Hariḥ Om.
The first leaf is not seen.
Thus one should apply the Gāyatrī-mantra to the ashes. By that ritual procedure, beginning with the head and following the sequence starting from Īśa (the northeast),
a *bhautika* celibate student should face the east, while a *naiṣṭhika* celibate student should face the north, applying the ashes to the feet and other limbs.
In some places it is said: "Having smeared [the ashes] over all the limbs, one should apply the *puṇḍra*.
The three—the seeker of progeny (*sāntānika*), the seeker of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), and the practitioner (*sādhaka*)—are for a duration of three lifetimes.
And one should place ashes upon the head with the Brahma-aṅgas and the water-pot mudrā.
Having shaken off the dust from the ground preceded by three claps of the hands, one should cast it far away; therefore, one should not step over that discarded flower-garland (nirmālya) in sequence.
In this manner, the fire-related bath (āgneyasnāna) should be performed by those practicing celibacy (brahmacārin).
At the three junctions of the day, at midnight, upon going to bed,
upon rising from sleep, after eating, after drinking water, and after performing the necessary bodily functions.
In the same way, upon touching a eunuch, a Śūdra, or a woman, one should perform the Āgneya penance;
likewise for contact with semen, or with a cat, a mongoose, a goat, or a rat.
When one has been touched by others in that manner, one should perform the fire-purification bath (āgneyasnāna).
Now, as for what was stated in the *Śrīmataṅga* and other texts: "The fire-related bath is performed with ashes, or with wild cow-dung and stones.
He was gazed upon by all the Vināyakas, who were set ablaze by the accumulated weapons.
And with that ash which has been reduced to powder and consecrated by the Brahma-mantra,
one should bathe using that purifying ash, whether applied by hand or as a paste.
The recitation of the scripture is a bath that removes impurities and cleanses all limbs; it is declared in the scriptures that the obstacles residing within the body are thereby destroyed.
Again, O Lord, one should rub the face with the [mantras] born from the Aghora and Vāma [faces], the bow and the heart,
the secret parts and the feet, and again the entire body with the Sadyojāta [mantra]. Then one should again bestow the consecration (abhiṣeka) with the Brahmā-aṅgas and with Śiva.
O gods, when one has become the mantra, the self becomes purified for all ritual actions;
or else, in the case of the Agnihotra, one who is skilled in the domestic ashes [attains this].
Therefore, the wise man should bathe with the purifier according to the previously mentioned procedure;
[he thereby obtains] whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices.
A person obtains that fruit multiplied ten million times by bathing in ashes.
Thus is the bath; having performed it in this manner, one should change one's loincloth (*kaupīna*). It should be as follows:
sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width and thirty-six finger-breadths in length. In some [traditions], however—
It is considered to be one cubit wide and two cubits long;
it should be beautiful, fine, and either white or saffron-colored. The loincloth (*kaupīna*) of a religious student (*brahmacārin*) consists of thirteen folds.
The waist-belt is well-observed, as are the girdle of muñja grass and the [staff] of palāśa wood.
From one, two, or three vowels up to the supreme fifty vowels,
one should arrange them as they appear beautiful; one should maintain this with the Vāmadeva mantra.
The measuring-line made according to the proportions of the *tāla* is multiplied by eighty-one;
having tripled it and tripled it again, one should rotate it repeatedly.
Above the navel it is not conducive to longevity; below the navel it causes the destruction of ascetic merit. When the navel is situated with a clockwise rotation, it bestows all accomplishments.
One should fashion the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) with three strands for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*);
that of a householder (*gṛhastha*) should have three times [that number], and that of a teacher (*deśika*) should have six times [that number].
Consecrated with the mantra of the respective lord of the [deceased's] caste, it should be accompanied by an upper garment,
neither too thick nor too thin, uncut, not knotted, and possessing the luster of being well-woven.
One should carefully avoid that which is covered with hair, joined [to something else], or decayed.
The wise man, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, should wear the sacred thread, which is visibly composed of all the gods, supremely pure, and auspicious.
The black antelope skin and the purifier (*pavitra*) should measure four or six finger-joints;
it is fashioned from two *kuśa* blades with their tips intact, or from two *darbha* blades,
and that purifier is joined with a knot in its middle.

One should wear that sacred thread (*pavitraka*), which is joined in sequence with [the syllables] beginning with *brahmā* at its root, middle, and tip, while reciting the *śiva-mantra*: "To Śiva, [obeisance]."
The staff, equal in length to one's own height, should have seven, nine, or eleven joints;
its thickness should be like that of a goat’s thumb, and it should be placed upon the left shoulder.
p. 5) The ash-receptacle, the gourd, the cloth, the deerskin, and so forth,
should be prepared as they are available, or else [the receptacle] should be eight finger-breadths high.
The practitioner, endowed with the observances and the constituent parts of the rite, adorned with his own ornaments,
sits upon a seat with a serene countenance, facing the eastern direction.
Having tied the topknot on his head and washed his feet and hands first,
he should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with that same water and with ash.
While reciting the Śiva-mantra, one should place the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb [together].
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) as a sectarian sign; one should place it horizontally and evenly.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the triple mark.
On the crown of the head, the forehead, the neck, the two throat-joints,
the two armpits, the heart, the navel, the back, the two knees, and likewise the two feet.
On the forehead, the heart, and the two arms, the length should be four finger-breadths;
the remaining parts are said to be one finger-breadth each—having thus applied the *tripuṇḍra*.
Brahmā himself resides in the place of the head, Skanda on the forehead,
Vināyaka in the ear, and Keśava abides in the two arms.
Īśvara is said to be in the heart, and Prajāpati is in the navel.
The Aśvins [are worshipped] with the knees, the god [Viṣṇu] with the feet, and likewise the serpent [Śeṣa];

a Cāṇḍāla is not at all fit for the purpose of a Śrāddha offering when one is impure from remnants. Likewise, that which has been kept overnight is unfit, as is the worship of Śiva performed without ashes.
Therefore, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be applied by those intent on the worship of Śiva.
On the crest-lock, the sacred thread, the neck, the arms, and the ears,
the best of practitioners should wear the rudrākṣa with the Śiva-mantra.
The mantra-practitioner who performs the worship of Śiva without wearing rudrākṣa beads [is ineffective].
The study of that scripture is a fruitless labor;
therefore, one should always wear a rudrākṣa during the auspicious sacrifice to Śiva.
With the hair between his knees covered, not looking at dogs or other such beings,
and becoming single-minded, [he should perform the rite] with clear and cool waters.
[Water] freed from froth and bubbles, strained through cloth, and drawn up.
One should sip water from a place not frequented by outcaste tribes, nor where it is defiled by worms or other impurities, such that a cow does not become free from thirst.
One [type of water] comes from leather bags, saline ground, or hot springs; the other is that which comes from the hands of the virtuous or from vessels.
Whether walking, standing, speaking, acting, spitting, seeing, sleeping, or touching;
whether in the air or on the ground, in a state of rest or diversion— with the body, feet, shoulder, tongue, and the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) placed within the cavity of the lips.
The vital breath (prāṇa) resides in the two nostrils; the moon and sun in the eyes;
all the directions in the ears; Brahmā and Agni in the navel;
and for the sake of purification, Viṣṇu and the fierce Rudra are stationed in the head and heart respectively.
Having consecrated it with mantras in due order, one who is pure in disposition should slowly and silently drink the soaked bean that has been brought forth through the *brahmatīrtha* channel.
Having recognized that it has entered the heart, one should then drink it again and again.
However, from time to time, having washed both hands repeatedly,
one should cleanse the lips in two ways with the base of the thumb using the *hetināma* [mantra].
The lips, nose, eyes, ears, navel, chest, head, and shoulders—these [parts] should be touched with the thumb and ring finger; it is impossible to touch them with the heart [the middle finger].
By that [offering], O gods, they become purified and indeed satisfied;
through them being pure, the practitioner becomes pure in body and pure in disposition.
And as it is stated in the Śrīprākhyatantra: "He should sip water at the nine sacred sites (tīrthas), drinking the consecrated water three times;
having placed that water in the palm of his right hand, he should fix his mind upon the heart."
By that, there shall be internal purity; those situated within the temple [should perform it].
One should wipe the door of that Ananta with those [materials], according to the measurement of its entrance.
Through purity and benefit, there should be action for the sake of the limbs;
those who follow that become pure, possessing the qualities of pure intention and action.

Then he should touch his limbs: the head, the eyes along with the nostrils, the ears, the shoulders, the heart, the navel, and finally the topknot. The gods are pure by their very nature; likewise, these places were established by the Creator.
The eyes of even Mārtaṇḍa were fashioned for those devoted to purity;
his nose was made of that wind, and his ears are the abode of all the quarters.
The region of the shoulders is the station of the Aśvins; the heart is that of Agni Kṛṣṇavartman;
and the navel is that of Prajāpati. By touching these, one becomes pure.
The touch of the thumb should be applied to the "healthy" (anāmaya) part;
the thumb is always Īśa, while the nameless finger (anāmikā) possesses the power of the Nameless (nāmābhṛtākalā).
Likewise, when the deities are of such a nature, being satisfied by the elements, they grant one's desires;
for the performer of that rite, they become augmenters of the state resulting from the ritual action.
Or even the external purification of the body is performed by means of earth and water.
How can there be internal purity for one who has acquired this object? However, through the complete purification of that state, the mind becomes pure in its dispositions and so forth.
When one possesses pure resolve through a pure mind, then,
by means of that yoga of pure resolve, the pure person attains its fruit.

Therefore, one should sip water twice for the sake of purity and stability. Having thus sipped water twice and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the householder and the student, with a tranquil mind, should first pay homage to the Vedic [deity].
Furthermore, the ascetic should perform either the Śaiva twilight rite or the twilight rite itself as being identical with Śiva.
It is stated in the venerable Svāyambhuva and other scriptures:
"Having performed a bath up to the head and having sipped water (ācamana),
one belonging to the two [upper] stages of life (dvirāśramī) should worship the Sandhyā established by the Vedas, facing north or facing east."
But the other, whose nature is dispassion and who is turned away from worldly objects, should perform the *brāhmī* [mudrā] and not the *śaivī*; such is the rule.
Likewise, in the Bṛhatkālottara it is said:
"Having first performed the Vaidikī [initiation], one should then practice the Śaivī [initiation]."

9) Likewise, the *bhautika* and *naiṣṭhika* [types of celibates] may or may not perform the *brāhmī* [initiation] beforehand;
however, the *śaivī* [initiation] must never be practiced during the observance (*niyama*), otherwise there is a fall.
"The triad beginning with the daily rites (nitya) is to be performed by all four [classes] without distinction;
likewise, the Vaiśvadeva and the Sandhyā are beneficial for the three [upper classes], excluding the Śūdra."
Once the water has been perfected through inspection and other rites, or wherever else it may be,
one should [consecrate] the moon, sun, son of the Sun (Saturn), and so forth, with the single Aṅkuśa-mudrā.
Having cast [the seed-syllable] from the heart into the city of the heart from the drop (*bindu*) by means of that which is called Udbhavā;
Alternatively, having recited the Saṃhitā ending with "Namaḥ," which is filled with the nectar of the power agitated by the Nāda, it is illuminated by the Dhenu-mudrā.
The sacred site of the Lord is protected by weapons such as the spear and by armor;
it is [consecrated] with those six limbs ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and with the nectar from the full jar of the *haṃsa*.
The wise one should join the body at the crown and envelop it with the armor;
this is what the discerning practitioner should do by means of the conjunction of the seed-syllables.
And it is said: having bound the *kalaśa-mudrā*, one should contemplate the concentration known as *sudhā* (the nectar).
The *tāraka* [mantra] consists of five syllables; it is like a water-pot turned upside down, very smooth and resembling the moon, from which nectar then flows.
Having likewise formed the Kumbha mudrā, one should recite the Saṃhitā even once;
thus, this should be performed three times, which bestows all accomplishments (siddhis). One thereby becomes as if bathed in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist upon the earth.
"He shall be the master of all dharmas, and he shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices. Thus it is said.

Then, having mentally recited the *Śivasaṃhitā* three times while holding the breath (*kumbhaka*), [one should perform] the conjunction of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the Brahman-mantras, which constitute the complete ritual procedure of the *Prāsāda*. What is this *saṃhitā*? It is the conjunction of the seed-syllables.
Oṃ hauṃ haṃ hāṃ hiṃ hīṃ huṃ hūṃ heṃ haiṃ hoṃ haḥ. Thus, for those who practice the Niṣkala Prāsāda, the conjunction of the limb-seeds (*aṅgabīja*) alone constitutes the *saṃhitā*. For example:
Oṃ hauṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ haḥ. By this, there is purification of the sins within the body. Then, having sipped water, performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and encircled oneself as before—
Having performed his purpose and tied the *mūrdhaka* (topknot), he should meditate upon the twilight according to the scriptures.
When the sun is at its first [rising], one should practice the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) prescribed for the Kṣatriyas; when it is at the last [setting], the twilight prayer of the Āryas;
and when it is in the middle, one should diligently practice the middle twilight prayer.
The morning twilight is considered to be threefold: the best is when the stars are still visible; the middling is when the stars have disappeared; and the lowest is when half the sky has turned rosy.
Likewise, at midday, it should be known as occurring during the three ghaṭikās marked by the sun's orb; it is excellent at midday and middling when the sun has set.
The youngest [sandhyā] is that in which the stars are visible; thus, the evening twilight is threefold.
For one who abides in the time of the morning twilight, there are two distinguished daily rites.
For one initiated into Nirvāṇa, the three junctions (sandhyās) are prescribed here;
however, for a householder, there is no [observance] at night, nor during eclipses or solstices.
This is always recommended for ascetics, without distinction for any of them.

In this context, the threefold *sandhyā*—namely *aparā*, *parā*, and *parāparā*—is of three kinds by way of its nature as *sandhyā*. Due to the influence of temporal adjuncts (*kālopādhi*), the *aparā* *sandhyā* takes the form of Brāhmī and so forth; it consists of three triple-samayas for both the *putraka* and *samayin* initiates.

And [these are located] in the heart, the forehead, and the apertures (*brahmarandhra*). Then, for the wise ones (*jñānin*), those initiated into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣitān*), and the teachers (*ācāryas*), there are three *parāpara-sandhyās*—the powers (*śaktis*) known as *mṛgī*, *icchā*, and *ṭa*—which are white in form like a lotus fiber, located respectively in the heart, the *bindu*, and the *brahmarandhra*. Then, that *parā* [power], which is the fourth (*turyā*), should be meditated upon at the *dvādaśānta*; it is like a lotus fiber and is either black in form or formless. Then, for those practitioners of breath-control (*prāṇayogins*), there are two *sandhyās* belonging to the sun and the moon. Then, for the supreme knowers who are established in the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and have dedicated themselves solely to Śiva, there is a constant union with Śiva; that is the *parama-sandhi*, and it is the supreme *sandhi* throughout all *sandhyās*. Thus says the Āgama:
Each one of these, however, possesses a supreme, stainless power through the Lords;
it is inseparable from Śambhu, O Lord, just as heat is inseparable from fire.
Because she joins the two Śivas and is intent upon the supreme awakening of Śiva, she is called Sandhyā;
yet she herself is considered to be threefold.

Those powers of action which, through the power of vision, exist on the pure path— by means of those powers of the Śivas, together with the powers called Ātman, Īśa, and Sadāśiva— that Sandhyā, reaching up to the Bindu, the end of Nāda, and the Samanā power, [is attained].
These three, both supreme and inferior, are said to be the junctions (sandhyās) by virtue of time.
It should be meditated upon by those initiated into Nirvāṇa in the cavities of the heart and the forehead;
it is called Parā, and she indeed resides within the mind at the end of the two [breaths].
And thus: "In that way, they are declared to be differentiated as Kriyā, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī;
through such transformation, they consist of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara. (p. 12)
Endowed with the three qualities (guṇas), they are likewise Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Śāṅkarī.
These three powers (śaktis) are to be known as the junctions (sandhyās) by the wise;
they are indeed declared as "lower" (aparā) by the sons of the Lord of the Rule (samaya).
These [energies] are to be meditated upon in sequence within the heart, the bindu, and the aperture of Brahmā;
according to the influence of time and limiting conditions, they possess specific colors, vehicles, weapons, and forms.
In this regard, their meditation and their ritual manual are described here as follows:
The Brāhmī goddess is white-clad with a sacred thread, adorned with red garments;
she has a youthful red complexion, four faces, four arms, and eight eyes.
The Haṃsa [is seated] upon a lotus throne; in his right hand, he holds a sruk-ladle, a sruva-ladle, and a rosary of akṣa seeds.
Vaiṣṇavī, holding a staff and a water-pot in her left hand and adorned with a black antelope skin,
is white in color and dressed in white garments; she has one face, wears a forest garland, possesses three eyes, and stands upon a lotus supported by Garuḍa.
And Kṛṣṇājinā, in the northeast and other directions, holds a conch, discus, mace, and the gesture of fearlessness;
Raudrī rides a bull and stands upon a lotus; Kṛṣṇā has dark-colored attire, one face, and three eyes, and is adorned with matted hair and a crescent moon.
Adorned with a black antelope skin and a sacred thread, her beloved is clothed in a tiger skin;
she holds a trident and a rosary in her right hands, while in her left is a spear that inspires fear.
She extends across a mandala of hundreds of millions of yojanas.
O Brahmāṇī, you who abide within the multitude of hearts that resemble a blazing fire.
In the mandala, which is two hundred crores of yojanas in extent and resembles the moon, the Vaiṣṇavīs reside within the center of the bindu.
In a body measuring four hundred million *yojanas*,
there is a lotus-like face; therein reside Raudrī, Kapilā, and Madhyagā—
these three twilight goddesses (*sandhyā*) in sequence, who are to be served by the sons established in the pledge (*samaya*).
They should be meditated upon in sequence during the morning, at midday, and in the afternoon.
They are to be known as resembling the tips of rice-ears or like long crests;
thus the three junctions (sandhyās), both higher and lower, are to be meditated upon by the wise.
Just as Turyā is proclaimed to have Kṛṣṇavāsā as her form,
so too the Sandhyās are always to be saluted, for they are the witnesses of all actions.
By means of the splendors of those [deities] spreading through the pores of his skin, he should contemplate that mountain as his own body; whatever he performs for them is considered their worship.
And it is said:
"One should imagine one's own body as having entered the expanse of their circle of light; whatever action one performs, that is considered to be a salutation to them."
The state of Śiva at all times is declared to be the *sandhi* (junction) of the knowers;
that *sandhyā* is called supreme among all Śiva-yogins.
The upward-moving breath (*prāṇa*) is the Sun, while the downward-moving breath is the Moon.
The union with that auspicious state which exists at its end is considered by yogins to be yoga.
And it has been said:
"Two tens of thousands, one thousand, and likewise six hundred."
The lord of yogis who performs the recitation with the Aghora weapon mantra, [attains success].
One should indeed make the root of the world consist of the form of *nāda*, which is both supreme and non-supreme;
through its practice, there is a coming and going from above the navel up to Śiva.
Therefore, for those practitioners of breath-yoga, there is no further exertion regarding the meditation described;
for them, both twilights are remembered as being at the ends of the Vaiḍūrya and Soma [kalpas].
Thus he praised [it], and thereafter performed whatever was to be done according to the scriptures.

Then, with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), one should take the three portions of water; then, by means of the "uttara-sañcāra" [movement], having poured the water from the *śivatīrtha* onto the palm of the left hand—which holds *darbha* grass—along with *kuśa* grass held in the right hand, one should perform a cleansing (*mārjana*) on the head with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*) ending in *vauṣaṭ* using the water dripping from below that. Then, having placed the remaining water in the right hand, one should draw the white-colored water into the stomach through the left nostril by means of the *pūraka* breath, while mentally reciting the *Śivāstra* mantra three times. Having washed away the sins residing in the body with that water, and having visualized the water as black in color due to the destruction of internal sins, one should expel the internal water through the right nostril by means of the *recaka* breath using the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. One should then cast it like an arrow (*nārāca*) upon the imagined *vajrī-śilā* (diamond-stone). This is the *adhamarṣaṇa* (the lowest form of atonement). Thus says the *Āgama*:
One should cause the water held in the full left hand to be poured out;
by means of the *recaka* breath-retention, one should cast far away the sins of speech, mind, and body.
Having entered the limb with the *soma* [mantra], one should exhale through the *piṅga* aperture;
then, with the *pāśupatāstra* [mantra], one should [perform] the sprinkling of water drops with the right hand.
And for the destruction of obstacles, one should cast the *nārāca* weapon upon the ground;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should offer a full *añjali* containing a *kūrca* grass-bundle, consecrated with the mantra.
Just as one might cast three jewel-flowers toward the sun,
so too, having performed circumambulation and recited the Gāyatrī, one should mutter [the mantra].

Regarding this, it is said that one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Following the sipping of water, the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) must also be performed. As stated by the Teachers:

"Whenever one performs the placement of the *samanya* and the placement of the mantras, at those very times the practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*) should perform them upon the hands and the body for the sake of attaining the goal of the mantra."
Here, "to Āditya" means to Śiva in his form as Āditya; and it has been said:

"One should offer water for honor (arghya), accompanied by fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, to the form of Āditya—that is, to Śiva together with his limbs (sāṅga), the sole witness of all actions."

"The power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) is embodied as residing in the center of a circle of light. Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Having meditated upon the Lord Sadāśiva, who is eternally situated within the orb of the sun, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī), having offered his joined palms (añjali), should cast [the offering] and, at the conclusion, remember Him with his mind."
The sequence for the rite of offering the *arghya* is as follows:

having placed the heart-mantra upon that joined palms (*añjali*) which are provided with fragrance, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and unbroken rice grains, and having meditated upon Śiva-Sūrya stationed within the solar disc, one should recite: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāyārghyaṃ svāhā*. Having performed this rite three times and offered the *arghya*, one should mutter the *Gāyatrī*. As it is said in the *Siddhāntas*:
"At the rising of the morning twilight, one should offer the *arghya* facing the east."
It should be offered to Āditya... [rest of the verse].
Having risen at the time of midday, likewise with the face turned toward the south,
and having risen again in the evening and offered the *arghya*, one should then sit and perform the recitation (*japa*).
Whether wearing dry or wet clothes, one should not recite the Gāyatrī;
it should be recited [only] when one is of the nature of the Sun and Fire, for otherwise there is contradiction.
"What must be done? [he asked]. * * * * * * * * * * * ||
At twilight, the sun’s ray, its form fully manifest,
stands within the solar disc like a second sun.
With arms raised, she stands upon two feet or on her right foot alone;
her right leg is extended sideways, while she rests upon the petals of the lotus of her left foot.
She has one face and three eyes, adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon.
"Clad in an upper garment of black antelope skin, [I meditate] upon that Maheśa; we know Mahādeva, we meditate upon him; may Śiva impel us"—thus is the Śiva-Gāyatrī stated. And it is said:
"Oṃ, we know that Maheśa, and after that, we know..."
At the end of the mantra for Mahādeva, it is joined with the word "dhīmahi."
May that [state] be for us a step toward auspiciousness.
"The Gāyatrī has been declared [to be] the bestower of the goal. Thus [it is said].
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should contemplate that the goddess, having gone to the orb of Umā, has entered back once again into the orb of the Sun. And it is said:
"Having recited the Gāyatrī, which begins with Oṃ and consists of twenty-four syllables excluding the word 'tat', as it has entered the Sun, at the end of the recitation [one should enter] the orb."
In this context, it is sometimes said that one should recite the three-syllabled Gāyatrī; and as it has been stated:
"Oṃ Hoṃ Hīṃ, or likewise the Gāyatrī ending with 'Namaḥ', is the bestower of desired fruits."
That [vow], having seven turns, shall bring the body back to heaven ten times;
but that goddess, when performed twenty times, leads one to the final abode.
Having recited it one hundred and eight times, one shall cause [others] to cross over the ocean of birth. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, having thus recited [the mantra] every day one hundred and eight times, having offered the *arghya* libation, and having performed circumambulation three times while worshipping the collection [of deities] together with its limbs (*sāṅga-saṅgraha*), one should ask Śambhu for forgiveness through the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
Otherwise, there would be no figurative usage; or one may worship him in his own abode. And it has been said:
"For the sun who has arrived, worship itself is the dismissal;
this is established by worldly convention. Thus, one should always worship him once."
Likewise, in the Śrī Kālottara: "One should offer arghya to the Sun with the Śiva-gāyatrī mantra, the Praṇava, and the Hṛdaya mantra; one should worship him daily once."

The libation (*tarpaṇa*). Since this is so, therefore—after the libation with the *gāyatrī*, having worshipped Śiva-Sūrya along with his limbs (*sāṅga*) within the house, having recited the Śiva-mantra and performed worship, and having dismissed [the deity]—one should perform the libation and other rites. Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra* [Tantra], it says "divyām" (the divine...).
Having performed the complete worship preceded by the offering of *arghya*,
and then having recited the mantra of Śiva along with its limbs (*sāṅga*), one should announce [the conclusion] with the word "uttara."
Now, they are briefly written out here. As for the libation (*tarpaṇa*):
*oṃ hāṃ sarvebhyo mantrebhyaḥ svāhā*. *oṃ hāṃ sarvebhyo devebhyaḥ svāhā*.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to all the ṛṣis!
Oṃ hāṃ, vauṣaṭ to all human beings! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the ancestors!

Thus, one should offer libations according to the procedure to be described hereafter. Alternatively, one may perform the libation in detail as follows: in that sacrifice—*oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Saṃhitā mantras;
oṃ, svāhā to all the hundred-million mantras*.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Śivāgamas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Śivas!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Rudras!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Lords of the Worlds (Bhuvaneśvaras). Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Ādityas.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Vasus.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Viśvedevas!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Maruts! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Bhṛgus!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Aṅgirasas! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the directions!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the lords of the quarters!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Mothers! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Gaṇas!

Thus, one should offer libations with water containing *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and finger-nails of men. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the ear—*Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to all the sages who are the incarnations of the Śaiva Āgamas.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the sages who are the incarnations of the Śaiva authorities.*
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the sages who have taken refuge in the Śaiva union. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to all the seven ṛṣis.
Thus, with the root of the little finger joined [to the thumb], he then recites: *Oṃ hāṃ sarvebhyo bhūtebhyo vauṣaṭ* | *Oṃ hāṃ sarvebhyo rākṣasebhyo vauṣaṭ* | *Oṃ hāṃ sarvebhyo yakṣebhyo vauṣaṭ* |
Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to all the Nāgas!
With this, using the root-mantra of the one who has performed the auspicious rite (lagnakara), he again becomes a wearer of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavyopavītī) and says:
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the Śiva-pitṛs!
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the gods and ancestors. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the ancestors. Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the kinsmen.

Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all the preceptors! Having thus gratified them with the root-mantra of that [deity] using sesame seeds and the roots and tips of kuśa grass, [one recites]: Oṃ, those in my family who have been consumed by fire and those who have not been consumed by fire...

"May those [ancestors] who have been satisfied by the water offered upon the ground attain the supreme goal. Having recited this, one should cast the water along with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds three times onto the bank using the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savyopavītī*), one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), execute the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*), and withdraw that water with the withdrawal gesture (*saṃhāra-mudrā*) while reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the heart. This is the procedure for the libation (*tarpaṇa*). As it has been stated by the Teachers:
Having sat down and recited the Śiva-mantra, one should satisfy the mantras ending with "svāhā," as well as the Rudras, the gods, the lords of the worlds, and human beings, ending with "namaḥ."
"Having known the *bhūtas* ending with *vauṣaṭ*, the *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, and *rākṣasas*; the *pitṛs*, the *devapitṛs*, and the *pretas* ending with *svadhā* as the teachers.

Here, "the *pitṛs*" refers to the ancestors of one initiated by Śiva; the meaning is that they are *Īśa*, *Sadāśiva*, and *Śānta*. Although the state of being a *preta* persists even after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* [rite],...
(20) Thus, because it has been stated that all elements are omnipresent, there is no fault.

[Objection: But surely, only one class [of mantra] should be employed for all [elements]. [Response: That is not necessary, because *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *namaḥ* have the same purpose as the classes [of mantras]. [Objection: True. Even though they have the same purpose, it is because they are prescribed in that way. And thus says the scripture:
In the purification of the mantras, one should offer libations to the sages, the gods, and the ancestors.
One should satisfy the atoms (anu), the gods, and the ancestors with water from the tips of the fingers while keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya);
and one should satisfy the sages with water from the middle of the palm using joined palms (añjali).

With *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and salutations (*namaskāra*), and likewise with the [mantras] belonging to the [respective] classes and limbs in their proper order, one should satisfy those who stand at the forefront by means of the tips of the hands— the faculty of giving— with those same tips for the mantras of the left-hand deities.
The abode of the ancestors (pitṛs) for the pretas and others is to their left in successive order;

O sages, because that [line] is in the middle of all [the offerings], it is therefore the middle of the ritual action. For this reason, the words *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *namaḥ* are prescribed for the act of giving.
Of these three, that which is given is equal;
for those inhabitants of heaven, the offering is *bhūta*, while *svadhā* is declared to be the food of the ancestors (*pitṛs*).
*Svadhā* is dear to the ancestors. *Hā-hāraḥ* is the substance in their own heaven. *Dhā-svadhā* is said to be dear among the ancestors.
"Salutation to Yoni, the celestial vault; in that [place], may the essence flow for me among men.
Having gratified these [deities] at the crest, the principal ones, [one should offer] in sequence with clarified butter. Thus it is said.

Here, "the place of the ancestors (pitṛsthāna)" refers to the place of the ancestors of the deceased (preta) and others; that is to say, the place of the *tīrtha* for the deceased ancestors and so forth is the base of the ring finger (*tarjanī-aṅguli*). This has been stated by the Teachers:

(21) For those whose root region is that of the ancestors (*paitṛmūla*), O Prajāpati, the words *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *namaḥ* are declared in grammar to be used with the dative case (*caturthī*) when they function as the primary agent (*pradhānakāraka*). Therefore, the meaning is that one should satisfy these principal mantras of the deities—beginning with "To Śiva, svāhā" and so forth—using the words prescribed for that purpose. In this manner, one should perform the satisfaction (*tṛpti*) of all beings from Īśāna down to the stationary objects (*sthāvara*).
Because Śambhu remained there out of compassion for all living beings;
thus, having accomplished everything, he was pure in being and fulfilled in his purpose.
Having bathed while standing in the middle of the *sūpacara* (the excellent path), one should ascend the steps;
having restrained speech and having purified both touch and what is handled,
one should proceed according to the scripture toward the divine abode (*dhāma*), which is pure, all-pervading, and beyond the supreme.
It is being written, by way of a discussion on the eyes, both in brief and in detail.
Next, I shall fully explain that which purifies the surface of the earth;
its examination, as well as the knowledge [required] for it, and even [the procedure for] another village.
Fragrant, endowed with a sweet taste, white, red, or yellowish-brown.
The ground enriched with dust is exceedingly auspicious and the accomplisher of all goals.
One should examine a white ground that slopes toward the northeast, is smooth, blackish, and pleasant to behold; it should be situated near a body of water and free from hair,
bones, thorns, saline soil, and fissures.
Free from snakes and anthills, cleared of ashes, charcoal, and husks,
with the three-cubit-long stakes dug out from the earth, it is devoid of all defects.
Having worshipped the site according to the scriptures and having prepared the ground,
one should construct [the hall] either of baked bricks or likewise of pure wood.
Or, having previously fashioned one made of clay, he should place it in the sacrificial pavilion.
That is to say:
having made the length double [the width], the width shall consist of one part;
the door shall be in the third part, with a measurement of one and a half cubits.
One should determine two parts for the mandala and one part for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
one should perform cruel rites in the intermediate directions (vidiś), but auspicious rites in the cardinal directions (diś).
Alternatively, one should construct a sacrificial pavilion that is square, easy to enter,
adorned with various paintings and other works of art, and surrounded by a perimeter wall.
One should construct its upper part firmly with well-seasoned wood,
making it spacious, and likewise provide a lattice-work at its top.
Thus has been briefly described the pavilion that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
as taught in the Sarvajñānottara Śāstra and likewise in the Kālottara.
The beautiful worship hall, situated in the northeast or the east,
should measure thirty-two cubits, or even twenty cubits.
It was provided with four pillars, possessed four gates with archways,
well-guarded, delightful, and radiant with scattered flowers.
It was perfumed with excellent fragrances such as sandalwood and other scents, adorned with a canopy above, and hung with strings of pearls.
Abounding with white cloth banners and raised with variegated white flags,
it was sprinkled with saffron water and rendered greyish-white by the powder of camphor.
Abounding with lamps whose flames were unwavering, it was filled with the rays [of light].
One should lead [the deity] through the western door or even the eastern door;
thus, in the daily worship, the temple is praised as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
A single-story structure with a roof-terrace is here called a *vitāna*.
Having divided the field into five parts according to the *ṛc*, the middle portion constitutes the altar (*vedikā*).
Those made of *aiṣuka* wood or clay are best, not those made of stone or plaster;
they should be sixteen or eight *aṅgulas* in height and provided with corner pillars and other such features.
Then, having set aside a portion, there is a wall adorned with four doors,
along with door-panels and door-keepers.
To the west of the surrounding veranda is the main pavilion;
that hall and its walls should be adorned with latticed windows.
To the south shall be the kitchen with its utensils, and to the west the dance hall.
To the north shall be the temple bathhouse and water reservoirs;
and to the east shall be the fire-offering hall, provided with a lattice for the smoke.
The characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa):
For daily homa, however, it should be located in the south-eastern quarter of the Vedāśrama, equal in measure to the ashes,
and likewise provided with a girdle (mekhalā) according to its width and height.
One should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) either in the northeast or to the east of the yoga-pīṭha;
it should be made of bricks, very firm, with a neck (kaṇṭha) one finger-breadth outside the excavation.
(On the first day) it is one finger-breadth in length; then, in sequence, three fingers and two fingers [in length];
it is four fingers in width and five fingers in height.
Make everything, including the lips, like the thumb, and shape them like the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
"Or it may be made in the western forest-district (vaṇacit), in the direction of Varuṇa, even if it is like that of an elephant or a camel. Thus [it is said].
And it has been said:
"In the daily fire-offering (nityahoma) for the elephant-temple, one should prepare either a circular or a square [altar] to the east or the west of the yoga-pīṭha."
The daily fire-oblation (homa) must be performed either there or in the domain of Īśāna;
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be provided with a neck and adorned with three girdles (mekhalā).

The first [Kuṇḍa] should be made with four finger-breadths; that which is three or two finger-breadths [in width], the depth of the Kuṇḍa is like its mouth, and the Yoni is remembered as being half [of that].
The navel is recorded as being nine finger-breadths in length, shaped like an elephant's lip;
it is situated above the girdle at a measurement of one finger-breadth.
The sacrificial pit (yoni) should be fashioned according to the shape of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), and not otherwise;
or else, one may conceive it within the interior of the yoni in the form of the fire-pit.
"Then, at the edge of the *yoni*, [the altar] should be slightly elevated like the dome of a water-pot (*kuṃbhikumbha*);
thus is the *kuṇḍa* for the daily rite described here, as well as that for occasional rites.
Thus has the incidental matter been explained; now the subject at hand is stated.
One should not perform any other action until Śiva has been propitiated.
And it has been said:
"Viṣṇu, with palms joined in reverence, and Brahmā especially as well..."
"For the sake of favoring the worlds, therefore, the best of men should worship the *liṅga* at dawn for the attainment of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). Thus [it is said].
Having washed his feet and sipped water, and having taken up a collection of garments and other items,
he should slowly place them upon the beam of the scale using pure ropes, away from the pegs.
Having adorned his own body with Rudrākṣa bracelets and other ornaments,
the practitioner should place all the requisites for worship nearby.
If one performs worship appropriate for that time according to the ritual rules,
one should then worship Śiva in the form of the Sun between the Lord of the Gods (Indra) and Fire.
"One should worship in this very manner between Śakra and Anala.
What is this restriction that "that place is right there"? It has been stated: "Eight cities are situated on the side... [and so forth].
Amarāvatī belongs to Maheśa, and likewise Tejovatī belongs to Vahni.

The daughter of Vivasvat belongs to Kṛtānta; that of Nīlārakṣodhipati is called Śubhā; that of Varuṇa is known as Gandhavatī; that of Vāyu is named Vimalā; and that of Soma is Manovatī, belonging to Īśāna.
Furthermore, there are eight other cities situated between the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Between Śakra and Anala, as far as the domain of Īśāna,
is the daughter of Viśvakarman named Prabhāvatī.
Raugryā is for the eleven Rudras, and Ruprāṇā is for the Pitṛs;
Maitrī is the city of Mitra, and Vasumadhyā is for the Vasus;
Gāndharvī is for Sarasvatī, and likewise Cakravatī is for Viṣṇu.
"Ananta [is the name of] the one known as Padmavatī, born from the Lotus-born One. Thus it is said.
Now, one might ask: why was it stated that "one should worship Śiva as the very form of the sun"?

Since the moon and other [planets] are also forms of Śiva, why is their worship not performed here? However, because the six supports (*ṣaḍādhāra*) alone constitute the constant limb [of the rite], their worship is not performed.
And it has been said:

"Attendance upon the Sun, self-sacrifice, the *liṅga*, fire, the Guru, and the book—thus is the sixfold support for the worship of Śiva declared as constant. Likewise, the Ācārya also [states]: "From bathing comes external and internal purity; from attendance upon the Sun comes freedom from sin."
The fruitfulness of one's actions is attained; liberation arises from the worship of the *liṅga*. Gain of wealth and universal affection are constantly produced by the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Knowledge comes from the worship of the seat of learning (*vidyāpīṭha*), and all of that [is obtained] from the honoring of the Guru.
Thus, the six supports are described here as being constant and occasional.
Established in the *liṅga*, he is the witness of actions; established in the *kumbha*, he is the protector of the sacrifice;
established in the fire, he is the chapter (*paṭala*) for men and the compassionate benefactor of the Guru.
"In the disciple, sin is said to be pacified; this is considered to be the fivefold stream.
Now, Daṇḍin, Mahākāla, Raudra, Daṇḍa, and Piṅgala—these are the Śiva-mantras, the Sūrya-mantras, the limbs of Śiva, the Mantra-deities, the Vidyeśvaras, and the Planets.
Now, as it was said in the *Alpaughasārakāla-jñāna* and other texts: "From that [state] arises a web of rays, and from that, fire; in its center is the solar disc.
Having brought the moon and the twilights into union, he remains there, having set."
The wise know it to be in the heart, the navel, and likewise in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) for yogins.
(27) "In that [space], there is a power (śakti) in the form of a lamp-flame, consisting of nectar;
the Supreme Śambhu residing therein should be meditated upon by those who know reality. Thus it is said.
As it has also been said by Kūrma:
"Therefore, having abandoned all the gods led by Brahmā,
one should worship Virūpākṣa, who dwells within the sun."
Now, the procedure for their worship:
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍin. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Piṅgala.
Thus, facing the east, [one should worship] the two door-keepers on the right and left with sweat [and other substances]: *Oṃ hāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*.

In the northeast, *Oṃ hāṃ gurubhyo namaḥ*. Having worshipped [the deities] in the southeast with the general *arghya* and other offerings, and having contemplated oneself as Śiva-Sūrya, one should prepare the special *arghya*. Having sprinkled the collection of materials for that [rite] and oneself, one should place Ananta, Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya upon the pedestal or the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*)—Ananta in the center and the others in the corners starting from the southeast—and above them...

Having worshipped the newly blossomed lotus with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lotus," and having worshipped the mass of radiant energy, the seat of Śiva-Sūrya, with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva-Sūrya," [one should worship] upon that.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva-Sūrya," and having recognized him as Sadāśiva— possessing the colors of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of his locus, subtle, five-faced, and of great luster— one should invoke the Supreme with the root mantra. One should then perform the rites of installation (sthāpana), presence (sannidhāna), confinement (rodhana), and the ritual integration of the limbs (sakalīkṛti).
Having performed the ritual procedure with the mantras of the limbs of Śiva-sūrya within.
Having consecrated [the offering] with the root mantra, one should display the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful oblation (*arghya*), one should proclaim its merit.
One should worship the deity and the limbs of enjoyment with bathing water, perfumes, and so forth.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the heart. Oṃ hīṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ haṃ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ haiṃ, huṃ to the armor.
Thus, [reciting] "Oṃ Aḥ, salutation to the Weapon (astra)" in the three corners starting from the northeast,
one should visualize and worship [the weapons] in the four directions beginning with the east as will be described hereafter, and then perform the purification of the planets.
In the east is Soma, gentle (Saumya), holding a rosary and a water-pot;
in the southeast is Maṅgala, whose face is red, possessing a spear and red eyes;
and in the south is Budha, who is yellow and holds a rosary in his hand.
The aged, fair-complexioned Guru (Jupiter) should be visualized in the southwest;
the clever, one-eyed, white Śukra (Venus) is in the water, wearing a bracelet on his wrist;
and Śanaiścara (Saturn), with crooked feet, a downward gaze, and a terrifying appearance, is below.
In the northwest wind-quarter, Khinkhirī holds a rosary and Rājāvarta;
Vyāvṛttāsya has an upright body, and Rāhu holds a black bull’s hide at his heart.
In the north, in the quarter of Śaṅkara, Ketu has three hoods and carries a sword and a shield.
And Dhūmra, whose body was enriched with human and serpent-like features, joined his palms in reverence.

Alternatively, O Soma, Budha, Bṛhaspati, and Śukra are to be worshipped in the directions starting from the East, while Maṅgala and the others are to be worshipped in the corners starting from the Southeast (Agni). The mantras are: *Oṃ Saṃ Somāya Namaḥ*, and so forth. Then, with the root mantra and with [mantras] such as *Śivasūryādibhyaḥ Saparivārebhyo Namaḥ* (Salutation to Śiva, the Sun, and the rest, along with their retinues), one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), flowers, unguents (*abhyañjana*), fragrant powders (*udvartana*), bathing materials, perfumes (*gandha*), garments, ornaments, flowers, incense (*dhūpa*), lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), drinking water, water for a second sipping (*ācamana*), hand-cleansing powder (*hastodvartana*), and mouth-freshener (*mukhavāsa*).
(Page 29)

After the services of betel, the mirror, and so forth, having offered purifiers such as *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā*, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and having consecrated them with the *amṛtīkaraṇa* rite by means of the *dhenumudrā*, one should offer the *mahārātrika* (the midnight offering) and perform the recitation (*japa*) of the root mantra according to one's capacity. Having offered a tenth part of the recitation to the limbs (*aṅga-mantras*) and others, and having praised, prostrated, worshipped, and offered the *arghya*, one should turn [the deity] away. Then, withdrawing the host of mantras with the *nārāca-mudrā* using the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and uniting [the deity] with the form in the icon by means of the *mūrti-mantra* and the *divya-mudrā*, one should cause [the deity] to enter the Sun of Śiva situated within the lotus of the heart by means of the root mantra.
Then, on the six seats: Oṃ, salutation to Caṇḍāsana;
Oṃ Oṃ, salutation to Caṇḍamūrti.

*Oṃ, obeisance to Antatejaścaṇḍa.* Thus, having worshipped Caṇḍeśvara—who is composed of light, whose four faces are formidable with his own fangs, who has the sun as his eye, wears a garland of skulls, and holds a water-pot and the *tarjanī* gesture in his hands—through the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth; and having offered the remains of the previous offerings (*nirmālya*) and dismissed him, one should perform the purification of the place where the *nirmālya* was taken. Then, having gone outside, one should perform the washing of the feet, sipping water (*ācamana*), and other such rites. Alternatively, according to the rule for the worship of the Sun, one should avoid the Sun immediately after the emission of the *Śiva-bīja*. Having thus worshipped Sūryeśa, one should thereafter worship Śiva in the *liṅga*. It is as follows:

The root *yaja* is used in the senses of worshiping the gods (*devapūjā*), bringing together (*saṅgatakaraṇa*), and giving (*dāna*). Thus, "one should sacrifice" (*yajet*) refers to the performance of the gathering for the worship of Śiva. This is the mutual conformity between the one worshipped and the worshipper, their coming together. In this worship of Śiva, there is a particular grace (*prāsādaviśeṣa*) on the part of the worshiper, such as the thought: "I am [subordinate] in the worship of Śiva," or "I accept this worship of Śiva, who is the object of worship. Giving (*dāna*) is the manifestation of consciousness colored by the desired fruit of Śiva. However, through the mutual conformity of both, [it consists of] the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, which is one's own self... (p. 30).

The giving [of offerings] ending with the *karpaṇa*; the bestowing of worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*); and the worship of the one who is both the object of adoration and the subject of adoration—these are the specific rules. For the sake of fulfilling this, there is sacrifice; this is known as the sacrifice to Śiva. Having performed the worship of the *liṅga*, which is the self of Power (*śakti*), the act of sacrificing to Śiva must be performed by that person.
Furthermore, the measurement extending up to the power of the Fire of Time (*kālāgni-śakti*) is non-specific.
That wherein one comes and dissolves is called the *liṅga* known as "dissolution."
Thus, from scripture:
"One should resort to the *liṅga* which bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) and grants all attainments."

"For even on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the swift accomplishment of mantras arises. Is this *liṅga* manifest (*vyakta*), unmanifest-manifest (*vyaktāvyakta*), or unmanifest (*avyakta*)? Among these, those ending with Sādākhya are manifest. The "mouth-liṅga" (*mukhaliṅga*) is manifest-unmanifest, and the "entirety" (*sakala*) is unmanifest. Furthermore, it is fourfold: moving (*cala*), non-moving (*acala*), moving-non-moving (*calācala*), and non-moving-moving (*acalacala*). Here, the moving is the *liṅga* made of mind; the non-moving is that which has been installed in temples and the like; the moving-non-moving is the *bāṇaliṅga*; and the non-moving-moving is the mandala and the sacrificial mound (*saraṇḍila*). This *liṅga* is of many kinds. Having taken up a substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), Śiva is worshipped [therein]. However, Śiva is to be worshipped in the *liṅga* itself. Thus, in the *Bṛhatkālottara*:
Whatever holy fords and sacred abodes exist upon the earth all reside at the base of the Liṅga; therefore, one should worship the Liṅga.
Whether once a day, three times a day, or even four times a day,
he who eats without having first worshipped the Supreme Lord does so out of negligence.
An expiation must be performed; otherwise, one shall fall into hell.
Worship must not be neglected during periods of birth-impurity or death-impurity.
The living being is like a bubble on the water; therefore, one should worship the *liṅga*.
Likewise:
"But by not sacrificing, one eats worms; even a goat [eats] urine and semen.
Alas! These [who do not give] eat filth, while the non-giver consumes poison."
And likewise in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He who eats without having performed the worship of Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, eats nothing but the five impurities; of this there is no doubt."
But he who worships with devotion even after the dissolution of the body is Śiva himself, the doer of all; such a living being is called one liberated while alive (jīvanmukta).
In whatever state one may be— whether standing, walking, sleeping, reciting prayers, eating, or engaged in sexual intercourse— one should remember Śiva.
He whose mind is dedicated to Śiva attains liberation, and not otherwise.
Without knowing the principle of Śiva (śivatatva), the maṇḍala of mantras, vidyās, and so forth, should be understood as being like a lump of clay; likewise, one who worships [it thus] is fallen.
Therefore, with every effort, one should not let that [maṇḍala] be stained by semen and blood.
Having realized the identity of the signified and the signifier, which bestows the fruit of the imperishable,
one should take refuge in the Vidyā, for all mantras reside within it.
Abiding in the *liṅga* and abiding in the fire, the Lord accepts the sacrificial oblation;
assuming the form of the Guru, He severs the flood of bonds.
Thus is the rule regarding the location for the worship and other rites of the Supreme Lord.
He who worships a deity or even a *liṅga* for the sake of a livelihood,
and who likewise presides over a temple, is indeed known as a *devalaka*.
That man who worships the deity for the sake of wealth, having fixed a time [for worship] for that purpose,
is indeed called a *devalaka* and is excluded from all ritual acts.
Likewise:
"Even in the calamity of starvation, or even out of fear,
or for the sake of a livelihood, one should never worship another deity."
A wise person should not remain having fashioned a linga with a deficient head.
Likewise:
"One should never pass by seeing a *liṅga* with a deficient head. Thus it is said.

Enough with excessive detail. Now, therefore, the worship of Śiva is described—it is twofold: external and internal. Among these, for those who perceive the inner self (*adhyātma*), there is internal sacrifice, because for them there would be the undesirable consequence of faults regarding flowers, ornaments, and so forth, in the context of external sacrifice. Therefore, external worship is for those engaged in ritual action (*kriyāvat*). And it is said in the Siddhānta:
"I shall fully explain the sacrifice according to the rules and in proper sequence."
And that [instruction] should be known as twofold, according to the fitness of the recipient.
"For ascetics and yogis whose external powers have ceased, internal sacrifice is prescribed;
likewise for those devoted to external worship.
As it is also said elsewhere:
Having worshipped with non-violence and other virtues, the Lord of Wealth (Śiva) should not be sought by yogis who have transcended external things; for Śiva is present wherever one goes.
Those who perform ritual actions should always worship the deity residing in the *liṅga* with flowers and other offerings— such as well-ripened *sphaṭika*, freshly gathered fragrant blossoms,
*campaka*, *karavīra*, and other forest-grown flowers collected for that purpose.
One should offer worship with as many flowers and other articles as are available.
Moreover, the life-force (*jīva*) is not taught to exist for the sake of the self’s enjoyment;
rather, it is taught just as the *āhṛkṣa* flower and so forth are [offered] for the sake of the king’s bodily enjoyment.
"No harm is seen in [taking flowers] from his garden grove;
likewise, one who takes flowers for the sake of worshipping the Lord incurs no fault.
Furthermore, those devoted to external worship must perform internal worship as well, for without that, it does not come to pass. And this has been stated in the Siddhānta:
Having first performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), one should then commence the external worship;
for the light-liṅga (jyotirliṅga) that resides within the heart is worshipped in exactly the same way externally.
Therefore, for that reason, the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) is said here to be performed first.
Likewise:
"He who performs an external sacrifice without having first performed the mental sacrifice, his labor is in vain; such is the settled conclusion of the scripture."
Likewise: "He who, abandoning Śiva who resides within himself, worships Śiva as being outside, is like one who,
casting away the lotus stalk held in his own hand, licks the elbow of his arm."

"How is it that even in the middle [center], the liṅga situated in the heart and on the forehead shines forth as visible? This is the ultimate reality (paramārtha) of Gārgya; behold, behold the form with a mind free from aversion. Likewise, in the *Mālinīvijaya*: "But surely the *Mālinīvijaya* is established for the Western [tradition]; why then is it cited here? Because it is prohibited in the Śaiva [context]. True. However, the prohibition therein concerns the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*), mantras, and ritual substances. Furthermore, since it is merely a statement of testimony (*sākṣimātra-vacana*) in this matter, no fault would arise. Even in those tantras, the worship of Śiva—
It is written for the purpose of making it known:
"Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret, which is difficult to attain by one who has not disciplined the self."
That which has not been told to anyone, I shall tell that to you today.
Abandoning everything else, one should focus the mind solely on the mind-only;
one should not worship a linga made of clay, stone, minerals, gems, or other such materials.
One should worship the internal *liṅga*, wherein the moving and the non-moving are dissolved;
for by this [internal principle], the external *liṅga* is presided over, thereby attaining the state of being beyond all *liṅgas*.
Therefore, one should worship this [liṅga], which rests upon supreme non-duality;
by constant meditation, O Goddess of Gods, it is the supreme, most excellent goal.
He alone attains liberation; he beholds the liṅga and nothing else.
When this so-called vibration is firmly established in the heart,
the Giver of Boons remains there for a moment, having gathered the mind within it.
As long as there is trembling in him, that is merely the experience [of the movement];
having attained tranquility therein, the knower of yoga, within one month,
beholds the *liṅga* arisen from the heart extending as far as the *brahmaliṅga*.
With a brilliance like fire, his entire body was illuminated by its own radiance;
then, once that had arisen, all perfections were attained within six months.
He who, without understanding this characteristic mark, takes recourse to the mark as a practitioner,
undergoes fruitless exertion and does not enjoy the fruit of the mark.
In this very way, the Śaiva [path] is perfected within the Great Liṅga by means of the Self-liṅga.
(35) By means of the perfected one, the bearer of the perfected sign (*siddhavalligī*) resides in the sign (*liṅgastha*), yet is devoid of the sign (*liṅgavarjita*).
O Bhava, what [else] should we worship? From this [perspective], what is the use of signs and those who bear signs?
When a yogin goes outside by means of this sign and the possessor of the sign, then those signs are to be recognized; even for him, there is the sign of the city.

From this knowledge of the signs, yogins are known as "possessors of signs" (liṅgin). It is no wonder that the mantras—whether peaceful, fierce, or otherwise—proceed when presided over by him; for he is like a reed (vetasa) that bends toward the Lord (bhagavat).
"If one should practice this yoga while relying upon a fierce disposition, one will become difficult for all to behold—gods, asuras, and humans alike. Thus it is said.

Having thus understood the nature of the Śivaliṅga as being established within the subtle liṅga, one should worship the external liṅga. Now, an objection may be raised: "The supreme Śambhu is partless (niṣkala); how then can he manifest in a physical form? This is true; however, because he is the bestower of grace upon all, he assumes a body through his own will by means of the mantra and takes on forms corresponding to the various dispositions of the minds [of his devotees]. And it has been said:
"In the supreme ether, situated at the tip of the flame, is the partless, supreme Śiva."
A mass of consciousness and bliss, subtle, and out of compassion for all living beings,
he became accessible through meditation and remained like a wish-fulfilling gem.

In the heart-abode of yogis, he exists in the form of an internal flame; for the sake of his own welfare and for the attainment of all prosperity, the ignorant one indeed resides there at midday, in the afternoon, and at the half-watch, facing eastward.
One should worship with every effort at the four junctions [of the day] as if one were healthy.
What is a day and night for humans is reckoned as a single *ghaṭikā* for the ancestors.
Thirty ghaṭikās are considered one day and night for the ancestors (pitṛs);
one should understand that thirty such ghaṭikās constitute a day and night beginning with the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa).

One should know that the night is for the Kṛṣṇa fortnight; that constitutes a day and night for the ancestors (Pitṛs). The eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) occurs at midday on the previous new moon (Amāvāsyā), while the full moon (Paurṇamāsī) falls in the afternoon, and the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) occupies the third watch of the day.
A year among humans is a single day and night for the gods. The northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is declared to be their day, while the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night.
The transit (saṃkrānti) at the beginning of the northern course is proclaimed to be the forenoon.
The month of Caitra and Viṣṇu [correspond to] midday; the latter half is the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana). Āśvayuja is declared to be the equinox (viṣuva), the mid-period of the gods.
From that [equinox], worship performed during those very three periods shall be dear to Śiva.
Mortals worship Sadāśiva at the junctions of days, the ancestors at the junctions of months, and the gods at the junctions of years.
Thus, the higher gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu,

and others who abide above also perform worship of the Supreme Lord during the four junctions (saṃdhyās) according to the measure of their own day, seeking the fruit of the accomplishment of their own desired goals.
Indeed, for the sake of meditation and worship, He assumes a body by His own will for the benefit of ascetics, ministers, the wise, and likewise yogis.

The form is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), as well as both-with-and-without-parts (*sakalaniṣkala*); that which is without parts is devoid of *kalās*, while that which possesses *kalās* and so forth becomes "with parts" (*sakala*).
That which is mixed with both the differentiated (sakala) and the undifferentiated (niṣkala),
therefore the Lord of Gods is always worshipped by means of the Liṅga and the Yoni according to the prescribed measure.
That which is devoid of meditative worship is partless and without a presiding deity;
therefore, one should fully worship Śambhu, who is both with parts and without parts.
There are many such statements; enough with this excessive detail, let us follow the subject at hand.
Having sipped water, performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), and completed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma),
one should [offer] ten times with the Dhruva mantra and the water of the general arghya.
Having consecrated the doors with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,

the practitioner should worship the door-keepers and others at the eastern and other directions, using flowers, perfumes, water-offerings (*arghya*), incense, and the sounds of bells and musical instruments, in the manner that will be described hereafter.
Or else, having closed the remaining doors, one should worship the western door.
And it is said:
"One should worship the gatekeepers at the western door;
one should worship Nandin and Svadhunī at the southern branch of the door."
One should worship Mahākāla and Yamunā on the northern branch of the door; Sarasvatī and Gaṇeśāna on the *dumbura* tree;
and one should worship the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya) with flowers, water-offerings (*arghya*), perfumes, incense, and oblations (*bali*).
Although this has been stated by means of an inversion of the sequence, nevertheless, one should first worship Gaṇeśa and the others, and then, having worshipped them,
worship Nandin and the rest. And it has been said:
One should place Gaṇeśa, Bhāratī, and Lakṣmī upon the upper udumbara;
then Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, Jāhnavī, and Yamunā.
And [he should place] those beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "namas" on the southern and northern branches, respectively. Thus it is said.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī.
Thus, [he places them] above on the udumbara post; and in the southern, northern, and middle [sections], he says:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā."
Thus, salutation to the Southern Branch.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahākāla.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Yamunā.

Thus, according to the Vāma-śākhā: for each of these [deities], one should perform separately the rites of seating, invocation of the form (mūrti), installation, making present, and confinement, as well as the offering of water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya-offering, flowers, and so forth; and the offering of perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), drinking water, water for sipping, betel, the purifier (pavitra), and other items, using their respective mantras.
Or, one may perform all the ritual offerings collectively with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to all the gatekeepers. Then follows their visualization (*dhyāna*), as follows:
[He is] dark-complexioned, pot-bellied, with a trunk, elephant-faced...
[with] a tusk and a rosary in his right hands, and an axe and a trident in his left.
One should worship the dwarf, three-eyed [form] above the right door;
and [one should worship] the white, youthful Sarasvatī, adorned with all ornaments,
intent on playing the lute with her left and right hands.
One should worship the two deities holding books and dice in the north;
between them, one should worship Mahālakṣmī, golden-hued and adorned.
Holding a *śrīphala* fruit and a lotus in her right hands, and endowed with a lotus and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands,
she consecrates [the practitioner] with streams of nectar from the *bhṛṅgarāja* plant, like the bathing of an elephant in a pool.
Śrī Nandikeśvara is red in color, with matted hair and a sacred thread;
he holds a trident and a rosary, is gentle in appearance, and has hands granting boons and fearlessness.
One should worship on the right branch the three-eyed one adorned with the moon,
[and] Jahnu’s daughter, who is white and gentle, seated upon a crocodile,
her arms resting upon a white chowrie and a vessel of nectar.
To the north of that, one should worship Nandin, adorned with all ornaments, dark-complexioned,
with tawny matted hair, formidable, and possessing a face made terrifying by prominent fangs.
One should worship on the northern branch the one who is terrifying with a frown, stout, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and bearing all types of drums;
and then, to his left, Yauvana.
"The wise one should worship the daughter of Karma, who is seated upon a tortoise, dark-complexioned, adorned with ornaments, and holding a jar of nectar and a lotus. Thus it is said.

Then, with the thumb and the tip of the ring finger of the hand that expresses the *haṃsa*—the self of Śiva and Śakti—one should place the *nāda* and, having fashioned divine eyes through that light, dispel the divine obstacles with the *nārāca-mudrā*. By casting flowers consecrated with the blazing *śivāstra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should expel the obstacles situated in the intermediate space from the temple. Having warded off the obstacles located on the ground by striking the earth three times with the right heel while discharging the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having taken hold of the southern doorpost, one should step over the threshold with the left foot and enter within the navel [of the mandala].

Having entered facing west, one should worship the abode of Śiva at the center of the threshold as before, through the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, and then meditate. One should meditate upon [Brahmā] in the middle of the threshold: four-faced, four-armed, with the color of blazing fire, holding the gestures of boon (*vara*) and power (*śakti*), the trident (*śūla*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in his right and left hands, adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon, and seated upon a lotus throne. Now, one should worship the Great Lakṣmī of the Boon (*varalakṣmī*) either above or within the range of vision, facing toward the sacrificial hall.
*Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the Lord of the Site (*vāstvadhipati*), together with his retinue.*

Thus, having worshipped [the deity] in the southwest corner as before with the rites of invocation and so forth, one should meditate upon Tundila— yellow in color, with matted hair of a tawny hue, endowed with a beard and earrings, seated upon a lotus throne in the *buddha-paryaṅka* posture, and holding a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), a rosary, a *śruk* spoon, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his right and left hands. Then, having offered the seat for the virtuous guru with the heart-mantra,
the practitioner, having gone and circumambulated the God of gods, Maheśvara, [should proceed].
Having thoroughly cleansed the outer ground with a soft,
fine broom, and having smeared it with cow-dung water, one should adorn it by scattering dust [of colored powders].
Then, according to the prescribed ritual, one should fill jars with water from the Gaṅgā and other sacred waters, along with auspicious vessels and so forth.
Whatever materials whatsoever are suitable for worship;
Having brought and gathered together, according to one's means,
special arghya vessels and the implements for worship,
and having purified them according to the scriptures, one should place each in its respective location.
Then one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to the scriptures and in the proper sequence.
Therein, [the seat] is either a black antelope skin or a pure one made of kuśa grass and so forth. (p.
O Lord, one should enter into the presence [of the deity] on a soft, pure seat to the right.
And it has been said:

"One should not worship Śambhu in the east, nor in front; not in the north, as that is the seat of women; nor in the west, since that is the back; therefore, one should worship him when he is situated on the right."
Likewise:
"One should not stand directly in front of the Lord, nor behind him, nor too close to his wife.
Standing to the right of the one who is skillful in destroying the flood of sins and bestowing liberation and so forth, one should perform worship."
Likewise:
"One should not [worship] at the front in the presence of a woman, nor at the back in her presence;
for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, one should worship while standing on the right side of the one who removes the flood of sins."

One might object: "Since he is not terrible (*aghora*), being peaceful (*śānta*), he ought not to be one who liberates from sin. True; however, this is due to the very nature of the Reality (*vastu-svabhāva*). And as it has been said: "Just as a lotus, though fearsome, soft, and cool, yet burns [the world], so too, even when perfectly tranquil, the Terrible One (*ghora*) acts as the burner of sins."

[Objection: "In the sacrificial pavilion (*nanuyāgamaṇḍapa*) or in a temple facing east, [the deity] faces oneself. But what if [the temple] faces west, since the Lord stands there facing west? Consequently, his terrible face (*ghoravadana*) would also be in the north; this should not be said. [Response: It is not so. Even there, the Lord indeed faces east. And it has been said: "Just as the body [of the deity] is like a temple, its faces—though they may be directed toward any direction at will—do not abandon their positions in the cardinal directions starting from the east. Whether a *liṅga*, an image, or something else is made, in whichever direction [it is placed], the sacrificer should worship Śiva while facing north."
How is it that for whichever deity facing the western door has been established, there too it is only Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna? And it is said:
"In the west, just as the door is, there one should meditate upon Īśāna and Puruṣa.
The "Just-born" (Sadyojāta) face should be in the east; the "Terrible" (Ghora) and the "Left" (Vāma) as before.
The limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅga) are as previously described, and the practitioner faces north.
One should place the food offering, the row of lamps, and so forth at the entrance. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere:
"Either facing east or west, O Śivā, one should be joined with the limbs of enjoyment;
or, in the state of Ghoratva, one should resort to the southern direction."

"Rudra bears the southern face; therefore, protect me always"—thus says the Śruti. By this very [statement], it is indeed declared that the worshipper should begin [the rite] in the presence of the Aghora face. Now, if Śiva possesses the quality of looking toward the western door, then in that case, one should cause him to proceed to the west and strike the doors.

"One who desires success, being composed in mind, should cause [the deity] to proceed through the western door"—from such statements as these, let the western door alone be used. Why then resort to the eastern door or facing the east? This should not be said. This is an beginningless convention; thus, the Blessed One faces the east. Furthermore, because he is for the benefit of all, he remains according to the established arrangement. And it has been said: "In whichever direction the door may be, one should imagine the west;
that which is facing the *liṅga* is considered the east."
"In that regard, the Tatpuruṣa face and the upward face should be turned forward;
the sacrificial pedestal, the bull, and the trident should be facing that [Tatpuruṣa] face.
Thus it is said elsewhere as well.
Śambhu always faces the east, while the practitioner faces the north;
however, according to the distinction of their specific desires, one should visualize Śiva as facing that particular direction.

In rites that are obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), or for the fulfillment of desires (kāmya), one should face the east; or else, facing west, one should arrange the orientation toward other directions at the junctions of the regions, provided it is not undesirable.
Thus, enough of this excessive elaboration.

Now, the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*) is described. [An objection: But what is accomplished by the purification of the elements at this point? For, previously on the occasion of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the very elements censured within the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) were already purified. [Response: It should not be said thus. Those elements are of two kinds: the elements [of the cosmic paths] and the elements that constitute the body. And it has been said: "Earth, water, fire, air, and space..."
These five principles, however, pervade all things.

"The bondage of the body is not established without the five principles. Thus it is said; "Having understood these through their division into gross and subtle, one should purify them. Thus it is said.
