In that regard, at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the external locations of experience—which are of the nature of the *tattvas*—and the karma to be experienced therein, are purified; however, the elements in the form of the body are not [purified] at that time, because there is no destruction of the *prārabdha* (commenced) karma. And it has been said:
"Just as when the production of a jar is complete, the wheel continues to spin due to the perfection of its prior momentum, so too does this body persist."
Karma that would have led to many future existences has been burnt away like a seed by subtle flames;
even that which was yet to come is obstructed by him through the experience of this [present] fruition.
"Or there may be liberation in the body itself, which bestows immediate nirvāṇa.

Therefore, it is improper for the self—which has been purified by initiation (dīkṣā)—to remain present in a pure physical body composed of the five elements, which is the locus for the experience of karma impelled by the unmanifest power of Māyā. (p.

The purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*) is performed daily and at every moment upon the body through the power of mantra; this must be practiced because of the instability of the mind. As it has been said by the Teachers:

"Therefore, for one who has been purified by initiation, whose self resides in the physical body composed of the five elements—which is the locus for experiencing the fruits of one's own past actions—and who is impelled toward a continuous stream of worldly experience by the powers of Māyā..."
That [placing of] honey in a defiled vessel is improper;
therefore, the wise one [should purify] the body consisting of *śakti* through the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
And she should always perform that [duty], because otherwise there would be no stability for herself. Thus it is said.
And it is said in the Āgama:
"Having meditated on a lotus bud in the heart, completely flooded with the water of nectar,
one should contemplate there one's own task as something divine, like a wish-fulfilling gem."
The "burning" is said to be by the fire of yoga, not in the manifest [state], but rather in the case of karmas;
those whose powers are manifest are accomplished through all mantras,
and they are established by the independent ones in their own respective places according to the sequence.
And when their task is completed, they return of their own accord to their own abodes;
for day by day, through contact with yoga, the powers of Śiva [attain their state].
Constantly sprinkled with the water of mantra, they gradually attain growth;
thus, being restrained by them, their powers become manifest.
"Being purified, they increase and remove all defects;
even those that are deficient become complete—of this there is no doubt.

For this very reason, one must certainly perform purification of the body through the retention (*dhāraṇā*) of the elements and *kalās* that are censured throughout the entire path. And it has been said:
Since the body is born from the elements (*bhūta*), purification occurs through the cleansing of the elements. The elements contain the essence of the *tattvas* and are endowed with five signs.
The intrinsic nature, color, and shape, along with the causes of the digits and the mandalas, as well as the colors, mantras, qualities, locations, and measurements, are all joined together.
"By means of the five concentrations (dhāraṇā) associated with earth and the other elements, [the yogi proceeds];
however, in this context, there is no concentration during the upward impulse (udghāta), as the earth and the other elements are already joined with their respective digits (kalā)."

This is its meaning: at the time of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśodhana*), there is specifically a distinguished purification of the Deity alone. This purification is performed by burning [the impurities] with the fire of yoga. Since that [Deity] has birth from the elements, delusion arises; that is, birth would occur along with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) from the gross elements. Thus, it is "born from the elements" (*sa-bhūta-janman*). And it has been said:

"The great elements (*mahābhūtāni*) are the principles (*tattvāni*); the body consists of the subtle elements. Its state is "being born from the elements" (*bhūtajanmatvam*). Regarding the phrase "from that": the elements are those known as earth, water, fire, air, and ether. By their very nature, they contain the principles; the principles are the thirty-six in number beginning with earth, and those which have these within their interior or midst are "containing the principles" (*tattvagarbhāṇi*). They are also endowed with the five symbols consisting of the vajra, lotus, svastika, six dots, and the power (*śakti*). He says, "the configuration" (*saṃsthānam*), which is a description of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). In that regard, their own form and intrinsic nature consists of solidity, fluidity, heat, motion, and space. Their colors are yellow, white, red, black, and bright white; their digits (*kalā*) are named Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Śāntyatītā; and their mandalas are square, semi-circular, triangular, hexagonal, and circular in form. Their causal deities are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Ananta, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. And as it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Ananteśa, and Sadāśiva are traditionally known as the presiding deities of the principles (tattvas), beginning with earth, in their respective order. Thus it is said.

(p. 46) Now, the *varṇas* are [the letters] beginning with *a*. The *mantras* are [the seed-syllables] beginning with *sadyojāta*. Alternatively, those joined with mantras are the *mantras*, namely the *varṇa-mantras*. Among these, the *varṇas* are the seed-syllables (*bījas*) *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, *ha*, and *kṣa* belonging to the earth element and so forth. The *mantras* are the seed-syllables of the heart (*hṛdaya*), the crest (*śikhā*), the armor (*kavaca*), and power (*śakti*). Thus, the *kalā-mantras* are extracted as *hlāṃ*, *hvīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hyaiṃ*, and *hrauṃ*. The qualities (*guṇas*) are smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. In that regard, the elements (*bhūtas*) are the locations (*sthānas*) possessing five, four, three, two, and one quality respectively. Alternatively, the "location" refers to the head and other parts of the body. And it has been said:
"All mandalas, from the head down to the feet, are situated there; all that is of the earth, marked with the vajra," and so forth. Likewise, in the Jñānottara:

"One should contemplate the *maṇḍala* of Mahendrī, beginning from the top of the yogin," and so forth. There is a tenfold increase starting from one hundred million (*koṭi*) *pramāṇas*. And likewise in that very same [text]: "Starting from the earth up to the *bindu*-tattva, one should understand the *tattvas* as being situated in a tenfold rotation."

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the four *pāśas* beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with the *praṇava*—that is, those preceded and followed by the *praṇava*—are included. These have not been forgotten here, as they will be discussed in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*). Having thus contemplated the elements censured as the entire path (*adhvan*), one should effect the purification of the body by means of those elements, earth and the rest, which are characterized by being conjoined with the five meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) beginning with that of earth.

Now, in this purification of the body (*deha-śodhana*), it is not even said that the eternal elements (*nityabhūta*) themselves are being purified; rather, those [elements] are purified by means of *dhāraṇā* and so forth. Therefore, because they have become one through the relationship of the purified and the purifier, *dhāraṇā* itself must be purified. To the question "Then by what are these purified?", he says: "In the *udghāta*, during the day, *dhāraṇā* joined with *kalā*. Thus, there are the five categories beginning with earth, which are censured by all the paths (*adhvan*); and there are the *kalās* censured by the *tattvas*. And it has been said (p. 47):
"When the [vital breath] is properly and completely restrained, the upward-moving wind proceeds;
this is reckoned as an 'udghāta' (upward thrust) here at will, even for the youngest. Thus it is said.

The purification of the five elements, beginning with earth, should be performed by means of the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) corresponding to the number of their respective principles (*tattva*) and qualities; or else, all may be purified by a single *udghāta*. Thus it has been said: "The five elements, which contain the principles within them, [should be purified] by the five diverse meditative concentrations, such as that on the head and others, by one whose mind is focused on nothing else."
The earthy, the watery, the fiery, the airy, and the one called *nāhasī*—
these are indeed the *kalās*, which are the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇās*) here, named after the object to be purified.
The maṇḍala, the configuration of the seed-syllable, and the form, each distinct [from the others],
together with breath control (prāṇāyāma) and meditation (dhyāna), are declared to be concentration (dhāraṇā).
Alternatively, because it holds those respective seeds within the lotuses of the sense organs,
this is called "concentration" (dhāraṇā) by the knowers of reality for the sake of the arising of a purified body;
then, having purified the elements through the yoga of striking down their qualities.
In that place, one should clearly contemplate the form of one's own Kalāmūrti;
or else, by means of a single upward thrust (*ekodghāta*), all [the forms] should be contemplated according to their true nature.
There, the tree of worldly existence (*bhavapādapa*)—which is the self of the body with its face turned downward—should be meditated upon. Thus it is said.

Now, as for the detailed exposition that one's own lineage of gurus (*gurukrama*) must be performed for the sake of fully understanding the various scriptures, it is impossible to elaborate upon it here. Furthermore, because they possess equal authority, the concise procedure (*laghukrama*) is commenced:
having smeared the hands with fragrant unguents and having exhaled the vital breath (*marut*), the wise one should touch the palms and the backs of both hands—once on the left and once on the right.
One should immerse both hands, which are like half of the flame of the fire of the weapons, with the *śakti* [mudrā];
the fingers form an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp of two finger-breadths.
Having meditated there, one should place the seat, the form, and Śambhu as its pervader;
then, having assigned the limbs beginning with the heart, one should assign them to the fingers beginning with the little finger and ending with the thumb.
Having consecrated [the hand] with the root mantra, one should encircle it mutually with the armor mantra;
then, having meditated upon the hand as consisting of Śiva’s fiery energy, one should [withdraw it] with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
Having withdrawn the self by means of the Mūrti-mantra through the vital breath (prāṇavāyu),
one should [place it] pervading one's own body; then, within that heart-lotus in full bloom—
which consists of fire and moon— one should place the solar orb within that fire.
One should place that which stands there, as far as the moon and the sruva-spoon, within the cavity of that [vessel].
Having placed that within the orb of the nectar of Śakti situated inside the sun, moon,
and fire, one should fashion the cosmic egg by means of the pair of orbs beginning with Śakti.
Then, having formed the tortoise mudrā, one should purify the tattvas in succession.

The sequence here is as follows: one should contemplate one's own body as a banyan tree—having the seed of *āṇavamala* cast into the field of *māyā*; rooted in *dharma*, *adharma*, and delusion; having *kalā* and the rest as its pith; the individual soul (*jīva-puruṣa*) as its trunk; *prakṛti* and the rest as its massive body; the senses as its branches and sub-branches; the sense objects as its sprouts; the manifold of states (*bhāva-prapañca*) as its flowers; pleasure and pain as its fruit; and with its roots above and branches below. And it is said:
"One should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) for the sake of the pure self, which is the substance of Rudra;
thereafter, one should gradually lead the Lord of the Senses (*akṣeśa*), who resides in the senses, [to the supreme state]."
"One should gradually perform the purification of the self by the self within the self;
one should purify the tree of the feet in sequence, consisting of the impurities (*mala*), *māyā*, and *kalā*. (p. 49)
Having rotated the kneecaps, one should snap the fingers of the mother [the hands] in succession;
with those twelve finger-snaps, there is inhalation (pūraka) and likewise retention (kumbhaka).
And thus is described the exhalation (recaka) of the minor breath control (praṇāyāma).

*Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Nivṛttikalā.* Reciting *huṃ phaṭ* five times with the mind during the first half of the inhalation (*pūraka*), while performing the earth-element concentration (*dhāraṇā*) for the purpose of destroying the five qualities (*guṇas*), one should contemplate that tree of the body as being devoid of leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth. Then, reciting *oṃ hvīṃ, salutation to Pratiṣṭhākalā; haḥ huṃ phaṭ* four times during the second half of the inhalation, while performing the water-element concentration (*dhāraṇā*) for the destruction of the [remaining] four qualities, one should contemplate it as having sprouted new shoots. Then...

Reciting "Oṃ hrūṃ vidyākalāyai haḥ huṃ phaṭ" three times with the *kumbhaka* (retention) breath and the fire-element concentration (*dhāraṇā*) for the destruction of the three qualities (*guṇas*), one should contemplate [the body] as dried up and burnt.

Then, reciting "Oṃ ke hyeṃ śāntikalāyai haḥ huṃ phaṭ" twice with the first half of the *recaka* (exhalation) breath and the wind-element concentration (*dhāraṇā*) for the destruction of the remaining two qualities, one should contemplate that ash being scattered in the ten directions. Thereafter—

Reciting "Oṃ hauṃ śāntyatītakalāyai haḥ huṃ phaṭ" once during the latter half of the exhalation (*recaka*), one should contemplate the stainless ether through the meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the element of space for the sole purpose of destroying the [remaining] qualities. Then, having contemplated the subtle form consisting of a *jyotir-liṅga* by means of the mantras beginning with *Śāntyatītā* ending in *namaḥ*, applied respectively to the head, forehead, nose, neck, and the region of the heart; and thereafter, having contemplated at the *dvādaśānta* the circle of power (*śaktimaṇḍala*), which resembles a full moon disc and consists of nectar.

Having expelled [the impurities] with the exhalation (*recaka*) while reciting "Oṃ hauṃ śaktaye vauṣaṭ," one should then, through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), consecrate that [deity] with streams of nectar in the form of cool, yellow light radiating from the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*). Having removed the upper mandala, one should purify all of this, including oneself, by means of five breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) accompanied by the *praṇava* (Oṃ). As it is said:
"One should purify everything with the *praṇavas* and with five breath-controls. (p. 50)
By means of the *recaka* [breathing], it is burned once from the feet up to the crown of the head.
"In the same way, one should flood that [space] with the ashes filling it;
together with those ashes, one should do so once with water containing charcoal embers during the half-exhalation in the Śāṅkara [mudrā]."

Then, with the mantra *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmamūrtaye namaḥ*, one should contemplate that very subtle form of the self—red and white, possessing undistracted hands, feet, and so forth—as being located within the heart-lotus. As it has been said:
"Endowed with four petals and resembling the orb of the rising sun..."
One should install the embodied form within this, recollecting it as having both manifest and unmanifest natures.
"One should place within the center of the *liṅga* the form called Ātman, possessing a brilliant white luster. Thus,

having meditated upon the *liṅga* as the all-pervading Self, and having contemplated the form of Sadāśiva— which consists of the five Brahmans and the [five] Kalās— reciting "Oṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*)."

Having meditated upon the venerable Paramaśiva as the officiant (yajamāna), bearing the [sacrificial] form, residing in the heart, and pervading all—that is, by reciting "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva"—and having mentally performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Heart-mantra and the others in the locations such as the heart, one should effect the supreme consecration (paramīkaraṇa) by means of the Root-mantra. Having performed all this mentally, one should again release the tortoise-gesture (kūrma-mudrā).

Then, having uttered "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva (śivāsana)" with the thumb and ring finger, one should place [the mantra] upon the *bindu* situated in the center of the pericarp of the sixteen-petaled lotus located within each of the cakras, in the midst of the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*) of the navel. Then:
"Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva (śivamūrti)."
One should place the subtle form, whose nature is the union of the *bindu* and the moon, [upon the forehead].
And it is said:
"Having meditated on the form residing in the *bindu* of the *bindu*, one should contemplate the gross body."

thus [it is said]. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Sadāśiva—who consists of the five Brahma-kalās—extending to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the one whose body is knowledge (*vidyādeha*)," and having invoked the venerable Supreme Śiva by reciting "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva" up to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] (*dvādaśānta*), and having performed the placement of the two pervasive forms (*mūrtidvaya-vyāpaka*), [one recites] "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the heart" for the purpose of the rite of making [the deity] possessed of all parts (*sakalīkaraṇa*).

"Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to the head; Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the crest-lock. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs—using white and their respective [colored] syllables—at the locations of the heart, head, and crest-lock with the thumbs and ring fingers, [one should proceed].

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the black-colored armor (*tanutra*) upon the two sides with both hands while reciting *oṃ hyaiṃ kavacāya namaḥ*, and having dispelled obstacles by clapping the three sounds of the palms with both hands while reciting *oṃ haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ*, one should place water in the cardinal and intermediate directions like a shower of arrows (*nārāca*) using the snapping gestures of the weapon (*astra-choṭikā*), thereby performing the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*). Then, having enveloped [the body] with the armor mantra ending in *namaḥ*, and having performed the supreme unification (*paramīkṛti*) from the head down to the feet with both hands using the lotus mantra (*kamala-mantra*), one should perform the invigoration of all mantras starting from the feet with the power mantra (*śakti-mantra*) ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*). And it has been said:
One should place Śiva as the seat-form at the navel, the white heart-form at the heart,
the golden "I" (Ahaṃ) at the head, and the ruddy crest-form at the topknot.
O warrior, place the black armor upon your chest— terrible to behold— and hold the weapon,
which resembles fire, in your hand, preceded by three claps of the palms.
One should expel the collection [of impurities] in all directions and intermediate directions by means of the *atikāstra* mantra;
having enveloped it with the *kavaca* mantra, one should perform the supreme consecration (*paramīkṛti*) with the root mantra.
Then, having pervaded it with that splendor, one should expel the subtle elements (*aṇu*) by means of the power (*śakti*). Thus it is said.
Thus, being one whose body is armored with mantra, the practitioner is not overcome by any obstacle. As it has been said: (p. 52) "And so..."
The *hṛdaya* is for protecting the heart; it is beneficial when bound like a bandage.
The *śirastra* is a head-protector, a wrap for the head. The *mūlikā* is a helmet for the top of the head, and the *kramaṅkaṭa* is a leg-protector.
"When a weapon is grasped in the hand, he stands like a terrifying warrior;
he would be invincible to the base, just as Tārkṣya is to the serpents. Thus it is said.

The sequence of placement (nyāsa) for those who perform the Niṣkala Prāsāda [rite] involves the limbs of Brahmā and the eyes. Furthermore, by those who perform the Sakala Prāsāda [rite], the placement must be performed with the limbs of Brahmā and the eyes. And it is said in the Siddhānta:
"Having thus performed the placement according to the rule, one should then perform the placement of the mantras.
One should purify the two hands with the Astra-mantra, counting them as one and then two."
With the power [of the breath], one should flood [the area] with the supreme nectars arising from the nostrils;
then, having meditated upon a lotus there, one should mentally place the *sana* (seat) within it.

The wise practitioner should perform the placement of the form and its pervader, Śambhu, with their respective individual *aṇus*, beginning from the thumb and ending with the little finger, starting with Īśāna and the others.
The mantras beginning with the heart and ending with the armor are assigned to the little fingers in sequence;
having placed the eye mantra on the palms of the hands, the weapon mantra is placed within the range of the thumbs.
Having consecrated [the object] with the root mantra and veiled it with the armor mantra,
one should thus fashion the Hand of Śiva and perform the preceding rites with it.
One should place the Āsanāṇu-mantra at the navel, then the Mūrti-mantra, and then the Śiva-mantra.
The faces are not arranged in the manner of a staff (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*), but rather in the manner of a skull-crown (*muṇḍabhaṅgī*).
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face.
Having placed Aghora in the heart and Guhyaka in the secret region,
one should place Sadyojāta from below that down to the feet.
Having fashioned one's own body with these mantras which are the abodes of the elements,
one should meditate upon that forest on the head by means of the Īśāna mantra;
first, one should [place] Tatpuruṣa as the face upon the face above the heart.
One should arrange Vāmadeva upon the right shoulder and the right face;
Sadyojāta, situated above the neck of Brahmā, [should be arranged] with Ajāṇu.
These are of various colors— white, yellow,
and red-and-white— and all of them are adorned with crowns and earrings.
One should place the white heart-mantra in the heart, the yellow head-mantra on the heads,
the red crest-mantra on the crest, and the black throat-mantra on the chest.
Having placed the eye, which consists of the sun, moon, and fire, into the eyes.

With the Astra-mantra, one should dispel obstacles in all directions by making three clapping sounds with the two hands stained red, and then place the Astra-mantra upon the head with the fingertips. Beginning from the crown of the head, one should touch [the body] with both hands while reciting the Mūlamantra.
When the mantras have dissolved into the body, then that becomes the mantra-body.
In some places:
"The emission of everything is performed with the Śakti-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Thus [it is said].
The procedure for the seed-syllable (bīja) of Brahman has been declared; now hear the sequence of the foot-Brahman (pādabrahma).
Having first divided those feet, one should place them with the ritual digits (kalās).
Īśāna is on the head as the fifth abode, and [Aghora] is on the face among the four faces.
The fifth [syllable] is placed in the *praṇava* itself; thereafter, one should assign the *ghora-kalā*.
One should assign [the syllables] to the heart, the throat, the navel, the belly, the back, and the chest.
In the secret place, the penis, the two thighs, the knees, the shanks, and the buttocks;
Then, O Vāmadeva, one should place a portion on the hips and the two sides;
[and likewise] on the feet, the hands, the nose, the head, and the two staff-like arms.
The *kalās* of Sadyojāta are to be joined; one should install the *kalās* ending with the mantras.
As follows: Oṃ, Īśāna of all sciences, Lord of all beings, Sovereign of Brahmā, Overlord of Brahman—may Śiva be mine; Sadāśiva, Oṃ!
Oṃ, we know that Puruṣa, we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra inspire us.

Oṃ, to those who are non-terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the most terrible—to all these forms of yours, O Śarva, O Rudra, let there be salutation from every side. Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to the Eldest; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Kāla; salutation to Kalavikaraṇa; salutation to Balapramathana.

Salutations, salutations to the Subduer of all beings; salutations to the Transcendent Mind (Unmanā). Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to him who is newly born. In every existence, in non-existence, and beyond existence, protect me; salutations to the Source of Existence (Bhavodbhava). On the right face: Oṃ, that Rudra, salutations to the Foundation (Pratiṣṭhā). On the left face: Oṃ, may he impel us, salutations to Cessation (Nivṛtti). On the rear face: Oṃ, to those who are not terrible, salutations to her.

In the heart: *Oṃ atha ghorebhyo mohāyai namaḥ*. In the throat: *Oṃ aghorakṣāyai namaḥ*. On the right shoulder: *Oṃ ghoratarebhyo niṣṭhāyai namaḥ*. On the left shoulder: *Oṃ sarvataḥ śarva mṛtyave namaḥ*. In the navel: *Sarvebhyo māyāyai namaḥ*. In the stomach: *Oṃ namaste'stu rudrabhayāyai namaḥ*. On the back: *Rūpebhyo jvarāyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ vāmadevāya namo'rajāyai namaḥ*.

In the secret place (*guhya*): *Oṃ jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ*, *rakṣāyai namaḥ*. In the *liṅga*: *Oṃ rudrāya namaḥ*, *ratyai namaḥ*. On the right thigh: *Oṃ kalāya namaḥ*, *pālyāyai namaḥ*. On the left thigh: *Oṃ kalakāmāyai namaḥ*. On the right knee: *Oṃ avikaraṇāya namaḥ*, *saṃyaminyai namaḥ*. On the left knee: *Oṃ bālakriyāyai namaḥ*. On the right calf: *Oṃ vikaraṇāya namaḥ*, *manobudhyai namaḥ*. On the left calf: *Oṃ balakāryāyai namaḥ*.

On the right buttock: *Oṃ*, salutation to Balamathanā, salutation to Dhatrī. On the left buttock: *Oṃ*, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanā, salutation to Bhrāmiṇī. On the hips: *Oṃ*, salutation to Manomohinī. On the right flank: salutation to Unmanā, salutation to Manonmanī. On the left flank.

Oṃ, I shall proclaim Sadyojāta; salutation to Siddhi. On the right side. Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation to Siddhi. On the right foot. Oṃ, salutation to Sadyojātā; salutation to Ṛddhi. On the left foot. Oṃ, salutation to the one called Bhava. On the right hand. Oṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī, the "Ahava. On the left hand. Oṃ, salutation to Medhā, the primordial Bhava. In the vital breath. Oṃ, favor me!

*Oṃ*, salutation to Kānti; on the head. *Oṃ*, salutation to Bhavasvadhā; on the right arm. *Oṃ*, salutation to Udbhava and salutation to Dhṛti; on the left arm. Or rather, one should place these [mantras] preceded by all the seed-syllables (*bīja*).
*Oṃ hoṃ*, salutation to Śaśinī; such are the mantras for the limbs. As before, this is declared to be the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*.
However, if he is a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) who is detached, [he should perform it] starting from the little finger with his own respective fingers.
And the wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement of withdrawal (saṃhāranyāsa) starting from the feet.
In that very same way, one who is peaceful, free from longing, and devoid of attachment should perform the dusting;
he should be constantly devoted to the practice of yoga, for otherwise it is held that there is no qualification [for this].
As it is said elsewhere: "The construction of the body occurs through the five unborn elements which remain as non-realities:
earth, water, fire, air, and ether."
"Īśa is the withdrawal; that placement, however, begins with the feet and so forth. Thus [it is said].
Having thus performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa preceded by the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should begin the internal worship (antaryajana).
That [worship] should be performed by yogis with flowers such as non-violence (ahiṃsā) and so forth. And these are described in the *Gama*:
Non-violence is the first flower, and the restraint of the senses is likewise a flower; patience is a flower, and beyond that, knowledge is the supreme flower.

Then there are the flowers: the flower of truth (*satya-puṣpa*), the flower of intention (*bhāva-puṣpa*), and likewise the eightfold [flowers]. Now, if non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the others are flowers, how can they be compared [to physical flowers]? For they lack form (*arūpatvāt*). True. However, the comparison is made because the Blessed One is gratified by non-violence and the rest just as He is by [physical] flowers. Now, if that yogin is a Mādhyamika on account of the commonality of form, he should worship the God through the *suṣumnā* channel at night, and perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) during the day.
Likewise, one should practice meditation during the twilights, and always recite [the mantra] by day and by night.
Now, if the perfected yogi thinks:
"One should not worship the deity by day, nor indeed by night;
one should worship him constantly, avoiding both day and night."
Now, if he is a beginner, he should visualize the seat of the heart as being located within the flowing *iḍā* channel.
Piṅgalā is at the navel-lotus, while Suṣumnā is at the crown;
the rite of worship should take place in the heart, and one should perform the fire-oblation at the navel.
And one should meditate on Īśvara on the forehead as having the form of smokeless light.
Alternatively, for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, he should worship Śiva through the central nostril;
for the sake of pacification or for malevolent rites, he should worship through the left and right nostrils respectively.
As it is said in the venerable Kālottara:
"In this matter, unify external time with internal [time];
then, having abandoned external time, one should contemplate the internal."
One should contemplate one's internal actions at the proper time;
for one who desires liberation from the realm of sense-objects, such worship is highly praised.

"For the sake of pacification, worship of Maheśvara is prescribed through the flow of the left channel (nāḍī); for Skanda, it is prescribed in the Mānalyā; and for malevolent rites (ābhicāraka), [it is prescribed] in the right. Thus [it is said].
Then, with flowers and other offerings imbued with the sense of existence (bhāva), one should worship Śiva in the heart-lotus.
And that [lotus] has arisen from the *kanda*. As it has been said:
"The location of the *kanda* for human beings is nine finger-breadths from the center of the body."
The height and the width of the platform should likewise be four finger-breadths.
"And the egg-shaped [form] has the appearance of a *dā* [syllable], adorned with the *tattvas*, *gās*, and so forth.

Now, that which is like a bulb (*kanda*) is the source of the leftward channels; from it arises the heart-lotus. In its pericarp, within the power (*śakti*) of the flames of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, Ananta, Īśa, Sadeva, and Paramaśiva abide by their very nature. As it is said in the venerable *Niśvāsakārikā*:
The heart of all embodied beings resembles the flower of a plantain tree;
situated in its center is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
The heart is one *vitasti* in measure, and the lotus is four *aṅgulas*;
it is situated above the navel, extending to a maximum dimension of eight *aṅgulas*.
The lotus has two openings for the stalk and is surrounded on all sides by a rim;
here, its pericarp is equal in size to a thumb-joint and is provided with filaments.
Within the pericarp there should be the sun, and in its center the moon;
within the moon there should be fire, and within the sun, Maheśvara.
Sadāśiva is Maheśa; he who stands in the opposite view is otherwise.
I shall fully declare the measurements established by Śiva for all of them.
One should know that the sun is slightly inferior to [the previous], and likewise the moon is inferior to the sun;
one should understand the supreme orb of fire to be inferior to the moon.
Free from smoke and stainless, divine, resembling the rising sun,
gentle and beautiful like the fifth state (turya), it is as pure as a flawless crystal.

"Always [meditate upon] Śiva, the Great Soul, who is beyond that [universe], both transcendent and immanent; whose state is perfectly pure, divine, ungraspable, and the supreme auspiciousness. Thus it is said.
Having thus understood all this, one should arrange the locations for worship, fire-offerings, and meditative absorption.
The heart is beautiful and expansive, with a canopy bound by the Vedas,
forming a circular expanse like a fully blossomed white eight-petalled lotus.
Seated upon the lion-throne of mantra, his body armored with mantra.
Having attained the excellent path of mantra-worship, one should there sacrifice to Maheśvara.
In the sacrificial fire-pit within the expanse of the secret cave of the navel-cakra,
having brought [the deity] into presence as before, one should satisfy him there with the supreme nectars.

"According to the statement: 'One should meditate upon the Lord Śiva, peaceful, smokeless, and consisting of light, within the cavity of the throbbing bindu in the expanse of the region of the forehead.'"

Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the stalks and pericarps of the lotus—from the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*) up to the power of consciousness (*śakti*), as will be described there—having meditated upon Īśvara there as consisting of the gross body of Sadāśiva, and having performed the placement of the two pervasive forms (*mūrti*) extending to the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*) of Paramaśiva, which is the supreme light; having consecrated [the deity] through invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, having effected the unification with all parts (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings; having worshipped with substances mentally conceived through inhalation (*pūraka*) via the *iḍā* channel; and having performed the recitation (*japa*) through the movement of the central breath (*nāsīcāra*) while offering praise and salutations, one should direct [the deity] toward the temple (*prāsāda*). Then, in the self-manifested navel-pit (*nābhikuṇḍa*) which has three ridges, one should kindle one's own elements with the mantra, abandon the portion for the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*), purify [the fire] through inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and other rites, and—having unified it with the fire of knowledge (*jñānavahni*) located between the heart and the eyebrows, ignited by the seed-syllable of fire, and led to the twelve-finger space—bring that Śiva-fire back to the navel via exhalation (*recaka*). Having worshipped it with the *Sadyojāta* mantras and others according to the visualization, one should offer five oblations (*āhuti*) with the root mantra (*mūla*).

Oṃ Hāṃ! Having given the name "Hutāśana" (Fire-eater) to Śivāgni, and having performed the worship of the four deities beginning with Brahmā upon the kuśa grass placed within the girdles of that sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the four directions, one should perform the *samidh*-oblation of sixteen kinds representing the elements, senses, and mind. Then, having meditated on the protective [deity], one should mentally install [the fire] there, from the *ādhāra-śakti* up to the end, in the center of the heart-lotus of the fire. There, having worshipped Śiva along with his limbs (*aṅga*) and ending with the *kuśa* purifiers, one should proceed with the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*).

By means of the *piṅgalā* exhalation (*recaka*), one should contemplate the internal nectar-like form of Śiva, who flows from the sphere of Power (*śakti-maṇḍala*) situated at the *dvādaśānta*, filled with the essence of supreme nectar, and who pours forth from the jar of the *kanda* through the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*)—reaching the throat, palate, ears, the unmanifest *brahmarandhra*, the lotus of the ear-vessel (*puṣkara*), and extending as far as the son of Brahmā (*brahmaputra*). Having offered the ten ritual ingredients (*daśāṅga*) and the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) by means of the ladle (*sruva*) whose form is the *suṣumnā* and whose handle is the ear, and having worshipped according to rule, one should unite the Śiva residing in the fire with the Śiva worshipped in the heart-lotus via the path of the channels. Then, having restrained the fire situated in the navel-pit by performing the *bhūr-ādi* oblations, and having performed the dedication of the rite (*karmārpaṇa*) to the Śiva worshipped in the heart-lotus, one should restrain [the fire] with the various offerings (*upacāra*) and meditate upon Śiva in the form of Power (*śakti*).

Then, having gone to the space between the eyebrows by means of the *suṣumṇā* exhalation (*recaka*), and having fixed the mind there through retention (*kumbhaka*), one should perform *samādhi*. Having contemplated one's own body as being filled with a mass of that [divine] light, and with a steady intellect thinking "I am indeed Śiva," one should again contemplate the self as divided into two by way of the relationship between the worshiper and the worshipped. This is the purification of the self (*ātma-śuddhi*).

In this regard, that which has been stated in the secret Tantras is as follows: "Śiva, the great-souled one, is the master of yoga who bestows the fruit of the world; residing in the hearts of all people, he is the witness of actions and the teacher of the universe."
The yogi is to be meditated upon by living beings, yet he is devoid of the qualities of living beings;
and the living beings produced from him are like the marks of Viṣṇu [imprinted] upon his body.
Having become objects of play, their vision and action constrained within the abode,
those bound by the *āṇava* impurity always go wherever they are impelled by the will of Śiva.
By the will of Śiva, dharma and adharma result for them in pleasure and pain;
those principles (tattvas) are the objects of enjoyment, the means of enjoyment, and the places of enjoyment, [all] through the powers (śaktis).
(61) Those [elements] are imagined as gross and subtle within great enjoyment;
the gross ones have the form of sacrificial rites, while others reside in the body.
These powers of Śakra are to be known as arising from the power of action;
they are to be understood as having various forms and acting in accordance with the will of Śiva.
And that activity, having arisen from among the powers of knowledge,
is the supreme and subtle power of knowledge, which constitutes the instrumental nature of all things.
And that [power] consists of the light of knowledge; she alone is the body of Śiva, assuming forms for his play, glorious, and colored by various states of being.
Independent, he sports with delight, his consciousness being one of perpetual bliss.

O fair-faced one, for those men who meditate constantly, the Truth truly and truly becomes manifest quickly within their hearts; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, with every effort, one should always remain steadfast in meditation.
Then he shall indeed become Śiva himself, and not otherwise, O one honored by heroes;
however, if his state of being is not yet firmly established, then he should worship externally.
When that meditation, preceded by worship,
conforms to the state of meditative absorption and the mind becomes established in meditation, then one should abandon the external.

Otherwise, if one should abandon it out of delusion, his twofold protection perishes. Therefore, that external [rite] should then be performed, preceded by the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi);
for five times, the body consisting of the power of Māyā [is purified].
Having performed the complete purification, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva.
Śambhu himself has become twofold through the distinction between the worshipped and the worshipper.
Thinking thus, O beautiful one, one should constantly worship Śiva as Śiva.
With mantras, mudrās, and so forth, and with flowers, one should practice until the mind becomes serene;
once the mind is serene, however, one should abandon even the state of Kaula.
The God, who consists of self-luminosity, abides within the heart of his own accord;
O beloved, he reveals himself through love with his whole being.
Therefore, being free from conceptual construction, one should always worship Śiva. Thus [it is said].

There are many such secret statements in accordance with the Śiva doctrine; however, they have not been written here for fear of excessive length in this work. Now, the subject at hand is discussed: For the sake of accomplishing the external sacrifice (*bāhyayāga*), one should perform the purification of the site (*sthānaśuddhi*). Having performed the triple *tāla* strike and the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the *cchoṭikā* [finger-snap] using the Weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having established the enclosure (*prākāra*), one should create a protective dome (*khādhikā*) outside that with the Armor-mantra (*kavaca*). Then, displaying the Great Gesture (*mahāmudrā*) with the Power-mantra (*śakti-mantra*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should contemplate the pavilion as consisting of Power (*śaktimaya*). This is the purification of the site. And it has been said:
One should dispel obstacles with the Astra-mantra by means of three claps of the hands;
one should perform the binding of the directions with snapping fingers and the construction of a rampart with the Astra-mantra.

Then, having covered the outer and inner spaces with the armor, one should thereafter form the Śakti-mudrā and contemplate [the self] as consisting of the flood of power (śaktiprāta). Thus it is said.
At this juncture, one should place the *vajra* and other weapons in the cardinal directions; so it is said in some [texts].
And it has been stated:
"Facing north and being pure, one should brandish the weapon."
One should diligently expel the obstacles with three claps of the hands;
one should threaten them with the index finger and then install the mantras of the spirits (bhūta).
The mantra-practitioner should again encircle that [deity] with the armor-mantra (kavaca).

Then, having performed the placement of the protective weapons (astra), he should place them in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the sub-directions according to the scripture.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, and likewise the goad;
the gāyatrī, the trident, the discus, and the lotus—these are [to be visualized] in their respective order.
Beginning from the eastern direction and extending as far as the domain of Īśāna,
one should place the lower wheel in the cardinal directions according to the scripture and in the intermediate directions as well.
Furthermore, one should worship the weapons with perfumes, flowers, and incense.
Then, having recollected Śakti, who consists of subtle nectar,
who pervades above and below, immeasurable and incomparable— thus [it is said].
Then, one should collect the materials that constitute the components of worship. These have been described as follows:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the collection of the components of worship:
water for the feet, water for sipping, the *arghya* offering, fragrance, flowers, and incense."
Then, having offered a lamp and the oblation, the eightfold [worship] is proclaimed;
one should worship the Supreme Lord endowed with these eight limbs.
Worship is said to end with the lamp, the fire oblation (homa) with the concluding rite, and the propitiatory rite (śāntika) with the offering of food (bali);
thus, worship is declared to be of three kinds.
Uśīra combined with sandalwood, along with dūrvā grass and white mustard seeds—
this fourfold substance is declared in the scripture as the material for the water for washing the feet (pādya).
Murā is the fruit of worship and other rites involving cardamom, cloves, and camphor.
Now listen to the six-limbed sipping of water (ācamana) and the substance for the arghya offering.
Arghya mixed with sesame and rice is said to be eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga).
In some cases, it is stated that flowers may be used in place of rice. And it has been said:
"Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, rice grains, jasmine (*sumanas*), sesame seeds, along with barley and white mustard—this is declared to be the eight-limbed *arghya*."
In some cases, it should be made filled with water alone; as it has been said:
"One should diligently have it constructed with eight components, or in their absence, filled with water."
The fragrant substances have thus been described; now listen indeed to the flowers:
those that are white, red, and black here are the sattvic and other types.
One should specify yellow-colored flowers as being of the *miśraka* (mixed) variety;
one should discard all others except for the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), which is of the *tāmasa* (dark) type.
The *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, and white *arka* are beneficial when used in the morning.
Karavīra, padma, and droṇapuṣpa are beneficial when offered at midday; mallikā and kṛṣṇadhurdhūra are beneficial in the evening, as is campaka.
Kadamba, kanaka, jātī, and cikarṇī in half-tātra;
and one droṇa each of white lotus, jātī, and bahukarṇikā.
The *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, *mandāra*, *śatapatrikā*, *śvetārka*, *mālatī*, *bilva*, *punnāga*, and likewise the *kurava*.
One should designate flowers such as these as *sāttvika*;
likewise, the red lotus (*raktotpala*), the *āpadma*, the *kuraṇṭaka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*,
the *palāśa*, the *pāṭala*, and so forth, one should designate as *rājasa*.
One should designate as mixed yellow flowers the karṇikāra, dhurdhūra, campaka, āragvadha,
and others of this kind.
Karañja, vakula, śāka, śirīṣa, and likewise ketakī;
phālgunī, pomegranate (dāḍima), and śrīparṇī, as well as vibhītaka; bandhūka, kunda, uddhā, cotton (kārpāsa), and the fruit of the nimba tree.
One should avoid the *kiṃśuka*, the *madantī*, and the *kumuda* flowers;
one should also avoid those that are over-ripe, unripe, or still in bud.

One should discard flowers that are infested with hair or insects, those pierced by thorns, those already strung on a thread, those that have fallen of their own accord, and those that are otherwise defiled.
Śamī, bilva, apāmārga, kuśa, dūrvā, sahā, as well as nāha, nandī, rudraparṇī, damanā, and likewise maruva;
dhātrī, bhadrī, mahābhadrī, and likewise droṇabhadra.
Among all species of leaves, the bilva leaf is praised as the best;
among all varieties of flowers, the bilva flower is declared to be supreme.
Thus the flowers have been described; now hear concerning incenses.
p.
66) There should be one part of *agaru* and two parts of resin (*niryāsa*);
*candana* is said to be three parts, mixed with a small amount of camphor.
It is prescribed that for one named Śrītāridhūla,
guggulu mixed with ghee and combined with bilva and bāhu should be praised.
One should burn kuṣṭha or sandalwood mixed with ghee as incense;
likewise, camphor should be lit as a wick-candle using cow’s ghee or oil.
The ritual for the axe-shaped vessel (paraśvālā) shall be performed with a length of four finger-breadths and so forth.
For the Blessed One, the God of gods, Sadāśiva, is indeed fond of lamps.
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"The lamp should be made with the ghee of a tawny cow, or with red or white [ghee]."
She obtained that benefit through clarified butter from a goat, or even through pure oil;
among these, ghee from a tawny cow (kapilā) is the best, while ghee produced from other animals is middling.
Now, from the goat-born [cow], there is clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and likewise pure oil;
these become *sāttvika* and *rājasa* respectively, in due order.
One should cause a camphor wick lamp to be offered, which bestows all accomplishments;
the best has a flame of four finger-breadths, while the middling is of two finger-breadths.
The lowest lamp is said to have a flame of two finger-breadths; one should avoid offering a lamp to Śiva with oils produced from the seeds of trees. Thus it is taught.
As it is stated elsewhere:
"Sandalwood, resin, kunduruṣka,
saffron, *megha*, black iron, and camphor, in this sequence."
The sky [should be drawn] up to the third part from the wing, slightly mixed with camphor.
This is known as the supreme incense, saturated with honey.

Uśīra combined with sandalwood, joined with honey and drenched in honey—its portion is said to be as previously described; this is called the middling incense. Guggulu mixed with clarified butter is declared to be the inferior incense.
Taking up an incense burner filled with glowing embers and provided with a bell in the left hand,
the wise practitioner should blow the bell while burning incense.
By the sound of which all obstacles depart to the ten directions,
as do all diseases, evil planetary influences, and all Vināyakas.

Bad dreams, malevolent *rākṣasas*, terrifying *vetālas*, and auspicious jackals (*śivās*); *sākinīs*, hosts of ascetics, and serpents such as Kārkoṭaka and others; some desiring offerings, some desiring to kill, and others desiring sexual pleasure.
"Upon hearing the sound of the bell, they become deprived of their power; therefore, one should always ring it with every effort at the time of worship. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"By the sound of the bell, the terrifying Dānavas depart, and the gods together with Śiva arrive, well-pleased. Thus it is said.
Having thus collected everything according to availability and preference,
water scented with perfumes and consecrated by the Astra-mantra should be placed in the *badhanyā*.
Having thus prepared the collection of substances, one should then sprinkle each of them individually with that [water].

Thus, having then consecrated two *vardhanīs* for the purpose of the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), one should prepare the vessel for the special offering (*viśeṣārghya*) according to the tradition. And it is said:
"The water for the feet, the water for sipping, the offering (*arghya*), and the water for rinsing the mouth (*tīrodha*) [should be arranged] in due order. (p. 68)
Then, according to worldly custom, one should offer [the funeral cake] for that body.
That is to say:
one should offer the vessel for increasing the water, as well as water for the feet and water for sipping;
and once the deity is established, one should present the arghya offering directly before him.
The rite beginning with the invocation and ending with the obstruction is employed, as well as the obstruction and the ablution.
From that [Viṣṇu-tattva] comes the Visarjanīya-tattva; the Arghya consists of four arms.
The Pādya extends up to the Īśvara-tattva; that called Ācamana includes the Sadāśiva-tattva.
The Śivārghya extends up to the Śiva-tattva; that called Rodha pertains to the sphere of Śakti.
Having recited the mantra, one should offer that vessel; its characteristics are now described:
the *vardhanī* should be twelve finger-breadths in height and provided with a pedestal.
The immovable [vessel] is joined at the neck and not provided with a lid;
the vessel should be known as eight finger-breadths wide, or even as much as fills the palm.
One should take five palas of copper and gold-tāla according to one's preference;
then, a vessel made of earth or a leaf-cup should be taken somewhere for this purpose. Thus it is said in the Āgama:
"The gold should likewise be known [to be placed] in a *bhṛṅga* or a vessel that holds the measure of a handful (*pāṇipūraka*)."
The Śivārghya vessel is marked with a lotus; this vow is devoid of the vital breath (prāṇa).
A real horn, a mother-of-pearl shell, a horn [of another animal], or leaves such as those of the *palāśa* or lotus—
these may serve as substitutes for cow-products even in the absence of horns and the like.
For the sake of prosperity, [the circles] are established by revolving with a diameter of six and a half finger-breadths.
When the ground is prepared, then no other [measurement] should be accepted until the final worship. And it is said (p.
On this ground, the daily rite is desired to be performed with that which is pleasing and appropriate;

for that which is employed on the eleventh day becomes *nirmālya* (remains of an offering). Thus, in some places it is said that one should not offer *viśeṣārghya*, water, *pādya*, or *ācamanīya*. Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*:
At the end of the *nirodha*, during the emission (*visarga*), the word "rodha" (obstruction) is employed.

Having become Śiva, one should offer the *bhūta-tarpaṇa* (libation to the elements), ending with the *bhūga* [mantra], and the *pādya* and *ācamanīya* [waters] at the end of the *prajā*. Now, the sequence: having prepared the *arghya* vessels according to one's capacity, having washed them with the *astra-mantra*, purified them by means of *nirīkṣaṇa* and other rites, and protected them with the *kavaca-mantra*, one should fill them with substances such as water in the form of nectar flowing from the *bindu*-location using the *śakti-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and consecrate them with the *brahmāṅgas* or the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) mantra.

Alternatively, having worshipped the *vāsana* here with the *aṣṭapuṣpikā*, consecrated it with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*), protected it with the *astra* and *kavaca* mantras, displayed the *dhenumudrā* and *mahāmudrā* with the *śakti-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having sprinkled oneself on the head three times with that water using the *śakti-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should thus worship the *nirodhārghya*.
And it is said:
"A vessel made of gold or one of the other [precious materials], placed upon the sacrificial base—
having then taken that vessel for the *arghya* offering, one should wash it with the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*."
Afterwards, he should enclose both the exterior and interior with the armor-mantra;
then, taking recourse in the station of the *bindu*, he should contemplate a lotus in the center.
One should place the three principles (tattvas) therein, and then again place the Śakti;
having filled it with the five Brahmans, the limbs of Śiva, and Śiva himself.
That water, combined with perfumes and flowers, is consecrated by mantra.
"In the places that are to be visualized, one should heat [the fire] drop by drop. Thus it is said.
Now follows the purification of substances.

Then, having gazed at the collection of substances with the root-mantra placed on the tips of the thumb and ring finger, one should strike them with the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having removed [impurities], sprinkle them again with the *kavaca* for nourishment. Then, looking upon them with an eye that perceives the abode of Śiva, one should consecrate this mass of splendor either with the *hṛdaya* or with the five limbs (*aṅga*). Alternatively, one should consecrate the perfume with the *sadyojāta*, the cloth with the *vāmadeva*, the ornament with the *aghora*, the food offering (*naivedya*) with the *tatpuruṣa*, the flower with the *īśāna*, and other items with the *gāyatrī*; then protect them with the *astra*, conceal them with the *kavaca*, and make them nectarine with the *dhenumudrā* using the *śakti* mantra, dedicating them solely for the sake of Śiva. Furthermore, those consecrated with the *hṛdaya* for others should be placed separately in another vessel. And it has been said:
One should sprinkle the horse that has been released with this armor using *kuśa* grass;
one should touch each of the aforementioned collection of substances as they are produced.
One should touch the unguent with the heart-mantra, or with the purificatory limbs, or with those [limbs] which are its own nature; and one should touch the garment with the left hand.
One should offer ornaments with the *rūpin* mantra, the food offering (*naivedya*) with the *puruṣa* mantra,
flowers with the *īśāna* mantra, and perform the final application (*ālabheta*) with the *gāyatrī*.
"Everything is protected by armor and weapons, and is preceded by the dhenu-mudrā. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
One who is inauspicious should never perform auspicious rites;
one should offer to Śiva only that substance which has been presided over by Śiva.
O son of Muktikā, it must be performed separately for the others.

O Śivā, that which has not been sprinkled with water should not be offered, nor indeed should anything be given without being designated. One should cause a drop to fall into every one of the satisfaction-vessels (*toṣakumbha*).
Again, the mantra is uttered with water and flowers;
thus, by means of the mantra, there is no separate collection of substances [required].
One should worship with flowers, incense, and so forth, and seal [the offering] with the mudrā called Amṛta.

Thus says the Teacher. Now, having sprinkled the vessels for the incense, lamps, and nightly offerings with the Astra mantra and worshipped them with the Hṛdaya mantra, one should sprinkle and worship them with the Ghaṇṭā mantra.
Next, the procedure for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is written here.
In a lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*koṣṭha*) consisting of the essential reality (*tattva*), adorned with five colors,
one should worship [the bell] and, having sprinkled it with water from a bell and cloth, perform the worship. Now, the procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is written here.
In a sacrificial pit consisting of the five principles and adorned with five colors,
one should prepare it with rice or kusha grass according to one's capacity.

One should place Śiva, Sadāśiva, Vidyā, the principle of the individual soul (puruṣatattva), and that which is designated as Time (kāla) in sequence upon the middle and the sections starting from the east and ending with the others;
likewise, one should place Su-pratiṣṭha, Su-śānta, Tejas, or similarly that which is born of jewels.
One should also join "immortality" (amṛta) as the fifth; thus, one should employ five vessels for the treasures.
Into these, one should place milk, curd, clarified butter, urine, and cow dung.
For the sake of conquering the five elements, one should consecrate the *pañcagavya*, which consists of those [elements],
with [mantras] dedicated to Īśa and the others, numbering according to their respective qualities in sequence.

If he is a householder or a celibate student, [he should prepare] water with cow dung and so forth from goats and other animals; having placed it in a vessel dedicated to Śakti in the northeast and adorned with kuśa and dūrvā grass,
he should consecrate it six times with the Gāyatrī mantra while adding fragrant substances.
Cast cow dung into cow urine; that water, combined with ghee, should be placed into curd;
and place that curd into milk.
Then, one should pour kuśa-water there with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and the *gāyatrī*. One should recite [the mantras] once with the *brahmadaṇḍi*, the *śivāṅga*, and the *gāyatrī*.
This is declared to be the *pañcagavya*; now listen to the *brahmakūrca*.
A cow that has recently calved, one afflicted by disease,
one whose calf has died, those that eat impure fodder, and a pregnant cow should be abandoned.
The cow dung is from a black cow, the urine from a blue one, the ghee from a tawny one, and the curd from a white cow;
having collected the milk with great care, these are to be known [as the ingredients].
Cow dung situated in the sky (the vessel) should be taken, measuring half the size of a thumb;
cow urine should be one *pala* in measure, likewise strained through a cloth and boiled.
Two palas of this [curd] should be taken, and three palas for the curd itself;
milk free from the calf’s saliva is considered to be five palas.
One *pala* of water with *kuśa* grass should be consecrated according to the previously mentioned procedure;
having placed it together in one vessel as before, one should recite the root mantra over it one hundred times.
p.

73) One should daily bathe the deity with the limbs of Brahmā, with a tenth part thereof, and likewise with the Gāyatrī mantra, as well as with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the nectars (amṛta), and so forth.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight and other such occasions, one should bathe [the deity] with the *śivakūrca* during the night after having worshipped the Lord of Gods; by that, a human being transcends that [cycle of] existence within the *bimba*.
The wise man is never defiled by even great secret sins;
rather, [the rite] should sometimes be performed with the heart alone. And it is said:
"Cow dung, urine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and water infused with *kuśa* grass..."
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are obtained through the heart-mantra by means of the qualities of the great elements.
Now, the ritual procedure for the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) is also written down.
Having prepared sugar, honey, clarified butter, curd, milk, and water infused with *kuśa* grass using goats and other animals as before, one should bathe [the image] with each of these individually.
Likewise, by whom can the path be filled with offerings of water (arghya) and incense? Those [vessels] for the head-measurements are two *prasthas* in capacity;
they should be filled up to the brim, starting from the smallest size.
Every day it should be bathed with ten [vessels], and on every festival day (parvan) with a hundred;
having established it in seven ways, one should arrange the positions for Brahmā and his limbs.
Now, the purification of the materials:

Then, having performed the self-worship (ātmapūjā)—consisting of the seat, the form, and the insignia—and having offered the *arghya* on the head with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should recite the root mantra ten times, offer it, and contemplate, "I am Śiva. With the body straight and the hands joined in the *mukula* gesture, [one should place] the two *siddhas*...

Having uttered the root mantra—beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, extending from the *brahmarandhra* to the *dvādaśānta* and the *śaktyanta*, and comprising the short, long, and protracted vowels—one should then utter the other limbs of Brahman (*brahmāṅga*) along with the *siddhandas*. This is the purification of the mantra (*mantraśuddhi*). And it is said:
"Having thus resolved upon the worship of the self with substances that have been purified in this manner, one should maintain silence and perform the purification of the mantra."
One should slowly recite the mantra upward through the sequence beginning with the three measures (trimātra),
until the state of culmination is reached; being devoted to that measure,
the purification of the mantra occurs thus, by taking refuge in the pure reality.
Thus say the teachers. And so says the Āgama:
"One should purify by reciting the mantra consisting of the *bindu* and *nāda* at the tip of the crest;
this mantra, which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), is always presided over by Śiva."
The remaining mantras, which possess the bindu, accomplish all things and grant desires.

If it is argued: "Since it is stated that 'mantras are by nature pure and possess the power to grant boons,' these mantras are pure by their very essence; therefore, even for those that are already pure, if purification were performed again, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress," we reply: True. However, they possess impurity in the form of *avidyā* (ignorance) which causes [the obscuration of] sovereignty and other powers. Consequently, for those whose powers are concealed, the manifestation of that capacity through contact with the power of the *vanā* (the forest/assembly of deities) is indeed established as purification. And it has been said: "Mantras consist of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), yet they are possessed of the impurity of [obscured] sovereignty."
"By their power, they possess ignited capacity; they are all bestowers of desired objects.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara* (p. 75):

O Guha, the wise one who is skilled in mantras has proclaimed the origin of the impurities and powers of mantras, which arise from the end of the mind through the purification of mantras by means of mantras.
The awakening power of those [mantras] resides within the mind of one who possesses the knowledge of Śiva;
thus, the purification of mantras has been succinctly proclaimed.
An interruption must be made at this juncture; it is appropriate to do so immediately after the purification of the mantra.
Having gone to the bathing hall with his companions,
he should place upon the bathing altar a previously prepared, auspicious seat made of copper.
Alternatively, that which is two cubits in length, measured by the hand, with its upper part twice as wide,
half of that height, beautiful, and provided with a girdle and cow-mouths (corners), [is the sacrificial altar].
When a mobile or immobile *liṅga* has been installed there,
having sprinkled it with water while reciting the *pūjā-mantra* and the *gāyatrī*, one should worship it with flowers.
Having visualized the pervasive [deity] as a mass of light, one should offer the general arghya water to Śiva, who is contained within it,
according to the distinction between emanation and reabsorption.
Having worshipped the five Brahmans in the same manner upon the five excellent heads,
one should thereafter place the flower from the *nirmālya* upon the head.
One should never leave the head of the Liṅga empty of flowers.
Whatever remains as floral offering (nirmālya) inside the inner sanctum should again be placed outside.
One should offer flowers and other items to Caṇḍeśa in the northeast, beginning with the heart-mantra;
one should sprinkle the excellent cloth, such as the turban and eye-cloth, with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra.
It is declared that this [cloth] becomes pure through contact with the rays of the sun and wind.
One should carefully cleanse whatever remains, free from perfumes and ointments;
golden and silver ornaments should be washed with warm water.
One should rub vessels made of precious materials and the like that have been smeared with oil using cow dung;
bell-metal is purified by ash, and [vessels] made of those two [gold and silver] are purified by both [ash and water].

Conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and the like are purified by water, while vessels made of wood or bamboo are cleansed with husks and curd; therefore, the purification of vessels appropriate for the occasion must be performed at every moment.
With water consecrated by mantras over weapons, one should perform the smearing of fragrance to remove [impurities], and likewise,
for the purpose of dispelling obstacles, one should smear the base of the linga while seated.
Having attained [the state], one should subsequently sprinkle [it]; then the mantras will attain their presence. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in some cases, one should wash the pedestal with the Śivāstra-mantra and the Pāśupatāstra-mantra.
And it has been said:
"At the conclusion of the daily worship, and in the midst of the assembly of mantras for Śiva..."
At that very moment, the form became tranquil within that linga and upon that pedestal.
They obstruct both worldly enjoyment and liberation; therefore, one should expel them first.
Having bathed them again with the Śivāstra-mantra at the liṅga and with the Pāśupata-mantra at the pedestal, one should bathe them with the waters of the Heart-mantra.
"Then that embrace shall be pure, and furthermore, the mantras will bestow their fruits. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the Sarvajñānottara it is said:
"Having washed the *liṅga* with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), which is proclaimed as the Śiva-weapon,
those obstacles that take the form of Rudras are thereby driven away."
Afterwards, one should wash the pedestal with water from the *vardhanī* vessel,
using the *pāśupata* weapon-mantra. [The goddesses] who have arrived assuming the form of Umā [should be addressed].
Having thus duly performed the expulsion of obstacles, the wise one should then perform the worship of Śiva, the Supreme Self. Thus it is said.
Then, one should perform the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* with the mantra "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva and Śivā, to Śiva and Śakti," or else by means of the *liṅgamudrā*.
At the time of bathing the *liṅga*, one should display the *liṅgamudrā*.
Having performed the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, one should install the collection of mantras.

In this manner, one should perform the appropriate purification—by means of bathing, sprinkling, and so forth—for fixed lingas, movable images, clay models, sacrificial altars, mandalas, and the like, using the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. Thus ends the purification of the linga.
Thus, when these five purifications are present, the worship of Śiva becomes fruitful. And it has been said:
"When this pentad consisting of the self, the locus, the substance, the mantra, and the liṅga is purified, the worship of the Śaivas occurs; otherwise, it does not."

Now, if the *liṅga* is mobile (*cala*), it is impossible to perform the bathing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth in the prescribed sequence, starting from the mounting of the vehicle. If the bathing with *pañcagavya* and other rites were performed [directly], there would be the undesirable consequence of a mixture of sacred remains (*nirmālya-saṅkara*). Therefore, for the purpose of performing the elaborate bathing with *pañcagavya* and so on, immediately after the purification of the *liṅga*, one should worship Śiva—who is now established upon a pure seat as a mobile throne—along with his limbs (the deities of the seats). Having gratified him with offerings (*arghya*), incense (*dhūpa*), and other articles, one should bathe him with the five products of the cow, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and so forth, preceded by an oil massage (*tailābhyaṅga*) according to the procedure to be described hereafter, while reciting the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

Having placed a flower with pure water and wiped it with a clean cloth, one should place a seat upon a pedestal set on the altar and covered with a silk cloth; having arranged a seat of flowers, one should worship that firm seat. As it has been said: "The pedestal should be two cubits in length, one cubit in width, and twelve finger-breadths in height, or even one cubit, and it should be firm."
"Adorned with various colors and decorated with a lotus in the center. Thus it is said.

Now, if it is a fixed liṅga (sthiraliṅga), immediately after the purification of the liṅga (liṅgaśuddhi), one should worship the fixed seat (sthirāsana). Therein, first, in the northwest: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Gaṇapati*. *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Gaṇapati*. *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati*. Having consecrated [the deity] with the rites of invocation (āvāhana) and so forth as before—

Having meditated upon the dark-complexioned, pot-bellied, and stout elephant-faced one, seated and holding a rosary, an axe, his own tusk, and a water-pot in his left and right hands, and having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings up until the recitation of mantras, one should pray: "O Gaṇeśāna, be gracious and grant freedom from obstacles for the sake of Śiva's work."

Then, having performed the worship from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the recitation (*japa*), ending with: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of the Guru; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of the Guru; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva and the others*, one should pray: "O Lord, grant me permission so that I may worship Śiva according to the path taught by you. Thus, in the *Bṛhatkālottara*:

"Oṃ, salutation to the Gurus beginning with Sadāśiva, to the Gurus, and thereafter [to the rest]. Having thus obtained permission from the feet of the Guru, one should worship the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*).
Likewise, it is stated in the Āgama:
"Oṃ! There, the Kūrma-śilā (Tortoise-stone) consisting of the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti) should be installed;
it is as pure as a moonbeam, gentle, four-faced, and four-armed."
Born from the midst of the Ocean of Milk, conceived through the heart-mantra (hṛdayāṇu),
the Śakti— whose form is the support— appears in some places like the shape of a seed and its sprout.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti. Some say:
"One should install that Śakti, who is the form of the support for all, by means of the root mantra.
[Then one installs] Ananta, resembling blue in color and adorned with a thousand hoods.
With hands joined at the heart in *añjali*, having one face and four arms,
he was born from the Ocean of Milk, possessing the appearance of a lotus.
One should place the mantra of the heart, which constitutes the seat, upon the foundation of jewels.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ananta. With this, one should worship the pervasive Śuddhasiddhānta. Then, one should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya, in their respective order, as white, red, yellow, and black, located in the corners starting from the southeast (Agni).
Having worshipped [the deity] with the Heart-mantra (hṛdaya) upon the Brahmapīṭha, one should worship the sandals in the form of lions:

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jñāna; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vairāgya; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Aiśvarya. Thus, with the intellect, one should worship those whose nature consists of the principles (tattvas) from Puruṣa down to Anādi Māyā, as they pervade these principles.
Likewise, one should worship Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya.
"Anaiśvarya" is thus declared; with the heart-mantra, there is a tetrad of Gāyatrīs.
One should worship Dharma and the others, mixed with their respective colors, above the lion by means of the heart-mantra:
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Adharma. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ajñāna. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Avairāgya. (p. 80)

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Anaiśvarya. Thus, one should worship the forms of the principles (tattvas) beginning with disease and ending with Time, such as Gāyatrī and the others. Then, having placed the upper lid, [one should visualize] a lotus with a pericarp, complete with filaments, accompanied by the Heart-mantra and endowed with the wheel of powers (śakticakra).
The powers beginning with Vāmā are white, four-faced, and four-armed;
their hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and their lotus-like hands are joined to Śiva.

Indeed, Śaṅkara is fanned with white whisks and lotuses. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lower covering; in the southwest (Nirṛti). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the upper covering; in the northeast (Īśāna). In this manner, one should worship the two coverings consisting of Māyā and Mahāmāyā, which resemble the color of blood. In some traditions, the lower covering consists of Māyā and the upper covering consists of Śuddhavidyā; in their center is a lotus bud composed of Ananta, which has blossomed. Here, the lineage of the Guru (*gurukrama*) should not be omitted. The procedure is now stated:

Saying "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lotus," one should worship the white lotus, which consists of pure knowledge (*vidyā*) and is endowed with eight petals belonging to the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*). Then, saying "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lotus-mudrā," one should display the lotus-mudrā. Saying "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the pericarp (*karṇikā*)," one should worship in its center the yellow-colored [lotus] which contains the fifty seed-syllables (*bīja*), or the seed-syllables of the nine-fold self (*navātmā*), and which is surrounded by the sixty-four powers of the filaments (*kesara*). And it has been said: "The syllable of Brahmā is at its center; the power (*śakti*) is the form of the support of the universe."
That is the Śiva-power of action (kriyā-śakti), which is the cause of the agitation of the universe.
As long as it constantly manifests among sentient beings and all entities.
That power, which exists within all seeds as the source of the sprout,
has emerged from the ocean of milk, pervading the entire cosmic egg.
Again, having burst through the aperture, it remains like a sprout from a bulb;
starting from the state of water, it has emerged as far as the cow's horn.
Reliability (aptatva) should be known as the sprinkler; fire is the cause of elevation;
the wind is the impeller for its growth; and space is conceived as the support.
The subtle elements (tanmātras) are like sprouts; the sense organs are hollow.
The ego (ahaṃkāra), situated between sattva and rajas, is endowed with vitality (ojas) and is the cause of accomplishment.
One should place this [deity] upon the Brahma-altar on the Ratnādhāra with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).

Regarding the instruction "one should place this upon the Brahma-altar" (*brahmavedī*): having meditated upon the Tortoise-stone (*kūrmaśilā*) as situated on the Brahma-altar, one should place it there in the form of *Śakti*. Subsequently, upon the Jewel-support (*ratnādhāra*) of the Brahma-altar, one should place Ananta in the form of a lotus bud. This has already been stated previously here. In that regard, it is said elsewhere:

"First, having meditated upon Śakti, one should install her upon the Tortoise-stone; and [one should install] Ananta upon the [altar] called Brahma. As for the name "Ananta," because the serpent is infinitely extended, his pervasion (*vyāpti*) extends only downwards and not upwards. Subsequently, Ananta shall be the Lord of the Vidyeśvaras, presiding over the altar of the stainless Ananta.
After that, the eight petals ending with Vidyeśāna are pure, having arisen from that very same [source].
Below that is the aggregate [of elements], ending with Māyā, and the collection of seats (pīṭha-sañcaya).
The qualities of the intellect (buddhi-dharma) are considered to be knowledge, dispassion, and that which is derived from primordial matter (prākṛta).
Sovereignty, virility, and the principles— these are considered the duties of the ages (yugas). Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the respective causes, which are a collection of qualities (guṇas).

From *dharma* comes existence, from the mind comes purity, and through knowledge, passion is overcome; detachment arises from these three, while from the *tāmasa* [aspect] of sovereignty, pride of mind is born;
it is said that everything is afflicted by this mental pride.
That which is to be abandoned is the lower reality; that which is known is said to be knowledge.
Having ascertained through his intellect that the reality of Dharma is to be accepted, the king of yogis [proceeded].
It accepts everything; thus it is called "dharma" in the sense of that which upholds. Having understood all worldly bondage to be a support arising from mental enjoyment, [one should abandon it].
Having attained detachment therein, one reaches the state of puruṣatva.
Considering the host of qualities beginning with *aṇimā*— the sovereignty belonging to the *tamas* aspect of the person—
