to be something that must be abandoned, and having utterly renounced it, one looks upward once again.

Attachment, limited knowledge (*vidyā*), limited capacity (*kalā*), time (*kāla*), and the self-principle (*ātmatattva*) are the bonds. Attachment is characterized by its own nature as being colored; through *vidyā*, it consists of false cognition.
Though skilled in the arts, one who is deluded and lacking in dispassion is overcome by time; for those who are not yogis, there is the misery of the face [of death] and a lack of sovereignty.
Having thus reflected, he then gazes further beyond the principle of Māyā— the seed of the universe which is essentially Śiva—
perceiving that the entire world, consisting of both the gross and the subtle, remains contained within it.
By means of the fear of great obstacles, it bestows the true path and illuminates the knowledge of Śiva;
furthermore, the principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā-tattva) grants liberation even to yogins.
The supreme abode of all sovereignty, possessing infinite and boundless enjoyment.
This very path, ending in reality, is the seat of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin),
where the vital breaths, known as the digits of knowledge (jñānakalā), are united.
Liberated through the state of the light of absolute isolation (kaivalya), they remain like those who are deluded.
The great village is the interior of the altar, the place of liberation;
furthermore, it is described as being like a machine for them.
Those known as Dharma, resembling lions, are the sustainers of Śambhu’s throne.
The corners beginning with the southeast are white, red, yellow, and white in radiance.
Deceived by illusion, they are auspicious and affectionate, looking at one another with mutual nourishment; extending as far as the Brahmāṇḍa and up to the end of the Māyā-tattva,
their limbs are adorned with various colors and qualities such as dharma and the rest.
The two coverings above and below are considered to be the two Māyās, resembling gold.
The seat of Śuddhavidyā is a lotus endowed with eight petals, consisting of Vidyeśā;
its expansion, the pedestal (piṇḍikā), is auspicious and resembles the autumnal moon.
The eightfold groups of eight filaments are known as the powers (śaktis) beginning with Vāmā, situated [therein].
In the center is the power Manonmanī, whose pericarp has the luster of gold;
it is joined with either fifty seed-syllables or nine seed-syllables.
In the center of that, O Lord, is situated the Liṅga consisting of the Śiva-tattva;
there one should place the subtle form which has the nature of the Īśa-tattva.
Having meditated upon Tattva as Sadāśiva, Śākta, Daindava, and that which consists of Kalās, and having meditated upon Vidyā as the embodied self, one should deposit the supreme Niṣkala.
In some places, the upper covering consists of the principle of *vidyā* (knowledge), while the portion below it consists of *māyā*. Thus it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should conceive of the altar of Brahma (*brahmavedi*) as beginning with earth and ending with *go* (the cow).
Upon that altar, one should place the feet, beginning with *dharma*, supported by the [principle of] *dhārakā*."

The four stages beginning with intellect (buddhi) and ending with the person (puruṣa), as well as the four courses of life (caraṇa), are bound together by the qualities (guṇas) which operate in mutual dependence.
The four limbs, however, are the obscurations such as passion and the rest.
Then, upon the upper covering, one should further fashion the Māyā and Vidyā [tattvas]. Having pierced the *liṅga* in its center, the oblation should be offered as far as the end of Śiva.
The light-ray of purity spoke with a radiance equal to ten million suns.
The support of all the gods, which bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation,
is its white lotus-form; it is beautiful with a lovely pericarp,
charming with its eight petals extending to the lovely filaments.
"The linga should always be conceived in this manner; one should establish Śiva within it. Thus [it is said].

On the tips of the eight petals of each of the eight groups [of lotuses], [one should worship]: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Raudrī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikariṇī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balavikariṇī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balapramathinī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamanī. Thus, from the east to the northeast, beginning with the medicinal herbs (p. 85).

Having worshipped the forms (*mūrtis*) and powers (*śaktis*) seated upon the lotus—two-armed and with palms joined in *añjali* facing Śiva—one should worship in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) with: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Manonmanī. Then, with "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Namaskārā," one should display the gesture of salutation (*namaskāra-mudrā*). And it is said:
"The powers beginning with Vāmā are considered to belong to the forms and their lords, beginning with Kṣa."
By the word "vāma," beauty endowed with five qualities is expressed.
Due to its possession of complete qualities, it is superior to water and the other elements;
whereas water and the others possess four, three, two, and one quality respectively, they are incomplete.

Here, Vāmā is the principle of earth (pṛthivī-tattva), whose nature consists of the elements and their manifestations; by her, emanation proceeds. She is Vāmā, and Śarva is the one who presides over the form of the earth.
That very Vāmadeva, or his Śakti, is celebrated as Meti;
there resides Jyeṣṭhā, whose form consists of water and who conforms to the nature of the waters.
Existence (*bhava*) is his eldest lord; from being the eldest, his power is declared to be Jyeṣṭhā.
Because he possesses the form of Rudra through his non-mastery (*anaiśa*), his lord is Raudrī, who is fiery (*āgneyī*). He is indeed Paśupati, that Rudra, and Raudrī is recognized as his power.
Because she is a fractional form (*kalā*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the power of desire (*kāma-śakti*) is of the nature of wind;
Īśāna, whose form is wind, is celebrated as "possessing all parts" (*sakala*).
The power that has been limited (*kālitā*) is space (*ākāśa*), which undergoes transformation over time.
Since time consists of parts, its modification is likewise [possible];
however, because space lacks parts, its manifestation is a modification of the unmanifest.
By that which is devoid of [the aforementioned], it is known as the portion of the arts (kalābhāga).
The Lord Bhīmogaganamūrtīśa is impelled by Kalavikaraṇā;
the Śakti is Kalavikaraṇā, lunar in nature, and preceded by Bala.
And here, Karaṇī is indeed the specific instrument of power;
having provoked Mahādeva, he, the Lord,
became Balavikaraṇa, whose nature is preceded by power.
The power consisting of the sun of action is that which, by means of the crushing of strength, [acts].
Because the sun possesses fierce rays, Rudra is remembered as having the form of the sun;
he is indeed the Lord who subdues strength with his noose.

She is the subduer of strength and the tamer of all beings; she is the manifestation of the arising of the experience of one's own flood of merit and demerit. Indeed, the Self is all beings, and it is remembered as the sacrificer.
Ugra is the lord of that form, and his mind is the joy of all beings;
she is proclaimed as his very power (śakti), the subduer of all beings.
Since the Śaiva power Manonmanī leads the bound soul (paśu), together with his mind,
to the supreme state that effects dissolution and brings about the unity of the individual souls (aṇu) with Śiva.
She is to be known as Manonmanī; the Supreme Śiva resides within her.
"These powers, beginning with Vāmā, have one face and two arms;
they should be meditated upon with palms joined behind the back, as well as those facing Śiva. Thus it is said.
According to some opinions, having meditated upon them in the manner previously described,
they are to be visualized as possessing the luster of the rising sun, with three eyes and beautiful earrings.
"In some traditions, they are adorned with a crown of matted hair and the crescent moon;
all of them are said to be of ten different colors and decorated with crowns and other ornaments. (p. 87)

Then, having placed the *vidyā-tattva* ending with *māyā* upon the two portions of Brahmā and Viṣṇu in the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should place [the *śiva-tattva*] ending with the *śiva-tattva* upon the portion for the image (*arcā-bhāga*). And it is said:
"The wise man should arrange the *ātma-tantra* ending with *māyā* in the portion of Brahmā;
he should place the *vidyā-tattva* ending with *vidyā* in the portion of Viṣṇu."
"One should worship that which is called the Śiva-tattva, ending with Śakti, situated in the portion of the image. Thus [it is said].
Likewise: "The seed, the sprout, and the infinite, as well as the dharmas and so forth in their proper order"—
thus one should worship the reality of the self (ātmatattva) below the seat in the place of Brahmā.
One should place the five *karṇikās* in the vessel upon the filaments starting from the left;
on the surface of the *Manonmanī-pīṭha*, within the range ending at the *Vidyā-tattva*,
the human [path] begins from *Ādhāra-śakti* and extends up to *Manonmanī*.
"Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, [the sequence] from Parameṣṭhin down to Īśvara and Śakti constitutes the form known as Rudra. Thus it is said.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the solar disc together with its presiding deity. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the fiery disc together with its presiding deity. Some worship the form and the fourth disc by means of the seven *kuṭis*. Likewise: "The seven syllables of the mantras are established upon the seat of Śiva.

Therefore, because she is the cause of the origin of the seventy million mantras, Śakti possesses the nature of the seven *kuṭis*. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the lotus petals, filaments, pericarp, tips, and edges, one recites: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kriyā-śakti.

Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the pervasive power of action (*kriyāśakti*) extending upwards and downwards, and having meditated upon the seat (*pīṭha*) consisting of that power, [one recites]:
*oṃ hāṃ śivāsanāya namaḥ*. (p. 88)

Having thus worshipped the seat with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should place [the mantra] "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jñānaśakti" upon the *liṅga* and contemplate the *liṅga* as being of the nature of Jñānaśakti. And it has been said:

The seat consists of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and the throne extends up to the principle of limited knowledge (vidyā-tattva). It rests upon the two lingas whose nature is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) and which have as their sphere of operation the principle of power (śakti-tattva).
Having invoked the two forms, one should worship the supreme deity Śiva. Thus it is said in the Āgama:

"One should place the pedestal (pīṭha) and the mantras upon the pedestal; then, upon the form of the linga and the image, one should place the principles (tattva), the limbs of the principles (tattvāṅga), and the power of consciousness (cicchakti), which is considered to be action (kriyā).
Likewise, in the Pratiṣṭhāsāra:
"One should place the power of action (kriyā-śakti) upon the seat (pīṭha), and that which is called knowledge (jñāna) within the form of the linga. Thus it is said.

[Objection: But surely the placement (*nyāsa*) of all mantras has already been performed at the very time of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). Why is it done again every day? [Reply: True. However, at that time [the placement was] elsewhere; for the sake of propitiation, the worship of the mantra itself must be performed daily. For some [mantras] may become averse. And it is said: "The worship of mantras must be performed daily for the sake of their presence; otherwise, they do not grant success and instead create obstacles."
"O Guha, if worship performed over many days is neglected, then the mantras turn their faces away and return to their own abode. Thus it is said.

Placing the *añjali* at the region of the heart, one should utter "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ śivamūrtaye namaḥ" ending with the nasal bindu, and then install the subtle form (*sūkṣmamūrti*), which is the form of Īśa, consisting of the principle of *tatva*, having the face of the *kāmaliṅga*, as the cause. And it has been said: "The complete supreme light, whose nature is action and whose sphere is the object of perception..."
One should deposit the cause called the Mūrti-tattva (the principle of form), ending with the *liṅga*, [with the mantra] "O Īśvara";
this is known as the Mūrti-mantra, which is indeed born from being encapsulated by the heart [mantra].
Now— this mantra, consisting of five mantras, is the manifest form of Sadāśiva;
those learned in the scriptures declare that he is the very body of Śiva composed of mantra.

Because of this statement: *Oṃ hāṃ vidyādehāya namaḥ*. Having thus recited [the mantra] up to the power (*śakti*) of Nārada, one should then, according to the statement "the principle (*tattva*) Sadāśiva is the body beyond Īśāna up to Āśā," perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the manifest form with its limbs and proportions, pervading the end of the Śiva-principle through devotion to Sadāśiva. And it is said: "In that same way, this root of Dharma is called the Sādākhya mantra;
one should place the Sadāśiva Vidyādeha within the central form."
In the ascent of the Śiva-liṅga, one should contemplate the Lord consisting of pure knowledge,
endowed with the thirty-eight kalās, whose body is composed of the limbs of Brahmā.
The supreme [deity] has three eyes and five faces, possesses three hands, and is endowed with twelve senses (the three—vision, action, and will; and the five organs of each).
He bears ten weapons, is serene, and is adorned with all ornaments.

Now, one might object: just as for the individual self (*ātman*) there is a subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) consisting of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) which is internal, and a gross external body consisting of the five elements; so too, Śiva possesses both a subtle and a gross body. Among these, how can it be said that His internal subtle form consists of the principle of Īśvara? True. Although that form is indeed declared to consist of the principle of Īśvara, one should understand that because of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakayor abhedāt*), it is essentially composed of the *bindu* which presides over the principle of Īśvara. Thus it is said: "The Blessed Lord, who delights in His own Self, is the embodiment of compassion; therefore, He is the subtle one who bestows grace upon all."

(p. 90) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. Among these, Mahāmati, the imagined self-nature consists of the various forms of names, signs, and conceptualizations that are falsely attributed to objects by ordinary people based on their own deluded minds."

If it is thought that the intellect (*buddhi*) assumes the form of the object to be meditated upon through a restrictive rule (*niyamāt*), then for the sake of conforming to all [levels of] understanding, it assumes a gross, subtler, and most subtle body. That body is *śākta* (consisting of power). And that power is inseparable (*avinābhāvinī*), consisting of the essence of supreme bliss (*ānandaghana*). Furthermore, that [power] indeed becomes differentiated as will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*). The Lord (*bhagavān*) whose nature consists of these three powers is designated as the *bindu*. And that *bindu* exists in three ways: as the partless (*niṣkala*), the whole (*sakala*), and the whole-partless (*sakalaniṣkala*). Among these, the partless *bindu*, which consists of the power of will, is called the principle of power (*śaktitattva*). Furthermore, that which is the whole (*sakala*) consists of four parts; it is the *bindu* composed of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), residing in the principle of Īśvara at the center of the eyebrows within the vital breaths such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*. Moreover, that which consists of the power of knowledge is the whole-partless (*sakalaniṣkala*); it is the subtle form of Sadāśiva-Bhaṭṭāraka, residing nowhere [specifically]. Nevertheless, because of the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*) between these two—the whole (*sakala*) and the whole-partless (*sakalaniṣkala*)—the form consisting of the *bindu* is cited as belonging to the principle of Īśvara. And it has been said:
Because he acts for the benefit of the worlds and for the cessation of the snare of bonds, Śambhu— the all-pervading, supreme, and self-sovereign— becomes accessible through meditation.
The power of will, knowledge, and action, whose form consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest,
exists as the cause of the universe— an undivided, stable power.
The Bindu, consisting of thirty-five aspects, is said to be the principle of Śakti;
it is denoted solely by the Kalā beyond Peace (Śāntyatīta). From that [arise] the principles of Peace (Śānti) and the Moon (Aindava).
That reality is to be known by all as the Bindu located between the eyebrows;
it rests upon the seats of Iḍā and Piṅgalā, which consist of the nature of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
(91) That which is proclaimed as the third, established in the reality of Īśvara and bestowing the perfection of yoga upon yogins, is the body of Sādāśiva.
Subtle, he is adorned with five subtle digits.
In the pure [state], Sadāśiva always possesses a gross form through six or five [faces].

Everywhere, the single Bindu is thus heard to consist of the principle of Īśvara. Therefore, it should not be asked how there can be three; for that [Bindu] consists of the [three] eyes. And this has been stated in the Sarvajñānottara, following the description of the state of Sadāśiva in the Ardha-paṭala: "And likewise..."
Then above that is the lunar principle (aindava-tattva), which is stainless, facing in all directions,
supreme among all principles, and infinite in the form of light.
There resides Skanda at the bindu, pure and stainless as clear crystal,
having the form of a kadamba bud, adorned with a garland of blossoms.
The Lord is to be meditated upon in five ways: as Sakala (with parts), Niṣkala (without parts), Sakalaniṣkala (both with and without parts), Sūkṣma (subtle), and Bhinnakala (of distinct parts).
Among these, He who is joined with the Kalās beginning with Śānti is traditionally taught as Sakala.
Partless and absolute, pervading the Bindu, it is both with parts and partless.
This subtle [state], joined with Jvālinī and the others, is proclaimed as such;
it is called the Bindu, which destroys the sixteen vowels and is of a distinct nature.
Therefore, O Six-faced One, there is no division into "S" and "tha" in any of the scriptures;
nor is there ever a lotus-bodied form among the mantras without the bindu.
The supreme power (Parāśakti) is partless, inconceivable, and faces in every direction.
It is subtle, stainless, infinite, and of the nature of nirvāṇa;
it indeed unfolds within all sentient beings and within all phenomena.
In this way, the entire world is like clarified butter within her, who is both one and manifold;
above her is that which is without support, without foundation, and free from all affliction.
"Immovable, all-pervasive, peaceful, and devoid of creation and dissolution. Thus [it is said].

If [the Lord] were not thus manifold in form, then for the sake of favoring all beings, He would not remain established in performing the fivefold cosmic acts—creation, maintenance, withdrawal, grace, and concealment—for the purpose of causing those living beings to abandon their karma. Consequently, due to that connection with karma, even the Blessed One would be bound by karma. To the question "Why is this not so?", it must be said: because of His divine power (*divya-śakti*). And it has been said:
"Sadāśiva, endowed with the thirty-eight *kalās* and possessing a manifest form, is *sakala* (with parts); otherwise, Śiva is *niṣkala* (without parts)."
The Lord, however, should be understood as possessing manifold forms;
established through the efficacy of yoga, he does not suffer on account of karma.
"O blameless one, this is indeed the form of the Supreme Lord as he sports.
Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"In the world, the vision and activity of the embodied one are just like ours."
Because of the impossibility of garlands and such, the body of the Lord is not of this nature, but is Śākta.
That, moreover, is [accomplished] by means of five mantras, which are employed for the five ritual acts.
"O Lord, [the installation] with the [faces] Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, beginning from the head and so forth, is for those with supports;
other [methods] in this Tantra are described by the wise. Thus [it is said].
Likewise:
"In whatever form the practitioner should always bring [the deity] to mind," p. 93.
The Lord becomes identical with that [object of meditation], just like a wish-fulfilling gem.

Since Śiva is worshipped by meditating upon Him in this manner, and since the attainment of the desired fruit would not occur without meditation, therefore the All-Sadāśiva must be meditated upon. And it has been said:
"For this very reason, He is the one to be meditated upon, for He bestows the enjoyment of distinguished fruits; they offer as a libation that vision which is the internal perception [of Him]."
"From Avalokita, there shall arise a man endowed with beauty;
his form shall be wondrous, entirely distinct from that of all other people. Thus it is said.

Now, one might object: "If the Lord grants desired boons only through meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*arcana*), and so forth, then He would be like us, enticed by the expectation of a return favor. Consequently, He would be subject to attachment, aversion, desire, and the like. This, however, should not be said; for even these [acts] are merely the causes of His maturation (*paripāka*). Furthermore, one might ask: "In that case, how could He be pleased by a vision (*avaloka*)? For a vision occurs only when He is manifest (*vyakta*). This objection is addressed by the term "vision" as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). The meaning is that when the full maturation—characterized by the equality of all actions—is properly brought about through vision, meditation, worship, and so forth, the Lord becomes pleased upon beholding that self which has become free from agitation. Therefore, the Lord is to be meditated upon (*sādhyeya*) there as possessing a specific distinction (*viśiṣṭabheda*). Both of these—the attainment of liberation as a distinguished fruit and the acquisition of the bliss of powers such as *aṇimā* on the pure path of enjoyment (*bhoga-śuddhādhvan*)—are impossible without the ripening of karma. And since that ripening does not occur without [the practice of] smearing ashes (*uddhūlana*) and other rites, the Lord is to be meditated upon with hands and feet. That is to say, He is to be worshipped. Because this is so, the form described in the scriptures, which is the basis for that [meditation], is now depicted.
One should fashion the five-faced [form] and meditate upon the western face adorned with three eyes;
thus is the five-faced one, whose head is covered by all the matted locks.
His crest is formed by the half-moon bound upward with a serpent-noose.
Having meditated upon supreme nirvāṇa, the best of men attain it. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, regarding the Śrīmukha image: one should place the western face slightly omitted, extending upward toward the northeast;
the eastern face, Tatpuruṣa, is adorned above the heart.
Aghora is on the right shoulder, while Guhyaka is on the left shoulder;
Sadyojāta is in the west, situated at the back of the neck.
Abounding in the splendor of various ornaments, bestowing diverse supernatural powers upon men,
eternally delighting in various sports, the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara) is the destroyer of misfortune.
One should display three faces, but one should not display Sadyojāta and Īśāna.

Thus [it is said]. When it is poured out, then the form of Śiva is drawn; "then" is the understood remainder of the sentence. One should place the white [form of] Īśāna by means of its shadow, and place Tatpuruṣa in the center.
Because the upward face of the Sun (the central face) is primary, its shadow is white all around. Thus [it is said].

Having contemplated the supreme Self as the supreme Brahman, and having contemplated the individual soul as the individual self, one should then contemplate the supreme Lord as
The lotus-face of the three [faces] consists of Īśāna, Śānti, and Atīta for the males;
Vāma bears Ghorā and Vidyā, while Pratiṣṭhā is the secret maṇḍala.
And [he should offer] water produced from immediate cessation to the tree that is the path of the worlds.
The phonemes are the blood of the mantra; the measure of the words is the network of veins;
the principles (tattvas) are the bones, marrow, semen, and so forth; and he who sits upon the lotus has ten directions as his arms.
He possesses the five senses—sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell—and is endowed with the moon of knowledge and its digits;
he resembles pure crystal and is adorned with the thirty-two major marks.
To the peaceful one with tawny eyes, adorned with a crown of matted locks, [the right hands hold] the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a sword, a spear, and a trident... [and so forth].
Indeed, the worship is complete; he holds a hand-drum and blue lotus seeds in his left hands, extending as far as the Śakti within the length of the Liṅga that pervades everything.
Likewise:
the syllable Oṃ on the right, and the full offering on the left;
similarly, the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and the hand-drum (ḍamaru), and likewise the trident and the serpent for the two [deities].
"Likewise, the sword is on the blue lotus, and similarly, the power, the eye,
and the thread are on the hands of the five faces beginning with Īśāna, in their respective order, known as the weapons."
Likewise:
"Seated with the face of a child, serene and with the luster of crystal,
one should behold one's own true nature as if remaining absorbed in meditation."
One should first contemplate that eastern face of Tatpuruṣa, which has the form of a youth, is yellow in color while standing, and has eyes motionless in meditation.
The non-terrible one is on the right, while the terrible one, endowed with black whiskers,
fearsome with fangs, and deformed, is situated upon the right shoulder.
The space-like face of a young woman, greedy for the fleeting display of illusion,
is like a creeper adorned with ornaments resting upon her left shoulder.
One should always meditate upon Sadyojāta, who has the appearance of a king’s face, is absorbed in meditation, and is white as snow, while remaining positioned behind and above one's neck.
One should meditate upon [the deity] as five-faced, with three eyes in each face,
possessing twenty smiling lips, and adorned with earrings.
With a broad forehead and a lofty crown, with auspicious and full cheeks,
it was adorned with various jewels and embellished with a golden tiara.
Adorned with necklaces and armlets, provided with rings and bracelets,
enriched with an upper garment and a sacred thread, he is gentle and wears a turban.
With a broad expanse of belly, full and with a well-developed waist-region,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and beautiful with a waist-band.
Clad in divine garments, fond of a tiger-skin mantle,
his feet adorned with anklets and decorated with bracelets and other ornaments.
The god, who had vomited forth the *sūkta*, possessed long arms marked with lotuses,
bore ten weapons, and was enchanting with his divine form.
One should thus meditate upon Sadāśiva, being praised by Viriñca and the other gods. Thus [it is said].
In the *Alakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:
"The five seats should be according to their respective signs, clearly manifest as a pentad;
the five-faced [form] is for those who do not desire [it], while the four-faced brings happiness."
The three-faced [form] is eternally bestowing peace; the two-faced [form] is for malevolent rites (abhicāra);
the single-faced [form] destroys diseases; and that which has the nose as its mouth is the eye.
On the four-faced support, however, one should place either the five-faced or the four-faced [deity].
The face of Īśāna, situated at the top of the Liṅga, is white and radiant, possesses three eyes, is adorned with a crown and earrings,
and is gazed upon by Kośa.
The face of Tatpuruṣa is red in color, has white eyebrows, is adorned with a crown,
possesses fierce lion-like eyes, and is richly endowed with hair.
The southern face should be black, with protruding lips, shaggy eyebrows, and blazing like a sword;
it should be formidable with fangs and have round eyes resembling a flaming fire.
The left face should be plump and remain as such for a fortnight.
Adorned with beautiful ornaments and rich in hair, decorated with a tilaka mark and a crest-jewel,
having a face like that of Varuṇa, white and lovely, wearing two earrings and bearing matted locks upon his head.
It has three eyes, is full-bodied, youthful in form, very serene, and most beautiful;
it possesses a face that is the destroyer of the enemy, with three mouths and its own ears.
Even if it is crooked, the face should immediately become a single form with the person; this is the *vaktraka* [ornament].

The *astra* [mantra] arises from all paths and is addressed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; it is the six-syllabled mantra ending with *rasadeśa*, worshipped by Vainateya among the *nāgas*. These many forms of Sadāśiva—designated as *kaivalya*, *sarvataḥ*, *sarvabhuvaneśa*, *padeśa*, *mantreśa*, and *kaleśa*—are differentiated. Furthermore, the divisions of the Lord above [the head], namely the *niṣkala*, *śānta*, *vyāpaka*, *ruci*, and *sadāśiva-bhaṭṭāraka*, are distinct. Moreover, the divisions of the mantra, such as *sadāśiva* and *sadā*, exist externally. All these consist of the nature of the density of consciousness-bliss (*cidānandaghana*), are composed of five mantras, bestow both higher and lower devotion, and are presided over by the partless Śiva (*niṣkala-śiva*). Of these—
p.

98) In the center, Rudra-Sadāśiva alone is to be worshipped by the Śaivas. Therefore, he speaks of the state of Rudra-Sadāśiva: "He possesses a trident, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and arms granting boons and fearlessness."
"Purākṣaḍiṇḍimī, Vyāla, Pālinī, and Prāksadāśiva. Thus [it is said].

By this stated principle, Sadāśiva Bhaṭṭāraka—who is both manifest and unmanifest, consisting of both [the individual] and the [supreme] Self, mobile and immobile, and who is worshipped as the cause of both worldly enjoyment and liberation—should always face the east. Just as that Blessed One faces the fifth [direction], so is the procedure declared: "In the case of the venerable Mukha-bimba, during initiation and the like, the Guru should contemplate Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Śānta, and Nitya, with the eternal face toward the west. Thus it is said.
In the *Śrībṛhatkiraṇodyota* and other texts: "Īśa and Tatpuruṣa are known as the faces in the east; Aghora is the face in the south;
Vāma is always the gentle-faced one in the north; and Sadyojāta is remembered as the face in the west."
Thus one should meditate upon the venerable Bṛhadvacas Bhārgava and the others.
"In initiation and other rites, that very [vessel] which supports the jar should face westward. Thus it is said.
In the *Lakṣmī-Keśa-saṃvāda*:
"In all rites—whether daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—Śiva is always the presiding authority;
he faces east while Lakṣmī faces west, and his body consists of [all] the digits (*kalā*)."
Likewise:
when the door is in the west, one should meditate on Īśa and Puruṣa there;
Sadyojāta should be in the east, and Ghora and Vāma as before.
The limbs of enjoyment are as before; and who is the one with the northern face?
One should place the food offering, the circle of lamps, and so forth at the doorway. Thus it is said.
One should always perform the inspection of the main entrance while facing the northeast.
It should always be installed facing east, or it may be installed facing west. Thus it is said.

(100) "Endowed with [faces] beginning with Īśāna, he is Sadāśiva. Regarding the faces beginning with Īśāna, which are the agents of worldly activity (*lokakartṛ*), their crystal-like nature refers precisely to their stainlessness. Therefore, in the ultimate sense, the faces of the body of Sadāśiva are indeed like crystal. This is the same for all of them.

For what purpose is the state of the faces beginning with Īśāna described as "serene" (*prasanna*) and "tranquil" (*stimita*) and so forth? If one asks, "Is it not like that of human beings?"—it is not so; rather, it is for the sake of the five-fold cosmic function (*pañcakṛtya*). Likewise, even during the dissolution of movement, for the sake of liberation, one should meditate upon him as having matted hair and being serene.
A slightly smiling, yellow face is used for acts such as pride and paralyzing;
a terrifying, black face, adorned with tawny matted hair and skulls, is likewise employed.
In the states of destruction and so forth, and in concealment, one should meditate on a beautiful red mandala;
in the generation of all phenomena, one should remember it as being attached.
"One should always remember the compassionate form [of the deity] as a woman in childhood, youth, or old age.
But is it not the case that [the deity] has a head, face, and mouth on the right, and resides in the terrible heart? Indeed, he is one.
"And this deity is immediately the embodied form; thus the 'sakala' (with parts) is fully recited," and so forth.

From the utterance [of the mantra], the Lord arises as the very form of the mantra, like a head emerging from the body. In that regard, how is it that the Blessed One has Īśāna as his head? Because the mantra of Niśāśana consists of phonemes (*varṇa*), he has those phonemes as his head; or rather, because of its clarity (*prasanna*), he has a clear-headedness arising from the nature of the path of qualities (*guṇādhvan*). If the head were composed of those [specific] harsh phonemes, then, because the pronunciation of phonemes is subject to destruction and lacks stability, the manifestation of the form would not be possible. Now, if it is argued that the heart of Ghorā is cruel-minded, that Vāmadeva is impure, and that Sadyojāta is the form of the Immediate (*sadyas*) which arises clockwise due to the [nature of] jewels and so forth—this should not be said. For the Blessed One, whose nature is formless and who is the self of all, is such by his very essence.
p.

101) There is no delusion (*moha*). However, because of the association with qualities and non-qualities due to the equilibrium of the two principles (*tattva*), it is metaphorically called "the Lord" (*deva*). And it has been said:
"That which does not rule over the entire world through the [ever-]changing quality (*guṇa*)."

Because its upper portion reaches as far as the region of the shoulders, it extends from the head down to the breasts. It pervades the body of each respective [deity] by means of which it is [designated].

Among the Tantras, that which is of a dual nature is the "face of Tatpuruṣa. The heart is a synonym for awakening (*bodha*); since Śiva is non-terrible (*aghora*) therein, he is [called] Aghora. This is because the [other] face is terrible due to its association with grasping (*parigraha*). The mention of "terrible" is used figuratively (*upacārataḥ*).
Because the three aims of life (trivarga) are contrary [to worldly norms], they are "left" (vāma), and because it is secret by its very nature, the supreme abode is "hidden" (guhya);
he who possesses that hidden, supreme left-abode is Vāmaguhyaka.
Because his forms arise instantly by his own will, he is named Sadyojāta;
because he bestows the form of a yogi instantly,
he is Sadyomūrti, for there is no delay in the manifestation of his form.
Thus, while performing the functions of the body, Śakti is designated by the word "body" due to the absence of [any other] body.
"Furthermore, whatever divisions of that [power] there may be, such as Vāmā and the rest, these too have been declared by the wise according to the distinction of their functions. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the passage beginning with "He rules here by which the entire world," and so forth, concerning those who abide above all paths: "By whom the entire world is a quality; the Lord (Īśa) is the object of Īśāna; because his place is at the summit (mūrdhan). This means that his place or station is similar to the summit; this is the similarity to the half-peak. Therefore, "the summit of him, of him," and so forth. Whichever [deity] has the *va* class and so on as its function, it matures through karma. (p. 102)

His city is that which fills the eastern city; because he descends into that city, he is Tatpuruṣa. Because he protects those persons (*puruṣa*) there, and because he manifests knowledge through their manifestation, he has Tatpuruṣa as his face. Alternatively, his body is filled with each and every delight; in that city, he exists as the protector of his own nature. He is Tatpuruṣa because the two powers of knowledge and action are manifested from him as a single entity to avoid the fear of [ontological] plurality; therefore, he has Tatpuruṣa as his face.

"Because its nature is to provide protection through its phonemes (*vyañjana*), it is called 'manifest' (*vyakta*)," according to the scripture. Regarding "the Heart" (*hṛdaya*) and so forth: since Śiva is not terrible (*aghorah*), therefore his heart is not terrible; rather, it is peaceful and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). She whose consciousness is that [peaceful] heart is the "Ghorahṛdayā" (She of the Terrible Heart). [Objection: If so, how is there a mention of "terrible" (*ghora*) here? [Response: True. Because the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) belonging to the one who moves within [her], which causes the dissolution of bonds (*pāśa*), is terrible, the term "terrible" is applied to her as well by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Regarding "Vāma": because she emits (*vamati*) the three letters—the three types of bonds—along with them, she is "Vāma" due to being contrary (*vaiparītyāt*) to them. In her true nature, she is secret, beyond the senses, and by her very essence, she is "Vāmamukhya" (the Chief of the Left), for she emits (*dhamayati*) the Vāma [path]. This is clear.

But if this is so, how can it be said that "the Blessed Lord bears ten weapons"? True; however, do those [weapons] indeed become instruments of violence? No, rather: they are called *āyudha* because by means of them one fights (*āyudhyante*), increases (*vardhante*), and cuts through the nets of bonds (*pāśajāla*). Thus, the [weapons] beginning with Śakti and ending with Ananta are the bearers of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and the rest.

As it is said in the *Caturviṃśatisāhasra*: "The supreme power, whose nature is consciousness, is known as the Self called 'Being' (*sadātman*); the powers of will, knowledge, and action are established as the trident."

By means of those very concentrations (*dhāraṇā*), does one also [attain] the Khaṭvāṅga of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow? Because the seeds (*bīja*) of these [mantras] are revealed, it is called Bījapūraka from the act of filling with seeds.
Māyā, in the form of a hand-drum (ḍamaru), is indeed that long-tongued Ambikā.
"The mind is said to be the blue lotus, and the senses are the untarnished garland. Thus it is said.

This is its meaning: that Blessed Lady who consists of the nature of consciousness (*bodha-rūpa*), whose essence is knowledge (*jñāna-ātmikā*), and who is united with both the supreme and the non-supreme Śiva—she alone is capable of severing all fetters (*pāśa*). Thus, she is called *Śakti*, like a power. *Sādākhya* [is explained as follows]: because it is eternal (*sada*), it is designated as such for all time; or else, that which possesses the name "Being" (*sat*) is *Sādākhya*. It is the state of eternal Śiva. When the Blessed One is endowed with all attributes, she is the one who possesses that true and auspicious designation (*sat-samākhyā*); thus, the state of *Aṇimā* is *Sādākhya*. As for the state of Śiva, there is no fear of returning [to saṃsāra]; therefore, it is *Abhaya*. It is *Abhaya* because it bestows fearlessness, like a hand granting security. Furthermore, that very reality of Śiva (*śiva-tattva*), when differentiated by the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*), becomes threefold like a trident (*triśūla*). Likewise, the single-rooted triangle has its root in the fundamental reality of Śiva, which is divided into the three powers. The *Bindu-tattva*, the *Sadāśiva-tattva*, and the *Īśvara-tattva* are thus established in a threefold manner. Moreover, those very powers known as will, knowledge, and action, through their transformation, constitute the *khaṭvāṅga* (the skull-topped staff) of Śiva. By his will, he intends the world as the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). His limbs are the auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*); he possesses these, thus he is the "possessor of limbs" (*aṅgī*), and therein he is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). This entire mass, ending in the *Śuddha-vidyā-tattva*, joined with the staff of the possessor of limbs, becomes like a *khaṭvāṅga*.

Now follows the exposition of the groups of seeds (*bīja*) and their expansion, which is the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). This [emanation] is the accomplishment of the fruits of karma, and because it bestows boons (*vara*), it is called "the Boon-giver" (*varada*). Furthermore, at the time of the completion of those very groups belonging to itself, its station is in the fullness of *māyā*; for that reason, it abides in the principle of *māyā* like a citron fruit (*bījapūraka*). Now, he describes the essential nature of that *māyā*-principle:

The *māyā-tattva* exists in the form of a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Now, the meaning is that just as a *ḍamaruka* drum is the cause of its own resonance, so too is the *māyā-tattva* the cause of the diversification of time and other factors. Furthermore, *māyā* itself, having become both long and short, transforms into effects such as time and approaches like a double-tongued serpent; for "double-tongued" refers to a snake, and just as a snake becomes agitated when pursued, there is a similarity [in the way *māyā* causes agitation]. Like a blue lotus (*indīvara*), the mind undergoes contraction and expansion due to its nature of shrinking and blooming; "expansion" refers to the outward movement of the senses. Alternatively, "expansion" is contentment when there is the enjoyment of existence, while its absence is "contraction. The mention of the "rosary of senses" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) which includes the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross elements (*bhūta*). Thus, this very world is the tree of experience, to be understood in both ways. Although the distinction of principles (*tattva-bheda*) stands as the cause of karma, nevertheless, that very [distinction] is also the cutter of the creeper of karma; thus it is figuratively called a "weapon," though it is not literally a weapon. Having fully understood all this, one should place the *mūrti* upon that lion-throne and perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) of Paramaśiva therein. Now, [one might ask: is the throne of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) from Śakti up to the end of Śakti, while the power residing in the *Śiva-tattva* is the *mūrti* consisting of knowledge? Indeed, it is so.
She has one face and three eyes, and she holds a spear, a trident, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
In some places, the reading is:
"She has one face and two hands, holds a citron, and is accompanied by Bhaya. In that case, having invoked the partless [form], one should contemplate all of Śiva as being without parts.
Having integrated the limbs with the limbs, one should worship Śaṅkara, who is Nirvāṇa.

(p. 105) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-svabhāva). Among these, Mahāmati, the imagined self-nature consists of the various names, signs, and characteristics that are falsely attributed to objects by ordinary people through their own deluded discrimination."

Such statements exist. Therefore, how can the Lord’s form consist of the principles of *sattva* and *śakti*? True. There are three types of established doctrines (*siddhāntas*): those consisting of half-verse units (*pādārdha-granthas*), those consisting of seed-syllable units (*bīja-granthas*), and those consisting of mixed units (*miśra-granthas*). Among these, in the *pādārdha-granthas*, there is authority for [the worship of] the [lower] levels; in the *bīja-granthas*, only the state beyond all (*sarvātīta*) and devoid of specific offices (*niradhikāra*) is to be worshipped; and in the *miśra-granthas*, it is taught that both are to be worshipped. Consequently, there is no fault here, as this distinction arises from the differences among the listeners in various contexts. Enough with excessive detail; let us proceed with the main topic. Now, the practitioner (*sādhaka*), having placed his hands joined in *añjali*—filled with flowers—at the region of the heart, should contemplate, according to the instruction of his own guru, the Root Mantra (*mūlamantra*). He should meditate upon Śiva, who is like a mass of light, foremost in the heart, the partless (*niṣkala*) Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*) at the "End of the Twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), self-luminous, endowed with all attributes, and identical with the Supreme Śiva. Then, through the exhalation (*recaka*), he should clearly utter the Root Mantra, transcending the network of bonds (*pāśajāla*) from the earth up to *Samanā* by means of the vowels beginning with *a* and *ā*, and reach the Supreme Śiva, who is beyond the power of *Unmanā*. As it has been said:
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and the bindu;
the half-moon, the rodha, the nāda, and indeed the end of nāda (*nādānta*).
"Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and likewise Unmanā; the net of bonds extends up to the level of Samanā, while Supreme Śiva resides at the end of Unmanā. Thus it is said.

If it is argued that this sequence of mantra recitation involving the *praṇava* (OM) does not concern the *prāsāda* [mantra], it is not so; for there is an intended non-differentiation between the phonemes *a* and *ha*. And it has been said:
"The phoneme *a* and the phoneme *ha*—these two abide as one.
One would find no distinction at all between them, like that between the wind and the sky.

Thus it is clearly stated: "The letter 'A', however, is the vital breath (prāṇa) when manifest; at its own dissolution, it takes the form of a consonant (halākṛti). According to this statement, the letter 'A' located in the heart becomes conjoined with the form of a consonant—specifically the form of the Bindu—which has emerged from the center of the Prakṛti-cakra situated at the navel. It is said that the entire veil, consisting of the vowels beginning with 'A', proceeds toward Supreme Śiva. In that regard, the mantra-garland, like a jewel, possesses the power of the deity of the mantra through the relationship of the signified and the signifier. One should contemplate the mantra-tejas, which is of the nature of bile (?), endowed with the six qualities such as omniscience, and appearing as a digit of the Bindu of supreme nectar. Having invoked [the deity] through the inhalation of Śiva-Śakti and established [him] with the Sthāpinī-mudrā, one should bring [the deity] to the Bindu between the eyebrows—which shines like a thousand autumn moons—by means of the Recaka (exhalation). Having meditated on [the deity] residing within the handful of flowers, one should invoke [him] with the Āhvanī-mudrā and the Mūla-mantra, and establish [him] with the Sthāpinī-mudrā. Having pervaded the two forms with the Mūla-mantra during the ritual placement (nyāsa) and contemplated [the deity] as having become present, one should restrain [him] with the Niṣṭhura-mudrā. Then, having offered the Nirodhārghya (oblation for restraint) and having dispelled obstacles with the Astra-mantra ending in "Phaṭ" (addressed to Kālakaṇṭhī), one should bind the Liṅga-mudrā and the Namaskāra-mudrā with the Hṛdaya-mantra, enclose [the deity] with the Kavaca-mantra, perform the Sakalīkaraṇa (unification) with the limbs of the body (Hṛdaya, etc.), and sanctify the ground. Finally, one should transform [the deity] into nectar by means of the Dhenu-mudrā and the Mahā-mudrā, accompanied by the Śakti-mantra. In this context: *Oṃ hauṃ haṃ, obeisance to the invocation of Śiva.*
Such are the mantras. And it has been said:
"This entire meditation is partless (niṣkala) and consists of creative contemplation (bhāvanā).
Within that [partless state], the part-manifested (sakala) [deity] resides pervading the body, situated like a human being."
"He who knows Sadāśiva as possessing both parts and being partless, abiding in both—being thus liberated from the body of bonds, he attains Śiva alone. Thus it is said.
In the Śrīparāśākha it is likewise stated:
"Having thus fashioned a body of peace (śānti), one should [place] the supreme cause within it."
The supreme, eternal truth, whose nature is knowledge and blissful happiness.
Pervasive among all principles, immeasurable, and incomparable;
devoid of the signified and the signifier, it lies beyond the sphere of speech and mind.
"One should especially manifest the unmanifest within the self that possesses parts;
this is called 'the supreme purification' (pārā-vāsana) because of the restraint [imposed] by the Śiva-mantra. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
there, having performed the invocation with the splendor of the sun by means of the invocation mudrā,
one should perform the installation by means of the installation mudrā, taking refuge in the embodiment of Śakti.
"Having brought [the deity] near through prostration, one should satisfy [him] with the mudrā of joy. Thus it is said.
Likewise: "The supreme seed-syllable, which is partless, joined with the bindu and the nāda, endowed with three internal mātrās, and ending with the self of the letter 'dva'."
One should mentally meditate upon Śiva as the embodiment of mantra within the creation, between the eyebrows;
having visualized him with a splendor equal to the orb of the moon, seated amidst a handful of flowers.
Having brought [the deity] back with the *āvāhinī* [mudrā], one should establish him in the heart with the *sthāpinī*;
one should perceive the Lord, who has entered the subtle form, throughout the entire body of the Vidyā.
O Lord, I remember [the body] as if pervaded by the Goddess, who has entered it as if it were insentient, having divided herself according to her portions,
and who has become present before me through the power of concentration.
There, according to the ritual procedure for worship, one should restrain the Lord by means of the [mudrā] called "the Harsh" (niṣṭhurā);
then, one should offer the water of restraint (nirodhārghya) to Śambhu for the sake of his presence.
Raising a flower with the weapon-mantra *phaṭ* ending in *kāla-kaṇṭhya*,
one should dispel all obstacles and display the *liṅga-mudrā*.
Having performed the salutation with the heart-mantra and having shielded [the disciple] with the armor-mantra, |||
The heart is white in the heart, and the head is yellow in the heads.
One should place the red *śikhā* [mantra] in the middle of the crest, the black *tanutra* [mantra] at the heart,
and the weapon [mantra], resembling a flame of fire, upon the groups of hands.
Thus, having thus brought [the deity] into proximity, the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the infusion of all parts) is declared;
one should meditate on those who possess the single color of Śiva, as well as on those who possess distinct colors for their limbs.
Having offered a flower with the root mantra, that indeed is the supreme consecration (*paramīkaraṇa*). One should perform the [milk-stream] action for the mantras by means of the *dhenumudrā*.
Having formed the mahāmudrā at the heart, one should perform the illumination;
saying, "Welcome to you, O Great God," one should supplicate the Lord.
"O Lord, Sovereign of the Entire World, until the conclusion of the worship, remain present in this *liṅga* with a state of affection for me. Thus [he prayed].

Now, one might object: if the Blessed Lord is invited, then there must also be his dismissal; in that case, would not his state of emanation (*sargaga-tattva*) be lost? It is not so. Here, "invocation" (*āvāhana*) refers to the manifestation of the all-pervading Śiva by means of the mantra. As it has been said: "The invocation is that which brings face-to-face the Lord Sadāśiva, who is omnipresent and tranquil."
"When the worship is completed, the dismissal of that [deity] is performed with averted face.

[Objection: But surely this too is contradictory, since that which is omnipresent is present everywhere. [Reply: It is not so. Because there is no purpose served by such a [general] presence, "invocation" (*āvāhana*) here is a presence characterized by the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, corresponding to the faith of the worshiper and the object of worship, within the context of the relationship between the worshiped and the worshiper. And because of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier, through the specific arrangement of the mantra—which is the signifier—there will also be a specific presence of Śiva, the signified; thus it is not contradicted. As it has been said:
"Just as the manifestation of fire situated from the root to the tip occurs in a tree..."
In the same way, the manifestation of consciousness in one place does not contradict its omnipresence.
Likewise:
"Just as fire residing within wood is manifested by means of friction and other such methods,
so too is Śiva manifested through the power of mantra and devotion."
"Just as there is the blazing of fire within the hearth by means of the wind, so too is the Blessed One manifested here by means of the *liṅga* mantra. Thus it is said.

If this is so, then what is the purpose of rituals such as the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth? True; those rituals are prescribed for the sake of stabilizing the mind of those who are devoted to ritual action (*kriyāniṣṭha*). Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Niśvāsakārikā*: "Although the Lord is omnipresent, He is not worshipped within the body;
rather, the Lord Śiva is to be worshipped in a Linga or in another auspicious [image]."
Invocation—meditation through the dance of the mind; one should contemplate union with Śiva through the restraint [of the senses] by means of the intellect.
One should worship the Sakala [form], offer what is to be given, and mutter the mantra of the Niṣkala [form].
One should meditate upon that which consists of light, subtle, and undivided from its parts;
one should satisfy it in the sky, possessing the pure luster of crystal, the destroyer of old age and death.
For the sake of attaining liberation through the mind, the practitioner should meditate upon that partless dissolution;
purified by bathing, the mantra-practitioner should perform recitation, for he is like fire in granting success.
Through worship, the two deities remain present, and at the time of the fire-oblation, they bestow the fruit.
Through meditation, one attains omnipresence; through yoga, the absence of yoga, and the [proper] measure; and through vows and initiation, liberation is sought.
Invocation, installation, presence, and confinement—
these are declared to be the constituent parts of the rites within the ritual procedure.
O Lord of Gods, it is not carried away by anyone, nor is it established by anyone; it is not obstructed, nor is its presence brought about.
One should contemplate the supreme Śiva as all-pervading in the form of mantra.
"Then it is called 'the vehicle'; 'forgive me' is the dismissal. Thus [it is said].

Regarding "invocation" (*āvāhana*) therein: it is called invocation because that by which one is invoked is "invocation. It is an activity of the mind, and that consists specifically of unsurpassed faith. Together with that [faith], there is the addressing by means of a mantra-word, which is the act of calling out. Invocation is the act of making [the deity] face toward oneself. The establishment of the Lord [in the heart] is the thought: "May the Blessed One, the treasure-house of austerity, whose nectar-like compassion is incessant, remain here for the sake of bestowing grace through the mantra," and it is the steadiness of the mind. Then, "presence" (*sannidhi*) is the relationship characterized by the benefactor and the beneficiary; it is the state of being oriented toward [the practitioner]. Then, the prayer: "O Blessed One, may you be ever intent on bestowing grace, becoming one with the Lord. This is the quality of the perfected ones (*siddhas*): that they act in accordance with the prayer of those who possess such concentration.

(As stated on p. 111: "Thus, for those whose eyes [of perception] have not yet matured, there is the manifestation of Śiva-nature; this is the 'veiling' (*avakuṇṭhana*) of those who are obstructed. Now, one might object: "Granted that the Vāma system is thus, but since locations such as the Heart (*hṛdaya*) and so forth are assigned to Śiva, does the suspicion of [Śiva having] a physical body not arise once again? If this is asked, it should not be said so. This [assignment of locations] is accepted as a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) because of the commonality of the locations such as the Heart and so forth. And it has been said: "The term *hṛdaya* signifies knowledge, intention, or purpose; it is, moreover, a designator [of Śiva]."
And because it consists of the light of knowledge, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is considered the heart.
The host of qualities beginning with *aṇimā* constitutes the most excellent state; because it occupies the region of his head, it is called the "head" (*śiras*) of the Yavaneśvara.
The power that brings peace to the universe is indeed the supreme command of the Lord;
because it is not dependent on anything else, O Śambhu, it is considered to be the crest-lock (śikhā) that has been severed.
The halo of the Lord is a mass of splendor consisting of dense light;
that body is of an unimpeded nature, for it is a protection and nothing else.
"The heat of Śiva is indeed unbearable, yet it is the tearer of all that is wicked;
it should be understood as being like a scripture, for in Śaṅkara, the weapon is unmanifest. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the invocation (*āvāhana*) with the *avāhinī* and other [mudrās], Śiva has therefore written down their characteristics as well: "In invocation, the *añjali* mudrā is that in which the thumb presses the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) full [of oblation] while the fingers are slightly bent by the mantra; likewise, in the *pātra* [offering], the fingers are not bent."
A fist with the thumb drawn up and well-joined with the flower-filled [fingers] is the Liṅga-mudrā; likewise, through this, Śambhu becomes present in the heart by means of the Heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
For those who are harsh, for pregnant women, and for those formed by the entire self as a fist,
a complete suppression should likewise be performed by the Lord through the rites of withdrawal and dismissal.
The ring finger is considered the mother; the thumb is the eldest, situated at the joint, and regarded as the substance.
From the joining of the fists with the palms raised and the releasing of the two thumbs,
that [mudrā] of the flower is known as Kālakaṇṭhikā, which destroys obstacles by means of the weapon-mantra.

The Liṅgamudrā, beloved by Śiva, is formed by raising the thumbs while the other fingers are bent inward; it is also formed when the thumbs are bent toward the palms while the other fingers are extended. A pregnant woman should perform this mudrā.
The *dhenumudrā* is formed by joining the middle fingers with the index fingers,
placing the tips of the ring fingers together, and interlacing the fingers of both hands.
And that is to be known as the Mahāmudrā, with the fingers extended in the añjali gesture. Thus it is said.

Now, one might ask: why is this finger-configuration (*namāṅgulī-sandarbha*), which consists of the act of joining the hands, performed as something other than the *naṭhī*? It is not so; for even in the form of a *mudrā*, it is indeed Śiva-Śakti herself. And it has been said:
"She liberates from all bonds and likewise dissolves what has been accumulated.
Because of this liberation and dissolution, she is celebrated as the *Śaktimudrā*."
Then, one should contemplate that Śiva has said, "Welcome to you, O Blessed One," and "Welcome, my child. And it is said:

"Having meditated in due order upon the invocation (āvāhana), the installation (sthāpana), the presence (sānnidhya), the confinement (sannirodhana), the welcome (svāgata), and the gracious favor (suprasāda)."

Then, having lifted the *astravardhanī* vessel with both hands and meditating upon the feet [of the deity] while reciting "oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya pādyaṃ namaḥ," one should likewise offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the mantra "svadhā" into the vessels facing east, south, north, west, and upward. Then, the special *arghya* vessel...

Having raised [the vessel] and not rotating it above the head, one should offer the *arghya* with the mantra "svāhā" using the tips of the thumb, ring finger, and middle finger with the palm facing upward, for the five [deities] beginning with Īśāna. With the mantra "vauṣaṭ," one should offer flowers, *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth. As it has been said:

"One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and *arghya*, along with *dūrvā*, flowers, unbroken rice, and the like, preceded by the rite of a warm welcome (*susvāgata*), according to the prescribed option."
One should offer water for the feet (pādya) and water for sipping (ācamana) at the two feet and the two sword-handles;
then, one should present these to the right and left of their blossoming lotus-faces.
Having raised up the special arghya, O Lord, one should present it face-to-face as the source [of the lineage];
one should offer the well-prepared flower-arghya upon the five heads. Thus it is said.
Alternatively,

one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, along with the special water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), while reciting [the mantra]. Likewise, the venerable teachers have stated that Śiva is the face [of all], whose form is free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The flow of supreme nectar has made the quarters of the sky white.
Having lifted up the vessel for the special arghya with the left hand.
One should first offer [the water] for the feet with the right hand facing [the deity];
likewise, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) into the mouths and the arghya offering upon the five heads.

Afterwards, one should offer *dūrvā* grass, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth, along with worldly customary offerings; the salutation (*namaskāra*), *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and *vauṣaṭ*, joined with the *jāti* mantras, should be performed with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
One should present these four there in their proper sequence. Thus it is said.

Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of offering water for the feet and other honors to the Blessed One? Since he is pure by his very nature, does not the act of bestowing upon him—his own abode, which is the supreme reality—the status of being worthy through the gaze of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted [constitute the purpose]?

The *pādya* (water for the feet). For this very reason, the mind is applied there. Regarding the word *namaḥ*: by means of it, one turns Śiva toward the temple (*prāsāda*). Because the verbal root *cam* has the sense of "taking" (*ādāna*), *namāsaṃ* means the complete tasting of the essence of Śiva; that is, becoming of one flavor with Śiva (*śivasamarasībhāvaḥ*). For this reason, the word *svadhā* is employed here. *Svadhā* bestows supreme delight upon oneself. This is because *svadhā* has the meanings of satisfaction, pleasure, extension, salutation, and offering. Therefore, since the head (*uttamāṅga*) is worthy of the highest state, the attainment of the manifestation of Śiva-nature occurs through the taking up of the *arghya* (offering water). For this very reason, the term *svadhā-jāti* is employed here, meaning that qualities such as omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and others are manifested. Now, an objection: *svadhā* is used for the purpose of a recipient (*sampradāna*), whereas the word *svāhā* is used for the purpose of one's own qualities. How could it have that meaning? True. However, there is no fault, because the fruit of propitiating those respective deities is obtained by the self alone.

Thus, when the state of Śiva (śivatva) has been manifested, that prior knowledge which discriminates between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted is like a flower; it is the "flower" because it is the cause for the fruit of the state of Śiva. Its "offering" (samarpaṇa) is its destruction, which is its ripening into the form of the fruit. For this very reason, the *vauṣaṭ* exclamation is employed here. It is established as *vauṣaṭ* through the derivation from the verbal root *vi-ṣvaḍ* with the prefix *vi* and the sense of "union" (*saṃvāya*). Consequently, the offering of the flower consists precisely in its becoming one with Śiva.

[Objection: But surely *śrauṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* have the sense of "giving" (*sampradāna*); how can this word *vauṣaṭ* possibly have the sense of "inherence" (*samavāya*)? [Reply: True; however, even through the act of giving, because of the intended expression of the relationship characterized by the benefactor and the beneficiary between the worshipper and the one worshipped, another internal state of inherence is indicated, so there is no fault. Furthermore, in that case, either the genus *vauṣaṭ* itself should be employed, since both *vaṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* have the same meaning in the two senses of "worship" and "giving. Thus [regarding] invocation (p. 115).

Having performed the tenfold ritual services ending with the offering of incense, water for sipping (ācamana), the guest-water (arghya), flowers, and the rites of installation (sthāpana), presence (sannidhāna), confinement (sannirodhana), veiling (avakuṇṭhana), and the making of the limbs whole (sakalīkaraṇa), and having offered incense and water for sipping, one should pray for the bath. As it is said:
"Invocation, installation, presence, confinement, the making of the limbs whole, unification, and veiling preceded by [the rite of] the left."
Having prepared water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering with [the appropriate] mantras, [he worshipped] Śaṅkara.
Having offered incense and water for sipping, and having made a formal prayer, one should bathe Śiva. Thus it is said.

But is it not the case that other purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as the offering of flowers and so forth, have also been mentioned? How then can there be the restriction that there are only ten? True; however, these ten purificatory rites alone are the primary ones, while others are merely their subsidiaries (*aṅga*). For this reason, they are established separately.

Then, having removed the flowers and other offerings, and having worshipped with fragrant oils and the like using the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should place dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) accompanied by auspicious songs and the sounds of conchs, trumpets, drums, and so forth; having offered incense, one should rub [the image] with camphor, sandalwood, barley powder, and the like using the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *namaḥ*, and then cleanse it with black mustard, salt, cotton seeds, *kāñjika* vinegar, and boiled rice using the armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*) ending in *namaḥ*.

Having requested, "Oṃ hāṃ, Śiva, arise for the purpose of bathing," and having visualized Śiva arising, one should bathe Him with fragrant, pleasantly warm water using the root mantra ending in *svāhā*. Then, one should bathe Him as desired with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth, using the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) mantras and the Brahma-mantras ending in *svāhā*, as well as hymns and mantras recited from the heart. And it is said:
"In this manner, the bathing should then be performed with scented oil, *āmalaka* fruit, and so on;
after rubbing [the body] with barley powder, one should then perform the bath."
One should bathe [the deity] with milk, then with curd, ghee, and honey;
thereafter with candied sugar and rock sugar, and then with the juices of fruits and flowers.
The bath should be performed with the *hṛdaya* mantra, using water from each vessel one after another,
combined with flowers, unbroken rice, *arghya*, and incense, and finally with water scented with all fragrances.
One should lead one hundred and eight [drops] in sequence through the *gassuka* [channels];
having placed the *gaḍḍuka* on the palm of the left hand, [one proceeds] from the top of the *liṅga*.
Likewise:
"Having bathed Śiva with perfumed waters, one should worship Him with jars made of gold, silver, and other materials, provided with a thousand holes."

Having wiped [the deity] with a clean, soft cloth and offered the *arghya*, one should smear [the image] with fragrant substances using the root mantra and the right hand, offer flowers, and perform worship with garments and other offerings. One should touch [the deity] with both hands, or with the left hand alone. And it is said: "Having wiped [the deity] with a pure, fine cloth and having offered [the *arghya*], one should apply ointments such as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron."
One should perform it with the right hand, or with both hands, or with the left alone.
One should not place the hand upon the top of the *liṅga* with the left hand, nor with both hands, nor indeed from the left side; one should neither rotate it around nor place the hand there.
[One should offer] the water for honor (*arghya*), flowers, incense, clothing, and ornaments.
"One should perform worship with various kinds of auspicious flowers strung together. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"One should not touch the liṅga with the left hand, nor should it be left with its top uncovered;
the cleansing of Śiva should be performed with a soft, pure cloth."
"One should smear the blue-throated [deity] with saffron and the lunar knots. Thus it is said:
"In the absence of these various substances, one may perform the rite mentally."
And it has been said:
"The golden [image] should be white and fragrant, with two red fruits;
one should adorn the maker with various jewels, such as earrings and necklaces."
If the fruit is not obtained, however, it should be given mentally in the form of a material substance.

Then, after the offering of form (rūpa), the waving of lights (ārātrika), the ritual purification with incense (nīrājana), and the sipping of water (ācamana), one should request permission and worship the limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅga). That is as follows:
having offered perfume, flowers, clothing, ornaments, gold, jewels, and so forth, with the root mantra ending in "namaḥ," and having bowed again and again—
Then one should offer incense and a lamp to Śambhu with the root mantra ending in "svāhā";
likewise, the water for sipping (ācamana) is offered first, followed by the worship of the night-guardian (rātrika) with the weapon-mantra (hetimantra).
Having raised that [liṅga], which possesses substance and is well-consecrated, with the armor-mantra (*kavaca-āṇu*) ending in *svāhā*,
one should again perform the encircling of Śambhu with flowers and water;
then, with the weapon-mantra (*hetimantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should offer the umbrella, the chowrie, and the mirror.
One should offer song, instrumental music, and dance with the root mantra *namonta*, according to one's means; may the mind find fulfillment therein. Thus it is said.
Likewise, immediately thereafter, one should fumigate [the area] with incense that is being intensely burned inside a vessel filled with smokeless, glowing embers.
"Always sounding with his left hand a beautiful bell of steady resonance,
and holding aloft incense as directed therein," thus it is said.
Likewise:
the *ārātrika* rite with many burning lamps filled with oil.
These [offerings], beginning with curd and consecrated with unbroken grains (akṣata), were placed in various worthy vessels.
Having wandered around three times, [he should drink] three handfuls of cool water. Thus [it is said].
And it is said thus:
"Having created a splendor with rows of lamps and the like, joined with a profusion of flowers,
and endowed with the fragrance of incense, one should thoroughly fumigate [the site]."
Having performed the *ārātrika* ceremony with wicks of five, seven, nine, eleven, and so forth, using lamps fed with ghee, accompanied by songs, instrumental music, and other auspicious rites.
Having sprinkled fragrant water— contained in vessels of gold, silver, and so forth, or placed in conch shells— three times, one should offer the *ācamana* with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should also offer the gift of the parasol and the chowries, as well as the mirror, song, and dance.
Having meditated upon the God, who is perfectly satisfied and an ocean of boundless compassion,
and having received the command from the Lord, one should worship the limbs of enjoyment.

Having worshipped Śiva with "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva," one should then attract Śiva’s heart with the "hook" (aṅkuśa) mudrā while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart," and worship that white-colored [form] in the southeast.
Then, having worshipped Śiva again with "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva," one should then [worship] with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart."

Thus, having drawn forth the heart of Śiva by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, one should worship it in the southeast (*āgneyī*) as white in color. Having fully worshipped Śiva with "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva," one should then draw forth the Heart from the heart of Śiva by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart" and worship it in the southeast as white in color. With "Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the Head," one should [worship] the Head-mantra, yellow in color, from the five heads in the northeast (*īśāna*). With "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the Crest," one should draw forth the red-colored Crest from the five crests; [one should worship it] in the southwest (*nairṛta*) with "Oṃ hīṃ ka haiṃ, obeisance to the Armor."

Thus, having drawn forth the black armor (*kavaca*) from all the limbs, one should worship the fire-colored weapon (*astra*) in the ten hands with the mantra "Oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ" in the four petals starting from the east, within the wind [quarter]. Likewise—
One should contemplate the collection of limbs as having arisen from the body of knowledge;
the heart, situated upon a lotus petal, is auspicious and white as cow’s milk.
One should worship the yellow-colored head, which has the form of a youth, situated in the northeast.
One should worship the auspicious Śikhā, who has the luster of vermilion, is bent by the weight of her breasts,
resides upon the leaf of Nairṛta, and is adorned with various jewels.
With a terrifying mouth of gaping fangs, formidable, massive, and radiant as a black bee.
One should worship [the deity] situated in the vessel of Vāyu with their respective mantras in due order;
one should worship the Weapon (astra) in the four directions, whose body is composed of jewels and who is most terrifying.
All these limbs are endowed with divine splendor;
they have one face, three eyes, and display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
"One should worship the god Sadāśiva, who is ever-content with the limbs of enjoyment. Thus [it is said].
In some places, the [deities] beginning with Hṛdaya are said to have four faces and four hands;
in both cases, they are described as having [the same attributes], such as the trident, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
As it is stated elsewhere:
"One should place [the syllable] near the right knee, the heart in the vessel of fire,
and the head near the left knee in the northeast."
One should place four formidable weapons in the directions starting from the east: the *cūḍā* near the right shoulder and the *varma* near the left shoulder.

Now, an objection may be raised: how can it be stated here that the heart and other organs are situated near the right knee and so forth, located in directions such as the southeast (āgneyī), given that there is the possibility of deviation in the case of a temple facing west?

It is not so; for even there, all the limbs remain in that very same state because Śiva is always facing the east. When, by some means, the grace [of the deity] becomes directed toward the west, then the five *arghya* vessels and the mantras of the *nidhana-sthāna* for the Blessed Lord Śiva-bhaṭṭāraka have already been stated by the words taken from the scriptures. It should be understood that it remains exactly the same now as well. Here, regarding the procedure for the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth of the limbs such as the Heart situated within the limbs of enjoyment (*bhoga-aṅga*), one should know the method to be described later in the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa-pūjā*) concerning the entire temple (*prāsāda*).

Thus, the worship pertaining to the *niṣkala* (partless) temple has been described as being appropriately performed with a single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*). Now, the [worship] pertaining to the *sakala* (manifested) temple is also described as having a single enclosure. [Objection: But surely this mantra is based on the phonemes of the *mātṛkā*; it is both *sakala* and *niṣkala*. If it is argued that the *sakala* denotes the *sakala*, while the *niṣkala* denotes the *niṣkala*, that is incorrect. For it was stated previously: "He who knows Sadāśiva here as both *sakala* and *niṣkala*... and so forth; it is not as you suggest. In this context, the state of being both *sakala* and *niṣkala* is intended merely as a distinction between the phonemes. And it has been said:
The supreme seed-syllable, the universal form, the imperishable Lord who is the self of the universe, should be known as the designator of Śiva; it stands pervading the entire universe.
Therefore, all that consists of speech is worshipped by yogis as the universal form,
the great seed-syllable, conjoined with the twelve vowels.
Having formed the eleven seed-syllables (*bīja*) joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*), and no others—
