beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with *namaḥ*— one should assign these minor seed-syllables to the faces beginning with Sadyojāta at the time of worship.
The six limbs, beginning with the heart, are long vowels accompanied by the *visarga*, in their respective order:
*namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *vaṣaṭ*. (p. 121) These are joined with [the six syllables].
The syllables beginning with *praṇava* (Om) should be joined [to the mantra], for they bring about the accomplishment of all rites.
One should place that seed-syllable, joined with the *bindu*, along with the three measures (*mātrā*).
Then, having placed the sixth spoke, one should join the letter *A* at the crown;
above that, there should be a circle of the *bindu*, shaped like the upper half of a crescent moon.
Then there is the sound in the form of a staff, situated between two points.
Then there is Trikuṭilā, Śakti, and Nādānta Viśvarūpaka; thus has the Sakala (with parts) been described. Now hear about the Niṣkala (without parts).
The single divine great seed-syllable *mū*, which is powerful through its dissolution,
is then said to be "partless" (*niṣkala*) when joined with the five limbs.
In this context, the limbs [of the mantra] end with *namaḥ* and begin with the *praṇava*;
the weapon-mantra (*astra*) should end with *huṃ phaṭ*, and there is no eye-mantra (*netra*).
"It is said that there is only one enclosure for both the daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites performed by people.

Now, an objection is raised: "In all cases, the requirement of five enclosures for the entire temple (prāsāda) is heard [in the scriptures]. How then can there be only one enclosure there? True. In some places, both the daily and occasional rites are said to have five enclosures; in other places, however, it is stated that the daily rite has one enclosure and the occasional rite has five. Therefore, this has been proclaimed here for the sake of clarifying those distinctions. And it is said in the *Ṣaṭsahasrika*:
"One should conceive of the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) as pervaded by the measure of the Sun."
Having joined it with the ray (the letter *aṃ*), the seed-syllable of the Moon becomes "unborn" (*anāsuta*).
(122) I shall explain the extraction of the mantra for the entire [deity] as it exists:
one should first utter the syllable Īśāna, which is pervaded by *ojas*.
Know the third to be Puruṣa, and likewise the fifth to be Dakṣiṇa;
the seventh is Vāmadeva, and after that is Sadyojāta.
The ninth [mantra] is endowed with the *rasa* (the syllable *vaṃ*); these are proclaimed as the five Brahmans.
These mantras are illuminated by the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning and joined with the word "salutation" (*namaḥ*) at the end.
The first two belong to Sadyojāta, and the heart is marked by the rays;
know that the fourth is the head, which is named after Īśvara.
The Prauka-hasta is to be known as Śivā, endowed with the universal form (viśvarūpa).
The eighth is celebrated as the armor (tanutra), while the tenth is considered the eye (netra).
The weapon (astra) is declared to be the Moon; it is named Śiva by Śikhidhvaja.
Namah, svāhā, svadhā, vauṣaṭ, huṃ, vaṣaṭ, and phaṭ, in this sequence.
One should sequentially apply the six seed-syllables (*jāti*) to the heart and the other limbs;
mantras ignited by the syllable *oṃ* and joined with these seed-syllables bestow their fruits.
Thus have the Brahmans and the limbs been described by me to you;
now I shall state the Śiva-mantra known by the name Prāsāda.
From Īśāna, one should extract the number of Rudras (eleven), known as the "upward-rising ray" (proddhaccāṃśu);
it stands upon the cool root (mūlaka) pervaded by herbs (auṣadha).
It consists of a half-moon and the Nāda situated between two Bindus.
That which is the universal form ending with that [state], its crookedness is the state of the three abodes.
Thus, this temple-mantra has been meditated upon by the God of gods;
it is known as the single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*), which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
At the time of initiation, one should worship Śiva together with the weapons of the world-protectors;
one should fashion the weapon-mantras of the world-lords beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of the *śikhā* (topknot), one should then utter *phaṭ* and *phaḍ*.

This is known as the "Half-Moon" (*ardhacandrasa*). One should not apply that [mantra], which consists of Kāmadeva together with the Ṛṣis, namely the Great Pāśupata weapon (*mahāpāśupatāstra*), to the body.
One should employ the Sadyojāta form-mantra as the Prāsāda mantra;
the Prāsāda has been described as having parts (sakala), and now it is described as being without parts (niṣkala).
The medicine is indeed the universal form, called Rudra, the solar orb;
it is the conjunction of the sound (nāda) for the sake of the moon, as well as the visarga and the curved letter (kuṭila).
The supreme, partless mantra is Śiva himself, the eternally auspicious (Sadāśiva),
the all-pervading Lord who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men, accompanied by his five limbs.
He who possesses the rays of light is the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa), while the Lord with his consort is said to be the Head.
The sixth [limb] is thus to be known as the *śikhā*, and the eighth shall be the *tanutra*. One should utter the *astra* mantra, which is the *viśvarūpa* with the moon (*śaśin*) and ending in *phaṭ*.
One should fashion the limbs of Śiva beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
"This is the enclosure, which accomplishes all desired aims. Thus [it is said].

But is it not the case that the mantra of the form (mūrti) has been declared to be partless (niṣkala) and identified with the Heart? How then can it be said, as previously cited, that one should fashion the form by means of Sadyojāta? However, there is another alternative view, so there is no fault.

And it is said: "The form [of the deity] may be by means of the Sadyojāta [mantra], or else by means of the Heart [mantra]. Now, one might object: "Since the primary [form] exists, what is the purpose of the secondary [one] here, given that the impartite (niṣkala) alone is intended? True. However, because this section is devoted to establishing the worship of both the with-form (sakala) and the impartite (niṣkala), both are presented as the form in both cases; thus, no distinction between primary and secondary intention is made here. In some places, even the temple is considered "with-form," and the limbs [of the mantra] also end with the word "namaḥ. And it is stated in the Sarvajñānottara: "All [the mantras] are joined with the Bindu, possessing the luster of pure jasmine and the moon."
The mantras, preceded by the syllable Oṃ and followed by the word "namaskāra," are thus joined.
O Six-faced One, the arcane mantras should be employed in the fire-oblation (homa) joined with the word "svāhā";
however, there are no *bindu* or crest-mantras (*śikhā-mantra*) for the group of six [mantras] belonging to that [deity].
"Those [mantras] which possess *viṣkaṃbhakas* and are always ablaze are remembered as having terrible power, like the sun.

Furthermore, one should not ask how this mantra, being deficient in its limbs (*aṅga*), can be worshipped, given the statement: "A mantra devoid of its *aṃśaka* is fruitless and brings suffering to men. This is because this particular mantra lacks *aṃśakas*. And it has been said:
"O Six-faced One, for the syllable of *Māyā*, there are the *prāsāda* and *pravaṇa* [as its *aṃśakas*]."
One should not assign a portion to the Navātman and Aghora deities.
"For these sovereign lords of the kings of mantras are considered to be beneficial to all;
they accomplish all purposes in all undertakings, so one should not destroy them through conceptualization. Thus it is said.
"One should always meditate eternally on Śiva, whose chest faces east;
Śiva faces the east, while Lakṣmī faces west, her body composed of [his] digits.
Likewise:
when there is a door in the west, one should contemplate Īśa and Puruṣa there;
Sadyojāta should be in the east, and Ghoratman and Vāmadeva as before.
The implements for enjoyment and the practitioner facing north, as previously described,
should place the food offering, rows of lamps, and so forth at the entrance.
"The observation of the root door must always be performed facing the northeast (Īśāna); it should always be established facing east, or else established facing west. Thus [it is said].

In this context, because the Lord Sadāśiva who is being worshipped possesses a purity like that of pure crystal, and because beyond that [crystal] there is the luminous form consisting of the five Brahma-mantras—which are fashioned as a manifest form through the configuration of a staff (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*) and are composed of white color—and because of the purity of the Supreme Niṣkala Śiva, who is established by the Niṣkala Śiva-mantra that touches Śiva at the *dvādaśānta* (the twelve-finger space above the head), which is condensed in the form of the supreme invocation (*parāvāhana*) and resembles pure crystal; and because after the rite of *sakalīkaraṇa*, he consists of the nature of supreme light (*paratejas*) pervading all limbs in the form of the rite of *paramīkaraṇa*; and because he has been rendered immortal (*mṛtīkṛta*) by the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) with the *dhenumudrā* showering nectar—it is stated that the purity of the Lord Sadāśiva, as well as that of the officiating priest (*yājaka*), is established as being like pure crystal, just like Paramaśiva. Likewise, in the ultimate sense, the faces of [the deity] must also possess purity like that of crystal. While the face of Īśāna, which resembles crystal, remains as such, the same would apply to the other faces; however, for the sake of stabilizing the colors—saffron, black, and white—of the faces starting from the East and ending with Indra and Kubera, the Lord Sadāśiva performs the worship of Śiva with the *Tatpuruṣa* and other faces using the *Sadākala Prasāda* mantra.
p.

126) Nevertheless, the practitioner, having worshipped Śiva—endowed with the Brahmāṅgas—in the manner prescribed and according to the method described up to the *layāṅga*, should request permission by saying four times: "Oṃ Hāṃ! O Blessed One, grant me leave; I shall worship the *bhogāṅgas*. Then, having worshipped the Mūla-mantra along with the Brahmāṅgas for Śiva, even in the case of the five-fold enclosure (*pañcāvaraṇa*), he should sequentially extract the mantras starting from Īśāna from the body of Śiva from their respective locations using their own respective mantras and the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*.
He should worship Īśāna in the vessels of the [four] directions, beginning with the East, and worship Nara in the eastern vessel.
Aghora is in the southern vessel, and likewise Vāmadeva is in the northern one.
The Unborn (Ajāta) is in the western vessel, the Heart is in the fire-vessel;
the Head and the Topknot are in the vessel of Īśāna, and Śiva is in the vessels of Nairṛta and Vāyu.
In front and in the four directions, one should place the King of Weapons, which is terrifying;
white, yellow, very black, red, and white, respectively.
They possess a uniform radiance of white, yellow, reddish-brown, blue, and red colors;
they have one face and three eyes, and are the incarnations of Śiva’s knowledge.
Starting from the east, [one should worship] Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śivottama,
Ekanetra, Atridra, Mūrti, and the supreme Śivā.
One should worship the deity named Śikhaṇḍīśa, known as Śrīkhaṇḍa, on each and every petal.
In the lotuses of the third enclosure, the lords of the Gaṇas are situated in sequence:
Nandīśvarī, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Mahākāla, and Bhṛṅgirāṭ.
Vṛṣabha, Kārttikeya, Pārvatī,
and Caṇḍanāyaka possess a splendor equal to that of rubies, as does the milk of the cow of speech.

In the fourth enclosure, the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped according to the sequence of their respective directions; they hold a trident and the gesture of granting boons (varada) in the right hands, and a garland and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in the left hands.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yakṣa, and Maheśvara;
Īśāna and Nairṛta are to be worshipped [in the corners], while Brahmā and Viṣṇu are on the left.
In the fifth [day], one should worship the weapons of the world-protectors (lokapālas), beginning with the discus (cakra) in their proper sequence.
The wise should perform the meditation upon Indra and the other world-protectors, as well as their respective weapons, in due order according to the procedure that will be described.
In that case, when the mandala is arranged, this is considered the indicative sign:
it is said to have only one enclosure, which is eternal and bestows all fruits.
And that is as stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasra*:
"Having thus performed the worship of the Lord, one should meditate upon Īśāna in the northeast corner as white as cow's milk and worship him with flowers and other offerings."
One should place the Puruṣa-mantra, resembling the petals of the Karṇikāra flower, on the eastern petal;
and Aghora, comparable to crushed collyrium, on the southern petal.
Vāmadeva, who resembles the pomegranate flower, is always in the north;
while Ajāta, possessing the luster of a conch, jasmine, and the moon, is in the west.
Having worshipped the Heart-mantra in the southeast, which has the luster of a pearl,
one should place the Head-mantra in the northeast, resembling clear lapis lazuli.
One should meditate on the tuft (śikhā) in the south-western quarter, possessing a luster equal to the form of lightning;
the armor (kavaca), however, is black in color in the north-western direction [and so forth];
and the eye (netra) is to be meditated upon in the east, possessing the radiance of the moon, the sun, and fire.
One should place the weapon on the tips of the petals, resembling a blazing fire.
In this manner, one should assign the faces and the limbs to the locations of enjoyment.
Indraka and the others, whose natures are like reflections, [are located] at the tips of the petals;
there, one should worship the Vidyeshas, beginning with Ananda.
One should worship the Gaṇeśas at the corners of the pedestal and the Lokapālas at the base of the pedestal.
"Then, when the weapon-mantras are situated in their respective places upon the Brahma-stone,
one should thus deposit the coverings of the pervasive Lord according to the distinctions of His own pervasion."
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should conceive of Vidyeśāna as merged at the end of the thirteen [vowels];
one should worship Gāyatrī, who is present therein, as the mistress of the Gaṇas."
The heart-mantra of the world-protectors should be known as that which fulfills all desires;
one should then formulate the blazing Pāśupata weapon-mantra.
Thus, for the purpose of their worship, the procedure for the mantras has been demonstrated;
alternatively, one may assign the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra) to all of them.
This has been described differently in various treatises; here, however, the primary [meaning] is stated.
Thus, the statements from various scriptures have been gathered together and arranged here.

Now, this enclosure (*āvṛti*) of Śiva is also treated like the royal service (*rājopacāra*). Therefore, having performed for the deities of that enclosure the eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and firm presence (*sannirodha*), followed by the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the guest-water (*arghya*), and flowers—up to the end; and thereafter, having offered perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, water for sipping, the waving of lights (*ārātrika*), and so forth, as well as the food offering (*naivedya*), drinking water, and another sipping of water according to the procedure to be described; and having placed a flower upon Śiva with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) and performed the act of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*), one should display the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*) and the great seal (*mahāmudrā*). Herein [is the procedure] for the deities of the enclosure. (p. 129)

Indeed, by means of Śiva’s splendor (*śivatejas*), there is the supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*) of the temple. Following this supreme transformation, one should offer the *āvaraṇa* (enclosures) and the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings to the deities. Here, the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) is for the purpose of attaining the qualities of Śiva for oneself. Furthermore, it is for the sake of oneness with the Lord and for the union of the limbs and the worshipper with Śiva. In this context, the offering of the water for the feet, the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and so forth, as a collective whole, should be performed according to the previously mentioned method. Having worshipped the limbs of enjoyment with their respective mantras and having displayed the *āvāhana* and other mudrās, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Śiva with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ sauṃ śivāya puṣpaṃ namaḥ*. Then, having displayed the *dhenumudrā* and the *mahāmudrā*, one should offer the water for the feet with: *oṃ hāṃ oṃ hauṃ śivāya pādyaṃ namaḥ*. Likewise, one should offer the water for sipping with the word *svadhā* at the end [of the mantra], and similarly offer flowers with *puṣpaṃ namaḥ*.

Likewise, one should offer incense with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with [the root mantra] ending in *svāhā*, the water of honor (*arghya*) with [the root mantra] ending in *svāhā*, and flowers with [the root mantra] ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Then, with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva, [I offer] fragrance," one should present the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) and so forth using the previously mentioned mantra. And it has been said:
"The components of enjoyment may be offered separately, or all at once as a single great offering.
Likewise, the food offering (*naivedya*) is prescribed as follows:
One should worship these [deities] in sequence with their respective mantras, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth;
however, for these, there is neither the veiling (kuṇṭhana) nor the eightfold immortalization (aṣṭamṛtīkaraṇa).
For each of these, the wise have prescribed a set of eight ritual acts;
bathing, lighting lamps, and sleeping [with the image] are not performed separately.
The meal for those [disciples] beside the Lord, as well as his own, is proclaimed;
half of that shall be the food offering (naivedya) for him, served in separate vessels.
Alternatively, when the [guests] have been purified, one may offer a single portion of sacrificial food consecrated by mantras;
or, once they are satiated, one should give them water for rinsing the mouth, preceded by the wiping of their hands.

One should offer betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) and mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*), which indeed causes its fragrance; likewise, the food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth, such as *khaṇḍana*, *pūrikā*, *jādu*, *upadhārikā*, along with roots, fruits, and various side dishes (*vyañjana*), scented with camphor, glistening, and accompanied by milk-drinks, fresh plantains, jackfruit, and mangoes, as well as various juices and drinks slightly scented with perfumes, together with water and other items. Having protected [the offering] with the Astra-mantra and the Kavaca-mantra, and having performed the *dhenumudrā* and the *bhṛkuṭīmudrā*, one should offer the water with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*. Then, having offered a flower upon the head of the deity with the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*, and displaying the *dravyamudrā* while saying "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Giver of Substances (*Dravyadāyai namaḥ*"), one should visualize the entire collection of substances as being complete. Then, having given the water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the root mantra ending in *svadhā*, and having offered hand-rubbing powder, mouth-perfume, camphor, nutmeg (*taka*), cloves (*kola*), and *jātīphala*, as well as fragrant betel leaf that has purified the mouth and other parts, all with the *dānamudrā* and the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should present the mirror, the parasol, and the fly-whisk (*cāmara*). And it is said in the *Śrī Kālottara*:
One should devoutly offer two kinds of food offerings in various vessels:
milk-rice mixed with ghee, as well as fruits, roots, sprouts, and curd.
Indeed, there were sweetmeat balls (*khaṇḍakhādya*), various kinds of rice dishes,
as well as *aśokavarti*, *śākulī*, *pūrikā*, and *dhārikā*.
One should heat pure tubers and roots, as well as many side-dishes and milk, for the deity.
These should be offered individually to the faces and limbs, or else all together as one.
One should offer water for drinking, water for sipping, and mouth-perfume to the Lord.
"And he [should offer] the moon and betel, preceded by the rubbing of the hands. Thus it is said.
Thus, at each junction of the day (pratisandhya), he should worship with these and other eight flowers beginning with *vāruṇa*.
And it has been said:
Water is for Varuṇa, flowers for Soma, ghee, milk,
and curd for Prajāpati, and likewise incense and lamps for Agni.
Flowers and the like are [the offering] of Bhava; the fifth is that of the Vanaspati (trees);
that of the Earth consists of bulbs, roots, and so forth; and that of Vāyu is fragrant sandalwood.

"The flower called Śuddha and the Śiva-flower— these eight flowers are said to be always auspicious for those whose minds are established in equanimity during the offering of the *arghya* and other rites.
Or alternatively:
First, a flower should be offered upon the seat with a pure mind;
the offering to the image should be performed with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), while another flower is used for the subsequent [offerings].
By the offering of five flowers, one should arrange the five limbs;
likewise, with the eighth, Śiva is worshipped—this is declared to be the "Eight-Flower Rite" (aṣṭapuṣpikā).
And these eight flowers are common to all;
they bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*) in all the scriptures (*āgama*).
One should worship [it] at one time, two times, or three times a day— common to all castes alike—
at dawn, at midday, and likewise when the sun has set.
One should worship with supreme devotion according to the rite of the eight flowers,
especially for the poor, the helpless, children, women, and the ignorant.
For those who enjoy worldly pleasures, for those afflicted by disease, for those whose souls are absorbed in meditation,
for those devoted to the scriptures of Śiva, and for those whose hearts are intent on various spiritual accomplishments— [for all these, there is no death].
p.
132) "The emission of those who are both attached and detached has been described as the 'Flower' (puṣpikā).
Thus [it is said] in the Kālottara.
One should properly worship with eight flowers during the invocation, the offering of arghya, the worship, the bathing, the incense, the unguent, and the dismissal of the food offering.
In the offering of flowers, in the arghya vessels, as well as in bathing, sipping water (ācamana),
washing, and sprinkling, one should employ the seven waters.
Incense should be offered everywhere; having understood what remains, one should perform worship.

Thus, having worshipped with the eight flowers for the sake of liberation arising from one's own speech, mind, and body, and for the sake of union with Śiva, one should offer a *pavitraka* made of *kuśa*, *dūrvā*, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ! To Śiva, who possesses all principles—the principle of the self, the principle of knowledge, and the principle of Śiva—together with His limbs, svāhā! Thus one should present the *pavitraka*.

If he is a householder, he should offer [the offering] while reciting the *mantra* beginning with the *Śivatattva*. Then, as before, after the offering of incense, lamps, water for sipping (*ācamana*), the waving of lights (*ārātrikā*), and so forth, he should place his own *liṅga* with the root *mantra* and display the *dhenumudrā* and the *mahāmudrā* with the *śakti-mantra* ending in *vaiṣaṭ*. Alternatively, at the conclusion of the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitra*), he should recite the root *mantra* up to the *dvādaśānta* and offer handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and the like. And it is said: "One should place the sacred thread, which has become like a crown, upon the head; it removes the exhaustion born from the activities of speech, mind, and body performed daily."
Because it protects one from falling, it is therefore called *pavitraka*;
immediately after its worship, there is the attainment of the state that transcends primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Having uttered the *paramāntika*, one should place the temple as before;
and upon its sprouting, one should perform the ritual according to rule with the previously mentioned mudrā and weapon.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth to Śiva as before,
[one should worship] with the five glorious great sounds, and with mirrors, parasols, and fly-whisks.
Then one should greet him with songs, dances, postures, and hymns of praise.

In accordance with this statement, the worshipper should meditate upon Śiva—who is accompanied by his consorts and attendants, who stands outside the sacrificial hall, who is being praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, who is gratified by the worshipper’s adoration, whose pair of lotus feet are the object of all Upaniṣads, who is an ocean of the nectar of boundless compassion, who grants the desired fruits to devoted suppliants, and who has turned his face toward him—and then, having consecrated the rosary with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [he should recite]: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the rosary*.

Thus, having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having formed the *mālā-mudrā*, one who knows the procedure for the protection of the self-mantra should begin the recitation (*japa*) preceded by the *sandhāna* (union). Furthermore, as it is said in the *Śrīkālottara*:
"One should diligently contemplate one's own body in the midst of both moons;
by that, the body becomes composed of nectar, and its meditation cannot be disturbed even by the gods."
Self-protection has been fully explained; now the protection of the mantra is being described.
One should install the mantras within the womb of the Śakti, neither in the Puruṣa nor in Śiva at that time.
Those situated in the Puruṣa are powerless, while those situated in Śiva possess peaceful splendor.
Therefore, mantras that have entered into Śakti bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation;
Śakti is the blissful Ādhāra-vidyā, the power of Śiva, which bestows the fruit of Śiva.
Auspicious, ever like the sun in its full orb,
she is the Mother of Mantra, the Supreme Power, the primordial Kuṇḍalinī;
she dwells eternally in the region of the heart, resembling the sun, the moon, and fire.
That one [nāḍī] should be known as threefold, according to the divisions of iḍā, piṅgalā, and so forth.
Hidden within the *suṣumnā* and known only through the mouth of the Guru, she extends from the navel to the *dvādaśānta*, pervading that space by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
For yogins, she travels along the path of Śiva— from the trident, the path, the water, and so forth, up to the end of the twelve— by means of the various movements of going and returning.
"By relying on the state of the Supreme (parābhāva), one attains supreme bliss;
having thus understood this through Śakti and the rest, one becomes capable of protecting the mantra."
As it is said elsewhere:

"The Śakti situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), having gone into the interior of the navel-lotus and having ascended the wheel of the foundation (ādhāracakra), should purify the supreme digit (kalā)."
"The fire at the pericarp of the heart-lotus, consisting of the digits of the sun and moon, creates the garland of phonemes; one should always recite the mantra situated therein. Thus it is said.

Likewise, in the Śrī Kālottara: "The signified (vācya), the signifier (vācaka), power (śakti), the self (ātman), and likewise the mind (manas)— having established the concentration of the mind, one should begin [the practice]."
The Supreme Lord, whose form is light, resides in the center of the heart-lotus;
he is stainless, resembling crystal, and the source of all radiant splendor.
His power consisting of sound has issued forth like a great flame; possessing those attributes, she is the pure substratum, and from her indeed has issued the succession of phonemes (*varṇa*),
which is the progenitor of all mantras and the king of mantras.
Just as a flower emerges from its stalk, and just as the beloved [seed] from the tip, O Śaṅkara,
so too should one remember that rosary and its arising in due order.
One should effect its dissolution into the heart, and likewise its dissolution within the center of the heart.
The mantras of Śiva, whether situated internally or externally,
if they are unified, that which is known as *japa* shall exceed one hundred thousand recitations.
Relying on the yoga of the equinox, one should collect a single akṣa until, indeed,
it has not yet emerged during the great impulsion.
Then one should perform circumambulation of Meru situated on the mountain,
and of the partless mantra situated above it.
And of the pervasive, stainless, and great-souled one who exists in the form of a knot.

O Six-faced One, that which appears as a back is to be avoided for the sake of liberation; however, one should see it as having the luster of crystal in rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika),
and as having the appearance of a *kiṃśuka* flower in rites of attraction (ākṛṣṭi), like a king or a mountain.

For killing, one should meditate on Śiva as having the luster of collyrium; for causing enmity, like the wing of a blue jay; and for expulsion, with a smoky appearance—having thus meditated, one should always recite the mantra.

Recitation is traditionally said to be threefold, according to its nature as *parā*, *paśyantī*, and *vaikharī*. Here, the two terms [recitation and sacrifice] are explained through the eightfold ablution (*snāna*).
Furthermore, the sacrifice is revealed as being performed either in a thousand [repetitions] or in a secluded place.

Concentration accompanied by the inner essence (*sagarbha*) is superior to restraint devoid of concentration (*dhyānavarjita*). Indeed, that which is free from the inner essence (*nirgarbha*) becomes a hundred times more fruitful.
This should be practiced by one who desires to ascend [to higher stages], as it bestows success in all accomplishments (*siddhis*).
Relying upon one's own capacity, one should begin the silent recitation (*upāṃśujapa*).
Capacity is declared to be of two kinds, O daughter, consisting of the nature of the Sun and the Moon.
Moving from the heart to the end of the three folds, she dwells within the fortnights.
On the day, at sunrise, when the breath is active, that which desires liberation should recite [the mantra].
At moonrise and during the night, it should be recited by one who desires devotion.
Having discerned the inhalation and exhalation, the recitation (japa) should be performed and not otherwise;
the recitation performed with the vital breath (marut) abiding in the suṣumnā bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
When the sun has set in the sky and the rays of the moon have not yet arisen,
that state should be known as pure consciousness alone, free from all grasping.
The wise know that knowledge, which consists of pure existence, is devoid of all means of valid cognition;
this Kālottara knowledge has thus been explained to you in brief.
Thus, in the heart-lotus, knowledge arises as pure existence alone;
this is the supreme secret, which must not be disclosed to anyone.
This knowledge, residing in the oral instruction of the Guru, is very difficult to obtain;
it should be given to those whose impurities have been fully ripened, and not otherwise, O son.
Then, by means of the movement of day and night, the breath (prāṇa) should flow with compassion.
Having attained contact with that there, the elemental being should always perform recitation.
In this teaching, the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is for those desiring both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
when the life-force (jīva) is established in Piṅgalā, one who desires liberation should always perform recitation.
One should recite [the mantra] while situated within the Suṣumṇā for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
likewise, the Iḍā and other [nāḍīs] are recommended for pacification and the nourishment of the body.
O son of Kṛttikā, Piṅgalā is to be known as present in battle, Suṣumnā in eating and sexual intercourse, and [the central channel] in all undertakings.
(137) One should recite the mantras while pregnant with their meaning, yet without knowing the names [of the deities] in reality.
O Destroyer of Krauñca, I shall now explain the pervasive mantra in brief.
The sun is situated in the midst of fire, and the moon is in the midst of the sun;
fire is the throat of the sun, and likewise the sixteenth digit is the moon.
With six, two, and three [breaths] in the three fires, one should proceed to that which consists of the power of the Sun.
The seat of the rasa is the region of the heart; there, Soma has attained its dissolution.
The lunar power (cāndrī-śakti) is said to have the form of a sprout of the principles (tatva).
Having understood this, the wise person should perform the recitation with diligent effort. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the characteristics of recitation and so forth are written down precisely according to the readings of various scriptures (*āgamas*). As it is said: "A right-hand thread (*dakṣiṇa-sūtra*) of one hundred and eight [strands] is always excellent; half of that is praised as middling; [half of that again] is the lowest."
Born from rudrākṣa, it brings great prosperity, bestows liberation, and is supremely auspicious—
whether with one face, three faces, four faces, or five.
Or it may be performed with six faces; however, one should avoid using mixed [faces] therein. That which has three times the measure of fruit is declared to be the "eldest" (jyeṣṭha).
A chickpea the size of a jujube fruit constitutes the medium and inferior [measures];
however, the *nivartana* has not been specified, and it should be performed auspiciously as previously described.
One should perform the binding with the *nāgapāśa*, the *sāvitra*, or the one called *brahma*;
however, the *meruvākya* must be used for the untying of the knot, and one must never transgress this rule.
One should wash it with the *sadyojāta* mantra and rub it with the *vāmadeva* mantra.
One should fumigate with *bahurūpa* and smear with *puruṣa*;
one should consecrate each [substance] one hundred times with the fifth [mantra].
With Meruṃca as the fifth, one should recite each mantra a hundred times;
likewise, one should recite with the Ghora-mantra, having Meruṃca as the fifth.
The eight mudrās should be displayed, and one should worship each one in succession;
having worshipped Meru with five [offerings], one should worship it according to the sequence, just as one worships Śiva.
Holding the ring finger and the thumb together, one should perform mental recitation;
one obtains merit a hundred crore times greater than before—of this there is no doubt.
One should perform the whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa) using the thumb and the middle finger;
thus, the fruit of a hundred thousand recitations is produced from a mere hundred recitations.
One should perform the recitation with the thumb and forefinger,
ensuring the connection between syllable and syllable is neither too fast nor too slow.
One shall obtain a thousandfold fruit; let there be no false speech.
For the sake of enjoyment, one should follow the path of creation, but for the sake of liberation, one should gradually attenuate [the self].
The practitioner of mantra should not cross over the *meru*; by crossing it, one incurs fault.
Having stepped over [the beads] with the middle finger and thumb, one should perform the recitation in a whisper (*upāṃśu*).
Then, by reciting it one hundred times, the fruit of ten thousand recitations is produced.
Having pressed the index finger against the thumb, one should perform the recitation while making it audible.
"Free from the conjunction of the perishable and the imperishable.
Likewise:
"One should perform mental recitation while pressing down with the ring finger and the thumb."
By performing one hundred and eight [recitations] in this manner, the fruit shall be multiplied ten millionfold.
One should perform the whispered recitation (*upāṃśu-japa*), moving the middle finger across [the beads].
Then, by reciting it a hundred times, the fruit of a hundred thousand recitations arises for him.
Pressing the index finger against the thumb, one should perform the recitation while speaking aloud;
or else, one should diligently prepare a rosary that is without a central bead (*meru*).
The merit of that [other] is a hundredfold greater than that of the rosary;
there is no fault in bypassing it, for it has surpassed even Mount Meru. Thus it is said.
Likewise—
one should perform mental recitation while pressing the ring finger and the thumb;
by means of one hundred and eight [recitations], the fruit becomes ten millionfold.
Pressing the middle finger and the thumb together, one should perform the recitation in a whisper;
then, from a hundred recitations, the fruit of a hundred thousand is produced for him.
Pressing the index finger and thumb together, one should perform the recitation and speech;
the joining of syllable to syllable should be neither too fast nor too slow.
One shall obtain a thousandfold fruit; there is no falsehood in these words.
Likewise:
"One should have a garland made from unbroken, fresh, thorny flowers—
either with one face, three faces, or especially with four faces."
With six faces for the sake of all accomplishments, and likewise with five faces.
And with seven, eight, or nine faces, and with ten or eleven faces.
The rosary should be fashioned; the pure garland of beads is thus described.
Having worshipped that thread with the heart-mantra and having smeared it with sandalwood paste, one should proceed.
One should rotate the thumb, the ring finger, the middle finger, or the index finger; then,
at the conclusion of the Meru [mudrā], there is the rotation of the Lord of Mountains.
One hundred and eight recitations should be performed for the crossing of Mount Meru.
Likewise:
"Placing [the thumb] at the base of the middle finger, while reciting the mantra, one should slowly draw out each bead. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"A wise man should not overstep Meru, the cause of creation and dissolution;
yet even if overstepped, it causes no fault, provided it is devoid of Meru and remains within the limits of the Gaṇas."
One should string the garland using gold, silver, lead, iron, and so forth;
having joined mouth to mouth, [one should fix] the *meru* bead with its face upward.
One should [fashion] the Nāgapāśinī [noose] visibly from linen cloth, silk bands, or threads;
it should have a clearly defined purpose, a cow-tail ring, be silent, free of flaws, and firm.

One should not employ a dilapidated swing, one with a broken rope, one with a frayed cord, one with an uneven opening, or one that moves unsteadily; for through such means, the mantra will certainly not be accomplished.
"O Six-faced One, the rosary must be kept hidden at the time of recitation;
if the rosary comes within the sight of another, the recitation becomes fruitless. Thus [it is said].
Likewise:
"Japa should be performed by those desiring liberation in a manner equal to the vital breath (prāṇa).
For the day is indeed the upward-moving breath (ūrdhvaprāṇa), and the night is the downward-moving breath (apāna)."
Having properly performed the self-identification with the Śiva-mantra and likewise with Śiva and Śakti individually, one should recite the mantra— whether aloud, in a whisper, or mentally.
The mantra-deity possesses a power known as the "garland of mantras" which is like a jewel;
the word "yat" (which) clearly generates that [power] for those who hear it indirectly.
In the commentary, it is stated that for rites such as eradication (*uccāṭana*), that [recitation] is whispered (*upāṃśu*); for pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*),
it is one where the sound is perceived by another at a distance of only a foot from the lips.
"The [repetition] consisting of ten thousand words is to be known as such; another is ten million times that.
By means of the connection of the syllables of its feet, reflecting from meaning to meaning and from word to word upon all words with an even mind, one shall attain liberation. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"O Six-faced One, one should not show even one's own end of the rosary to the guru; during the time of recitation, the prayer-bead garland must be kept secret."
If the garland were to belong to another's view, the recitation would be fruitless.
Enough with excessive detail; let us follow the subject at hand. One should mutter [the mantra] beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, preceded by "to Śiva. And it has been said:
"The mantra beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, likewise 'to Śiva, obeisance' (*śivāya namaḥ*)—one should mutter this mentally, with the inner self absorbed in Him."

Having thus recited the aforementioned mantra one hundred and eight times, one should contemplate that recitation as being like the full moon, emerging from the power of the sprout of the moonlight of the heart. Having placed the syllables situated upon the heart-mandala in the palm of the right hand—worshipped with the six limbs and protected by the armor and weapon [mantras] of the heart—and having rested that hand against the region of the heart, one should kneel on the right knee upon the ground and say: "Oṃ!
You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by me.
May accomplishment arise through you, O One who abides everywhere, by your grace."

Having recited thus, one should offer [the mantra] with the words "Accept the recitation for Śiva, svāhā," etc., together with a single *ācāma* (mouth-rinse) into the hand of the one bestowing the boon (*varada*). According to some traditions, this is done with three *cūlikās*. And it is said:
"One should never perform a recitation that is uncounted or confused."
Having performed one hundred and eight repetitions while reciting the root mantra, the wise one—
Placing the right knee upon the ground, one should offer that recitation;
with Śiva on the left, [one should offer] scents with three handfuls of water. Thus it is said.

In this context, it should be understood that the threefold [performance] of the single recitation (*japa*) is for the sake of its stability. Then, having performed the recitation for the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadeva*) for one-tenth of that amount and having offered [the oblation], one should worship Śiva with three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Having displayed the *dhenumudrā* and the *mahāmudrā* with the *śakti-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having offered incense and a lamp with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* as before, and having offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the root mantra ending in *svadhā*, one should take up the *sarṣapa* mixed with salt. Having purified it by means of the previously mentioned rites such as *nirīkṣaṇa*, and having worshipped it with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) upon the heart, one should take out the great lamp—provided with camphor wicks, consecrated by the *dhenumudrā*, and protected by the armor-mantra (*varma*)—three times as before with the *kavaca-mantra* ending in *svāhā*. Having encircled it with three handfuls of cool water and having offered water for sipping, an umbrella, chowries, and so forth, one should address him with this hymn:
Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, who is devoid of qualities, free from action, and the wielder of the trident;
salutation to Śambhu, whose sphere of experience transcends both Śiva and Śakti.
Salutations to Śiva, the partless, the stainless, the yogi;
salutations to Śiva, the cause of perfection and liberation, the self of consciousness.
Salutation to Śiva, the eternal, who brings death to the god of desire;
salutation to Śiva, the man-lion, who wears the skin of an elephant as a garment;
salutation to Śiva, whose lotus-eye is worshipped by Viṣṇu, O beloved!
Homage to Śiva, whose splendor transcends the moon, the sun, and fire;
homage to Śiva, the bestower of the yoga of Śaiva-siddhi and the yoga of the yogis.
Salutations to Śiva, who is within the range of the arrow and who transcends speech and mind;
salutations to Śiva, who dwells upon the mountain peaks of all principles;
salutations to Śiva, the witness of all deeds, the great-eyed one, the Great Soul.
Salutations to Śiva, whose essence is the seed-syllable within the cavity of the heart and who possesses a subtle body;
salutations to Śiva, whose self is permeated by the mantra of true grace.
Salutations to Śiva, who abides in the void-dwelling of mantras;
salutations to Śiva, whose crest is the moon, who wears the crescent, and who is the source of bliss;
salutations to Śiva, who is adorned with sacred ashes and who is the cause of prosperity.
Salutations to Śiva, the lord of all beings, the mass of consciousness, to you.
Salutations to Śiva, the cause of the cessation of the sufferings of birth, old age, and death;
salutations to Śiva, whose mind is eternally contented and whose nature is immortal;
salutations to Śiva, the abode of divine prosperity and the embodiment of compassion.
Salutations to Śiva, the essence of all things, the sole embodiment of excellent qualities;
salutations to Śiva, the kinsman of all worlds, who desires the welfare of others;
salutations to Śiva, who brings about the dissolution [of karma] at the time when actions reach equilibrium.
Salutations to Śiva, who consumes the fire of one’s own delusion and the bonds of karma;
salutations to Śiva, the embodiment of consciousness, the ordainer within the lotus of existence.
Salutations to Śiva, the singular light that expands through the consciousness of the knower.
Salutation to Śiva, who dwells in the lotus of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *śakti*;
salutation to Śiva, whose essence is the sprout of moonlight and whose nature is nectar.
Salutations to Śiva, the lover of the royal swan of the mind-lotus.
Salutations to Śiva, whose form is divine awakening, the Supreme Self;
having worshipped the Lord of Gods with devotion, whoever recites this before you—
By means of this hymn of praise, he goes to that peaceful, supreme state.

Having praised the Supreme Lord with these and other verses, having performed a circumambulation and a prostration with eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*), and having requested, "O Master, I shall perform the fire-rite (*agnikārya*)," he should, by the Lord's command, prepare the general offering water (*sāmānyārghya*). Then, having gone to the fire-sanctuary (*agnyāgāra*) with his own materials, he should kindle the fire produced from the *araṇi* wood or other means in a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) purified by the four rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), or on an altar (*sthaṇḍila*) six fingers high and one cubit in measure. Having ignited it with fuel, he should protect it with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. He should then cast away the portion of the fire belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) toward the southwest corner (*nairṛtikoṇa*) using the weapon-mantra. Then, having purified the remaining materials for the regional oblations (*deśāṃśa-homa*) and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles by means of inspection and the other rites, he should unify the fire with the fire-seed syllable (*vahnibīja*) as will be described. Having worshipped the fire with the *Sadyojāta* and other mantras for the sake of the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), and having offered five oblations with the root mantra (*mūla*), he should address it: "Oṃ hāṃ, you are the Śiva-fire, O Consumer of Oblations. Visualizing the fire as thus consecrated by the five rites beginning with conception, he should offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Then, having sprinkled the girdle of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍamekhalā*) with the water of the general offering while reciting the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*, he should place the armor-mantra upon the Kuśa grass in the east, north, west, and south. Specifically: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā" in the east; "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu" in the west; "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra" in the south; and "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ananta" in the north.
In the north, having worshipped Brahmā and the others, [one should recite]: *oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ vahnaye namaḥ*.

Having thus worshipped and offered five oblations with "svāhā," and having prayed as will be described hereafter, one should visualize the desired face of the fire according to the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Then, [visualizing] the father of the essences (*rasas*)—that fire—in the heart-lotus as before, one should worship Śiva, who is the form of the support for that Gaṅgā and the command, along with the ritual offerings (*upacāras*) ending with the purification (*pavitra*). Having requested the command, "O Blessed One, please satisfy me," and having first performed the placement on the channels (*nāḍīnyāsa*), one should perform a hundred-fold oblation of ghee and other substances according to rule in the place of recitation using the root mantra ending in "svāhā. Having offered oblations with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantras*) at a tenth part of that amount, and having performed the oblation of food and so forth with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ," and then perform the rinsing of the mouth, the rubbing of the hands, and so on. Alternatively, having purified that consciousness of the fire within the heart-lotus by means of the fire, and having drawn it up through the *suṣumnā* channel by exhaling while reciting the root mantra, one should unite it with Paramaśiva. Then, one should satisfy Śiva in that fire of knowledge (*jñānāgni*). As it is said in the *Kālottara*: [The text continues with the citation: "Then, having brought the fire from the hearth (*kuṇḍa*) into the body, one should contemplate the fire of knowledge in the heart. Having united the fire of the body with the fire of knowledge, one should satisfy Śiva in that fire of knowledge. ...and so on, until: "...having satisfied Śiva in that fire of knowledge, one should again bring the fire from the fire of knowledge into the body-fire. Then, having brought the fire from the body into the hearth, one should worship the fire of the hearth as before. Thus ends the section on the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*). Now, the procedure for the offering of the sacrificial pap (*caruhoma*). First, one should prepare the sacrificial pap (*caru*) according to the prescribed method. Then, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the placement of the vessel (*sthālīnyāsa*), and the invocation of the fire (*agnisandhāna*), one should worship the sacrificial pap as before. Then, having offered the sacrificial pap with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," and having performed the oblation of the limbs (*aṅgahoma*) with the limb-mantras, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ. Then, having performed the concluding rites such as the rinsing of the mouth, the rubbing of the hands, and so forth, one should proceed with the dismissal (*visarjana*). Thus ends the procedure for the sacrificial pap. Now, the procedure for the offering of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). One should prepare the sacrificial cake according to the prescribed method. Then, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sprinkling, the placement of the vessel, and the invocation of the fire, one should worship the sacrificial cake as before. Then, having offered the sacrificial cake with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," and having performed the oblation of the limbs with the limb-mantras, one should offer the full oblation with the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ. Then, having performed the concluding rites such as the rinsing of the mouth, the rubbing of the hands, and so forth, one should proceed with the dismissal. Thus ends the procedure for the sacrificial cake. Now, the procedure for the offering of the clarified butter (*ājyahoma*). One should prepare the clarified butter according to the prescribed method. Then, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sprinkling, the placement of the vessel, and the invocation of the fire, one should worship the clarified butter as before. Then, having offered the clarified butter with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," and having performed the oblation of the limbs with the limb-mantras, one should offer the full oblation with the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ. Then, having performed the concluding rites such as the rinsing of the mouth, the rubbing of the hands, and so forth, one should proceed with the dismissal. Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the clarified butter. Now, the procedure for the offering of the parched grain (*lāja*). One should prepare the parched grain according to the prescribed method. Then, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sprinkling, the placement of the vessel, and the invocation of the fire, one should worship the parched grain as before. Then, having offered the parched grain with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," and having performed the oblation of the limbs with the limb-mantras, one should offer the full oblation with the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ. Then, having performed the concluding rites such as the rinsing of the mouth, the rubbing of the hands, and so forth, one should proceed with the dismissal. Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the parched grain. Now, the procedure for the offering of the sesame seeds (*tilahoma*). One should prepare the sesame seeds according to the prescribed method. Then, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sprinkling, the placement of the vessel, and the invocation of the fire, one should worship the sesame seeds as before. Then, having offered the sesame seeds with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," and having performed the oblation of the limbs with the limb-mantras, one should offer the full oblation with the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ. Then, having performed the concluding rites such as the rinsing of the mouth, the rubbing of the hands, and so forth, one should proceed with the dismissal. Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the sesame seeds. Now, the procedure for the offering of the rice-grains (*taṇḍulahoma*). One should prepare the rice-grains according to the prescribed method. Then, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sprinkling, the placement of the vessel, and the invocation of the fire, one should worship the rice-grains as before. Then, having offered the rice-grains with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," and having performed the oblation of the limbs with the limb-mantras, one should offer the full oblation with the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ. Then, having performed the concluding rites such as the rinsing of the mouth, the rubbing of the hands, and so forth, one should proceed with the dismissal. Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the rice-grains. Now, the procedure for the offering of the sacrificial grass (*darbhahoma*). One should prepare the sacrificial grass according to the prescribed method. Then, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sprinkling, the placement of the vessel, and the invocation of the fire, one should worship the sacrificial grass as before. Then, having offered the sacrificial grass with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," and having performed the oblation of the limbs with the limb-mantras, one should offer the full oblation with the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ. Then, having performed the concluding rites such as the rinsing of the mouth, the rubbing of the hands, and so forth, one should proceed with the dismissal. Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the sacrificial grass. Now, the procedure for the offering of the water-oblation (*arghyahoma*). One should prepare the water-oblation according to the prescribed method. Then, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sprinkling, the placement of the vessel, and the invocation of the fire, one should worship the water-oblation as before. Then, having offered the water-oblation with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," and having performed the oblation of the limbs with the limb-mantras, one should offer the full oblation with the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ. Then, having performed the concluding rites such as the rinsing of the mouth, the rubbing of the hands, and so forth, one should proceed with the dismissal. Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the water-oblation. Now, the procedure for the offering of the flower-oblation (*puṣpahoma*). One should prepare the flower-oblation according to the prescribed method. Then, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sprinkling, the placement of the vessel, and the invocation of the fire, one should worship the flower-oblation as before. Then, having offered the flower-oblation with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," and having performed the
Then, having prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should proceed to the fire-chamber;
it is taught that the marking of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is performed with the *astra-mantra* and its sprinkling with the *varma-mantra*.
One should place there the fire of knowledge, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns;
[one should draw] that fire from the center of the heart-lotus by way of the suṣumṇā path.
One should join that mass of splendor, glowing like a cluster of fire, at the station of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta).
By the mere placement of it, the eightfold group of all rites is accomplished.
The rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and even the final rite of liberation do not equal even a sixteenth part of the water of knowledge; therefore, in obligatory,
occasional, and optional rites, one should perform the worship of the fire of knowledge.
By the mere act of sprinkling once, the consecration of the *sruk* ladle is accomplished;
then the offering of the *pūrṇāhuti* should be performed accompanied by meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
For the fourth [rite], having drawn out the fire for the purpose of incense and lamps, one should guard it;
having diligently worshipped Śiva according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should worship Him with flowers, perfumes, incense, and so forth, together with the mudrās.
"One should satisfy [the deity] joined with the faces, mouths, and limbs of Śiva by means of clarified butter and other offerings. Thus it is said.

Then, having worshipped that Śiva with the eightfold offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā) according to the rules and having bid him farewell, one should unite [the deity] with Śiva residing in the liṅga through the path of the channels (nāḍīmārga), and after dismissing Brahmā and the others, [one should cast] that [liṅga] into the fire.

Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ agniṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*, and *oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*; and having worshipped the fire with *oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ vahnaye namaḥ*, one should then prepare two mandalas with cow dung in the south-eastern corner of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Then, reciting each once and worshipping them with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings, one should present a *bali* offering to Rudra and the others using water mixed with *viśrānta* [incense] ending in *svāhā*, and dismiss them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. Thereafter, in the eastern mandala: *oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ* (in the east) *oṃ hāṃ rudrebhyo namaḥ* (in the east) *oṃ hāṃ pitṛbhyo namaḥ* (in the south) *oṃ hāṃ gaṇebhyo namaḥ* (in the west) *oṃ hāṃ yakṣebhyo namaḥ* (in the north) *oṃ hāṃ grahebhyo namaḥ* (in the northeast) *oṃ hāṃ asurebhyo namaḥ* (in the southeast) *oṃ hāṃ rākṣasebhyo namaḥ* (in the southwest) *oṃ hāṃ nāgebhyo namaḥ* (in the northwest) *oṃ hāṃ nakṣatrebhyo namaḥ* (in the southeast) *oṃ hāṃ viśvebhyo namaḥ* (in the southwest) *oṃ hāṃ kṣetrapālebhyo namaḥ* (in the northwest) *oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ* (in the east).
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni—thus [he offers] in the southeast; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yama—thus in the south (p.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti—thus in the southwest; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa—[thus in the west].

Thus, in the west: *oṃ hāṃ vāyave namaḥ* for Vāyu; in the north: *oṃ hāṃ kuberāya namaḥ* for Kubera; in the northeast: *oṃ hāṃ īśānāya namaḥ* for Īśāna; pointing toward the upper region: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; and in the northeast, at the region of the vulva and anus: *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. In the southeast... [text truncated]

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nīlalohita"— having thus worshipped Indra and the others in the center of the maṇḍala as before, one should offer a *bali* ending with "svāhā" and then dismiss them. Then, outside the maṇḍala, one should worship all those residing in the eastern direction and so forth— namely the lords of the directions (*digīśas*), the spirits (*bhūtas*), the hosts of mothers (*mātṛgaṇas*), Rudra, and the field-protectors (*kṣetrapālas*)— according to their respective directional names, offering a *bali* ending with "svāhā," and after bowing, one should worship at the front of the pavilion and the front of the maṇḍala with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the crows and others who violate the covenant (*samayabhedins*)," and a *bali* ending with "svāhā" should be offered there.
Those Rudras whose deeds are Rudra-like, who dwell in the terrible abodes,
the Mothers, those of Rudra-form, and those who are the lords of the hosts;
Likewise, all other obstructing spirits residing in the ten directions,
with well-pleased minds, may accept this bali offering.

"May there always be success and merit for me; may you protect me constantly from all fears. This is the *rudrabali* mantra. Having thus offered the oblation (*bali*) and paid obeisance, one should ask for forgiveness. Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should perform the ritual placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*). This, in brief, is the procedure for the fire-rite (*agnikāryavidhi*). Thereafter, having gone near Śiva, worshipped Him with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), and prostrated, one should recite the *aghora* mantra twenty-one times for the sake of liberation from defects of omission or excess. And it is said:
Whoever recites the Aghora mantra even once at night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight is liberated from all sins; he becomes free from the pairs of opposites and devoid of distress.
By merely remembering [this] once, the destruction of all sins shall occur.
By reciting it five times, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
by chanting it seven times, one obtains here the fruits of all sacrifices.
By reciting it twenty-one times according to the rule at the conclusion of the worship, one shall obtain the entire fruit of the worship; there is no doubt in this matter.
"There is no mantra other than the Aghora that bestows accomplishment upon reaching the Kali age. Thus [it is said].
Having performed the recitation (*japa*) and worshipped as before—
whatever we do, O God, whether good or evil,
destroy that for me while I abide in the state of Śiva; O Śaṅkara, [grant] peace.
Having recited this, [the practitioner] places [the offering] into the hand of the Bestower of Boons (*varada-hasta*). Then the Blessed One says: "Oṃ [etc.]...
Whatever has been done by me through delusion, whether deficient or even in excess, may all that become complete for me through your grace, O Lord."

Having thus prayed and contemplated the entirety of the fruit of the worship as complete, and having worshipped Śiva with the eightfold offering of flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), one should worship that fruit—which resembles the autumnal moon—just as one worships [the deity] during recitation: "Oṃ * * * *! Whatever merit has been performed by me through worship, recitation, fire-sacrifice (*agnikārya*), and other rites, that fruit I offer to You, the Supreme Lord. Accept it Yourself with pleasure; O Lord, let this not be for my own enjoyment."
O Maheśvara, you are my refuge through action, mind, and speech.
Having spoken thus, one should offer everything with the right hand of the Lord.
p. 149) Herein is the sequence:

*oṃ hāṃ hauṃ bhagavan pūjāhomādi puṇyaphalaṃ gṛhāṇa svāhā* (Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, O Blessed One, accept the fruit of merit from the worship, fire-oblation, and so forth, svāhā). Thus one should offer it to the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*). If he is a seeker of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), he should offer it after reciting: *tatphalaṃ me'stu deveśa bhuktimuktyartha sādhanaṃ* (May that fruit be mine, O Lord of Gods, as a means for the sake of enjoyment and liberation). Both should perform the offering of themselves (*ātmasamarpaṇa*). That is stated as follows: *oṃ*—
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the cause of the three causes;
I offer myself to you, O Supreme Lord—you are my refuge.

Having recited thus, then clearly pronouncing the root mantra at the peak of the sound (nāda), one should, through the exhaling breath (recaka), bring the individual soul (jīva)— consisting of a sphere of radiant energy— to each station;
having attained a state of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya), one speaks within the great ocean of the bliss of knowledge.
Having brought it back and placed it in the excellent hand of the body,
one should [unite] one's own heart-lotus through the yoga of joining the channels (nāḍī).
Having entered [the body], one should contemplate the meaning of the practice as it is practiced; without distress, one should reflect:
"Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire world."
"Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere; that which is Śiva is indeed I myself.

Then, having worshipped Śiva with the *aṣṭapuṣpikā* (eightfold flower offering), one should offer the *virodhārghya* with the hand turned downwards while reciting the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, from Sadyojāta to Īśāna—that is, across the five faces—and the *arghya* should be offered with the face turned away (*suparāṅmukha*). One should then offer [the offerings] to the limbs starting from the Moon (Soma) in the east and ending with the Tejas-kavaca, up to the Heart. And it is said: "Then the *arghya* is offered with the face turned away, beginning from Sadyojāta and ending with Śiva."
"Up to his heart, [one should worship] with perfumes, incense, garlands, and so forth. Thus it is said.

150) Now, having offered the aforementioned *arghya* with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*—visualizing the light-linga (*jyotirliṅga*) as the lotus of the entire temple—and having propitiated Śiva with the power-mantra (*śakti-mantra*) ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the *dhenu-mudrā*, one should pay obeisance to the devotees and offer the special *arghya* (*viśeṣārghya*). Then, having worshipped the Guru and others, and having given them *arghya* for the sake of their turning away, one should restrain them with the harsh [mantra] and dismiss them by means of the withdrawal-gesture (*saṃhāra-mudrā*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), using each of their respective mantras. Thus is the dismissal from the linga along with its characteristics.

Now, if [the deity is] on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), after the formation of the image, one should withdraw it with the *saṃhāramudrā* and, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), join it to the light-liṅga (*jyotirliṅga*) marked by Śakti within the lotus of one's own mind. Regarding the dismissal (*visarjana*) while the liṅga is still present, it is said: "Having meditated upon [the deity] as risen like a flash of lightning, one should lead it to dissolution in its own places; the mantras residing in the place of dissolution are themselves dissolved into the root-mantra."
Then one should meditate on the root mantra as it dissolves into a throbbing bond;
it reaches dissolution in the Bindu, the abode of the gods, within the Nāda, where the Nāda possesses the power of pure consciousness.
"The power of knowledge is dissolved in the Supreme; he who is established in the space of the heart—from him the mantra is born, and into that very place it is dissolved. Thus [it is said].

Is it not the case that a mantra capable [of denoting a specific object] should be employed only for that which it denotes? How then can a mantra expressive of Śiva be employed for the Śakti? True. For without that [Śakti], its capacity as a denoter is destroyed. Therefore, there is no fault, because of the scriptural injunction: "One should diligently worship Śiva by employing the individual souls (aṇus) within the Śakti. Likewise, elsewhere it is said:
"One should not employ a mantra capable [of denoting Śiva] toward the Supreme Reality, which is neuter."
"They attain the power of the male principle, but they are fruitless regarding the other principles.
Likewise:
"The mantra that has attained the state of Śiva makes the practitioner turn away [from lower goals]."
Therefore, one who seeks the goal through constant austerity should employ the remaining [means] according to one's capacity.
"The mantra situated in the center of the Śakti bestows all desires.
Even though it is thus [situated],
the mantra is not perfected if it has not been recited (*japta*), nor does it grant fruit if it has not been offered with oblations (*āhuta*).
Since he did not come having been honored by that [offering], one should perform the triad [of rites].
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva.

Now, for one who desires a concise mode of worship, one should perform it upon a book or similar object by means of the seat (āsana), the form (mūrti), the root-mantra (mūla), the limbs (aṅga), and the eightfold offering of flowers (aṣṭapuṣpikā). As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"In the case of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) as well, having reflected thus, one should worship the Lord with garlands, perfumes, incense, and food offerings, using a single utterance and delighting in the abbreviated ritual."

In the solar or lunar mandala, in the sky, or likewise upon the sandals of the Guru; when the light [of the deity] is situated upon the head, one who possesses faith should [perform the rite] as it has been described. Now, if the daily ritual (nityavidhi) is performed at some other consecrated linga—however it may be, or due to some deficiency—and if the practitioner is one who follows the same procedure, then a concise ritual should be performed there. A mixed ritual (miśra-vidhi) must never be performed. And it has been said:
Having performed the eight auspicious rites equally, one should complete the ritual procedure.
Action should be performed by those who possess action with a mind as declared in the Siddhānta;
for he whose intellect is deluded would perform action according to both [the Siddhānta and the dualistic] systems in a confused manner.
"His supreme sin should be known as equal to the drinking of liquor. Thus it is said.
Now, in the case of the common *liṅga*, worship should be performed with the common mantra alone. Likewise:
"The *praṇava*, the *mātṛkā*, the *māyā*, the *vyomavyāpī*, and the six-syllabled [mantra]."
The Prāsāda and Aghora mantras are considered to be common to all seven.
"With these, the wise one should worship Śiva, who is common to all.
Now, the worship of Caṇḍeśvara is described:
one should worship him [to purify] the transgression of the rules (samaya) committed by those who worship Śiva.

Caṇḍeśvara is said to be the one who removes the terrible evil of the village. Outside, in the northeast direction (Īśāna-kāṣṭhā), having fashioned a lotus representing infinite dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty upon a cow-dung maṇḍala shaped like a half-moon using the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should perform this mental worship: "Oṃ caṇḍāsanāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Above that: "Oṃ caṇḍamūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. [He is] with the luster of blue collyrium, four-faced, with eyes like the sun, wearing a sacred thread and armlets, and possessing the radiance of fire and the sun.

Having meditated upon the Supreme Goddess— who is exceedingly fearsome with four arms, blazing with flames and rich in sacrificial ghee, holding a *śūkta* (sacrificial vessel) and a *kamaṇḍalu* in her left and right hands respectively, and adorned with an axe and a rosary; who has originated from Rudra-Agni— one should invoke Her with the root mantra.

Oṃ dhuni caṇḍeśvarāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having rendered [the offering] supreme and made it nectar by means of the *dhenumudrā*, having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and so forth with the heart-mantra, and having worshipped [the deity] fully endowed with the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) such as perfumes and the like, one should perform recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, offer the oblation (*nivedya*), and then [proceed] with the *praṇava*.
Having set aside cows, land, gold, clothing, and so forth, as well as jewels, gold, and ornaments, one should offer the remaining remains of the offering (nirmālya) to Caṇḍeśa.
Liquids to be licked, foods to be sucked, meals, drinks, and so forth, as well as betel, garlands, and ointments—
these remains of offerings are given to you by the command of Śiva.
Having recited this and offered the *nirmālya* of Śiva, [one says]:
*Oṃ*,
"All this ritual section has been performed by me according to the command of Caṇḍa."
Whatever has been done deficiently or in excess through delusion, may it always be complete for me.
Having thus informed Caṇḍeśa, one should dismiss him like Śiva with the offering of eight flowers (aṣṭapuṣpikā).

Then, having smeared the area with cow dung and water to remove the remains of the previous offerings (*nirmālya*), having sprinkled the place with the *astra-mantra*, and having offered the *arghya* and performed the ritual placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*), one should recite the *Śivasaṃhitā* according to one's capacity.
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*: "One should worship Caṇḍanātha in the northeast with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*."
Having offered garments, food, perfumes, water for drinking, water for honor (arghya), flower garlands, and other purifying items,
and having set aside the vessel of honor-water (arghapātra), one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and touch [the various parts of the body].
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), the Śivasaṃhitā should be recited according to one's capacity.
"Thus the worship of Śiva has been fully described in due order.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The offering of perfumes and flowers to the deity who has been bid farewell..."
One should know that to be *nirmālya*; one must avoid consuming *nirmālya*.
Having made him fast once more, one should present him to Caṇḍeśa. Thus it is said.
Now, [one might ask]: "In the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, a mobile liṅga, a Siddhaliṅga, or a self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) liṅga...
"And in the case of all images, one who is fierce should not be appointed;
this also applies to the ritual for the Lord of the Altar (Sthaṇḍileśa) when it is joined with the contemplation of non-duality (advaita-bhāvanā). So say some.
Others, however—
"Even for a consecrated deity, there is no worship with fierce [offerings].
How then was this other view formulated? In the Śaiva Siddhānta, however, the rule is that [the deity] must always and everywhere be worshipped. And so it is said in the Kālottara:
"Whether [the image] is stationary, mobile, or likewise red, it is conceived as the Immortal Enemy."
The fierce Nivāmaka resides within the iron arrow adorned with variegated patterns.

Likewise— in the unmanifest, in the manifest, in the linga, in the mandala, on the sacrificial ground, in the fire; likewise in the mobile, in the stationary, in gems, and in various jeweled objects and the like.
In a linga made of earth, ash, or fruit, where fragrance is not present,
as well as in a linga made of flowers, [the mantra] is "Caṇḍa...mikā."

Then, the wise one should worship the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) to the extent of ten million times, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, including food offerings and garlands, just as one would for Śiva.
Thus: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati*.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the gurus beginning with Sadāśiva.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to those worthy of knowing Śiva.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the harakas who have descended through the knowledge of Śiva.

Then, having worshipped Śiva with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) and prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness. Next, having approached the feet of the one whose worship has been performed, having washed the lotus-feet, having anointed them with perfume, and having honored them with three handfuls of flowers, one should prostrate three times with the eight limbs (*sāṣṭāṅga*) and ask for forgiveness. This has been stated in other Āgamas:

One should address the Ācārya as being near, even if he is far away, by virtue of the yoga of the twilight [mantras]. Even when he is absent, one should properly worship his sandals placed upon the pedestal.
One should not salute a Guru who is eating, absorbed in meditative concentration, walking, engaged in ritual action,
or standing nearby with a mind of disrespect.
One should not follow behind someone who is walking, nor should one wake someone who is sleeping. One should not question the words of such a person.
Likewise—
one should diligently recite [the mantra] while prostrating before the Guru under the pretext of offering flowers;
by bowing at the feet of the Guru, the fruit of giving a thousand cows is obtained.
"A teacher who is of noble birth, endowed with ritual action, and devoted to the study of his own scriptures.
Then, one should also perform an appropriate salutation toward other ascetics who are well-disciplined in the absence of the teacher. Likewise:
"An initiate, and one who is an initiate who is senior—that is, one who was initiated earlier."
The son of the son is the accomplisher of the son, and the accomplisher of the practitioner.
He is declared to be the teacher even of the teacher, according to the instruction of the Samaya;
one should also pay homage to those who are senior to oneself, as well as to the assembly of the teacher’s brothers.
Then he should also salute other pure Śaiva ascetics who have taken refuge in all four paths, beginning with the Laukika.
Therefore, I greet with affection those who are senior in learning and austerity;
likewise,
in the teaching of Śiva, one who has undergone the purificatory rites is senior to those who have merely taken vows.
However, birth, seniority in age, or preeminence in learning are not the grounds [for authority];
for when an elder son remains as a child, the younger son may be consecrated.
