"Between the teacher and the one who has been initiated by the teacher, or even between those who have been initiated later, mutual respect must be maintained, except for the act of formal salutation. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"One should know that their fire-rituals, recitations, worship, initiations, knowledge, and vows are in vain; for among such gurus, there is no deity."
"The guru is the father, the guru is the mother, the guru is the deity, the guru is the friend;
there is nothing higher than the guru—thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śiva."
He opens the eyes with divine knowledge upon those eyes overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance; therefore, he is perfectly enlightened in all things.

The senior never performs a greeting for the junior, even if the junior is superior in austerity or learning; this applies even when the greeting is performed through an intermediary. All those who have been initiated previously are to be known as gurus.
O Six-faced One, all of them are to be honored and worshiped, with the exception of your preceptor.
Enough with excessive detail. Some desire the worship of Kapila at the conclusion of the worship of Īśa. By the will of Śiva, five cows descended from the city of Śiva to the earth;
these five cows were born as the mothers of all the world.
Nandā, Subhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā;
[the cows] were Kapilā, Kṛṣṇā, Śvetā, Dhūmrā, and likewise Raktā.
Thus has the armor-mantra for those beginning with Nandā and ending with Sumanā been proclaimed,
for the benefit of all the worlds and for the propitiation of the gods.
The mothers of the cows stood upon the ground for the sake of Śiva’s ritual bath;
[they provided] the cow dung, the *rocanā*, the urine, the milk, the curd, and the ghee of the cows.
The six limbs are pure and bestow all accomplishments;
by means of them sacrifices proceed, and by means of the Vedas the gods are established.
The Vedas, along with their auxiliary branches, word-for-word commentaries, and phonetic recitations, have been vomited forth by the cows.
At the base of the cows' horns, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are eternally stationed;
at the tips of the horns are all sacred fords, both stationary and moving.
For I am in the center of your head, my child, surrounded by the elemental beings;
and your brother, in particular, is stationed on your forehead.
The two nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara reside in the nostrils;
the two gods Nanda and Upananda are in the ears; and the moon and sun are in the eyes.
The Marut gods reside in the teeth; Varuṇa is situated in the tongue;
Sarasvatī is in the syllable *huṃ*; Yama and Yakṣa are in the two cheeks;
the two twilights are likewise in the lips; and Indra has taken refuge in the neck.
In the middle of the hooves are the Gandharvas, and in the tips of the hooves are the Pannagas;
at the rear tips of the hooves reside the Gandharvas and Apsarases;
the Rudras are located in the ten joints, and the Vāyus are in all the articulations.
The ancestors are in his blood; Umā is in his chest;
Śrī is always in the drinking of cows; and Dharma is stationed upon his trident.
The rays of the sun, the garland, the deer, and the Gaṅgā herself,
as well as all the sages, are stationed upon the tips of his body hairs.
In his belly is the goddess Earth with her mountains, forests, and groves;
the four oceans are full within him, and the udders are the waters in his limbs.
O Gajānana, it has been told how everything is established in cows:
whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, eaten, or all that is moving and unmoving, resides in cows.
The urine is from a tawny cow, while the dung is from one of black color.
If it is white or smoky, it is milk; if it is red in color, it becomes ghee.
It arises as cow-urine, an aṅgula in size, fragrant, and pleasing to behold.
The food of all the gods, and especially that of Śiva,
is the glorious Bilva tree, which rose from cow dung and is dear to Śiva.
Thus Śrī remains with a lotus in her hand, and for that reason she is called the Śrīvṛkṣa;
furthermore, the seeds of blue and red lotuses are produced from cow dung.
Whatever in the world has grown from milk should be known as originating from that; all products born of curd are auspicious for the attainment of one's goals.
Since nectar has arisen from the Soma and is dear to the one who is free from death,
therefore one should bathe that which is dear to Śiva with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
And gorocanā is auspicious, purifying, and the granter of all desires.
Thus, having honored the cows— who have come forth for the sake of the five products of the cow—
with their respective names and with the *dhruva* mantra, one should look upon them before entering the village.
One should pay homage with perfumes, flowers, purifiers, and so forth, preceded by the mantra. It is as follows:
"O fragrant one, arisen from the churning of the nectar of immortality, O sustainer of the world!"
"Take this morsel; this indeed is my supreme vow."

Having thus praised [the cows] with supreme devotion, the wise man should then cause them to accept the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or, in the absence of those [cows], [he should do so by other means].
One should take [the substance] from only one [cow], preceded by worship with the previously mentioned *śambara* mantras;
even in this case, Kapilā alone is praised among all [cows].
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of Kapila.
Then, until midday, the person should remain established in samādhi upon the Liṅga composed of the light of knowledge, radiant like the autumnal moon.
One should fix the mind and the vital breaths there, situated between the eyebrows; absorbed in that and becoming one with it, the yogi should gradually lead the consciousness into emptiness.
When the [dualistic] consciousness has perished, the supreme bliss of pure consciousness shines forth spontaneously.
Thus has samādhi been described, the abode of qualities such as aṇimā and the rest.
"Śiva is the generator of true existence and the simultaneous awakener of the universe;
having thus understood him in the upward flow (ūrdhvasrotas), one should practice this, O Sūta. Thus [it is said].
Likewise:
"Concentration may be of a single form, devoid of place and objective support; for cognition by means of the object alone is the supreme means for accomplishing yoga."
Relying on non-existence as existence, one should practice emptiness within non-existence;
that samādhi which is empty, utterly empty, and liberated is the domain of Śiva.
In the lotus of the heart, at the navel, or on the summit of the head,
or in such locations as these, concentration (dhāraṇā) is practiced by one who maintains Śiva.
"The mouth of the Guru is the mountain peak.
(p. 160) Likewise:
As before, one should take hold of its summit, which is the assembly of gurus;
there, the peak of the mountain is traditionally known as that which is worshipped by the gods in turn.

"The continuity of mental modifications, like a garland of flowers placed in water within milk, being intermingled with other modifications, is that meditation which, when offered by the Liberator, brings about liberation. Thus [it is said].

But surely, in the Kaula tradition, supreme liberation belongs only to the Kaulikas and not to the Śaivas? It has been said in the *Śrī-nigūḍhajñānasadbhāva*: "O Dear One, for the sake of worldly conduct, the Śaiva system consisting of the five currents—the external path originating from the Five-Faced One—has been taught."
However, in this world, the five streams have been made manifest for the sake of devotees.
Deluded by these five, people do not understand their own lineage;
they know only their pure family, which is honored in the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya).
Beyond this tantra, there is another tantra that is difficult to attain, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it exists within the Śaiva tradition consisting of five currents, which is endowed with both the supreme and the non-supreme.
"And even those who have been initiated do not attain success, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. Thus it is said.

It should not be said that this is merely a figurative expression for the cause of its manifestation. Otherwise, how could this Tantra—the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya) issued from the western face—be primary for the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), the beginningless agent and independent being? And how could that Blessed Lord be secondary? Therefore, this is indeed a figurative expression. Furthermore, the body of the Kula is insentient; the practice and so forth occurring therein is called "Gaula. But as for the venerable Śiva, who transcends all and is a mass of supreme consciousness and bliss—how could the Śivas residing within him not be partakers of liberation? Thus it is stated in the *Kulālikāmnāya*, in the twenty-fourth chapter of the eighty-four thousand [verse] work known as the *Kukhāra*, in the section on the descent of the Siddha-pīṭhas:
The Goddess said:
"The Brahmins are Śaivas in their inner hearts, but outwardly they follow worldly customs."
O Goddess, these three have been indicated by you, but not fully revealed.
O Lord, please graciously explain this matter of curiosity.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall tell you the supreme secret in its proper sequence.
O fair-faced one, that which is called Kaula resides within the body;
therefore, O beautiful lady, the practice of Kaula must be constantly taught.
O Dear One, that which is proclaimed as the internal Kaula is always to be practiced;
it is that which has been declared in the determination of the six systems of philosophy.
O sinless one, everything regarding the poison-foot and so forth, as well as the determination of the internal sacrifice within consciousness, has indeed been previously explained to you in detail.
Having understood the knowledge that pervades both below and above, one should practice the Kaula path.
Now,
O large-eyed one, listen to what is called "external Śaivism": whether among those born from eggs, those born from sweat, or those born from a womb or from sprouts.
One should contemplate that which is all-pervading, all-bestowing, peaceful,
and auspicious, remaining present even amidst all the objects of the senses and all sensory domains.

Wherever there exists some auspiciousness for those who have been wounded by what is called a "yakṣiṇī," wherever it may be discerned, one should contemplate that very thing as the object of knowledge.
A steadfast person should forcibly restrain restlessness, which grants yoga even to yogins.
Whatever is to be known, therein its being is always stable, full, and eternal;
having moved, where could it go? For everything is of the nature of Śiva.
Having realized that Śiva is outside as well, one should never be deluded in this way;
he whose being is thus all-pervading shall himself become all-pervading.
"This has been declared to you as the supreme, the most secret of all secrets. Thus [it is said].
Now, as it has been stated in the *Mahākaulajñānanirṇaya* brought down by Matsyanātha, which emerged from Candradvīpa:
"In the midst of knowledge, action is dissolved; the will of the Knower has gone to dissolution. Where the power of will (icchā-śakti) dissolves, there is that God, the Supreme Śiva."
As it is stated regarding the disclosure of the secret:
"I am the letter *a*, said to be the sun; the ocean is called the moon.
Together with *ahaṃkāra*, O auspicious lady, the letter *sa* is called night."
The syllable *haṃ* is the pure Śiva, while the syllable *sa* is said to be Śakti.
The syllable *haṃ* is partless and eternal; the syllable *sa* is said to be equal.
O auspicious lady, the syllable *haṃ* is called day, while the syllable *sa* is called night.
The syllable *Haṃ* is Śiva, pure, both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), O Beloved.

Or [the text] beginning with "not established" (*na sthita*) refers to that which is devoid of trees; nor is the city (*pūḥ*) devoid of that [deity]. Therefore, Śiva is stainless (*nirañjana*), peaceful (*śānta*), and the cause of power (*śakti*).
Śiva is the all-pervading cause of all powers indeed.
It is not maintained that he is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe because power is dependent upon him.

There are many such statements capable of establishing the state of Śiva-hood. Therefore, it is clear that only the pure Śaivas are those who follow the supreme authority; enough of this excessive detail. Thus it is determined. (p.

163) Although worship beginning with the internal [meditation] and ending with the final [external] rite has been described in this way, [it is most] beneficial when performed by one who is humble and free from pride. And it has been said:
Concentration, retention, meditation, recitation, fire-offerings, and austerities—
[these are performed] in one's own form, in the form of the Guru, in the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), in water, and in fire.

"Worship performed upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or before a fixed linga, or in the presence of a mobile image, is excellent; however, among these, worship before a linga possessing the prescribed characteristics is said to be the best.
Therefore, one should always perform the propitiation of the linga with diligent effort. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the Kālottara: "He is to be worshipped everywhere, always present in all substrates;
yet it is in Laṅkā that the Lord Dhūrjaṭi accepts worship."
O Six-faced One, even if a worship performed with my materials, rituals, and qualities is incomplete,
it becomes a complete worship when performed upon a linga.
The worship on the sacrificial ground and other sites must not be performed deficiently or excessively;
indeed, any worship that is deficient or excessive is proclaimed to be fruitless.
"For this reason, my child, one should begin the worship of the *liṅga*. Thus [it is said].

And likewise, for the sake of the fire, she was to be supported; under the pretext of maintenance, O King, she acted as a thief out of malice toward the Pāñcālī’s heart. Therefore, her gender has ceased to exist.
Just as worship performed upon a *liṅga* in the presence of the Preceptor yields fruit,
so too does that which is performed with the concluding rite (*pūrṇāhuti*) become most excellent.
Likewise, O Śaiva, for those whose minds are well-established, worship performed upon the sun, the moon, water, fire, the preceptor, knowledge, and the forms of the void is said to be fruitful.
Austerities, mastery over the vital breaths, withdrawal of the senses,
concentration, meditation, and absorption— this is the means for those whose minds are established in steadiness.
"For the wise who are free from passion and view the world as mere straw,
even the worship of the *liṅga* is unreal in nature, though it grants a physical form to their minds."
Likewise, in the Sarvajñānottara: "They call it the Space-Linga; the Earth is its pedestal.
It is called the Linga because it is the abode (ālaya) of all beings and because [all things] dissolve (layana) into it."
That which is the primordial sovereign splendor, consisting of all the gods,
and which is the massification of the principles— that is called the *tejo-liṅga*.
"One should know Umā-pīṭha to be of pure gold and radiant;
it is the meritorious Mother Ambikā, the Sustainer, and likewise the Mistress of Yogins. Thus it is said, and likewise in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
That wherein all beings dissolve and from which they emerge again and again—
therefore, the supreme ether is the *liṅga*, partless and the highest Śiva.

By whatever state [of being] the Blessed Śiva is marked or characterized, that state is the *liṅga*; through yoga, it is joined in three ways, whether by the unjoined, the joined, or the nature of fear.
That which is manifest is to be known as having parts (sakala), while that which is unmanifest is considered partless (niṣkala).
The Liṅga consisting of the light of knowledge is known as both manifest and unmanifest;
likewise, the image made of clay and so forth is considered a constructed form presided over by that [Liṅga].
In that regard, it is said that the *liṅga* may be made of clay, wood, or metal; thus, it shall become auspicious.
May this *Jñānaratnāvalī*, composed by the illustrious Jñānaśiva— who has taken refuge at the lotus feet of Śambhu— be victorious among people, bestowing the fruit of spiritual perfection.
The wise Śrī Jñānaśambhu— who knows the true scriptures and established doctrines that dispel the weariness of travelers on the six paths, who dwells at the feet of the Supreme Lord,
and who is a knower of the Vedas— performs the bathing and other rites, the worship of the lotus feet of Śiva, and the fire-sacrifice.
This ocean of true asceticism, born in the region of Saccoka, performed [this] for the sake of the Brahmins.
Thus concludes the ritual for the daily worship of Śiva from the *Jñānaratnāvalī* composed by the venerable Jñānaśambhu.

O you who dwell in the well of the fragmented vine of ignorance, listen! You who have been purified by initiation, from the presence of the most venerable Vyomaśambhu, hear the essence of the Śaiva Siddhānta—divine, non-divine, and mixed—which has issued from the mouth of Śiva;
I bow perpetually to that [Lord] through whom all knowledge, whose words are known by the Vedas, is attained.
Oṃ, homage to Śiva!

Having briefly described the fire-ritual for Śiva (śivāgnikārya) performed at the conclusion of the worship of Śiva— which is accessible even to the poor— among those who worship Śiva, I shall now explain the extensive fire-ritual, which constitutes a constituent part of the triad of rites.
Having approached the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with all auspicious characteristics,
the preceptor should gaze upon it with a gracious eye and sprinkle it with the Śiva-weapon (mantra).

The wise one should strike [the ground] and sprinkle it with water using the *varman* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. With the *astra* mantra, he should remove the excavated earth; with the *hṛdaya* mantra, he should fill the pit and level it.
Then one should perform the sprinkling with the armor-mantra and the pounding with the weapon-mantra.

One should begin with the sweeping and the smearing, and then proceed with the armor. The kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā should be deposited starting from the center and moving eastward. One should encircle [the site] with the three threads and the protective armor.

Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings while reciting "Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the pit (kuṇḍa) of Kalāmāyā," one should perform three [lines] starting from the east using fuel-sticks, darbha grass, and the weapon-mantra (hetimantra), one by one.

With the mantra for making [the area] adamantine (vajrīkaraṇa), one should form the shape of a vajra using three blades of kuśa grass. At the crossroads, one should fashion [the boundary] with two blades of kuśa from the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) until the moon and sun [are reached].
Thus, the eighteen purificatory rites have been briefly described for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
For the enclosure of the axle (akṣavāṭa), one should place eight kuśa grasses upon the pit while reciting the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Having performed the ritual placement with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vāgīśvara," one should visualize a divine lion-throne in the center of the grass mat.
There, one should install the form with the form-mantra, and through that form, one should invoke Śiva.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī.
[I meditate upon] the goddess Vāgīśā, dark-complexioned, having bathed after her menses and adorned with ornaments;
she has two arms, one face, three eyes, and is the beloved of Īśa.
Having invoked with the heart-mantra the one who has ten arms, who is white and gentle, who has five faces and fifteen eyes, and having worshipped him and meditated upon the union of those two;
The fire for the *agnihotra* sacrifice should be produced from the *araṇi* wood or from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*); or it may be brought from the hearth of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya.
With the Astra-mantra, one should cause the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) that is situated in the vessel to be discarded.
Having gazed at it, sprinkled it, and struck it, one should sprinkle the remainder as before.
Having taken up the consciousness with the seed-syllable of fire (Raṃ) by means of the heart-mantra and the saṃhāra-mudrā,
one should then join it to the bindu within the heart through inhalation (pūraka).
Or, having unified [the breath] with fire at the navel through the practice of *kumbhaka*,
one should lead it outward by means of *recaka* and properly join it to the blazing fire.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire;
having consecrated it with this mantra, one should protect it with the six-limbed rite using the armor-mantra.

One should rotate three times with the heart-mantra the fire, which has been worshipped with the heart-mantra and rendered nectar-like by the *dhenumudrā*, above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the purpose of agitating the womb.
One who is of divine nature should not feel distressed even when being cast into adversity.
"Oṃ hrāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the seed-syllable of fire.
Having placed both knees upon the ground, one should cast [the water] facing oneself;
then, having unified [the mind] through the heart, one should perform purification, sipping water (ācamana), and so forth, up to the navel.
Having given the clothing to be worn as well as the binding of the turban and so forth,
and having bound the protection for the hand of the Goddess with a golden thread and the like, he should proceed.
Then, having covered it with poisoned arrows, kindled it with a fan,
and worshipped the fire of the womb (garbhāgni) within his heart, he should perform the rites beginning with the conception ceremony (garbhādhāna).

Having worshipped the fire with the Sadyojāta mantra for the purpose of the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*), one should offer five oblations with sesame seeds and parched rice using the Heart-mantra and the Śiva-mantra; then [one worships] Nandana, who has ten bodies, with the Puruṣa-mantra and the Varma-mantra.
Having kindled the fire with *darbha* grass and other materials, and having bathed the newborn child who is the son of Śiva, as well as the affectionate Goddess, with divine ornaments;
and having offered five oblations (*pañcāhuti*) with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, one should meditate upon the embryo remaining [within].
In the third month, one should worship with the left hand and offer oblations with the head.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the body consisting of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka). One should first offer a drop of *arghya* with the heart-mantra; this is remembered as the *puṃsavana* rite.
In the sixth month, the *sīmanta* rite is performed, followed by the conceptualization of the limbs of the mouth of Agni.
Having worshipped with the Ghora mantra, one should perform the expiation for the opening of the mouth;
for each [opening], five oblations should be offered with sesame seeds and parched grain using the Śikhā-mantra.
On the tenth day, Nandana should be performed with the Puruṣa-mantra and the Varman-mantra.
Having kindled the fire with darbha grass and other materials, and having bathed the young son of Śiva along with the goddess— who is gentle and adorned with divine ornaments— [one should proceed].
Having sprinkled the sacrificial pit with the Weapon-mantra for the immediate pacification of birth-impurity,
and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should contemplate Śivā as being well-pleased.
To remove the fire's saliva, five oblations soaked in ghee should be offered with a piercing [mantra] into the five faces; thus, the five offerings are to be made at the edge and the base.
The auspicious sacrificial fires, which are like one's own vital breaths and are the masters of all beings, are sevenfold;
they are to be offered into for the purification of the seven tongues of fire.
The characteristics of the sacrificial grass mats and other items are as declared in the Śiva-āgama:
the enclosing sticks (paridhi) should be made from trees suitable for sacrifice, equal in length to a forearm.
It should be as thick as the little finger, green in color, and free from blemishes.
A triple-braided cord (*veṇī*) made of thirty *darbha* blades, measured by the length of the forearm,
with a *brahmagranthi* knot at the front, or a circular auspicious seat (*viṣṭara*), should be prepared.
The *haritā* grasses, which are similar to that [in color] and pleasing to the heart,
are always used for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) in the place of the *kuśa*, provided they are not slightly shorter than a man's height.
Having been employed in the Śiva-sacrifice and other such rites, they are praised for gentle activities.
Grass with three characteristics is excellent for rites of subjugation and illusion;
likewise, it is beneficial for rites of pacification, nourishment, and invigoration.
Grass that is inferior, hard, and slightly cut is considered neuter.
"O gentle one, those who are censured should be employed in fierce deeds, not in peaceful ones. Thus [it is said].
One should spread a girdle of *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward upon a seat consecrated with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, arranged toward the east, west, south, and north.
[Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśāna, and Ananta],
and in due order the world-protectors situated around the perimeter, together with their vehicles and weapons.
"O gods, well-equipped Bhoga, protect this child by the command of Śiva"—
having thus addressed them, he should perform the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*).
Because it was purified by clarified butter (ājya), its purification by ājya was established in ancient times;
and because that [impurity] was also [removed] by [the breath of] Vāyu, its purification is thus declared.
To eliminate the state of being mere wood, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, purified by gazing and other rites,
should be rotated three times in the fire with their faces upward and downward respectively.
Sprinkling [the area] once more, one should place that [offering] in the center of the mandala:
170) Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the Śiva-principle together with its presiding lord; Oṃ, homage to the Self-principle together with its presiding lord.*
Thus,
having worshipped the two [images] whose necks are wound three times with armor using the *varma* mantra and the heart mantra,
one should place them on *kuśa* grass to the right side of oneself in the sacrificial hall.

One should worship Śakti in the *sruk* ladle and Śambhu in the *sruva* spoon with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*. Then, having taken cow's clarified butter that has been purified through the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, one should whirl it three times over the sacrificial pit; this is the beneficial rite of circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Having brought it down with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and placed it in that pit in the southeast corner,
one should take up the tips of the kuśa grass after meditating on one's own body as consisting of Brahman and as being pure.
One should offer a drop to Brahmā with the heart-mantra ending in *svāhā*;
that is declared to be the *tāpana* [purification], having taken up that clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Having said, "One should give that to Rudra for Rudra," it has been proclaimed;
in some places, this triad is taught by means of the heart, the head, and the handful (culuka) mantras.

Kusha grass with unbroken tips and roots, measuring a span in length, should be used for the consecration of the clarified butter; others that are auspicious but thin [should be used] for other purposes.
Two *kuśa* blades should be placed in the middle of the vessel with a *brahmagranthi* tied at their base;
they should be two cubits long, with the thumb-width as their girth at the tips, and one should grasp them by their roots and tips.
One should worship three times facing the fire with the Astra-mantra or the Varma-mantra;
one should perform the *utplava* and *saṃplava* with the Hṛdaya-mantra, or indeed perform the *kiṃtvāna* with the mantra three times.
One should perform the joining of the mantras within the faces;
one should contemplate the earth dissolved into Varuṇa with the Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva [mantras].
The western [element] is dissolved into the north, and one should bring the triad into oneness.
The fire merged into the wind, and likewise [the wind] into the Person;
one should lead those three together into the southern face and the eastern face.
One should place Īśāna in the sky, facing it, as the dissolution into the principle of Śiva.
The method of joining the mouth has been explained to you in detail with due respect.

Then, with the mantra "Oṃ heṃ huṃ hiṃ haṃ svāhā to Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta," one should perform the pouring of a stream of ghee from the southeast corner up to the northeast. Having meditated on the dissolution of the remaining faces into the face of Sadyojāta, one should visualize that face as having its mouth wide open and equal in size to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). This concludes the daily rites regarding the unification of the faces. Now, in the rite of unifying the faces starting from the northeast according to the sequence of the Vidyās, one should meditate on the remaining ritual acts in accordance with the specific rite within the station of Īśāna, and then meditate upon that within the station of Īśāna itself. This is the unification of the faces. And it has been said:
Having understood the subsequent ritual action through the [deities] such as Vaiśāna and others, along with the *sadya* and other *Īśānāmbara*s,
one should meditate upon the fivefold activities before oneself— by means of which whatever action is desired is accomplished.
One should fashion its primary face upward; in that position, the other faces should be directed upward as well.
The other faces are included within it, and it should be of the same measurement as the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
"Śiva, Rudra, the Grahas, the Ādityas, Brahmā, Candra, Acyuta, and the others—all these have fire as their mouth; yet even he [Hara] consists of all the gods."
172) Now, the face [of the fire] is also according to the ritual action. As it is stated in the *Kālottara*:
"The oblation is for the form of Īśāna; and in the case of Puruṣa, there is [the attainment of] powers such as aṇimā."
In such a terrible situation, there should likewise be expiatory rites and the like, as well as harsh measures.

One should perform the fire-oblation in the Vāmadeva face for the purpose of subjugation, attraction, and delusion; however, the performance of daily rites is beneficial in this western face. Having understood this, O Mahāsena, one should determine the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) accordingly.
"O son, one should effect the unification of the faces in this manner and not otherwise;
for those other faces which are not primary are merely secondary to the fire-offerings. Thus it is said.
Therefore, one should perform the placement of the tongue and other rites upon that face.
It is as follows: Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and thereafter Suprabhā.
The seven tongues are proclaimed to be excessive and multiformed.

The seven tongues, beginning with Hiraṇyā, are situated in order: in the directions of Īśa (northeast), Agni (southeast), Nairṛta (southwest), Varuṇa (west), and Anila (north), as well as in the center.
One with the great luster of refined gold, one with the radiance of gold and silver,
one resembling the red hue of saffron, and one with the dark blue luster of a sapphire.
She possesses a beautiful luster like that of pearls and moonlight, and is deep red like a ruby;
she takes many forms, distinguished by the light of the moon-gem and the autumnal moon.
The fruit is proclaimed according to its individual distinctions: the *kravyādā* is for subjugation and attraction; the first (*vaśyā*) is beneficial for paralyzing;
the *kanakā* is for causing enmity and delusion; and the *raktā* and *kṛṣṇā* are for the act of killing.
Suprabhā is prescribed for pacification (*śāntika*); Suraktā is considered suitable for eradication (*uccāṭana*).
Ekā and Bahurūpā, however, bestow [the respective results]... [as desired].

That which begins with *hiraṇya* and is situated on the tongue in the proximity of fire (*vahni*) should be known as such; the path that occurs at the commencement of the *hotṛ* priest is a slayer of Brahman (*brahmaghātaka*). [The mantra] beginning with *yā* and ending with *hā*, excluding the letter *ra*, has the letter *ra* and the sixth vowel (*ū*) situated therein.
Joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*, one should perform the kindling of the tongue;
having established a continuous flow by means of each pair, one should lead it to dissolution in the center.

Thus is the unification of the tongue. The application of the mantra begins with: *oṃ bhūḥ hiraṇyāyai svāhā*, and so forth. For the purpose of the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), one should say: *oṃ īśānāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped [the deity] and offered five oblations (*āhuti*) with the weapon-mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should designate the name: *oṃ hāṃ śivāgni tattvaṃ hutāśana*. Then, having offered five oblations with *oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ śivāgnaye svāhā*, and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as will be described for the sake of completing the remaining consecrations (*saṃskāra*), one should then worship the parents, satisfy them with ten oblations each, and dismiss them with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). Thus is the naming ceremony.
And it is said:
"The naming rite (nāmakarma) should be performed, giving him the name Śivāgni;
for the sake of perfecting the refinement of his anger, one should subsequently offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), preceded by the previous [rites]."
The rites beginning with the departure from the womb, the first feeding, and likewise the investiture with the sacred thread,
up to the tonsure and the offering of the cow, have been commenced and completed in full.
One should dismiss Vāgīśvarī and Śiva with the heart-mantra. Thus it is said.
Or else, O Guha, one may maintain the Śiva-fire in another manner.
"One should cause the threefold full [offering] to fall by means of the knowledge of the Self and those called Śiva;
through that, the fire of Śiva arises, which is devoid of all residual impressions. Thus it is said.

Then, having removed the fire for the sake of incense and lamps and preserved it in another place, one should offer sixteen oblations of sacrificial wood (*samidh*) with their roots and tips intact, reciting: *Oṃ hrūṃ śivāgnaye svāhā*. Thereafter, [one should recite]: "O Agni, since you are the supreme purifying splendor of Īśvara, I therefore establish you within the lotus of my heart and satisfy you."

Having thus prayed to Agni, by his command, one should worship Sadāśiva—the object of meditation—within the lotus of his heart as before, in detail, together with his support, limiting adjuncts, and the [mantra] syllables, ending with the Pavitra.

Or else, having uttered the mantra of the seat-form (*āsana-mūrti*), one should worship it. And it has been said: "Having invoked the seat and the form, one should spread the three [mantras] there once; or else, according to the application from the heart, one should cause the fire of Śiva to be established."
The seat is as before, and the deity’s form here is also as before; one should unite that form with the Supreme Reality (paratattva), ending with Śiva.
Having performed the worship according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as before.
Then, having established a connection with Śiva residing in the *liṅga*, one should again connect [the fire] with Śiva residing in the fire. It is as follows:
"The thread from the spider's web, which has gone out through the joy [of emission], enters through the non-joy [of reabsorption];
and that which has gone out through the non-joy enters through the joy."

"The Guru should not contemplate her entering [the body] while the *ānena* has not yet been uttered. Thus it is said. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter (*sruta*) using the root mantra, [he should perform] its tenth part...
And one should satisfy the limbs with a portion [of the offering]. As it has been said:
"In the absence of clarified butter, the oblation (homa) should be performed with black sesame seeds;
or else the oblation may be performed with rice or barley, which grants success in all matters."
The oblation for the vow of all desires consists of sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter;
it should be offered into a fire that is not blazing, and its smoke serves as the binding agent.
When the fire is blazing and licking [the offerings], the oblation (*homa*) succeeds;
when it is glossy, turning clockwise, and its sound issues from the base of the flame's tail;
when it constantly rises upward and is free from soot—such a fire is auspicious for the performance of *piṇḍa* rites by the Śivas. Thus it is said.
Having offered three morsels of food to Śambhu, one should offer five morsels to Agni,
and one to each of the deities born of his limbs, according to the full procedure as it is taught.
Having filled the *sruk* with clarified butter and placed the *sruva* face downwards,
having placed a flower at its tip with the *śaṅkha*-like mudrā,
and holding the *sruk* and *sruva* with both hands, one should place their bases at the center of the navel.

Having performed [this], one should rise and stand with the body straight and composed, clearly reciting the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. That which is the bulbous vessel (*kanda-kalaśa*) is this very thing; the stalk (*nāḍī-daṇḍa*) has arisen from it.
The heart is the beautiful altar-platform and the cavity of the palate is the large vessel;
having filled the *sruva* ladle with the clarified butter that has emerged from the drop and issued forth through the nostrils, one should offer it into the fires of the *śānta* [state].
Having offered water for sipping (ācamana) to the fire, as well as betel leaves and other offerings,
one should conclude [the rite] by praising, prostrating, worshipping, and saluting it.

In this context, as a relevant digression, the substances for the *soma* offering, their measurements and so forth, and the characteristics of the final fire-oblation (*agni-pūrṇāhuti*) are written here according to the scriptures:
"With clarified butter or with milk, or with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter;
or with barley or rice, or with *guggulu* resin and clarified butter."
The daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) must be performed, and likewise the optional oblation (kāmyahoma) is described:
for the sake of pacification, one should offer three pieces of dūrvā grass and aśvattha wood soaked in ghee and honey.

For those desiring prosperity (*śrī*), an oblation of *jātī*, *campaka*, and *padma* flowers, as well as fruits, is beneficial; likewise, an oblation adorned with *karavīra* flowers, along with black mustard (*rājikā*) and salt, is for the purpose of paralyzing (*stambhana*). *Puṣpa* (flower) is used here as a neuter noun.
Indeed, clarified butter weighing one karṣa should be offered for the accomplishment of the rite;
one should offer sesame seeds with the *tilāmṛgī* mantra and barley and other grains with the *kambu-mudrā*.
One should offer rice with the *muṣṭi* (fist) mudrā, flowers and so forth with the *kumbhaka* (vase) mudrā,
and items including side-dishes and the like with the *patāka* (banner) mudrā.
One should always offer oblations of guggulu resin the size of a jujube fruit,
and one should perform oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with clarified butter according to one's capacity.

One should always offer a mouthful as an oblation; three such oblations constitute the measure for the stomach. Of side dishes, one should offer only a dripping amount; of solid foods, one should offer according to one's own capacity. And of salt, one should offer only a *karṣa* (one ounce).
White mustard seeds, in the measure of a handful, should be offered as oblations while reciting the mantra.
(177) O Six-faced One, for fruits and flowers, one's own desired measure is prescribed; the same applies to bulbs, roots, and fruits when they have been thus prepared.
Roots, tubers, fruits, and the like are recommended for both daily and optional rites;
however, for the cessation of hemorrhoids, one should use barley meal (*saktu*) in cases of pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣmā*).
For the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), one should offer parched grain, conch shells, and the bones of a crow as oblations;
likewise, fuel-sticks produced from the *vibhītaka* tree should be offered with pungent oil.
In the rite of inciting enmity, one should perform the homa with all the limbs of a hostile creature;
having made a firm resolve, one should likewise cut up that [victim] when it is upright and dried.
It is recommended that [the ritual] be performed with substances mixed with blood, using wood from a *preta* tree or arising from a cremation ground;
one shall cause the wheel to be eradicated—of this there is no need for deliberation.
In rites of malevolent magic (abhicāra), trees with thorns on their trunks are to be known [as appropriate];
for rites of pacification (śānti), rain-making (vṛṣṭi), subjugation (vaśa), and attraction (ākarṣa), milky trees are prescribed.
Honey is praised for use in the *homa* sacrifice and with the sacrificial ladles (*sruva*) according to the teaching;
the milk of all four-legged animals is praised for longevity.
A measure of one *pala* of sweet [substance] always yields two excellent fruits.
For the sake of accomplishing all nourishment, one should offer oblations together with honey;
an offering made in a smokeless fire is praised, and not otherwise is it auspicious.
When a fire blazes with a clockwise curl, an oblation performed therein grants the accomplishment of all aims;
likewise, the colors, fragrances, sounds, and shapes within the fire [indicate success].
The practitioner must recognize both the *vikāras* and the *śikhās*;
their radiance is like that of rubies, with a luster equal to liquid lac.
The sacrificial fire, possessing the color of the rising sun, is commended for the success of men in their quest for victory.
Resembling a hibiscus flower, he is intent upon enjoyments;
he is like fire, resembling a discus, a bow, a sword, and likewise like saffron water.
At that time, a red-colored fire is praised as bestowing all accomplishments;
it resembles molten gold or has the luster of yellow orpiment.

A [pigment] with the color of turmeric or realgar, ending with that of gorocanā, is praised for the purpose of immobilization (stambhana). A yellow color is used for paralyzing, while a red color is used for subduing (dhaukita).
A color resembling a bee or collyrium is not conducive to success.
One who is concentrated on this [mantra] performs the rites of killing, expulsion, and cutting.
Even one who possesses a complexion like that of a conch shell, crystal, jasmine, or the moon does not bestow accomplishment.
In rites for pacification and nourishment,
a fire that is always auspicious is one resembling the eyes of a cat or the color of a parrot’s plumage.
Like the ear of a peacock or resembling a pigeon,
the fire, being invoked with various mantras, is produced suddenly in this manner.
Having understood the wind according to its correspondence with each respective action, it should always be adopted when it is favorable to that action, or avoided when it is contrary to it.
The fragrance of fragrant substances, the scent of fire, and the pleasant smell of ghee are auspicious;
O Six-faced One, the lotus-scent and the bilva-scent belong to longevity.
A pungent odor is recommended for rites such as malevolent magic (abhicāra), while fire is always auspicious.
Having a fragrance like that of the blue lotus, he is always praised for his good fortune.
When the sacrificial fire, emitting sounds like those of a lordly elephant or a rain-cloud, is constantly fed with oblations,
then one should know that the desired success of the rite has been achieved for the sacrificer.
The forms of the sounds of clouds, lutes, conchs, and drums are auspicious for the success of the oblation;
any other form is the opposite.
The *chatraka* is the best of the *bhrigus*, resembling a banner and a fly-whisk;
equal to a bull or an elephant as a vehicle, it is a fire that always bestows nourishment.
There may be a multitude of celestial chariots, mountain canopies, and palaces.
And when the sun appears in the form of a swan, sweet-sounding and without cause, it is praised;
the wise have declared that such a day brings immediate success.
The clouds are thick, glossy, and compact, and the sun is intensely radiant.
Soft [sounds] are always praised for the accomplishment of all things;
likewise, a rough sound like the crackling of firewood brings success here.
However, the forms of donkeys, camels, buffaloes, and the like do not succeed in this matter.
If the sound is smooth and turns clockwise, it should be known as leading to the accomplishment of one's purpose; otherwise, it will be fruitless.
Bhrigus of such a kind are praised; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should also engrave the syllable *Sudhā* and this very *Śikhā*;
for the sake of liberation from bondage, these are not to be practiced in the scriptures consisting of the *Kālottara*.
Likewise:
one should offer [oblations] in this manner into Hiraṇyā; into Kanakā, one should offer clarified butter;
into Raktā, chariots are prescribed; and into Kṛṣṇā, one should offer grain.

One should offer parched grain (saktu) into the Suprabhā fire, sesame seeds into the Suraktā fire, white mustard seeds into the Bahurūpā fire, and it is said that an oblation of cooked rice (caru) is prescribed for all [the fires].
All [the substances] other than the primary substance (*dravya*)—[one should] offer the oblation in sequence.
With offerings of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one should meditate upon her; with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), one should offer to Daṇḍinī.
One should remain lying down during the *ājya* oblations, but seated during the remaining rites;
at the time of the oblation, however, the specific class (*jāti*) of mantras is determined according to the nature of the ritual action.
*svāhā* is for peace (*śānti*), *svadhā* for nourishment (*puṣṭi*), *vauṣaṭ* for subjugation (*vaśya*), and *namaḥ* for worship (*arcana*).
*ṭhaṭha* is for paralyzing (*stambha*), while *bandhu* is for eradication (*uccāṭa*); with *māra*, one should say "strike him yourself" (*ghātayasva yam*).
The syllable *vaṣaṭ* is proclaimed as the genus for the rite of attraction;
likewise, nourishing rites are performed in the late winter (*hemanta*), and the supreme rite of killing in the cool season (*śiśira*).
Subjugation (*vaśya*) occurs in the spring, while in the summer there is enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*).

In the rainy season, there is always eradication (*uccāṭana*), and in autumn there is peace (*śānti*). They know that at dawn it is the union of *uṣā*, and at daybreak it is the cold season (*śiśira*).
In the forenoon, however, it is spring; at midday, it is known as summer.

The rains last for three *praharas*, and autumn begins at sunset—thus says the wise one. Enough with this excessive detail. Then, having worshipped Śiva residing in the fire as before and dismissed him, one should unite [the fire] with the Śiva residing in the *liṅga* via the path of the channels (*nāḍī*). Having also dismissed the deities of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) along with their offerings, one should thereafter offer the *bhūḥ*-oblation and so forth as before. Having extracted the fire from the pit and preserved it in a new vessel (*bhāṇḍa*), one should worship Caṇḍeśvara in the residual fire, satisfy him according to one's capacity, and dismiss him. Having offered the internal and external oblations (*bali*) like cakes and wiped [the area], one should reduce the collection of materials in the pit to ashes. Having removed that, one should smear the pit, both inside and out, with cow-dung water. Then, once again performing the purification of the pit at the time of the *homa*, one should kindle the fire established there, worship Śiva within it as before, and satisfy him; in this manner, one should perform [this rite] every day. And so it has been said:
Every day, the ritual actions such as the scraping of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth are known to be performed during the waking state;
therefore, there is no fire in that regard, but rather in the daily obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*).

The meaning here is that the initiation of the deceased (śava-dīkṣā), whether it be the foundational (pratiṣṭhā) or another [type], must be performed according to the occasional (naimittika) injunctions. As it is said: "Once [the fire] has been consecrated, one should daily deposit into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) the fire previously consecrated.
Likewise:
"By the command of Śiva, the maintenance of the Śiva-fire is meritorious for as long as one lives."
Having drawn it from the vessel with ease, one should place it in a sturdy container.
One should well protect the fire with merit using parched husks and kālapa seeds;
having consecrated the sacrificial pit as before, one should circumambulate it every day.
Having deposited [the deity] there with the *anuṣṭubh* verses, one should perform the propitiation and the auspicious rite;
at the conclusion of the ritual, the initiates must diligently perform the protection as before.
Having thus made it well-protected, whoever should satisfy [the deity] even at the cost of their life—
the fruit of that merit cannot be described by anyone here in this world.
If that effect does not occur in others— namely, among ordinary beings—
then the dismissal of the fire should never take place at any time, such as in a specific location or on a particular occasion.
Having joined the fire of knowledge with the thought within the heart, one should dismiss it;
then, one should perform the expiation consisting of remaining in that very state.
"When the mind is again composed, one should act as previously described. Thus it is said.
Then, having gone to the presence of Śiva and performed the offering of the Śiva-homa and other rites, one should bid farewell to Śiva as before.
May there be well-being! Śrī Jñānaśaṅkara, a bee at the lotus feet of the illustrious Viśveśvara and whose abode is Śiva, has composed this extensive *Vahnikārya*.
Thus ends the Great Fire Ritual in the *Śrījñānaratnāvalī*.
Salutation to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.

Then, even at the time of midday, one should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) in detail, preceded by the bath and the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), and worship Śiva. Alternatively, having waited for five *muhūrtas* while the Lord is occupied with worship, one should certainly complete the midday rite preceded by the twilight prayers and the offering of eight flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), and then take food. As it is said: "Having performed the midday rite in this manner, one should eat; not otherwise. If one eats without performing it, that meal is [as if] offered to the gods."

Those established on the seat of yoga do not preside over that which resides in the mantra. When five muhūrtas have passed, having performed the midday rite, the mantras of Śiva become destroyers of inauspiciousness for one who is eating. Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"That twice-born man who, having committed evil, eats without first performing worship of Śambhu, will undoubtedly be devoid of virtue,
wealth, and food."
Now, it might be argued that even a goat eats worms and consumes urine and semen;
oh! a non-giver would eat such impurity, yet he experiences the unevenness [of his own actions].
Having performed these four through yoga, one partakes of the nectar of immortality.
Now, the procedure for eating is described: (p.
183) [Food] given by the gurus out of compassion and accepted with devotion by the disciples in their hearts.
Or [he may give] vessels of grain and so forth by means of other pure devotees, such as the twice-born.

That which is offered with devotion should always be accepted, and not by others through the power of mantras and such; one should avoid the property of the deity, the property of the guru, and that which belongs to the mantra.

He who cooks for his own sake alone is called a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*). Cooking is said to be *proḍāśa*; [one should cook] with dry fuel on a great seat that is free from insects and the like, pure, and smeared [with cow-dung].
The cooking should be performed by oneself, or by other pure persons from the left side.
When the cooking is finished and the house has been smeared [with cow dung], and once the cooked food has been brought inside, the pure preceptor—
having performed the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) and being surrounded by consecrated waters— should sprinkle the cooked food with the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra.
Having set aside the first portion of that cooked food, he should offer it to Śiva.
Then, having offered the remainder with the half-verse and purified that skull-cup,
one should generate the fire of gnosis there and worship it with the heart-mantra.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to all [the deities]. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Having thus worshipped from Agni up to the end of the east, and having performed the *haranā* (carrying away of the remains) and so forth with mantras ending in *svāhā*, one should ask for forgiveness and dismiss them. Then, at this point, some [authorities] say: "The body of dharma and adharma, the male form, the vessel, the water-pitcher, as well as the machine, together with the *mīla* and the pestle."
One should worship the mortar and pestle, as well as the grinding stone and the winnowing basket,
at the main door of the house; and on the path, one should worship Vighneśa and Sarasvatī.
One should worship Lakṣmī on the door-jamb, Maheśvara in the middle of the door,
Śakti on the threshold (udumbara), and the one called Ādhāra at the base of the door.
One should place Skanda at the central pillar and the presiding deity of the site (Vāstunāyaka) below it;
one should depict Kāma holding his own arrow at the tip of a bow, as well as a sword and a seat in the hand.
A vehicle, one’s own mount, a young maiden, and a brightly burning lamp;
with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, water, incense, lamps, food, and so forth.
And they worship this foremost [mantra] for the sake of bringing about all prosperity. Thus it is said.
Having washed his feet, sipped water for purification, performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), and composed his mind,
he should take his seat in the previously described place and proceed to eat.
There, the preceptor, facing east, seated comfortably on a comfortable seat with his hands between his knees— or externally— should remain silent, either in the *vīrāsana* posture or otherwise.
The practitioner [should face] the east for the gentle-faced [deity], while the others are situated facing west or north;
he should not eat facing south, even if it be only one of these [directions].
If he eats out of negligence, he will be tormented by diseases.
He [should be worshipped] with syllables arranged in rows, unmixed and unconfused.

Together with those who have arisen from the pure tradition— those who are disciplined and devoted to their guru— one should perform protection all around three times using ashes and the sword-mantra.
In a vessel made of bell-metal, copper, or lead, adorned with ashes,
[one should place] leaves of plantain, lotus, bhṛṅga, madhūka, and jackfruit,
as well as those emerging from the kumbhī, campaka, punnāga, kūṭaja, and jāti flowers.
The ellipsis "one should eat" is to be supplied with these and other well-known items of a single genus.
With *aśvattha*, *eraṇḍa*, *bhallātaka*, *nyagrodha*, *arka*, and *vibhītaka*.
A meal should not be served in a vessel made from the wood of the Śūka, Udumbara, or similar trees;
rather, it should be served in a vessel provided with a handle and a base, or one fashioned from leaves.
When the food has been purified by the recitation of the *ghora* mantra seven times over the sacrificial thread and the fingernail-scraper, and having meditated upon the nectar of Mṛtyuñjaya,
one should sprinkle the rice and other offerings there with the *mṛtyuñjaya* and other mantras.
By that [means], one should obtain those seven [offerings] and cause the water to be pleasing;
one should cast the bali offering, consisting of food in the measure of half a morsel, upon the ground for the Nāgas and others.

Namely: *Oṃ nāga kūrma kṛsara devadatta-dhanañjayebhyaḥ upaprāṇavāyubhyaḥ svāhā*. Having thus offered the *bali* to the *vāyu*s such as *nāga* and the others with water dripping from the hollow of the left hand, one should satisfy the deities residing in the vital airs (*prāṇa* and so forth) by means of the tips of the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger, saying: *Oṃ hāṃ apānāya svāhā*, *Oṃ hāṃ samānāya svāhā*, *Oṃ hāṃ udānāya svāhā*, *Oṃ hāṃ vyānāya svāhā*. Then, one should offer this food into the fire of Śiva located within the stomach-fire. And it has been said:
The Self resides in prāṇa; the sources of all beings reside in apāna;
the gods reside in udāna; and the ancestors reside in samāna.
The Nāgas residing in Vyāna as well as those dwelling in Pātāla are situated there;
[they are reached] by means of the thumb, the middle finger, and the tips of the ring finger of the right hand, which serves as the tip of the sacrificial ladle (sruk).
[He saw them] stationed in the midst of the flames of the fire situated within the clarified-butter pit.
With single oblations, one should satisfy these [deities] who have been subdued; one should not touch them.
One should offer the remainder, mixed with ghee and condiments, as a *homa* to Īśa.
"The Prāṇāgnihotra is said to be more than a hundred times superior to [ordinary] Agnihotra.
Likewise:
"Garlic and the meat of the chin (cibuka) yield swift results."
Gṛñjana, honey, meat, and visible salt [are forbidden].
One should not consume food remnants, nor clarified butter from the sea (sāmudrikam). One should not eat stale cooked food, except for that which has been fried in oil.
Furthermore, one should not drink water with hands that have merely been washed.
One should not eat from the hand of another, nor drink water that remains after someone else has drunk;
one should not blow on fire when it is blazing, nor should one strike the mouth with a stone.
One should not recite mantras while yawning or coughing; one should meditate on the *kukkuṭāsana* posture.
One should drink water that has been poured through a leaf, never with a distracted mind.
If [food] has been touched by fish, thorns, snails, nails, hair, cowrie shells,
or by flies and the like through negligence, one should remove those [impurities] from it.
Having sprinkled the remainder with water and ashes, he should eat it with washed hands;
he should avoid the remnants of [offerings to] Tantras, as well as dogs, donkeys, mules, and pigs.
At that time, one should not look upon Caṇḍālas, leather-workers, and the like;
hearing their speech is undesirable, and likewise, one should not make worldly noise.
If, through negligence, one should fall into water while still possessing half-eaten food,
and should see it [the food] there, then that is considered a bath.
Having heard those words, one should perform the rite of consuming raw grain (āmamācara) while remaining within the mouth.
Having taken [the food], one should not be intoxicated nor distracted; having approached [the meal],
one should eat with the left hand, making little noise, in a very gentle manner, and silently.

At midday or at night, having first comfortably performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should, for the sake of purifying the defects of eating, consecrate Kālāgnirudra—who resides on the tip of the big toe of the right foot—with water poured from the tip of the thumb of the right hand, reciting: *oṃ hāṃ kālāgnirudrāya svāhā*. Then, one should form the *parigha-mudrā*. And it has been said:
One is smeared with as much sin as there are morsels of food;
therefore, one should eat only a very small amount, just enough to sustain life.
To purify even that sin, [one should consume] the tip of the nail of the right foot.
The practitioner, reciting the heart-mantra of Kālarudra, should sprinkle [the disciple] with his right thumb;
then, having placed the little finger of the left hand at the region of the navel.
One should join that very [thumb] with the left thumb of the right hand;
having extended both hands, one should place the right thumb in the mouth.
This has been fully described as the protective enclosure (parikheya) that destroys unwholesome food;
then, having performed the ritual smearing (uddhūlana), completed the ritual placement (nyāsa), and prostrated before the Guru and the Deity.
Having recited the Aghora mantra seven times, one should subsequently release the vow of silence.
And it is said:
"Having sipped water and become pure, one should meditate upon Śiva and then recite [the mantra].
Upon concluding the recitation, one should release speech and make truth most dear."
One should perform the cleansing of the mouth. If one places betel—though it is sometimes used as a cause for coloration—along with *pathyā* and other such items, [it is permissible].
Thus concludes the rule for the meal of alms (*bhikṣābhojana*) belonging to the *santānika* [period].
What is the use of the fault of receiving gifts, or the fruit of giving,
or the labor of cooking— that which is the locus of many defects?
If one is detached from these and desires to perform great merit,
one should construct a hut made of grass and leaves at a sacred ford (tīrtha) that serves as a refuge for the Liṅga.
May his retinue be sufficient for as long as he exists,
illuminating the imperishable foot that is separated from the body by a mere quarter.
Constantly absorbed in consciousness that consists of the infinite, unattached to Śivā by the command of Śiva,
he has accomplished his purpose, is a purified soul, and his body is white with ashes.
Having exchanged his loincloth for a saffron robe,
having made it his upper garment, wearing a rosary of rudrākṣa beads,
and arranging his matted locks according to the tradition of the lineage of teachers;

The weapon, which is its own support, should be twelve finger-breadths in height and as wide as a finger of the auspicious measure; it may be made of iron or other materials, or likewise of tiger or deer skin— light, or whatever is obtained, or whatever is auspicious.
Likewise, having become a restrainer of the senses, having washed his feet and hands,
and having sipped water according to the rule, he, with a tranquil mind, performed the ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should practice the *mādhukarī* mode of begging for alms as prescribed for ascetics in the scriptures;
having made one's own body the staff, it should be as thick as a thumb.
Alternatively, this staff may be made of elephant-apple wood, bamboo, or of the *vaiṇava* or *khadira* species;
it should be twelve finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths in thickness.
Having pierced it, one should fashion a bowl, or a vessel made of copper may be prepared;
[one may also use] vessels of *palāśa*, honey, *kadamba*, or *campaka* flowers.

One should avoid the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *piṭha*, *akṣa*, and *kesara* trees. Furthermore, one should perform the task of begging for alms according to the prescribed rule, as it is said: "The weapon is in the staff, the heart is in the bowl; thus, one should meditate on Śiva."
One should eat almsfood received in one's bowl, placing it on the ground;
having withdrawn from worldly life, one should not remain for a long time among those who have not withdrawn.
One should practice silence with diligence, or by filling one's alms-bowl;
or one should subsist on morsels of grain, or even for many days at a time.
Even if it is very small, when brought by the feet of Somaśambhu and given with faith for the purpose of sipping water (ācamana),
that alms— extending from food down to a mere morsel— is called *ayācita* (unsolicited).
One should not accept food from outcasts, barbers, those accused of crimes, or those of the lowest castes;
rather, one should seek alms with a mind fixed on dharma from those who are pure.
Just as a bee, even while gathering honey, does not harm the flower,
so too should one collect the "honey-gathering" alms from the master of the house.
One should not eat food from a single source, even if that person were equal to Bṛhaspati;
for one who is intent on begging alms from these [many sources] attains both his own and others' welfare.
A monk, seeking what is to be accomplished, should avoid an inferior vessel for the offering of cessation;
for the purpose of alms, he may use one made of copper, iron, or leaves from large trees and the like.
For one who desires worldly enjoyment, a vessel is prescribed; for one who desires liberation, a gourd-bowl and the like.
It should be pure, white, suspended [from the neck], and consecrated with the *bahurūpa* mantra.
Clad in a saffron robe consecrated by many recitations, covered with pure garments,
bathed with purified ashes, he wears a loincloth and an upper cloth.
Having turned back and sipped water, remaining silent and meditating upon Śiva and the Guru, and having received their permission, he—
holding a staff consecrated with the Astra-mantra and an umbrella in his hand— proceeded for the sake of alms to the houses of the pure.

At that time, one should not disregard the vital breaths, the intellect, or the sense of touch; nor should one revile those who have strayed onto wrong paths. One should abandon a horse and so forth, even if it is crowded with many others.
[Dharma is realized through the intellect; a mendicant should not take alms from one who has not yet entered the gate.]
Just as a bee, even while taking its honey, does not harm the flower,
so too should one accept the "honey-gathering" alms from the master of the house;
having reached the courtyard of the homes of the four pure castes.
Having mentally recited "Give alms," he should fix his gaze on the tip of his big toe.
The sage should wait for as long as it takes for the cow to yield milk through union with her calf;
once she has yielded the flow, he should go elsewhere.
Even while traveling, one who has become equanimous should not return from that place;
he should bring back the alms obtained there from people engaged in sacrifice or giving.
One should not take it from a well, nor with one's hand, nor at the wrong time; nor indeed by means of the hand of a low-caste woman, a pregnant woman, or one wearing soiled garments.
Then, having wandered for alms in this manner until his bowl is full, and wishing for the welfare of the world, he should go to his own hermitage. Thus it is said.
Having brought alms and placed them in a pure, level, and auspicious spot,
he should wash his hands, feet, and so forth, and then perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) as previously described.
Having sprinkled those materials with water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should again offer them into the mouth of Śiva.
The food should be consecrated with the three-syllabled mantra (*tryakṣara*) and placed all around; thus it quickly becomes nourishment, and its consumption shall be the conqueror of death.
One should eat while maintaining silence and not causing excessive disturbance;
thus is described the wandering for alms, which is the common characteristic of all [orders].
There is no merit equal to alms-giving; what austerity is equal to begging for alms?

Whatever merit exists in all sacred fords, whatever fruit exists in all sacrifices, and whatever merit exists in all acts of charity as well as in penances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa—[all that is attained through alms-giving].
A man who receives alms from such a person shall obtain ten million times that fruit, O Śrī.
When the cooking is completed, the lunar day (tithi) turns its back and departs;
likewise, all the gods and ancestors turn their backs and depart from that place.
When the time has arrived, however, it should be given with careful deliberation and effort;
such a person uplifts ten generations of ancestors and ten generations of descendants.
Among all worthy recipients, a guest is indeed the most excellent;
even one who is deficient in limbs is superior to one who is complete in limbs if he is without brothers and is pure.
He is worthy of worship even without formal deliberation; he shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
But he who, when the proper time has arrived, avoids a mendicant standing before him—having seized all his merit, that guest departs.
p.
192) When one seeks to understand through inquiry that which is not yet fully realized during the process of maturation,
even he who is called a slayer of a Brahmin is always pure, O Bahurūpa.
Knowing this, one should always diligently engage in the practice of begging for alms;
for him whose senses are restrained and who is intent on the life of a mendicant, spiritual perfections are accomplished.
O Śikhidhvaja, all forms of receiving gifts are said to be permissible except for alms;
having given water into the hand of an ascetic, one should give the alms, and then water again.
That food would be equal to Mount Meru, and that water would be like the ocean.
Likewise:
"The giving of alms is a great gift; indeed, the alms are not a formal acceptance.
The fruit of both is equal for both the giver and the receiver."
Therefore, having taken up faith, one who is constant in his vow should always practice mendicancy.
Thus ends the procedure for eating alms-food in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
Thus, salutations to Mahāgaṇapati.
Until the time of evening, one should contemplate the established conclusions regarding the task at hand;
and at that time, according to one's ability, one should perform either a bath or the cleansing of the waist.
Having washed his limbs or wiped his body with a cloth,
and having performed the ritual dusting as before, he should salute the twilight and worship Śiva.
If one becomes purified by means of bathing water, milk, and so forth,
then one should bathe or wash oneself in sequence, either above or below the navel.
Having sipped water and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should spread ashes upon a bed of kuśa grass on the ground;
having strewn it there, one should enter with a serene countenance, placing the unconquered *khaṭvāṅga* upon it.
As long as he remains under the influence of sleep, so long should he be intent upon meditative concentration and dhyāna;
then, having returned, the householder should sleep with his head toward the west and his feet toward the north.
By saying "Namo nandīśvarāya" with the *yonimudrā* at both sides,
he shall never experience fear from *kūśmāṇḍas* and other such beings.
Then, one should go for alms during the day itself; however, at midnight, as before, one should perform the twilight worship, the worship of Śiva, or even the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
Having slept again, she should rise and perform everything previously mentioned;
by doing this daily with a sense of constancy, she herself shall not [be deprived of] the fruit of her merit.

Thus, this daily ritual procedure has been composed by the venerable Jñānaśivācārya, a scholar who follows the path of virtue, at the request of his disciples. Thus ends the "Ritual for Daily Duties" in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Now, regarding that which is called the "daily" [rite], it is accompanied by mantras, substances, and ritual actions;
yet, due to negligence, divine influence, delusion, or preoccupation with other tasks, [it may be omitted].
From the king, thieves, [and] laziness, as well as from physical calamity, a vulnerability inevitably arises; for the purpose of filling that vulnerability, [one must act].
Now, for the benefit of men, the eternally constituent and purifying [element] is being described—
that which was obtained by the gods from Śambhu in ancient times through difficult penance.
And it is said in the venerable Mṛgendra:
The Creator himself is declared to be the remover of one's own defects;
he was obtained by the gods through austerity from Hara.
"In the month of Śrāvaṇa, his near-pupil, like one being instructed, having obtained the purifier (pavitra) of Śambhu, should complete the rite in its entirety. Thus [it is said].

[Objection: Is this not a case of overlapping? Since the *pavitra* is an obligatory limb (*nityāṅga*) of the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), and since this [specific rite] is to be performed at another time, how can it be understood as an obligatory limb? Therefore, it must be either occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), or a penance (*prāyaścitta*). [Reply: This should not be said. Because even when that daily *pavitraka* is performed with substitutes for the thread, such as flowers or *kuśa* grass, it remains incomplete. Consequently, by means of this very [rite], its completion is brought about; thus, this too is indeed an obligatory limb. Furthermore, because a penance is prescribed for its omission—just as for the omission of the daily twilight prayers (*sandhyā*) and other obligatory limbs—it is certainly an obligatory limb, and not occasional or optional. In this context, "occasional" refers to initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*); "optional" refers to the attainment of powers like atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth, or subjugation (*vaśya*) and the like. As it has been said:
Bathing, the twilight rites, worship, recitation, and fifthly, the fire sacrifice—
these are declared as the daily duties, as is the ritual of the sacred thread investiture (pavitrāropaṇa).

"Initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (pratiṣṭhā)—these two are occasional (naimittika). That which is for the sake of attaining powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth is optional (kāmya); even that has been forgotten. Thus [it is said].

Just as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed for the violation of a religious observance (*niyama*), so too, since an expiation is heard of even for its performance, there would likewise be no need for an expiation [for its non-performance].

Alternatively, if this very act were somehow considered the expiation itself, then it would necessarily follow that its non-performance would also be established as an offense, because there is no other means of atonement for it. And it has been said:
"An expiation declared in the scriptures and taught by the Guru must be performed."
"Otherwise, his initiation (dīkṣā) and the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) would indeed be fruitless. (p. 195)
Therefore, this is indeed an obligatory limb [of the ritual]. And so it is stated in the *Kālottara*: "The obligatory [limb] is remembered as being twofold therein—the permanent and the occasional.
For men, that which is devoid of substances, mantras, and ritual actions is defective and fruitless."
Therefore, this Pavitrāropaṇa is considered to be an obligatory constituent part [of the ritual].
Because it purifies through the non-terrible [aspect] despite its partiality, it is called *pavitraka*.
Therefore, at that time, one should perform what was previously prescribed for the Supreme Lord;
by that, the annual worship clearly becomes complete.
But as for one who would worship Maheśvara for even a single day according to my word,
I, the six-pathed one (Ṣaḍadhvaja), am unable to describe the fruit of his merit;
she was worshipped in ancient times by the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Upendra.
Having established [the deity] in the supreme abode, who then would not worship it?
Because it is an integral part of worship, it should be performed either daily or according to fixed rules.
Furthermore, one should certainly not perform it within three months;
likewise, on the fourteenth day at the end of Āṣāḍha, or similarly in Nabhasya and Nabhas.
Or on the eighth or the fourteenth day of both fortnights, equally.
The Pavitrāropaṇa rite must be performed; it is not beneficial to postpone it to another time. If this time has passed, one should perform an expiation.
"This rite is specifically for material beings during the bright fortnight.
This being so, however, it must be performed only after the sleep of Viṣṇu. And it is said:
It should also be performed in the month of Āṣāḍha when Madhusūdana is fast asleep;
this time is declared to be fixed for it—now hear the determination of the ritual procedure.
One should perform [the rite] on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha,
and on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada.

[Objection: But does not the phrase "on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha" itself establish that [the Lord] lies down at the time immediately following Viṣṇu’s sleep? What follows from this, namely, that Madhusūdana is already fast asleep? [Response: True. Furthermore, Āṣāḍha is of two kinds: lunar (*cāndra*) and solar (*saura*). Among these, he sleeps throughout the entire period of the lunar month. Moreover, when there is an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), Viṣṇu [lies down] specifically upon the solar transit (*saṅkrānti*) into Cancer. This was stated for the purpose of such recollection; thus, there is no fault. And it is said in the Jyotiḥśāstra: "When the Sun, situated in Gemini, touches two new moons (*amāvāsyā*)."
"A second Āṣāḍha is to be recognized; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer. Thus it is said.
It is said:
When the sun passes beyond two new moons,
that should be known as the intercalary month (malamāsa), excluded from all ritual acts.
According to this statement, the intention is that the *pavitra* rite should not be performed during Pūrvāṣāḍhā. Thus it is said.

If this were so, then when an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) occurs in Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada, there would be a specific rule for the knower [of time] regarding the intervening period; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that vows and other such observances would become useless. It is not so; for even if an intercalary month should occur within any of the six months beginning with Caitra, the restriction of time remains exactly the same there as well. Therefore, no fault arises. Thus it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"Among the six months beginning with Mādhava (Vaiśākha), two of them always possess one [intercalary] month. (p. 197)
"Then there may be two Āṣāḍhas, and [the festival] in Śrāvaṇa, O Śveta, O Cyuta.

This is stated in the *Māheśvarottara*, a scripture of Śiva: "O Śatakratu, initiation and so forth, as well as the installation [of icons], the Pavitraka rite, and so on, [should be performed] according to the Śiva-āgama."
One who desires their own welfare should not perform [rituals] during an intercalary month;
for that which occurs during the new moon (*darśa*) would be devoid of the transition of the sun (*saṃkrānti*).
That month is to be known as an intercalary month; Viṣṇu sleeps during the month of Karkaṭa.
Regarding that:
"The *pavitraka* should be prepared during the month of Āṣāḍha, specifically in the month of Śrāvaṇa;
