for if it is done otherwise while Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, one becomes a partaker of fault. Thus [it is said].

[Objection: Why not simply take the solar month itself as the lunar month? In that case, there would be no suspicion whatsoever of an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*). [Response: It is not so. For in the *pavitrāropaṇa* rite, the lunar month alone is intended, because it is prescribed—preceded by an expiation (*prāyaścitta*)—when the Sun enters Virgo (*kanyāgati*).
And it has been said:
"The three months beginning with Āṣāḍha are indeed those when Janārdana is asleep."
Just as it is auspicious for the stringing of the thread during the bright fortnight, so it is during the dark fortnight;

however, one who is afflicted by disease, engaged in travel, or oppressed by a king will suffer an increase of ailments. It is said that if one does not perform the stringing of the thread within these three months, [misfortune follows].
When the sun has entered Virgo, one should recite [the mantra] joined with the *dakṣa-ṛṣi* and prepare the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) for Śambhu; this may also be done in some way during Libra.
"One who has these two impurities for even a single day is censured in all ritual acts. Thus it is said.

Enough with this prolixity; let us return to the subject at hand. One should avoid from afar a thread made by a twice-born girl, or one that is otherwise poorly dyed, unwholesome, excessively thick, thin, cut, full of many joints, knotted, dirty, or abounding in other defects.
A [line] that is stained produces sin; one that is burnt brings fear of the king;
a thick line is said to cause disease; and a thin one causes the loss of wealth.
Death would sever the thread; it is joined by the junction of the *sandhi* and *gulma*.
From this, the knot and the sheath become stainless and firm through forceful penetration.
One hundred and eight threads, equal in number to the Rudras, are always most excellent;
in the absence of that many threads, one should arrange half of them, or half of that again.
Alternatively, there may be eighty-one flags, or a number measured by fifty.
Alternatively, a measurement marked by thirty-eight *kalās* is approved for all *liṅgas*;
or else, it may be one hundred and eight, or less by ten, in successive order.
And it has been said:
Beginning from Nāgakhendu (187) up to the limit of Nāgayama (298),
when nine times twenty (180) have elapsed, you shall attain the state of the youngest.
O Purandara, best of gods, ten oblations have been declared;
beginning from the dot (bindu) and the arrows (bāṇa), up to the eight (vasu) and the moon (candra),
the knots have been declared by you, O most excellent of the wise.
The procedure for water-clocks (ghaṭikā) is proclaimed [as applicable] in these cases, but never for others:
on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), a mobile liṅga, a Bāṇaliṅga, and a self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga.
There is no fixed rule regarding the number [of repetitions] starting from one hundred; as was previously stated, one should never perform more than one hundred and eight.
O Supreme Goddess, O Śakra, this is the command for all:
the *pavitraka* rite must be performed upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and other such sites using one hundred and eight [threads].
One should take half of this, or half of that, or according to what is available;
or, in the absence of thread, one may use *darbha*, *muñja*, and so forth, to fashion the *pavitraka*.
The worlds of excellent sound should perform atonement as follows:
Oṃkāra, Candra, Agni, Brahmabhā, Guhā, and Nṛpi.
And all the gods, together with their respective regions, as stated in the Kālottara, [worship] Jaya, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
One should place the deities Soma, Sūrya, and Agni upon the threads;
the width of the top of the liṅga is the Ātmatattva.

Therefore, the Vidyās are of the nature of Śiva; each subsequent one is more auspicious than the preceding. Having fashioned it like a bracelet—whether for a stationary or mobile [object]—measuring eight finger-breadths in length and provided with ten knots at equal intervals, one should perform the rite.
One should recite the Vāmadeva mantra and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the heart and the other [limbs] according to the Śakti;
[the deities are] Prakṛti, Pauruṣī, and Parājitā.
O Sadāśiva, the sixth day is Vijayā, which is abandoned by Japā;
the ninth is Manonmanī, and the tenth is Sarvatomukhī.
Alternatively, when nine knots are made, the powers (śaktis) such as Vāmā and the others are likewise [represented].
Regarding this, some say:
"The knots should be made equal, or more, according to what is aesthetically pleasing."

The fourth Śaktisūtra, named Gaṅgāvatāraka, extends from the top of the head to the end of the pedestal; this applies to a fixed liṅga and not otherwise. For a mobile liṅga, it should be made the length of an arm, or otherwise as [specified].
"Having made four knots there with a space of two finger-breadths between them,
one should then leave a space of one tāla and make another four knots. Thus it is said.
Śiva, within the delusion consisting of Śakti, further creates two knots.
And those digits (kalās) are written here in their proper sequence as before:
Ā, U, Ma, Bindu, [Nāda],
Nādānta, Śakti, and Vyomarūpiṇī, Vyomarūpiṇī.
She is infinite, unattached, the protector, equal, and likewise like the sky.
One should visualize three bracelets for the forms located at the secret place, the navel, and within the heart;
one should arrange a fourth from the head down to the knees.
On a cloth or a painting, [the image] should extend down to the knees and consist of twenty-seven threads;
it may also be placed upon the limbs of enjoyment, or according to the opinion of some, on the eight subtle [limbs].
One should prepare a nine-threaded cord reaching to the navel for the Guru and oneself;
it should possess the qualities of the Sun, the Water-pot, Fire, and the Moon, as well as those of the Guru and Śambhu.
For all the world-regents (lokapālas), the thread [of the cloth] should be eight finger-breadths;
that shall be the measurement for the book when it is chosen from among the options of horn, flowers, or wool.
One should fashion this afterwards, and then one should fashion those [other items].
Then, having discarded the ancient bamboo vessel produced from the Pātrabhṛt-veṇu tree— which was spread with the essence of reality— one should take up a newer one,
consisting of a single knot, twelve finger-breadths in length.
Having prepared the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitra), or that which is devoid of the left [hand].
p.
201) That which is joined with all adjuncts (upādhi) is to be conceived as corresponding to each deity;
likewise, the flesh of the city [of the body], the thumb, the stone, and the two types of turmeric.
The entire collection of medicinal substances is traditionally said to include *śadīśavyaka* and *musta*.
In the evening, one should [decorate] the sacrificial pavilion with garments, mirrors, flowers, and other such items.
Having adorned one's own body, one should decorate it as is appropriate.
And it is said:
"The rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) should be performed at whatever twilight [is appropriate] for that occasion."
"Therefore, it is called 'indicative' (naimittikī), because it arises from that indicative action. Thus [it is said].
In the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"Then, having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), [he should worship] the Sun and the Moon as before;
having sprinkled the doors with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) and with the water for the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) and so forth."
The door of Śāntikalā is in the east, while the door of Vidyā is in the south;
Nivṛtti is the western door, and likewise Pratiṣṭhā is in the north.

Having worshipped the presiding deities— some beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ), ending with *namaḥ*, and in the dative case— either in the water-pot (*kalaśa*) or upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
One should install Gaṇeśa, Bhāratī, and Lakṣmī above all the doors;
and with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should install Nandin, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgīśa, Vināyaka, Vṛṣabha, Kārttikeya, Gaurī, and Caṇḍeśvara.
Starting from the eastern gate, however, in a clockwise and counter-clockwise sequence.
The wise man should worship each pair [of deities] upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or in a water-pot (kalaśa):
Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sindhu, Śāradā, and the river Narmadā.
p. 202) Or else, one should worship the Tāpī, Godāvarī, and Pauṣṇī in order from the east,
honoring them all with extensive offerings of perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Entering through the western door as if it were permanent,
one should place a flower with water for Vāstunātha upon an udumbara branch at the station of Brahmā.
Then, having seated oneself on one's own seat in the courtyard of the physician’s sacrificial ground, one should remain established there.

Having performed [the rite] at will as if it were permanent, one should worship the deity together with his limbs upon the fragrant mandala using the palm of the right hand, placing [the offering] upon the head.
Uttering the root mantra very clearly up to the *dvādaśānta*,
he should place the Hand of Śiva, which is the primordial embodiment of splendors.
One should contemplate: "I am indeed Śiva himself, whose body is composed of mantras.
[Then one should take] jātī, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and unbroken grains of rice.
Having measured the proportions and fashioned the thirty-six petals of the lotus,
one should sever it into seven parts with the Astra-mantra, and prepare the five products of the cow as previously described.

Having offered the *arghya* and sprinkled [the area] all around with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), standing at the left armpit with the sword of awakening (*bodhāsi*) held there, facing north and situated toward the southwest, one should perform the mental purifications of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) within the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇṭapa*).
Having scattered above us weapons in the form of various missiles,
they stand positioned within the intermediate spaces between the principles (tattvas), from the fire of time (kālāgni) up to Śiva.
Having arranged canopies for them and cleared the space,
he should collect the scattered offerings with a bunch of kuśa grass while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra.
On the northeastern corner of the altar, one should then collect the *vardhanī* water;
having extracted the *vāstu-puruṣa* in the southwest, one should worship him with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and other offerings.
Or, in a jar rich with all ornaments, one should worship the deities of the site (vāstu) according to the scriptures;
or else, having first performed meditation, one should worship the single Lord of the Site, Brahmā, as well as Mahālakṣmī, who dwells upon a lion in the western direction.
Having meditated upon the Great Abode (Mahālaya), which fills all directions and faces the pavilion,
as being Śiva himself, or by means of his seed-syllable or heart-mantra,
one should place it upon a base made of seven kinds of grain on the northeastern part of the altar.
A jar made of gold, copper, or auspicious clay— copper-colored,
with a small mouth, neither too thick nor too light.
It should be endowed with unblemished sesame seeds, wrapped in a white thread,
placed in the eastern vessel, provided with fruit, having sprouts at its mouth, well-adorned,
filled with fragrant water from sacred bathing places, containing gold within, and accompanied by cloth.
Having placed [the deity] upon the back of a white, tall bull on that movable seat,
one should worship the Lord in the water-pot lotus (kumbhapadma), facing east with his consort, together with His radiance.
To her left, one should place the vessel for scattering (vikiro) and the vessel for increasing (vardhanī);
above the lion, one should place a lotus-like object and there a terrifying weapon.
Then, at the corners of the lines of the sacrificial ground and upon the wooden planks,
[one should worship] Indra, Agni, Yama, the Cruel One (Nairṛta), Varuṇa, Vāyu, and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).
And again, Viṣṇu spoke to Īśāna, who was going toward the lord of the Nairṛtas.
He holds in his hands a sword, a shield, an iron arrow, a bow, a measuring cord,
a water-pot, a spear, a trident, an axe, and the staff of Brahmā.
One-footed, two-footed, or with feet evenly placed, brilliantly radiant,
with all limbs endowed with serpents and wearing a sacred thread of nagas.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Weapon-mantra (astra), which destroys the suffering of those who bow before it:
Oṃ oṃ astramūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Oṃ śaṃ paśuṃ huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the eyes of the weapon: huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ! Oṃ phaṭ, homage to the weapon, to the weapon: huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ!

Having thus performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), having consecrated [the object] with the root mantra, having displayed the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*) and the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), and having sprinkled it with earth and the other elements, one should satisfy and worship it with perfumes and other offerings.
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutations to Śiva and Śakti!
For you are indeed the Lord of this sacrifice, and this moving form is likewise [your] manifestation.

Having made this request with the words *iti vijñāpya*, one should offer it into the right hand, which displays the gesture of granting boons (*varada-hasta*), of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva, whose face is turned toward the east. And it is said:
"The cloth placed upon the right hand of Śiva is indeed consecrated."
Now, one might object:
"In initiation and other rites, one should always meditate upon Sadāśiva to the left of the [initiate] facing east; however, the support for the water-pot (*kalaśa*) faces west."
Thus, in the *Śrīmacchivodaya* and likewise in the *Bṛhatkiraṇodyota*, regarding initiation and other rites, the Guru should contemplate the object of instruction within the jar facing the west.
The Lord, Tatpuruṣa, the peaceful, the eternal, whose face is eternally ancient.
According to this statement, the support for the pitcher (kalaśādhāra) must indeed face westward.
How is it that [Śiva faces] east in the Mantra [system], while [in the Tantric system he faces] west? True;
however— "In the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites, Śiva is the presiding authority in all cases;
Lakṣmī always faces east, while his body has its back toward the west. Thus it is said.
In the dialogue between Lakṣmī and Keśava:
"Because the scriptures are manifold, the procedure of one's own tradition is what grants the desired goal;
Śambhu is the authority for all, and therefore he is considered the one whose face is turned toward the east."

And because of the statement in the *Siddhāntasāra*, "The ritual procedure of one's own tradition must be performed," there is no fault. Furthermore: "This sacrifice has been initiated by me for you, O performer of sacrifices; it must now be protected by you until its completion."
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods and having bowed down properly with devotion, [he remained].
One should worship Gaṇeśa in the north-west corner and the Guru in the north-east.
Having prepared a seat for the Lord of Devas, one should worship Him with the nectar of the moon and other offerings, and with an abundance of flowers, as if in a pavilion of blossoms.
Then, having prostrated and received permission, the Guru goes to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
having consecrated the pit and the fire, he should extract a small portion of the fourth [offering].
Having again invoked the Lord of Gods along with his limbs (retinue) and worshipped him, he should offer libations (tarpayet).
And it has been said:
"Thereafter, the beautiful sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) [is offered] into the fire that has been consecrated by the five purificatory rites;
even if uninvited, the oblation (homa) becomes effective when the fire has been invoked. Thus it is stated.
The single libation for all mantras, ending with *svāhā*, is as follows:
*oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ svāhā*. (p. 207)
The same applies to the head and the other limbs as well.
The head (śikhā) is consecrated by the seed-syllables joined together, ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, which serves as its illumination (*dīpana*).
*Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hṛdayāya huṃ huṃ phaṭ*— these and other such mantras [are used].
Having thus purified the *liṅga* three times by means of gazing and other rites,
one should install it in the south-eastern corner of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and recite the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) one hundred times from the west.
Having recited over the body, which consists of dharma and adharma, seven times with the mantra according to the scripture,
one should cast it there, kindle the Śaiva fire with fragrant fuel, and set it ablaze.
In front of that, having placed a washed vessel upon a seat formed of the six syllables within the mandala, one should contemplate the deity as having become manifest in its form inside it.
Having worshipped Śiva mentally and having worshipped him with flowers and clarified butter,

and having obtained eight hundred recitations of the root mantra, one should place milk along with rice such as śāli and other grains into it according to the requirements of the cooking process, and then prepare it accordingly.
Having wrapped his neck with a triple thread and,
out of a desire for virtue, having diligently placed both merit and demerit upon the hearth for the sake of the body,
he who seeks auspiciousness should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) facing east while moving it with his heart.
Once it is well-cooked, having performed the consecration with the *saṃhitā* mantras and the sprinkling of mantras,

one should then fill the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter ending with the word *svāhā*. Having removed it from the hearth and placed it upon the *maṇḍala*, one should wipe it with the *hṛdaya* mantra and smear it.
Having performed the cooling sprinkling with the Śiva-mantras ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
one should diligently protect the fire on the hearth for the sake of incense and lamps.
Having placed [the vessel] upon the mandala at the edge of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), by means of the application of the *seti* and *heti* mantras,
one should perform the *sampāta* rite twenty-one times with clarified butter from the *sruva* ladle into the fire and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Oṃ hauṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ haṃ śivāya svāhā—these are the Saṃhitās.
Having consecrated it with mantras, protected it, and then made it palatable, one should divide it into three parts;
having offered two portions to Śiva and Agni, one should take the portion for oneself drenched in ghee.
Having placed [the materials] in a vessel and preserved them, one should establish it facing east;
one should install it with the mantras of Īśa and the others for the very sake of pleasing the faces.
And it is said in the Kālottara:
"In the northeast, one should place the five products of the cow; for the tooth-cleansing twig, [place it] toward the east;
one should offer ashes to the southern face and fragrance to the northern face."
One should cause a clay vessel to be given to Sadyojāta by means of the Sadyojāta mantra.
Thus it is also stated elsewhere:
"O fair-faced one, all the substances for the fire-oblation,
along with kuśa grass, the staff, the rosary, the loincloth, and the alms-bowls, [should be placed] on the right."
Rocanā, saffron, oil, and the hair-purifying agent for the practitioner;
likewise, another part of his body, betel—these should not be given to a Kinnarī.
In the northeast, there is a seat, an umbrella, sandals, and a yogic belt;
so say some.
In the northeast, one should offer water with the Īśāna mantra or the root mantra,
as well as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) placed within a cup made of *pālāśa* leaves.
One should place a flower in the northeast and a stone in the southeast direction.
"Aloe wood [should be placed] in the direction of Nairṛta and in the direction of Vāyu, [each] four units apart.
209) Now, near [that], in the maṇḍala... in an auspicious vessel... setha.
Having placed the purifiers (pavitra), they are purified by means of the rites of inspection and so forth.
Or, having consecrated it with the limbs of Brahmā or with the *svadhā* mantra over that substance,
one should purify it twenty-one times with the *saṃhitā* mantras beginning with "adhastvā."
Having consecrated it once more and protected it, one should pour [the water] out with the *dhenumudrā*.
Having encircled it with the thread and the armor-mantra (*varman*), one should wear it for the sake of the primary cause.
Herein are the seat, the vessel, and this incense burner.
The lamp-vessel, the *dhallī*, the lamp, the *bhañjala*, and in sequence the *vardhanī*, the fan, the umbrella, the chowrie, and likewise the mirror.
The drum, the trumpet, the conch, and so forth; the sacrificial pit, the altar, the canopy, the flagstaff, the sword, the treasury, and the granary.
Likewise, other houses and so forth,
as well as the house itself and all household utensils, one should envelop with a single thread.
Then, having bestowed the weapon-purifier (astra-pavitraka) in sequence upon the Sun and the others,
[one should likewise bestow it] upon the Śiva-vessel (śivakumbha), the Vardhanī vessel, Gaṇa, and the Guru.
Having likewise offered incense soaked in perfumes and all medicinal herbs to himself,
and having presented an *añjali* of flowers along with *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā*, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
he stood gazing at his own bow with the compassionate glance of the Lord.

Constantly meditating with devotion upon Lord Sadāśiva, and having known the deity Āvaṃtya, he performed the entire sacrifice according to the prescribed rites, including the fulfillment of any deficiencies.
"By virtue of its power, because it is the master of mantras, it brings about the attainment of your will;
recognize that as its accomplishment, O Lord of the conscious and the unconscious! To you, O Sadāśiva, who are always Śambhu, let there be salutation! This is also the meaning of this [verse].

In all days, the ritual consists of the agent, the materials, the mantra, and the action; therein, when it is incomplete, You Yourself are the Lord regarding its fulfillment. Since You are endowed with all sovereign qualities, for that very reason You are "Sakala" (the Whole), meaning You are capable of fulfilling the entire process of ritual action. Since You are the Lord, by the mere act of remembrance, You possess the nature of bringing about the accomplishment of every task; therefore, this [prayer] is also a word directed toward You alone. O Lord! O Master! toward You—the one who guards the great mantras—I am distinguished as the one who effects the attainment of Your will. By Your desire, by Your command, I have obtained the collection of instruments, causes, and materials; therefore, grant success to my work as I apply myself to the sacrifice (*makha*), the worship, and the ritual.

"I command, O Lord of the conscious and the unconscious! O Lord of the father, of myself, of my thoughts, and of Māyā and the rest! In every way, by all means, at all times—* * * salutations to You; be gracious, become propitious. Such is the meaning of the mantra.
Having uttered the root-mantra up to the end of "Śiva," it is rendered nectar-like through exhalation (*recaka*).
Then, having brought [the deity] down from Śiva, one [offers it] to the limbs and the various parts of speech individually.
One should offer incense, lamps, and food offerings, while reciting prayers, hymns, and salutations;
having first performed worship according to the prescribed method, one should present these with devotion.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations and having given the full offering, one should cast the internal *bali* within;
then, one should give it along with the *pavitra* outside to the lords of the directions in their respective quarters.
Having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should offer oblations according to the prescribed rite;
having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the root mantra and the weapon mantra, one should bow down again and again.
In a purified vessel, one should place the *kavaca* and the *hṛdaya*;
having placed the purifiers there and consecrated them with the limbs of Brahmā (*brahmāṅga*),
one should then apply the *hṛdaya*, the *varma*, and the *śastra* above that, along with the others.
Having wrapped it with a thread and armor, one should place it upon the mandala at the front of the jar;
then, one should worship the collection of jars with perfumes, purifiers, and other offerings.
Having propitiated the pair of lotus-feet and worshipped them with devotion,
and having adorned the face of Śiva with canopies and other ornaments, he bowed down before him.
Having gone outside by his command to the courtyard, [they should perform] in three mandalas;
or else, the members of the assembly, with the right hand, [should do so] at the western full-mouthed [fire].
Having sipped water with the *sakuśa* mantra, and having sipped again at intervals,
he should consume three mouthfuls in the middle while touching his seat; then,
in the third [round], he should cleanse his teeth with a tooth-stick while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra.

Having washed it and lifted it with its tip pointing upward, and having observed it in the morning, [one should know that] what is seen in the east and west is auspicious, while the remainder is not drying [and thus auspicious]. The northern weapon is praised; the rest is non-drying.
And for the sake of purification, having offered oblations with the *tama-astra* mantra and having dismissed the deity,
one should perform the *ghora* rite with the *vyāhṛti*s and likewise offer a single oblation.
Having purified the fire right there, as well as its mouth, eyes,
and teeth, a vigil (jāgara) should be performed before Śiva with song and instrumental music throughout the three watches of the night.
Householders and ascetics alike should perform recitation, hymns of praise, and circumambulation;
then the fruit of the Shiva-jāgaraṇa vigil should be known as having ninefold merit.
On Darbha grass or ashes, this vigil is appropriate;
having fasted for only one day and night, one should consume the sacrificial porridge (caru).
O Śivā, the rite of placing the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) must not be performed without [these].
Then, one should perform the immediate consecration (adhivāsana) by playing musical instruments, even without the sacrificial porridge (caru) made from cow products;
this involves the preparation of the ritual substances through mantras for the purpose of worship.
This is declared to be the "adhivāsa" by the illustrious Ājñānaśambhu.
Thus ends the ritual for the consecration of mantras in the Jñānaratnāvalī.
Then, having risen at dawn and performed the purificatory rites such as the ritual bath,
he should worship the Lord with the eightfold flowers (aṣṭapuṣpikā) as well as the water-pots.
Having taken up the purifying materials, one should place them within the range of the Lord;
then, having dismissed the deity as before, one should remove the used floral offerings (nirmālya).
Having set aside the gods and having offered flowers to Kumbhīśā,
gradually purify that place, sprinkle it with water, and contemplate it.
Having adorned [the deities] with flowers and other offerings after the completion of the two daily rites,
one should unite the gods within the jars with auspicious flower garlands and the like.

(212) Having performed the *ārātrika* ceremony with auspicious sounds such as the chanting of hymns, songs, and the waving of the parasol, fly-whisk, and colored banners, one should offer betel leaf and water three times from the hollowed palms.
Repeatedly reciting the mantra, hymns of praise, prostrations, and circumambulations with the eight limbs, accompanied by three offerings of handfuls of flowers.
With bliss as his refuge and his purpose accomplished, his body bristling with joy,
he stood upon the ground on his knees with palms joined in devotion like a handful of flowers.
She should inform Mahādeva with palms joined:
"Oṃ! You are the refuge of all beings; you abide within the moving and the unmoving."
Through the internal movement within all beings, you are the witness, the Supreme Lord;
by deed, mind, and speech, I have no other refuge but you.
Whatever has been performed by me that is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in material offerings—[may it be accepted].
"O Maheśvara, please fulfill those daily rites of recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, which were not performed by me and for which I am devoid of words."
O Maheśāna, you are perfectly pure, a purifier that destroys all sin;
by you, the entire world—both the stationary and the moving—is sanctified.
O Lord, whatever portion of my vow has been broken by me,
may all of that become whole again, bound together by the thread of your command.
Thus, having immediately sought forgiveness for the multitude of her offenses,
she made this petition and prostrated herself again and again with the eight limbs touching the ground.
O Lord, by your command, I shall observe the four-month vow and the restraints according to my capacity;
may he who has undertaken it likewise fulfill it.
Having bathed the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other substances upon the auspicious throne below,
one should worship him in the center of the altar with divine perfumes and ointments.
With various kinds of garments, diverse flowers, and even ornaments,
together with all articles of enjoyment, one should worship Śambhu amidst auspicious sounds such as constant singing.
Having worshipped Śiva stationed in the fire and offered oblations with the mantras beginning with *amūla* and ending with *iśambare*,
and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to Sūrya who has been worshipped in his own place;
Having placed the purifiers upon his heart, and likewise for his retinue,
he should thereafter prostrate before the Sun with incense, lamps, and other offerings.

Having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings in due order to the guardians of the gates, the world-protectors (dikpālas), Lakṣmī, and all the gods, and having prostrated before them, one should offer the purified [substance].

As for Śiva, [one offers] to the Kumbha and Vardhanī vessels; as for oneself, to the Gaṇas and the Guru, [an offering] endowed with flowers, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice, made fragrant and pleasing by incense.
Having placed the purifier (pavitra) in his joined palms and facing Kumbheśa slightly,
he should address this prayer while remembering Śiva as the embodiment of Time (Kālātman).
O God, by you, whose nature is Time, everything has been seen within my own ritual procedure:
that which was joined, that which was cast away, that which was hidden in the heart, and that which was marveled at;
let that which was done be either afflicted or unafflicted, whether it be a flower or treated as worthless.
By the pure power of Śambhu, through your will, [I have been granted] the state of being the soul of all.
Oṃ pūraya pūraya maravavṛta niyameśvarāya svāhā. The meaning of this is as follows:
[the divisions of time consisting of] truṭi, lava, nimiṣa, kāṣṭhā, kalā, muhūrta, ghaṭikā, yāma, ahorātra, pakṣa, the two months, and ayana.
(214) He, whose nature is Time, maintains the essential form of this jar-like [deity], who is measured by the divisions of years, yugas, intermediate kalpas, and great kalpas. And it has been said:
"The Lord, consisting of all states of being, exists within the entire universe of moving and non-moving things."
"O Maheśvara, whose form is the universe, a fraction of you is Time in its embodied form. Thus [it is said].

"For the sake of my rite—my own ritual performance—may that which has been seen as *kliṣṭa* (defiled) by you in the form of Time be [rendered] *samutsṛṣṭa* (abandoned). It is said that when the Lord Sadāśiva is worshipped with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), an act performed deficient in those offerings is called *kliṣṭa*. Not only is it defiled, but it is also abandoned; that which is performed according to the rules of worship through the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth—if one omits any of those purificatory rites while performing the action, that act is called *samutsṛṣṭa*. Likewise, even the *hṛd* (heart) is established as a constituent part of that: whatever is performed having extracted [the essence] from that very purificatory rite, that action is called *hṛdaya*. Similarly, even the *gupta* (hidden): whatever other action, produced by speech, mind, or body, one conceals out of fear of penance, that is called *gupta*. May all that fourfold action performed by me—which was done by me as *kliṣṭa*—become *akliṣṭa* (non-defiled) and *akṛta* (unperformed) through your grace. This is the remainder of the sense.

Moreover, O Śambhu, may even that which is performed by others—the threefold [offering] beginning with *samutsṛṣṭa*—be rendered complete as a flower; for you are the supreme one for all beings in every way and at all times. Therefore, for this reason, by means of this purifier (*pavitra*)—which is of what nature?—that which has its own nature (*svarūpa*) as the fulfiller (*pūraka*) in all fourfold ritual action (*caturvidha-karman*), and which is thus the purifier that completes all rites, [may it be offered] by your will, by your command.

"Fill, fill"—by this repetition, through the intensity of a wretched supplication, there is an excellence in the fulfillment of one's own duty; upon that, [the mantra] is placed. Now, sacrifice (*amara-vī-yāga*), the act of sacrificing (*yajana*), and the vow (*vrata*) beginning with the eighth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*) constitute the ninth stage, which follows what has already been set in motion. Sacrifice (*makha*), vow (*vrata*), and restraint (*niyama*)—these are the "sacrifice-vow-restraints" (*makhavrata-niyama*). He is their Lord (*īśvara*), for by his command alone all things become complete for the Mothers. He is their master; this is the meaning. To that Śiva, *svāhā*. "May there be the bliss of nectar (*amṛtānanda*)"—this is the meaning of the mantra. Alternatively, one should recite the supreme mantra of the Hero against delusion (*moha-śūrottara-mantra*) upon the seat (*pīṭha*).
Having taken up the purifying thread (pavitra) together with perfumes, flowers, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), one should address the Lord with this:
The God who abides in all gods, the omniscient, omnipresent, and all-pervading Lord—
this inferior song was seen by you as the Lord’s work, yet it was composed by me.

"By this sacred thread (pavitra), may [the rite] be completed through your grace. Having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods, one should offer the sacred thread (pavitra). This sacred thread of the essential nature of the Self (ātmatattva-pavitraka) should first be offered by those seeking liberation.
The deities beginning with Brahmā abide, relying upon that which is the primordial reality.
From the root up to the end of Māyā, one should offer [the purification] to Śiva in its true sense;
then, taking up flowers again, [he offers] the purificatory thread of the Vidyā-tattva.
Having presided over the principle of Māyā and being established as the deity Śrīvatsa,
one should utter the root mantra up to the end of dissolution and place it upon the head of the Lord of Gods.
And it is said:
"O Śakra, now hear the procedure for the Pavitrārohaṇa rite.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra with a well-concentrated mind, one should proceed until the end."
p.
216) One should superimpose that upon Śiva, who is the sovereign of the reality of the Self.
Now—
And one who desires to enjoy [the fruits] should cause the purifier to ascend in the natural (anuloma) order.
In some cases, the ritual slaughter (ālabhana) is prescribed according to the sequence of one hundred and eight [recitations] and so forth.
And it is said:
"The *pavitraka* of the Śiva-tattva, joined with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
should be heated upon the form of Śiva after reciting the mantra of Śiva one hundred and eight times."
It should be offered by way of emanation, resembling the world of nectar;
half of that consists of the nature of knowledge, and a quarter is the self-purifier.
"But by those seeking liberation, it is [realized] in reverse order as consisting of the Self-knowledge and Śiva. Thus [it is said].
Now the mantras are written as follows:
Oṃ hauṃ, to the Lord of the Principle of the Self, the purifier, svāhā!
Oṃ hauṃ, to the Lord of Knowledge, the purifier, svāhā!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Lord of the Śiva-tattva; or one should recite this ending with "namaḥ. And it has been said:
"Reciting the mantra for these [deities] either ending in 'svāhā' or ending in 'namaḥ'."
Having recited the root mantra ending in *namaḥ* and offered three handfuls of flowers,
one should offer *dūrvā*, *kuśa*, unbroken rice, and the *arghya* drop, and then cause [the deity] to rejoice.
Having meditated upon the eternal God of gods, who is being praised by Viriñca and the others, with contented and pure offerings, according to the path previously described.
Having offered incense, lamps, and other items, purified by his own mantra,
[he should offer them] to the gods, such as those residing in cows and trees, and to his devoted followers.
Then, O Śambhu, as before, he should offer according to his capacity and in due order:
hand-ointment, betel, mouth-perfume, and a mirror.
Having offered the sacred threads (*pavitra*)— including incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), water, *śālmanā* and so forth— to Śiva residing in the fire, [one should proceed].
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations along with the ancillary rites, he should perform the final full oblation according to the prescribed rule.
Having removed the defects of deficiency or excess with the weapon-mantra and the full [mantra],
one should dismiss the deity and, having restrained the fire within, offer the oblation.

Having offered the outer *digbali* (oblation to the quarters) with the *sūtras* as before, and having sipped water (*ācamana*), O ascetic rich in penance, one should satisfy the other [deities] according to one's ability and with devotion, by the command of Śambhu, through the discernment of the various [mantras].
With a thread of fried food, as well as with cloth and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
one should proceed to the preceptor’s lotus feet according to the *Āgamas*. Having washed them and seated him upon a throne, one should then smear [the area] with sandalwood paste.
Having worshipped with flowers, incense, and so forth, one should offer [the gift] as in the Gaṅgāvatāra rite.

Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ! To Śiva, the embodiment of the object of worship, who is the presiding lord of all principles—the principle of the self (ātmatattva) and the principle of Śiva—this sacred thread (pavitraka), svāhā!
Having worshipped him like Śiva himself and having prostrated again and again, one should devoutly offer the sacred thread; and likewise, the brothers should offer it to one another.
One should keep vigil as before with stories of Śiva’s divine play and so forth;
then, having brought the threads in the morning and performed the preliminary bath, one should establish them.
Having performed the obligatory and occasional rites, and having offered a beautiful purifying thread (*pavitraka*), [he should proceed].
Having offered four oblations with sesame seeds at the end of all [the rites] along with the *pūrṇāhuti*,
one should apply the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) to the *liṅga*. Then, having addressed Śambhu and heated the fire with the *vyāhṛti* mantras,
and having offered the *bali* sacrifice in detail, one becomes pure in body through the mantra oneself.
Having worshipped Śiva with eight flowers, one should offer the merit as if it were a recitation of mantras.
O Maheśāna, accept the merit that I have acquired through this Pavitrārohaṇa rite, together with its limbs and sub-limbs; be gracious to me.
Having thus informed him, one should hand it over at the eastern door-post;
then, having prostrated and worshipped him again, one should ask for his forgiveness with due respect.
Having dismissed the sacrifice, he should worship Caṇḍeśa outside on a half-moon mandala as before, and having given him the fourfold purified offering.
Oṃ, to the Lord of the Principle of Self, to Dhvanicaṇḍeśvara, huṃ, the sacred thread, svāhā!
These and other such mantras [are used].
Having gratified [the deity] with incense, lamps, and the like, one should then offer the food oblation (naivedya).
Preceded by perfumes, flowers, sacred grass, and other offerings such as food oblations.
As it has been said:
"O Lord, by the command of Śiva, this Prasāda, the remnant of Śiva, is most pure;
O Master, please enter here out of compassion and accept it."
Having thus offered libations into the fire and bowed down, he stands with a handful of flowers in his hands and recites:
"Oṃ, whatever annual rite has been performed by me, whether deficient or excessive..."
By your command, O Caṇḍanātha, may that be fulfilled for me.
O Lord Caṇḍanātha, O God of gods, O Sadāśiva!
May your grace be upon me; protect me, O Śambhu, O Mahodbhava!
O Caṇḍanāyaka, you are the refuge for those who have fallen from their conduct and are without a protector;
protect us who are fallen and devoid of proper conduct.
Having thus made this request and prostrated with the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma) out of devotion, one should bid them farewell;
then, having washed one's feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one becomes pure.
On a thoroughly purified ground, having bathed the *liṅga* and worshipped it according to the daily rite,
and having asked forgiveness with great devotion, one should dismiss the God of gods.
One should discard that offering and other remains in a temple courtyard, a pit, a lake, or similar location;
having smeared the place with cow dung and water, one who has bathed should touch it.
If the rite of the sacred thread (pavitraka) must be performed in this manner over three days, or if one is unable [to do so],
then one should perform all that was previously described in its entirety according to the sequence over two nights.
If on a single day the work is completed by the lunar days (tithis), then...
And it is said:
"When one desires to perform the Pavitraka and other rites on the day of the Sun (Sunday),
having performed the obligatory daily rituals, one should then perform the occasional rite once."
Having extracted [the substance] and given it to Caṇḍa, one should bathe the liṅga and worship it.
One should worship Īśa upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), for there is no other prescribed rite for Him.
Having bathed, one should not offer flowers or oblations to a linga, nor should one wear the ashes above [the navel].
If it is full, it should be mixed equally in the middle; or rather, one should do so at another time; or else, if there is distraction, it should be performed right then and there.

Having performed the milking of the cows and prepared the consecrated *pavitraka* with perfumes, one should perform the rite on the fourteenth lunar day; the remaining rites should be carried out on the following lunar day.
And it is said:
Having prepared the fragrant *pavitraka* on the seventh or the thirteenth [lunar day],
one should likewise prepare the *pavitraka* on the eighth or the fourteenth.
It is established that [the rite] to be performed on the following day is most pure;
however, others have declared that it may be performed by two people on one day, or by one person on the following day.

On the thirteenth day, others, with minds free from agitation, should perform the ritual for the acceptance [of the vow] according to the rules, having performed it at intervals between the milkings of the cows.
On the fourteenth lunar day, one should perform the consecration (*sādhivāsa*) of the sacred thread (*pavitraka*);
it should be well-consecrated on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).
This sequence for the mounting of the thread (*sūtrarohaṇa*) is to be understood as applicable even on the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*).
Having performed the ritual bath and personally sprinkled water upon the children,
he should afterwards honor the teacher with garments, ornaments, and garlands.
One should give the teacher a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) without any stinginess regarding one's wealth.
When the Guru-Lord is pleased, Śaṅkara becomes pleased;
for him whose Guru himself is satisfied, everything becomes pure and fruitful.

Then the Blessed Lord Śiva said: "The wise man should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) with the mantra 'niṣphalacchāyām' even while situated five yojanas away from the presence of the Guru; it shall be pure and effective, whether performed in his presence or in one's own place."
"Otherwise, one would go to hell; such is the command of the Supreme Goddess."
And it is said:
"If one should perform the *pavitraka* rite out of greed, delusion, or ignorance,
he shall remain in a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings."
When, by the will of Śiva, a sattvic creation occurs once again,
then he, having returned to the mortal world, shall enter a hundred births as a dog.
Furthermore, he who is joined [to the path], yet free from the fruit of further existence,
performs or causes to be performed [rites] by means of the armor [of protection] seen in the scriptures.
Together with ten generations born of his father and ten generations born of his mother,
having abandoned all sins, he goes to the world of Śiva.
At the conclusion of the vow, having worshipped Śiva, one should perform the formal dedication of the vow;
or, at the end of the vow, having performed the *pavitraka* rites, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
And it is said:
"There, one should observe the Cāturmāsya vow dedicated to Śiva;
it should be performed according to one's own capacity by both householders and lifelong celibates."
For two months, or for a fortnight, or for seven days in the absence [of a recipient],
one should rise and place that alms-bowl in a clean location.
Then, at the conclusion of the worship, having carefully placed the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) upon the linga-form [of the deity],
all your rites— such as worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth— shall become twofold day after day.
Without having discarded the purificatory blades (pavitra), one should not go to another place.
And it is said:

"One who has not been dismissed and whose purification is incomplete must not overstep the boundary. Otherwise, even by divine chance, he may encounter obstacles at every step, though success might otherwise be attained."
Likewise:
"O Thousand-eyed One, one must not go while the sacred thread has been consecrated but not yet released;
once it has been released, however, one may go wherever one pleases according to one's own will."
This ancestral rite was performed by the venerable Jñānaśiva, a brāhmaṇa of the Coladeśa, who was rich in asceticism.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
In the *Svacchanda-bhairava-tantra*, according to the mantra proclaimed by Bhairava,
he was born from the ashes of Smara, moistened in one place by tears of joy.
In the established doctrine (siddhānta), no regard is shown to him even by means of scriptural expiations;
nevertheless, his disposition is common [to others], as it is proclaimed in the *Puṣpāñjali* hymns.
Because it has been taught by the former teachers, that procedure is now being described:
on the seventh or the thirteenth day of either of the two fortnights in the month of Caitra,
having performed his daily rites and having prepared a beautiful seat for the deities in the evening;
Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the Astra-mantra and purified it,
the wise one should worship it with the Saṃhitā mantras, using perfumes, flowers, purifiers (pavitra), and so forth, as well as incense, lamps, and other offerings.
Having prostrated according to the scriptures, he should then address Dāma:
"Oṃ, O Hara Prasādasambūta, be present here."
"You must be led away for the sake of Śiva’s work by the command of Śiva;
having worshipped him again, protected him, and uprooted him, one should lead him to one’s own home."
If it has been carried far away, one should bring it back near;
or, having placed it in a full vessel within the house, one should perform the rite preceded by the recitation of mantras.
Having performed the sacrifice as previously described, one should purify the sacred objects (*pavitrāṇi*):
fruit, flower, leaf, lotus stalk, and whatever else originates from those [plants], the various products of the cow (*gavyaugha*), the tooth-stick, ash, and the fruit of the *śr̥ṅgāṭaka*.

One should place [the offerings] in three vessels starting from Īśāna and ending with the North; having offered scents and so forth, one should install the Sun and the others in their proper sequence.
Having worshipped the Lord with *damanaka* flowers and the five limbs [of the body] unseparated,
one should offer incense together with the *damanaka*, accompanied by *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Having formed the añjali gesture, one should utter this address while standing in the middle:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, you have been invited by me at the time of dawn."
However, the Dāma-parvan must be performed at the proper time according to your command.
If the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) is to be done immediately here, let it be proclaimed for the immediate time.
Having recited the root mantra ending with Śiva, let it be offered to Īśa along with his limbs (aṅgas).
Having gratified [the deity] with incense, lamps, and food offerings as previously described,
and having completed the remaining rites, one should remain awake throughout the night;
this is known as the procedure for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), which follows immediately after the daily morning rituals.
She should worship the Lord in Śambara with flowers, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, incense, and water-pots at the gates and directions, having formed an añjali of adamanaka flowers.

Having offered three handfuls of water with the mantras beginning with *āvidyāni* and ending with *śivastadvai*, starting from the root mantra and ending with the mantra for Īśvara, and concluding each with the word "namas," one should worship with a fourth handful of water.
Oṃ hauṃ! To Magheśvara, fill, fill with wine; to the wielder of the trident, Damanaka, obeisance!
Having offered these to the limbs and to the fire of Śiva, and having performed the two bali-offerings:
Oṃ, O Blessed One, whatever has been done by me in excess or deficient—
May all that be fulfilled; may all [the fruits] of the act of giving be complete.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods and having surrendered his own self as an instrument of action, [he remained].
Having concluded the sacrifice and performed the Caṇḍeṣṭi, one should perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Whatever merit exists in all sacrifices and whatever fruit exists in all sacred fords—
The fruit of that [practice] is obtained through initiation multiplied ten millionfold.

Here, the specific distinction regarding this was stated by the venerable Śambhu and the feet of Somaśambhu. Having thus performed the rite of the cord (*dāma-vidhi*), one should perform the worship of the Guru.
Afterwards, one should satisfy the twice-born and others as well, providing them with complete satisfaction.
Whether he be a householder or a celibate student, this is the rule for him:
his recitation, worship, and so forth, as well as his movable and fixed seat in the month of Caitra. Thus it is said.
The procedure for the offering of leaves and garlands was composed by the venerable Jñānaśambhu, a compassionate lord of sages born of the Golakī lineage.
That which is to be performed must not be violated;
furthermore, the expiation (prāyaścitta) should be understood as it is described in the Kālottara.

Īśvara said: "O dear sons, by the command of Śiva, this daily practice has been taught in due order for the practitioner, especially during his state of meditative absorption (samādhi), to be maintained throughout his entire life."
Bathing, worship, recitation, meditation, and fifthly, fire-offering—one should always perform these daily; this is further declared to be the "daily limb" (nityāṅga).
And on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights.

On the fifteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] and so forth, at the destruction of a lunar day, during the transit [of the sun], during the southern solstice, upon the increase of a month, and when there is an excess of days— even at these junctures, it is called the *ṣoḍaśī*.

During both solar and lunar eclipses, as well as during the Cāturmāsya period, the recitation of mantras and other rites should be doubled; likewise, one should observe the vow of eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya) at all times.
"One should never eat on the eighth or the fourteenth [lunar days].
Thus, this has been declared as a mandatory (nitya) limb; now the occasional (naimittika) is being described:
initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (pratiṣṭhā) are likewise to be known as occasional.
The threefold [ritual]—daily, occasional, and optional—has been prescribed for the teacher;
O son, the preceptor must likewise perform these three, except for the installation ceremony.

The exposition of the triad beginning with the obligatory (nitya) rites, as well as the optional (kāmya) ones, should be performed by the preceptor; O Six-faced One, the obligatory and optional rites are to be conducted according to one's own scripture, just as in the case of the Sun-god.
It is proclaimed that for both the initiate (samayin) and the spiritual son (putraka),
one should perform what is taught in one's own scripture and abandon the scriptures of others.
A spiritual son must always regard his guru’s brothers as his own;
whether he is established in the observances (samaya) or not, this must be performed by the practitioner.
When afflicted by disease, when intent on medicine, or likewise in fear of a king or thieves, the preceptor or the practitioner must always provide food for others.
Those who are skillful should not perform rites for their own desires; rather, one should practice penance.
The Guru is to be worshipped like Śiva; one should not employ him in ritual labor.
One should worship him daily, and especially in rites for specific desires, in expiations, and in recitation and worship.
Mahādeva is to be worshipped; one should not remember anything else with the mind.
One should behave toward the wives and sons of one’s guru as toward the guru himself. One should never look at a naked woman, and one should always honor young maidens.
One should not engage in jesting; one should perform the worship of the Guru, the gods, and the sacred fire.
One must avoid voiding urine, spitting, and other such acts into that water.
One should carefully avoid censuring those who are devoted to their own names and customs.
One should diligently avoid association with, laughter at, and likewise censure of those who have deficient or redundant limbs, as well as those who are low in birth, learning, or character.
One should never eat food that has been left over, especially by a woman with a frail body;
likewise, one should not eat from the wife of a hero, nor from a woman who is menstruating.
He should approach his wife during the fertile period, but avoid her on the forbidden lunar days (parvan).
He should likewise avoid mental derangement, negligence, lust, anger,
rashness, doubt, excessive pride, and the secret key of the household.
Lack of effort, lack of enthusiasm, atheism, and agitation;
an atheist, one who has broken the bounds of conduct, and one who reviles the scriptures—[these are to be avoided].
One should never engage in conversation with those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātaka). One should likewise avoid jesting, idle talk, delusion, and worldly pursuits.
And one should avoid all that has been mentioned by others, such as the worship of the *pūta* and so forth.
One should perform the ritual section (*kriyākāṇḍa*) exactly as taught in one's own scriptures without omission;
likewise, one should avoid fear and laziness during those very rituals.
One should not revile the Lord who is the cause, nor the scripture spoken by Śiva;
one should avoid backbiting with effort and should not step over the shadow of a liṅga.
One should avoid cooked food touched by a woman in her courses,
as well as a couch, a bedstead, a pestle, a threshold, and a broom.
At that time, he should not touch the grinding stone or the hearth with his feet.
All those living beings who have been saluted by the twice-born observants of vows [attain merit].
One should not touch with one's feet horses, cattle, maidens, or women;
nor should one eat the remains of offerings made to a deity, nor step over them.
One should not apply the property of the gods or the property of Rudra to one's own use;
rather, it must be protected with great effort through fasting or by means of giving it away.
One should cause even contradictory rites for the Guru, the deity, and the fire to be performed;
likewise, the ritual of the preliminary homa and so forth [should be done].
Those who abide in the Śiva-tattva should be served by the wise, as they are like the gods.
Those who desire Śiva’s favor should regard the devotees of Śiva as Śiva himself;
they should be protected with great effort from fear, poverty, and calamities.
One should not expel ascetics who have been cursed; one should never kill them in such a manner.
One should never do so at night, nor when there are many people present, nor ever with an associate.
In a cremation ground, a temple, on the bank of a river or a well,
in an empty house, or likewise in a forest, one should avoid taking shelter. One should not engage in conversation that is indistinct or meaningless.
One should prepare separate, auspicious clothing, bedding, and seating, each suitable for oneself.
One should avoid association with fools and procrastinators;
one should also avoid contact with the cruel and those who harbor secret sins, as well as with talkative people.
One should never cause censure to be directed toward the gods, cows, or Brahmins.
One must not seize the property of a Brahmin, nor the property of others; whatever belongs to another should be avoided, and one should refrain from speaking ill of Śiva.
One should avoid lack of fortitude, which is a violation of the bounds of conduct and a misery among miseries.
One should completely avoid ingratitude, envy, and meanness;
one should also avoid the sense of "mine," egoism, and violence toward living beings.
One should not cause false speech regarding living beings to be uttered among cattle, women, or children.
One who has entered into all sacrifices must not act with shamelessness;
one should avoid playing with poison, food, water, or weapons.
Never concealing his own scripture, as well as his self-restraint and vows,
he should constantly protect his own dharma and avoid the dharma of others.
One should avoid from afar stories concerning kings and thieves,
as well as negligence, rashness, and [the improper touching of] those wearing sacred marks or the sacrificial thread.
The physician should likewise avoid treating one who bears the marks of another gender or one who is deficient;
he must not step over a funeral pyre, nor Śiva, nor a living being.
One should avoid contact with an uninitiated person at the time of worship.
One should not sleep at all; one should avoid sleeping during the day.
During the time of worship, recitation, fire-oblation, and especially during the evacuation of waste,
as well as at the times of bathing and eating, one should diligently maintain silence.
One who has renounced should always avoid initiation, ritual exposition, and the consecration of temples;
those who have reached the fourth stage of life are considered renunciants (sannyasta) and ascetics (yati).

Since the state of degradation for both the one who acts and the one who causes it to be done arises from the same cause, favor should be shown to both; for their designations are indeed identical in that regard.
One should avoid such and other similar idle chatter;
one should diligently refrain from harming living beings even in thought,
and one should not, even mentally, cause anything that is disagreeable to living beings.
This alone is the supreme duty; this alone is the supreme austerity:
one should never go away after seeing a headless trunk or a linga.
Thus, this conduct of the samaya must be observed by those who seek Śiva.
Thus concludes the procedure for proper conduct.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati!
Since practitioners on the path and others have lost their proper conduct and are devoid of mantras,
one must therefore maintain right conduct with a disposition toward Śiva.
One whose conduct has been corrupted by negligence should perform an expiation;
for through fear of that [negligence], one's mind is generally further overwhelmed even while engaged in austerity.
Success proceeds constantly; this is considered the expiation if a fault has arisen through fate, disease, or likewise through delusion.
Bathing, recitation of mantras, fasting, daily fire-offerings, the *gaṇḍuka* rite,
consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and giving gifts— these destroy the evil deeds committed on the path.
O Mahāsena, even the god [Śiva], having understood the strength and weakness of karma, [acted accordingly].
The word "must be performed" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. [This applies] when the body is extremely afflicted by disease, or during terrible royal fears and the like.
The same applies when both have died by fire, during a journey abroad, or during the two periods of birth-impurity.
In the case of the service to the Guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, a daily omission does not constitute a fault;
however, both the householder and the student are traditionally held to be liable for penance.
Each [type of penance] should be known as being of various kinds, distinguished by whether it is performed with desire or without desire.
For one who acts with desire, [the penance] is fruitless; however, one should prescribe double the purification for such a person.
The [practice] of one who possesses desire and is materialistic is proclaimed as *bhautika*;
for one free from desire it is *naiṣṭhika*, and for one with desire it is twice that amount.
Now, since it is impossible to know them all in their entirety here at present,
various statements from the established doctrines (siddhāntas) are being written down in succession as follows.
Without the morning meditation, one should perform twice as much [recitation] within that period;
or else, one should complete four times as much, or two hundred root mantras.
If one should discharge excrement without having performed the rite of *apasavya* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder) after sipping water (*ācamana*), it is impure.
If one sips water (ācamana) with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one should go outside,
shake off the dust, fast, consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and recite the Ghoramantra three hundred times.
When nasal congestion, spitting, sneezing, yawning, or similar occurrences take place,
one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and recite the Praṇava twenty-one times.
Previously, you were seen upon the watchtower at Ātāraṇa and within the cave.
And at a crossroads, on a mountain peak and the like, in the middle of a river, and at a confluence.
Likewise, when one voids excrement or urine under a single tree or by a well;
If one enters a terrible place unintentionally, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times; if intentionally, three hundred times.
In this way, in other sacred fields as well, one becomes pure through the recitation of the terrible [mantra].
Likewise:
one should look at the moon, the sun, and so forth, and recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times;
however, if the twilight ritual is omitted even once, one becomes pure by reciting the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times.
If the three times [of recitation] are omitted, the recitation is considered to be threefold when accompanied by fasting;
this is declared for unintentional omission, but if done intentionally, one should perform double the penance.

The duration for a householder is declared to be double that; for those committed to the ultimate goal (naiṣṭhika), it is considered fourfold, beginning from that point, as stated for celibate students (brahmacārins).
The loss of luster for one who is ill is said to last for the duration of a fast;
however, in the case of a fall from a great divine station, it lasts for ten thousand years respectively.
Having understood this, the wise one should himself recite what was then imparted by his own guru;
he too, having offered the bali-oblation, should do so after discerning the time, the worthy recipient, and the age of the son.
In that regard, for the elderly, the sick, children, and others afflicted by hunger and so forth,
as well as for women, [the ritual] should be concise so that no distress arises.
Or one may have business with disciples, brothers, sons, or wise kinsmen.
When a threat to life has arisen, those initiated into their own tradition must perform double the penance compared to other people;
likewise, this applies to general rites such as penances for the sake of protecting one's accomplishments (siddhi).
One's own mantra must not be employed [otherwise], for success will be otherwise. Furthermore,
as it is stated in the *Sārasaṅgraha*:
If one fails to perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) even once, one should recite the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times;
whether healthy or afflicted by illness, one should likewise recite the Dvādaśikā once through the officiating priests.

Due to the omission of the three daily rites, one becomes deficient in the three qualities (guṇas) and loses the essence of the fast; therefore, being free from illness, one should recite the mantra and perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) as before.
If one is afflicted by illness and has omitted the bath, or if one has missed three Ekādaśīs,
one should perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) after reciting [the mantras], and then perform the bath while still ill.
And three hundred newborns exhausted by bathing in the Niruja [fire]—
at the fourfold junctures of the day (saṃdhyā), as before, it is fourfold.
For one who is ill, [the fine is] one thousand; for one who is healthy, two myriads. When many days have passed and [the debt] is lost, it is [recovered] through monthly fasts.
The remainder [of the phrase] is "bathing and twilight rituals. As it is stated in the *Varadevīya* regarding ritual action in the home:
"When one performs the voiding of urine in a grove sacred to Śiva or in the courtyard of Śiva..."
Having fasted, one should recite each [mantra] one hundred times in succession.
At a crossroads, at the foot of a tree, or in a barren place, one should not perform the recitation (*japa*).
However, the practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*) should perform five hundred recitations as an expiation for negligence.
[This applies when reciting] in saline soil, in water, in ploughed land, on a riverbank, or on a mountain peak.
Even one who has committed a perverse act should mutter the Aghora-hundred;
or the wise practitioner should mutter it twice over with the Sandhyā-mantra.
Then, having completed the remainder of the recitation, one should perform the twilight worship (sandhyā) as before;
however, if the three twilight prayers have been omitted, one should recite the Īśāna mantra three hundred times.
Whether free from disease or afflicted by it, the practitioner should perform the *saṃhitā* recitation in three ways;
or the practitioner may begin the mantra recitation three times over with the *sādhya* mantra.
Even at the fourth twilight, this fourfold procedure must necessarily be performed as before for the sake of purification through expiation.
In the event of a lapse regarding many daily rites, one should perform recitation while fasting;
for the fifth [offense], one thousand recitations are prescribed for the informant.
Likewise, for one who has broken the vow, [the penance lasts] twenty thousand nights;
having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should worship Śiva and the fire. Thus it is said.
Since a householder should therefore worship Śambhu constantly— whether once, twice, thrice, or at midnight—
at the times of morning, midday, and the final half-watch; |||
When the sun has set, one should avoid performing worship and giving gifts;
likewise, except during a lunar eclipse, one should avoid ritual practices and covering the sacrificial fire.
If there is an omission of worship for a single day, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times with the right hand;
if it occurs through unintentional negligence, one should perform twice as much as intended.
For those who perform worship at a single time and for those who perform worship at the three times of day,
the expiation for all of them shall be neither less nor more.
For those whose worship occurs three times a day, or even until the ritual image is removed,
purification must be performed there using what was previously prepared, and not otherwise.
The previously mentioned characteristics should be understood for the purification of those committed to the final stage (naiṣṭhika),
[even when hindered] by fate, disease, great delusion, or terrible fears of kings and the like.
One should know that a friend free from these defects may go wherever he wishes; however,
starting from one day up to ten days,
one should increase the number of oblations (*homa*) by three hundred from the prescribed amount, as well as the *gaḍḍuka* vessels.
If there is an omission due to evil deeds, the practitioner of mantra should clearly recite the southern [mantra];
but if there is an omission in the double repetition, he should thereafter increase it by twenty thousand.
Month after month for a year, during the Mahāsena rite,
one should perform the expiation if there is a lapse in the daily fire-oblation.

As it is also stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "The fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) which must be performed immediately after initiation— without that, one has no authority over the chariot, the weapons, or the initiation and so forth."
"If the preceptors do not perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) due to negligence, it must be performed with a count of one hundred thousand [repetitions] for every year [of omission]. Thus it is said.

On the eighth and subsequent lunar days, rites such as worship, recitation, and fire-offerings yield fourfold benefit in this world; O dear one, they are superior to the penances previously mentioned.
When the Pavitrārohaṇa rite for the gods has been performed during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha,
one becomes pure by reciting the Aghora mantra two hundred thousand times, as well as by performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And as it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"He who performs the *pavitra* rite when Janārdana has fallen into the sleep of delusion or ignorance is a sinner, deluded by sin."
One should recite [the mantra] while fasting for five days;
in this way, one attains supreme purity through the five weapons, and never otherwise.
One should not perform [this] after the Bhadra [period]; in the Siddhānta, one would become a partaker of fault.
By reciting the Aghora mantra two hundred thousand times, one becomes purified even if,
by chance or through ignorance, one has performed [the rites] during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha;
O Purandara, such is the expiation prescribed for that case as well.
In the event of the omission of a vow, a ritual act, or a restrictive rule,
one should recite the *niyatya* mantra one hundred times and perform the same rite for the rectification of the breach.
If the vessel for the *arghya* offering has been discarded, broken, or overturned,
one becomes pure again after two hundred, one thousand, or five hundred [repetitions of the mantra], respectively.
They say that on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and in the fire at that time, the merit is twofold;
one should maintain the Śiva-fire with diligence, for [otherwise] it may be lost through negligence.
Having recited the Aghora mantra ten thousand times, one attains purity, and not otherwise;
however, it is taught that the recitation should be doubled when performed before one's own chosen deity (Sveśvara), in the sacred fire (Agni), or at a site of liberation (Nirvāṇa).
And as it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara* (p.
"In Nirvāṇa, or in the auspicious Fire, [the seed] is nourished..."
Having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times for one possessing form, one becomes capable of perceiving purity; of this there is no doubt.

"Even when Nirvāṇa has been protected, the practitioner becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and reciting the Rūpiṇī mantra a thousand times. Thus it is said. [If] meat is [offered] to the God through negligence, [then] ghora... [etc.]
Upon seeing the offering defiled by insects, meat, bones, and the like that have fallen [upon it].
If one offers incense made from the limbs of a living being, one should recite the *pañcamahāśata* mantra.

If one should step over the shadow of a *liṅga*, the shadow of a guru, or other *liṅgas*, one should recite the *ghora* mantra three hundred times; [if one steps over] a blazing cow or a Brahmin, one hundred times.
If there is damage by incense and the like, one should recite ten thousand [mantras] excluding the *saindra* [formula].
If there is a strike from nearby, or if it is noiseless, one should recite ten thousand [mantras] including the *saindra*.
If the *liṅga* is touched by a foot or stepped over, one should recite twenty thousand [mantras].
By implication, Kapardin has stated that purity is attained through the touch of the dust of [the guru's] feet.

When a thousand revolutions have occurred, purification occurs; when two thousand, it is doubled. When three or four thousand revolutions have occurred, this applies to the *liṅga* on the surface of the earth.
In ten thousand [drops], one is purified by being clean; in a hundred thousand, one is purified by water reaching the thighs;
in three hundred thousand, when defiled by phlegm, one is purified; and in four hundred thousand, one is purified by that water after it has been offered in worship.
One should declare purification after falling one hundred thousand times into a pit for discarded offerings;
and by falling into a pit of excrement, one is considered pure after half a lakh [fifty thousand] falls.
Purification occurs through the uprooting of a firm tree, and likewise through its re-establishment.
If a *śasamutśaka* linga should fall due to negligence,
then a portion measuring one cubit (*hastamātra*)— neither less nor more than that— should be fashioned as a replacement.
If the Śiva-linga, having been released from its casket, should fall through negligence,
it becomes pure again by measuring one cubit, which is twice the previously mentioned distance.
If luster is produced by the fire having licked it for thirty thousand [years],
then purity is achieved when it is devoid of luster after being abandoned for a hundred thousand [years] once the city has been constructed.

Then, when the linga— though established for all time— was led away by those who defiled it with wind and other elements, you were struck down, rendered lusterless, and cast into river chasms and the like.
If a place is frequented by those who have stolen royal edicts or by thieves, or by outcastes (śvapacas),
or if it is touched by two opposing factions, its abandonment is ordained.
One should diligently recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and firmly establish that form;
then the practitioner attains purity and washes away his sins.
Otherwise, it could not be performed at all, due to the possibility of a deficiency in the ritual procedure;
the assembly consists of the four castes, with actors and dancers as the others.
Through the ritual sipping of water (*upasparśa*) and by means of these two types of touch,
the triad of groups beginning with "ka" (the gutturals) arises, whereby [the phonemes] do not fail to be produced.
If, however, after [the third], he should enter the water on the fourth day, it is called *paścāt*.
As it is stated in the Tilaka and the Parameśvara: "If one's own chosen *liṅga* is stolen, lost, or burnt,
the atonement (*prāyaścitta*) is considered to be a hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣa*) of the mantra, along with its re-implantation."
Or if it has fallen on the ground through negligence, or even been touched by an animal;
Having recited ten thousand [times], as well as the fundamental consecration (*maulika-saṃskāra*),
one becomes pure by means of fifty thousand [recitations] if the *liṅga* has fallen from the hand.
If [the substance] falls from both hands due to negligence, then there would be no purification for the linga; a fundamental consecration (saṃskāra) must take place.
When a *liṅga* made of clay falls from the hand and is broken through negligence,
there is no expiation for it, because the *śālikā* has been split apart.
The *liṅga* is considered to be of two kinds: stationary (*sthāvara*) and moving (*jaṅgama*).
When it is intentionally or unintentionally burst open or split asunder, [it is a transgression].
"There is no atonement for him," said the Blessed Lord Śiva,
"who performs the most terrible uprooting of a linga or who insults ascetics."
O best of the twice-born, O lord of Brahmā, I do not tolerate even the transgression of the two paths;
if there should be a lapse of a *śalākā* or a *ghaṭikā*, no expiation exists.
Upon seeing a fallen divination-stick (śalākā), the country must be abandoned along with its inhabitants;
for in that place, famine, diseases, and calamities will occur incessantly.
"And in that Īśāna [kalpa], O Brahmin, men will live for nine long lifespans; for when the *liṅga* has fallen, there is no doubt that [this] occurs. Thus it is said.
One becomes pure by reciting the mantra eight hundred times from the *liṅga* for faults such as those concerning the rosary (*akṣasūtra*);
however, for a fault regarding the bell (*ghaṇṭā*), one becomes pure by reciting it eight hundred times as prescribed for the *liṅga*.
If one's own chosen *liṅga* is touched by uninitiated persons such as Brāhmaṇas and others,
then its purification shall occur through one, two, three, or four hundred [repetitions of the mantra].
If [the water] has been touched by a group of fishermen, purification occurs after ten thousand recitations;
if it has been touched by a group of crows and the like, one should prescribe purification after thirty thousand recitations.
If one is seen by outcastes (śvapacas) and the like, purification occurs through ten thousand arrows;
however, when an image is touched or embraced by these, purification is held to require double that amount.
When the *liṅga* is touched by those initiated in their own stream (*svasrotas*), they incur no fault;
