likewise, even if the *liṅga* is touched through negligence by those established in the left or right paths (*vāmamārga* and *dakṣiṇamārga*).
The mantra-practitioner is purified by ten thousand repetitions and by great ablutions, and not otherwise;
[so too are those] who revile the Guru, the Linga, the Shaiva scriptures, or the wearers of the Linga.
One should depart far from that place and recite the *sadyojāta* mantra a hundred times.

The Guru is threefold: the purifier (*śodhaka*), the awakener (*bodhaka*), and the giver of liberation (*mokṣada*). For [offenses against] the giver of liberation, the awakener, or the one who inspires [practice], purification is achieved by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, fifty thousand times, or a quarter of that; one should determine the penance accordingly.
If injury occurs sixfold, one who is stained [by sin] gains a twofold luster;

through weapons, purification is a hundredfold. Having understood this, one should apply it elsewhere accordingly; thereafter, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* and other penances according to one's ability.
At the conclusion of the vow, the initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed as before, preceded by the five lotuses of the Gṛhya ritual;
one should give all gold to the Guru, for then the purification of men occurs.
For a preceptor who always observes the Śiva-vow, or for a practitioner (sādhaka) and others,
purification occurs by means of one hundred thousand offerings made with red-footed [animals].
It was given until the blow of the staff, so that it could no longer be seen as it was when dyed.
The mantra-practitioner is purified by half of that [time]; one should pray with prostrations at his feet.
When acts such as malice toward the guru have been committed, the great ablution and other rites must be performed.
A great ablution (mahāsnāna) should be performed with milk, curd, ghee, and so forth, yielding two thousandfold fruit; the same applies to [offerings of] fruits.
Likewise, one should arrange a great red wick made from aṅkola, jāti, punnāga, and śrīphala flowers before Śiva.
A great ablution (mahāsnāna) should be performed, and a great worship (mahāpūjā) half its size;
two days of fasting should always be observed for ten thousand and for another ten thousand [recitations].
From the recitation, one-tenth of the portion should be offered as oblations (homa), and one-twentieth of the portion as water-pots (gaḍḍuka).
This is accompanied by truthfulness, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at night.
The procedure for recitation should end with an oblation of clarified butter, provided it is not already accompanied by an offering of sacrificial food.

One should always drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and likewise copiously when the [recitation] is completed; for when the book has fallen [from the hand], one should bathe it wherever it may have landed.
Having placed that sūtra either on a high place, or on the ground, or in a book, or upon a seat, a bed, or within a house,
one should offer five hundred terrible arghyas and recite the mantra twice to grant all desires.
An old scripture together with its established tenets—that book soaked in ghee—[should be offered].

One should offer oblations into the fire-pit; having offered them, one should recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times. There is no defilement from [the touch of] those who have traveled a krośa, nor from those who have touched [the ground] a hundred times, nor from speaking with such persons; purity is attained by half of that [number].
One should not engage in dispute with those who have five faces and mouths at the half-time;
likewise, one should avoid conversation and physical contact with them from afar.
One should avoid conversation with the Sāṅkhyas, the Snātakas, the Cārvākas, those who [wear] cloth-paintings and the like,
as well as with the Bhāgavatas.
One should never commit an offense nor ever engage in a dispute;
if one who is deluded in soul commits such an act, he shall attain purification by performing a rite of expiation.
One should avoid the sight of those who are guilty of the five great sins;
purification from conversing with them and so forth is considered twice as difficult as that resulting from physical touch.
Purification from [the sin of] lying on a bed occurs after thirty thousand [repetitions], and one becomes pure from [the sin of] eating after one hundred thousand;
[these apply to] killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife.
They call it a great sin (mahāpātaka); through association with that, one becomes the fifth [category of sinner].
If a twice-born man, out of desire, performs an oblation, he should then recite [the mantra] in a cow-pen;
if he drinks liquor out of desire, he should then recite it in the temple of Śiva.
Having committed theft unintentionally, one should recite [the mantra] in a cremation ground for a year.

Having committed adultery with the wife of a guru out of lust, or having practiced yoga with all [the aforementioned women] while smeared with fire, one should recite the fifth mantra five hundred times before a Naga.
In the case of a public act committed intentionally, one is purified by repeating [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
if it was committed unintentionally in secret, purification is held to be achieved by repeating it one thousand times.
These two myriads belong to Kāmadasya Rahasya and Trita;
and in Akāśatapraprakāśa, there too are two myriads.
The Cāndrāyaṇa, the Parāka, and the Kṛcchra penances,
as well as the Tapta-kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra, are prescribed in their respective order for the five great sins beginning with the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
And here, the cow-pen and so forth constitute the maṇḍala, just as in the case of the lotus.
Brahmā said:
What is meant by "in the midst of cows," and what is meant by "the abode of Śiva"? What is the cremation ground, and what is the house for the Agnihotra sacrifice?
O Lord of Gods, you ought to tell me in truth what this mountain is.
Īśvara said: "They say that the middle of the cows, the cow-pen (*goṣṭha*), is measured by a *dyogahasta*;
O Brahmin, a *koṣṭha* is [measured] from a thousand cows; this is the general rule."
The cow-maṇḍala is proclaimed as the "Saurabheya";
it is so called because therein eleven cows along with their calves are worshipped.
Brahmā is situated in the eight directions, and three [goddesses] are located in the center of the mandala;
in their midst, the Bull himself is established.
The goddesses are the source of the fulfillment of desires; their mandala, which consists of that sinful nature, extends to eight cubits and may be ninefold or tenfold.
It is square, with four gates, four faces, and is supreme over all.

Amantra mantrā yathā [insert mantra] svāhā. In the center is the lotus; in the south is Jagadyoni; in the north is Oṃ Amoghamātṛ; and likewise, Vṛṣabha is in the pericarp (karṇikā). Furthermore: Oṃ Jagaddhṛdaye in the east; Oṃ Amṛte in the southeast; Oṃ Tejomālini in the south; Oṃ Jagaddheto in the west; Oṃ Śivaśakti in the northwest; Oṃ Sarvalokasañjīvini in the north; Oṃ Sa[insert syllable]de in the northeast; and Oṃ Tejaḥsaṃhāriṇi svāhā. Thus, [this is performed] in front of the tree. (p. 244)
Oṃ sruva sruva gala gala, may [this] become the nectar of pleasure and pain, svāhā! Thus for all the calves. This concludes the worship of the circle of cows (dhenumaṇḍala).
O Brahmin, the Maṇḍala is declared to be a general term for Śiva’s abode, possessing a single gender; however, it is specifically designated as "Śivāya" (the abode of Śiva).
Where Śiva and those preceded by the Creator (Brahmā) are worshipped according to the prescribed rite,
there stands alone in the center the Great Śiva, pervading the void.
His emanation is situated on the right side of Śiva;
Śiva himself remains established on the left, upon the lotus-center (karṇikā) which serves as the seat of Śiva.
In the northeastern quarter of that [place] stands the one named Saṃhāra;
in the east is Anugraha Śiva, and in the southeast is Muktida Śiva.

Tirobhāva is on Śiva’s right; Śiva bestows prosperity upon the Rākṣasas. Having established Bhukti and Mukti in the remaining directions in due order, this Mahāśiva is to be known as abiding in the state of the "all-pervading void" (vyomavyāpin).
One who stands upon the two stages of existence (bhava) should be known as such, and not one who is beyond existence (aśiva).
Śiva, established in the state of existence, shall always abide there.
"Release, release! Śiva, who abides in the state of withdrawal, remains established as the one situated in the stage of the feet."
Anugraha is declared to be Śiva, the bestower of happiness upon all beings;
these three—bhukti, mukti, and śiva—are thus proclaimed.
That mandala should be fashioned as a square, just as before.
The mantras here are as follows:
Oṃ, salutation to the Great Śiva, the all-pervading space.
Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, the source of existence and creation.
Oṃ, homage to Bhavodbhava, the auspicious one who brings about existence! Oṃ, homage to Saṃhāra-śiva, the auspicious one who releases and releases!

Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, the bestower of happiness upon all beings, the compassionate one; Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, salutation, salutation! Salutation, salutation to Śiva! Salutation to Mukti-Śiva! Oṃ, salutation to the first of the firsts, to Tirobhāva-Śiva! Oṃ, Śiva is the giver of everything, existing below the thousand [petals] of the Karavīra and other [lotuses]. Here, the general speech is without distinction; here indeed is the Maṇḍala. By means of the words of Bahurūpa, beginning with Aghora and ending with Rūpa: there, Aghora is the first, while the second is called Ghora.
Another is Ghoratara, and yet another is Sarva, as well as Rudra.
Indeed, these four are known as the Śivas within the cremation ground mandala:
Aghora is situated in the center of the lotus, and Ghora is established in the east.
Ghora and Ghoratara are in the southern direction, and all [the others] are situated in the western direction;
likewise, Rudra is stationed in the northern quarter, and the mandala has four petals.
All [the deities] mounted upon the skulls of four pretas are to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
The mantras for this are as follows:

*Oṃ aghorebhyo namaḥ* in the pericarp (*karṇikā*). *Oṃ atha ghorebhyo namaḥ* on the eastern petal. *Oṃ ghora-ghoratarebhyaśca namaḥ* on the southern [petal]. *Oṃ sarvataśśarva sarvebhyo namaḥ* [on the western petal].
"In the west: 'Salutation be to you in the forms of Rudra; salutation in the north. Thus is the cremation ground mandala.
O Brahman, the fires are offered there in the fire-sanctuary (agnihotra-gṛha);
because thousands of oblations are poured there, the purifier (pāvaka) is highly honored."
p.
246) There, the fire-sanctuary (*agnihotra-gṛha*) is specifically remembered as the mandala;
it consists of three lotuses for the sake of the deity and for the person (*puruṣa*).
The specific distinction here is proclaimed as being in the form of the three eyes of Hara.
In the east, it is a square; in the west, it is circular; in the south, like that of Yama; and in the north, like that of Indra.
Wherein the Gārhapatya fire, the divine being, is situated;
there Agni, the Great God, is Rudra, and the southern wind is his breath.
In the west is the personified deity Mahādeva standing in front;
Rudra, however, is proclaimed to be on the southern side within the maṇḍala.

The mantras for this are as follows: Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa; salutation to Gārhapatya. We meditate upon Mahādeva; salutation to Āhavanīya. To the east: Oṃ, may Mṛtyu impel us toward that... [wealth] to the south. Thus in the Agnihotra maṇḍala.
The mountain peak, however, is proclaimed to be the common Śikhara.
The [names] of the Adṛṣṭaparvatas and the Kulādri mountains are thus proclaimed.
O Brahmin, it is established that the mandala is the specific feature, namely the mountain peak.
Mount Meru is proclaimed as the preeminent among the regions; the Vindhya alone is the foremost among the principal mountain ranges. Furthermore, the mountain known as Catuḥśṛṅga is also there;
the mountain Parvavān is to be known as being to the east of Īśāna.
By virtue of its meaning, the technical name consists of syllables and words denoting the object [of worship];
however, the objects of worship on the seat are said to be fourfold.
That which is denoted by the name Sadāśiva is proclaimed as the foremost.
In the center of that, the object of worship is situated with its four joints at the top;
Īśvara is to be worshipped in the south, and the Lord of Brahmā in the west.
One should worship the northern joints in the circle of the head.
The mantras for this are as follows:

*Oṃ sadā śivāya namaḥ* in the center of the maṇḍala; *Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānāṃ namaḥ* in the eastern part; *Oṃ īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ namaḥ* in the south; *Brahmādhipatirbrahmaṇodhipatirbrahmā namaḥ* in the west; *Oṃ śivome'stu namaḥ* in the north. Thus ends the worship of the mountain peaks.
Having approached the wife of his guru out of delusion even once, he should abandon her with remorse;
having undergone internal penance, he should proceed toward expiation.
One hundred thousand recitations of that [mantra] should also be given without conceptual distraction.
One should not abandon it out of desire or delusion; otherwise, that lowest of men shall become a denizen of hell.
There is no atonement for one who obstructs the fruit of initiation;
however, having seen the guru’s wife with a wicked intent, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
If, however, due to negligence one's garment becomes exposed while wearing the Bahurūpa mantra, one should recite it one hundred times.
By selling images, lingas, or scriptures, one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin;
he is likewise a murderer of his guru, a killer of his mother, and a killer of his father;
he is also a cow-killer, a drinker of intoxicants, and a thief of gold.
Together with twenty-one generations of their lineage, they shall remain as long as the moon and stars endure.
One attains a terrible hell; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
For all sins whatsoever, the expiation has been declared as [the gift of] cows.
"There is no atonement for the sale of images, lingas, or scriptures;
there is no one more sinful than such a person," the Blessed Lord Śiva has said.
In the same way, there is no atonement for the sale of *piṇḍikās*;
however, if they are sold through negligence, one becomes pure by reciting [the mantra] ten million times.
In other cases of lust, it is proclaimed that his [penance] is threefold; however, what is the use of saying much more here—there is no atonement anywhere for this.
Regarding the sale of lingas and piṇḍīs, those words were indeed true, truly true.
Now, in the Śivadharmottara:
"O Mahādeva, he who, out of anger, hatred, fear, or negligence, speaks of a Brāhmaṇa in a way that strikes at his vital points, is proclaimed to be a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa."
Now, regarding the *lalitabhedas*: he who, acting out of his own will, kills a Brahmin who has committed a minor offense,
or a woman who embraces a maiden while being a knower of the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.

There is no atonement for that; therefore, one should not kill them. Even when reviled or beaten, or through the course of worldly dealings, such as the seizure of property or land, a renunciant must not fall under the sway of anger.
If a Brahmin should die with desire for anything, he becomes a slayer of Brahman;
even for thousands of offenses, one should not commit suicide.
He who commits this is a sinful soul, the lowest of men; he shall become a denizen of hell, a slayer of his own self by himself, and must dwell for a long time in the Kumbhīpāka hell.
And so says the Smṛti: "Whether it be a woman or a man, if they should hang themselves and die under any circumstances due to insult, anger, greed, humiliation, or fear..."
There, those men go to the place named Asūrya;
having filled it with blood, they are cast into this dreadful [hell].
A man who kills himself by piercing himself with weapons in battle,
in defense of a cow or his home, in a state of enmity, or for the sake of one who steals his seed and so forth—
even if he increases his own pain in the act of killing— he does not become a slayer of a Brahmin on that account.
Having swiftly slain those who revile Śiva, the Śiva-mantra, or the Śivācārya out of desire, one is not tainted by the sin of killing;
for the [sin] is destroyed by the fault [of the victim], even if the *liṅga* has been placed within him.
Bound by any fault whatsoever, or by wicked and contemptible actions, or even by iron shackles— that [bond] is not found in a blameless woman.
One must never inflict punishment upon women or upon those who practice asceticism.
The determination [of punishment] for the virtuous should be like that for a daughter of the Udika clan:
even for a thousand offenses, one should neither strike nor [inflict] [punishment]; even toward gurus, there is no [inflicting of] punishment, as in the case of a deposit.
It is a terrible act of hostility toward Śiva, censured by the gods and the Vedas;
it destroys the vigor and intellect of one's beloved friends and others,
and once promised, it brings ruin upon the wise.
To cause an obstacle to food for one afflicted by hunger, or to obstruct water for one who has gone to a sacrificial session (*sattra*),
is a sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin; it is a defilement of the lineage.
Eating what is forbidden to eat, sexual misconduct, false testimony that causes harm to others,
and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The theft of a lord’s property, a human being, a woman, land, or a milch cow,
as well as the misappropriation of a deposit— all such acts are equal to the theft of gold.
Sexual intercourse with a female friend, a wife, a maiden, women of one's own age,
women of the lowest castes, or the wives of one's sons or of those of the same lineage (gotra) is recorded in tradition as equal to violating the bed of a guru.
One who approaches a paternal aunt, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother’s sister,
a mother’s co-wife, a sister, a teacher’s daughter, a teacher’s wife,
or one’s own daughter, is a violator of the Guru’s bed (gurutalpaga).
What has been called a "great sin" (mahāpātaka), the "secondary sin" (upapātaka) is now described.
The killing of a cow, theft, non-payment of debts,
failure to perform sacrifices, not maintaining the sacred fires, the mendicancy of a householder, and the selling of censure.
Studying for a fee, teaching for a fee, acting as a matchmaker,
lending money at interest, usury, and the manufacture of salt;
and subsisting by censured occupations involving women, Śūdras, Vaiśyas, or Kṣatriyas.
Atheism, the neglect of religious observances, the sale of one's own children,
the theft of grain, forest produce, and livestock, and officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice;
Abandoning one's father, mother, or son; selling a pond or a grove;
defiling a maiden; and officiating at a sacrifice for one who has married before his elder brother.
Eating the food given by a maiden, practicing crookedness toward her, breaking one's vow for the sake of one's own interests, and consorting with a woman who drinks liquor.
The abandonment of Vedic study, the sacred fire, and one's son, as well as the abandonment of one's kinsmen;
Cutting down trees for fuel, living by the killing of women or by medicinal herbs,
the construction of murderous machines, vices, the selling of oneself,
serving Śūdras, friendship with the low-born, and consorting with those of inferior birth.

Likewise, dwelling in a place where no stage of life (āśrama) is observed, subsisting on the food of others while being devoted to others, studying false scriptures, and being intent upon improper conducts.
"For those for whom there are various [transgressions] regarding their wife, each one is a minor offense (upapātaka). Thus it is said.
The statement of Smṛti—alternatively, in the Kālottara: "One is purified from the sin of making oneself a participant in the injury of living beings by reciting the Śataghora mantra;
for intentional abortion, one should recite it joined with the third [mantra]."
Having killed a woman, a Śūdra, or a child, one becomes pure by [the recitation of] ten thousand *bahurūpa* mantras;
having killed a cow through negligence, one becomes pure by the recitation of one hundred thousand *ghora* mantras.

Having killed a hundred cows, one is purified by [reciting] three hundred thousand [times]. When a swarm of boneless living beings or those born from sweat has been killed, one should recite the Ajāta hymn a hundred times; if it was done intentionally out of desire, half of that [number].
And with a hundred [strokes] like a cat, he [cleansed] them by the thousands.
For killing dogs and jackals, the penance is doubled; for monkeys and cocks, it is one-eighth; for snakes and the like, it is one-sixteenth; likewise for swans and other such birds;
and for killing wild animals, it is equal to the penance for killing a non-domesticated animal.
If one is bitten by a dog, a jackal, or any such animal unintentionally, one becomes pure by reciting the appropriate mantra four hundred times for each of the four hundred [stages].
However, if one is bitten by any of these while in water,
one should bathe and, standing in the midst of cool water, recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times.
If one wishes to practice the science of poisons, medicine, or the *jālaka* [spell] against Indra,
three hundred [recitations] are required for the eradication of *bhūtas*, *grahas*, *piśācas*, and the like.
Having performed rites for pacification and nourishment out of necessity or affection,
purification from the three hundred [impurities] occurs through the Bahurūpa mantra and not otherwise.
Having recited the Aghora mantra ten thousand times while remaining pure through fasting,
one may [attain] the knowledge that is the compendium of the reality of the principles, even without knowing the true essence of the scriptures.
If anyone, out of delusion, performs initiation and subsequently feels regret,
he should recite the Ghoramantra five hundred thousand times if he desires auspiciousness.
One's own guru’s brother, and especially the guru’s son.
However, for those who have committed it unknowingly, purification is achieved by consuming a hundred thousand units of that [substance].
Furthermore, the rite of *pavitrārohaṇa* must likewise be performed by those who have received initiation.
When one who is qualified installs another person as the son of the Guru,
his initiation indeed becomes fruitless, and he goes downward for a great kalpa.
Having brought a companion even from afar, one should mutter [the mantra] twenty-four thousand times;
having muttered a fourth part of that for oneself, one may enter the house.
In the Śivadharmottara:
"The resolve regarding another's wife or property, these eight reflections, and the intent toward what should not be done— [one should abandon these] with the mind."
Excessive chatter, falsehood,
that which is unpleasant, slandering others, and backbiting— this is the fourth type of vocal action.
Eating what is unfit to be eaten, violence, and indulgence in false desires.
In the *Śivabhedatantra*, among the thousands [of verses],
it is said: "Speech, action, and words— he who punishes this triad [is the true teacher]."
He should be known as a tridaṇḍin; he attains the supreme goal.
And hear, O beloved, the expiation for all three of these as well:
in the case of mercury (rasaka), there should be silence for three days, along with fire-rites, worship, and recitation.
In secret, he should offer humble words to his guru and deity;
thus released from vocal bonds, he should understand the bondage of karma.
By fasting for three nights, immersing oneself in water at the three junctions of the day,
practicing celibacy, and observing silence, one is liberated from the bonds of karma.
"When breath-control (prāṇāyāma) has been performed in water for mental sin, one is liberated from a hundred mental [sins] by means of the Śivagāyatrī mantra. Thus it is said.
Alternatively, according to the *Vāmadevī-kriyāsaṅgraha*:
"Having recited the mantra ten thousand times for Śiva in order to remove all defects,
the practitioner, by drinking the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) just once, is liberated from all sins."
Having become satisfied by the Aghora [mantra], he stood before Śiva;
facing the eastern direction, he remained with the root mantra beginning with Oṃ.
Upon merely drinking it, one becomes pure and stainless like the autumn moon;
though born of mother and father, it is both innate and adventitious.
The Brahmakūrca [rite] would instantly burn away the evil that has reached the very marrow of the bones.
The rule is that one should speak of the Guru’s faults when they are concealed from others, but reveal them openly.
Likewise, out of negligence, one might [speak ill of] the Linga, the Guru, the scripture, or the image.
If he has been touched by the foot, he should recite the Ghorā mantra twenty thousand times.
Having offered three hundred water-pots with six qualities according to one's desire,
as well as a teacher’s bed, seat, vehicle, sandals, and shoes;
Having committed an act of malice unintentionally, one becomes pure by reciting [the mantra] a thousand times;
however, when a wise person knowingly commits such an act, he must perform the penance sixfold.
One should not allow the garment that adorns the body of the Guru, nor his umbrella, to touch one's feet;
or, if one desires victory for oneself, one should recite [the mantra] five hundred times.
For violating the command of a divine, fierce, or preceptor-like teacher, one hundred thousand [repetitions] are prescribed;
for doing so unintentionally, ten thousand are declared, along with fire-oblations, water-vessels, and fasts.
And for one who intentionally breaks the command regarding the directions, [the penance is as prescribed];
and unintentionally, it is a thousand [units]. Likewise, for sleeping in the presence of those [objects], or when semen and the like flow while one is sleeping unintentionally.
Having bathed previously while still unclothed, one should mutter the weapon-mantra a hundred times.
Having touched [the liquor] with skull-bearers and Kolikas, who have five faces and half-moon-shaped mouths,
and having brought Soma from the cremation ground— which is difficult to behold— along with dog-cookers, Mlecchas, Caṇḍālas, Buddhists, the naked (Jainas), white-robed ones, and Cārvākas;
Having performed his bath, that devotee of Śiva becomes pure after the three hundred [repetitions];
even by means of a wooden bed, a wall, a water-pot, a house, or an elephant.
O gods, even when touching [the corpse] during processions and the like, in sacrificial rites, and at all festivals, such contact does not cause defilement.
Then, in the Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa]:
"One should not revile Brāhmaṇas or cows; one should not revile the forms of Śiva, nor the gods, nor the sages, nor the Gaṇas, nor the Mothers."
If one should utter censure against even one of these, [one incurs great sin].
Having bathed, one should perform sixteen rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with all one's being;
however, if there has been an emission of semen at night, one should perform this same practice reduced by six.
The dog, however, is said to perform the previously mentioned rite with the Aghora mantra;
having united with a woman, the practitioner of mantra [should do so] for the sake of the Great-Souled Praṇava.
By restraining the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*), one purifies oneself by encompassing the *lakṣa*;
this indeed pertains to the domain of ascetics.
And it is said in the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
An ascetic who is attached to sense objects may take a wife after first performing the rite for the lifting of his vow; otherwise, his downfall is certain.
For as many moments as there are hairs on his matted locks or particles of ash on his body,
for that long shall the observer of the vow dwell in the most terrible Raurava hell.
O Vāmadeva, he who should approach a woman [of another caste] even once—whom shall he marry again?
They are purified by a thousand [recitations of the] Vāmadevya hymn; of this there is no doubt.
If one emits semen by force during the day, one should recite [the mantra] four hundred times;
if at night, two hundred times; and if one has slept during the day, one should recite it one hundred times.
When he should witness the play of cattle unintentionally, he should recite [the mantra] one hundred times;
likewise when his wife has bathed after her menses, for a period of five days.
The sky [should be purified] by a Brahmin for the sake of obtaining a son; otherwise, one becomes a slayer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā).
Thereafter, one who is proficient in asceticism should perform recitation, fire-offerings, and other such rites.
That brahmin who constantly engages in sexual intercourse, deluded by lust, should be known as a donkey; the mantras turn their faces away from him.
There is no fault in [eating] at the beginning of the Kṣatra period and so forth; however, one incurs fault by eating during the day or on a festival day.
One should not, according to one's desire, consume food that has been served [inappropriately] through action, mind, or speech.
"If one should perform [the rite] out of delusion when it is intended for the purpose of purification,
the recitation must be doubled in the case of a maiden, and likewise among other castes."
Now, in the Parākhya:
"At all the junctures of the lunar phases (parvan), having occasionally engaged in sexual union during the day,
the wise man, established in his vow, should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times while prostrating."
Having performed half of the number at night, one should recite it ten thousand times during the twilight.
Having engaged in talk concerning sexual intercourse, one should recite the heart-seed mantra a hundred times;
a wise man who has failed in celibacy should perform this atonement as a householder.
One should diligently avoid a prostitute, a Śūdra woman, and the wives of others;
having approached them through negligence or delusion, a man must perform penance.
In the *Parāsaṃhitā*:
"Having had sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, one should recite the *Vāmadevya* hymn a hundred times;
likewise, if one who is initiated should approach a Brāhmaṇa woman or any other [forbidden woman]."
A Brahmin, having recited it one hundred and eight times, is liberated from that sin.
A Kṣatriya [attains success] by reciting it two hundred times, a Vaiśya by three hundred,
and a Śūdra by four hundred times, having recited the Vāmadeva [mantra] before Śiva.
Having stayed there for one night, he is liberated from that sinful nature;
so too is he who approaches a woman who has renounced the world, or a Brāhmaṇa woman, or a woman of noble family.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with the Īśa [mantra], the initiated one shall be freed from defects.
If at any time one should, through negligence, have sexual union with a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī),
he shall be freed from that sin by reciting the mantra of Īśāna one hundred times.
When one learns that a Caṇḍāla woman is staying within the house,
one should discard earthenware and other such vessels and, having bathed, purify that house.
Having recited the *Narasiṃha-mantra* five thousand times, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance;
having eaten at night out of desire,
one becomes purified by performing the *taptakṛcchra* preceded by ten thousand recitations of the *Aghora-mantra* and the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
If one eats out of desire even once, having committed [the act], one should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances;
likewise, the recitation of the Vāmadeva [hymn] is prescribed as the vow for approaching another's wife.
If, having known [her to be another's wife], one eats [with her] for a long time, then he becomes equal to her [in guilt].

Having touched a washerwoman or a leather-worker while staying in a temple, one becomes pure by discarding the vessel [of food]; for five thousand [repetitions of the mantra], purity is attained after three days.
If one has unintentionally touched or eaten [forbidden things], one should recite the mantra intensely;
if done intentionally, one should perform twice as much, practicing this once through yoga.
If many [impurities] have been mixed unintentionally, even when those two have arisen, then the Cāndrāyaṇa penance must be performed; indeed, one is not purified by merely following [the rules].
If a sexual union occurs out of desire for many days,
then one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance using water alone.
A Brahmin should remain [on one morsel] for half a month during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight;
this is declared to be the rule for Cāndrāyaṇa, which, consisting of water, is composed of water itself.
One should eat a single meal for three days, remain without food for three days,
eat only at night for three days, and subsist on air alone for three days.
Thus has Kṛcchra been fully described; now hear about Atikṛcchra. Drinking three palas of milk for twenty days is declared to be Atikṛcchra; now hear about Parāka.
This Pāraka vow, consisting of twelve days without food,
is declared to be equivalent to thousands of Atikṛcchra penances according to the various divisions of Śiva’s tradition.
The wise man should eat a single morsel at midday for three days;
then, in the same manner, he should eat for another three days by begging for alms.
"One should remain without food for three days and one night;
this procedure for the Atikṛcchra penance has been described to you in brief. Thus it is said.
Salt, sugar, various kinds of fragrant substances,
milk, curd, clarified butter, oil, honey, meat, and so forth, as well as coriander; likewise, silk cloth, cotton, wool, linen, and that made from muñja grass.
Having accepted a hide, one should mutter the Ghoramantra three hundred times;
likewise for a collection of metals such as gold, or a heap of jewels such as those found in Vraja.
Yellow orpiment and other minerals, mercury, a store of grain,
a bull, an elephant, a village, a field, a horse, and likewise a man.
Through effort regarding the store-consciousness and so forth, one becomes pure by means of many forms.
By carrying hundreds of loads of wood, stones, grass, and the like,
one becomes pure even when confronted with the accumulation of many sins.
Having understood and thoroughly mastered the terrible thirty-two-knife mantra, the wise one should recite it.
Having accepted the gift of a monastery, one should then recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with great intensity.
The meaning is: "if it is a new [temple] built by disciples, devotees, and others";
those of evil intellect who, having taken refuge in a monastery (maṭha), worship the Liṅga.

The meaning of the phrase "having resorted to a monastery" (*maṭham āśritya*) is as follows: the sense is that householders or celibate students (*brahmacārins*), out of a desire for food and other necessities within the monastery, worship the stationary or moving phallus (*liṅga*) of another—devoid of their own [resources]—using materials mixed with the property of the deity (*devadravya*).
Those men who are free from passion would have the worship of liberation;
if one desires that Nārada, however, along with sons, friends, and kinsmen.
Therefore, one should establish a monastery and a temple for Śiva.
In this regard, the primary cause is either the status of being a monastery head or [the dedication] to a temple of Śiva.
In this regard, either the status of *māṭhāpati* (founder of a monastery) should be established as the primary cause,
or whatever is performed according to the procedure for one permanently attached to the root [of the lineage]— this is what that statement means.
He who worships either an image or a linga for the sake of a livelihood,
as well as one who is the master of a temple, is indeed known as a *devalaka*.
Soma, Brahmā, Ravi, Skanda, Viṣṇu, and the Goddesses, as well as the Mothers—
whatever living beings there are who subsist on offerings, they live by worshipping these.
O God of gods, contact with them is said to be their atonement.
The distinction is that [this applies] to one who will be mentioned later. In some places it is said:
"Whether he be a Śaiva, a Vaidika, a Tantrika, or even a Pāśupata; whether he be a Kapālin, a Kālavaktra, or whatever other kind of human being he may be."
He who worships the Lord, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds, for the sake of material wealth—
even if he is endowed with the conduct of the sacred observances— is fallen and the lowest of men.
Thus, when the vessel has been touched after being prepared with the *samparka* mantras, one should,
without hesitation, offer it to that deity whose essence is Brahman.
Iron, copper, as well as bronze, and those originating from gold, silver, and so forth—their purification is by fire; in that case, their reduction to ashes constitutes the cleansing of impurities.
One should purify conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and other such items with water and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having thus understood each of these various objects, one should purify them after repeated examination.

When one intentionally associates with those who are outcastes or those deficient by birth, one should recite the Ghoramantra twenty thousand times; if the association was unintentional, one should recite it ten thousand times.
The property of the deity, the substance for the deity, the offering, that which has been offered, the substance for Caṇḍa, and the remains; thus the sixfold *nirmālya* is traditionally taught.
One should know that a gift of land, a village, a field, a granary, or a crossroads is the property of the gods; one should cause it to be delivered to its rightful owner.
One should drink heated water for three days, then heated milk for three days;
having drunk warm ghee for three days, one should subsist on air alone for three days.
This is known as the Tapta-kṛcchra, which destroys sins committed against the property of the gods.
When garments, ornaments, relics, and whatever precious jewels there may be—
designated as the property of the deities— are consumed through desire;
One should recite the mantra of Bahurūpa two hundred thousand times at a tree according to one's desire;
likewise, by giving four or five times that amount, you shall be purified.
Whatever food, drink, and other edibles have been prepared for the sake of the deity—
whether already consumed or properly offered— becomes the *naivedya* (food offering) of the deity.
Having offered that [oblation], there should be purification;
then, on the following day, having withdrawn [the deity] from above the pedestal (piṇḍikā) and gathered it together at the corner of the pedestal—
Whatever food, drink, and so forth has been prepared for the deity,
that is to be known as *caṇḍa-dravya* (the "fierce" substance) when it is consumed out of desire.
One should recite the mantra of Bahurūpa two hundred thousand times;
if one has acted without desire, one becomes purified by reciting it four or five times that number, or even by giving [the prescribed gift].
With half of that [measure] one is a *saṃyogin*, and with half of that again, a *saṅkarin*.
Having recited half of the *Pratisaṃkaraṇa* and observed a fast for two nights,
[the power of those] who were present at that time and whose minds were then defiled [is neutralized].
Their purification shall occur by means of a thousand [repetitions], otherwise they are excluded;
this applies whether the linga has been recently installed, or is mobile, or even immobile.
The fourth [day] lasts until the conclusion of the ritual; that which arises from it remains as the offering of remains (nirmālya).
(272) [One should perform] circumambulation around relics, jewels, golden lingas, and images;
likewise during a discourse, or when a painting moves, or when one has entered the middle of a river or a lake.

Just as the remains of offerings (nirmālya) belong to Śiva, so too do they belong to the Gurus, the Fires, the seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭhas), the lords of the serpent-hosts, the Yogins, the Mothers, Akṣobhya, Kāmbikā, and the others.
If a wicked-minded person, out of greed or craving, should eat that which was requested for the sake of a fire-sacrifice, or for the sake of his guru, or for the sake of the *liṅga*, [he incurs sin].
One should recite one hundred thousand [mantras] and a quarter; however, due to negligence, it may be deficient by a quarter.
Thus, a learned man may incur a fault; he should always subsist on pure food.

Whatever he might eat himself without having first offered it to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), or if he does so through negligence regarding his gurus, he should then recite the mantra eight hundred times.
Then, being pure, he gave them oil and meat, along with all the cooked food.
One should always avoid sitting in the same row while eating with those of low birth;
for by such contact, people generally become afflicted and fall into lower states.
When there is contact with the leavings of food from all those of the same caste,
the penance is written down as stated in the *Kālottara*.
If one touches someone initiated into their own caste, they become pure by sipping water (ācamana).
Having sipped water, even one who is initiated should mutter [the mantra] a hundred times according to his own caste;
likewise, such should be the expiation when an initiated person is touched in close proximity.
If that initiated person is touched while not yet consecrated, one should recite two hundred and fifty [mantras];
likewise for the touch of a Vaiśya, whether he be initiated or otherwise.
One should recite [the mantra] three hundred times upon touch; the recitation should be performed while fasting.
The same applies upon touching one known as a Śūdra or one who has been initiated.
Even for one who has been initiated by mere touch, having fasted for two nights, [he should recite] a thousand [times].
In the midst of a thousand [repetitions], the remnant of a twice-born (dvija) is considered to be three [quarters];
for the remnant of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, it is one quarter less than that, and for the remnant of a king, half of that.
A Śūdra should recite one thousand and a quarter [repetitions] when there is the remnant of a Vaiśya.

One should avoid the food of a *gaṇa*, the food of a courtesan, the meal of the husband of a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*), the food of a single person, the food of an outcast (*patita*), and food obtained through trade. One should also avoid the food of a Vaiśya, the food of an outcaste (*antyaja*), and the meal of those belonging to the class of artisans.
One should not accept food from a woman in her courses, and one should avoid the food of those who have lost a limb.
If one should, through negligence, eat the food of cowherds, florists, followers of the Bhaṭṭa school, or singers,
and other such classes of people;
One who steals cows or gold should perform twice a thousand repetitions of the *saurya* mantra according to his desire. Whoever recites it thus is purified.
That Brahmin who holds the property of a Brāhmaṇa in his hand is the husband of a Vṛṣalī. Two ascetics should be fed at a time—namely, the student (brahmacārī) and the householder (gṛhī).
The food of others, as well as that of those bearing other sectarian marks (liṅgin), is not to be eaten.
If he should eat out of negligence, he becomes pure again after ten thousand Bahurūpa mantras;
and by observing the Jaina vows and carrying the skull-bowl (kapāla), he is purified even through initiation.
He may eat from the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, provided they are initiated souls.
But for Śūdras who are established in their own duty,
there is never any fault whatsoever in eating the food of a virtuous Śūdra, whether done intentionally or unintentionally.
One should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred times for a virtuous Śūdra, and one thousand times for others.
Having fasted for one night, even a Brāhmaṇa initiated into Śiva who has turned away from the three castes is purified by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should give nine or ten [mouthfuls] without hesitation to initiated members of the castes;
likewise, Kṣatriyas and others who are of the same caste and endowed with purity and proper conduct.
One who avoids their food would be subject to a light expiation. One should not eat the food of one belonging to a different caste who has been invited;
likewise [the rites] for the male organ, the *sīmantonnayana*, and so forth.
Having eaten at the birth ceremony (prasūti) or the postnatal rite (sūtaka), one should mutter the Ghorasahasra mantra;
this is likewise prescribed for the naming ceremony, the emergence [of the infant], and the first feeding of solid food.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred times during the caulakarma, the vrata, the vaṭa ceremony, the godāna, and the marriage;
after eating the food of the fourth day, one should recite it one thousand times.
During a pākayajña, a haviyajña, and a somayāga, one should recite it one hundred times.
For one who has departed, having observed the vow for a period of one year,
one should begin the true Śrāddha rite and recite ten thousand [mantras] facing the south.
Alternatively—
when one eats at a *sadyaḥ-śrāddha*, one should then recite the Aghora mantra one hundred and eight times;
on the tenth or twelfth day, one should recite the Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra three hundred times.
At an Ekoddiṣṭa or a Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times.
p.
265) After that, having eaten at the time of a *śrāddha*, one should recite the *ghoraśata* mantra.
When one eats at a *śrāddha* for Śiva, no fault exists therein.

Having performed penance in the manner previously described, one who has eaten at the aforementioned places and has fasted should bathe as stated before and then worship the Lord; it must not be done otherwise.
Just as a woman with her menses or a man who has recently given birth, one who is not pure should not worship the God; yet their purification is now being declared.
On the first day she is a Caṇḍālī; on the second, a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa;
on the third, she is called Rajanī; and on the fourth, she becomes pure through bathing.
Having performed a bath with clay and consumed the products of the cow (gavya), one should worship Śiva; likewise,
the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) should be performed during the three preceding days,
at night, during the conjunction of the three lunar phases (triyāraja), and on the anniversaries of one's birth and death.
One should accept a panegyrist three times on the left [side] as long as the sun has not yet risen.
For all [such occasions], there is no period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*) because the wise enter into the fire;
therefore, one should perform acts such as giving gifts and worship with materials previously intended for that purpose.
Likewise, when death has been previously resolved upon, the Sun [is the witness].
One whose soul is always pure may have the deity worshipped by others;
however, for ten days after the death of a Brahmin, one is oneself not authorized to perform the ritual.
A Vaiśya who does not drink liquor, is of noble birth, and is constantly devoted to dharma, shall observe a fifteen-day penance for twelve days.

The period of birth-impurity for them would be ten, six, three, and one day respectively.
For kings, what [impurity] is there from the death of a beautiful woman?
And for those initiated into Nirvāṇa, no impurity from birth or death exists at all.
For those who follow the worldly initiation, impurity (sūtaka) exists;
for where there is an initiation through the cutting of the topknot, that initiation belongs to the worldly path.
For those whose wealth consists of illusion and grief, the cutting of the topknot (śikhā) is ordained.
Impurity due to birth or death (sūtaka/bhūtaka) does not apply to them in the worship of Śiva.
One who cooks for others should stay far away; one should avoid contact with them.

If one recites [the mantra] of Bahurūpa a thousand times unintentionally during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka), one should recite it twice that amount if done intentionally.
Even for one abiding by the worldly laws,
during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or likewise when performing worship, an expiation must be observed, provided it is without the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
The internal sacrifice must be performed even by worldly initiates;
the recitation of mantras, circumambulations, and other rites must be performed day after day.
Having bathed and fasted, at the conclusion of that, Śiva should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Furthermore, according to the Vāmadevīya-śivāgama,
for all householders who have been initiated into the Śiva-sacrifice,
purification occurs in exactly ten days during both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka), even if the period is increased by one day for each of the four [castes].
By increasing [the number] by one, there are four classes, as well as the days unfit for study (*anadhyāya*).
One who performs his own duty, is devoted to ritual action, and relies upon the increase of knowledge—
One is purified by bathing at that very moment; otherwise, there is a constant loss of merit.
One should prepare food separately and avoid contact with them at that time.
If he is connected with that practice, he becomes equal to it;
therefore, purification for him lasts only as long as he does not eat from a beloved woman.
He is purified by bathing at the three times of day and likewise by three hundred *ghora* [mantras].

There is no separate portion [of impurity] for those who possess the splendor of purity; likewise, the house and dwelling of ascetics is not affected even by birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). This is the rule for those established in their observances, situated in their proper places, and engaged in austerity.
In matters concerning the gods, the sacred fire, and the preceptor, there must never be an interruption;
one should maintain celibacy, recitation, silence, forbearance, moderation in food, and contentment.
This formidable austerity, characterized by five features, has been fully described;
it must be performed constantly and without interruption by those practicing celibacy.
Purification for the miscarriage of a full-term fetus occurs at that very moment;
for one from the time of naming until the end of birth, it is immediate, up to the conclusion of the *ekāha* sacrifice.
For one whose tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) has been performed, it is declared that purification takes three days; even more than this is required if the rite was not completed.
Beyond that, purification is as previously stated. This rule applies to all castes.
In a corpse, the intellect is purified; Śiva is not purified by growth.
If one is born as a living being, or if one speaks regarding these two states of existence, [then purification occurs].

268) However, the impurity due to death (śāvāśauca) must be observed; one should likewise perform [the rites] for a birth. For a daughter given away, it shall last one day; for one already given in marriage, it shall be three days.

The same should be understood regarding sisters and others; this is the opinion concerning those who are incomparable [in merit]. Upon the death of a brother-in-law, his son, a friend, a daughter’s son, a sister’s husband, a son-in-law, and so forth, one becomes pure simply by bathing.
In the case of those who have renounced their vows (*saṃnyasta*), those whose strength has been taken away (*balahṛt*), those consumed by fire (*agnibhūta*),

and those who have died in a foreign land (*deśāntara*) with a separate funeral cake (*pṛthakpiṇḍa*), there shall be a ritual bath (*snāna*) except for the Guru. This applies to pilgrimages (*tīrthayātrā*), marriages (*vivāha*), and so forth, excluding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.
One should not observe a single day of impurity for the death of a *mahāguru*;
likewise, for children who have not yet cut their teeth, and for those who have just emerged from the womb,
there is no purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) nor any ritual such as the water-libation (*udaka-kriyā*) for them at any time.
Upon the death of her husband, the father shall observe a fast for one night;
the mother shall do so for three nights according to the prescribed rule, partaking of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

A wife, however, should perform the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such penances. Immediate purification (sadyaḥ-śauca) is ordained in the case of giving gifts, performing sacrifices, marriage, battle, national upheaval, and even in times of dire distress.
When one who is not ill touches a person who is afflicted by disease while that person has undergone a bath, he should touch him repeatedly and bathe outside; only then will he attain purification.
Pilgrimage to sacred sites, falling from a cliff, renunciation, entering the fire,
setting out on the Great Path (mahāpatha), mental delusion, fasting, and so forth.
(269) One who has been initiated should not perform [the rites] of animal species and the like.
However, if one's body is extremely afflicted, being tormented by the exhaustion of [past] faults, [then one may do so].
Having likewise obtained the consent of the virtuous teachers and Brahmins,
and having considered what is appropriate for that time, he performed the preliminary rites of atonement for the fourth [offense].
Even then, there is no impurity from the food of one in childbirth; one becomes pure simply through bathing.
The purification of vessels and other items touched by a great person’s elder brother is now described:
for the sake of removing oiliness, odor, and residue, one should wash them with cow dung and water.
The impurity of bell-metal (bhairava) is removed instantly by means of an alkaline substance;
that which originates from copper is purified by acid, and bronze used for eating is purified by ash.
A vessel made of bamboo, gourd, or similar materials attains purity by being scrubbed with cow-hair and water;
however, an earthen alms-bowl attains purity through water alone.
An iron vessel becomes pure when heated with fire, but a conch shell, a mother-of-pearl shell, or a horn is not purified by heating; rather, they are cleansed by scrubbing with alkaline water.
Then one should rub [the stain] with wheat husks or rice husks;
the purification of garments is declared to be by means of alkaline substances and water. As it is for cloth, so it is for leather, ropes, and likewise for wooden planks.
One should always purify the food, condiments, and vessels with water.
Likewise, even after the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa),
a vessel known as *kīṭa* is purified if it has been licked by cats,
provided it is scrubbed seven times with ash and likewise subjected to the rite of circumambulation with fire.
One should abandon what has been smelled or licked by a donkey, a camel, a dog, or other such animals;
indeed, one must completely discard that which has the form of a vessel of clarified butter.
But a vessel that has been licked by a mongoose, or even merely smelled by one, [is unfit].
Indeed, that which is broken after seven [days] attains purity through fire;
first, it becomes clear, and then it attains purity like a vessel.
One should avoid abundant food that has been frequented by crows and other such creatures,
as well as food that has come into contact with the leavings of others, even after setting aside another portion of it.
Having sipped water and sprinkled the food and other items, one should touch them with the Astra-mantra;
for oily substances, purification comes from cleaning, and for those with stains, from removing the stain.
The purification of foul-smelling objects is declared to consist in the removal of the odor;
seats, beds, and vehicles become pure by means of earth and water.
Women are always pure; a bird is purified by plucking fruit;
speech is purified by truth; and a river is purified by its current. A woman is considered impure due to her menses, but she is purified by the cessation of that defect.
Thus, having understood what else is impure and how it is to be purified by one possessed of wisdom—so it is said.
As it is stated in the *Śivadharmottara* as well:
"In the case of a heap of grain, cooked food, and so forth, when only one part has been defiled..."
Having set aside just that much, the remainder deserves to be sprinkled with water for purification.
Purification with water, milk, and clay is required;
for vegetables, roots, fruits, and the like, purification is prescribed in the same manner as for grains.
That which has been licked by a cow, or by a fly, or touched by worms, becomes pure by being licked by a goat; for anything else, purification is achieved by sprinkling water over it.
Having removed only that much [of the impurity] which has been licked by donkeys, camels, horses, jackals, and the like, or by village pigs, the wise man should purify the remainder.
When touched by one who is intent on radiance, it is indeed as if smelled by the three branches;
it is purified, as it were, by golden water—of this there is no doubt.
If food is mixed with flies or hair, or has been touched by the edge of a foot, or contains dust or ants, or if one eats while sneezing or belching,
one should remove that portion alone and then sprinkle it with water.
Purification occurs through the sprinkling of clarified butter or by the scattering of ashes.
Water is considered most pure when it quenches the thirst of a cow,
provided it is not pervaded by impurity and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste.

One should not, through some practice, allow the two nails of the hand to enter the mouth from the lips while they are stained by food or saliva; nor do those other drops of water from the rinsing of the mouth that fall upon the feet touch the teeth.
They are to be known as equal to kings; one should bow before them according to their respective faculties.
Having performed [rites], having eaten, having slept, having drunk, or having spoken with the lowest of men;
while holding wealth in hand, being impure from food remnants, or having placed [something] nearby—one should sip water (ācamet).
"The purification of substances, however, as previously described, should be performed according to the nature of the substance. Thus it is said.

A teacher who has studied one hundred thousand chapters is excellent, having severed all doubts; he is one who prescribes atonement according to each specific fault and in accordance with the circumstances.
One should not give less or more than that; in its absence, it should be given by ten or five most excellent gurus who are teachers well-versed in the scriptures.
He too, relying on devotion to that [deity], pure and with his mind fixed upon it,
should recite the mantra in a solitary and clean place until it is completed.
When that recitation is completed, one should subsequently offer the merit of the recitation to them;
food should be given to them so that satisfaction arises,
or else one should gratify them with flowers, betel, sandalwood, and other such offerings.
And they should perform his rite with the first water according to their capacity;
once the penance has been completed, they may increase it without contradiction.
If it is not uttered at that time, no expiation for him is prescribed.
This expiation has been extracted from the root [tantras] as taught in the Āgamas.
Where a statement occurs with the same meaning, it is not to be considered redundant, for it arises from various doctrinal perspectives. Thus it is said.

Thus, by the wise Śrī Vijñānaśiva— a bee at the pair of lotus feet of the illustrious Lord of the Dabhra Assembly, a knower of the Vedas, a resident of Vārāṇasī, and one who possesses a steady conduct— this procedure for the Prāyaścitta (expiation) has been composed according to the words of the Lord, as a cause for the destruction of the great sins of men, for the sake of attaining the state of Śiva.
Thus ends the procedure for expiation in the illustrious *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
p.
273) || Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati!
I bow to Vināyaka, who is intent on shattering the mountain of obstacles,
his cheeks colored by the swarms of bees falling as they drink the flowing ichor.
Having bowed to the Lord of the Universe, who is restrained by the supreme limit,
and to Umā’s husband, the son of the Mountain,
as well as to those named Śrīkaṇṭha, Aghora, Śambhu, Nīla, and so forth; I [compose this] here.
The pair of lotus feet of Śiva, preceded by the venerable Vyoma.
Thus, I have established the ancillary elements of initiation through concise and brief arguments;
likewise, the fact that initiation is the sole ground for all purposes has also been determined.
Moreover, the entire [subject] is described here by means of three verses.

The fool is possessed of innate impurity (*sahaja-mala*), deluded by *māyā*, bound by destiny (*niyati*) and limited agency (*kalā*), and stained by passion (*rāga-rakta*) due to the power of knowledge (*vidyā*); thus he is called the "Person" (*puruṣa*). Furthermore, his body is bound by primordial nature (*prakṛti*). How is it that this one, whose purpose remains unfulfilled, is described as being subject to the unfolding of karma through the discernment of the qualities of *prakṛti*? *Prakṛti* itself drives him like a beast toward the city of Yama; even if he is somehow impelled by fate, he remains within the womb of *māyā*. At the time of dissolution, he becomes utterly distraught, having been released from the functions of *kalā*.
"This entire world, though unattached, attains the state of reality through Māyā, if [the Self] constantly perceives it as its own form even by a fraction.

If there were discernment regarding the manifest (sakala), then one who has understood fear and enjoyment would attain the isolation of knowledge (jñāna-kaivalya). This meaning, found even within these three verses beginning with "deluded by innate impurity" (sahaja-mala-vimūḍha), is as follows: one is deluded by the innate impurity called *āṇava*, and the eye of consciousness (cic-cakṣus) is obscured. And it is said in the *Pārākhya-saṃhitā*:

"Through the Śiva-tattva and the purification of the self, one attains knowledge; from that [knowledge], one obtains the attainment of the Self, which is free from the obstruction of impurities. Thus it is said.
One is deluded by Māyā through its power (śakti), thereby creating attachment to sense objects. And so it is stated in the Kiraṇa-tantra:
"Māyā is said to be delusive due to the enjoyment of the savor of sense-objects.
This is its meaning:

The objects (*viṣayāḥ*) are garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth; their "taste" (*āsvāda*) is the quality of the object itself. "Experience" (*bhoga*) is the enjoyment or perception thereof. From that experience of the taste of objects, *māyā* is "delusive," meaning it produces delusion—that is, attachment—by presenting objects as delightful. Then there is *niyati*, which is the time of a *truṭi* (the smallest unit of time) and so on; by these two, [the soul] is enveloped. Here, *truṭi* is time, which performs calculation and enumeration. *Niyati* restrains one within the fruits of karma earned by oneself. The principle of *kalā* fashions (*kalayati*), manifesting a limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*). Furthermore, *avidyā* establishes limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), which is merely the cognition of objects. *Rāga* colors [the soul], bringing about constant attachment to objects. Thus, this existing self, the *puruṣa*, is called the twenty-fifth. Moreover, he becomes one whose body is bound by the twenty-four principles of *prakṛti*. The phrase "by his own will alone" is to be understood as the ellipsis. And it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*:
From Śiva, the *kalā* comes into connection with that pure [soul];
by it, his power is activated, and its sphere of experience is made manifest by *vidyā*.
Passion (rāga) is also primary by virtue of its coloring nature, yet it is subordinate in its essential character;
through its connection with the array of instruments such as the intellect (buddhi), the bound soul (paśu) perceives.
"Then, through the conjunction with Niyati, one is constrained within what has been earned by oneself; subsequently, Kala also becomes associated in the reckoning of time. Thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is as follows:

Regarding the phrase "of that pure Self": [the Self] is one whose innate impurity has been obscured by knowledge, who is entwined by the many sprouts of karma, and for whom the creation has been set in motion by the power of Māyā. From Śiva—who is intent on bestowing grace upon such a bound soul (paśu)—there is the principle of *kalā*, impelled by the will of Śiva. Through that *kalā*, the soul attains *māyā*, characterized by the relationship between the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment. Bound by that *kalā*, its power becomes unmanifest and diminished, distinct from its capacity to act as it was before; thus it is rendered powerless. On the impure path, *vidyā* (limited knowledge) is that which makes things known; it is that by which the range of objects is slightly revealed. Furthermore, at the very moment *vidyā* is connected [to the soul], *rāga* (attachment) is also connected to it, acting as the generator of desire through its nature as the revealer of the objects of *vidyā*. Thus, enveloped by these three coverings (*kañcuka*), this Self attains the state of a person (*puṃbhāva*) and exists within the principle of *puruṣa*. *Tamaḥ* (darkness/ignorance) is for him the principle of *pradhāna* (primary matter), which undergoes transformation into the form of the *guṇas*—such as the state of being gentle (*saumya*) and so forth. Then, due to the connection with the host of instruments beginning with *buddhi* (intellect), there are those starting with *buddhi*; these are the instruments beginning with *buddhi*. This group or collection of instruments, along with their effects, is grasped as the tenfold effect beginning with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). By means of this connection with the instruments beginning with *buddhi*, one perceives pleasure and so forth, as well as people and other objects. Now, *kāla* (time) and *niyati* (fate) are connected with the *puruṣa* even prior to the three coverings. Nevertheless, it has now been explained that all principles exercise restraint and calculate time. Among them, the connection or union of this Self with *niyati* is equal to that [of the others].

276) Due to the conjunction with *niyati* (destiny), one is constrained to the fruits of one's own performed actions, which consist of pleasure and pain. Since *niyati* is that which governs, its meaning is that it causes one to experience exactly what is to be experienced—neither less nor more—in whatever place and at whatever time one is led. Time (*kāla*) also acts as the agent. Regarding the reckoning of time, having established the divisions such as *truṭi* and *lava*, when there is a reckoning of time such as "bubbles of time" or "childhood, youth," and so forth, the meaning is that the connection of that [individual] with a body occurs in accordance with that [reckoning].

Thus, with his body thus equipped through the [eight] seats (*āsana*) and so forth, the person is said to have accomplished his purpose (*kṛtārtha*) by means of the collection of actions performed through *prakṛti*—actions that bring about birth. How can one be called "one who has not accomplished his purpose" (*akṛtārtha*) if the entire goal has been achieved by the compassionate Śiva? This is explained as being "covered. The meaning is that even by hundreds of worldly knowledges [this state remains hidden]. He says this very thing: through the discrimination of the qualities of *prakṛti*, that is, through the thorough knowledge of the nature of *prakṛti*. *Prakṛti* is the state of equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; it is insentient, and it becomes the cause of action and the basis for the subtle and gross bodies by transforming into effects such as the intellect (*buddhi*). By the thorough knowledge of this, one is liberated from the products of *prakṛti*. Why is it that he [the Self] does not see her again? Because that aforementioned eternal *avidyā* is the impeller; therefore, *prakṛti*, being impelled by *avidyā*, enters into a relationship with the *puruṣa* once more through the connection characterized by the states of the enjoyer and the enjoyed. If liberation were merely the abiding of the Self in its own nature through the thorough knowledge of *prakṛti*, it would not be so. Now, if it is argued: "Whoever possesses the state of being a product of *prakṛti* must have karma to be experienced; it is only for him that *avidyā* can be the impeller. But for one who has no karma to be experienced within *prakṛti*, why is liberation (*kaivalya*) not appropriate? [The answer follows: *Note: The provided text contains several lacunae marked by asterisks (*). The translation reflects the available portions of the Sanskrit text.*

It should not be argued thus: even though he lacks *prākṛta* (material) karma, because he lacks the thorough knowledge of reality (*tatvaparijñāna*) after [the dissolution of] *prakṛti*, since there exists karma to be experienced therein, how could there be the consequence of liberation? And it has been said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Because of the non-perception of karma for the experience above the *guṇa-tattvas*..."
"Even for the Sāṃkhyas, this [liberation] is not possible as absolute isolation (kaivalya), because [the afflictions] are not utterly destroyed. Thus [it is said].

Now, those proponents of *avidyā* (ignorance) assert that the knowledge of Brahman, which is beneficial to all yet enveloped by *avidyā*, is connected to *prakṛti* by its very nature. For them as well, because their knowledge consists of ignorance and lacks true comprehension, their *avidyā* dissolves into the Supreme Brahman within the individual soul (*jīva*) from whom *avidyā* has been cast off. However, even this [view] is inconsistent. Furthermore, how could it be so? If, by some means or another, through the mere word "ignorance" (*avidyā*)—which denotes wealth—one were to understand [the state of] being known by ignorance, then one would be liberated by that [word], yet remain unliberated from its auxiliary effects such as time and other causal factors. In that case, this Self would also be devoid of dissolution only within the midst of the principle of *māyā*, and would thus be designated as a *pralayākala*. It would not be liberated, because pure karma (*vimalakarma*) still exists. Consequently, at the time of creation, one would certainly be bound again by the effects of *māyā*. Thus, it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"True liberation arises from the discrimination between the Puruṣa and Prakṛti; or else, it is the cessation [of bondage] by realizing that everything is Brahman.
Whatever various liberations there may be that are produced by fetters, they all return to differentiation at the time of creation. Thus [it is said].

Then, [the author] says "the whole" (*akhilam*) to explain what would happen through her self-recognition: the power of *māyā* eternally brings the entire group of selves under her own control for a long time by means of generating the state of being made one's own; having thus brought them under her sway, she [acts] through her powers ranging from the *akalā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*).

If he perceives, counts, and pervades [the universe], then it is true. Certainly, the entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, attains reality; that is, its state becomes like that of the Real (satya). It "attains reality" means it reaches it. If there were a thorough discernment—that this world, though real, exists as if it were merely an appearance—along with the "sakala" (the whole), which exists together with *kalā* (limited power) and the effects of *māyā*, then that person, being one whose worldly enjoyments are unknown, attains the isolation of knowledge (*jñānakaivalya*). This means that through the practice of wisdom, yoga, and renunciation, while not yet liberated from the effects of *māyā*, even in the absence of the enjoyments of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), because his innate impurity (*sahaja-mala*) remains veiled, he attains only the isolation of higher knowledge (*vijñānakaivalya*). Yet, he does not become fully liberated, because of the absence of Śiva’s desire to grace him. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
Even those who are born of Māyā may be innate (sahaja) and designated as pure;
and Śambhu, who transcends the paths and is stainless, beholds them.

For this reason, it is exceedingly pure because it has been proclaimed by those with clear vision. Therefore, the authoritative word (*āptavākya*) composed by the Omniscient One, which has come down as tradition, is indeed the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). And it is said in the *Raurava*:

"Śiva, the Lord of Beasts (*Paśupati*), is the one who has attained the enjoyment of the beasts; that which is the authoritative word of him is the *Āgama*. Likewise, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, in the dialogue between the venerable Upamanyu and Kṛṣṇa:
That knowledge which is declared in the Śivāgama is indeed the supreme knowledge;
the Śivāgama was spoken by Śrīkaṇṭha Śiva for the sake of Śiva himself.
"Compassion is the sole means for those who have taken refuge in Śiva to attain the highest good. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, when karma has become equalized according to the logic taught in the scriptures, for one who is enveloped by the power of Śiva (śiva-śakti), liberation in its specific excellence occurs only through the means known as initiation (dīkṣā). And so it is said in the *Kiraṇa*: "When karma has become equalized, by the power of time, this one becomes Śiva because of omniscience; free from dualities, he [attains] the destruction of the body at the end of the path."
"One who is fully perfected in the manifestation of Śiva-nature shall not undergo rebirth. Thus [it is said].

This is its meaning: there is a certain other "time" (*kāla*) consisting of the repeated experience of the soul's dissolution (*pralaya*), beginning with its *kalā* (limited agency) and so forth; by the power (*vaśa*) of that interval of time, even a fraction of its capacity manifests in millions of ways. Therefore, when the equilibrium of action—which consists of merit and demerit—is established through the influence of that interval of time, there occurs from Śiva, who desires to show grace, the descent of the power known as compassion (*kṛpā-śakti*), which is capable of uplifting both women and men. That descent of power proceeds solely for the sake of favoring the individual soul (*puruṣa*). Because of that descent of power, which causes the destruction of impurity (*mala*), one approaches a Guru out of a desire to know reality (*tatva-jijñāsā*). Then, having obtained the vision of reality from that Guru—who is satisfied by [the disciple's] service and other such qualities—one receives initiation (*dīkṣā*). When one has been thus initiated by the Guru, at that very moment this soul becomes just like Śiva; it becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). However, upon the dissolution of the body, being free from dualities (*nirdvandva*)—that is, released from the pairs of opposites consisting of pleasure and pain—it understands that this entire world is the abode of experience for all individual souls (*māṇava*) through their karma, and that it is the realm of *māyā*. When there is the manifestation of Śiva-nature (*śivatva-vyakti*)—meaning that fullness of Śiva-nature, which consists of pure knowledge and action, is manifested in him—he is no longer [bound].

Furthermore, the meaning is that he becomes liberated just as one who [attains the state of] number and so forth enters into the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Now, why is there this restriction here—that for one enveloped by Śiva’s power, liberation occurs only through the means called initiation (*dīkṣā*)—given that knowledge, action, and the rest are also causes of liberation? True. That is being explained: in a previous birth, during an initiation [performed] by a teacher who was not a true initiate (*asikanda*), when the fault of violating the rules (*samaya*) occurred, those who did not perform the required penance may, in subsequent births, eventually experience the exhaustion of that *karman*. At that point, their intellect begins to apply itself to knowledge, action, and so forth, which are the very fruits of the previous initiation. Thus, although knowledge, action, and the rest are indeed causes of liberation, the emphasis is placed on initiation alone—stating that liberation arises from initiation itself—and therefore there is no fault. And it has been said:
From this extensive bondage, through its cessation for the sake of others,
initiation alone liberates one and leads [the soul] upward to the abode of Śiva.
Someone [is the master] of unstruck powers and of mantras whose nature is measured.
The power of those of immeasurable majesty is inconceivable in its valor;
the word of the Lord is truth, and mantras are accomplished by their very nature.
All things roll along according to their own nature; they act and they obstruct.
All are performers of Śiva’s will, always presided over by Śiva.
They bring about creation, maintenance, destruction, and even ultimate dissolution;
yet the Puruṣa never attains liberation through his own power alone.
The initiation of Śiva is the primary means for protection everywhere;
apart from initiation,
one is not liberated through knowledge, yoga, or conduct alone.
For even here, the capacity for [bestowing] the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*) and so forth does not belong to oneself;
this applies likewise to children, the ignorant, the elderly, women, those addicted to sensual pleasures, and those who are diseased.
Without initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is no liberation distinct from [ordinary] knowledge and so forth; therefore, she is the liberator.
By his very nature, Lord Śiva is the cause of grace for all.
In this world, through initiation, liberation shall come to all living beings here.
Therefore, liberation for everyone is accomplished through the power of Śiva;
it does not exist for anyone through their own power, as that is impossible.
Likewise, in the *Kiraṇa* it is said: "Because he acts for the benefit of all—including children, the ignorant, and serpents—the Lord must bestow grace;
and that grace is preceded by ritual consecration (*saṃskāra*)."
When it is stated in the Tantra that liberation occurs through ritual action alone, then what is the distinction between ritual action, knowledge, and vows? There is no difference whatsoever.
The Blessed One said:
"O Tārkṣya, those who are established in whatever state are likewise made so by the grace of the Lord.
