Some among them are fit for ritual action, and their liberation is likewise."
Likewise, others are fit for knowledge, and those beyond them are fit for the status of a teacher;
thus, for whomsoever liberation has been proclaimed, it results from being united with that Lord.
Knowledge and the other means are held to be the cause of initiation;
initiation itself is liberation, while the means is that which regulates it.
"And they are proclaimed as the means (upāya) because they effect the benefit of all. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in the Pauṣkara: "The Lord, Vidya, as well as Avidya, the bound soul (paśu), and the bond (pāśa) are the causes.
The categories (pādārtha) that have ceased from that [state] are said to be six in number:
Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara, together with their respective worlds and so forth.
This object of knowledge, characterized by the mantra and the Lord of Mantras, should be understood as the meaning of the term *patipada*.
Śakti and Vidyā, along with the worlds, are proclaimed as that which is called Vidyā.
The category of power (śakti-padārtha) consists of the realm of Māyā, known as ignorance (avidyā), together with the latent impressions of karma,
for all souls here who are designated as Vijñānākala.
The consciousness of the *pralayākala*s and likewise that of the *sakala*s,
due to its conjunction with the impurity of bondage (*paśutva-mala*), is the category designated as "bound" (*paśu*).
The collection of bonds consisting of Māyā extends from Earth up to Kalā;
it comprises the existing elements and worlds that act as the cow of Māyā.
The category known as "bond" (pāśa) is to be understood by the yogis of Śiva;
the supreme Śiva is the category called "cause" (kāraṇa), which is the cessation of that [bond].
"This initiation (dīkṣā), whose nature is ritual action, is proclaimed as the means to liberation. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in the Vāsiṣṭha Purāṇa and the Laiṅga Purāṇa, Lomaśa said:
"Even one who is devoid of initiation and mantras, if he always worships Hara, [attains the goal] even while running toward a forest that has been fortified as a citadel."
Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva—
he who, endowed with initiation, ritual action, and mantras, worships Hara.
In all worlds, that man is eternally liberated;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship that very Lord whose banner is the bull.
"Indeed, when Śiva, who bestows the peace of liberation, is pleased by being propitiated, [he grants this]. Thus it is said.

In this context, it is called "the bestower of the pacification of dualities" (*dvandvapraśāntida*) because, through the initiation of Akṣuṣī, it grants supreme liberation (*parāṃ muktiṃ*) and brings about the cessation of the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*). And it has been said:
"Those who, though devoid of the knowledge of initiation, are intent upon the worship of the Liṅga, they go to the abode of Hara, which brings the bliss of all sovereignty."
"From this point on, O Goddess, one does not return again to the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra;
rather, having been gazed upon by Śrīkaṇṭha, they proceed from there upwards to Śiva. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the Vāmana Purāṇa,
it was instructed by Śrī Upamanyu to Śrī Vāsudeva:
"Indeed, I shall tell you that which purifies all sins."
This supreme meritorious rite was proclaimed by Śiva.

Since a person who has properly performed their duties regarding worship and other rites is said to have undergone the purification process known as the cleansing of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva-pariśodhana).
"By means of which knowledge is indeed bestowed, and the bondage of the fetters is destroyed;
therefore, this very *saṃskāra* (purification/transformation) is both bestowed (*dīyate*) and called [the initiation] (*kathyate*).
Thus [it is said]. The investigation of the feet of power (*śaktipāda*) and so forth is as stated in the *Kiraṇa*:
Garuḍa said:
Initiation occurs through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), not from omnipresence;
for, O Lord, because Śiva is immanent [in all], the fettered souls (*paśu*) remain as they are.
Since power is always present by virtue of its permanence, why would it not exist?
Or rather, what is time? If time is said to be Śiva, then what [is the purpose]?
O Blessed One, that which was previously stated by you—that initiation (*dīkṣā*) occurs through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—is incorrect.

Because there is no possibility of the descent (*nipāta*) of power (*śakti*). Why? Because of its omnipresence (*vibhutva*), that is, its pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*). For a pervasive entity, a "descent" characterized by movement or displacement is not possible, as it would be like [the descent of] a fruit. Furthermore, because it is inherent (*samaveta*) in Śiva—just as heat is inherent in fire—how could there be a descent of the power that is inherent and inseparable from Śiva? It is impossible; such is the meaning. Thus, due to its eternity and pervasiveness, power remains always and at all times connected even to the bound soul (*paśu*). Therefore, since power exists at all times and pervades all selves, thereby binding all, why would this power not be attached to all selves today? Indeed, it certainly is. Now, if you think that although that power is all-pervasive, it becomes the agent of grace (*anugraha*) only at a specific time, then what is that time said to be, and how is it characterized? If you say that some cause for the descent of power exists, then let that very time be the maker of liberation; what is the need for Śiva? To this, the Blessed One says:

In this context, the application of words is seen to occur through figurative usage (upacāra), as for example: "The person is all-pervading and eternal; having perished, he has attained the state of Śiva."

"Thus, even the 'falling of power' (śaktinipāta) is explained through investigation. O Garuḍa! Because you lack a thorough understanding of the meaning of the word *nipāta*, you have spoken thus. How then do the applications of the meanings of words occur? They are twofold: primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*). Therefore, in this case, it is a secondary application of the word. As for the primary application—for example, when it is said in common worldly usage, "The sight of this man has fallen upon this woman," at that time, from whom would the sight have fallen away, and upon whom else would it be seen to have fallen? It is seen [as such] by virtue of the mere relationship between the seer and the object. (p. 285)

The "connections" (*sambandhāḥ*) are metaphorically said to be "fallen views" (*dṛṣṭi-patitā*). Likewise, even in the case of a single person, because of the relationship characterized by the benefactor and the beneficiary (*anugrāhyānugrāhaka-lakṣaṇa*), the "connections" are metaphorically said to be "fallen powers" (*śakti-patitā*). This is not in a primary sense; thus there is no fault. He confirms this very point: "Just as the person," and so on. Just as the person, although eternal by nature, is metaphorically said to be "destroyed" due to the falling away of the body; and just as the all-pervading one (*vibhu*), although omnipresent, is metaphorically said to have "attained Śiva-hood" through the metaphorical designation of manifested Śiva-nature; in the same way, the "falling of power" (*śakti-nipāta*)—when analyzed—is metaphorically called the "falling of power" because it is a relationship between power and the self characterized by the benefactor and the beneficiary. It is not in a primary sense; thus there is no fault.

Now, let it be granted that this attendant is capable of making the soul (ātman) assume a state of being situated within the site of the piercing; but what does that soul do immediately after that piercing? To this, he says:
"Just as an object, when suddenly struck by fear, moves away from that very place to another location, so too does the soul move toward the instructor."

Just as in the world, when there is the occurrence of some event regarding a certain object, it is said, "In this village, a king will arise"; although this word is formless (*amūrta*), it is perceived by the people living in that village from both sides. And those people, becoming afraid, consult with one another and depart suddenly and swiftly from that place to another location capable of removing their fear. And just as that [word] is able [to do so], even though this descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is formless, it bestows fear upon the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of living beings. Since the descent of power, though formless, bestows fear upon the latent impressions of living beings, because of that descent of power, the previous enjoyment of worldly essence [is seen to be] merely supreme [delusion]; then, having had the eye of consciousness opened by that descent of power, and having perceived the worthlessness of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), he [seeks] a single teacher from his own station who is skilled in removing the fear of worldly existence.

"Yāti" means "he goes," that is, he attains. Now, does that power awaken the agent by itself, or not? To this, the Guru says: "Just as one might awaken a sleeping disciple from the front with a staff. Thus.

Likewise, Śiva is also called *māyin* because He possesses *māyā*, since He is the cause of delusion (*moha*) by generating the desire for the great ocean of worldly experience (*bhoga*). Furthermore, *karma* is designated by the term "sleep" (*nidrā*), and *māyā* is likewise referred to as sleep because it is the cause of such experience. Śiva awakens certain *vijñānākala*s—who were previously asleep and unawakened due to *māyā* while in proximity to the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*)—by means of His own power (*śakti*). He awakens others—the *pralayakevala*s—who were asleep in the sleep of *māyā*. And He awakens those who are submerged in experience (*bhoga*), whose minds are immersed therein, and who remain unawakened due to a lack of knowledge regarding the nature of the Pure and Impure Paths while the sleep consisting of the nature of *mala*, *karma*, and *māyā* persists. Therefore, it is Śiva alone who awakens them through His power; thus, *śakti* is the instrument (*karaṇa*), while the independent Śiva is the agent (*kartā*), meaning that [the power] is not the agent herself.
Now, how is it known that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred for him? To this he says:
"When the knowledge of one's own true nature [arises] once [the veil] has fallen away, then it is so called. Thus.

In this context, because the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) for those who have attained isolation of consciousness (*vijñāna-kevala*) or isolation of the self (*kaivalya-kevala*), being bodiless, is difficult to discern, the characteristics of these two states are now described: when, at a certain time, a person who is still bound (*sakala*)—desiring liberation after having repeatedly reflected, "Who am I? What is my nature? What is this cage of suffering?"—seeks out a Guru, that very state constitutes their essential form, their knowledge, and their sign; at that moment, it is said that power has become manifest. And it has been said: "For those embodied beings upon whom power descends for the sake of cessation... (p. 287).
Their characteristic sign is this: they possess eagerness for liberation, freedom from aversion toward stability, devotion to the devotees of Śiva, and faith in the discipline that teaches him.
By this [verse], even for those of dull intellect, the obstructive power of the reason connected with the inference is somewhat removed; thereafter, [the state] of the Lord [is attained].
"These signs indeed appear for embodied beings when [the impurity] remains slightly;
for, by means of the fourfold descent of power (śaktipāta), the result is exactly the same. Thus [it is said].
"Likewise, [the poison is] very intense, intense, mild, or even very mild;
immediately there is fainting, trembling, and horripilation, remaining as such.
Now, he provides the answer to the statement, "Furthermore, the cycle of abiding (vāsacakra) is proclaimed at the [proper] time":
"Whether the time for actions is equal, exhausted, or unequal."

The time at which there is equality—that is, a state of balance—between the actions of one whose nature consists of both dharma and adharma, that time is said to be the cause of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Whether that power is pervasive, deficient, equal, or excessive, it then becomes the bestower of experience; however, it does not manifest when [the actions] are merely balanced, nor does it manifest immediately thereafter. When, at a certain time, there is an equality of action, and that very time has arisen as the [proper] moment, how is it that the state of being a bestower of experience ceases? To this he says: "either exhausted or equal. Therefore, when the action is either exhausted, deficient, or unequal (i.e., excessive), then it becomes the bestower of experience, but not when it is merely balanced. And that manifests immediately thereafter. When, at a certain time, there is an equality of action, that very time is the cause of the descent of power. Consequently, because there is no simultaneous equality of actions for all [souls], the power of Bhava would not exist [for everyone at once]. This is the meaning.

288) Now, if it is argued that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) occurs only when there is equality of karma, then how can it occur for those who are "isolated by knowledge" (*vijnana-kevala*), given the absence of karma? To this he says: "In this way, at whatever time that subtle equality always exists, it quickly illuminates one's own nature through the full force of the signs of awakening. Thus [it is said].

As for what was said—that for the *vijñānakevalas* there is no karma—it was stated that they lack the cause of karma, which is *māyā*. It does not mean, however, that the destruction of all karma has occurred; rather, the state of being a *vijñānākala* is indeed the fruit of some residual karma. This karma was acquired by them previously during their state as *sakalas*, and because it exists in a subtle body, it is difficult to perceive. One must understand that this similarity [of karma] is the cause for the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Otherwise, there would be no descent of power at all. At the very moment when the karma becomes similar [to that of others], at that same moment, that Power—though all-pervasive—bestows grace. Therefore, that Power produces a certain distinct state of pure consciousness (*vijñānamātra*) even for the *vijñānakevalas*, just as it does for the *sakalas*. Or rather, he says "its own nature" (*svarūpa*) and so on, meaning that it attains a specific knowledge. Since for the *vijñānakevalas* there is no experience of the body or of the fruits of commenced actions (*prārabdhakārya*), an extremely intense descent of power occurs. Consequently, that very intense and specific nature of theirs illuminates and manifests the nature of the pure Self, characterized by omniscience and other qualities. Now, one might ask: if the manifestation of the attributes of the Self occurs for the *vijñānakevalas* simply through contact with Power due to the removal of impurity (*mala*), why should it not be the same for the *sakalas*? To this he replies: "Enough with the signs of awakening. This means that for the *sakalas*, the manifestation of the Self's qualities does not occur merely through the removal of *mala*, but requires other factors such as the strength of the signs of awakening.

Because all [souls] must experience their *prārabdha* karma, according to the intended degree of temporal variation in the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*), the power (*śakti*) falls—whether slowly or very slowly for some, or intensely or more intensely for others. Then, for the sake of understanding and recognition that "the power has fallen upon this one," there are signs such as horripilation, delusion, and bristling of the hair; yet the strength or efficacy of those signs is diminished, and they become exhausted below. For all those of equal birth, when there is contact with the remnants of the remnants (*ucchiṣṭocchiṣṭa*), it may be shorter, longer, or even more excessive than the end of the time-period (*kāla*). By means of those signs and the waters [of initiation], one is sufficiently characterized by the gradations of the signs. Therefore, the meaning is that the manifestation of the qualities of the Self does not occur for them at that very moment.

This clarifies what was stated previously—that karma which is either exhausted or equal becomes the giver of experience. [The text asks: "When one portion of karma is greater, it gives experience first; but when they are equal, how does that experience arise? To this extent, there exists karma for the self to be experienced over many births. And that is of two kinds, consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Among these, that which consists of merit—such as great acts of charity—is the cause of heavenly enjoyment; that which consists of demerit—such as killing a Brahmin—is the cause of attaining hell. Here, the word "portion" (*aṃśa*) refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the action. Therefore, between these two types of karma consisting of merit and demerit, whichever portion of karma—whether meritorious or demeritorious—is greater and more powerful, it occurs first. When that karma has given its experience and ceased, then another subsequent karma of its own nature gives experience. But if the two are equal, how can that experience arise for that self? The meaning is: not at all.
(290) "If the initiating karma were mixed, there would then be no equal experience [of pleasure and pain];
otherwise, nothing more than pleasure [or its opposite] could be predicated."

The Sūtra: Or rather, the word "atha" (then/therefore) has the sense of "yadi" (if). Now, as for what was said—that [action] is equal to a dream and thus does not bestow the experience of karma—that is incorrect. For instance, in the *Gomedhā* sacrifice and others, the slaughter of an animal is indeed of the nature of demerit (*adharma*), yet that very same act is the cause for ascending to heaven; thus, even though it is of a dual nature, it is observed to bestow the experience of karma. If this is argued, then even so, the enjoyment of two types of karma would have to occur at the same time, for no such simultaneous experience is heard of in scripture. If, while being equal, one were to drink from the stream of karma that bestows experience, then the self would simultaneously experience both the bliss of heaven and the suffering of hell. But that is not the case. Therefore, in those instances as well, it must be stated that one portion of the karma is greater and the other smaller. Otherwise, if there were no such inequality in the portions of karma there, then for those who perform sacrifices, the prior fruit of the sacrifice—namely the bliss of heaven—and the subsequent fruit of the other, which is the suffering resulting from various demerits such as eating meat, would not occur. Yet, that certainly does happen. And it has been said:
"At that time, even animals were gods, and gods were in the state of animals;
likewise, Brāhmaṇas were dogs, and dogs were Brāhmaṇas.
And so say the wise:

Therefore, the wise devotees of Śiva cherish devotion to you—whose nature is that of a householder’s sacrifice, who has performed the sacrifice desired by the twice-born, and whose fruit is not the slaughter of living beings as in animal sacrifice, but rather the cause of heaven and liberation, your power being well-known. Thus it is said.

Therefore, the meaning is that it is only action—whether deficient or excessive—that bestows experience, not action that is equal. Consequently, when there is equality of action, at that time, for all those who have reached tranquility through the conjunction of the descent of Śiva’s power (śaktipāta), initiation (dīkṣā) is performed.

Furthermore, that [initiation] is of many kinds according to the three types of persons: with support (*sādhārā*), without support (*nirādhārā*), dependent (*sāpekṣā*), independent (*nirapekṣā*), characterized by the nature of Śiva (*śivadharmiṇī*), characterized by the nature of the world (*lokadharmiṇī*), with office (*sādhikārā*), and without office (*niradhikārā*). It is said: "Support" (*ādhāra*) means the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the place (*sthāna*), and the teacher (*ācārya*). By means of that, when one becomes independent in the act of sustaining, the venerable Lord Paramaśiva performs it through his intense power (*tīvra-śakti*); that is initiation. That which is without support belongs only to the *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala*. And it has been said: "In the case of those two, [initiation] is performed by Śiva himself through the descent of his intense power."

"It is performed without support; that initiation is considered the supreme state. In this regard, even within initiation, it is heard in scripture that for some there is the attainment of the state of union (*sāyujya*), while for others there is the attainment of the state of authority (*sādhikāra*), due to the intention of describing the equality of action (*karma-sāmya*) even amidst the two [levels] of the "pure" (*kevala*).
Initiation is performed by Śiva himself, whose nature is compassion, through his power.
"The union (sāyujya) of a certain [liberated soul] with the Supreme Self should be understood as being accompanied by residual capacity (sādhikāra). Thus [it is said].

However, among those who are subject to dissolution alone and for whom there is no possibility of the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*), the connection with Time and other factors arises at the very moment of their manifestation. As it is stated in the venerable *Lalitasamhitā*:
"The principle of Māyā is the seed of the universe, eternal, all-pervading, and likewise imperishable;
having placed his own group [of souls] within it, the Lord simultaneously agitates it."
What is it like? O friend, when the *badarī* trees are struck by a staff,
their fruits emerge on all sides— horizontally, upwards, and downwards.
But where food is offered after [the soul] has been liberated, those [souls] are indeed led by Śiva;
they all go upward to the supreme, partless Śiva.
But those who are vessels for this knowledge become the very form of mantra.
But those who possess the vessel of formative forces (saṃskāra) and are endowed with impurities, karma, and its subtle portions;
"Moving swiftly downward upon this terrible path, he is now in a state of great suffering. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"Those whom Śiva releases during his sleep immediately become [liberated],
whether they were withdrawn [at the time of dissolution] or newly arisen, or even lords of the Vāṇas."

The meaning of this is as follows: during the sleep of Śiva—that is, at the time of delusion—because there is a state of the self devoid of knowledge in the condition of the *vijñānakala* and *pralayākala*, therefore, those whom He does not favor at that time remain below that [level]. However, at that very moment, they become Śivas. Then, whether during the withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*) of all things, or when the dissolution of the *pralayakalas* has occurred, or at the time of creation when the connection with *kalā* and the other categories arises—since their creation occurs precisely then—those whom He favors at that time become the *aṇus*, the *mantreśvaras*, or even the *vidyeśvaras*. Thus it is said: And likewise:

The Self is said to be of many kinds; among these, the first is remembered as the Sakala (the conditioned), who is possessed of the impurity of karma and whose sphere of experience consists of the objects of the senses.
Another is the *pralayākala*, who is conjoined with the *kalā* of purified *karma*;
he is above *māyā* and below pure *vidyā*, yet is covered by the impurity (*mala*) of *māyā*.
The meaning is that this is the state of the *vijñānākala*. As it has been said elsewhere:

"There are many selves (*ātman*) as well, whose nature is consciousness yet defiled by impurity (*mala*). This impurity, which obstructs knowledge, should be understood as being like the blackness on copper."
It is innate to all living beings and is the cause of their capacity to experience;
therefore, for the sake of its enjoyment, it is the cause of this body and the sense organs.
Subsequently, Māyā arises as the sole cause of pleasure and pain;
the possessor of Māyā (māyin) enters into connection with karma, consisting of the five kalās and so forth.
Bound for the sake of experiencing knowledge through their own nature as cause and effect,
living beings indeed exist in three states throughout the succession of all time.
"Having first [attained] the state above, they proceed by means of the second;
however, their abiding in the beginning of the *kalā* and so forth is proclaimed by the third. Thus it is said.

Enough with further elaboration. Śiva is "possessing authority" (*sādhikāra*) because he functions together with that authority. By him, in his entirety, [the initiation] is performed through a power that is either weak, intense, or otherwise, corresponding to the gradations of the karma of all individual souls; thus it is "with its basis" (*sādhārā*). And it has been said: "Assuming the form of the Preceptor (*ācārya*), and with the intention of equalizing karma, that which is performed by Śambhu through a power distinguished as intense and so forth is indeed [the initiation]."
She is declared to be the common ground for all individual souls; thus it should be understood.

This initiation (*dīkṣā*) is twofold: the "common" (*sādhārā*), which conforms to the body and lacks specific authority, and the "dependent" (*sāpekṣā*), which should be understood by the wise as requiring the performance of rules (*samaya*) and so forth; the "independent" (*nirapekṣā*), known as "seedless" (*nirbījā*), bestows liberation even without such requirements. And it has been said:
"That which leads the person—this is the ellipsis—to the abode, following the rules (*samaya*) and so forth.
The wise declare that one who possesses preeminent personal qualities is "dependent" (sāpekṣa),
whereas one who is aged, foolish, lacking in strength, and so forth, is incapable of observing the rules of conduct.
"That which, because it is independent [of causes], is called 'without dependence'. Thus [it is said].

In that regard, the initiation involving dependence (*sāpekṣāpekṣā*) is of two kinds: that characterized by the way of Śiva (*śivadharmiṇī*) and that characterized by the worldly way (*lokadharmiṇī*). Among these, the *śivadharmiṇī* is associated with the insignia (*liṅgin*) of ascetics, while the other is devoid of them for householders. And it has been said: "The initiation for liberation is twofold: the worldly and the *śivadharmiṇī*. The worldly is to be known as that of householders; the *śivadharmiṇī* is that of those bearing the insignia."
An initiation that does not involve the cutting of the top-knot is one belonging to the worldly way;
an initiation joined with the cutting of the top-knot is one belonging to the way of Śiva.
Likewise:
"But for one whose topknot (śikhā) is indicated as being purified of that illusion (māyā),
and who is devoted to the Dharma of Śiva— that initiation is indeed the 'Śivadharmiṇī'."
"Without the cutting of the top-knot (śikhā), that other initiation is one belonging to the worldly path.
Likewise:
"By means of the initiation belonging to the worldly path, the Guru should initiate a householder."
"In the same manner, one should initiate those whose wealth is austerity by means of the Śivadharmiṇī initiation. Thus [it is said].

In that regard, the Śivadharmiṇī is of two kinds: the Naiṣṭhikī (lifelong) and the Bhautikī (temporary). Among these, the Naiṣṭhikīs are ascetics for whom there is no limit [to their practice]; their state is called "Naiṣṭhikī" and also "niravadhi" (limitless). The second is that which, after observing the vow for a few days, leads one back to the household life. As it has been said: "The Naiṣṭhikī lasts until the fall of the body; the Bhautikī grants liberation from the vow."

Now, for one who is free from desire (*niṣkāma*) and possesses equanimity toward all beings, there is the attainment of Supreme Śiva. Regarding both [the seeker and the teacher], it remains to be considered whether that initiation (*dīkṣā*) shall be accompanied by authority (*sādhikārā*) or not. In that regard, the lifelong initiation (*naiṣṭhikī*) is of two kinds, according to the distinction between having desire (*sakāmā*) and being free from desire.

295) In that regard, for one who possesses desire (*sakāma*), having granted the enjoyment of the pure path (*śuddhādhva-bhoga*), she subsequently bestows the state of Śiva; thus she is "with desire" (*sakāmā*). And it has been said: "But the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for one who is free from desire (*niṣkāma*) occurs without [the exhaustion of] commenced action (*ārabdha-karman*)."
She is the destroyer of all sins without exception and the bestower of seedless non-duality. Thus [it is said].
And thus:
"With seed and without seed—thus the two types are proclaimed as imperishable."

"That [impurity] has seeds; it should be known as being merely by means of the *samāna* [breath]. By means of the body alone, one should conquer the state of having burnt seeds therein—the fruit of what was previously worshipped. Thereafter, its future [impurity] must be suppressed like the potency of poison.
Its commenced [impurity], becoming attenuated, proceeds like a desire for experience. Now, that which pertains to the elements (*bhautikī*) is likewise twofold. And it is said:
In this very way, through the yoga of action, even the earth becomes both supreme and non-supreme;
however, for those who are deluded, there remains the *prārabdha* karma that leads to separation from the body.
Having united with that which is to be accomplished through the Śaiva means of practice, one should preserve it;
then, once the fire of initiation is kindled, one should burn away everything else along with its consequences.

The meaning of this is as follows: "In this very way. For both the *naiṣṭhika-sakāma* (the lifelong seeker with desire) and the *kāmayad-bhautika-sakāma* (the worldly seeker with desire), there is the application of *kriyā-yoga*—that is, both ritual action (*kriyā*) and yoga. For the one with desire (*sakāma*), the ritual action consists of the purification of the paths up to *Māyā*. For the one without desire (*niṣkāma*), yoga consists of the purification of all the paths. Furthermore, on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), for the one with desire there is the yoga of enjoyment (*bhoga-yoga*), while for the one without desire there is the yoga of Śiva (*śiva-yoga*). Nevertheless, even when the yoga of Śiva is to be performed, for that embodied being who is a worldly seeker without desire, there exists the *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma) as the cause for the purpose of maintaining the body through yoga. Therefore, having joined those two—the body and the karma—with the state of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should preserve them; anything other than that must be restrained. Thus, that which is bound by the experience of *prārabdha-karma* is the cause for another birth.

(296) Karma accumulated in the past, along with its "concomitant" (*sānubandha*)—meaning it persists as a continuous connection—is all that pertains to the sacrificial ritual (*āmāmika*). He should burn all of that away. Then, upon the falling away of his body, there shall be liberation; or else, there is immediate nirvāṇa. Now, the worldly power (*lokadharmiṇī*) is of two kinds, according to whether it is higher or lower. Among these, the higher bestows the state of Śiva. And it has been said:
"The auspicious [power], having purified the karma pertaining to the path which consists of the nature of Śiva..."
"Whichever [attainment] reaches nirvāṇa is another, characterized by worldly phenomena. Thus it is said.

The *śeṣā* (residual) [form of karma] has as its nature the worlds of the hereafter (*paraloka*) once the fall of the body has occurred; it pertains to those desired worlds. On the other hand, the *aparā* (other) [form of karma], when the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*) has been accomplished, bestows the powers (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā* and so forth upon the lords of those worlds even in a desired world, provided that impure karma has ceased. And it is said: "When there remains [the fruit of] evil deeds in all the planes of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*), the residual [karma] has the nature of the desired worlds for the sake of the body and powers such as *aṇimā*."

After the fall of the body, one should perform the Śivadharmiṇī rite, which is desired for those remaining in the world of the Lord, which possesses the nature of the universe, and which gives rise to the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇimā*. And so it is said: "Having purified the Śivadharmiṇī and recited [the mantra] in the supreme state, upon the fall of the body there shall be liberation through the observance of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*)."
Having established the one who abides by worldly dharma in the station of the Creator of the universe,
he should carry out the protection of that dharma for those seeking liberation in Śiva.
"In the reality of Sadāśiva, one attains enjoyment at every step. Thus [it is said].

For one who desires liberation, it is not only this [liberated soul] who attains Śiva; even for those who have attained the station of Bhuvaneśvara, there is indeed the attainment of the Śivatattva after the exhaustion of their enjoyment. And it has been said (p.

Those who are purified by initiation (*dīkṣā*), born from the maṇḍala of Gaṇapati and the Guru, and are perfected (*siddha*) through mantras, possess bodies resplendent with the solar orb. Whether they are devotees or [enjoyers] of pleasures for a long time, they are endowed with celestial female forms and, possessing unshakable sovereignty, become partakers of the supreme Śiva-sovereignty. Thus, it should be understood that [initiation] is manifold, being both dependent (*sāpekṣā*) and independent (*nirapekṣā*); furthermore, it is twofold as higher (*parā*) and lower (*aparā*), and as immediate (*sadyas*) and non-immediate (*asadyas*) liberation. Of these two, the non-immediate liberation is also twofold: the lower-higher (*aparāparā*). In this regard, for those who enjoy [pleasures] such as children and women, the first [type] bestows enjoyment upon the path of purity (*śuddhādhvan*) even without the performance of the rules (*samaya*), and thereafter grants liberation. And it has been said:

However, for those who are capable but still attached to enjoyment, one should perform the previously described initiation which purifies the observances (*samaya*) and so forth, leading to the state of being seedless (*nirbīja*).
One should effect absorption (laya) into the supreme reality; having bound one's experience, one should remember the Sound (dhvani).
And with devotion, one should always perform the worship of Śiva through those [means] for as long as life lasts.
"Likewise, one should perform the worship of the teacher for ascetics according to one's capacity.
This duty must be performed for one who is free from desire for anything else and is solely devoted to meditation. And why?
Because he has burnt away his karma with the fire of initiation, and his bonds have been severed by Māyā.
Having attained the supreme state of steadfastness in knowledge, he remains as Śiva, free from seeds;
for him there is no need for observances, nor indeed for the worship of the *liṅga*.
"Not by visiting sacred fords or pilgrimage sites, nor by the nine bodily restraints. Thus it is said.

Now, when those whose impurities have reached full maturity develop equanimity through right action, they attain immediate nirvāṇa, being enveloped by an exceedingly intense power. Beyond that, in the state of "having attained" (*sāsādya*), one experiences the stainless [state].
On the side of immediate nirvāṇa, the supreme fruit of austerity is obtained.

Thus [it is said]. This is its meaning as well: "It bestows liberation at the end of the body; it is called the seedless (nirbījā) Parā. This [state] of the supreme Parā, which is the most supreme, instantly—that is, at that very moment—renders the self free from affliction; it makes it stainless. That is the initiation of immediate liberation (*sadyo-nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*). And that occurs when the ripening of karma has taken place. When it is attained by a person through the power of the vow (*vrata-śakti*), then that person also reaches the state of Śiva—the supreme knowledge beyond darkness. And it has been said: "The removal of impurity arises from knowledge born of the descent of Śiva’s power."
"Having manifested its state as Śiva, it proceeds from the characteristic of impurity. Thus [it is said].

Now, that [initiation] with seed (sabījā) is of two kinds: that which possesses authority (sādhikārā) and that which lacks authority (niradhikārā). Among these, that which possesses authority bestows the authority for performing the initiation, installation, and so forth, upon the seeker (sādhaka) and the teacher (ācārya). And it has been said: "That which possesses authority is the 'seeded' [initiation], by which there is authority for the seeker and the teacher during the initiations, installations, and ritual unions."
Because it pertains to two [categories], equality is not an authority.

It is heard [in scripture] that for these two—the teacher and the practitioner—liberation occurs immediately after the destruction of the impurity of their office (*adhikāra-mala*), following the experience of enjoyment upon the impure path. And it has been said:
"That initiation is always possessed of seed, possessed of office, and possessed of the practitioner;
it is for the sake of fitness for installation, and for the bestowing of the consecration of office."

When one has ascended to the state of authority (*adhikāra*), their impurity (*mala*) becomes an obstacle; therefore, there would be enjoyment (*bhoga*) on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). [The teacher] should bestow [initiation], whereby the destruction of impurity occurs.
"When the latent tendencies (adhikāra-mala) are exhausted, there shall be supreme, imperishable liberation. Thus [it is said].
And thus:
"That seed is to be known as twofold, distinguished by the presence or absence of a qualification.
The [mantra] of the two Aryanīs should be performed with its authority (sādhikā) and enriched by its functional status (padāḍhya).
Here, purification has been previously explained; their enjoyment (bhoga), however, resides in Sadāśiva.

Whether by the will of the practitioner or through the power of sovereignty and pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), dissolution should be contemplated in the supreme reality; for both [the teacher and the disciple],
there is no distinction once the impurity of office has perished in the eternal state.
The book [is the authority] for one established in the observance, and there is eligibility for the daily rites;
therein lies the firm conclusion regarding both, which is the supreme state of ultimate bliss.
Because they lack the qualification for initiation and so forth, there is no impurity of non-qualification for those two;
and because they lack qualification even for the obligatory rites, there is no transgression for those who are seedless (nirbīja).
Therefore, there would be no liberation for them immediately after the fall of the body. Thus [it is said].

Now, one might object: "If the impurity of office (*adhikāra-mala*) is the cause of concealment for one who has ascended to the rank of *ācārya*, then what is the purpose of that office? This should not be said. For the office is indeed authorized so that the transmission of initiation and other rites may not cease from the supreme state of the *ācārya*, and so that all obstacles to the self may be removed for those who are fit. And it has been said: "The Lord, a treasure-house of compassion, because he effects the grace of all, assumes the form of the *ācārya* and liberates individual souls (*aṇu*) through initiation."
In this teaching, there can be no liberation for living beings without initiation;
and that initiation cannot exist without a teacher—thus is the lineage of the teachers.
It should be known that one attains the wealth of the meaning of the scriptures of the established tenets through this cause. Thus [it is said].
Since the mantra is partless (anniṣkala) without an instructor, those who mutter it after merely looking at the mantras written in a book [act in vain]. (p. 300)
The sin of those [who do so] is proclaimed to be equal to the drinking of liquor.
Then, one should take refuge in a teacher who is the best of sages;
initiated by him into the sacrifice of Śiva through devotion and other means,
one becomes authorized in the mantras and becomes a vessel for both spiritual perfection and liberation.
"For this reason, O Goddess, the eligibility of teachers, disciples, and grand-disciples should be understood by those learned in the scriptures. Thus [it is said].
And thus:

A disciple should be one who knows the reality of proper ritual application, is endowed with beauty, virtuous conduct, and good qualities, is born of a noble lineage, and is a constant protector of the daily rites.
Even if he is detached from his office,
he should be appointed to a position of honor by the best of gurus, even by force, for the sake of protecting the lineage.
The Lords of Knowledge praise the protector of the lineage of gurus,
the noble preserver of teachers who is rich in the Āgamas and full of joyful insight.
Even if he is attached [to worldly life], for the sake of his disciples, by the command of Śiva,
he should hand over that [knowledge] to his own disciple for the sake of learning for some time.
For him who has thus entrusted his office, she [the power] is joined to the supreme state.
"His entitlement consists in the perpetual enjoyment of the state of Śiva;
at its conclusion is eternal liberation—such is the certainty of the scripture. Thus [it is said].

301) Depending on the equality of karma, the inclinations of disciples become manifold. Consequently, the initiation (*dīkṣā*) performed by a teacher who acts according to that intention and with a corresponding understanding likewise becomes so. And it has been said: "The initiation of the Śiva-āgama is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as threefold: the Vāma, the Śāmbhava, the Śāntī, and the Māntrī."
By the mere sight of the Guru, or even by touch or conversation,
the Command (ājñā) is immediately produced, which brings about the destruction of the bonds (pāśa).

That initiation is declared to be Śāmbhavī; it further exists in two ways, namely *tīvra* (intense) and *tīvratarā* (more intense), according to the distinction in the destruction of the fetters (*pāśa*).
Whatever immediate relief there may be is considered to be the most intense [suffering];
yet that intense [suffering] causes a man to live on until his karma is completely purified.
The initiation consisting of power (*śaktidīkṣā*) is that which, possessing knowledge, enters the body of the disciple by the Guru through mere yoga and the eye of wisdom.
The initiation consisting of mantra (*mantradīkṣā*) is preceded by the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the mandala, and is characterized by ritual action (*kriyā*).
The teacher should perform it outside with very slow and gentle movements.
According to the descent of power (śaktipāta), the disciple deserves grace;
for it is the root from which the qualification for the dharma of Śiva arises.
Wherever power has descended, there success does not arise.
There is no knowledge, no auspicious conduct, no liberation, and no supernatural powers;
therefore, one should observe the signs of the abundant descent of power (śaktipāta).
The Guru should purify the disciple either through knowledge or through ritual action;
the dull-witted one who acts otherwise out of delusion perishes.
Therefore, the teacher should examine his disciples in every possible way.
The characteristic sign of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is the arising of awakening and bliss;
for that [power] is the supreme energy, whose nature is supreme bliss.
The *liṅga* awakens bliss through a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
just as there are modifications such as horripilation, goosebumps, and the expansion of the eyes of a deity.
The disciple is so called because he is to be trained, and the teacher because he is the cause of respect;
therefore, one should practice respect toward the teacher with every effort.
He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru.
The Guru is indeed Śiva, or else he is established as the very form of Vidyā.
As is Śiva, so is Vidyā; as is the discourse on Śiva, so is Śiva himself. The fruit resulting from the worship of Śiva, Vidyā, and the gurus is equal.
Because he embodies all the gods, he is the Guru who consists of all mantras;
therefore, with every effort, one should carry his command upon one's head.
If one seeking the highest good should not transgress the teacher’s command even in thought,
for the one who observes the teacher’s command [attains] * * * * * * * *.
Regarding the perfection of knowledge:
whether walking, standing, eating, or performing any other action,
if it is in the presence of the Guru, one should perform all of that with the Guru’s permission.
In the presence of the guru, or in his house, one should not sit as one pleases.
Since the Guru is the deity manifest, his house is a temple of the deity;
and just as one who shaves [his head] through association with him becomes a partaker of the fruit of that sin.
In the same way, through association with a teacher, one becomes a partaker of the fruits of that teacher's qualities;
just as gold, through contact with fire, abandons its dross.
In the same way, through contact with a guru, a human being abandons sin,
just as gold melts when placed near fire.
In the presence of a teacher, even sin may be dissolved;
just as a blazing fire consumes both wood and gold,
so too may this satisfied Guru burn away one's sin in an instant.
If a wise man seeks his own welfare, he should diligently practice the conduct of salutation— saying "namas"— toward his teacher through thought, deed, and speech.
Thus, a disciple who possesses proper conduct, is devoted, always has a diligent mind, and acts for the pleasure of the Guru, is worthy of the abode of Śiva.
The disciple should also examine the guru by these characteristics;
for in association with him, one's own [inner] winds become those of the guru during the worship of Śiva and other rites.
The Guru is virtuous, wise, and the illuminator of supreme bliss;
he is united with Śiva through the realization of reality (tattva) and is not wavering from liberation.
Reality is the generator of consciousness, arising from supreme bliss.
He by whom that reality is known is indeed the one who reveals bliss.
Furthermore, that which lacks the power of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) cannot cross over [the ocean] by mere name alone;
can a boat rescue one stone with another? Can one stone rescue another stone? (p. 304)
For those by whom liberation is indeed attained through that name alone.
Furthermore, for those who have realized the liberation of the already liberated, how could there be awakening in the absence of reality? And how could there be the grasping of a self?
Furthermore, he who knows all these principles— earth and the rest— as they truly are, is declared to be a Guru, not merely an equal; he is the one who reveals the potency of mantra.
One who is devoid of possession is called a beast.
Even for one impelled by the bound souls (paśu), the state of being a bound soul does not cease;
therefore, even when they have reached the stage of reality (tattva), they are indeed considered liberated only within the Wheel (cakra).
Even if one is endowed with all auspicious marks, even if one is a knower of all scriptures,
and even if one knows the application of all means, if one is devoid of the ultimate reality (tattva), one is fruitless.
For one whose intellect proceeds toward reality until it reaches direct experience,
extending as far as the principle of Śiva, supreme bliss arises through the primordial lords of the worlds.
Therefore, a wise person should bow only to that very guru through whose contact the bliss of awakening arises, and to no other.
Skilled in the conduct of discipline, he [restrained] his angry teacher by means of his disciples.
As long as he is known [to be qualified], he should be served by those seeking liberation;
once he is known, if one possesses firm devotion, one should take refuge in him. One should never abandon such a person, nor should one ever neglect him in any way.
Wherein the awakening of bliss is obtained after a kalpa,
who would not especially resort to a guru through the excellence of the words?
Even when one has attained a higher guru, one should not disparage the former one,
nor the guru’s brothers, sons, instructors, or those who have exhorted him.
Likewise:
"In that regard, first having approached a wise Guru who is an expert in the Śiva scriptures, endowed with good fortune, and pleasant to behold, one should worship him."
One should strive to please him— who bestows fearlessness upon all and whose mind is overcome with compassion— through thought, deed, and speech.
The disciple should propitiate [the guru] until he becomes pleased;
when he is pleased, the disciple’s bonds are instantly destroyed.
Therefore, [one should offer] wealth, jewels, fields, and houses.
One should also give ornaments, as well as inferior houses, beds, and seats to the preceptor with devotion, according to one's means.
One should not practice stinginess with wealth if one desires the supreme goal;
he alone is father, mother, brother, kinsman, wealth, happiness, friend, and companion— therefore, one should offer everything to him.
Having first offered himself, his accumulations, and his possessions,
and having surrendered them along with water into that [fire], he should remain perpetually under its control.
When one has offered one's own self to the Self of Śiva—that is, to the Guru—then that embodied being becomes a devotee of Śiva; from that point on, I am his rebirth.
"Having assumed a creative form, the Lord leads this bound soul, by means of his power as the Guide, entirely beyond the fetters to the supreme state of Śiva-nature; such is the sacred revelation."
A guru who is learned in the scriptures, wise, ascetic, affectionate toward people,
and adorned with worldly propriety is remembered as the bestower of liberation.
The teacher should examine the disciples who have taken refuge in him for one year,
by means of such tests as the giving away of his life or wealth, by making them sit in improper places,
by treating the superior as inferior, and by assigning the lowliest tasks to those who are not of the lowest character.
Those who are satisfied or even pacified, as well as those who have transcended sorrow, are fit, disciplined, and pure for the rite of Śiva-consecration;
indeed, by the command of their master, they are joined with enjoyment by the lords.
In the same way, for a woman who is bereft of her husband, there is indeed the authority to act with the permission of her two sons,
or by the command of her father.

For those who are non-existent, Śūdras, those of the lowest castes, and especially the fallen, as well as for those born of improper sacraments, purification through the path is not prescribed; yet even they, if their disposition toward Śiva, the supreme goal, is natural, [are eligible].
One should effect the purification of the bonds by means of offering water for the feet and other such rites.
In this regard, for those born in the natural order (anuloma) among the twice-born and other classes,
one should perform the purification of the path and so forth in accordance with what is appropriate for their maternal lineage.
A maiden who has been dedicated to the Śivadharmas by her father and others should be given to a devotee, and not to one who is an offender or an adversary.

If she has been given to a husband who is hostile, she should, out of negligence, seek to awaken him [to righteousness]. If she is unable to do so, she may mentally abandon him and practice her religious duty.

Likewise, in the Śiva Purāṇa: "Just as in former times, a devoted wife, having propitiated Śaṅkara through austerity, became one who had fulfilled her purpose after abandoning even the mantra of the best of sages."
Now, the examination of the teacher and the disciple is written down with various statements.
First is declared the Śaiva [system], then the Pāśupata;
the third is Kālarātri, and the fourth is Kālavaktra.
The fourth is the vision of Śambhu; those joined with that and identical to it are the five-and-a-half [groups] and the Kālavaktras, who know the Soma-siddhānta.
Since these [three types] are renunciants because they have renounced the fire of existence and material substances,
they are therefore not at all qualified for initiation or the installation of deities.
Nevertheless, those who have renounced must recognize their own teachers within their own philosophical system.
Those who act for the benefit of the world are indeed neither to be known nor crossed over;
they have arisen from those possessing pure authority and are endowed with knowledge and action.
The wise say that the support is the locus and the place.
The place known as Govindāna where curd was established is heard of;
and there is the place named Āmardaka, frequented by the illustrious Durvāsas.
From that [place] emerged the site of Raṇabhadra and Golakī;
[there dwell] the celibate student, the householder, the forest-dweller,
and the ascetic— whether wearing matted hair, shaven-headed, or with a top-knot, and whether bearing a staff, a loincloth, or a girdle.
Wearing a girdle of muñja grass and a deerskin, their bodies white with ashes,
they were all marked with the triple horizontal lines (tripuṇḍra) and adorned with rosaries of rudrākṣa beads.
Devoted to service of the guru, worshipping the fire of Śiva’s knowledge,
wearing either saffron or white garments, truthful in speech, pleasant of address,
bathing three times a day, and subsisting on alms— he is declared to be a *brahmacārī*.
And he should be known to be of two kinds: the lifelong (naiṣṭhika) and likewise the temporary (bhautika). A lifelong celibate (brahmacārī) is one who remains so for as long as life lasts.
Established until the end of his life as a celibate student is the seeker of the elements (bhautika).
The householder, through union with a wife, is likewise considered to be of two kinds.
The *vratārthaka* was proclaimed first, and thereafter the *sāntānika* is considered;
these two are to be known as the auspicious rites for worldly prosperity (*laukika*).
These [devotees] should bathe either three times a day or at least once;
their entire bodies should be marked with the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) and they should be adorned with bracelets of rudrākṣa beads.
Those established in the injunctions declared in the Vedas and observers of Śaiva conduct;
and the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) who resides in the forest, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits.
Whether alone or with his wife, remaining celibate and engaged in spiritual practice,
having renounced all worldly activities, he is peaceful, possesses equal vision, and is devoted to his duties.
Subsisting on alms, using only his hands as a bowl, wearing only a loincloth or being naked,
the ascetic (yati) should always remain established in meditation while walking, standing, or sleeping.
Both the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and the ascetic (yati) are not entitled [to perform rites involving fire].
The student (brahmacārī) and the householder (gṛhastha) are qualified for initiation and other such rites.
And it has been said:

"Only two types of ascetics are true celibates of the secret [path]: the wandering mendicant and the forest hermit; for neither the world-renouncer nor the ascetic [in the ordinary sense] brings about grace for the worlds."
The Brāhmaṇa is always intent on bestowing favor upon all castes;
his own caste is his primary concern, followed by the teachers, the Sūdras, and the kings and others.

Those who are engaged in the three stages of life are not considered true *varṇins* [if they lack other qualities]; rather, one who does not drink liquor, is of noble birth, and is devoted to the *Śivadharmas* is so regarded.
The Śūdra should be understood as being like the Kṣatriya; the remaining [castes] are far inferior to Indra.
For those devotees, during initiation and other rites, there are three [levels], which are considered to be the eyes.
And so says the Garuḍa:
"Tell me, who possesses the weightiness [of authority] in the midst of the four castes?
He is declared to be the liberator from all [bondage], like Śiva, at the end of midnight."

When a wife, a relative such as a father through devotion, or one who has approached [as a disciple] becomes [a spiritual guide], then initiation for them would occur; in that case, would they not possess the status of being his sons?
And another who has approached is an outcaste (antyaja), and he too is untouchable;
how much more so if he lacks initiation and has no guru who liberates all?
Īśvara:
Here, the status of being a teacher for all four castes is declared;
among the fourfold group beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the twice-born is [the teacher] by virtue of his capacity for grace.

Among the three [castes], the Kṣatriya [is superior] by two [factors], and the Vaiśya and Śūdra by one, according to their origin; however, the favor shown toward wives and others depends on their disposition.
Since mantras are independent, their cultivation is exactly like that;
by means of the state as it truly exists, mantras bestow grace.
Since for that reason, even for one born of the lowest caste, initiation is indeed mental.
"One should not designate a Hotṛ priest from among artisans due to their physical contact;
for if one were to know their supreme devotion, the world would incur fault. Thus it is said.
Now, the initiation (dīkṣā) categorized as cākṣuṣī and so forth is being described;
having meditated upon the supreme, utterly pure reality, one should lead [the disciple] to the removal of the eye-veil.
Then, for the sake of purification, one should look; this is considered the "ocular initiation" (cākṣuṣī dīkṣā).
Here, the word "vain" (vyartha) refers to [the lack of need for other means] regarding enjoyment and liberation.
Having meditated upon the supreme Śivapura together with the Brahma-aṅgas in the hand—
The Guru should touch the body of the disciple, including the head, back, and other parts.
Thus, the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā) occurs, performed through the knowledge of dissolution and enjoyment;
having gathered the mind into the reality (tattva), it is augmented by the supreme splendor.
One should recite the Saṃhitā mantras; initiation is the cause for [attaining] the Lord.
And that [consciousness] is not eternal; it is neither power nor insentience.
Relying upon a mental process, this consciousness possesses knowledge.
Initiation (dīkṣā) should be known as consisting of ritual action for the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa;
it consists of the triad of Rudra, Rudra-śakti, and the Guru, together with their mantras.
That other initiation which is entered into through devotion is appropriate for him;
it should be accepted by the disciple as well when the Guru is satisfied by means of his body,
wealth, knowledge, faith, ritual action, qualities, and so forth.
And likewise:
"That man who is devoted to the Guru, by means of the vital breaths moving both externally and internally,"
He alone would be worthy of grace and capable of liberation, and no other who has not performed [this practice].
Likewise:
"He who maintains the gravity of body, substance, consciousness, speech, action, qualities, and the vital breaths,
deserves praise and refinement."
As it is stated in the Vidyāpurāṇa:
"One who is rich in virtues or has few defects is praised as a devotee of Śiva;
one who is endowed with [all] qualities is [praised], but never one who is devoted to two [deities]."
Whoever desires this and is a devotee of Śiva is to be favored; of this there is no doubt.
One who is devoid of devotion and possessed of characteristics contrary to a brahmin is not to be initiated;
[rather, one should be initiated] by one whose devotion to Śiva is firm and who is constant in the rituals of the Guru.
Be eternally detached while established in the seat of the knowledge of Śiva; initiation is praised for one whose mind is focused on nothing else, but not for anyone other than such a person.
And he is worthy of the position of teacher if he is endowed with the qualities of moral conduct; he who possesses graceful and truthful speech is dear to the Lord of Speech.

One with prominent veins, a weak voice, emaciated, or obese; one with a protruding belly, or one who is excessively large; likewise, one who is dark-complexioned, has protruding teeth, or deformed nails;
one who is wicked, or whose hair and eyes are reddish-brown; and even one whose intellect is harsh with logic.
One-eyed, with squinting reddish-brown eyes, with tawny eyebrows, whiskers, and hair;
a practitioner of the Garuḍa-mantras for spirits, and a seller of the three types of funeral monuments (caityas).
One with a crooked nose, mouth, ears, or eyes is sinful, diseased, and envious;
he is deceitful, cruel in his actions, fraudulent, a base artisan, and merciless.
Thus, one who is devoid of the qualities of a learned man, yet is skilled in discerning what is appropriate and inappropriate,
is diligent, of noble birth, tranquil in soul, and born in a virtuous land.
Likewise:
one who is one-eyed, thin-waisted, humpbacked, deficient in limbs, or having extra limbs;
or one who is black, hairless, has deformed nails, or has protruding teeth.
One who is squint-eyed, one afflicted by consumption, one who is a barbarian, and one with a corpulent body—
this person is free from such characteristics and possesses a complete form.
One who knows the essence of the Śaiva Siddhānta, who turns away from the scriptures for the bound souls (paśu),
who is compassionate toward all living beings, and who is free from dry logic.
Though he may be deceitful, cruel, deluded, slanderous, envious, or wicked,
one who is entirely free from the nature of the base and who delights the minds of others [is truly noble].
One who possesses virtue should recognize him as being intensely devoted to compassion;
through the wisdom residing in his heart, he is truly virtuous, like a well-trained horse with a bit.
Does a neem tree become sweet because of honey located within its hollow?
One knows knowledge through practice; character is an innate quality.
Knowledge, truthfulness, compassion, fortitude, humility, and steadfastness—these are declared to be the qualities of the sattvic person; yet they arise from association.
Having personally examined the scriptures, the most excellent of teachers speaks.
Those who speak thus in this matter are indeed to be abandoned by the Self-Existent One (Brahmā).
He who, having abandoned another liṅga, takes refuge in a stone liṅga,
should be known as a "reborn" one (punarbhava), censured in all ritual acts.
(313) They are to be known as gurus only so long as they are observers of proper conduct;
however, those who have fallen away from proper conduct are to be abandoned like one whose *liṅga* has been broken.
That which arises from one who has broken his vows is known as the "broken sprout" (bhagnāṅkura);
those born from that are to be known as *kandhakas*, and they are considered to have become *kogikas*.
"For those desiring the auspicious, there exists [the path] between initiation (dīkṣā) and the establishment [of the lineage]. Thus it is said.
One who possesses all the auspicious marks but does not know the Śiva-śāstra is neither a yogin nor one purified by vows; he is not called an ācārya.
However, even one devoid of all auspicious marks is a guru if he knows the meaning of the Śiva-śāstra.
"O Six-faced One, [this] has been fully declared in the Śiva-śastras regarding the rites of installation and so forth."
And he was born in a noble region and of noble lineage, as stated in other scriptures:
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and the Ṛkṣa mountain.

The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra— these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvata). From these principal mountains flow the meritorious rivers, which descend and flow through those various regions.
Those holy places favored by sacrificers are approved in all the scriptures.
The Gaṅgā, Revā, Mahītāpī, Gautamī, Sarasvatī, Yamunā, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Kāverī, and likewise the Gaṇḍakī.
The Gomatī, Sarayū, Sindhu, and Devikā— these fourteen sacred rivers are to be known as bringing welfare to all the worlds.
It is to be resorted to by great sages, by those who perform sacrifices, and by those whose wealth is austerity;
it is filled with self-manifested Śiva-liṅgas and various other divine sages.
The regions situated on its banks are considered holy lands by the virtuous.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras residing in that land—all of them [attain purity] through service to that sacred site; hence, it removes all sin at all times.

If those who have been purified by Śiva are fit for the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva-śodhana*), then surely here [in this region], the Kāverī and the eight *karkara* stones are included within the center. Consequently, the inhabitants of that land are not qualified [for initiation].
And it has been said: "Those born in Kashmir, Kauśala, Kāñcī, Kaliṅga, and Kāmarūpa..."
The Kāverī originates from Koṅgaṇa; which other regions are its sources?

Likewise, there are others from the Ruru kingdom who subsist by gathering *kuśa* grass. The four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, are the authorized persons by virtue of their status as preceptors.
This should not be said—
that this is a Śākta statement— for there is no such restriction even within the Śaiva Siddhāntas.
And it has been said:
"Or, according to the established doctrine, one should follow the left-hand path (vāmācāra) through the left [channel], not the right.
Whatever rule is proclaimed for a specific [path], it yields its fruit only therein.
Likewise:

Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are pure are indeed practitioners (sādhakas). O Six-faced One, they are teachers according to their respective castes in due order— those who possess faith, are free from malice, know the ritual, and are devoted to that rite.
Permitted and consecrated, they thereafter desired to be protectors;
O Six-faced One, that place where the black-colored deer roams—O Kṛṣṇa!
One should know that region as fit for sacrifice which is inhabited by Brahmins,
where there are Brahmins of virtuous conduct and ascetics whose wealth is their austerity.
The Sāntivedas and likewise the gods designate that as a meritorious place;
the teachers born in that region are approved by the scriptures.
They are constantly devoted to the Śiva scriptures and intent upon the worship of Śiva and the sacred fire;
likewise,
the teacher should be one from a meritorious region, righteous, and a knower of the state of Śiva.
Those who know the true meaning of the Śiva scriptures and who impart that knowledge of reality reside in Kaliṅga,
Siṃhala, Vaṅga, and Kiṃdhāra, which is frequented by Mlecchas.
One who has been initiated into the Śiva-maṇḍala should avoid this with great effort.
By such statements from the Śaiva Siddhānta scriptures, the status of being an *ācārya* for those born in cities and regions such as Kashmir is indeed intended.

Now the path (adhvan) is described, because initiation (dīkṣā) is prescribed therein. That path consists of the path of worlds (bhuvādhvan), the path of mantras (mantrādhvan), that known as the path of words (padādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), and the path of words (padādhvan); these six are considered to be the enlighteners.
A person must experience two kinds of karma: that which is currently being performed and that which was accumulated in the past.

Here, "of the person" (*puṃsaḥ*) refers to the individual soul (*puruṣa*). The "object of experience" (*bhoktavya*) consists of pleasure and pain in places such as heaven and the netherworlds; this is the "dharma" which is the nature of the self, consisting of two types of karma. He extends the principles (*tattvas*) and worlds (*bhuvanas*), which are the objects of purification, as well as the purifiers; however, these [latter] exist by their very nature.

This Lord should be known as fivefold: the Subtle (*sūkṣma*) and the One with Divided Parts (*bhinnakala*).
Among these, he is considered "with parts" (*sakala*) because he is endowed with the *kalās* beginning with Śānti.
Partless, devoid of parts, all-pervading, both with parts and partless.
Endowed with the kalās beginning with Jvālinī, this subtle one is called Bindu;
differentiated by the sixteen vowels, the Bindu is said to be manifold in nature.
There, that omnipresent power resides as the partless *bindu*;
she is renowned as the *bindu-śakti*, and that is also known as the *śakti-tattva*.

The wise one should recollect here the world-sphere (*bhuvana*) and the plane (*pada*), enriched by the mantra of the Eye of Īśāna and endowed with the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*), as previously described.
Then, the principle of Sadāśiva, endowed with the Kalā-śānti [tattva],
interpenetrated by the sixteenth vowel, resembles a lotus marked with the letter Kṣa.
The Lord Śiva is always established there in the form of mantra;
this is the lineage of the five Brahmans, abiding as all-pervading space.

it rests upon the two words "to Śiva," who is all-pervading.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—these three are considered the one supreme city.
That which is established upon the lotus of the letter 'A' is the undivided essence of the excellent state;
it is declared to be the Īśvara-tattva, whose power is the night-lotus and whose digit is the lotus-fiber.
The Lord, the Blessed One, the four-faced one, remains established in existence;
and in the eight positions beginning with Ananta, the eight Vidyeśas are well-established.
Ananta, Āyupama, Ananta, Sūkṣmarudra, and Svānāthaka reside in Anāśrita; Śivotkṛṣṭa resides in Dhruva, and Netrakam likewise.
In the eternal [state] is Ekarudra, and Trimūrti is the pedestal of Yoga (yogapīṭhika).
Śrīvaktranāyaka is to be known as eternally present in the state of the Knowable (jñeyapada).
Residing in the state of one whose sustenance is meditation (dhyānāhāra), he is Śikhaṇḍī, the Lord of the World (bhuvaneśvara).
The Puruṣa, the armor, and the two mantras accompanied by the digit of Peace (śāntikalā) are here;
then follows that which is enriched with sixteen syllables, situated upon the lotus of the letter *sa*.

Within the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with Aśuddhavidyā, there is the path of Vidyā and Kalā, belonging to the Ghoramantras. Therein, the sovereignty of the embodied forms beginning with Vidyā is surrounded by the arrays of Rudras.

Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Rudra, Kāla, and again Kālavi-kṛt.

Namely:
Aghora, then Ghora, Ghoraghoratara,
Sarvatassarvasaṃjña, and the omniformed Sarvarudra.
The Queen is Vyūhombikā and so forth; she is established in the word "Śivāya."
Namely:
Ambikā, Brahmavetālī, Triguṇā, and Asthāṇumatī.
