she is also Suveṭālī, Gaurī, Aghorā, and Nandininditā.
He stands as the array of limbs, like all radiance within the words and phrases.
And that— Vidyādhipa, Brahmā, Śiva, Rudrāṇī, and he who is made of Puruṣa,
as well as Mahāpāśupata— is declared to be the array of the limbs of Vidyā.
Then, in the state of Śiva, there exists the Rudra-array, beginning with Mala and others:
Halāhala, Mātaṅga, and the one known as Nīlalohita.
The Ucchuṣmas, the Śālavaras, and the mighty Padarudras;
In this context, "mahābalāḥ" means these [deities] known as the Rudramahābalas; the sense is that they are [possessors of] prowess.
Then the Māyātattva is a hexagon situated within a lotus of vowels;
it consists of the letter Ā, possesses the muṇḍamudrā, and is filled with the group of the Self (Ātman).
O Goddess, Māyā is situated there, filled with blue rays;
likewise Īśāna, Puruṣa, Ghora, Vāmadeva, and Aja,
as well as the Praṇava and "Namaḥ"— these constitute the eight words.
In sequence, there is Aṅguṣṭhamātra, and Bhuvaneśa as the leader;
likewise Īśāna, Piṅgala, Udbhava, and Bhava.
"Vāmadeva and Mahādeva"—thus the eight Rudras are established. Thus it is stated in that text:
"It is surrounded by Gaganeśa and the others, situated in the upper and lower caskets. For example:
"Gaganeśa, Asādhya, and Viṣṇu are remembered as the principles of the sacrifice (tattvādhvara)."
Deśeśāna, Mahāvīrya, Antyula, and likewise Gopati.
320) Now, these two should be known as being situated above the *sampūṭaka*;
they are Kṣemīya, Brahmaṇo-hantā, Vidyeśāna, and Parastathā.
Vaidyeśa and Śiva— these six are said to be Ananta.
Then, joined with Sāga, situated upon the mud of the vowels (svarapaṅkama),
the principle of Time (kālatattva) resides there like Kālarudra, the end-maker.
"To the one more secret than the most secret" and "to the protector"— of these two [mantras],
the Ekavīra and the Śikha reside in the two worlds.
In the lotus of the vowel *va*, the principle of Time (*kālatattva*) is present;
there, in its center, is the goddess Kalā, whose nature consists of variegated limbs and ornaments.
The one who stands at the limit of the five stages has reached the reality that is truly indestructible;
the hero is established in the stage for the sake of presiding over all yogas.
The syllable *ya*, situated upon the lotus of vowels, is known as the source of the principles (*tattvas*).
Therein resides Rudra himself, the omniscient Nīlalohita.
Beyond that is the Light-Rudra (*Jyotīrudra*), who abides in the state of the form of light.
And at the two highest points, "para" and "parāca," the tawny-eyed one stands.
The lotus of the vowel joined with the letter *repha* (ra) is present as the reality of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*);
there resides the goddess Vidyā, who dwells within the source of all knowledge.
O Rudra, within that pair of insentient [elements], Saṃvartaka resides;
O God, thereafter Rodharudra resides in this void-state called Khyāti.
Pervading from Vidyā up to Śuddhavidyā, [the power] remains within Avidyā and Kalā.
Aghora is joined with the *śikhā* [mantra]; these are proclaimed as the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*).
From *rāga* onwards, in the *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā], there is the state of being the end (*vāntatva*) and the accumulation (*sañcaya*).

In some cases, within the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*, it is held that there are twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) ending with the *vādipuruṣa*. In the *vidyā-kalā*, seven principles beginning with *rāga* and ending with *śuddhavidyā* are observed. Since both views are declared in the Śiva Āgamas, they should be accepted accordingly.
Now, the *vāma-śiras-mantrādhvan* is described separately:
it is situated upon the lotus of the letter *dha*, interpenetrated by the sixteen vowels.
The principle of passion (rāga-tattva) is likewise colored red; therein, passion has a crimson luster.
It is to be known as pervasive within the pervasive state; Śiva resides in the eastern sector.
The formless [elements] arise from two [factors] at the beginning of each pair;
fire resides in fire, Umā in the moon, and light in the two luminaries.
From the center of the lotus of the letter *A*, differentiated by the sixteen vowels, there arises a great radiance, red in color, consisting of a hundred million *ruṣāmāta* principles.
There dwells the subtle, all-pervading Person, whose body is the city of eight.

Passion (Rāga) possesses knowledge (vidyā), limited power (kalā), time (kāla), necessity (niyati), the individual soul (aṇu), and karma; it is fierce in its nature and resides in the eighteen-fold state.
Sarveśāna resides in his own smoke (svadhūma), while he who is known as Agra resides in the ashes (bhasma).
Bhīma is to be known in the station of Nāda, and Vāmanātha is situated in the station of Pada.
The vowel, enriched with sixteen petals, is located in the center of the lotus of the letter Bha.
That reality has been declared as the primordial nature (prakṛti), which exists as the cause of the world.
The unmanifest *prakṛti*, abiding there in the form of consciousness—
*dhū dhū dhū dhū*. First, [one should recite] while stationed in the world of Śrīkaṇṭha.
The goddess Umā is to be known as the body; thereafter, the syllable Oṃ is the earth at her feet.
The realm of Kumāra is to be known as the syllable Oṃ, which is indeed the ancient city of Viṣṇu.
The syllable *oṃ* is to be known as the *Brahma-bhairava* at the station of *bhuvaḥ*;
furthermore, it is called *Kṛta* and *Akṛta* during sleep and at the time of death.
Then, situated in the center of the left lotus is the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), which is reddish;
here, intellect previously resided, endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
In the position called Nidhana, the world of Brahmā is proclaimed;
situated there, in the midst of the vowel of the letter Pha, is that principle of Garva.
There, in the two [mandalas] of Śiva and Sarva, one should place the Saumya and Aindra [deities] in front in sequence;
then, the principles (tattvas) beginning with the ear and ending with sound (nāda) follow in due order.
The five [organs] beginning with speech and those beginning with the nose are also [associated] with the letters from *ṭa* to *ṇa*.
As it says in the Āgama:
"The nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears are indeed the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*)."
The anus, the genitals, the hands, the feet, and the voice—these are the organs of action;
thus, O knower of the reality of sound, the nature of the phonemes resides within the lotus.
There, in the state of the Supreme Self, lies the world of the Gandharvas;
there, in the state of Maheśvara, is situated the world of the Yakṣas.
The reality of form (rūpatattva) resides within the phoneme 'va', its own nature being situated between 'ka' and 'ja'. There, in the station of Mahādeva, the world of the Rākṣasas is established.
The state of being the subtle element of taste is that [realm] whose lotus has the letter Śa;
there lies the Paiśāca world, situated at the side of Sadbhāveśvara.
And the reality of fragrance resides in the letter *ka*, situated in the center of the lotus of the vowels.
Chagala, Dviraṇḍa, Bhūkoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara,
Kālāñjara, and the city of Śaṅkukaṇḍa— these six are located on the plateau.
O one of great splendor, Sthūleśvara is situated at the station where the eight Sthāṇus reside.
The essence of space resides within the letter *da*, situated upon the lotus of the vowels;
there dwells the Blessed Lord, the Great Lord Maheśvara, whose form is space.
Vastrapāda, Rudrakoṭiraṃ, Mukta, Mahālaya,
Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svakarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu—
these constitute the eight purifying sites established at Gādhipatika.
The element of air (vāyutatva) is established there as the essential nature of the syllable *gha*;
it resembles a cloud, and within it, the wind possesses the luster of collyrium.
When it manifests the field, it becomes Nakharu, the Lord of Nakhala.
Vimala, Aṭṭahāsa, Mṛgendra, and Bhīmakeśvara—
this is known as the Guhyāṣṭaka (the Eight Secrets), situated in the word *muñca muñca*.
It is the principle of fire (*tejas-tattva*), located in the letter *ka*, between the king of vowels (*a*) and the letter *ya*.
The red [element] is situated in the eye as fire, possessing a luster equal to that of Padmanābha;
Hara and Candrī are Śrīśaila, with the filaments consisting of mere speech and so forth.
Madhyameśa, Makākāla, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava.
(324) This is indeed the most secret of secrets, situated between the first two;
then there is the state of water (aptva), the abode of the red (aruṇa), located in the lotus of the vowel Kha.
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Raimeśa, Puṣkara,
Āṣāḍhīśa, Caṇḍīśa, Bhārabhūti, and Calākula—
these indeed are the eight primary secret [shrines], O Śarva, established in the state of Śarva.
Upon its cessation, the royal reality resides in the midst of the lotus of the letter Ka.
There, situated upon the earth on Mount Meru, she is golden-hued and adorned with all ornaments;
the two mantras are born from the heart like the worlds from their constituent parts.
Thus, outside the Brahmāṇḍa, the hundred Rudras are established.
Śambhu, the all-pervading Lord, the presiding deity of the qualities, the three-eyed one, who is worshipped by the thirty gods.
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, Namolipsu, and Vicakṣaṇa—be present, be present! O Rudras, you who abide here in the city of Brahmā.
Kapālīśa, the unborn Buddha, Vajradeha, the crusher, Vibhūti, the imperishable Śāstṛ, Pinākī, the lord of the thirty gods—
having surrounded the city of Indra, he shall abide in the state of Bhava.
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśin, Piṅgala,
Khātaka, Hara, Jvalana, Udhana, Babhru, Bhasman, Antaka, Kṣaya, and Vāntaka.
These are the Rudras who existed before Agni, bestowing happiness upon all beings:
Yāmya, Mṛtyu, Hara, Dhātṛ, the one known as Varakākarṇa,
Virūpākṣa, Dhūmra, Udaṃśu, and Lohita.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra abide within the supreme city.
Bala and Atibala, the mighty Pāśahasta,
Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, and Jalāntaka.
And Sandhava, Ashva, and Bhima, who dwell in the abode of Varuna.
These Rudras stand here: Anarcita, Anarcita,
Pada, Ugra, Śīghra, Vegasūkṣma, Tīkṣṇa, Kṣayāntaka, Pañcāntaka, Pañcaśikha, Kapardin, and Meghavāhana.
Though unacquainted, she was as if an old acquaintance; they remained in the city of Vāyu.
He wore a crown of matted locks, a lake of various jewels, possessed the form of the Lord of Treasures (Kubera), was fortunate, gentle of body, and the bestower of grace.
This illustrious Prakāśa, who can assume any form at will, is the tenth in the higher series.
These reside in Somapura, established in the two former positions:
Vidyādhara, Jñānadhara, Sarvajña, Vedapāraga, Mantravrata, Piṅgākṣa, Bhūtapāla, and Balipriya.
The creator of all knowledge, the one who brings about pleasure, pain, and tranquility, O Lord of the world, you abide as the witness, established in the state of witnessing.
Ananta, Pālaka, Dhīra, Viṣāgni, Viṣalocana,
Vṛkṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Vīra, Nāgāsena, and Bandhapālana.
These gods in Anantapura are established in the station of the two Rudras.
Now, [I shall describe] the sequence of the cities and so forth situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), starting from the beginning.
Formerly established in the world of Rudra, he was endowed with the qualities of *aṇimā* and the rest; there,
in that supreme city of Rudra, many Rudras were likewise stationed.
Then, in the world of Vaikuṇṭha, Viṣṇu dwells with his ten and twelve forms,
accompanied by his principal attendants headed by Viṣvaksena.
In the world of truth (Satyaloka), the Grandfather (Brahmā) [is worshipped] with the Vedas, their auxiliary limbs, the Purāṇas, and so forth.
And these three worlds are situated in calamity for the sake of the winged one;
O tawny one, in the tawny station, they are thereafter established in the world of penance (Tapoloka).
The great sages, Sanaka and others, sons of Brahmā, were stationed there;
the world known as Janaka was filled with sages who had attained the perfection of knowledge.
Śabda, Śabda, the great light, the abode of the perfected ones and the Vidyādharas;
it is to be known as subtle within the subtle state, and this is the land of enjoyment in its own world.
The assembly hall of the gods is situated there, along with the circle of planets and constellations;
beyond that, in the state of Śiva, one should know the world of Bhuvaḥ, which moves within the intermediate space.
The vital airs, beginning with prāṇa, are located there; the perfected ones (siddhas) and others reside within the measurement of Śiva.
Then he established himself in every station upon the field of action for the world,
together with rivers, forests, mountains, and the seven continents with their oceans.
Since it is the abode of all those who perform actions for the sake of accomplishing their karma;
since its nine regions, including Meru and Meru itself, are like islands in the salt ocean of worldly existence;
this land is remembered as the supreme among all lands.
From this, both heaven and liberation are attained by men.
In this meritorious land of Bhārata, having attained this transient human birth,
he who works for his own spiritual welfare has not deceived himself for long.
Heaven is considered a land of enjoyment; this [earth] is regarded as a land of action.
Whatever karma is performed here is experienced in heaven or elsewhere;
just as a tree whose roots are severed inevitably falls to the earth,
so too do the denizens of heaven fall when their store of merit is exhausted.
Human birth is extremely difficult to attain for all the gods and asuras;
having attained it, one should act in such a way that one does not go to hell.
And as for one who has attained the state of a Brahmin in human form— a status most difficult to obtain—
if he does not work toward his own supreme welfare, who else is more senseless than he?
Since for hell-beings, O God,
a body arises from the elements in a mere instant through unrighteousness alone,

*Oṃ yama dīkṣā*. Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Since it leads to nirvāṇa without causing the emergence of the double-tongued one,
its status as the "twice-born" is proclaimed according to the scriptures.
And it has been said:
"One who is not a twice-born is not fit for success, nor does he attain nirvāṇa;
since even a twice-born [may fail], therefore one should make him a most excellent twice-born."

[Objection: Is it not improper to establish the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*) here for one who does not possess it in the Vedic sense? However, for one who already possesses the Vedic status of the twice-born, it is improper to establish that status once again. [Reply: True, because that would lead to a lack of systematic order; however, that Vedic status of the twice-born was stated with reference to the body, not the self (*ātman*). And thus says the Smṛti: "The purifying refinement of the body should be performed both in this world and the next by means of the Gārgya oblations, the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), the tonsure (*caula*), and the investiture with the girdle of muñja grass (*mauñjinī*)."
There is no purpose here for that refinement (saṃskāra), because even when that Vedic status of being twice-born exists, one's destination is dependent upon one's actions. And so says the Smṛti:

"One may be a Brāhmaṇa by birth, or he may be a Śūdra; whichever is the highest [is determined] by future action. Those whose intellects are fixed on what they have done are overtaken by their future karma."
"Those who are peaceful and those who are cruel at the end of their lives [lead] to heaven or to hell;
a Brahmin who dies [as a sinner] becomes a Caṇḍāla, and he [the Caṇḍāla] may become a Brahmin. Thus it is said.
For instance, it is said even in the *Bhārata*: "As beasts are to gods, so are gods to beasts;
as Brahmins are to dogs, so are dogs to Brahmins."

As it has been said: "In this world, one [type of person] possesses the power of merit arising from pure deeds; another brings forth the fruit arising from a previous birth; and yet another performs a sacrifice for the sake of a specific purpose. Among these, they consider that which is performed by one who has integrated all these to be the true 'done' (*kṛtam*). Therefore, the purification intended here is that of the self (*ātman*), not of the body. And it is further stated:
"The purification of the body is not considered to be for the sake of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)."
If that [perception] belongs to the genus, then what is the perception of this [individual] when it has been consecrated?
"By that multitude of elephants, [the state] has been attained; but because of our matted hair, you do not understand.
Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, bestows grace upon all.
Thus it is said in the *Kālottara*:
The consecration (saṃskāra) of the body is not for the sake of beautifying that action;
rather, one should cause the Self to undergo initiation (dīkṣā), which removes the impurities of primordial ignorance.
This [initiation] is not prescribed by means of conjunction or disjunction, nor by birth or destruction, nor even by [the concept of] genus (jāti).
"Even for that conscious, pure knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the embodied being, whose nature is knowledge and who is the agent—that [purification] is desired as its refinement. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: here, unlike in the Vedic [tradition], no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the body is performed, because that too would become a cause for being an enjoyer; thus it is said, "not in the case of conjunction and disjunction. Like a sacrificial act, a refinement is performed for the sake of attaining a superior fruit and for the sake of dissociation from the fruits of inferior actions. For when that [refinement] has ceased, by the force of time, the occurrence of other actions necessarily arises. Therefore, what is the certainty in that? Nor is the refinement performed for the destruction of karma through birth and death—that is, for the destruction of creation and dissolution—for even when that exists, there remains only the state of dissolution (*pralaya*).

And liberation would not occur; nor is it prescribed for the *jāti* (the generic class), because there is no limit to the effects initiated by the body. If so, for whom is the purification (*saṃskāra*) performed? He says: "of the conscious one," and so forth. Consciousness (*cetanā*) is the power characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion. Through association with that [power], the conscious Self (*ātman*)—even though pure, yet joined with the three impurities such as the *āṇava*—is called a "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*) because he knows pleasure, pain, and so on within the field, which is the body. Furthermore, he possesses a subtle body (*piṅga*), hence he is "embodied" (*śarīrī*). For this Self, whose nature is that of a knower, who is established as an agent yet is not independent and is incapable of experiencing enjoyment or attaining liberation by himself, the meaning is that he is dependent upon the gods. And it has been said:
"This ignorant creature is not its own master over its pleasure and pain;
impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed to the pit. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that this is the *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) for the manifestation of the *śivatva* (state of being Śiva) of that self which has been thus distinguished. Enough with this excessive detail; the subject at hand is now stated:

having performed everything beginning with the sacrifice as before, including the testing of the disciple, and having bestowed the *śivahasta* (the hand of Śiva), one should take up the *śakti* and place it within the fire.

Here, on the many-winding surface of the path of Māyā, having invoked, worshipped, and gratified the goddess Vāgīśvarī— the power whose nature is action— and Sadāśiva as Vāgīśa within the lamp of Śuddhavidyā, one should contemplate their enjoyment.

In some cases, one should offer five oblations of each of the five [substances] with a single grain of rice into the Fire of Speech (Vāgīśvarī), who is the form of Sadāśiva, for the sake of obtaining desired garments, food, and wealth.
Then, having intentionally [visualized] them as either red or dark-complexioned according to the previously stated procedure, [one should proceed].
(348) May this twice-born man, pure in his sustenance and possessing purity of seed and place, become a true portion of the gods.
Then, with the water of the scriptures,
[the teacher], possessing the seed-syllable of the Self as a weapon, should strike the disciple on the chest.
Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ ātmane haḥ huṃ [svāhā]. Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hūṃ ātmānaṃ gṛhṇāmi haḥ huṃ phaṭ, and so forth.
Having caused [the deity] to enter within by means of the inhalation (*pūraka*) of the left [nostril], the Guru, through his own self,
having established a state of aesthetic union (*sāmarasya*), and then during the retention (*kumbhaka*)—
[visualizing] the root mantra situated at the end of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), like a net resembling the glow of fire.
With the *recaka* breath, one should bring [the deity] from the crest of the head through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) by means of the left [nostril], O Vāgīśa;

having caused him to become the Goddess, he should be cast in, yet not [forcibly]. Contemplating thus, one should cast [him] with the Goddess, and perform the purification (*śauca*) and other rites with the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Self— having worshipped with this and offered libations for the satisfaction of yoga, one should offer five [libations];
and for the perfection of the stages of the womb and so forth, one hundred and five [libations] with the Śiva-mantra.
One should offer oblations into the fire with wood that has been split according to the prescribed form; by this, one burns away all impurity.

Even a killer of a Brahmin, one who violates the teacher’s bed, a drinker of liquor, a slayer of his guru, a killer of a cow, or one who destroys what has been done—each of these becomes a purifier of the earth through the sixth [offering] involving fragrance.
In the case of black [hair], fire, the smell of a corpse, or a fetus, one should not make a distinction among the brothers regarding the eldest;
when the tuft of hair is joined with the *saṃpuṭita* [mantra], it brings about the state of Rudra even for that which is deficient.

Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ! When the fetus moves, when it trembles in the three types of fire, when it is supported by gold, when it is bound, when it bursts forth in the child, when it is devoid of luster, or when it causes the destruction of the womb— in these and other such signs, one should recite the mantra of the Thousand-formed One a thousand times.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) either with the mantra for consuming sins or with the ninefold self-mantra.
Here, the mantra for consuming the sin-mantra is as follows:
"The peacock-crested one, the crescent-moon-marked one, the one of universal form, situated in the heap."
The Nārasiṃha mantra consists of fire (Ra) and wind (Ya), conjoined with the sixth vowel (Ū).
The orb of the moon, endowed with a crest and adorned with two *khaṭphiṭ* syllables,
preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, is joined with the mantra for devouring sins (*pāpabhakṣaṇa*).
One should extract the mantra of the medicinal herbs; now hear the *kūṭāṅga*.
That which is joined with the six long vowels is declared to be the *kūṭāṅga*.
The form of the god Pāpabhakṣaṇa has the luster of crushed collyrium;
it is licking [its lips], invincible in its onset, voracious, and exceedingly difficult to conquer.
With his mouth wide open, possessing great fangs, a red face, and three eyes;
with a mass of matted hair tied in a topknot from which blood flows, he is adorned by a circle of serpents.
One should meditate upon the terrifying destroyer of evil, who holds a trident and a half-moon, who has been granted boons,
who is clothed in a tiger skin, who wears a serpent as a sacred thread,
and who sits upon a lion in the lotus posture.
Oṃ khaḍgahaste kṣayarudro khaṭphaṭ pāpatra* * bhakṣaṇāya namaḥ. Thus is the application of the mantra (p. 350).
Now, the Navātman is also written.
One should place Viśvarūpa, established in prosperity and situated within the splendor;
then, below that, one should assign Nārasiṃha at the two ends of the wheel.
Below that, one should place the syllable of Indra (Ś),
which is the sixth vowel (Ū);
then, having placed the vital breath (Pra) ten times, one should again place the syllable ŪH below that.
Aṃśumān should extract Navātmā, who resides upon the head of Viśva.
Thus, having extracted [the soul] from the womb of Māyā and uniting it with the womb of Śakti,
the state of the Self as the seed of Śiva is declared to be Garbhādhāna (Conception).
For that which is the re-emergence from the path at the boundary of Māyā is indeed that [rebirth].
The parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) is to be known as the birth [of the child], and the state of being a son [is established] therein;
for this very reason, it is called "awakening" and "glorification" by way of Śiva-hood.
Then one should offer [the oblation] according to the color, consisting of the letters of the name and the syllables of the mantra,
ending with Śiva and Deveśvara, in sequence across the three colors.
For one born of a noble family, [the initiation] ends with the word *deva*; for a Śūdra, it ends with *asacchūdra*, and for a Vaiśya, it ends with *ṛṣi*.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the remaining sacraments (*saṃskāra*), one should cause the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) to be offered.
Having entered [the fire] as before, one should especially refine [it];
then, having led it to the station of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta), it should be applied to the body of the disciple.
To nourish him, the teacher should sprinkle water from the vessel of sin upon his head;
then, having worshipped, gratified with offerings, and dismissed the two parents, the teacher [should proceed].
Having offered oblations of the various colors into the fires of Śiva one hundred times for each deficiency in the ritual procedure,
he should afterwards cause the disciple to partake of the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti) and [thus] lead him to Śiva.
Having made the gods, Agni, Guṇeśa, and Īśāna, as well as the world-protectors, his witnesses,
the virtuous [preceptor] should cause that capable person to hear [the oath].
And one should perform the fire-ritual daily together with the previously mentioned observances.
One should not perform teaching for the sake of worldly existence;
one should prescribe only a minimal code of conduct for those who are incapable of following the full rules of conduct.
Desiring to conquer the five elements, he should lead back the limbs of his vow—
namely the staff, the loincloth, the ashes, self-restraint, and the *śivomaṇi*—
which have been purified by the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and consecrated with the sacred threads (*pavitraka*).
Having placed the vessel containing the purified *sampātāhuti* offerings for a mere moment within the *kumbha*,
one should take it and present it to the disciple who has prostrated.
Alternatively, as he dwells there, he should not mention the rules regarding food and so forth,
nor [speak ill of] Śiva, the Śiva-scripture, the Śiva-fire, the practitioner, or the Guru.
One should never, under any circumstances, step over even the shadow of these [gurus].
One should avoid eating their remains (nirmālya), giving gifts on their behalf, and stepping over them.
The worship of Śiva, the fire, and the guru must be performed for as long as one lives;
likewise, even for those who are incapable, all these previously mentioned commitments (samayas) must be observed.
Then, having worshipped the Supreme Lord in the mandala, the pitcher, and the fire, the preceptor, having entered the ocean of Śambhu’s knowledge, should perform the purification accordingly.
The lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras), Gaṇeśāna, the world-protectors (lokapālas), and Anala, in due order.

(353) ... Thus it is said. Now, some [object]: "The wearing of matted hair and ashes by Brāhmaṇas is improper. That is incorrect, because it contradicts the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas. Likewise, in this very Sūtra:
"The tonsure ceremony (*caulakarma*) is for the twice-born, especially for the Brahmins..."
"In the first eon, one should wear matted hair; such is the Vedic injunction.

Likewise, in the Vāyavīya-Sāvarṇa-Saṃhitā: "The fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possess their own forms; they have four arms, all their limbs are auspicious, and they wear bright sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*)."
Adorned with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on their limbs, they all wore matted hair and rudrākṣa beads; they carried water-pots and were resplendent with rosaries.
Having placed the lotus-feet of Śambhu upon her head and offered a garland to the worshiper,
this highly fortunate Sāvitrī appeared with a form like jasmine or the moon,
adorned with rudrākṣa beads, radiant, and wearing a crown of matted locks.
With their hands placed upon rosaries and holding water-pots,
their bodies draped in black antelope skins and sacred threads, they were clad in Āṣāḍha grass garments and renowned for their merit.
"O Mahādeva, [the Self] has not entered the heart-abode of the yogins. Thus [it is said].
Then, in the *Lokṣi-sūtra*, one should apply ashes consecrated with the mantra *mā nastoke*.
A learned Brāhmaṇa should not transgress the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) even in his mind;
since it is ordained by the Śruti, he who abandons it becomes fallen.
"That which is made on the forehead with ash using the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—that is the *tripuṇḍra*, which is auspicious and the destroyer of great sins. Thus [it is said].
There are numerous such statements found in the Vedas and Smṛtis;
therefore, that statement should not be understood as a mockery of the world.
Thus concludes the procedure for wearing matted hair as part of the initiation into the specific observances.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Thus, for one who is firmly established in this final state, the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) becomes perfectly stable;
having understood this, one should perform the supreme initiation known as *nirvāṇa*.
Here too, as before, having performed the sacrifice which concludes with the satisfaction of the mantra,

one should perform the placement of the path of the *kalās* through emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) within Śambhu, the water-pot, the fire, and the self; then, placing the hand of Śiva upon his own, he should address the Lord thus:

This Blessed One has been examined; he is the essence of Māyā, born from the power of Śiva, of noble birth, a portion of Rudra for a very long time, and established in the observance of the Rule (samaya).
And when the child, afflicted and longing for nirvana because of the suffering of existence,
then stands before him seeking liberation, let the Lord remain there for his sake.
Therefore, this body presided over by Him is the Teacher himself, the Lord.
Having gone outside, here too [the teacher performs] the placement upon the mandala and so forth,
as well as the binding of the eyes, the entrance, and the hand of Śiva, just as before.
Having performed the fire sacrifice and the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the mandala to the south of the sacrificial post,
he should place the deceased's body upright and bathe the disciple who has observed the fast.
One should not tie that thread upon the crest; rather, it should be as follows:
neither too thick, very white, odorless, uniform, and auspicious.
Having spread out the *kākarkita* cloth, tripled and then tripled again,
it is washed with the weapon-mantra until it is bright white, especially with the special water for the *arghya* offering.
For the sake of enjoyment, [one should proceed] from the big toe up to the crest, and for liberation, in the reverse order;
one should apply the seven puruṣas on the right side and water and the other elements on the left.
And it is said:
"The thread spun by virgins, tripled and then folded three times,
should be sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then again with scented water."
O Goddess of gods, having honored that thread with water for the guest-offering (arghya) according to his capacity, the wise preceptor, being well-composed, should then proceed.
Having placed the thread at the region of the big toe, one should stretch it out;
the thread [should extend] from the crest-lock down to the foot.
"Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon that thread with all the mantras, the wise one [should proceed]. Thus [it is said].
One should meditate upon this thread of power as the effect that binds one to the fetters.
And it has been said:
"The bonds are to be cut and pierced; however, in the context of the body, they reside in the Sūtra-sthāna.
Therefore, the body should always be meditated upon by the teachers as consisting of Sūtra. Thus [it is stated].
Now, the sequence of the ritual application.

Having worshipped [the deity] in that body with the mantra "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Kriyāśakti," and having extracted [the consciousness] by means of striking and other methods, one should place it upon the thread and perform the *apāda* rite. Then, having worshipped in the body of that disciple with the mantras "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śuddhā," "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Piṅgalā," and "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Suṣumnā," and having performed the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), one should—after the entry and separation through striking and piercing with the mantra beginning "Oṃ hāṃ, to Iḍā, haḥ huṃ phaṭ"—[extract the consciousness] from the disciple's body, which resembles a lotus fiber.
Page 356.

Having severed [the thread] with the *pūrakasaṃhāriṇī* breath, having joined it to the *dāya-sūtra*, having worshipped and restrained it, one should place it in the fire of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), worship it, and satisfy it. Then, regarding the [five] daughters: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā; Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmā; Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā; Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Raudrī. Having thus assigned [these mantras], having worshipped them, and having worshipped them in the fire as well, one should offer oblations five times for the sake of satisfaction and for the sake of their presence. Then, having again restrained it in the thread and having confined it, one should perform the loosening of the bonds and so forth by means of those [mantras]. And it has been said:
And the three powers of Śambhu are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrikā; they are omnipresent, their energy proclaimed in anger, separation, and extraction. Thus it is said.

Then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon that thread which corresponds to the continuum of his body as it was manifested, at the region of the heart, with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the heart-lotus adorned with the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire*, one should place [it] therein.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śakti," having worshipped, having bound and shielded [the disciple], and having offered libations even into the fire; then, having clearly placed and worshipped the form of light there with "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge" (*vidyādeha*), and having established it; then, having struck the heart of the disciple with a flower over which the *saptārṇa* mantra has been recited, using "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Self; haḥ huṃ phaṭ," and having visualized the Self as terrified by this; then, having performed the piercing (*vibhedana*) again with this same mantra (*aṇu*), and having visualized the consciousness (*cit*) moving upward from within the calyx of that heart-lotus; then, with the seed-syllable of the Self enclosed by the *śikhā* mantra and ending in *namaḥ*, [one should imagine] it exiting from one's own body through the *raudrī* channel during exhalation (*recaka*), and entering [the disciple] through the left [nostril] during inhalation (*pūraka*). Then, with "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ hūṃ, I seize the Self; haḥ huṃ phaṭ," taking [the Self] from there by means of the *pūraka* and the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā], and having made it reside in oneself, one should make it of one flavor (*samarasa*) with one's own self through the *kumbhaka* [breath-retention] by means of the *jyeṣṭhā* [channel].

Having separated [the soul] by means of the *raudrī-ārecaka*, one should lead it—resembling a spark of fire situated at the tip of the root-mantra—through the piercing of the knots up to the purification of the path of the twelve *antadhvan*s. Then, having brought it to the middle of the eyebrows by means of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), and having expelled it by means of the *piṅgalā-ārecaka*, one should cause it to enter either the body of the thread (*sūtradeha*) or the *māyā-pūraka*. Saying "Salutation to the Self" (*ātmane namaḥ*), one should separate the self—which is dark-colored and obstructed by the bonds (*pāśa*) such as impurity (*mala*)—by means of the *udbhavā* [kalā], and having enclosed and restrained it with the *varman* [mantra], one should effect its presence within the fire.

Then again, having meditated upon the black form of the *mala-pāśa* (the impurity-bond), one should worship with: *oṃ hāṃ mala-pāśāya bhoktṛtvakāraṇāya namaḥ*. Next, having meditated upon the white and black forms consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), one should worship with:

*oṃ hāṃ karma-pāśāya sukhaduḥkhamoha-bhogakāraṇāya namaḥ*. Then, having meditated upon the manifold form which is the effect of *māyā*, one should worship with: *oṃ hāṃ māyā-pāśāya śarīrendriya-viṣaya-kāraṇāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped, one should also perform the rites of invoking the presence (*sānnidhya*) and so forth within the fire.

Then, having placed upon the head of the disciple the threads that extend continuously from the pure power (*viśuddha-śakti*), one should perform the worship and other rites after depositing [the mantras] whose nature is darkness (*tamas*) and which pervade up to the end of the *pada*: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the self of the path of reality (*tattvādhvātman*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the path of words (*padādhvan*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the self of the path of reality; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the path of limited powers (*kalādhvan*). Accordingly, the Āgama states: "Here, the mantras are constantly pervaded by the words, and the words are pervaded by the phonemes; those [words] are in turn pervaded by the realities (*tattva*)."
"Likewise, the tattvas are pervaded by the kalās in their respective order;
having first conceived of the inner sin, these [tattvas] must be purified with effort.

Then, with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva-śakti, the presiding deity over the impurity-bond," one should worship Śiva-śakti—who is of the nature of darkness—within that body, take her up, join her to the thread, and perform the worship and other rites.

But surely, how can that Śiva-Śakti, who is stainless, become of the nature of a bond (*pāśa*)? True; however, because she is colored by the relationship between the object of purification (*śodhya*) and the purifier (*śodhaka*), she is called a "bond" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). And it has been said: "The auspicious power of Maheśvara, which bestows grace upon all, is metaphorically designated as a 'bond' solely because it follows after [the individual's] *dharma*."
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Tirobhāvikā, who has a crooked form and is thus attached.
One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites as if offering it to her crest or into the fire. And it is said:
"From the two powers of action (*kriyā-śakti*), Vāmā and Kuṇḍalinī are born."
"The Kuṇḍalinī, afflicted within the body, is the downward-moving breath that obstructs knowledge. Thus [it is said].
Having offered oblations with the hundred-fold root mantra and the full [mantra] for the sake of rectifying any deficiency or excess,
one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the lamp-offering (*dīpa*), as well as the rites beginning with *śāntyatītā*.
But in cases such as striking with nooses, binding, and so forth, it is for the sake of exercising power.

Namely: *Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Mantras, who has transcended peace; to the bond of the *kalā*, *huṃ phaṭ*. Likewise, there is the kindling. Having thus performed the rites for pacification and so forth, one should then mark the crest-lock, the eyebrows, the ears, the navel, and the knees with saffron and other substances upon the *pāśasūtra* in order to fully understand the pervasion of the *kalās*. Then, having worshipped Śiva along with his limbs (*aṅgas*) and the *pāśas* upon that [sūtra] on the head with eight flowers for the purpose of disjunction, and having offered oblations ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* into that arrangement using the root mantra a hundred times, one should then perform the inspection of the bonds (*pāśas*) and so forth. Namely:
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ! To the one whose form consists of the impurities of mantras, worlds, and principles, as well as karma, āyā, and māyīya, together with their ripening fruits.

Having observed the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the *Pratiṣṭhā* Kalā within the body—starting from the joints of the fingers and toes up to the navel—one should say: "Oṃ Hāṃ Hāṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the *Pratiṣṭhā* Kalā-pāśa, which consists of the Mantras, words, phonemes, worlds, principles (*tattva*), impurities (*mala*), actions (*karman*), Māyā, and the nature of the Māyīya Śiva. Then, having observed the pervasion of the *Nivṛtti* Kalā from the region of the knees down to the tips of the toes, one should join [the soul] with the bonds of *Śāntyatīta*, *Śānti*, *Vidyā*, *Pratiṣṭhā*, and *Pratiṣṭhā-Nivṛtti* using the following mantras: "Oṃ Hāṃ Hauṃ Hyaiṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the two Kalās, *Śāntyatīta* and *Śānti*, which are censured by the bonds of the Mantras and so forth," and so on. Next, having performed the piercing (*vibhedana*) of each [bond] individually with the mantras beginning with "Oṃ Hāṃ Hauṃ Hāṃ, Haḥ Huṃ Phaṭ" for the bond of the *Śāntyatīta* Kalā, and so forth; and having again recited the previous mantra and observed the pervasion of the *Śāntyatīta* Kalā-pāśa; then, having pierced it with the *Kalā-aṇu* ending in *phaṭ* as before, and having entered and determined it accordingly; one should take [the soul] from its own place by means of the *Pūraka-saṃhāriṇī* [breath] with the mantra: "Oṃ Hūṃ Hāṃ Hūṃ, I seize the *Śāntyatīta* Kalā-pāśa, which is censured by the bonds of the Mantras and so forth, Haḥ Huṃ Phaṭ. Having placed it within oneself, one should then join it to the thread of entry (*tatpraveśasūtra*) during the *Recaka* [exhalation] with a mantra ending in *namaḥ*. In this regard, there is a specific distinction mentioned by the venerable Somaśambhu: [The text continues with the specific ritual details.]
In that initiation which possesses seeds (*sabījā-dīkṣā*), there exists a continuous bond distinct from the fetters of conventional conduct (*samayācāra-pāśa*),
from the qualities that initiate the body, from the fruits of mantra-perfection,
and even from the merit of sacrificial rites and public works (*iṣṭāpūrta*).
"One should meditate on that which obstructs consciousness within the subtle *kalās*.

Thus, having tied a knot in the thread at the region of the crest (*śikhā*) with the mantra "Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ hūṃ, I bind the noose of the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*)," [one proceeds] with the mantra-word "Oṃ hauṃ" (p.

Having worshipped [the thread] and the fire with the mantra "Obeisance to the censured one, whose mass of parts has transcended peace," one should offer five oblations, including the libation (*tarpaṇa*), ending with "svāhā. In this same manner, regarding the knowledge of peace (*śānti-vidyā*) and the other arts (*kalā*) such as establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*), one should look at them in their respective places with their own mantras, strike them, divide them, enter them, grasp them, perform the taking up and so forth, and join them to their respective locations. Having tied a knot in the thread at the place of the dyer, one should worship it and offer libations.

Thus, the sixteen rites beginning with *tarpaṇa* and ending with *tarpaṇa* have been described. And it is said: "Satiating, kindling, coloring, worship, oblation, anointing, breaking the joints, instantaneous [action], half-[action], entering, seizing, and joining."
And you should perform the sixteen rites, ending with the libation (tarpaṇa), within the [sixteen] digits (kalās).
Regarding this, the meaning of "seizing" (*grahaṇa*) and "binding" (*bandhana*) is as stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"Seizing is the subjugation of the fetters (*pāśa*) and so forth;
binding, moreover, is the complete prohibition of their activity with respect to the person (*puruṣa*)."

"Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the Śiva-Śakti who presides over the bonds (pāśa) of the Kalās. Having thus extracted [the essence] from the body of the disciple, having performed its binding with the thread, its worship, and its libation into the fire, one should then worship Śiva there with the eight-fold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*). Having seated the disciple upon the seat presided over by Śiva and placed the bond-thread on his right shoulder, one should offer one hundred and eight full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the sake of liberation from defects of deficiency or excess. Then, having offered oblations with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), if it is the method of immediate consecration (*sadyo'dhivāsana-pakṣa*), one should first perform the pouring of the remnants (*saṃpātana*) and then purify [the disciple] according to the procedure to be described in the sequence beginning with Nivṛtti. On the following day, having placed the thread on the head of the seated disciple and performed the pouring of the remnants, one should remove the thread from the topknot and place it either in a copper vessel or within the belly of a male [linga].

361) Having placed that thread within a casket consisting of the weapon (*astra*), armor (*kavaca*), and heart (*hṛdaya*) mantras, and having worshipped it with the limbs (*aṅga*) of Śiva, one should perform the *sampātāhuti* offering from the second *saṃhitā*. Then, having wound it with a five-colored thread, one should hand over the thread to the child by the Guru’s command, saying to the Lord Śiva residing in the jar: "O Blessed One, protect this binding-thread (*pāśasūtra*). Now, [one might ask]:
"Having prepared the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and offered it into the divine fire, the Guru [should take] two portions."
Having gone outside by the command of the deity, [he should perform the rite] in the courtyard upon the three mandalas.
Whether situated facing south or north, or standing facing west;
for the offering, one faces east, and for the child’s consumption and liberation, one faces the north.
One should offer the fivefold Brahman-group (pañcabrahmagaṇa) with the left hand;
with kusha grass, one should drink [the remaining liquid] three times from within, using the principles of the Self (ātmatattva) and so forth, at intervals.
Having sipped water and consumed three morsels of sacrificial porridge (caru) at the second [round],
at the third [round] one should clean the teeth with a tooth-stick made from a milky tree as if cleaning the teeth.
Having performed the *adhauti* rite, one should lift up the fierce [sacrificial post] and observe its fall upon the ground;
it is auspicious when it falls with its tip pointing west, east, north, or northeast, and not facing any other direction.
Then, for the sake of liberating it from those defects, one should recite the *astra-mantra* one hundred and eight times.

Having offered oblations with the *pāśupatāstra* mantra and the root (*mūla*) mantra until the end of the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), for the sake of pacifying other forgotten [faults], one should inform Śiva.

O Lord, this ritual of sipping water (ācamana) which you have performed up until the end of the *śānti* rite must be abandoned here; your presence should not remain for the sake of spoiling the cooking of the husbands.
Having thus informed [the disciple], and having again offered [oblations] for the sake of cessation, one should completely suppress that which resides in the fire.
Afterwards, having sipped water (ācānta), one should offer the internal oblation (antarbali) for the sake of liberation;
then, having worshipped the deity in the form of the mantra upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and having informed the Lord Śiva, one should cause him to remain [there].
And one should place Śiva, situated in a water-pot,
there at the eastern side of the Lord, on ground smeared with cow dung.
Covered with cow-dung ashes and a cloth, and having seated the disciple— who is seeking both worldly enjoyment and liberation— facing east on a festival day, the Guru [proceeds].
Having performed the placement of time and space, having tied the topknot with the Śiva-mantra,
and having worshipped with the eight flowers, one should impart the dream-mantra.
Oṃ, salutations to Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
salutations to the Auspicious One, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Dreams.
Speak, O Lord of the Gods, for I have come into your presence seeking refuge.
In a dream, all activities situated in the heart become otherwise.

With the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ hlīṃ śūlapāṇaye svāhā*, having initiated the disciple seven times with this, and having covered him with a cloth while protected by the armor-mantra (*varma*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should bathe the child.
Protection should be performed all around with kuśa grass, ashes, and sesame seeds using the Astra-mantra;
having gone outside, the preceptor should offer oblations to the lords of the directions.

Having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), while partaking of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances, he should remember the entire procedure of initiation; then, having offered the sacrificial ground, the grass, and the fire to Śiva, he should sleep.
This consecration for initiation has been performed by Śrī Vajrajñānaśambhu, born of the Golakī lineage, in accordance with the meaning of the Siddhānta.
Thus concludes the procedure for the destruction of obstacles to initiation.
363) Now, having heard the morning bath as it was seen for a child,
or having determined it as seen by oneself, one should speak it for the sake of Śiva or for one's own desired purpose.
One should rejoice in the auspicious therein, as it appears like a dream.
For example, as described in the *Śrīmṛgendra*: mounting upon a crest, a cow, a horse, a bull, a goat, a sheep, or a measure;
a mass of water, a river-bearer, a lake, mud, and so forth; wealth;
a fire-oblation, a star, a great jewel, a fine flower, a fruit, or yoga.
The attainment of the kingdom of intelligence, the milk of wisdom, the smearing with excrement,
the flooding with the drinking of blood, and the devouring of living beings by fish, lions, and men.
The attainment of royal insignia, the sun, the moon, fire, and the enemy of the serpents (Garuḍa); white copper, variegated gems, lightning, the stars, and Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
The manifestation of the perfected Māras, Apsarases, and Brahmins at the sacrificial enclosure;
the sea voyage; and the taking of refuge in the sun, moon, and fire.
The perfection of weapons such as the discus, and the attainment of wealth, constitute success.
He ascends the pericarp of the great lotus, taking refuge in the purifying field;
he is like the fruit of a milky tree, and there are flowering groves as well.
Weeping, traveling upon those who should not be traveled with, and so forth, are taught for the sake of attaining renown;
while mounting a donkey, a camel, or a pig, and falling into a pit, result in extreme degradation.
Bathing in water mixed with the liquid mud of cow dung, wearing white garments,
and avoiding lac, salt, iron, and the skins of crows and jackals— this is the rule for one who has committed a minor offense.
Wearing red [garments], white garlands, ointments, clothes, and ornaments.
Dancing, instrumental music, singing, the display of graceful gestures,
running about, snapping the fingers of the mouth, playing, and serving spirits.
The falling of the sun and moon, Śeṣa [emerging] from the ocean, the supreme red chalk,
the destruction of the city of Dhūmaketu, and the collapse of the archway and Indra’s banner.
The disappearance of royal insignia, a terrible shroud of mist,
and the attempt at sexual intercourse with those of improper species indicate that what was cooked will succeed only after a month.

Among these, the best [time] is at the end of the night, the middling is in the middle, and the lightest is at the first watch; such is the threefold classification for those who possess the three abodes.
A fire-oblation of more than a thousand [offerings] performed with the *ghora* weapon is for the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable];
that which consists of a hundred is for the *śakti* [seed-syllable], and the ritual procedure for others is for the *śakti* [deity] by those who are not unrighteous.
Having thus fixed this in his mind, the Guru, having performed his daily rites (*nitya-kriyā*), [proceeds].
Having performed the sacrifice as before, concluding with the assumption of the guise of a disciple.
In order to accomplish that within one's own dream, one should perform a hundred [recitations] with the root mantra and the full oblation;
or, if the dream occurs at dawn and other such times, then with the terrible weapon-mantra.
He [placed] five hundred and fifty [disciples] on the path of the sequence;
the disciple, having performed his daily rites, stood present within the mandala.
Having worshipped him with the eight flowers, the Guru, whose body is composed of mantras, [proceeds].
With that very [thread], one should raise the water-pot and offer oblations into the fire for Śiva;
then, taking the thread, sprinkling it, and binding it to the top-knot of the child.
Having arranged everything as before, including the channels and so forth, [he should place] Śiva upon the thread.

Having offered oblations to Śiva with the root mantra until the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), for the purpose of joining the paths located within oneself, the water-pot (*kumbha*), and the fire of Śiva, in the presence of all those [deities].
Having offered a hundred oblations, one should perform the rites of withdrawal and so forth, satisfy the kalās, and then kindle [the fire].
The application for the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is: *oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ svāhā*, and so forth. For the kindling (*dīpana*), it is: *oṃ hūṃ hlāṃ hāṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, and so forth.
Having worshipped and offered libations into the fire, [one worships] Śakti in her form as the Support (*ādhāra*):
*oṃ hāṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*.
Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Iḍā. Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Piṅgalā. Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Suṣumnā.

Having worshipped and offered libations into the fire, and having performed the union of the channels (*nādī-sandhāna*), the disciple should likewise do so; then, for the sake of bringing [the deity] into proximity, he should offer five oblations with the root mantra and perform the inspection for the presence of sins and so forth. Reciting: *Oṃ hlāṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the syllable of the mantra-word, which is the impurity of the world-level, the companion of Māyā, having the form of a woman, having the nature of the Tattvas, and being the noose of the Nivṛtti-kalā.* Having thus perceived the entire path (adhvan), beginning from the immobile beings up to Brahmā—the fourteen classes of beings and all that is censured—within the thread of the *jāñcayā*, he strikes it with the syllable *haḥ* and *huṃ phaṭ*. Having pierced it, he first enters by means of the *pramā* [mantra] with the *pūraka* breath at the end of the *namaḥ*. Then, having separated it with the *jyeṣṭhā* [mantra] and the *kumbhaka* breath ending in *phaṭ*, and having drawn it out with the *raudrī* [mantra] and the *ārecaka* breath ending in *svāhā* while forming the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, he seizes the noose.

Having grasped [the substance] with "Haḥ Huṃ Phaṭ," having brought it forth, having established it within oneself through the left nostril by means of inhalation (pūraka), having separated it from the body through the right nostril by means of retention (kumbhaka), having manifested it through exhalation (recaka) with the Raudrī mantra ending in "Namaḥ," having united it with the fire, having worshipped it, and having offered it with "Svāhā," one should present it with five oblations and establish its presence (sānnidhya).

Then, having invoked the Brāhmaṇa Āvārya with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, having worshipped him and gratified him with libations, [one says]: "Oṃ, O Brahmā, in this office of yours, I initiate this person for you."
By the command of Śaṅkara, may you become favorable to this seeker of liberation.

Having thus made this declaration, [one should recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hvāṃ hauṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāgīśvarī, who consists of the phonemes and words of the mantra, who is the embodiment of the three-fold reality (*trirūpatattva*) through the impurities of worldly existence, karma, and *māyā*—both the *māyīya* and the *sacintya*—and who pervades the bond of the *kalā-pāśa* of cessation (*nivṛtti*). Thus, having invoked Vāgīśī—who has bathed after her menses and whose form is non-dual and like a staff (*daṇḍa-rūpin*) within the two [fires] simultaneously—into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and having worshipped and gratified her with libations, one should then recite the beginning of the mantra-words: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hlāṃ hauṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāgīśvara."

Thus, Vāgīśa, having meditated upon the agitator of all wombs (*niḥśeṣayonikṣobhaka*), having invoked, worshipped, and gratified [the deity], and having visualized their union as before preceded by meditation, he should display the *yonimudrā* and the *aṅgulimudrā*. Having obtained permission from the two, he should then perform the piercing of the body at the heart with a flower over which the *astra-mantra* has been recited seven times, using the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ hāṃ ātmane haḥ huṃ phaṭ*. Then, having entered through the left [nostril] as before via the *vāmā* [power], and having separated [the self] via the *jyeṣṭhā* [power] with the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ hūṃ ātmane svāhā*, he should draw out the self—which resembles a savior (*tāraka*)—by means of the *raudrī* [power] and lead it to the *dvādaśānta*. With this very [mantra], he takes hold of the self; having taken and brought it back, he establishes the *ātmasra* (self-weapon) through inhalation (*pūraka*). Having made it one with flavor (*samarasīkṛta*) through retention (*kumbhaka*) as before, he leads it upward to the *dvādaśānta* and the limit of the *śakti* through exhalation (*recaka*). Having grasped the principle (*tatva*) through emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), he causes the self—meditated upon as Vāgīśa and Vāmatā—to enter. He should pray: "O Blessed One, let the first yoga be performed for all wombs simultaneously. Then, by that Blessed One, for the sake of accomplishing the arising of forms such as the lame and others from objects divided by manifold distinctions, [the self is placed] within the womb of the *vāgīśī* in the world consisting of various kinds of wombs.

Having visualized the self as having been cast [into the womb], one should perform the rite called *udbhava* by means of the *recaka* breath, joining it with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, [this] world is joined with the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) in all wombs. Then, having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the self" (*ātmane namaḥ*), and having gratified [the deity] at the end of the *svāhā* syllable, one should offer five oblations with that root-mantra for the sake of its presence. Thereafter, having prayed, "O Blessed One, may there be the simultaneous impregnation of this [soul] in manifold wombs," one should offer five oblations with the Heart-mantra ending in *svāhā*.

Now, the *puṃsavana* rite should not be performed for him, lest there be the appearance of a neuter being; likewise, the *sīmantonnayana* should also not be performed, lest there be the appearance of a hunchback, a lame person, or similar deformities.

Then, having prayed, "O Lord, let the birth of this animal proceed from all wombs," and having offered five oblations with the *śiras* mantra; having prayed, "O Lord, let there be authority for this [animal] everywhere," and having offered five oblations with the *śikhā* mantra; having prayed, "O Lord, let this animal simultaneously exhaust the experience of karma arising from transmigratory existence through the mantras and so forth," and having offered five oblations with the *varman* mantra; having prayed, "O Lord, after the exhaustion of that experience, let there be the dissolution, the withdrawal, and the complete separation from the earthly body of this animal," and having offered five oblations with the root mantra (*mūla*); having prayed, "O Lord, let there be no further wandering for this animal in the worlds already experienced; let there be the purification of the paths of those respective worlds and the cessation of its karma at this time," and then having offered five by five oblations with the *astra* mantra ending in *svāhā*; then, for the sake of the specific purification of the earth element, he should offer five oblations with the *hṛdaya* mantra; then, for the sake of the removal of water, the removal of pride, and the removal of the bonds of the *pāśas* belonging to the entire group beginning with the *dānavas*, he should offer one hundred oblations with the *hṛdaya* mantra as an expiation (*niṣkṛti*).

368) Likewise, even in the case of the *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) and other rites, having performed the rituals beginning with *garbhādhāna* (impregnation) up to the purification of the *tattvas*, one should again perform the expiation (*niṣkṛti*) in sequence by means of the head-mantra (*śiras*), the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), and the root-mantra (*mūlāṇu*). And it has been said:
"The re-establishment of the *tattvas* in the fire should be joined with the mantra by means of the self."
One should perform the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) with the heart-mantra and the rite of birth (janana) with the head-mantra.

Having prayed, "O Blessed One, may there be authority everywhere," one should offer five oblations with the *śikhā* [mantra]. Then, for the sake of removing the bonds (*pāśa*), one should offer five oblations each in sequence during the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*: the portion for *tvam* with the *kavaca* mantra; that known as *laya* with the *śiva* mantra; the purification of the stream (*srotaḥ-śuddhi*) with the *śiva* mantra; and the purification of the principles (*tattva-śuddhi*) with the *hṛdaya* mantra. Thus, one should offer five oblations at each stage.
In the case of cessation, there is no [need for] establishment in the heart;
in the case of knowledge, purification is performed with the head-mantra and the tuft-mantra; in the case of peace, it is by means of the armor-mantra.

Thus, for the sake of the soul’s (*paśu*) return [to its source], five oblations should be offered with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) by one skilled in the noose (*pāśa*) to obstruct the impurities (*mala*). Then, having moved the cord with the thumb and forefinger, and having offered five more oblations with the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ* for the purpose of severing the noose, one should then pray: "O Blessed One, please sever the noose of the soul. Thereafter, the recitation (*japa*) should be performed seven times with: *oṃ haṃ haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ*. Then, having severed the cord of the noose—which is censured by the mantra-pāda beginning with *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ*—along with its attendants and its cessation, one should consecrate it elsewhere as previously stated with the mantra *ka * * * rīṃ*. This should be done seven times with the aforementioned sword-weapon mantra (*kṣurikāstra*).
Having purified those who have descended through the Śivāsana, one should unite them with the three sweets (madhuratra);
then one should purify the bonds (pāśas) by means of the collection of weapons (astras).
The bonds of the knots are indeed severed, for those are the joints of the knots; even in the world, one who has escaped from a jointed enclosure is released from the fetters of that enclosure.

Thus, for the purpose of removing the state of being bound again, one should rub the mantra with both hands while reciting "haḥ huṃ phaṭ. Then, having rolled the mantra [into a ball] and placed it at the tip of the *sruc* ladle filled with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one should offer the oblation while reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ! I sacrifice here the mantra, the words, the phonemes, the worlds, the principles (*tattva*), impurity (*mala*), karma, Māyā, that which pertains to Māyā (*māyīya*), the assistant, the female form, the form of the principle, the form of the principle, and the bond of the *kalā* of Nivṛtti—haḥ huṃ phaṭ! Then, for the removal of the noose and the hook, one should offer eight oblations as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) using the Weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in "huṃ phaṭ. After that, having invited and worshipped a Brāhmaṇa and gratified him, one should separate the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) from the pit (*kuṇḍa*) by means of striking and other methods. Then, one should offer the white [element] with five oblations while reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ! O Brahmā! Sound and touch, the white, the cave (the heart)—svāhā! This is because the earth possesses five qualities (*guṇa*); thus, all five qualities are to be offered. Alternatively, since [Brahmā] is "without qualities" (*nirguṇa*), only fragrance is to be offered. If it is asked: "How can sound and touch, which are qualities belonging to the element of space (*ākāśa*), be offered to Brahmā during the purification of the earthly principle (*pārthiva-tattva*)?"—it should not be said thus. It is not those qualities that are offered; rather, through the purification of the principles (*tattva-śuddhi*), the purification of the individual soul (*āṇava-śuddhi*) occurs. What then is meant? It is this: the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) of the self, consisting of the inner group of eight (*puryaṣṭaka*) such as sound, touch, and so forth, is thereby dissolved. And it has been said: [The text continues: "Just as a snake sheds its skin, so the embodied soul casts off the subtle body. And: "The subtle body is composed of the eightfold group beginning with sound. Thus, the subtle body, which is the internal organ of the self, is dissolved. Furthermore, it is said: "The subtle body is the aggregate of the eight, beginning with sound. Therefore, the subtle body, which is the internal organ of the self, is dissolved. Furthermore, it is said: "The subtle
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
intellect, mind, and ego—these they know as the 'City of Eight' (puryaṣṭaka). Thus [it is said].

Therefore, these objects—sound and the rest—are presented as belonging solely to the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), which arises from the impairment of the sense organs beginning with hearing. Among them, sound is produced by the impairment of the ear and the organ of speech; touch, moreover, is produced by the impairment of the skin, feet, hands, anus, and genitals, and since both of these are portions of Brahmā (*brahmāṃśau*), they are presented to Brahmā. Then, taste arises from the impairment of the tongue and is presented to Keśava. Likewise, [the objects] are presented through the impairments of the eyes and the nose. (p. 370)

Form and fragrance are offered to Rudra. In this way, the delusion (*vipluti*) of the intellect and ego is considered to belong to Īśvara. Furthermore, that delusion, which is the cause of all transformations, as well as the *bindu-śakti*, is separated from the child through striking and other means, and is joined to Sadāśiva. And it is said: "The *śruti-vipluti* belongs to Brahmā; it bestows a womb among the eaters of raw flesh (*kravyāda*).
The *rasanā* belongs to Viṣṇu, the *raudrī* to Rudra, and the *haitakī* to Prāṇa and the eyes."
The goddess Aiśvarī, whose root is the pride of intellect and who is the deity of the mind,
and the four deities of action, because they have touch as their object, are all established within you.
The wise maintain that because they are the objects of words,
external things are included in the three internal functions along with the ear, the hand, and the injunction (*vidhi*).
"Having performed [the rite] like the loosening of a noose, one should install the deities.
Now, returning to the subject at hand: "O Brahman, you must again cast away the noose of the first Lord of Kalās."
By the command of Śiva, no obstruction should be placed within one's own sphere of activity.

Having thus prayed and dismissed Brahmā, one should offer five oblations with the root mantra for the sake of one's own liberation. Having approached the fire with the Vāmā [mantra] and separated it from the Jyeṣṭhā [mantra], one should draw oneself—resembling the lunar orb emerging from Rāhu’s mouth along with the five meats—with the Raudrī [mantra]. Having placed oneself within the self and joined it to the body of the thread, one should offer five oblations with the root mantra for its presence. Then, for the nourishment of that head, one should offer the water of the *arghya* with the ring finger while reciting the root mantra ending in *svadhā*. Having worshipped the two ancestors and gratified them with ten oblations each, one should dismiss them. Finally, for the fulfillment of all rites, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*: *oṃ hāṃ hāṃ hīṃ hāṃ namas to the knots of the bonds of the kalās of Nivṛtti and Pratiṣṭhā, which are censured at the beginning of the mantra-padas.*
Thus (p.

371), having effected the union of the pure and impure principles by means of short and long utterances, one should offer five oblations with the root mantra for the sake of their stabilization; in this way, there are twenty-four rites beginning with the seat and ending with the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). And it has been said:
Striking, piercing, entry, separation, extraction, gathering,
joining, honoring, satisfaction, concealment, and awakening—
these eleven functions of the bonds have been described to you.
Having struck and split it, having entered and separated the atom,
and having drawn it out and grasped it, one should unite the power within the womb.
For the purpose of implantation by means of the heart-mantra, likewise for generation by means of the head-mantra,
for authority by means of the tuft-mantra, and for enjoyment by means of the armor-mantra.
Then, for the sake of purification, one should perform ablutions with the root mantra while dwelling in the purity of the stream;
thereafter, for the sake of expiation, one should recite the heart-mantra one hundred times.
When the power of *kalā* is concealed, one should perform five oblations with the ritual weapon (*śastra*):
cutting, crushing, burning, and the prevention of sprouting.
Having offered white [substance] with water for the sake of the cause, one should extract the subtle [essence].
"Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should perform the reconnection (*sandhāna*) between the pure and the purified;
twenty-four rites have been declared for the purification of the self.

Now, how can it be said that there are twenty-four rites, since only eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) are heard of in the *Brahmakavaca* of the *Bhārgava* [tradition]? And it has been stated:
Thus, these eighteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras) [are performed] for the sake of the disciple who is bound by reality;
one should perform them, omitting the triad beginning with the throat, for the satisfaction of Śiva.
Your application consists of the acceptance of striking and urging yourself.
The first [section] concerns origination; then the authority over the streams [of scripture], their enjoyment, and their cessation;
followed by purification, the purity of the principles (tattvas), and the restraint of the power of the bound soul (paśu).
The loosening of the bonds, their severance, and the ritual of transposition upon their burning.

"The Karaṇeṣṭi, the extraction of the animal sacrifice, and others among these [rites] are to be understood as purificatory rites (saṃskāra) for the intermediate state, performed with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Thus it is said.

True; however, it should be understood that this is established by implication: that it is impossible to perform drawing and so forth without first effecting entry through differentiation and separation. And it has been said:
"Striking is for the purpose of separation, and separation is for the sake of drawing;
drawing is indeed for the sake of grasping, and grasping is the cause of union."
The interruption is for the sake of distraction; distraction is the cause of that state. At its end, it becomes full, having as its cause the extraction of the subtle atom (*aṇu*) and so forth.

But surely, even when beating or pulling is performed, how can there be a union with the womb for the Self (*ātman*) residing in that very body, since it is omnipresent? When a person has been commanded, they ought to undergo conception and so forth; yet this is not possible. That is true. However, because the states of Śiva, Śakti, and the Self are all-pervasive, all of this is indeed possible. And it has been said: "Śiva is subtle everywhere; Śakti is omnipresent; and the Self is everywhere the bringer of those respective states."
When a state of being has been commanded such that it shall come to pass exactly as so directed.
And so it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Alternatively, O Six-faced One, what is the use of saying much more?"
By means of a particular mental construction of speech that causes delusion.
Whatever one conceives regarding the nature of all phenomena as it has been taught, that very thing comes to be for one who constantly contemplates its reality; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, the knowledge of the self has been explained to you in brief. So it is said.

[Objection: But then, how can there be such things as the depositing [of seed] or the generation [of offspring] for a self that is omnipresent? [Reply: True; however, its nature consists in the union of Śiva and Śakti, and it is through this that the depositing and so forth occur. And it has been said:
"Deposit, immersion, generation, the arising of vision and action, authority, sovereignty, bliss, and the supreme [state] born of the womb."
"Beyond the noose, great, eternal, and possessing an age equal to that [of the universe]; thus [it is said]."

The meaning of this is as follows: the "absorption" (*laya*) of those two, Śiva and Śakti, who are essentially partless (*niṣkala*), is their immersion (*samāveśa*), their union (*samavāya*), which is the beginning of the manifestation of such a nature. And "birth" (*janana*) is the arising of supreme knowledge and action for that Great Soul (*mahātman*). "Authority" (*adhikāra*) is the sovereignty over even all those who rule the wheel of the paths (*adhvacakra*), because he is superior even to them, being impelled by Paraśiva. "Enjoyment" (*bhoga*), however, is the innate joy (*āhlāda*) born from the source of all latent impressions; it is enjoyment characterized by bliss (*ānanda*). "Absorption" (*laya*) is the Self (*ātman*) that stands having transcended all the paths beyond the state of the bound soul (*paśu*). For this very reason, the Lord (*bhagavān*) is eternal and free from any other excellence, because there is no state of perishability. To the question "What is this absorption characterized by such qualities?", he says: "Possession of equal yoga with Him" (*tattulyayogitā*). This means possession of equal yoga—that is, co-existence—with that Śiva, having become one in essence (*samarasībhūta*).
Thus concludes the purification of the *nivṛtti-kalā*.
Salutation to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.

"Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the beginning of the mantra-words, the censured installation, and the bond of the *kalā*s. Having thus observed the pervasion of the *kalā*s, the most excellent of teachers, having taken up the cord of bonds according to the previously mentioned procedure, should apply this very mantra and rite to the disciple in the sequence beginning with the striking [of the body].
Having worshipped and gratified [the deity] in the fire, one should make this request:
"In this office, I shall initiate the seeker of liberation;
by the command of Śiva, may you be favorable to him who desires the welfare of Śiva.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśvarī), one should perform the invocation and other rites for the Fire-god.
And having subjected the disciple's self to beating and other such treatments as before,
O Goddess, one should take him and perform the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna).
Having performed [the rites] for expiation and offered oblations hundreds of times with his head bowed,
he likewise effects the removal of the obscuration of the power of impurity and the loosening of the bonds.
Having performed the cutting of the bonds and other rites, one should offer the white [substance] to Viṣṇu;
having invoked, worshipped, and gratified him with oblations in the fire by means of the heart-mantra.

Oṃ hāṃ! To Viṣṇu’s tongue, born from the overflowing [of the sacrificial vessel], for the grasping of the essence that dries up worldly existence—svāhā! As he, whose bonds are burnt, proceeds to the imperishable state of Viṣṇu, you must not perform any adornment; he has been bound by the command of Śiva.
Having thus informed Govinda and dismissed him as before,
he should extract the animal from the fire and join it with the *bindu* by means of the cord of bonds (*pāśasūtra*).
Having sprinkled [the offerings] into the fire for his parents and having satisfied them, he should likewise dismiss them.
Then, at the conclusion of the full oblation, one should perform the reconnection with the Root mantra and the Knowledge mantra.

"Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ huṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the bond of the *vidyā-kalā* of *pratiṣṭhā*. Having joined [the mantras] as before, one should offer five oblations with the root mantra. Thus ends the purification of the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*.

Salutation to Mahāgaṇapati. Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ hāṃ. With the mantras of the Vidyākalā—beginning with the words of the mantra for the one who is censured, who has the form of a woman, who is the form of reality (tattva), and who is the bond (pāśa) of the Vidyākalā—one should perform the rites of inspection and so forth as before.
Having taken up the Vidyā-pāśa and cast it into the fire, one should offer libations (tarpayet).
Having invoked [the deity] here and gratified [them], one should make this request there:
"In this office of Rudra, by the command of Śiva, you must perform an act of compassion and initiate this seeker of liberation who has reached the summit, through the grace of the Lord."
