Thus, having first joined the disciple’s self into the womb [of the fire] within the water, and having performed here also the rites of impregnation and so forth as before for himself, he should effect the purification of his own self by means of the topknot-mantra (*śikhā*), thereby concealing the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*).
And having performed the rites such as the loosening of the noose, one should offer white flowers to Rudra.

"Oṃ hāṃ! O Rudra, accept the white form and scent produced by the impairment of the eyes and nose; svāhā! Thus, for Rudra, whose bonds have been consumed, there is the characteristic of being marked by the scent of Śiva. Furthermore, by the command of Śaṅkara, you must not again cause obstruction.
Having thus informed Rudra and dismissed him as before,
one should contemplate the sequence beginning with the elevation of the self (ātmoddhāra) and ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), by means of the Vidyā-śānti mantra.
Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vidyā Śāntikalā and the two nooses;
with this mantra, one should offer five oblations using the root mantra.
Thus ends the purification of the Vidyā and Kalā tattvas.

Oṃ, obeisance to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati. Oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the one whose essence is the feet and other parts of the mantra, who possesses the form of woman and the form of reality, and who is the bond of the *śāntikalā*.
Thus, having observed the state of peace, and having bound [the victim] as before with beatings and other means, one should take the noose of the *kalā*, cast it into the fire, and offer libations.
Having invoked the Lord there into the heart, one should awaken Him according to the rule:
"In this office of the Lord, [awaken] this child who desires liberation."
O Lord, out of the impulse of compassion, I bestow grace within my own sphere;
then, the Self of the disciple is joined to the womb of Vāgīśvarī and so forth.
Having performed everything as before, one should perform the expiation with the *varman* mantra;
for the concealment of the power of impurity (*mala-śakti-tirodhāne*), one should offer five oblations with the *mala* mantra.
Having thus purified the path for the enjoyers, one should bestow [the powers] as follows:

Oṃ hāṃ! O Self, may *aṇimā* (atomicity) be yours, svāhā! Likewise, may *laghimā* (levity) be yours, svāhā! May *mahimā* (magnificence) be yours, svāhā! May *prāpti* (attainment) be yours, svāhā! May *prākāmya* (efficacy) be yours, svāhā! May *īśitva* (lordship) be yours, svāhā! May *vaśitva* (subjugation) be yours, svāhā! May *yatra-kāmāvasāyitva* (the power of abiding wherever one desires) be yours, svāhā!
Having proceeded in this manner, one should offer three oblations there with the *sruva* ladle itself in due order, and finally the *pūrṇāhuti* with the *śiva-mantra*.
Endowed with these qualities of sovereignty, one should unite [the soul] in the state of the Lord.
Therefore, having taken [the essence] from that body, one should join it to the Guru according to the prescribed rite;
then, for one who is detached from worldly enjoyment, there is the cessation of the power of impurity (mala-śakti).
The impurity of [lack of] qualification arises for him spontaneously;
because of that, there would be no attainment of the supreme state, and therefore he should bestow that [qualification].
Then, with the twentieth weapon-mantra, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*);
here also, according to the rule, if it is seedless (*nirbīja*), it is done with the *Śivāṇu* mantra.
Having offered two hundred full oblations, one should petition Śiva:
"O Blessed One, forgive me for any failure in maintaining the conduct of the observance."
Therefore, through this oblation, make all of that forgiven by yourself.
Having thus made the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), Gaṇeśāna, and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) witnesses,
the best of teachers should cause him to bind himself by the rules of conduct (samayas).
Then, O Blessed One, having performed the rite for the severance of the fetters of the sacrificial animal,
one should hold that cord of the fetter with the thumb and forefinger and move it,
as before, for the purpose of loosening the bonds of tranquility.
Having performed the oblation, the Guru should act as before with the *tattvāyus* thread.
Having performed the cutting of the bonds and other rites, one should offer the white goat with [the mantra]:
*oṃ hāṃ īśvara sarvaviplutikāraṇaṃ budhyahaṃkāra śukla gṛhāṇa svāhā*.
O Compassionate One, for this bound soul whose every fetter has been completely burnt away by Your lordship, there is no theft on Your part in exercising Your authority as its binder.
Having thus petitioned and dismissed the Lord, and having taken [the fire] from the hearth as before,
one should join the *aṇimā* at the end of the full oblation and perform the union of the digits (*kalā-sandhāna*).
Oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hauṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the bond of the *kalās* Śānti and Śāntyatīta. Having thus performed the union as before, one should offer five oblations with Śiva.
Thus concludes the purification of the Śāntikalā.

Oṃ, obeisance to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati. Having visualized with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the one who possesses the syllables of the mantra-words, the worlds, the principles (tattvas), impure karma, and Māyā; to the companion of Māyā; to the principle in the form of a woman; to the bond of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*)," one should take up the bond as before and cast it [into the fire].
Having invoked Śiva, known as Sādākhya, into the fire, one should address him thus:
O Blessed One, under your authority, I initiate this seeker of liberation.
You, being compassionate, must be favorable toward him;
having honored his parents and his garment as before, let there be salutation.
Having taken [the victim] by means of beatings and other such methods, and having joined him to the womb of the Goddess,
one should thus bring about for the sacrificial animal (paśu) everything from the rite of impregnation (garbhādhāna) onwards, as before.
And having first attained the expiation through Śiva as well as the qualities of the enjoyer,
one should unite [the soul] with the reality called Sādākhya, endowed with its own qualities.
For a detached animal (paśu), the rite to be performed is the attainment of sovereignty and confinement;
the weapon-mantra is recited twenty times with the root-mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the cessation of future karma at the conclusion of the rite,
the Guru likewise offers it for the cessation of the power (*śakti*) presiding over the fetters (*pāśa*).
Having performed the previous rites with the Astra-mantra during the application of the cords,
and having performed the cutting of the cords and so forth, one should offer the white [flower] to Śiva.

"Oṃ hāṃ! O Blessed One, accept this white [oblation] consisting of the *bindu*, which is the cause of all transformations; svāhā! Having thus offered three times with the ladle filled by means of a hymn, [one should recite]:
"This supreme Śivakara, who transcends the origin of worldly existence, has fulfilled his purpose through you; therefore, Sadāśiva must never be obstructed."
Having made this request, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra and perform the dismissal (*visarjana*).
For the sake of liberation from what was forgotten and so forth, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra and the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having offered oblations, struck, and separated [the bonds], one should restore the disciple's self to its former state.

Having gratified the Self with five oblations, saying "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane svāhā," and having thus purified and made it radiant, one should extract the Youthful One— who resembles the full autumnal moon— from the ear-ring; then, having joined him to that body and presented the *arghya* offering,
one should properly gratify the two Parents and, with devotion, address them as follows:
O Lords of all, you two parents have been troubled for the sake of your disciple through my artifice;
this offense of mine must be forgiven out of compassion.
Having made this request and having offered libations, one should give the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and perform the dismissal.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
One should perform the *sandhāna* (reconnection) for the Śāntyatīta [tattva] by means of the power of the *śikhā* (topknot).
Reciting "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Kalā and Śakti of Śāntyatīta," one should offer five oblations with the root mantra according to the procedure to be described hereafter.
Possessed of the supreme state through the sequential yoga like Viṣṇu,
he should unite the disciple— who abides in worldly dharma— with the highest station.

For one established in the Śivadharmas, the crest-lock (śikhā) is like a seed; one should consecrate the small knife (kartarī), which is the form of the digit of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), with the sword-mantra.

Oṃ hūṃ haḥ, *astrāya* huṃ phaṭ. And it is said: "The *kartarī* is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*); just as it cuts the bonds in the lower realm, so too is that supreme, subtle *kalā* the ultimate awakener of mantras."
"The cleaver (kartarī) should be known in the form of the agent by the best of teachers. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in the venerable *Haṃsapārameśvara*:
"The power of Śiva is to be known as inseparable; she is the *kartarī*, the destroyer of sins.

Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hauṃ hāṃ hūṃ tirobhāvikāṃ kuṭilaśaktiṃ cinasmihaḥ huṃ phaṭ. With this [mantra], one should cut the tuft of hair (śikhā), which is the nature of the obstructive power (ārodha-śakti) and the cause of all fetters (pāśas), at a distance of twelve finger-breadths.
For another [deity], it is eight finger-breadths higher; that which is called "seedless" (nirbījā) is for those with seeds (sabīja).

Having placed [the substance] mixed with honey and clarified butter into the middle of a cow-dung ball, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and performed the topknot-offering (śikhā), one offers five oblations with the Weapon-mantra (śastra).
With clarified butter and the mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ," one should reduce the topknot to ashes.
Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ hūṃ, I sacrifice the crooked power (kuṭilā-śakti) that causes concealment; haḥ huṃ phaṭ.
In the Kālottara:
"Initiation has been described previously as being both with seed (sabījā) and without seed (nirbījā)."
But for those beginning with the *kalās*, it is seedless (*nirbījā*) and devoid of the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*).

"For those who possess the seed-mantra (sabījā) and for those capable [of performing rituals], the offering of the crest-lock (śikhāhuti) should be performed together with the observance of the rules (samayācāra); this applies to both types of initiated ones.
Alternatively:
In some places it is stated: "Having performed the tonsure of the top-knot (śikhā), one should perform the bath for removing impurities.
And it has been said:
"The praise of worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti) is seen in the Śiva scriptures."
Therefore, immediately after that, the shaving of the head including the top-knot (śikhā) must be performed.
"Bathing with ashes should be performed by ascetics (*yatis*), while for householders it should be done with water;
and as bathing is prescribed in this world for one who has undergone a haircut, so it is here as well.
Regarding this, some state that only the "bali-bath" (*balisnāna*) should be performed by the word *yajati*. And it has been said:
One who desires liberation, or one who longs for release, having cut off the topknot,
should plunge into water and, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), become pure.
Thus ends the procedure for the cutting of the topknot.
Salutations to Śrī Mahāgaṇapati! Having bathed with water and also with ashes, and having sipped water (ācamana), the Guru himself,
having performed the purification of the elements (bhūta-śodhana), [should place] the radiant Hand of Śiva (śivahasta).
One should place it upon one's own head and contemplate the non-duality of Śiva.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the purification of the self (viśuddhi), the disciple, whose body is now composed of the recited mantra,
should, illuminated by the light from Śiva’s hand, behold the Guru and the Deity.
Having worshipped Śiva along with his disciples, and having satiated the mantras in the blazing sacrificial fire, the Guru, having kindled [the fire], should address a petition to Śiva as follows:
O Blessed One, by your grace, the six stages have been established;
having seized and purified the sacrificial animal, [the ritual proceeds] with the fire for the cutting of the crest-lock.
And by the method spoken from your own mouth, the worlds have been turned back by me;
therefore, through your power, one must go swiftly to the auspicious state of Dhruva.
Now, having followed your command, give me the order for that which must be performed by me; then, having joined this disciple [to his master], I shall depart.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods and received his permission, the Guru then took the two [disciples] and,
having washed them with warm water as before, made them listen [to the teachings].
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should meditate upon [the deity] as consisting of Śiva and Śakti.
And it is said:
"The base of the staff is the *kalaśa*, its purification is the *maṇḍala*-staff which ends in the *kalā*;
the hollow at the tip of the staff is *māyā*, and the altar (*vedi*) is the forgotten *vidyā*."
The placement of Indra and others upon variegated leaves is the binding of the flow of the corners.
That which is the hollow support is the lotus-seat;
that which is the locus of sound is the ear, whose opening is the form of Śakti.
p.
382) This power, which pervades all times, is that which fashions the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*);
likewise, it is the sacrificial spoon (*sruva*).
The staff is shaped like a sacrificial ladle (sruk) and a thread-measuring tool (sūtra), while the circle of the bindu is formed by its circular rotation.
"By the designation of the *sruk* and *sruva*, Sadāśiva is the mass of power (*śaktipiṇḍa*). Thus [it is said].

Then, having sprinkled the disciple who stands on his own left side in the mandala as before, and having performed the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the prescribed rule,
some authorities maintain that at this juncture— one which serves to block future karma subsequent to initiation— one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra.
"Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, which consist of the *pūrṇānta* [mantra], and having smeared and worshipped them,
one should make the fire blaze with its crest of flames and then draw in the self of the disciple"— thus they say.
O Śiva, whose form is pleasing to the eye, the Śakti [in the form of] the *sruva* ladle pours the nectar;
thus, holding the two [ladles] filled with clarified butter at the navel with the *śaṅkha-mudrā*.
Taking that child from his own left mandala as before,
he [places him] within the lotus of his own heart, shimmering like a radiant star with light.
Having established the two gurus in a state of aesthetic resonance (sāmarasya) by means of the self through the self,
standing with feet together, the mouth slightly open, and the mind serene.
Having joined the palate, the tip of the tongue, the throat, the heart, and the two eyes,
and having attained divine perception while maintaining the elevation of the body,
he performed the yoga of union through Śambhu, Kumbha, Ātman, and Vahni.
Having joined the tips of the sacrificial ladles with the nostrils for the sake of tasting the portions, [he should proceed].

Having performed inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*), one should pierce the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) with the exhaling breath (*recaka*) using the Śiva-sword: *oṃ hūṃ hāṃ huṃ phaṭ*.
Having performed the *vyāpuṭa* breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), one should contemplate the equinox (*viṣuva*) seven times;
the conjunction of the disciple’s self, vital breath, and mind is designated as "prāṇa."
Above the *mūlādhāra*, at the navel of the *kanda*, the heart, the tip of the pericarp,

the middle of the eyebrows, the forehead, the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*), the *śakti*, and the end of the twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśānta*)— these are indeed the ten knots (*granthi*) in sequence.
Having abandoned the root mantra by means of the trident, the resonance proceeds.
Through the union of the sound (nāda) and the nose (nāsī), that channel is considered the equinox (viṣuvat).
Having meditated upon the dissolution of the self's sound into the center from the navel,
through the conjunction and separation of the letters beginning with 'A' and 'U'.
From the heart to the aperture [of the crown], there is that which is designated as the Viṣumantra;
it consists of the phonemes *a* and *u*, and the phoneme *m* known as the Bindu.
Having abandoned the states known as *nāda* and *nādānta* in succession within Brahmā and the others,
one should lead the disciple’s self into dissolution in the seventh state, in the midst of Śakti. One should know that to be the state of perfect peace, wherein the range of the senses is stilled.
The Nāda situated within the Śakti spreads forth as the Samanāda;
that is declared to be the Viṣuva of the Śakti, while in Umā it is known by the name Kalā.
Having thus meditated upon these sevenfold [aspects], the best of teachers performs the Viṣuva.
Above that, in the eternal bliss of the mass of consciousness, the abode of all qualities,
obeisance to the Reality that transcends causes and is free from even the primordial source;
having gradually led the self to dissolution, one should offer it into the Fullness.
There, for the sake of stabilizing non-duality, one should again offer the *pūrṇāhuti*.
Having brought [the deity] back through re-emanation and having joined him once more to the fire of the *pūrṇā*, [one should proceed].
The practitioner of mantra should bring about qualities such as omniscience and the like.
Oṃ hāṃ! O Self, become possessed of infinite power; svāhā!

Having thus attained the sixfold qualities, and having taken up the self of the fire with a stream of clarified butter by means of the *sruva* ladle, it is purified by means of meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*).
Having assigned that [knowledge] to his body for the sake of experiencing the *prārabdha* karma,
one should join it to the head with the *arghya* water and impart the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Likewise, having resorted to the root ritual procedure of the mantra through the dual method,
and having relied upon the divine instrument, he is endowed with the supreme state.

Having gathered the two paths from the disciple, the self, the pitcher, the fire, and the mandala, and having projected them onto the path, one should take the breath as the sacrificial ladle situated at the nose.
At the outset, one should utter the *guruktaka* of the *dādi* [mantra] as follows:
the *kanda* above the penis, the navel, the heart, and the *karṇarūpikā*.
The tip of the *varṇikā*, the middle of the eyebrows, the forehead, the fruit of Brahmā,
the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*)— these ten are the knots of movement (*cāragranthi*).
For the sake of the accomplishment and liberation of mantras, this must be understood by the teachers and others:
having pierced the knots in due order with the trident of the root mantra.

Having led the self, which is endowed with the nature of consciousness, from the tip of the crest-lock to the palace [of the heart] until its dissolution, one should indeed withdraw all mental activity.
Meditating upon Śiva— the supreme, who is complete with the six qualities and a mass of consciousness and bliss— one should gradually dissolve the self and cause it to descend into the full [state].
"One should remain in the kumbhaka breath-retention for as long as the flow of clarified butter [is perceived];
when stability is attained, one should perform the unification and further cast the full oblation. Thus it is said.
In this state, when one is established in the self, one may cut off the topknot (śikhā); thus it is said in some places.
One should perform all rites on the entire path as before;
likewise, O Six-faced One, one should maintain the state of the Unmanifested (unmanī) at the end of the oblation.
Thus the external procedure has been declared; now hear that which pertains to the body, by means of which, when purified, the person (pudgala) attains purity—of this there is no doubt.
By means of the previously mentioned procedure and through the five concentrations (dhāraṇās),
one should purify all the principles (tattvas) residing within the body in their proper sequence.
Having yoked the sacrificial animal there as well, according to the previously mentioned procedure,
[he should offer it] into Śiva, who possesses authority, who transcends the crest-lock (śikhātīta), and who is as pure and stainless as crystal.
When this ritual action has been performed in this manner, the cutting of his topknot (śikhā) is ordained.
Having consecrated a pair of scissors seven times with the weapon-mantra (astra),
one should apply them to the site of the topknot, joined with the three sweets (trimadhura).
The knower of mantras should deposit [the deity] with the seed-syllable of the crest (śikhā) ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
thereafter, he should render it mindless, liberating it from its office.
One should employ the instrument [of consciousness] situated in the middle of the enclosure of the *śakti*,
within that which is inexpressible, supportless, ungraspable, and devoid of the mind.

The firm conclusion of the scripture is that liberation consists in being joined to the state beyond all ontological categories (niṣṭattva). With reference to this [state], ritual action is performed, preceded by the mantras and the deities.

O Six-faced One, that which is performed on Sunday according to the procedure seen in the scriptures certainly yields its fruit; however, that which is performed on Sunday without the prescribed rite does not.

"By that karma there is no accomplishment, no happiness, and no supreme goal. Now, one might object: "If the soul, though conjoined with the supreme reality (*paratattva*), is again assigned to a body of *māyā* for the sake of experiencing the fruits of its *prārabdha* karma, then how could the consequence of its return [to saṃsāra] not occur? This should not be said. Because there is nothing further to be experienced, immediately after the fall of the body, he attains union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*). And it has been said:
"Thus, one whose self is purified by initiation, even while remaining in the body, does not belong to the body."
Because all remaining bonds have been utterly consumed, he is liberated while living, with his consciousness fixed solely on Śiva.
"When the body has fallen away and one has attained the state of being of a single flavor with Śiva, who is consciousness and bliss,
one does not undergo division again, just as the water of a river [does not separate] from the ocean.
Thus it is stated in the Raurava.
Just as darkness quickly perishes upon the rising of the sun,
so too do merit and demerit perish upon attaining initiation.
Just as the sun illuminates these worlds with its rays,
so too, O Goddess, may the mantra-sacrifice illuminate the path to liberation.
Just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire,
even so have all the powers (śaktis) emerged from Śiva;
directed toward arrows, they pervade bodies.
Just as the sun, by means of its rays, draws up the water from the earth,
so too does the Lord, by means of His powers, draw forth the bound souls who have been initiated.
Just as water thrown into water, or milk poured into milk,
so too does the knower of mantras attain oneness with the Lord through initiation by means of the mantra.
Just as when a blazing fire is applied to a heap of cotton,
it is consumed and extinguished everywhere, and can never again become cotton;
even so, having attained the sacrifice of service arising from initiation and mantra—
Furthermore, that best of men who has been initiated does not undergo rebirth.
When the body has perished, having become Śiva and being endowed with the nature of Śiva,
one attains the bliss of Śiva and becomes fit for non-conceptualization.
Just as a river carrying pure water, upon reaching the ocean, attains the state of salty water through the power of that great sea; so it is here.
Thus, indeed, one whose self is separated from the body attains Śiva alone. Thus it is said.
Now, the procedure for the union with Śiva (*śivayojanikā*) as taught in the venerable *Mṛgendra-tantra*, which establishes the specific meaning of this [rite], is written here:

Having filled the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), while meditating, "May the purity of absolute freedom and the rest shine forth," one should cast it into the consciousness of Śiva.
Having superimposed the ladle (*sruc*) as the meditation, the neck of the jar is the *gaṇḍikā*;
the altar is the neck, and from the divisions beginning with *nivṛtti* arise at the tips of the mouth.
Having joined the channel (*nāḍī*) to its tip, one should deposit and take up the individual soul (*pudgala*).
Resembling the solar disc, transcending all bonds, and oriented toward Śiva,
it is the body of the Lord, the Praṇava, mounted upon the power of the vital breath.
The wise one, recollecting the infinite garland whose parts pervade all time, perceives the body of the garland as consisting of the final letter of the *bindu*, extending as far as the *puṣkara*.
That [state] is to be conceived as having grown forth from a stream of smooth sounds;

having been uplifted by the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti), one should lead it to the supreme abode of Śiva. Having brought the qualities (guṇas) right there, one should offer three oblations (āhuti) for the perfected ones (siddhas).
"The wise indeed desire that the injunction [of giving] should be independent and so forth. Thus it is said.

The explanation of this is as follows: "By the female serpent," and so forth. May the independence of this Self, along with its qualities such as satisfaction and beginningless consciousness, shine forth until the consciousness of Śiva. Meditating thus until the completion of the realization that is identical to the knowledge of Śiva, for the sake of that completion, [one should contemplate] within the ladle (*sruc*) the path of the *kalās* in the sequence beginning with Nivṛtti. Contemplating the trunk of the *kalās* upon the neck, the altar, the throat, the mouth, and the parts of the ladle, one should join the Suṣumṇā channel—which is the form of the Supreme Power—at its tip. Having thus taken up the individual soul (*pudgala*), which is the Self, by means of that Power, one should place it on the tip of the primary sacrificial ladle (*mukhyasruk*) within Śiva—the unspoken, supreme liberation—[the Self] being like the solar orb because its innate luster spreads forth, radiant and transcending the bonds (*pāśātīta*), having passed beyond the bonds such as those of the individual nature (*āṇava*). Then, regarding what one does next, he says: "Then, mounted upon the strength of the vital breath" (*prāṇabalārūḍham*), and so forth. That divine body, which is the form of the Praṇava and the form of the entire sacrifice, is non-different from the ladle and is mounted upon the power of the vital breath.

(p. 389) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-svabhāva). "Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is the grasping of names and characteristics (nāmanimitta) based on the dependent self-nature; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and imagining it to be a snake. This is called the imagined self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of various appearances arising from the causal conditions of ignorance, karma, and mental impressions (vāsanā); it is like a dream or a reflection. This is called the dependent self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state in which the dependent self-nature is seen as being eternally free from the imagined self-nature; it is the realization that all phenomena are originally unborn and non-dual. This is called the perfected self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the Great Vehicle? It is the realization that all phenomena are the Tathāgata-garbha, which is the Dharmakāya, the realm of reality (dharmadhātu), and the ultimate truth (paramārtha); it is the teaching that transcends all conceptual proliferation (prapañca) and is the domain of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. This is called the self-nature of the Great Vehicle. "Mahāmati, if one does not understand these four kinds of self-nature, one will fall into the views of eternalism or nihilism. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should cultivate wisdom through skillful means and enter into the stage of the Tathāgata. Thus spoke the Blessed One, and the World-Honored One, having thus spoken, further addressed the Venerable Mahāmati with these verses: "The imagined nature is like a flower in the sky, The dependent nature is like a dream or illusion; The perfected nature is the absence of duality, This is the self-nature of the Great Vehicle. When this was taught, the Venerable Mahāmati and the assembly of great Bodhisattvas, having heard the Buddha’s words, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

One should meditate upon [the Self] as abiding in unity with that which has been divided. To the question, "Having done what after that, what should one do?", he says: "At the end of the *bindu*," and so forth. That which has the *bindu* at its end, existing as the cause, is the *praṇava* (the syllable Om). By the phrase "according to the rule of the lotus," the meaning is that it should be visualized as far as the ear-lotus. Then, "arisen from that": having arisen from that lotus in the form of the *praṇava*, the *dhvani* (sound) which is smooth (*snigdha*), which—by the root-meaning of *uṣṇīha* in the sense of "delight"—vibrates with supreme bliss (*parānanda-spandī*), is of the nature of that [bliss]; [this is] the praise (*stuti*) of that [bliss]. Upon that [praise], one should mount—that supreme power (*parā-śakti*) should be placed above it. Having joined the disciple’s self with Śiva, who resides within the flame of the fire, by means of that Śiva-power, and having lifted him up and drawn him out from there, one should lead him to, or cause him to reach, the supreme, most excellent abode of Śiva, the splendor of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-tejaḥ*).

Now, as to what should be done, he says: "The qualities," and so forth. In that very fire, one should cause the qualities of that Self—such as omniscience and the rest—which are established for oneself, to be attained individually by means of three oblations each; having thus caused those qualities, which are established for all, to be stimulated because they were situated within the *pāśakūṭa*, one should join them [to the Self].

[Objection: Surely, by the mere removal of the veil of impurity (*mala-āvaraṇa*), the manifestation of the qualities such as sovereignty (*svātantrya*) occurs naturally; what is the purpose of this [further] effort? To this he replies with the words beginning "of the injunction regarding sovereignty, etc. (*svātantryādividheḥ*): The wise ones—the learned masters (*sūri*), omniscient ones such as Śrī Nandikeśvara and others—desire such ritual action precisely for the sake of establishing the unsurpassed firmness of the realization of one's own nature, which consists in the awakening to the qualities such as sovereignty, fullness, and satisfaction. Now, that which was introduced is being stated.
Thus, when the matter has been introduced, the initiation that bestows liberation has been declared;
having joined [the disciple] who is fit for the rank of an Ācārya to the supreme state, (p.
Thereafter, one should arrange for his enjoyment in his own office;
having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as before with the root mantra and a hundred-fold oblation.
Having taken [the substance] with the *pūrṇā* [offering], having joined it at the end of the flame in the reverse order, O Śivā,
and having brought forth the Gaṇas, one should enjoin them into that body according to the rule.
This Ananta should offer the *arghya* on the head at the tip of the ring finger;
this is for the pacification of the exhaustion born from the descent of the intense *aṇu-śakti*.
Then one should perform the worship in this manner and measure the proportions of the *liṅga* and so forth.
Having established the self as Śiva and the fire in the southern mandala of Śiva, he should then inform Śiva regarding the disciple:
"May this one, favored by you alone, attain my liberation."
Therefore, O Lord, increase the enjoyment of this [debt] through the fires of the qualities;
by your grace, may his unbroken ritual practice be restored.
O, let there be no cause for bondage through negligence or transgression on his part.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, he then went to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit and,
for the sake of liberation from deficiencies and other faults, performed one hundred and eight recitations with the root mantra.
Having performed the concluding oblation (*pūrvāvasāna*) and likewise the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*),
he should then offer the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) as before and present the great final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Then, having dismissed the Lord of Devas, he should offer the *bhūḥ*-oblation and the others.
Having offered the inner and outer bali offerings, one should perform the dedication of the ritual action.
Or, in the northeast quarter, upon a full mandala marked with a svastika.
One should perform the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) for Śambhu with a water-pot (*kumbha*), preceded by the water of the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Then, in the fire, one should offer the remainder of the sacrifice with a thousand or a hundred [oblations].
Having gratified him, one should dismiss Caṇḍanātha with the words, "Forgive me."
Thus, at the request of his disciple, this procedure for the initiation of *kalā* has been composed by the venerable Śivajñānaśambhu,
in accordance with the scriptures and according to his own understanding.
Thus concludes the initiation of the Kalās.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Now, the initiation of the three principles (tritatva) is described here according to its application:
having prepared the water for sprinkling as before, one should proceed in sequence through the five streams.

Having performed the placement (vinyāsa) of the three principles (tattva-traya) and placed the Hand of Śiva upon his own head, one should then contemplate the non-duality with Śiva; then, having joined the disciple’s crest-lock to the maṇḍala with the cord of bonds (pāśasūtra), one should likewise join the channel of power (śaktināḍī) as before.
Having taken from the body of the disciple the powers beginning with Vāmā and the others in that same manner.

Likewise, having placed the self, along with the water for the *āṇava* and other initiations, within the thread from the body of knowledge, one should then place that body— which is censured by the sixfold [impurities]— into the thread.
Beginning from the crest-lock up to the forehead, from the forehead to the ends of the ears,
and from below the throat down to the feet— these are known as Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman.

Having performed the placement of the three principles through emanation, and then having satiated and inflamed the fetters with the *śambhara* mantras "HŪM HĪM HĀM," one should worship Śiva upon the crown of the head.
One should perceive the pervasion of the kalā beyond tranquility within the Śiva-tattva.

"Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ hāṃ! To the fetters of the world of phonemes (*varṇa*), the worlds (*bhuvana*), the principles (*tattva*), the aspects (*kalā*), impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*), illusion (*māyā*), and that which belongs to illusion (*māyīya*)—to the Śiva-principle of the woman, obeisance! Having thus observed, the Guru, according to the previously mentioned procedure, should apply the striking and other rites to his head and thread. Then, he should contemplate the pervasion of the *śāntikalā* within the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*). "Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ hāṃ! To the womb of the mantra-words and so forth—to the fetter of the principle of knowledge, obeisance!"
Having taken it from that body, one should place it upon the thread at the mouth;
then, one should contemplate the pervasion of the remaining kalās within the principle of the Self (ātmatattva).
Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, salutation to the fetter of the reality of the self, which is encapsulated by the beginning of the mantra-words.
Having thus taken up that [substance] with the *aṇu* mantras and so forth, and having performed the striking and other rites in sequence,
one should worship and satisfy it within the thread from below the throat down to the feet.
Having worshipped the power (śakti) that resides at the limit of the noose and likewise the one that obstructs knowledge,
one should take her from that body, join her to the thread, and offer libations.
At the end of the plow, and upon the neck-thread dyed with saffron and other pigments,
one should worship the Lord of Gods there, as before, using the seed-syllable.
Having set aside the pledges and so forth, the supreme guru, recollecting [the disciple], should bind the noose of the disciple's vital energy (tejas) by means of confinement, just as before.
Having performed the striking and the separation, one should perform the seizing and binding.
Having placed the thread upon the shoulder of the disciple seated below,
and having offered a hundred oblations with the root mantra ending with the full oblation, the descent of the thread is accomplished.
Having performed [the rites], one should offer it into the water-pot as before, beginning with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having given that, one should cause the deity to rest upon what is called the "superior seat" (adhicāsana).
Salutations to Śrī Mahāgaṇapati.
Having performed all daily and occasional rites at dawn,
[the master], preceded by the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), [proceeds] for the disciple situated within the mandala.
One should bind that thread upon the crest [of the disciple], preceded by the ritual convergence (sampāta);
then one should install the Śakti, the channels (nāḍīs), the path (adhvan), and the Self (ātman) as before.
One should worship the deity on the crown after offering a hundred oblations into the fire with the root mantra;
at the conclusion of the full oblation, one should perform the satiation and the kindling for all the mantras.
Then, having placed the power (śakti) of the girl into the vessel, and having worshipped and gratified her,
one performs the rites of striking, piercing, entering, separating, drawing out, gathering, taking,
and establishing within oneself; then, having extracted [the essence] from that, one performs the application.
Having performed that with the *tattvāṇus*, one should worship and offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) into the fire beginning with the *tattvas*.

The mantras are as follows: "Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *pāśa* (bond) of the *ātmatattva*, including the mantra-words, phonemes, worlds, *tattvas*, impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and the *māyīya-saciva*. These and others are the mantras.
Having first informed Brahmā and the other causal deities there as before,
and having performed the invocation and other rites upon the son while recollecting the Yoga, [he should proceed].
Having sequentially performed the striking and other rites, and having placed the *aṇu* within Vāgīśī,
one should prepare the *arghya* for oneself and the desired [deity], and then perform the formal petition in due order.
Just as one who knows the ritual procedures previously [described] [acts] simultaneously in all wombs.
Having performed the installation and the generation [of the deities], and having withdrawn the enjoyment of the Lord,
one should perform everything— the purification of the principles of the currents (srotas-tattva)— in the same manner as for all [other rites].
One should contemplate atonement with the Śiva-mantra within the three principles (tattvas).
The concealment of the intermediate power, as well as the severance of the fetters,
must be performed by means of the *tattva-weapon* itself; likewise, the cutting and crushing of the fetters [are to be done].
From those two, there is the absence of that sprout and the expiation as before.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] and having invoked Brahmā, one should offer the white [garment] to him.

Having made this request: "Oṃ hāṃ, O Brahmā, accept the sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, which are white; svāhā," and having bound an atom (aṇu) to his body to prevent obstruction, one should release the power (śakti) at the end of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and perform the reintegration of the principles (tattvasandhāna).

Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ hiṃ hāṃ, salutation to the two principles of the Self (ātmatattva) and Knowledge (vidyātattva). Then, having performed this likewise for that which consists of Knowledge, one should abandon the white [syllable] with the syllable *haḥ*.
"Oṃ hāṃ, O Viṣṇu, accept the intellect and ego, which are white, svāhā!
Having thus applied the *aṇu* (the soul) to that body, one should perform the conjunction of the principles (*tattva-sandhāna*).
"Oṃ hāṃ hiṃ hūṃ hāṃ, salutation to the two principles of Knowledge (vidyā-tattva).
Having performed everything there as before, one should invoke Rudra into the principle whose nature is Śiva, satisfy him with libations, and offer the bride-price (śulka) to him.
"Oṃ hāṃ, O Rudra-mind, accept this bride-price, svāhā! Having thus employed the subtle mantra at the end of the full oblation, one should cause the principle (tattva) to dissolve into the Śakti.

"Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ hauṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Śiva-tattva and the two powers of the crest (śikhā). Having thus severed that crest as before and offered oblations, one should perform the bathing and other rites. Thereafter, one should purify the body with the five subtle mantras (aṇus).
Having become the embodiment of the Śiva-mantra, one should place the hand of Śiva upon oneself;
having done the same for the disciple, one should then proceed through the five streams in due order.
Having fully worshipped the devotee of the Paśu [tradition] and having gratified the mantras, one should kindle them; then,
having informed the Lord of Gods and received his permission, one proceeds as before.

Having taken the disciple's self through beatings and other means, having cast it into one's own self and made it of equal flavor (samarasīkṛtya), one should contemplate the piercing (vedha) in seven ways.
The Guru, stationed within the tip of the lotus of the palace in the supreme state,
having united [the disciple] with that which is preeminent in qualities and having brought him into his own body, should employ him.
The venerable Jñānaśivācārya, who knew the essence of the Śaiva Āgamas and turned his back upon the scriptures of the bound souls (paśu),
performed the initiation consisting of the three principles (tritattvika).
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for initiation into the three principles (tritatva).
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇapati.
Now, the initiation into the single reality (ekatattva-dīkṣā) is taught in brief:
having completed all the preliminary rites such as the sacrifice, and having performed the binding of the thread with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
One should place the Śakti, the Weapon, the Body, the Knowledge-mantra, and the Self as before; one should then conceive of the thrill of that body, the threefold resonance, and the Śiva-principle.
One should then join the power presiding over the noose (pāśa), as well as the obstruction of knowledge (jñānarodha),
and subsequently the pervasion of the five kalās, into the Śiva-tattva.
"Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the bond of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva-pāśa) which is censured by the words of the mantra.
Having applied [the mantra] through striking and other rites, one should perform the binding upon the thread.
Then, having worshipped Śiva and offered a hundred oblations upon its head, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Then, in the morning, having performed all the ritual acts in their entirety,
he should bind the thread upon his crest-lock with the Śiva-mantra until the conclusion of the expiation.
The remainder [of the ritual] is as before, up to the offering of water for the feet and the conclusion of the expiation;
having fully worshipped Rudra and offered libations, one should present a white garment to him.

Having prayed thus: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ! Accept the white form of the drop (bindu) consisting of sound, touch, taste, form, smell, intellect, ego, and mind—svāhā!"—one should unite the self with the body through the worship that effects liberation from bondage. Then, having dismissed the two parents and offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should [dissolve] the principle (tattva) by means of the Śiva-mantra.

"Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ haiṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Śiva-tattva and the powers of the crest (śikhā-śakti). Having thus joined [the mantras], having cut the crest with the crest-mantra, and having offered it into the fire, he should immerse [the disciple].
There too, the Guru should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth, as previously described.
Having united the self with the Pūrṇā and attained the qualities as before,
one should then join it to that body and sprinkle it with the water of Śiva.
In this manner, one should likewise release the sacrifice; such is the single reality and the sequence of the ritual, as taught by the venerable master Jñānaśivācārya, the mountain of existence.
Initiation is declared by the knower of the Siddhānta to consist of a single reality.
The thirty-sixfold initiation pertaining to the principles (tattvas) has been taught in the Kālottara-āgama;
it is now being written down for the sake of understanding its function and pervasion.
Beginning with Kālāgni in due order, join each [element] with its respective deity;
then, having again joined the progenitor, eliminate the attributes by means of the attributes.
By means of all the duties toward a husband, cast off the duties toward a beast;
and by means of the auspicious duties, O Niṣka-less one, cast off even those duties toward a husband.

Furthermore, during the ritual bath, one should again offer oblations in sequence for the sake of [attaining] birth, sovereignty, the procurement of its enjoyments, and the dissolution of the qualification.
For example:
having first joined with the reality (tatva), the wise one should sacrifice in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
397) One's own name [should be placed] in the ritual of grasping the mantra of all the principles (*tattva*);
however, in the midst of the principles, one should place the *gāyatrī* fashioned according to the procedure of one's own mantra.
Having grasped the *paśu*, the knower of reality should unite it within the womb of reality;
the tip of the nose is the fixed point for the act of seizing the *paśu*.
One should meditate on the individual soul (jīva) as consisting of the short seed-syllable, having the nature of knowledge and the form of a mass of light;
then, having struck it with the weapon-seed syllable, one should withdraw it by means of the heart-mantra.
Having withdrawn [the breath] through the path of the yoni, one should direct it toward the left;
the *garbhādhāna* (conception) rite is performed with the *sadya* [fire], while the *puṃsavana* (male-making) is traditionally taught for the left.

One should bestow sovereignty with the seed-syllable of the weapon (*astra*) during the birth-rite (*jātakarman*); Īśāna during the naming ceremony; Hṛdaya during the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*);
Authority with the Head (*śiras*); and Enjoyment with the Topknot (*śikhā*).
One should offer oblations for the dissolution of sovereignty with the seed-syllable of the weapon and the armor-mantra.
Having offered a full oblation with ten offerings for each [deity] by means of Śiva,
the purification of the channels is performed with the ten Brahma-aṅgas in successive order.
With Śiva, one should perform the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi) among all the principles.

The tenfold oblation should be described here; whatever is unsurpassed in this regard must be understood through the various sections of the text. One who knows the mantras should perform the severing of bonds, as well as their burning and the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*), by means of the *astra* seed-syllable, and thereby purify the hells.

In this regard, although the sequence of ritual action has been presented here in brief, that supreme and excellent [practice] should be understood clearly through the instruction of a guru. It is as follows:
397) Having unified reality with reality, one should pierce it with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.
Having joined [the breath] with the Jyeṣṭhā [vowels], one should then again extract it with the Raudrī [consonants].
O Six-faced One, this rite should be performed in detail according to that specific injunction for each respective reality within the world of action, on the surface of the earth.
In the principle of Kālāgnirudra, one should purify the state of Kālāgni;
having offered the Dharma into the hell-beings in Naraka, one should lead them to the state of Kūṣmāṇḍa.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) with the seventh [syllable] Ananta in Pātāla, one should purify;
here, "Ananta" refers to the Lord of the Kaṭāha, who consists of Rudra-Ananta.
Then, one should subsequently join the principle of Hāṭaka to the world of Bhūloka.

Having purified the city of Hāṭakeśvara—this being the remainder [of the process]—one should join the disciple’s self to Vāgīśī in the belly of Bhūloka. Then, with the Sadyojāta mantra, one should offer oblations in sequence: for stationary beings with the Viṣātmā (Vāmadeva) mantra, for reptiles with the Ghora mantra, for birds with the Puruṣa mantra, and for domestic animals with the seed-syllable of Īśāna. For the immobile, however, one should use the Sadyojāta mantra. Thus, having joined the disciple’s self to the immobile, one should perform the homa for the mobile beings starting from the reptiles. For the bird-nature, one uses the Ghora; for the animal-nature, the Puruṣa; and for the human-nature, the seed-syllable of Īśāna. One should perform the homa in this successive order.
Having offered each [oblation] with ten mantras, one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in due order.
At this point, it is stated elsewhere: "The state of being a dog-cooker (śvapaca) and the Caṇḍāla-mantra should be recited seven times;
one should offer oblations of their various divisions and subdivisions with the Saṃhitā mantras."
The knower of the ritual procedure [should worship] with the Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and Hṛdaya mantras.
"For one should perform the *homa* [offering] starting from the status of a *śūdra*, in successive order up to the status of a *vaiśya*.

Having thus performed the *homa* for himself, the most excellent teacher [should proceed]; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. And having united [the disciple] with the external womb (*bāhyayoni*), he should perform this ritual procedure."
The impregnation ceremony (garbhādhāna), the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana), and likewise the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
Birth, the rite of departure from the womb, and the first feeding of solid food— among these,
the rite of departure from the womb is to be performed with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, while the remainder is prescribed by the *brahma-mantras*.

In this context, among the seven sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*, the *niṣkrāmaṇa* is not [performed]; it should be performed with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. It should be understood that the remaining six sacraments are traditionally prescribed to be performed with the ten oblations (*daśāhuti*) using the *brahma-mantras*.
The *caula* and *upanayana* should be performed in sequence with the ten *brahmāṅga-mantras*.
The girdle, the upper garment, the staff, and likewise the black antelope skin.
Vedic study, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions;
begging for alms, respectful salutation, silence, celibacy, compassion, and self-restraint.
Approaching the guru, recitation, non-censure, lack of longing, silent prayer,
non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, forbearance, and absence of malice.
Likewise, among living beings, there is worldliness, gentleness, modesty,
steadiness, vigor, forbearance, fortitude, purity, lack of malice, and freedom from arrogance.
One should offer these ten times with the Gāyatrī mantra according to all the prescribed sequences; likewise, the Upākarma, Godāna, and Mahāvrata rites are performed three times.
One should offer the Naiṣṭhikī and the Asidhārā oblations with the Pāśupata mantra;
thereafter, the homa performed with clarified butter is said to consist of the limbs of Śiva.
One should again perform the union with the wife by means of the limbs of Brahmā;
having made the wife consist of the embryo, one should unite her with the syllable "Om."
Together with her, one should perform sacrifices in sequence, beginning with the *pākayajñas*;
for the sake of expiation regarding offspring, one should offer twenty-five oblations.
Then, knowing the ritual procedure, he should perform the *pākayajña* with the heart-mantra,
as well as the *aṣṭakā*, the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, the *śrāvaṇī*, and the *āgrayaṇī*.
The full moon days of Caitra and Āśvayuja are known as the *pākayajñas*.
Each [rite] consists of five *brahmans*, and for each there are ten oblations.
[These are performed] fivefold among the gods, the ancestors, humans, the spirits (*bhūta*), and the *brahmans*.
The Āgneyī brick, the Agnihotra, the Darśa, and likewise the Paurṇamāsī;
The Cāturmāsya, the Nirūḍhapaśu, and likewise the Sautrāmaṇī are declared to be the Havis-yajñas; one should perform the oblations with the limbs of the Brahman in their proper sequence.

Each [deity] is addressed with ten mantras, and there are ten oblations for each. The Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Vājapeya, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Atirātra, and Aptoryāma are known as these forms of the Soma sacrifice.
With the limbs of Brahmā, the Śiva-gāyatrī, the Great Weapon, and Śiva himself.
One should offer twenty oblations for each [deity] for the sake of purification;
thereafter, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in all rites involving consecratory refinements.
In whichever purificatory rite one performs the fire-oblation with Śiva— who is fully immersed and raining nectar—
one should omit a single *pūrṇāhuti* and perform that [remaining ritual] twice over.
At the conclusion of the Soma-saṃsthās, however, one should offer oblations of Soma-drink with all the mantras, each recited once, using curd, milk, ghee, and honey.
In the midst of a thousand sacrifices, one should offer ten supreme sacrifices.
Then, having performed thirty oblations with each of the thirty [verses] and with the *jana* verse,
the wise one performs twenty-five oblations for the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
By means of the Śiva-mantra, the knower of mantras certainly becomes a householder;
thereafter, in the forest-dweller stage (vānaprastha), he performs the fire-oblation (homa) with all mantras in five ways.
Having performed the renunciation of everything in that [fire], one becomes a monk (bhikṣu). One should offer the state of being a monk into that [fire] with all the mantras, once each.

Then, having contemplated the separation from the body in this world of beings (bhūloka), and having completed the rites beginning with the purification of the channels and the purification of the principles up to the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should unite the world of beings with the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka). Having then completed that realm, beginning with Mohana and ending with Śānti, one should then—once the rites in the worlds such as Svaḥ, Mahas, Jana, Tapas, Satya, and Dhruva have been performed—establish the self, purified of all taints, once again in the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka).
Having performed the reconnection as before and likewise having divided [the vessel] again,
one should worship the deities as previously done and perform the ritual procedure prescribed for the full oblation.
One who knows the ritual rules, being well-composed, should offer oblations for the state of Brahmā, the state of Vāsudeva, and the state of Rudra, according to the sequence as before.
Having split the cauldron as before, he should [offer for] the ten Rudras and the lords of the directions.
One should worship the seed-syllable on the crown of the head according to the previously described procedure.
One should place Śambhu upon the Mantra-siṃhāsana; one should place Śambhu in the east, Agni and Rudra in one's own directions, Kāla in the south,
Bhayānaka in the southwest, and Mahābala in the west.
Having assigned Śoṣaṇa in the northwest and likewise Kāmarūpa in the north,
one should then assign Rudra, the locus of all vidyās, in the northeast.
One should worship all of them with their respective mantras— Śiva, Śambhu, and Īśvara—
having performed the libation in the mandala according to the previously described procedure.
Then, having ignited the state of Śambhu-Rudra, one should purify it;
for the remaining [impurities], one should offer expiation with twenty oblations each, in due order.

Having thus purified the principle of earth (*pārthiva-tattva*), one should apply the principle of water (*vāruṇa-tattva*). "As before" is the specific instruction. Likewise for fire, air, and ether; and for the ego (*ahaṃkṛti*) and the quality of passion (*rajas*). Here, having reflected with the intellect of the preceptor that the purification of the subtle elements (*mātrās*) belonging to the principle of ether must be performed, and that the eleven organs—the organs of action, the organs of perception, and the mind—are included within the principle of the ego, one should understand that a fire-oblation (*homa*) must be performed for their purification.
In the principles of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, which consist of Rāga, Vidyā, and Kalā;
in the principle of Kāla, which consists of Māyā; and likewise in Vidyeśvara and Vidyeśvara.
[He meditates] always upon Śiva, likewise upon the Tattva, and likewise upon the Sakala and Niṣkala [forms];
upon the dharmas that are lords of all tattvas, and likewise upon the supreme dharmas of the tattvas.
"Having purified in the manner described by this rite, one should place [the consciousness] into the cause (kāraṇa) and the emergent (udvaṇa).
Thus it is said regarding mantras, phonemes, worlds (bhuvanas), and states (padas).
An enlightened teacher should perform initiation for those previously mentioned who possess the [required] pervasion (vyāpti).
Likewise, in the *Siddhāntasāra*:
"The Guru should first project the sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidham adhvānam*) into the body of the disciple;
having determined that which is to be purified as one, [he does so] through pervasion, drying, and transcendence."
Having observed [the thread] with the *sṛṣṭi* [mudrā], having made it into a thread according to that rule, and having bound it with the *tāḍava* [mudrā],
one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsa*) and then carry out the purification three or twice over.
The mantra consists of the letters beginning with *sa* and so forth for the one to be purified, while the letters beginning with *ka* follow the sequence of the *ātman*.
Alternatively, one may purify the groups of consonants (*varga*) according to the sequence of the group beginning with *śa*.
Having first established the fire of time (kālāgni) and the worlds in their proper sequence,
one should worship the Śakti there, having joined oneself to it.
Having performed the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, one should unite [the disciple] in the supreme state;
starting from the final *praṇava*, I shall declare eighty-one [syllables].
One should purify [the soul] in due order, beginning with *garbhādhāna* and so forth as before;
having performed all rites sequentially from the *pārthiva-tattva* up to the *śiva-tattva*, one should unite the individual soul (*aṇu*) with the eternal [Śiva].
The kalās, which are censured throughout all the paths and consist of the cessation of that [ignorance] and anger, must be purified with effort; their procedure is now being stated.
Having sequentially joined Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti,
one should then again bring them all together simultaneously with Śāntyatīta.
Having worshipped Brahmā, Keśava, Rudra, Ananteśa, and Sadāśiva within the heart and having gratified them, one should invoke Śakti and offer libations.
"Having joined [the disciple] with the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, one should perform the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*.
Purified by initiation, being born within the maṇḍala of Gaṇapati and the Guru, they become perfected beings (*siddha*) through mantras, their bodies radiant like the orb of the sun."

Having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time, those who have taken on the forms of classes of immortal women become possessors of the sovereignty of the supreme state of Śiva, free from longing. Thus it is said.
Thus, by the power of the merit of meditating upon the lotus of Śiva’s feet,
having had the flood of his sins removed and attained the awakening to the Siddhānta,
[he reached] the severer of the dense, partless bonds— the sixfold path— ...
Śambhu performed the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*) which makes [the truth] clearly manifest.
Thus ends the procedure for the sixfold path initiation (*ṣaḍvidhādhvadīkṣā*).
Thus, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*, the procedure for initiation has been proclaimed.
Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati!
Having performed one of these initiations for the disciple,
the preceptor [should possess] those characteristics previously described for preceptors in the Śiva-āgama.
For one who possesses the characteristics [of a practitioner] and is devoted to the *saṃhitā*,
the teacher should prescribe the *saṃhitā-vrata* for the sake of attaining success in that mantra,
[staying] on a holy mountain such as Śrīśaila or in a sacred field (*kṣetra*) within a forest retreat.
There, in a place endowed with flowers and fruits, prepared with earth and kusha grass, auspicious, filled with the presence of the illustrious Maheśvara, or otherwise delightful;

One should abandon a place of practice that is infested with disease, thieves, or wild animals; frequented by rogues, women, or atheists; or which is a field for other sects such as Buddhists, even if it is a site of spiritual accomplishment.
In that regard, one should take refuge in a self-manifested (svayambhūta) linga that is complete in all its limbs, facing westward— or, in the absence of such, facing eastward.

A wise person should avoid a site that has been established by sages, perfected beings, and others, or one conceived by oneself, even if it is claimed to have been consecrated by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, or the Mothers.
Together with Umā, Maheśvara, Skanda, Kṣetrapāla, and Gaṇeśvara.
One should avoid the Śatalinga, the Sahasrāka, and the Mukhalinga;
one should also avoid the Bhogalinga, which consists of dance, instrumental music, song, and the like.
One should avoid a linga that faces south when it is intended for the north, as it is deficient in its characteristics.
Having selected the desired linga, one should place it to the south, outside the Jagatī (enclosure), and staying in a pleasant monastery with a serene mind at evening... [the rest of the verse].
Or, one should practice the attainment of the body (kāyasiddhi) in the vicinity of one's own chosen *liṅga*,
either by means of *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, or by subsisting on sacrificial oblations (*haviṣya*) and eating only once a day.
Endowed with the observance of fasting and subsisting even on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should constantly practice the Praṇava by restraining the functions of the vital breath.
Having resolved to complete one hundred thousand recitations within six months,
one should chant the Aghora-weapon mantra and the Aghora mantra ten thousand times each.
At the conclusion of that, having worshipped Śiva and offered libations, one should perform the recitation (*japa*).
This is declared to be the purification of the body (*kāyaśuddhi*). Having performed the sacrifice as before, one should consecrate oneself with the *prāsāda* mantra using the water of Śiva.
Then, joined by his companions, he should perform the rites of concealment;
he should carry out the daily duties of bathing, worship, recitation, fire-oblation, and other regular rituals.
When one's own chosen *liṅga* is stable and under one’s own control, or likewise in water,
one should subsequently recite the root mantra five hundred thousand times without being bound by formal constraints (*atantrita*).
Neither delayed, nor indistinct, nor hurried, and free from confusion.
Having determined that "the recitation shall be this much every day," one should carry it out;
likewise, one should daily perform the subsidiary rites and the fire-oblation (homa) at one-tenth of that amount.
With cow’s ghee, offerings of food mixed with clarified butter, black flowers, or auspicious sesame seeds,
one should offer to Śambhu the fruit of the multitude of recitations and burnt offerings according to one's capacity.
One should pass the days considering the body to be impermanent, O Lord;
at the conclusion of the recitation, one should especially worship the God, the Lord of Gods.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) especially, having fed the ascetics,
and having gratified all other Māheśvara brāhmaṇas according to one's ability,
one should dedicate all actions, bow to Śambhu, and ask for his forgiveness.
Thus one should recite this mantra according to the number prescribed by Śrī Śivajñānaśambhu,
so that the teachers may possess the power to sever the bonds.
Thus ends the ritual for the Saṃhitā vow in the Jñānaratnāvalī.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Now, [the teacher should initiate] a disciple who has fulfilled his vows, who is proficient in the meaning of the Saṃhitās,
whose limbs are complete, and who belongs to the highest of all castes and lineages.
One should sprinkle the most noble being, whether he be one observing vows or one who has taken possession [of the state].
And it has been said:
"In this Siddhānta, the status of being an Ācārya has been established by Śiva for all four castes, as well as for those bearing sectarian marks and those observing vows."
In due order according to their castes, he [chose] one among those boys—
Satyavrata— who was supremely devoted to truth, peaceful, endowed with self-sacrifice, and full of compassion.
One who has a serene countenance, is skillful, the most excellent of teachers, and free from fickleness.
One who is perfectly endowed with purity and right conduct, disciplined in yoga, having conquered the senses,
a devotee of Śiva, always self-controlled, and one who has reached the further shore of the Śaiva Siddhānta.

"Having performed the sacrifice as prescribed and completed the initiation, the knower of mantras should then consecrate the disciple who is proficient in discerning what is appropriate and inappropriate.
Thus it is said. Furthermore:

He who thoroughly understands this compendium— consisting of three categories and four quarters, which brings about the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation— is indeed worthy of being a disciple.
Likewise:
"The Guru is said to be twofold—consisting of four mantras—due to the distinction in his mode of conduct;
their characteristics are now correctly stated for the sake of brief understanding."
In that region, he should be endowed with virtue, conduct, devotion, power, and action; he must always be vigilant regarding the restraint of violence and be accompanied by assistants.
The teacher should be of steady intellect, endowed with sattva, having conquered the pairs of opposites, and having mastered his senses;
he should also possess unwavering application due to the firmness of the practitioner.
Furthermore, such a teacher must be well-proportioned in form and possessed of learning and virtuous conduct.
He was neither lacking a limb nor possessing an extra limb; he was neither too tall nor too short; he was neither too dark nor too fair; and he was neither too stout nor too thin.
He is neither too young nor too old, neither lustful nor excessively so;
his conduct is unimpaired, and he does not possess divided wealth.
Nor [should one initiate] one who is like ashes, one called "sprout," a eunuch, a *kuṇḍa*, or a *golaka*;
nor a logician, an atheist, a sick person, or one whose medical treatment is directed against poison or spirits.
Thus, one who is pure should consecrate a disciple who possesses the [proper] characteristics and is self-restrained;
however, one who is censured and devoid of the characteristics should never be consecrated. Thus it is said.
Then the teacher, having performed the preliminary rites at an auspicious place, time, and planetary conjunction,
should perform the sacrifice as before, to the west of the jar of Śambhu.
On the sacrificial mound to the south, having fashioned a lotus on the altar with unbroken grains of rice;
Having worshipped the partless Śiva in the pericarp with the Śiva-mantra,
[one should worship] Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, Pārvatī, and Hara.

One should worship Brahmā, Kārttikeya, and one’s own preceptor on the permanent seat, and then worship them extensively with the *hṛdaya-mantra* in the locations starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
One should worship Caṇḍeśa, who stands near the lineage of gurus (gurupaṅkti),
together with his limbs (sāṅga), having gratified each one with a hundred oblations using one's own mantra.
The disciple, having likewise worshipped Śiva, should make this request:
"O Great Lord, you yourself shall manifest in embodied form and instruct me."
O you of excellent vows, this instruction on initiation and its exposition is for the purpose of cutting through [ignorance];
it has been correctly understood by you through thorough knowledge, O you who possess the form of virtuous conduct.
It should be bestowed upon one's own disciple immediately after the consecration of the head;
through your power, it has now come to me.
Therefore, by your command, I offer this second portion of food to him.
Having been thus authorized with the words "Do so," [the master] should, outside [the hall], in the east, the north,
the northeast, or the west, face westward toward the maṇḍala.
The two auspicious altars (vedikās) are situated from east to west;
they are said in some places to be four cubits [in length], while twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) are considered the best [for their width].
In other cases, they are two cubits in breadth and one auspicious finger-breadth (maṅgalāṅgula) in height.
Having prepared a design such as a svastika or lotus, adorned with a perimeter of flowers,
and having placed them upon seven kinds of grain like a hero in battle;
One should offer red sandalwood paste, gold, all medicinal herbs, and consecrated rice; there should be garments made of mango sprouts, along with full vessels and fruits.
One should place nine jars— saturated with a hundred recitations of the root mantra and filled with the power of the sacred waters— in the directions starting from the northeast and in the center.
The alkaline ocean, the milk ocean, the ghee ocean, the sugarcane ocean, the *kādambarī* ocean,
and the *darbha* water— these eight oceans are to be placed in sequence;
within them are to be established Śikhaṇḍin, Rudra, Śrīkaṇṭha, Trimukta, and Ekarudraka.
The single eye is the most excellent Śiva, subtle and known as Ananta.
Resembling pure crystal, with many faces and four arms,
holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a trident, and a rosary in their hands, and possessing three eyes.

Having sprinkled these six substances— alkali and the rest— with water, one should place the seat (āsana) marked with its own name, using either the root mantra or the Praṇava, or else the heart mantra.
One should place the Śakti in the central jar, which is filled with waves of nectar.
One should worship Śiva with extensive offerings such as incense and perfumes from that previous [substance],
or else with jars in the four directions that are red, blue, white, and crimson.
Furthermore, in the jars starting from the southeast (āgneya), one should place [the Rudras] beginning with Ananta and ending with Ekanetra;
and [the Rudras] beginning with Asita and ending with Khaṇḍa, starting with Ekarudra and ending with Nīlalohita.
One should worship those who bear the weapons of Śiva, whether they have five faces or four faces.
Alternatively, having fashioned five portions, one should place two Sindhus and likewise two Rudras in each of the five jars starting from the east.
One should worship Śambhu in the central jar, or in the northeast according to some traditions;
or one may worship everything in a single jar or in a vessel made of leaves.
One should offer a hundred oblations for each [deity] with its own mantra, ending with the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Then, on a portion of ground smeared with water, upon a mandala made of flour,
where unbroken rice grains and a *svastika* have been placed, one should establish the seat (*pīṭha*) there with the nectar of the hand.

For that purpose, on a site with a wide extent and height, marked by a lotus and possessing excellent characteristics, the disciple— having performed his daily rites, bathed, dressed in white garments, and observed a fast— stands ready; with a full face for the sake of enjoyment, and with a serene face for the sake of liberation.
Having performed worship and the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the Guru, together with his disciples,
should surround [the site] with the armor-mantra for protection and perform the rite of defense with the Vajra and other weapons.
Having cleansed [the site] with cow dung, earth, ashes, sour gruel, rice, and mustard seeds;

with cotton, water from the ocean, and abundant [water]; accompanied by the auspicious sounds of Vedic recitations and the like; having had women perform the purification and having enveloped it with the water of the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Having drawn out full jars in sequence with alkaline water and the other substances,
by the practitioners and the teachers who are the embodiments of the eight Vidyeśvaras.
This body of one who possesses the nature of Śiva is sprinkled by the retention of nectar;
that of one who possesses the nature of the world is [sprinkled] by the jars of the lineage beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin.
Then, with water from the pitcher of Śambhu, the Guru, who is the very embodiment of Śiva,

should offer the ceremonial rinsing (ācamana) with a stream of weapon-mantra water, and present two white garments upon the seat on the western altar, which is adorned with ornaments and other such items.
Having adorned the disciple, one should worship him with elaborate offerings beginning with the *ārātrī* ceremony.

Having arisen, one should cast balls of yellow rice, curd, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) [into the fire], and perform the initiation three times by encircling it with a stream of water. Then follows the purging (*recanā*), the rinsing (*camana*), *dūrvā*, flowers, curd, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
One should worship white mustard seeds mixed with honey for the sake of auspiciousness.
The instructor, grasping his right hand with his own right hand and leading him clockwise, should direct him toward the sacrificial hall.
Having worshipped the disciple, who is seated upon the mandala on the southern seat of the deity, as if he were Śiva himself, one should address a request to Śiva.
O Lord, you who are the embodiment of the Guru have compassionately consecrated this disciple; O Blessed One, he possesses the qualification for initiation and the other rites.
O All-pervading Lord, the capacity, the expectation, and the impulse must now be bestowed upon the one who has been impelled.
Thus instructed, the Guru should bestow the authority as it is described:
the turban, the variegated crown, the palanquin, and the fly-whisks.
A bracelet, a finger-ring, a necklace, an armlet, and a jeweled earring.
Having bestowed upon him the *saṃhitā*, the *saṃhitā-sūtra*, the *karaṇī*, and the *yoga-paṭṭaka*, the Guru, by the command of Śiva, places him on the lion-throne in the row of teachers.
And just as one should proclaim to the prostrating disciple his eligibility for initiation and so forth, one should likewise proclaim the Supreme Reality,
the observances (samayas), and Caṇḍeśa, with the Guru as witness.

Since you, as the authorized officiant, reside in a holy place, you must— from this day forward and with due reflection and by the command of Śiva— perpetually perform the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites that have been handed down through the lineage of gurus.
Having thus commanded, having offered a hundred oblations, and having given the full oblation with the Śiva-mantra,
[he should perform the rite] for the salinity of the bonds in the sequence beginning with the left thumb.
One should properly mark [the disciple] with weapons, mantras, and so forth, using a blazing blade of darbha grass;
thus, having offered himself, he is bound by the fetters by the Guru.
Having fully worshipped Śiva, one should place his hand— illumined by the oblations cast into it—
upon the head of the disciple, which consists of a circle of radiant light.
One should perform the daily worship and other rites for Śambhu, Kumbha, Ātman, and Vahni;
having worshipped the lineage of gurus and bowed to one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
For the sake of purifying the bonds of initiation (*dīkṣā-pāśa*), the Guru should offer himself [to the deity].
And it has been said:
"The Guru, too, for the sake of his own purification, having worshipped the Lord according to the prescribed rule..."
One should worship the lineage of gurus, beginning with Śiva and ending with one's own spiritual teacher.
Following the path taught in the scriptures, the practitioner of mantra,
with a mind fixed upon the maṇḍala, should worship the lotus-dwelling deities of the Lord of the West (Varuṇa).
Sadāśiva and Ananta, Vidyārudra together with Umā,
Viṣṇu the knower of the gods, Brahmā, and Skanda as well.
Having honored his own guru and his excellent disciple-son, as well as Śambhu and the guru,
with perfumes, flowers, purifying threads, garments, ornaments, and vehicles;
