Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should offer oneself [to the deity], saying:
"O Blessed One, from this day forward, this body which is my very self—"
Those belonging to you may be either female or male according to your choice;
having thus come under the power of the Guru, they shall remain so for as long as life lasts.
When he has been authorized by him for the duties of the present time—
namely, the fire-ritual, worship, initiation, exposition, and vows— then [he may proceed].
Thus, one should act according to his command, neither far from him nor in his immediate presence;
one should know that the efforts of those for whom the Guru does not grant joy are in vain.
"The Guru is the father, the Guru is the mother, the Guru is the deity, the Guru is the friend;
there is nothing superior to the Guru," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
With the divine ointment of knowledge, he clears away the eyes that are overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance; therefore, he is the one who removes the serpent of all [defilements].
By the path instructed by the Guru, they attain the supreme state;
therefore, first the Guru is to be worshipped, and afterwards the stainless God.
"Through initiation, [the Guru] leads one from the lower state to the supreme abode, the eternal station.
Therefore, O Guha, it should be understood that there is no one higher than the Guru. Thus it is said.
Is this rule indeed for many disciples? But for a single disciple, this is the procedure:
having entrusted his own authority, he himself should always practice yoga.
Then, being unattached and free from desire, whether in an empty house or in the forest,
one should perform initiation when this self is unable to renounce [the world].
Having projected the reality consisting of the principles (tattvamaya) into the fire and having gratified the foundational power (ādhāraśakti),
one should unite one's own self with that [reality] through the yoga of the virtuous and the blind.
Having offered a thousand oblations with the root mantra and performed the *pūrṇāhuti* while radiant,

he should extract himself and unite his self with the supreme Śiva at the *dvādaśānta*. Then, through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), he should rejoin [the self] within his own body and present the *arghya* offering.
O Lord, with my hair standing on end and acting in accordance with Your command, I shall perform upon myself and others the consecration previously described.
"Therefore, O Lord of Gods, be gracious and grant authority over this disciple. Having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods, and having been granted authority by Him,
he should offer one hundred oblations with the root mantra up to the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and after bowing, he should ask for forgiveness.
And it is said in the Kālottara: "When that office has been relinquished, he enters the state of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha);
or he should offer a thousand oblations with the Śiva-mantra."
Furthermore, the office was bestowed upon Śaṅkara by Padmanābha.
You must exercise your authority as you desire.
"Until the end of this body, [this has been] given by me according to the prescribed rule. Thus [it is said].
Then, having worshipped and dismissed the Lord, he— remaining under the authority of the true preceptor as well as that new teacher— should perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) for the disciple.
Having performed the daily rites there in the sacrificial hall in their entirety,
one should worship the lineage of gurus, beginning with Śivā and ending with one's own guru.
With a heart in the manner of one liberated by Śiva, [one should worship] Sadāśiva,
as well as Ananta, Hara, the Goddess, Acyuta, and Kamalāsana.
At the end, one should worship the six-faced one and one's own guru seated upon the *praṇava*-throne;
and having likewise sought out and satisfied those worthy of offerings, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the fallen (*pātakin*).
Having taken the disciple who has performed the previously mentioned rites and the worship performed by him,
and having led that non-dual [deity] outside, one should consecrate him.
In the northeast, the north, or the west, upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring two cubits in width and height,
auspiciously marked with lines,
immediately smeared with cow dung, and adorned with lotus and svastika symbols.
On a ground strewn with dūrvā grass, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice, and with the sky adorned by a canopy;
Seated upon the seat of the *dharmodaya*, facing east and with a face turned toward the north,
white in color, adorned with a white garland and white garments, and [worshipped] with white perfumes, white mustard seeds, and unbroken rice grains.
It was honored with offerings of flour and cow-dung fashioned into the forms of the world-protectors' weapons,
and it was cleansed by lamps kindled by virtuous daughters.

One should sprinkle the seeker of enjoyment (bubhukṣu) with water from a conch filled with the previously mentioned *anuśāstrālu* [substance], and the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) in the reverse order.
Having taken away the bathing garments and other items that were discarded, he provided her with another set of ornaments.
Having made him purified and honored, and having led him into the presence of the Guru,
he should say to him: "Listen, my dear, to this account of human endeavor."
The Supreme Self has ordained that the merit of the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) belongs to one whose mind is undistracted,
who is situated in the lake Mānasa, and who is free from mental affliction.
A disciple with a serene mind should always worship the guru as if he were Śiva;
likewise, a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should stand to the right side [of the guru].
By the command of the Guru, the Vaiśya and the Śūdra should always sit on the left side;
they should sit on a mat of grass, or on a low seat, or on a bundle of Kuśa grass.
While traveling, sleeping, or sitting, one should remain out of the Guru’s sight.
When addressed by the guru, one should always say, "I shall do as commanded";
likewise, when desiring to speak further, one should say, "I wish to inform you," and not otherwise.
One should not speak with familiarity;
even while desiring to serve, one should not step upon the Yoga-pīṭha, which is the seat of honor.
Indeed, one should maintain the same distance from the Guru as one would from his own seat.
The measurement of the bed is according to the one lying upon it;
one should not provide a pretext, for if he is released, there is danger to his life. While [the teacher] remains, [the disciple] must remain... [text fragment].
One should not rouse someone sitting at ease, nor should one awaken someone who is lying down.
Except when there is a risk to one's life, one should not utter anything else;
one should always perform service for the Guru with the root mantra, having offered one's own self.
One should abandon pride regarding wealth, noble birth, and learning;
and having acquired anything whatsoever— be it sacred knowledge, wealth, or even the merit of visiting holy sites— one should offer that to the guru.
Having understood the intention of his teacher, he further fixed his mind upon that [teaching].
Without transgressing the command, one should act wherever it is enjoined;
even though he knows, the Guru should not speak before his disciple.
Likewise, one should always dwell like a dull-witted person, devoid of pride in one's knowledge;
the Guru should reveal his name only at the feet of the worshipful Lord.
Whatever has been said or whatever has not been said, one should carry it out by the command of the guru;
the disciple must never eat anything without [the guru's] reason, remaining always devoted to the guru until the end.
"Even after hundreds of millions of eons, it cannot be recovered, like the property of the gods. Thus [it is said].
Likewise:
Whether possessed of qualities or devoid of qualities, one should bear the Guru’s command upon the head;
when he is informed [of this], the fruit of all sacrifices shall accrue to him.
When his faults are made known, even he shall partake in the fruit of being devoid of virtue;
therefore, one who seeks the highest good should not transgress the command of the preceptor, even in thought.
By properly carrying out the command of the guru, one attains the perfection of right knowledge;
one should never speak any word that is contrary to the guru.
Speak! If one should go to the Raurava hell due to great delusion, they will approach him out of anger and destroy him; their sacrifices shall be fruitless.
"Neither recitations nor observances should be performed here by those who are wise. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, at the Śākta Mūlapīṭha and in the Ulāvatāra, there is the enclosure and the renunciation of life; one must not transgress the word of the Guru.
When the Guru is pleased, Śiva is pleased; when he is angry, Śiva is angry—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, one should strive to please the Guru.
Those who hate behind one's back but speak kindly to one's face— these most sinful people go to the Kumbhīpāka hell and attain the lowest state.
The disciple who reviles the guru who has bestowed even a single syllable goes to the city of Asita; of this there is no doubt regarding the transgression of the samaya.
O illustrious lady, he who hears of malice toward his guru in his absence, and having heard it, approves of it, goes [to that same fate] as well; of this there is no doubt.
He who abandons devotion to Śiva and praises another deity—
initiation does not take effect for him, and even if it has been performed, it becomes fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in the path of Śiva.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the initiation of an Ācārya.
Oṃ, salutation to the glorious Mahāgaṇapati.
He who was previously called "the desirous one" (kāmī) is here remembered as the practitioner (sādhaka).
For him also, according to this same procedure, immediately after the consecration of the head (śiras-seka),...
One should offer the *uṣṇīṣa* and the *kartarī*, as well as the deficient and the excessive;
by performing this in the temple, his accomplishments (*siddhi*) will be attained through the grace of the Lord.
The preceptor should observe the vow of a preceptor while in the presence of the preceptor;
the practitioner of mantra should observe the mantra-vow before the liṅga or within a maṇḍala.
And this has been stated in the *Svāyambhuva*:
"Now, the preceptor himself should indeed observe the excellent vow of the preceptor;
he should practice the collection of mantras beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Śiva."
For three fortnights he should sleep on the ground, eating only at night and always subsisting on sacrificial porridge.
Silent, bathing three times a day, undisturbed by dualities, self-restrained,
wearing white garments, peaceful, and adorned with white garlands and unguents.

Wearing a yogic belt, a thread, a girdle of muñja grass, and holding the pure victor’s [rosary], one should perform the recitation daily; at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the ritual sequence according to one's ability.
With ghee, or with sesame seeds smeared with ghee, or with milk, rice, or grains;
or with sacrificial fuel-sticks, or likewise with curd and barley.
With bilva fruits, bilva leaves, or auspicious flowers fit for sacrifice.
Then, upon the completion of the vow, the preceptor and likewise the practitioner should worship the previously mentioned mandala at the time of receiving the consecrated substances.
Having consecrated oneself by means of the self, one should then sow the seed;
the practitioner of mantra should observe the mantra-vow according to the path prescribed for the sādhya mantra. Thus it is said.
Now, as it is said in the *Kālottara*:
"Then, for the purpose of the initiation of the Ācārya, one should fashion a nine-fold [mandala];
it bestows the fruit of a nine-fold [attainment] even for all those [rites] performed for specific desires."
In the northeastern direction, the worship of Parameṣṭhin should be performed—
[him] who is skilled in the meaning of the four categories and who knows the multitude of the six categories.
Then, [the teacher] should consecrate that heroic Sāhasika, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings and who has excellently fulfilled the vow of the vidyā, as his guru.
The Śiva-mantras and the Brahma-aṅgas should be recited in the abode of Śiva.
Having fully restrained the collection of his senses for one year as prescribed,
he subsisted solely on alms and slept upon a pure mat of kuśa grass.

One who is intent on worship with a mind cultivated by self-realization should know that when one hundred thousand recitations of the syllables of the Vidyā-aṅga are completed, the maṇḍala is formed; the Guru,
having thus fashioned it with nine lotuses, should perform the sacrifice as before.
Likewise, for one who is fit for consecration, it must never be done by any other [woman].
Because of the Guru’s power to both curse and grace, this vow is praised by him;
it is supremely meritorious, and once perfected, she shall employ it.
For the sake of the practitioner’s own accomplishment, he should perform this vow at all times.

On an auspicious lunar day during the bright fortnight, under a favorable conjunction (*yoga*), and during the northern course of the sun, when there is the *mūlārka* yoga or the moon is in conjunction with the *śravaṇa* asterism;
Consecration is recommended on either the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day.
Thus, this ritual for consecration (abhiṣeka-vidhi) was composed by the illustrious Jñānaśiva, a bee at the lotus feet of the venerable Viśveśvara. Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati!
Now, as an incidental matter, a very small mandala is being described:
it is a square field of equal dimensions, resembling the interior of a mirror.
Having stretched a thread extending from east to west, one should mark the center;
then, using that same measurement, one should mark the two endpoints to the south and north.
For the sake of the northern field, one should mark the corners from the center with a cord;
by means of four cords, the wise man should fashion a square.
When four cubits are divided into eight parts, two parts are considered for the lotus;
the pathway outside is one part, and the doors are two parts each,
provided with cheeks, sub-cheeks, and eaves.
One should fashion that auspicious two-footed design with variegated corner-bindings;
the petals are white in color, and the pericarp has the luster of gold.
One should arrange sixty-four filaments— yellow, red, and white—
at the base, middle, and tip of the stalk for the practitioner who seeks stability or liberation.
The Aruṇāvīthikā should be fashioned, adorned with leafy creepers;
one should complete the doors in accordance with the [directions of the] world-protectors (lokapālas). Furthermore, the space between the lines of the sky should be made to resemble the sun.
The corner-junction is reddish, while the base is yellow or white.
Thus has Bhadra been fully described, the supreme support of Śiva;
it should be performed in both daily and occasional rites for the sake of attaining auspiciousness.
Now, the procedure for the lotus is briefly described by me:
the lotus is considered to be of two kinds, the unattached and the attached.
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men; it is always beneficial when practiced independently.
O son of Pārvatī, that which is eternally beneficial for those seeking liberation is to be understood as one,
yet threefold, by a Guru who knows the ritual manuals (kalpa).
Considering that [the practitioner] may be a child, a youth, or an old man according to their name for the sake of accomplishing the fruit,
one should then fashion the lotus in successive order.
One should cast the lines upon the lotus-field in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
likewise, there are sixteen lines, numbering thirty-two in total.
The five kalpas have passed, and they are equal in the lotus-field.
In the first [circle] there is the pericarp, surrounded by nine lotuses;
the second, however, consists of twenty-four filaments.
At the third joint, however, it should have the shape of an elephant's frontal globe;
at the fourth, the tips of the petals; and at the fifth, the form of space.
At its end, a line of the sky is established, neither thick nor thin;
this is called the "attached lotus," and now the "evenly attached" is described.
The tip of that petal should be unattached and extend outwards according to the respective directions;
by omitting two parts, one should fashion the petal using eight parts.

One should mark that petal with the *Sandhivistara-sūtra* according to the sequence of left and right; thus, it becomes a "grown lotus" (*vṛddhapadma*). Then, from the center of its joint, one should rotate [the line] like a half-moon.
The joining of the two seams and the thread for the young lotus should be done in that manner;
however, when inferring the thread for the seam, one should turn it back from behind.
A lotus with a sharp tip and young petals bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for the sake of liberation, an old lotus is used, while a young one is desired for the joints [of the ritual]. A petal from a youthful [lotus] is recommended with effort for all rites.
One should perform four circumambulations, remaining closely attached [to the path] and avoiding the sky.
p.
423) One should also rotate the sky-line slightly at the tips of the petal-ends;
thus, by way of brief indication, the eight-petaled lotus has been demonstrated.
O child, the Maṇḍala of Vighneśa is common to all;
O beloved, listen as I describe the Maṇḍala known as the Nine Lords (Navanātha).
It should be a square field of eight cubits, or even ten cubits.
One should divide the city on all sides into seven hundred and four parts;
in its center, there shall be a lotus divided on all sides into eight parts.
The *pādukā* and the *vedikā* should be made with a width of half a *pakṣa*;
it is joined with the *kalpa* and the *upa-kaṇṭha*, and its *kaṇṭhya* consists of a rounded form with two bands (*varta*).
In the middle of this is a lotus provided with four doors;
this has been described to you in brief, and outside of that is considered to be the pathway (vīthikā).
Its length being five parts, it should extend ten parts on all sides;
then, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, an eight-petalled lotus should be made as previously described. Outside of that, there should be a five-part path adorned with petals.
The throat of the door should be like a lotus, with a *kañjuka* (petal-base) of one *padika*;
the cheek (*kapola*) should be made of one *padika*, and clearly there should be three doors in the cardinal directions.
The three-legged and two-legged [pedestals] should be like a vajra.
In the center is that white lotus; the eastern lotus is yellow. In the southeast it is red in color, while a blue lotus is situated in the south.
Smoky-colored in the northwest corner, and red-yellow to its north.
In the northeast, there should be a fresh lotus resembling a pearl, white,
or pale like a lotus, or perhaps reddish-white.
The nine-fold [mandala] of Śiva is declared to be called Prasāda;
Śiva is to be worshipped in the central lotus, and the world-protectors (lokeśas) in the others.
Then, one should worship the weapons with devotion below the outer path.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit from the worship of this maṇḍala.
He is not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
one should perform the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I shall now describe the Great Maṇḍala, which bestows all accomplishments.
One should first divide the eight-cubit field into twenty parts.
In the center, one should fashion a two-petaled lotus; outside, there is a path for the vehicles, and likewise, one should arrange eight blue lotuses in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The central lotuses are of appropriate size, sharp-tipped, and auspicious;
they are devoid of petal-joints, and from them proceed the pathways and the footpaths.
Having divided the squares into two types, one should place eight svastikas in the directions;
there is a path of single squares on the outside, with doors and a lotus as appropriate.
The central lotus should be fashioned with its neck and sub-neck joined, and its cheeks and sub-cheeks; the pericarp should possess the luster of gold.
The filaments are variegated, being yellow, red, and white.
A detached petal is recommended, conceived as the sky within the sky;
the corners are marked by the color of horses, while the walkways possess the luster of gold.
The blue lotuses are dark-hued, with their pericarp like a *karṇikāra* flower;
the paths are of various colors, adorned with swastikas and leaf-patterns.
One should fill the various-colored doors with colored powder;
this is known as the Great Maṇḍala, the heart of Śiva, O Lord.
It is recommended for ascending the ladder of purification and especially for initiation;
one attains all desires through the worship of the great maṇḍala.
Salutations to Śrī Mahāgaṇapati!
I shall now fully describe the fivefold lotus offering for the dedication of vows;
it must also be performed during the purification of the *liṅga* and for the attainment of the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) such as *aṇimā*.
In a square field measuring five cubits on each side, divided equally on all sides by Indra (four),
there is a two-pada lotus in the center, and from that, a one-pada pathway.
One should arrange four lotuses in the four directions as in the center;
outside of that is the path (pathikā) and the courtyard (ālīthi), and the doors are two units (dvipada) wide.
The neck and its vicinity should be joined with variously colored intersections;
the central lotus should be made very white, and the filaments yellow.
The right [hand] holds a full yellow lotus with the luster of lapis lazuli;
the northern [hand] has the appearance of cinnabar, while the western lotus has the luster of the moon.
The first path is considered to have a reddish luster, while the next has a golden luster.
O Śikhivāhana, the gates are like those of Lokeśa;
this is declared to be the Maṇḍala of the Five Lotuses, which grants the accomplishment of all desires.
Thus has the mandala described in the Kālottara been written down for you;
now I shall speak of the Prāsādatilaka, as taught in the Maṇḍalārṇava.
One should set aside sixty-four square units, excluding the nine-cornered [sections].
With one part, the pillar [is formed]; with six parts, it is above; the head [of the pillar] is three [parts] across.
Having set aside one part from the pillar, there shall be a single liṅga as it occurs.
From the feet to the shanks and the throat, [the proportions] are respectively six vedas (twenty-four) and six kalās (six).
The *kaṇṭhapāṭhī* and the *vedī* should be formed by the six Vedas respectively;
in the middle, having set aside a portion consisting of pairs of *liṅgas*, the pillars and so forth are as described before.
In this manner, one should arrange five lingas with six pillars;
these are situated between the lingas and the pillars, as well as positioned above the lingas.
Having obtained the storehouse, one should turn back toward the white-peaked summit.
For the sake of the pavilion (vimāna), one should remove five or seven parts above the pillar;
from above the two corner pillars, one should remove eighteen parts.
In the corners, beautiful tilakas should be made together with creepers;
above that, a pathway (vīthikā) should be constructed, joined with the [appropriate] divisions.
Then, having set aside the portions at the corners as previously described for the sevenfold [mandala],
one should fashion three lingas provided with four pillars.
Having established the corner as before, according to the measurement of the portion for the pathway (vīthikā).
A svastika should be formed with four [lines], omitting two pairs of corners.
Above that, a pathway (vīthikā) should be constructed all around with a measurement of one part;
in the center, one should fashion a lotus using twelve parts.
In some [traditions], a pathway is said to be outside, beyond that by five parts; in others, it is considered that the arrangement of eight doors in the cardinal directions occurs with half a lotus.
The seed-syllable at the pericarp should be yellow, while the letter *ka* is green;
the bases of the filaments should be like jasmine, snow, or the luster of the moon,
and their middles should indeed be made red with colored powder.
The tips of the filaments are [marked] with yellow powder, while the petals are white;
the ground is considered square by means of three types of white powder.
The liṅga is marked with black powder, and the path is adorned with petals.
White [pigment] is produced from the powders of barley, wheat, or white rice;
red [pigment] may be derived from mineral cinnabar or from burnt brick.
Black [powder] may be made from burnt husks of grain or from pulverized charcoal;
yellow [powder] may be derived from turmeric, from *śāmbhava* (orpiment), or indeed from red ochre.
One should fashion a green-colored [image] using powdered green leaves;
these [images] of all colors may be made by some using grains such as *śyāmaka* and others, or with rice that has been infused [with pigments], or with grains endowed with their respective lusters.
In this way, the wise one should visualize the mandala, the ornament of palaces,
upon a perfectly pure ground that resembles the surface of a mirror.
Whether above the altar or on the ground, in a place delightful to the auspicious gods,
adorned with rows of banners and other ornaments, one should act as if it were Bhava himself.

Having sprinkled the mandala of the Supreme Lord with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra, the practitioner, having adorned it with incense, flowers, and other offerings, should begin with the Nipāta, Dīpa, Ārambha, and so forth.
There, one should worship Śiva as the Tilaka of the Palace within the central lotus.
In one particular palace, together with the individual soul accompanied by the limbs of Brahmā,
one should worship the primary Vidyeśvaras in the svastikas, starting from the east in sequence.
Then, with the root mantra and the heart mantra, one should worship the five and eight Rudras in the center of the lingas,
on the tilakas, in the mirror, and on the mandala to the right of that mandala, using the heart mantra.
And [he should worship] Indra and the other world-protectors first, in order, starting from the east.
And in their respective directions.
There, the best of gurus should mentally worship all these, beginning with Śiva and ending with the world-protectors, using the two external seed-syllables and the heart-mantra.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to the scriptures and preceded by meditation,
one should perform the recitation of the root mantra as many times as possible, exceeding one hundred repetitions.
Having given [the offering] among the gods to Śiva, one should dedicate a tenth part of that to the fire;
likewise, one should worship in the fire and satisfy it with the sacrificial porridge (caru) according to the prescribed rite.
Thus has been described the Prāsādatilaka, proclaimed by Droṇa and beloved of Viśvaṃkara.
In rites that are obligatory, occasional, or performed for specific desires, this should be practiced, for it bestows all success;
whatever fruit is found in all sacred pilgrimage sites and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices [is obtained here].
Whatever merit is obtained from all forms of giving accompanied by austerity and meditation,
ten million times that merit shall be gained from worshipping Śiva in this [temple].
That man who, with devotion, beholds even once the Tilaka-prāsāda [shrine], [attains such merit].
By that [practice], one is not stained by sins such as violating the *liṅga* and so forth,
nor by the transgressions of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*), just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Enough with further elaboration.
For the rites of initiation and installation, the learned one should worship Śiva in the *kumbha* (the ritual jar) alone;
or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or in a mobile *liṅga*, but by no means in a mandala.
Since atonement must be performed for the stain of menstrual blood, it is like a tail.
Thus, the path of the maṇḍala has also been described by me incidentally,
for the sake of attaining the realization of its function, by the venerable Śivajñānaśambhu.
Thus ends the ritual for the mandala.
Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
The rules for residing [with the teacher] and the lifting of vows are now described.
At the end of the period, the disciple should inform the guru of this as follows:
Just as this much capacity has carried out my vow for so long,
now, for me who am incapable, you must act with compassion by granting the vow.
Having thus performed the sacrifice, the Guru, being skillful and requested by the disciple,
[prepared] that which was resplendent with lines of colored powder upon the water-pot and the sacrificial mound.
Having fashioned a mandala of five lotuses with unbroken grains mixed with fragrance, or with sandalwood alone, one whose body is presided over by Śiva [should proceed].
One should worship Īśāna in the central lotus, Puruṣa in the eastern lotus,
Aghora in the southern lotus, Vāma in the northern lotus,
and Ajāta in the western lotus— these [five faces] together with the limbs of Brahmā.
Indeed, they are white, yellow, white, red, and the color of milk, respectively.
One should visualize her as having five faces, fifteen eyes, and bearing ten weapons;
and having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, and so forth, [one should worship] upon the petals as well.
Likewise, the limbs of Brahmā are of their respective colors, each having three eyes and one face,
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and holding spears and tridents.
Having gratified each [deity] with a hundred oblations using their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), the mantras are as follows:
*oṃ hauṃ śivāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hauṃ īśāneśāya namaḥ*,
*oṃ īśāne tatpuruṣe namaḥ*, and so forth.
Having performed his daily rites and completed a thousandfold expiation, the disciple— having bathed, observed a fast, and being endowed with the five mudrās— is [prepared] for the Brahman.
Having caused [the disciple] to enter the sacrifice and having worshipped the Lord of the Jar (kumbheśa) and the Fires with that [offering],
he should then bow to the Lord of the Altar (sthaṇḍileśa) and address the Guru as follows:
"O Blessed One, you previously bestowed this vow upon him for a limited duration;
now, having taken up your abode here, you must perform the ritual for the release from that vow."
Having been granted permission with the words "So be it," his body presided over by Śiva,
he offered oblations one hundred times each, according to the number of limbs of the vow.
Having offered the full oblation with the root mantra, one should present the ancillaries of the vow;
having presented each individually, one should offer one's own staff to Sadyojāta.
The loincloth and the waist-thread, which constitute the essence of the vow of celibacy;
likewise, the Vāmadeva [mantra], the Ghora [mantra], and the sacred ash belonging to Agni.
The sacred thread belongs to Vāyu; it is purified with the Tattvapuruṣa mantra and its own seed-syllables.
One should apply the nature of the sky and the matted lock to the northeast;
then, the preceptor should release the matted locks using this [deity’s] weapon-mantra.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and having given the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Śiva-mantra,
one should then worship Caṇḍanātha and offer the constituent parts of the vow (vratāṅga).
Having cast [the image] into the current of river water, the preceptor should cause it to flow away;
then he should give two white garments to the child who remains.
Having given the command for the sake of marriage and for the realization of one's former births,
and having offered a hundred oblations with the mantra for the sake of the birth, he should dismiss the sacrifice.
He may be a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī) whose mind is nonetheless attached to the objects of the senses.
If she is to be given [the initiation], then one should recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times.

If [the mantra] has not slipped from the memory of one whose celibacy has been violated and whose mind is intent upon sense objects, then it may be recovered by reciting the *lakṣaghora* mantra one hundred thousand times.
In this very same way, the ritual procedure should be performed for those two as well, without distinction.
And it is said:
"Now, regarding the optional vows above [the householder stage], both the householder and the one who bears the marks (liṅgin) [the ascetic]..."
When he is addressed as "householder" once again, the renunciation of those two is described:
the vow, the topknot, the sacred thread, the ashes, the loincloth, and the staff.
Because it is the cause that manifests the vow, this is the vow of the ascetic:
he whose devotion is firm and whose celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is unimpaired;
yet he who is unable to properly maintain the vow of a celibate student.
Having first abandoned that [first one], he who then desires the second;
One should liberate that which is the support for the glory of the household vow; perform the vow of that elemental being.
One should worship the Brahmāṇīs as before upon a pure and variegated five-petaled lotus.

The reading may also be "vrateśāneśvaraṃ śivāhamiti. For one who is purified by fasting, who has performed his obligatory rites, who has honored Śiva, the fire, and the guru, and who is thus free from debt: [He attains the state of Śiva.]
Having removed those limbs of his vow in reverse order and having offered them to Caṇḍeśa within that maṇḍala, one should perform the ritual dismissal (pravāhaṇa).
The vow is performed through the yoga of withdrawal for the one who has bathed and is wearing ochre robes;
then, having performed the ritual dressing for the one praised as a cutter, he should cause the two feet to descend.
He should say, "You are a Snātaka," from the time of taking up the staff onwards.
And until your marriage, [protect] your wives... [and so forth].
Having committed offenses such as those involving women of the same caste (*savarṇā*) and others,
and having incurred defilement by violating the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
The phrase "having performed expiation" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Having been thus instructed, he should observe the vow of eating at the other stages of life,
namely the householder stage (*gārhasthya*). As for the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*), if he has fallen from his celibacy through negligence, [he must perform penance].
One should unite him who is unattached, having purified him with vows as before;
or else, one should unite him from the stage of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
The Guru should cast Sāgara, who is attached to enjoyments, with the *cañcala* [mantras];
and that which was stated regarding the previous lineage (*pūrvagotra*) is indeed stated in exactly the same way here.
As it has been said:
"One should diligently avoid those kinsmen who are devoid of initiation."
But a woman who has not been initiated—one should likewise avoid association with her.
He is born bearing the marks of the Self (*ātma-liṅga*), a worshiper of the gods, the fire, and the guru.
Here, the "marks of the Self" refers to the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and so forth.
Nevertheless, even one devoid of initiation possesses authority in this Śaiva [tradition].
One whose soul is solely absorbed in the Śiva-scriptures, who is proficient in the knowledge of Śiva,
and who has been initiated, should properly establish a formal relationship with another who is likewise initiated.
One who is uninitiated should not maintain social or ritual relations with one who is initiated;
this includes explaining the scriptures, listening to them, giving gifts, and receiving gifts from a pure person.
Initiation and the establishment [of the lineage]—these are the six duties of the Guru at all times.
Thus has been declared the abandonment of the Śaiva vow.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
For those initiated Śiva-devotees who have fallen away at any time, the extraction of initiation (dīkṣoddhāra) must always be performed; how that is to be done according to the rule is now declared.
From Śiva down to the earth, that entire collection of principles was cast into the fire.
Having simultaneously caused [the disciple] to conquer [his senses], he should satisfy him with his heart, saying:

"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the multitude of principles from Śiva down to the earth. Having established consciousness there by means of striking and other rites, he should unite it [with that consciousness].
For the removal of the merit [accrued from previous] initiation, [he should perform this] with the Pāśupata mantra.
Having offered a full thousand oblations, one should abandon the power of the mantra.
Having extracted the subtle soul (aṇu), one should join it to that body through its prior karma;
otherwise, the teacher or the expounder of the scripture goes to hell.
And it is said:
[One should not give] to one who is deceitful, dishonest, cruel, devoid of truth, fond of quarreling,
joined with lust and greed, afflicted by disease, or a mere logician.

This should not be given to one devoid of devotion to Śiva, to one who procrastinates excessively, to one who is utterly contemptible, or to one who walks the path of wicked reasoning contrary to the true nature of Śiva.
Those who give [to such a person] go to hell;
nothing should be given to anyone for whom devotion to a guru arises that is greater than devotion to Śiva.
To him this knowledge is to be given—initiation and exposition—and nothing else.
Thus concludes "The Extraction of the Fruit of Initiation for Persons Devoid of Devotion to Śiva."
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Now, as a secondary point, the [mantras] of other practitioners of signs (liṅgin) are also stated:
for those whose faces are five, half, one, and four [units long], they reside in the lower cavity of Māyā.
Liberation is declared to exist in two places, at Vakula and at Kṣetrarudra;
liberation is said to belong to the Kapālins at Ūrdhva-kaṭeśa.
Liberation occurs through the principle of the Person (puruṣatattva) for the proponents of Sāṃkhya and Vedānta;
it occurs through the womb [of the Goddess] for the followers of Pāñcarātra and Vaikhānasa.
The end of the Jainas is to be known as being in the intellect; for the Buddhists, it occurs in the consciousness;
and for the Cārvākas, the place of liberation is said to be in the wind.
Having performed the sequence beginning with the principles (tattva) up to the duality ending in earth, one should perform the accumulation.
p.
435) One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of those who reside in the triple superimposition (*trirāropa*) upon the body of the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth—
those who are engaged with their respective mudrās and remain within the outer mandala.
By means of the yoga of channel-union (nāḍī-sandhāna) and through the sequence of striking and so forth,
one should take up [the essence] and join it to the fire once the upward accumulation has been performed in the sacrifice.
One should offer five oblations for each principle (tattva) with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaṇu*).
The mantras begin with: *oṃ hoṃ māyā-tattvāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
[The general mantra is: *oṃ hāṃ namaḥ to the principles and observances beginning with Māyā and ending with Dhārā*.
Thus ends the application of the Vāma mantra.
Having offered the full oblation with the root mantra, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) that night.
Then, in the morning, having performed the remaining rites such as worship and so forth, one should proceed.

Having caused [the disciple] to enter the outer mandala, one should perform the accumulation of the principles (tattvasañcaya) as before; having assigned them to the bodies of the principles and having invoked their presence, one should satisfy them with libations.
Having taken them up with beatings and other means, one should place them in the fire in reverse order;
having likewise placed the tattvas and the negation (nañ), for the sake of purification through their respective consecrations.
With a concentrated mind, the Guru should offer eight thousand oblations for each [deity] using the Pāśupata weapon-mantra, and five [oblations] for each using the Śiva-mantra.
For the sake of purifying the reality (tattva), having offered a full oblation with the *śikhā-mantra*,
one should extract the reality up to its end and then place it in the previous birth.
Having cast their ritual observances into water, they should maintain their status as householders;
thus, for those devoted to Śiva, initiation is characterized by the absence of desire for worldly seeds.
Because of his eligibility for initiation and other rites, there is no lack of accomplishment in the attainment of the goal.
And it has been said:
"There is no accomplishment, nor even in the rite for the attainment of powers or for the act of favoring the bound soul (paśu)."
"Even one situated within the ocean of the scriptures may render rebirth fit [for liberation].
Or else: "In an eight-petaled lotus, adorned with pathways and gates, one should worship Śambhu in the pericarp (karṇikā) with the syllable *kṣuṃ*, together with its limbs."

Indeed, having worshipped the eight letters beginning with *Śiva* and ending with *Varga* in their respective order within the [eight directions] starting from *Īśāna*, one should worship and satisfy them in the fire.
Having offered five oblations each with the heart mantra, and having joined the principles (tattvas) therein,
one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra accompanied by the limb mantras, concluding with the final full oblation.
Having extracted the individual soul from the group beginning with Śiva, one should unite it within that body;
in this manner, one should purify the groups beginning with Śiva, either all at once or individually.
Having joined the Aṇu-mantra to that body, one should cast the components of the vow into the water.
Thus, in the Śrī Śaivāgama, this [work] has been extracted by me,
Śrī Śivajñānaśambhu, from the ocean of the scriptures, based on a mere fraction of the ritual procedure for the restoration of vows (vratoddhāra).
Thus ends the extraction of vows for other ancillary limbs.
Salutation to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Now, for those engaged in yoga who have renounced all worldly responsibilities,
this purifying procedure is written for the purpose of proceeding upon the path to Brahman.
Having first prostrated before the Guru as a deity who is seated comfortably on a comfortable seat,
one should remain in a solitary, secluded place with the body held straight.
First, one should slowly dissolve the hundred objects of the senses into the Lord of the Senses (Akṣeśa);
having deposited that within the place of the heart, one should then withdraw it back again.
To the extent that whatever has arisen remains [in its place], that is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
One should fill the abdomen with air as much as desired;
such is the prāṇāyāma known as pūraka, which fills the body.
Having closed all the openings of the body and being devoid of inhalation and exhalation, one should remain like a completely filled jar; that is the *kumbhaka* breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Then one should exhale the breath upwards through the head along with the breath;
this is known as *recaka*, which causes the cessation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Having performed a circumambulation with the hand of the foremost [deity] while observing the vow, one should snap the fingers at its conclusion; this is proclaimed to be the measure.
Prāṇāyāma with twelve mātrās is known as the lowest;
that which is double [that] is declared the middling; and that which is triple is remembered as the highest.
The best among those who know yoga should practice one *mātrā* each day;
he should neither hasten nor delay, but increase it gradually.
Thus, retention (dhāraṇā) is considered to be twice the duration of the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) as described;
yoga is twice the duration of retention, and yoga itself is likewise doubled.
This is declared by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as the "junction of yoga" (yoga-sandhi);
one who desires to go to that supreme state [should proceed] through the divisions of the heart and other centers.
In sequence, the yoga beginning with Brahmā arises, and its fruit shall likewise be so;
the heart-lotus is to be known as primordial (prākṛta), and its presiding deity is Brahmā and the others.
In that regard, whether he is to be meditated upon as the very nature of Brahman or as possessing the form of the phonemes (varṇa),
he then becomes the Lord on the path beginning with earth and ending with primordial matter (pradhāna).
Viṣṇu, pure and situated in the throat, is located in the middle of the second syllable;
one should practice meditating on Viṣṇu either in his essential form or in the form of the phoneme.
Then, through that practice, accomplishment consisting of the nature of the Puruṣa will arise effortlessly.
Rudra resides in the lotus of the palate, situated in the middle of the third syllable.
Through the practice of that, one attains the state of Ananteśa;
one should meditate on the Lord in the forehead as the flawless form of the *bindu*.
He shall become the creator of all, endowed with the eight qualities of sovereignty:
*aṇimā* (atomicity), *laghimā* (lightness), likewise *mahimā* (greatness), *prāpti* (attainment),
as well as *prākāmya* (efficacy), *īśitva* (lordship), *vaśitva* (control), and *yatra-kāmatā* (the power to will anything).
These qualities have been fully described; now their true nature is being stated:
when, by one's own will, one suddenly abandons this gross body, [these qualities arise].
It attains the state of having a body the size of an atom; therefore it is called "atomic" (aṇu).
In the former [view], however, through the *tattvas* of the Guru, the state of having a body arises instantly like cotton-wool by one's own will; this is the accepted [position].
Whenever and wherever one may go by one's own will, one is honored everywhere by those residing there; for that reason, his greatness has been celebrated.
When an object of desire appears spontaneously, then there shall be the attainment of all wealth; this is the sudden acquisition of the self.
When one enters into a form created by oneself within one's own self,
having performed an imitation according to one's will— that is declared to be *prākāmya* (the power of irresistible will).
If the world, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Sūrya, and the rest, were merely aquatic creatures;
In this context, that which is lordship (*īśitva*) is sovereignty (*prabhutva*); this is what is called "lordship" here.

That which is mastery (*vaśitva*) in various respects is mastery whose essence is the *praṇava*. Through the force of *haṭha*, there is the power of determining one's desires (*yatra-kāmāvasāyitā*) regarding that mastery.
These qualities certainly manifest there through the constant practice of Īśa;
above the *bindu*, the *nāda* arises, subtle like the fiber of a lotus stalk.
Those desiring the state of Sadāśiva should practice the resonance of the bell-sound; they should meditate either on that which ends with sound (nādāntaka) or on Sadāśiva in his own essential form.
Beyond that as well is power; it is called the power of the bindu. The subtle bindu situated above is also known as Kuṇḍalinī.
Through the practice of that [state], one becomes omniscient and the creator of all;
beyond that, its power is heard of in the scriptures as Unmanī, the sacrificial offering.
For she indeed abides in the center of the lotus, extremely subtle and difficult to perceive;
yet through practice of that, one then becomes all-pervading.
And beyond that is its station, partless, eternal, and imperishable;
consisting of knowledge and bliss, pure, all-pervading, and the sovereign lord of all.
O Lord, the yogi who has been slain by the sequence does not depart from that place;
between the navel and the genitals is the *kanda*, and there resides the channel whose essence is Śiva.
The Suṣumnā, rising through the central path as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
is as pure as a crystal and resembles the coral stem of a lute.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā are on the two sides of the neck of the lute;
they are red-limbed and tawny-colored, emerging from the pair of yokes.
The letter *sa* is situated in the center, having the form of its own inherent *ha*;
it is established in that place upon the lotus of *ha*, encompassed within the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*).
Through the practice of that [yoga], liberation occurs even for one who has fallen into the mire of sin;
such a yogi remains at will as long as he desires, even until the time of Brahmā.
Or if the yogin, by his own will, effects the departure for the supreme state—
thus has yoga been fully described as the unsurpassed among all yogas; it is to be understood and practiced by one who desires the state of the Lord of Yoga.
Or [the disciple] should be enjoined by the teacher who knows reality to apply himself to the self.
Now, the procedure for the departure [of the soul] (utkrānti) is written down briefly and in sequence:
having performed inhalation (pūraka) and retention (kumbhaka) until the culmination of yogic perfection,
the wise one should pierce the cranial vault (kapāla) by means of exhalation (recaka).
Having gradually abandoned the principles that are difficult to traverse and having dried up the causal factors,
one should enter the imperishable state through the yoga of exhalation (*recaka*).
And it is said in the *Triśatikālottara*:
"Having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), or otherwise as is comfortable,
one should take hold of the vital breath (*vitta*) at the crown of the head and mentally utter the name of Hara."
Having gradually withdrawn the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), which was established within the Brahma-nāḍī, I—
One should meditate on oneself as being seized by the power of Rudra, with a ruddy luster.
One should cause alms to be collected for as long as it takes to reach the path of the small bell.
Having worshipped, one should cast the bulb (kanda) into the wind situated in the channel;
having pressed it upward, one should not release it until it has reached the vicinity of the palate.
Above that is Sadāśiva, and above that is Bindu and Nāda;
having transcended Bindu and Nāda, one should then follow Śakti.
"Abandoning the *śakti*, one should go to the peaceful Śiva, the supreme cause;
having gone there, one is not born again—this, my dear son, is my promise.
Thus, O observer of good vows, has the process of departure (*utkrānti*) been briefly explained to you."
It should be given constantly to one's own disciple who is endowed with devotion,
for whom devotion to the Guru is established as greater than [devotion] to Śiva.
This knowledge is to be given to him, and never to anyone else;
thus, having transcended all the paths, there is the sole atonement for the experience of karma.
The abode of Śiva has been described by the illustrious Jñānaśambhu through the heart;
now, the procedure for the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi) is also briefly recounted by me.
In this regard, for that yogi who has passed away through the process of *utkramana* (the upward departure) with his impurities completely burnt away,
there is a pure body made of mantra, which is the "body beyond the body" (*videha*) by means of the fire of Śiva.
Neither the rite of offering funeral cakes nor the water libation for him should be performed;
rather, the disciples must always perform the worship of Śiva in order to discharge their debt.
442) By way of incidental discussion, it is stated how that [attainment] occurs for all others as well—
for men who are established in reality through initiation and who possess virtuous conduct.
For those who have passed away while diverting themselves with the meaning of the Siddhānta, one should cremate their body with the fire of Śiva; however, there is a specific rule regarding that.
The purification of the path, known as the forest of improper conduct (*anācāra-vana*), is prescribed.
And it is said:
"After the time of initiation, one should not transgress the rules of conduct (*samaya*)."
One becomes a partaker of great sin by [neglecting] the Lord and the gurus;
for those who remain in doubt and others whose natures are defiled,
O Guha, the final sacrifice (antyēṣṭi) is ordained for the removal of their sin.
"One falls into the abode of one's own conceptualization by transgressing the commitments and so forth. Thus it is said.
And likewise: "Especially for those who have not been liberated from doubt, who possess impurities,
who profess other scriptures, and likewise for those whose ritual duties have been abandoned."
"For the funeral rites must indeed be performed at the end; otherwise, one shall not attain the supreme state. Thus it is said.
The teacher, the adept, or the spiritual son should perform the purification of the paths for those who are spiritual sons;

however, he should not do so for one who merely observes the pledges (*samaya*) or for one who desires liberation. The teacher, the adept, or even the spiritual son [should initiate] only the one who observes the pledges (*samayin*).
Having bathed a deceased person, whether they were an observer of vows or a householder, one should adorn them;
one should then bind their two thumbs with a white thread so that they touch the spokes [of the wheel].
Upon a celestial chariot (vimāna) richly adorned with red garments, garlands of flowers and banners— constructed from moist bamboo as a stairway to heaven for the sake of health—
Conches, cymbals, trumpets, and so forth, were sounded by the sons of Vidhi.
443) Together with noble ones, those equal to them, or those of other castes,
as well as with initiated Sāṃkhyas and those whose heads are covered with [ashes].
Then, while maintaining [the ritual], one should scatter the bali offering in all directions along the paths;
furthermore, [one should do so] on the bank of a meritorious river, in a sacred field, or by a reservoir of water.
On a pure float facing south and west, one should hold the head toward the south;
having constructed a mandala measuring nine cubits and encircled with gold.
Or, measuring seven cubits, it goes toward a gate equipped with an archway;
it should be known by the name Avasānaka, though in some places it is called Kṛtānta.
There, in the northwest, one should fashion a pedestal out of that same clay, measuring one cubit in length, square in shape, with a single girdle,
and raised by six finger-breadths.
To the southeast of the sacrificial pit, one should prepare a trench for the funeral pyre, four cubits in length,
two cubits in width, and as deep as the auspicious finger-breadth.
In some traditions, it is held that one should construct the funeral pit to the south of the sacrificial fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having prepared these three [sites], one should smear them with cow dung.
Then, having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*) and performed the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), one should remain composed.
With the sacred thread over the right shoulder and facing north, the Guru,
having gone to the site of the *padam* within the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*),
sits upon a pure seat and performs the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
The wise one has performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in reverse order and has manifested the end-maker (Kṛtānta).
One should purify the ritual substances with water over which the Astra-mantra has been recited seven times.
Having sprinkled oneself and performed worship, and having purified the mantra,
one should sprinkle the ground all around with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra and with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having consecrated it with the rites at the end of the four paths, even if it is scattered, one should cast it back,
bring it forth, and join it together in the northeastern sector of the funeral pyre.
One should worship the Pāśupata weapon in the *vardhanī* vessel at the southern nozzle,
and the weapons of the world-protectors in the jars located in the directions beginning with the northeast.
Having performed the protection of the bath with the stream of the Astra-mantra,
one should worship the Vardhanī vessel there and worship the Astra-mantra on the movable seat.
"Enjoyment, this place, and protection shall last until the completion of the rite"—
having thus informed Hetiśa, one should take refuge within the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having performed the protection over the sacrificial mound with kuśa grass, ashes, and sesame seeds;
Having worshipped the gatekeepers and others with the Astra-mantra and with the Hṛdaya-mantra as before.
In a jar adorned with a royal mass of pollen, fashioned into lotuses using sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains, or otherwise endowed with all beauties and containing the seven types of grain;
One should worship the one called Ādhāra, who has an infinite lotus, as well as Aiśvarya and the other [powers], and the three sins beginning with Anaiśvarya;
these are of various colors, as before.
Upon cutting [the cord] from top to bottom, one should place the lotus with Manonmanī in the pericarp (karṇikā),
and the deities beginning with Sarvabhūtadamanī and ending with Vāmā upon the filaments (kesara).
One should offer the mind enriched with Śakti, Agni, Soma, and Sūrya;
having invoked the two forms, one should [worship] the kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, in due order.
Having placed [the mantras] beginning from the feet and having invoked Śiva as before,
one should perform the ritual of integration (sakalīkaraṇa) with the weapons-mantra and others, and then effect the supreme transformation (paramīkaraṇa) with the root-mantra.
Having made [the offerings] immortal through devotion and accompanied by the rite of welcome,
one should offer water for the feet and other items to Śambhu and worship the limbs of his enjoyment.
From the weapon-mantra (astra) to the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), [one should worship] in their respective places as before;
having offered incense, lamps, and other food offerings (naivedya), one should recite the mantra and present it.
Having consecrated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and having circumambulated the fire from left to right (apasavya), one should scatter [the embers],
generate the fire, and perform the purification beginning with the blindfold.
Having worshipped Śiva, offered libations, and given the final oblation according to the rules,
one should thereafter perform the worship of the deities after having prepared a grid of twenty-five squares.
The site known as Vetāla is provided with bamboo ropes;
there, the preceptor, having meditated upon the site in its true form and having worshipped it, [proceeds].
One should remove that single square with yellow powder;
from the southwest, one should draw four squares as a boundary like a reed-weaver.
One should fill the four [squares] in order, starting from the east, with the colors white, red, black, and white;
and then with yellow, black, white, and red.
In those [circles], one should worship the principles (tattvas) beginning with the Earth, together with their presiding deities, as follows: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Earth-principle;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā.
Thus, in the center:
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the water element;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu.
Thus, excluding Nara: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of fire (tejastattva);
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra.
Thus, in the fire [mandala], [one recites]: *oṃ hāṃ vāyutattvāya namaḥ*.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśvara; thus [one offers] in the northwest. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of space (vyomatattva).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva; thus at the Īśāna [corner]. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Indra.
Thus in the east; "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yama" in the south.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa" in the west, and "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kubera" in the north, and having offered an oblation of black-gram and rice in the cow-pen, one should then offer clarified butter and other substances in sequence;
thereafter, one should cause that fire to burst forth again.
Having prepared the ground with the *kuṇḍavatsa* rite and fashioned a square with the *vīta*, one should worship Brahmā in its center within a variegated-cornered space.
Having fashioned [an image] from red pigment, one should worship the tree as Kālāgni:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālāgnirudra."

Having recited the Astra-mantra seven times over four dry wooden stakes that have their roots pointing upward and their tips downward, and having fixed them in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Nila (Nairṛta), and Rakṣas,
one should encircle them with a red thread.
Having filled it with sandalwood and other materials, and with sacrificial fuel sticks,
and having covered it from the southern direction to the northeast with a cloth, one should worship it with the Astra-mantra.
Oṃ hāṃ haḥ, homage to Citā.
Having performed the protection of the enemy with ashes, *darbha* grass, and sesame seeds in reverse order,
and having worshipped and offered libations into the fire, one should [dispose of] the lifeless dwellers of the funeral pyre.
Having washed the auspicious [image] with clay, cow dung, and water, and having raised it up, one should bring it forward;
setting aside the sacred thread and other such items, regardless of its previous caste,
one should place it facing north on the seat of the Praṇava within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
When the body composed of mantra has been fashioned according to the rules for *dhāraṇā* and so forth,
one should bring [the soul] from the Great Net down to the size of an atom by means of the *jīvasaṃhāra-mudrā*.
Oṃ hūṃ hauṃ hāṃ hāṃ hūṃ, salutation to the self of [Name].
Having joined [the mantra], one should place the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) within the heart-lotus;
then, one should offer libations to Śiva, the Hand, Śakti, and the Nāsīs in the fire.
Starting from Śāntyatīta and including all the Kalās censured throughout the entire path,

having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) through emanation upon their summit and worshipped Śiva as before, one should offer oblations with the root mantra accompanied by the limb-mantras, numbering one hundred and ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having projected the *ādhārikā-śakti* and worshipped it at the throat, and having offered libations,
one should take up the *kalās* beginning with Nivṛtti in their proper sequence by means of striking and other rites.
Having worshipped and offered libations into the fire according to the procedure prescribed for initiation,
and having informed the causal deities as well, one should [worship] Śivā, who pervades all the paths,
and Śiva, the agitator of the womb, simultaneously in every lotus.
Having struck the living soul and entered into the wombs in the form of disciples—
namely, all those beginning with Nivṛtti— the Guru [should perform the rite] according to the procedure prescribed for initiation.
Having simultaneously performed the foundational rite (ādhāna), which establishes the authority for birth and experience,
[the practitioner] proceeds toward dissolution, purification, the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi), and expiation (niṣkṛti).
The concealment by the power of impurity (*mala-śakti-tirodhāna*), the warding off of future karma (*bhāvi-karman*),

and the present [karma]— having joined these with the remainder of what has been experienced, the severing of the fetter (*pāśa*) by the sword of Śiva, and the offering of the body along with all its impurities (*sarva-guṇḍa*).
And in all the causal deities, beginning with Brahmā, as before,
one should extract consciousness and, as previously described, unite it with Śiva.
At the conclusion of the vision, through the practice of the equinox sequence,
the Guru himself performs the union for him by placing [the consciousness] beyond the crest-lock into Śivā.
In that regard, the masters maintain that one's own guru and one's own lineage must be honored.
Having prepared the funeral pyre, one should not place Śiva upon it with his head to the south;
rather, one should arrange the cloth in reverse order using the available fuel.
Having employed the Lord of the Altar (Sthāṇḍileśa) with the fire connected to the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
one should offer [the oblation] starting from the head until the completion with this mantra:
"Oṃ, you, O Agni, [are the witness] of this [offering] prepared at the time of the southern [solstice]."
Accept this great oblation, born of mantra, which is auspicious and free from deceit.
Having thus heated them, one should cast the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, with their openings facing downwards, into the blazing fire.

This is its meaning: O Agni, you who are the Lord Sadāśiva in the form of the southern fire; O Kāla, the Lord who is Rudra of the impurity of time (kālamala), accept this great oblation. Of what nature is it? It is that which has been brought forth by Time itself for the enjoyment of karma to be experienced. It is produced from mantra, purified by the mantra-offering deposited during the higher initiation (dīkṣā), and even now performed as a sacrifice for you. The sense is: "Accept also the mantra."
Having released Śambhu who resides in the fire while uttering the syllable "Śakra," the preceptor places the Vardhanī vessel upon his left shoulder and [the other] on the right.
Releasing the rear-stream [of breath], one should then cast it into the northeast;
having gone to the limit of time, one gazes at the back...
As long as the skull remains broken, one should wait there;
then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, having bathed and sipped water, one should wear it over the right shoulder.
Having spread excellent *darbha* grass on the bank— with the tips pointing toward oneself and the bases facing away—
one should offer three handfuls (*añjali*) of sesame, *darbha*, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), while reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ, O pure-souled one named [so-and-so], be present, svadhā!"
Oṃ hāṃ, O [Name], pure self, become Sadāśiva, svadhā!
Oṃ hāṃ, O [Name], pure self, become peaceful, svadhā!
Having bathed again and sipped water for purification (ācamana), one should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) as before, after offering salutations.
The preceptor should mutter the *Ghorasata* mantra two hundred times for one who gives [the gift] to Skanda;
having gone to his own hermitage, he should worship the deity according to his capacity.
One should deposit the bones at a sacred ford on that very day or on the third;
having performed the collection of the bones, one should then place them inside a full water-pot.
On the peak of the holy ground, having performed the rite of establishing the sacred ford (tīrtha),
he should then bathe, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and consume ghee along with fire.
Having bathed again and performed the ritual placement [of mantras], one should pay homage to all the Gaurīs. Thus it is said.
And when someone has died out of sight, or at that time among those who debate, he says:
Having fashioned an image out of darbha grass and other materials, one should perform the remaining rites as previously described;
however, for one who has broken their vow, no final rite (iṣṭi) should ever be performed at the conclusion of the task.
Whether it be perceptible or imperceptible, [this applies] to the disqualified person who has fallen away.

Just as a guide for one who desires liberation, when that person is afflicted on the path, is of low character, remains in a state of pride, and has failed while traveling toward another land, provides him with a higher initiation.
Having fashioned an image of that [deity] out of kuśa grass or from cow dung,
one should prepare that linga after it has been immersed in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
By means of the application of the Great Net (Mahājāla), endowed with the power of mantra and the power of mudrā,
one should withdraw that which resides in the portions of the mantra-body, and having performed it thus,
one should yoke the fetters (*pāśas*) to the stainless state (*amalapada*).
Having caused that milk, clarified butter, and honey— endowed with the splendor of Śiva—
to be consumed by fire, one should then perform a Śrāddha rite consisting of half of that [remaining portion].
This is the procedure for one who has passed away, even when a sapinda relative is present, according to the worldly customs of the Śivadharma.
The external water-offering should be performed just like the rite for immediate liberation;
there is no distinction in the final funeral rite, and thus it is prescribed that nothing further need be said.

It should be understood that the final rite (*antyesti*) consists of the departure (*utkrānti*), protection (*saṃpālana*), preservation (*pālanā*), and the various [offerings] ending with the sound of the *śivāgni* fire.
Just as fire arises from the friction of wood and twigs,
so here the locus of experience falls upon the earth for the experiencer when his enjoyment is exhausted.
That which is to be enjoyed, together with various means of enjoyment,
is of two kinds according to desire: that which arises from desire and that which does not.
That which is prohibited and forbidden, and that which is other than these by choice, is not considered [as such]; the prohibited is of three kinds: sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic.
If it falls into water, fire, or on the ground, it is tāmasa;
if it falls into the hand, it is sāttvika. One should perform the act of friendship with that [stone] in the house of a cowherd.
The thought, "Death comes from protecting what has been taken," is said to be rajasic;
for it arises in one who is unable to retaliate against benefactors out of resentment.
In times of calamity—
having himself been struck down by iron and severely censured—
the knower of reality, having mentally renounced the means of enjoyment and having calculated the number of others, [remains steadfast].
One who performs the rite of departure (utkrānti) brings an end [to his life]; that is his perfected state.
In this case, the sacrifice (iṣṭi) should be performed, excluding the purification of the sacrificial fee (bhārga).
Nevertheless, one of lower caste who has abandoned his vows should not be made to recite [the mantra];
having followed [him] and bathed in water, he should mutter the hundred names of his own clan-lord.
Whoever carries a deceased Brahmin who was initiated into the Śiva-dīkṣā— whether he was established in his vows or had ceased his vows— shall not suffer death in the celestial realm.
He who takes a deceased Śiva-yogin who has passed away alone and honors him with due rites shall be liberated from all undesirable things.
O wealthy one, for one who observes the Śiva-vow, there is neither death nor impurity;
because he does not regard his previous stages of life, the momentary rite of cremation for the bones does not apply.
Even for one who remains in a previous stage of life, [liberation is attained] through initiation.
For the knower who possesses the seed of the purification of sound and performs the true rites,
that [impurity] which would otherwise persist for even a moment is removed simply by bathing.

Otherwise, there would be a loss of the ritual placement (nyāsa), and that [loss] belongs to those who perform the rites for the sake of final liberation; however, one who has become Śiva desires a Guru.
In the absence of a guru, [the lineage passes to] the disciple; in his absence, to one's own progeny;
and when, over time, even that progeny should cease to exist here, [the lineage continues through another means].
For others, that [gift] is not to be accepted; then it goes to its own proper domain. Or else, that substance should be offered to Śiva or to the Śiva-fire.
And those who contemplate the established order must not transgress his word, which is to be respected.
"Otherwise, one should employ that which is suitable for its own purpose accordingly. Thus it is said.
Now, in a certain scripture:

having prepared the Śiva-vessel, the weapon-vessel, the *vardhanī*, and the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and having performed [the rites] as before, one should mentally offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to Śiva alone in the fire-pit; then, having dismissed Śiva who resides upon the sacrificial mound, [one remains] alone.

"Burn the citri with the fire of the crest alone. And it has been said by the Teacher: "For the four [initiates] by the preceptor, for the three by the practitioner (sādhaka), for the two by the spiritual son (putraka), and for the one who knows the pledges (samayajña) within his own lineage."
Out of fear as well, one who knows the samaya should cause all [beings] to do so.
Having reached the riverbank, one should smear it with cow dung;
then, having duly worshipped the jar and the scripture-jar according to the rules.
On a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit, having worshipped Śiva as before,
one should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa); having gratified the mantras, one should cause them to blaze.
That ash, rubbed with cow-dung and purified with the Śiva-sword mantra,
should be brought and placed there upon the body of the fire in the [southern] direction.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] and shorn his hair, he should meditate on the Praṇava in the heart;
having performed the ritual of Sakalīkaraṇa and worshipped [him], he should then perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having meditated upon Śiva by means of the path [of breath], one should offer that to the God;
O Lord, accept this great oblation, whether it be [offered] with the breath or with the span of the arms.
Having spoken thus and having dismissed Śiva, who abides as fearlessness within the body,
one should then lead the fire, which has been kindled with that fuel, to its place of worship.
Then, one should maintain an unbroken stream from the vessel of the weapon, in the form of an unfragmented circle; may there be auspiciousness for you now.
Having offered bathing water on the bank and having bathed again, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) on the bank;
for the purification of Śiva, one should repeat [the mantra] from the west up to the eye.
Or, through their connection with the guru, the disciples, as well as those related to the guru,
should likewise perform rituals such as recitation (japa) and fire-oblations (homa) for one another.
Having recognized his own disciples as sons, another brother is considered a "little son" (putraka);
how then can one who is eternally devoted to the observance of the rules (samaya) not be a "little son"?
The practitioner (sādhaka), the spiritual son (putraka), the brother (bhrātā), the initiate (samayī), and the spiritual grandson (putraputraka)—
of all these who perform the rites, the teacher (ācārya) shall be their father.
For them, there is impurity for one day due to the occasion of Śiva’s ritual impurity;
however, a householder should not transgress the path of the world even in his mind.

Birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) is recognized as such by worldly custom; however, for men who have been initiated, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no birth-impurity regarding the sacred fire.
"The final funeral rites for them have been described by me here in detail. Thus [it is said].
Now, for those whose lives have been taken through negligence— whether by thieves, snakes, fire, tigers, the current of a river, or in battle— [there is this rite].
Having first extracted [the heart], he should silently burn the body of others who have committed suicide or are devoid of the Self, using the Śiva-fire.
Having recited the Aghora-mantra one hundred thousand times, one should offer the Rudra-bali according to the rules.
On the Raudra ground, the wise man should worship the Kṣetrapālas and satisfy them, [reciting]:
"Those Rudras who dwell in the Jana-loka and Sthāna-loka..."
May the guardians of the fields and all others, such as the Piśācas, Dānavas, and so forth,
with well-pleased minds, accept this bali offering.
Having prayed, "Release [him]! He has attained the state of a piśāca through the power of a fierce death," one should clench the fist and cast it down with palms joined in añjali.

Oṃ, homage and svāhā to Raudrī, the Kṣetrapāla, Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Dānavas, Bhūtas, Grahas, and those who desire the maṇḍala-offering; such is the application of the mantra for worship, the offering of bali, and so forth.
Having properly performed his ablutions, he should cause those whose wealth is austerity— the eight who uphold the great vows, such as the Pāśupatas and others— to attain enlightenment.
Having satisfied them with garments and ritual fees, one should dismiss them;
having fashioned an effigy out of *darbha* grass as a likeness of that body.
Having established the remainder as before, one should apply it to the stainless state.
Thus is known the procedure for the final sacrifice (antyesti) for those whose souls have reached every possible condition,
according to various Siddhāntas and reasonings, by the venerable Śivajñānaśambhu.
Thus ends the ritual for the final oblation in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Now I shall describe the ritual for the *śrāddha*, which removes the debt owed to the gurus and others.
And it has been said:
"The rites of worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth, extend from the gods down to the grass."
"One should always offer unswerving conduct even toward sages, as well as libations and other offerings.

Having been initiated, one should discharge one's debt to the guru and others through the performance of *śrāddha* rites. Otherwise, by neglecting this injunction, how could the disciple become free from debt? Thus it is said.
Whatever wealth is given with faith by learned men to worthy recipients on behalf of their preceptors, that indeed is declared to be *śrāddha*.
After the day of the funeral rites, on the third day, one should perform the Śrāddha for ascetics (tāpasas).
After that day, for those remaining at home, this is the rule:
until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed, Vedic rituals are prescribed;
thereafter, they are for the sake of worldly social interaction for the sons and others.

A Śiva-śrāddha should be performed by those whose souls are established in the Śiva-dharma; it should be done regularly when there is prosperity, and specifically on the day of the lunar anniversary of the deceased.
The consecration (pratiṣṭhā) should be performed on the new moon day, or once every year,
or on the anniversary of death, or during the fortnight of Śrāddha rites, by qualified disciples or even by sons.

Out of compassion for their disciples, the teachers, or the groups of brothers, out of a spirit of affection for their brothers, established the convention regarding the arrangement of the scriptures.
