On the preceding day, with devotion, the disciple should invite the preceptor and other ascetics, as well as those established in their vows, householders, and those who have been initiated.
On another day, having properly performed their two daily rites,
they prepared various kinds of foods and grains when the cooking was completed over the auspicious fire.
In a secret, smeared, and auspicious place, having prepared a washed pedestal and other such items,
one should worship the chosen *liṅga* with extensive offerings of incense, lamps, and so forth.
Having offered abundant food oblations and performed the fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rules,
he requested permission from Śiva, saying, "May this be so for me throughout my births."
Having constructed two circular mandalas on the eastern courtyard, each measuring one cubit and ending at the edge of another cubit,
with their orientation from south to north and their shape being four-cornered (square).
Having sprinkled the mandala with the general *arghya* water using the *astra-mantra*,
one should [offer] barley, *darbha* grass, unbroken rice, and white flowers in their proper order.
Having worshipped those seated on the eastern seat upon the pedestal with their own respective names using the *hṛdaya* mantra,
one should offer a handful of flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) at the feet of both with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having sipped water (ācamana) in the south and north, one should wrap both [feet];
as follows: *Oṃ hāṃ, to Kālāgnirudra, this water for the feet (pādārghya), svāhā*.
"Oṃ hāṃ, to Ananta Viṣṇu, this water for the feet, svāhā. (p.
457) In the western circular mandala, one should offer three handfuls of sesame seeds at the feet.
Oṃ hāṃ, to Īśa, the father, this water for the feet, svadhā!
Oṃ hāṃ, to Sadāśiva, the grandfather, this water for the feet, svadhā! Oṃ hāṃ, to Śānta, the great-grandfather, this water for the feet, svadhā!
Having given [the gifts] as before, he should cause those who have performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) to enter within;
then, having himself performed the sipping with his sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should lie down among them.
Having first established two [liṅgas] facing east on the right side of the deity,
the Guru should then place three [liṅgas] facing north upon the pedestal.
"Today, at this [specified] Śrāddha, a rite is being performed for you;
one should perform the rites of seating, invocation, and so forth with the heart-mantra and one's own name.
Beginning from the feet up to the head, one should worship the two [deities] with unbroken rice grains (akṣatas)."
Afterwards, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds— beginning from the head— with these three, as well as with incense, lamps, purifiers, garments, and auspicious ornaments.
Then, having performed the ritual knowledge at that time, O Lord, he should draw a mandala in the south,
provided with kuśa grass pointing westward and abundant with sesame seeds, while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
Having set aside the finest portion of all the cooked food and mixed it with honey, ghee,
and sesame seeds, one should fashion there three funeral balls (piṇḍas) shaped like hen’s eggs.
For the sake of attaining proximity with the ancestors, one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) starting from the east;
having worshipped Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta among them with elaborate offerings,
one should offer incense, lamps, and food oblations (naivedya), and perform a hundred oblations for each individually.
Having worshipped [the deity] in the fire with Kālānīla and the others as before,
and having offered three morsels of food as an oblation, one should go into its presence.
Having offered each item individually as before, or having placed them all together in the vessel and so forth,
one should say, "Everything is complete," and then recite the *sannidhāna-arghya* (the offering for the presence of the deity).
Then, having heard their words,
he recited "Saṃpūrṇam" seven times, offering it for the sake of invoking the presence [of the deity].
Then, having placed the vessel in his left hand, the wise one should perform the recitation;
saying "Thou art the station of the ancestors," he should proceed according to the sequence of right and left hands.
Then, having arranged [the offerings] on the western side and having himself washed his feet and hands,
he should present the food to be chewed and eaten, as well as drinks and so forth, preceded by the remnants of the oblation.
Having offered food for this purpose, even when the five [deities] have been worshipped,
one should recite the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra over the food and offer the *āpośana* water with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having said, "May you partake of the nectar," he should present it;
then he should feed the Brahmins and the guests without any hesitation.
When they are satisfied, he should then ask, "Are you fully satiated?
Having placed food with water near their remains, he should then offer it.
He should offer water for sipping (ācamana) to the ancestors with two verses, and afterwards he should dismiss the vessel;
at the conclusion of the sipping, having given betel-leaf accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), and having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the fire of Śiva,
one should dismiss the Lord after worshipping Him and dedicate the rite of the śrāddha.
Having knelt down on both knees, one should worship with the left hand— adorned with flowers, water, and unbroken grains— the white fruit of the merit of the *śrāddha*.
O Lord, having granted the means for the attainment of union with you—the feet of our worshipful masters—Māyā has performed this Śrāddha; please accept it.
Having spoken thus, one should offer the *arghya* into the left hand of the God of gods;
then, having lifted up the *arghya*, one should ask forgiveness from the Lord of Gods and from Īśa and the others.
One should cause those who are meritorious and noble—women seeking sons—to consume the middle portion;
that woman shall give birth to a son of Śaṅkara, radiant with knowledge.
Or one may bestow the merit as one pleases upon a cow, a Brahmin, fire, or water;
thereafter, the performer should address the ground with people mentioning their lineage and other details.
One should likewise consume the remaining food, drink, and so forth, which are purifying.
Thus has the *śrāddha* been briefly described for those who follow the path of Śiva.
Now, [I shall describe] the worldly duties preceded by the *śrāddha*.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the *śiva-śrāddha* is prescribed;
one should perform the *śrāddha* for the Lord of those objects that belong to the Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśa*).
And it is said in the Kālottara regarding those who follow worldly customs:
"Then his ritual action should be performed either in his own hermitage or by a body of water;
having placed the hearth facing north, he should cast fire into it with the Astra-mantra."
Having placed [the vessel] on the stove, one should pour rice with water into it using a ladle;
once combined with honey, milk, and clarified butter, it is perfected within the circle of light.
Having drawn the mandala upon the ground, free from hair, insects, and the like,
one should prepare an arghya vessel and sprinkle it with that water using the Astra-mantra.
There, having brought down the faithful Bhadrāsana consecrated three times with mantras,
and then having recited the mantra once, one should prepare the seat.
There, one should worship the Supreme Lord with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and by means of the internal sign (saṃjñā),
first offering water for honor (arghya), flowers, and so forth, without the sequence of mantra-installation (mantranyāsa).
O Śambhu, the worship in the fire is performed with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), not in such detail as for the body; likewise,
having taken up a beautiful portion in a silver or copper vessel with the heart-mantra,
one should prepare the sacrificial ball (piṇḍa) with sesame seeds, the size of a hen's egg.
Having established that [liṅga] in the place of Śiva, facing north, [he should do so] with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra).

Immediately thereafter, one should worship him with flowers, water for the feet, perfumes, incense, and so forth, as well as garments, food offerings, and other articles, pronouncing his own name followed by the word *svadhā*.
*Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā, obeisance to [Name] of such-and-such lineage, possessing such-and-such qualities*—
this is the mantra. Into that [water], one should place sesame seeds, honey, kuśa grass, and scented water.
Having filled his joined palms or a vessel— either silver or made of rhinoceros horn— with various kinds of food mixed with curd, milk, and ghee, while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should sprinkle that rice-ball all around on the outside with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
having paid obeisance according to the rule, one should dismiss it, saying, "Forgive me."

O son, having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with water from the heart-mantra and with the previously mentioned mudrā and mantra, [he should offer] the jar containing sesame seeds to the six-faced one.
One should present that, together with a garment and accompanied by gold, to the preceptor.
Having cast the rice-ball into water, or into fire in its absence,
one should offer sesame-water upon the ground with the name [of the deceased] and the *hṛdaya-mantra*, together with the word *svadhā*.
Having washed his hands and feet, he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
then, having withdrawn the pedestal that was placed there and having dismissed that which resided in the fire.
Having bathed and anointed himself, and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), he should enter the house;
having established protection with the weapon-mantra (astra), he should eat light food consisting primarily of air.
Facing east, the Guru, with practitioners facing north and the sons of the lineage abiding by the samaya facing west, should partake of the meal.
O Six-faced One, one should always avoid a single row among those of different castes;
the mandala for the Brahmins and the others consists of four, three, two, or one line.
The vessel should be protected by joining it with white powder;
having stood upon a seat oriented toward the east or one arranged according to the ritual sequence.
On a vessel either twelve finger-breadths long or twelve finger-breadths in circumference,
one should then recite the Aghora mantra for eating according to one's capacity.
At the end of the day, having scattered white mustard seeds with the Astra-mantra, one should go to bed;
this entire ritual procedure must be performed with diligence for ten days by the wise man, desiring to bestow grace upon the deceased.
One should perform [the rite] for five days with the mantras beginning with the Heart and ending with the Eye;
and for the subsequent five days, with the faces beginning with Sadyojāta.
Having thus completed the ten-day period, when the eleventh day arrived, he said:
p.
462) Then, for him who abides by worldly custom, there is the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
as follows:
One should then perform the śrāddha rite when the daily fire-oblation has been successfully completed.
For that purpose, one should worship the Guru, or else the Guru’s son;
or, in his absence, the Sādhaka, or the Putraka who abides by the rules (samaya).
O son, having washed each individual person— whether one observing a vow or a devotee of Śiva— and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), they should be made to enter within.
Then, having offered a seat and established [the deity] facing north,
one should worship the limbs of Brahmā together before him in the same manner as previously described.
Thereafter, according to the prior injunction, [one should perform the rite] accompanied by the name and lineage.
Then, having honored the teacher, he struck the one who had been invited by name.
Then, having offered all the funeral requisites to him according to one's ability— with perfumes, flowers, purifiers, garments, and so forth— [one should proceed].
Then, having received permission from Śiva, one should commence the piṇḍayāga in front of him,
using sesame seeds, the tips of mustard stalks, kuśa grass, and honey.
There, having worshipped the Lord of Gods with perfumes, flowers, and sacred threads,
one should diligently offer the food oblation (*naivedya*) into the *piṇḍa* while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
Having offered the *piṇḍa* according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped with devotion,
one should perform the recitation (*japa*), form the ritual gestures (*mudrā*), and then carry out the fire-oblation (*vahnihoma*).
Having given alms, food, and so forth to the Guru with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra),
at the conclusion of that meal, one should [perform the rite] before the seat of the mantra (mantrapīṭha).
Having offered water with sesame seeds upon the ground from the *arghya* vessel while reciting the *astra-mantra*,
and having taken the prepared food along with the remnants of the meal together with water;

For the purpose of satisfying the elemental beings (bhūtas), one should scatter an offering (bali) outside; one should ask, "Is it complete? and give water for sipping (ācamana) to the preceptor. Having also collected the remnants and sprinkled the ground with the weapon-mantra (hetinā), [one should perform the purification].
Taking the right [hand], the Guru should perform the propitiation of Śiva;
he should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) with the *śivamantra* to the Deity residing in the fire.
Having withdrawn the Lord of Mantras, who possesses a splendor equal to ten million suns, from the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus into the middle of the fire of the *piṇḍa* upon the seat.
O Śikhidhvaja, one should perform this rite month after month;
once it is completed, when the thirteenth month has arrived, one should remember it in this way.
For the sake of pacifying his state as a preta, one should perform the ancestral śrāddha ceremony;
having first completed the daily routine beginning with the ritual bath and ending with the fire oblation (homa).
When the consecrated fire has been established and the food prepared therein has been saturated with ghee and milk,
one should respectfully invite the preceptors who are observant of their ritual duties;
having performed the washing of their feet, one should lead them into the interior of the house.
Having first placed two [deities] upon two seats in the eastern face.

One should conceive of both Rudra as the Fire of Time (Kālānala) and Viṣṇu as Ananta; standing on one's knees before the fire, one should first worship the two from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head with unbroken rice grains, flowers, incense, and other offerings.
Having placed the three-eyed one facing north according to the sequence of the deposition on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa),
one should conceive of Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta as the third among them.
There, the invocation of the Lord should be performed with the heart-mantra using the designation "Son";
one should conceive Sadāśiva as the Grandfather by means of his own mantra.
One should conceive of Śiva as the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha) by means of the root of one's own knowledge;
then, according to the prescribed rule and in due order, one should worship these [deities] with offerings of water, flowers, and so forth.
Then, having requested permission, one should worship the Lord of Mantras (Mantreśa) in his form as a Liṅga with the great seats and so forth, with perfumes, garments, ornaments, and abodes.
Having gratified Maheśvara with incense, lamps, and other offerings, with food oblations consisting of various kinds of fresh delicacies, and with hymns, mantras, and prostrations;
And having brought that very fire close together, one should offer libations;
with the sacred thread over the left shoulder for those [deceased] on the right, and over the right shoulder for those on the left.
Having recited the seven weapon-mantras and lifted the vessel of *arghya* with devotion,
one should offer the *arghya* for the sake of attaining the presence of the ancestors and then place it beneath that [vessel].

Having said, "May it be complete," and also, "Thou art the seat of the ancestors," one should offer three types of food offerings (*naivedya*) upon the mandala near Śiva, using *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south, for the purpose of attaining the presence of the ancestors.

Equipped with condiments and the like, and saturated with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, one should sprinkle it with the water of the *arghya* vessel empowered by the *astra-mantra*, while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra* over the three locations.
By means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal, [he should place it] upon the darbha grass in the counter-clockwise direction.

Having recollected what was previously remembered and meditated upon the ancestors with their respective mantras individually, one should then worship Śiva as before by means of their names, lineages, and so forth.

In this case as well, having inferred the meaning from the two words, one should perform the monthly *śrāddha* preceded by this formula: "On such-and-such a lunar day, during the conjunction with such-and-such a constellation, for the sake of [the ancestors] of such-and-such a lineage and such-and-such a name, in this sacred field on the bank of the Gaṅgā or another river, in the presence of such-and-such a Lord, I shall perform the monthly *śrāddha*.
Having thus honored the ancestors, one should worship the deity residing in the *liṅga* with flowers and other offerings.
The meaning is that one should please [them].
Having gratified those whose fathers have been cut off, one should satisfy them through the offering of oblations into the fire;
then, O son, one should give food to those who have been honored previously.
Thereafter, according to the tradition, one should ask whether they are satisfied, using the words "May there be satisfaction."
With a heart full of devotion at the end of the evening, one should present the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) before Śiva;
then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should bid farewell to Śiva and the fire.
One should cause [the disciple] to consume the central ball of food, which has been consecrated with the root mantra.
Just as that noble woman gave birth to many daughters,
may she give birth to a son named Śaṅkara, who increases prosperity and good fortune.
To him who is devoted to the practice of knowing the Dharma and dedicated to the vow of truth,
he then lifted up the arghya vessel that had previously been consecrated with the heart-mantra.
One should visualize all the ancestors present there, whether situated on earth or in the sky, with their respective mantras.
Then, with the water from the *arghya* vessel and the *netra-mantra*,
one should wipe the eyes and sprinkle that water in a pure place.
Thus, the *śrāddha* consisting of mantra, endowed with knowledge and meditation,
should be performed by those who know the *samaya* and so forth, through the Guru, for the sake of attaining success in mantra.
The sons must perform [the funeral rites] for their fathers and others out of compassion for their teachers and disciples;
likewise for those former disciples who were self-realized and had been fully initiated.
Even there, one who is attached to action should act for the sake of attaining his own welfare.
This Śrāddha rite pertaining to initiation (dīkṣā), which bestows a favorable rebirth, has been described by me;
it must be performed by those who have been initiated, according to the ritual manual, by one who knows the sacrifice along with its ancillaries.
One should perform the *śrāddha* rite at the proper place and time for a worthy recipient;
for when the *śrāddha* for Śiva has been performed in this manner, I, who am eternally of the nature of Śiva, [am gratified].
They attain satisfaction here through Śiva, who is pleased and permeated by Śiva; thus,
according to the *Jñānaratnāvalī* of the illustrious Jñānaśaṅkarācārya and in accordance with the meaning of the Siddhānta, this ritual procedure for the *śrāddha* has been composed.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.

Now, we shall recite the Śivāṣṭaka for those whose souls are free from desire, should they inadvertently come into contact with the remains of offerings (nirmālya), in order to remove each respective fault.
That rite should be performed with pure substances on festival days such as the eighth day of the dark fortnight;
one should invite twelve ascetics on the preceding day.
On another day, having prepared pure food for those who abide by the pure tradition, who are tranquil, and who are firm in their vows through devotion to Śiva, he performs the ritual actions.
Having summoned them, one should wash their feet with the *hṛdaya* mantra according to the procedure;
the mantras begin with: "Oṃ hāṃ, to Soma, this water for the feet, svāhā," and so forth.
One should place eight [images] facing north in the vicinity of the liṅga;
two facing west in the east, and two in the west of the eastern [section].
Having established them, one should worship the twelve deities therein as follows:
Somaśambhu, Śiva, Śūlin, Sarvajña, and Śaṅkara.
Śitikaṇṭha and Śarva—these reside upon the gentle faces;
all are endowed with various forms of Śambhu, white in color, and seated upon lion-thrones.
All of them specifically hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a trident and a lotus;
I shall now describe the specific characteristics of these eight in their proper order.
Śambhu holds a noose and a goad, O Soma; another bears a bow and arrows;
yet another holds a bell and a staff; and another holds a rosary and a water-pot.
Another holds a book and a rosary, another bears a parrot and a mynah; another holds the moon and the sun, and the eighth likewise plays the lute.
Then Brahmā and Śakra stood in the two eastern positions,
while Viṣṇu and the serpent Ananta stood in the two western positions, [along with] Nīla.
With palms joined in reverence, all [of them] remain; what remains of these is now described: Brahmā holds a staff and a water-pot; Hari holds a thunderbolt and a threatening gesture;
Viṣṇu holds a mace and a discus; and the Nāgas hold a water-pot and a rosary.
Those Rudras, beginning with Brahmā, should be known as having six feet and four arms.
The *praṇava*, the *hṛdayāṇu*, or the [other] mantras are proclaimed as these;
having worshipped them all with perfumes and other offerings, with garments, flowers, and ornaments.

Having gratified [the deities] with one hundred oblations for each [deity] using the heart-mantra (hṛdaṇu), one should feed them with sweet foods and the like; when they are satisfied, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Kneeling on both knees, one should request these [deities] for betel leaf, saying:
"O Devas, out of negligence, I have previously consumed once the remains of offerings (nirmālya) such as divine substances; [I pray for this] to remove those respective faults."
"O Mother, you should now bestow your grace out of compassion;
may my liberation in the supreme state come through your favor or by other means.
Having thus made this petition and received permission, one should bow to the God and ask for forgiveness.

Having resolved upon liberation for the deities presiding over the iron mountain, the deer, and so forth, one should install them in a temple of Śiva— a sacred field of the gods— or in a painting, and then feed those whose wealth is austerity.
Then, O Lord, the controller of substances attains purity.
And it is said—
the venerable Goddess said:
I have heard of the lineage of the divine path and have heard much concerning initiation;
now I wish to hear about the presiding deity. [Exit. O bearer of the *kalā*, I [speak] of the many various lords of austerity resulting from the sin of *kṛta*.
By consuming the remains of the offering (nirmālya), one is liberated from terrible sin that is otherwise very difficult to overcome.
O Lord of the gods of gods, does such a thing exist? Let its full extent be told:
[the accumulation] of all impurities, whether arising from ignorance or even from knowledge.
Īśvara said:
There is one supreme expiation for those who destroy the remains of Śiva’s offerings.
By reciting this hymn of eight verses to Śivā, one is liberated from that sin.
Whether made of stone, clay, wood, or metal, or even fashioned with various materials before a deity,
by performing the installation according to the rules, a person is liberated from sin.
O Goddess, among the great sins previously mentioned and those associated with women,
this burning of the discarded flower offering (nirmālya) is known to be the most censured;
it is certain that there is no sin greater than these eight offenses against Śiva.
O Maheśvarī, the truthful word of Maheśvara should be reflected upon:
Soma, Śambhu, Śiva, the wielder of the trident, the omniscient, and likewise Śaṅkara.
Śitikaṇṭha and Śarva—this, O beloved, is the Śivāṣṭaka;
one should recite it oneself when alive, and again when deceased.
O Goddess, no sin exists for him on whose behalf [the offering] was made.
O Goddess, having used the remains of the offering (nirmālyaka), a man should avoid displeasing others.
Furthermore, by consuming [the offerings] together and so forth, one goes to hell; there is no doubt about this.
These eight are auspicious and peaceful, endowed with various amorous graces.
Sixteen years of age, adorned with jeweled earrings,
their chests covered by necklaces of longing [gems], their feet graced by anklets,
they have three eyes, wear masses of matted hair, and have their heads adorned with the moon.

Adorned with armlets, bracelets, and the ends of divine garments, they are beautifully decorated; they have six arms, assume the triple-bend posture (tribhaṅga), and are seated in the lotus position (padmāsana) facing upwards.
Seated upon jeweled lion-thrones, all [the deities] bear the bull-emblem;
they primarily hold the blue lotus, the gesture of fearlessness, and the trident.
Afterwards, one should bestow the two weapons as I shall describe them:
first the noose and the goad were mentioned, and likewise the wielder of the bow and arrow.
Another holds a bell and a half-moon; another is a bearer of the *kuṇḍikā* water-pot; others bear garlands and books; and another is a bearer of parrots.
Another is Candrasūryadhara, and the eighth is Vīṇāvādī. Alongside these who are arranged in a row, one should worship four other deities; I shall state their names and forms.
With palms joined in reverence, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Vināyaka [spoke].

In sequence, [the deities] hold a vajra and a tarjanī, and another holds a spear and a staff; others hold a discus and a mace, while yet another holds a rosary and a water-pot. Thus, these four-armed ones are to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
O Goddess, the eightfold worship of Śiva must indeed be performed through celibacy and other such virtues;
it cannot be accomplished by others who have minds fixed on impurities or by heretics, even through the removal of physical dirt.
O ascetics rich in penance, grant initiation to these twelve who have committed minor offenses;
they are devoted to another [teacher], yet are endowed with purity and right conduct.
"They should be worshipped according to the previously mentioned ritual for the sake of destroying all sins. Thus [it is said].

Thus has the Śivāṣṭaka been proclaimed by the venerable Śivajñānaśambhu, in accordance with the meaning of the Siddhānta, for the purpose of removing all impurities resulting from the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati. Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
On the thread consisting of the network of channels, one should place the heart-lotus together with its mandala;
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) there with the Heart-mantra, one should then place the foundational Śakti right there.
Then, with the supreme ray, one should project the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) there;
then, taking the disciple’s self, which is shrouded in impurity (*mala*), one should project it there.
One should project the black noose of impurity (*malapāśa*), as well as the white-and-black noose of impurity.
That manifold noose of Māyā resides within the self as its eighth part;
it constitutes the state of being an enjoyer, while the stainless self experiences pleasure and pain through that karma.
The illusory body has its cause in the sense objects;
one should worship the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) and Śiva upon that body at the head.
Then, the knower of mantras should place that thread upon the head without interruption.
One should deposit the sixfold path, pervading down to the feet of the disciple;
likewise, having deposited the power (śakti) that presides over the impurities and fetters, one should offer libations.
Then, one should place the Vāma-śakti upon his crest-lock (śikhā) according to the rule;
furthermore, one should offer libations into the fire for the sake of Nirodha, which is crooked in form.

Having offered oblations with the hundredfold root mantra and the full mantra for the sake of rectifying any deficiency or excess, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the kindling (dīpana) of the Śāntyatīta and other levels.

Oṃ, salutations to Śiva; Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati. The work concerning the Lord of the Universe, the Light residing within the expanse of the maṇḍala, is now declared by the venerable Jñānaśivācārya as the characteristics of the liṅga.
Although there are many kinds of supports for worship for a deity with a physical form,
nevertheless, for the sake of daily rites, the *liṅga* bestows the complete fruit.
Likewise, in the Śrī Kālottara: "O son of Kṛttikā, I shall explain in brief the supports of worship;
at the commencement of worship, one should diligently perform the worship of the embodied form."
For yogins, worship of one's own form is always prescribed;
at the commencement of a sacrifice, one should always perform worship in the form of the Guru.
Or, having offered the benediction, one should worship Śiva in this manner for the sake of the child;
for the worship of Vidyā must indeed always be performed.
One should worship the Vidyāpīṭha, the Kośa, and the Vasusaṃhitā for the measure of a cubit.
O son, Sadāśiva is to be worshipped in the water at the conclusion of the bath, and this should be done once.
At the conclusion of the worship in the fire, having worshipped him, one should perform the oblation (homa);
for the sake of removing obstacles, one should thoroughly worship the weapon of Śiva upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).

Śiva should be worshipped on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and a water-pot (kalaśa) is likewise desired; for those desiring spiritual perfection (siddhi), worship should always be performed with effort upon a fixed liṅga.
The worship of Śiva at a mobile liṅga bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
One should worship [the deity] as reflected in a mirror while situated within the solar orb;
likewise, one should worship [him] while situated within the lunar orb for the purpose of evading death.
He is to be worshipped everywhere, always present in all substrates.
Even there, in the linga, the Blessed Lord Dhūrjaṭi accepts worship.
O Six-faced One, even if worship is performed incompletely— lacking the full array of mantras, ritual substances, and rites— nevertheless, that worship becomes complete when offered to the Liṅga.
O son, the worship on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) must indeed be neither deficient nor excessive in its form.
"However, worship that is deficient or excessive is proclaimed to be fruitless.
For this reason, my dear child, one should begin the propitiation of the Liṅga. Thus [it is said].
That wherein all beings dissolve and from which they emerge again is the supreme Liṅga, the unmanifest ether, the partless Supreme Śiva.
O Blessed One, Śiva is characterized by means of signs, water, and the internal state;
that *liṅga* is threefold for yogis, consisting of the manifest, the unmanifest, and both.
That which is manifest is known as the "with-parts" (sakala), while the unmanifest is considered the "partless" (niṣkala).
The Liṅga, consisting of the light of knowledge, is traditionally remembered as both manifest and unmanifest.
That which has its form, is devoted to it, is artificial, and is presided over by it is called a *liṅga*; and that artificial one, presided over by it,
[is established] by the learned Ācārya with all auspicious rites during the recitation of the *Tāmra* [scripture].
On an auspicious lunar day and at a favorable moment, the officiant, honored by the patron,
should worship the jar of Śambhu along with its weapons and accompanied by ritual offerings.
Commanded by you, the God of gods, I perform the sacrifice for the sake of the *liṅga*;
that *liṅga*, worthy of being presided over by you, has been produced instantly.
Having made this request and received permission, the preceptor, together with the artisans and the auspicious birds,
should take up all the necessary materials and worship the shoulder-pole.
In a forest, on a mountain, at a riverbank, or likewise in a sacred field—
having obtained a gentle stone there, in a pleasant sacrificial hall;
He should worship the Lord, the Scripture, the Sovereign of the World, and the virtuous Gatekeeper within the pitcher;
having sprinkled them with the Śivā-mantra and worshipped them with the Hṛdaya-mantra, he should protect them.
At night, one should cast an offering to the directions with ashes while reciting the *astra* and *varma* mantras;
then, having fully worshipped all the implements such as the chisel and the mallet.
Having consumed the product of the cow, the Guru, purified in body, should sleep in the midst of the sacrifice;
one seeking worldly enjoyment should lie with his head toward the east, while one seeking liberation should lie with his head toward the south.
In the location of the head, one should worship the sevenfold Māṇavaka Śiva in the pitcher—
resembling pure crystal, with three eyes and a single face.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a serpent as his sacred thread, he has the crescent moon as his crest;
he is gentle, adorned with a crown and earrings.

Having meditated upon [the deity] holding a trident and the gesture of granting boons in the right hands, and a skull-bowl and the gesture of protection in the left, adorned with armlets and anklets, one should recite the mantra while dreaming.
Oṃ, salutations to Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
salutations to the Auspicious One, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Dreams.
Tell me the truth in a dream regarding the matter of the Lord of Sacrifices.
*Oṃ hili hili, salutation to the Trident-bearer.* Having performed the morning ablutions and other rites, one should worship the Supreme Lord.

One should recount a good dream to a beloved person; in the case of a bad dream, one should perform a rite of pacification with a thousand recitations of the Aghora-weapon mantra, or half of that, or a hundred.
In the east, the north, and likewise the northeast, the body and the head should be manifested in sequence.
One should mark the head at the lower part and the back portion at the upper part;
the stone slab is to be taken at the position of the feet, and likewise, the bull is placed in the remaining space.
One should mark it with that [specific] sign using either the *praṇava* or the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
When the work on the leaf is not yet complete, one should carefully extract the stone.
Having placed it in the work-sheds, one should perform the ritual as before;
then, having drawn out the stone, one should examine its qualities and defects.
As it is said in the Kālottara: "That stone is declared to be of three kinds—female, male, and neuter;
likewise, [it may be] a child, a youth, or an old man; and it may be rough or devoid of royal [marks]."
Deep with its profound sounds, it was lovely with its smooth luster.
Emerging from the water, firm, heavy, level, and gentle, yet not facing downward;
with deep shade, fragrant, glossy, very sweet, and solid.
Among those of white and other colors, as well as those that are colorless, a line that is too thin is censured;
in the case of an excellent [line], a thin line is to be avoided, as are dots.
The lower lines are inferior, while the marks (bindus) are likewise praised as supreme.
O son, a stone that is level, not false, unbroken, and praised— specifically one from the Kṛttikā asterism—
should be taken as a vidyā-stone, provided it is free from pegs, ripples, and fissures.
Those with many lines, deficient lines, or deformed lines,
those that are constricted, accompanied by cracks, abounding in [unfavorable] marks, and marked with crow-feet— these are inauspicious.
Situated in an impure place, she resembles a pigeon; she is like a female owl, and her laughter, gait, and voice are like those of a donkey or a camel.
Those with the luster of fire, madder, or a *bhṛṅga* insect, resembling a snake or a frog,
and those marked with the footprints of a lion, tiger, camel, elephant, or donkey;
(476) That which has the luster of a fish, mud, or smoke, which is grey or of a soiled radiance,
which is joined with the sound of sacrifice or the cry of a crow, and which is accompanied by a foul odor.
One should avoid that [water] which is disturbed, heated by the sun, or possesses many defects;
however, one should always accept that which is free from defects, for it bestows all accomplishments.
In the case of manifest [lingas] and those beginning with the unmanifest lingas, the "male stone" (puṃśila) is prescribed for the pedestal;
however, for female-form piṇḍīs, the "female stone" (strīśilā) is highly recommended.
One should recite the third verse to Gaurī for the successful opening of the door,
and especially for cutting, carving, or pulling [the materials].
Having thus explained, by means of their defining characteristics, both those with embryos and those without embryos,
[the teacher should observe] when his own mandala or some other part of it becomes distorted.
Then it should be known as "with embryo"; one should examine it preceded by a coating of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), horse, and the region itself.
Having smeared the root of the *ṛddhi* plant together with flowers, a wheel, a vajra, and a bulb, along with a combination of *viṣṭhāra* and lotus stalks, one should apply it to the linga at night.
One should recognize that the fetus has been deformed by observing the discharge of fluids;
one should diagnose the specific humor (doṣa) responsible for the fact that the characteristic signs do not disappear.
If it is soft, or circular, or has a distorted sound, one should indicate a frog;
if it is madder-colored, one should indicate a monitor lizard.
If the leaf is dark green and variegated, it becomes a scorpion;
if it is reddish, however, there will be a portion of its essence, and if it has the luster of a sword, there will be water.
"O Cātre, is he dark-complexioned? He might be a bird; perhaps he is covered in ashes.
Such musical instruments and the like should be recognized with diligent effort.
Having rubbed it with hemp and other materials, one should examine the marks;
if they are of auspicious color and auspicious form, they grant good fortune for the attainment of the serpent-siddhi.
Through colors of an inauspicious form, it yields contrary results.
Likewise, in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "White, red, yellow, and black—one should assign these respectively to the Brahmins and the other castes."
The lotus, clarified butter, red cow urine, fragrance, and the beautiful, firm *akṣa* fruit.
She is the sound of clouds as well as the lute; she is the supreme and the non-supreme in the bell and the conch;
she is the child, the youth, and the old man; she is female, male, and neuter in form.
Though it possesses various colors, is soft, and even fragrant with the scent of the forest, the young girl should be known as a mere child; like a young girl, she is fruitless.
It is considered firm, cool, smooth, deep, resonant with a beautiful sound, solid, preeminent in brilliance, weighty, pleasing to the mind, and well-proportioned.
Bestowing success in all undertakings and endowed with all auspicious characteristics,
[the tongue] that is parched, excessively hot, hard, crooked, or deficient is censured.
A frog, a fish, a bell-less woman, a serpent-woman, and one who carries a light load—she destroys all undertakings; like an old woman discarding her prosperity, she should be abandoned.
There, the form of the plantain leaf among one's own women grants all desires;
however, the scent of the road is like the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *palāśa*, and *arka* trees.
One who is smooth, long-lasting, and deep-toned is a stone-like person;
one who is rough, hot, and very hard is like a kettledrum or a water-pot.
A place that is veiny, rough, and dry bestows success upon one who is impotent;
it is joined with bell-metal, oblations, vultures, and leaves resembling copper.
If it is devoid of dots and lines of that same color,
it brings affliction to the patron, the king, the kingdom, as well as the artisan.
One should avoid that which is joined with the *niganti* plant and is free from impurities;
likewise, one should avoid that which has black or white sprouts, or is attached to a *kaupīka*, or is red like a mountain.
These, being golden in color, are auspicious; all others everywhere cause defects.
A white line resembling a lotus brings welfare to Brāhmaṇas;
for kings it should be yellowish-red; and for Vaiśyas, a dark-red line bestows wealth.
For Śūdras, green and black [sandalwood] is always considered to bestow health.
A line resembling a rainbow is considered auspicious for everyone at all times.
A low line is superior to a high one; a low line is auspicious when it is superior to a high one.
When it is endowed with all characteristics and possesses only slight defects, it is auspicious.
"Then, having offered a thousand oblations with the Aghora mantra, the Guru should perform the union. Thus it is said.
That which is produced from wood is praised as beneficial and accompanied by a sound of great joy;
that which arises from the two types of sandalwood—campaka and nandabībhatsa—is likewise auspicious.
Auspicious [wood] arising from the Śāka, Sāla, Tamāla, Khadira, and Aśoka trees;
and that of the Aśvattha, Vaṭa, Śrīparṇa, Bilva, Tinduka, and Gālava.
One should avoid wood from withered trees, or that produced on funeral mounds or anthills; likewise, one should avoid wood from trees growing within three or four villages,
or that pierced by insects, broken by itself, fallen during a great calamity, or carried by an elephant.
It is withered, possessed by anger and other afflictions, and frequented by those of the lowest castes.
One should abandon a tree that is wounded, knotted, deformed, or lacking in core strength;
however, an old tree possessing the auspicious marks should be consecrated as before.
Having marked the upper foot of Śiva and his face according to the eastern and northern traditions with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should cut it away at that very moment.
Having placed [the image] on a chariot with due ceremony and having brought it there with great care,
one should install it in the form of the ritual object in the northern part of the temple.
A *kaṃsa* should be known as inferior, middling, or superior according to six, seven, or eight *yava*s;
it should also be known as threefold up to one *aṅgula*. A *kara* consists of twenty-four [finger-breadths]. The small [size] is threefold: one cubit, two cubits, and three cubits.
The middle [section] of this [structure] is divided into three parts by four, five, and six cubits.
The three types of the best [size] are considered to be seven, eight, and nine cubits.
There are nine pure liṅgas, both made of stone and of clay;
their measurements range from eight to sixteen aṅgulas, with sixteen intermediate sizes here.

Some authorities say that [the height] increases by six *aṅgulas* for each of the thirty-four [types], or they say it is thirty-four [units]. A stone temple situated below one cubit (*hasta*) is auspicious within a palace or house. Thus Maya said: "A stone temple situated below one cubit is not recommended for palaces."
"Even a calamity occurring at home may lead to success for householders.
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*:
"One should avoid a mountain situated below the Hasta constellation when constructing a temple."
"But that fierce barley-mark [belongs] to Mārasā in the cremation grounds and other such places. Thus it is said.
The wooden [image] should begin at sixteen finger-breadths and have six arms;
the metal one is considered to begin at eight finger-breadths and have three arms.
And so it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
The Liṅga produced from stone, clay, wood, and metal is [worshipped] by Tuṣṭi, Graha, Rasa, and Anila;
it is the most excellent, bestowing excellence, according to the fourfold distinction of materials.
By abandoning one-third of that middle [portion], it becomes the best;
the tip of the small [portion] is from this [middle portion]; thus the linga is described as being threefold according to its petals.
They are divided according to their respective portions of names so that there may be nine *liṅgas*.
The *liṅgas* beginning with Jyeṣṭha and ending with Kanyasa have been described to you.
And likewise, in the *Kālottara*:
Starting from one cubit, I have not described the limit;
[an image] made of clay or stone is equal [to the prescribed size], while one made of wood should be three cubits less.
One made of metal is best when it is half that size, and it is proclaimed that [the measurement] is based on the cubit.
In the temple, the wooden structure is joined up to a limit of sixteen finger-breadths.
Likewise, iron [weights] of eight finger-breadths, or half that size, are beneficial in the home;
however, one should avoid those made of stone or wood in one's own house.
"Metal that bestows enjoyment and liberation is [mercury], except for lead and iron;
gold bestows great enjoyment; silver-born [metal] is middling;
and the remaining [metals] bestow other forms of enjoyment, up to the size of a finger's breadth. Thus it is said.

Or, if a temple has been constructed, it should be made according to the measurement of its inner sanctum (garbha). That which is equal to nine times the measure of the sanctum is seen to be the best. When that sanctum is divided into five parts, the [measurement] by three parts shall be the most excellent of the excellent (uttamottama).
Furthermore, by dividing [the remainder] by nine, the middle and superior [types] are obtained;
when divided again into two, one part of the womb is the inferior-superior.
Starting from the eldest and proceeding downwards until two below the youngest.
Nine superior *liṅgas* arise according to their own names.
And so it is stated in the *Kālottara*:
By the devotees, [the measurements] of the elements, apertures, and eyes should be applied all around within the interior of the temple.
Through the divisions of the fire, earth, and self-natures, there would be the superior, the middling, and the inferior Śiva;
likewise, among those, in the two pairs, there are the two for the maiden and the eunuch.
"Indeed, there are nine liṅgas according to the measurement of the interior of the temple (prāsāda-garbha).
By dividing each one threefold, the number [of divisions] arises.
Thus it is said; and likewise in the Piṅgalāmata:
Or, as before, one may first establish the palace and subsequently arrange the *liṅga*;
beginning from the smallest (*kanyasa*) up to the largest (*jyeṣṭha*), according to the measurement of the womb (*garbha*).
When the womb is divided into nine parts, the smallest is half [of that], and the largest consists of five parts.
The middle is declared to be the fire of the elements (bhūtāgni), while the superior is the eldest of the eldest.
Between the eldest daughter and the youngest, one should determine the placement of the divine lingas.
One should assign two daughters to each of those positions with equal measurement.
Just as before, one should arrange each of those intervals in a threefold manner.
"In this case as well, the number and the characteristic of the linga should first be clearly determined.
Alternatively:
"The lowest linga is half the height of the womb (garbha), while the best should consist of three parts of the elements (bhūta)."
In the middle of that, there are indeed seven threads and nine liṅgas.
And so it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*: "If the temple stands facing the east, then one should determine its measurement;
when [the height] is divided into five parts, the smallest *liṅga* should occupy half of that."
When the most excellent *trimāgha* liṅga is divided ninefold,
the middle liṅga with five [parts] shall be the "middle-middle."
p.
482) Above and below that, within the womb (garbha), there should be lines divided by threes;
thus, according to the application, there are nine lingas in a single womb.
"O bird-like sage, these [dimensions] should be determined by the learned according to the desire of the sacrificer;
for as the sacrificer is the share, so too is the fruit the sign. Thus has the vertical measurement been fully explained; now the detailed dimensions shall be told.
Having divided the sacred site (tīrtha) into sixteen parts by means of six, five, and four sections.
The width should be four parts; the channels (nāḍī) [should be] within each channel for the worship of the gods.
And that should be made entirely equal, again with five parts including the corner (satri).
And so it is stated in the *Kālottara*: "The height of this [liṅga] is as follows, and its width is further described:
the abode of the liṅga, whether modified or unmodified, [should be made] with five [parts], excluding Indra."
I shall now describe the width of the liṅgas in three parts:
the first is the *āḍhya* (abundant) liṅga worshipped by the gods, and the third is the *nāḍya*.
"All else is the same; the *liṅga* is proclaimed according to its divisions.
And likewise, regarding the characteristics in a house:
"When the stated length is divided by eight parts and [the width] by nine parts in sequence..."
It shall be [calculated] by the sixtieth part of the ocean of flavors (sixty-four), increased by three parts, and then by the arrows (five).
"The prosperous [mandala] is called the 'kingdom of the asuras' (āsurājya); for those who are equal, it is square. Thus [it is said].
And so it is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"In the case of the navel, the devotee, and the purpose of the *liṅga*, [the measurement] should be made by six, five, and four [units].
In the case of the *āḍhya* and *nāḍī* [types], among those favored by the gods, the *viṣkaṃbha* is equal on all sides."
"With the akṣas increased by one-third, the Brahmāṅga [altar] shall be square. Thus it is said.
Having clearly displayed his fingers, he should examine the signs.
Inflation is said to be fourfold according to the divisions of its locations, as taught in the scriptures.
And it is said in the Kālottara: "The seats of the *liṅgas* consist of the *pīṭhas*, and those of the *gaṇas* are joined with the *dhvajas*;
through the effort of purification, the *neryās* [are assigned], while the *draṇas* are joined with the vowels."
The purification of beds and vehicles is performed by those known as *bhūtas*;
now, another method for the purification of ponds, wells, and tanks is prescribed.
Dhvaja, Udghūma, Siṃha, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, and likewise Pañcama.
Daivata, Niṣāda, Svara, and the others are proclaimed as the seven;
likewise, the destruction of fortune, prosperity, tranquility, and greatness [are their effects].
The staff is poison, the great power is the fruit arising from the seven notes;
the elements beginning with earth are considered to be the five elements,
which are nourishment, burning, and movement in their respective order.
"The fire known as Āhavanīya, the Gārhapatya, and others, as well as the Bhakṣaṇāgni—in this order, their fruits are bathing, clothing, and a dwelling. Thus it is said.
Just as a linga that is deficient in its dimensions should be cast away for the sake of auspiciousness,
so too has that which is called *vardhamāna* (increasing) been described by the Supreme Lord.
In this case, one should multiply the length of the *liṅga* in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) by its width in finger-breadths;
then, dividing by the [standard] dimensions, one should observe the remainder as the first [figure].
When an auspicious sign is seen by the master, he should then cast the *āya*;
that is called the "present" [measurement], which is the means for determining the proportions. There, the body [of the image] should be one cubit and a finger-breadth, or two or three cubits.

(On the penis) there are four [finger-breadths] at the base, five in the middle, and five at the tip; on the two testicles there are six, seven, and seven [respectively]; and on the two scrotal openings there are nine finger-breadths.
Within the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu (Vaikuṇṭha), and Rudra, the measurement should be divided softly;
one should grant [the space] in the order of one, two, and three finger-breadths, otherwise one incurs fault.
Likewise, for those with internal spaces, this same rule applies to the entire uniform arrangement.
They know that even when there are three shares, the distribution of the three shares is equal. Thus it is said.
Just as the defect of shadow does not occur in the triad beginning with Āḍhya,
so too one may make the portion of Brahmā or the portion of Rudra either deficient or excessive.
And so it has been stated in the venerable *Pārameśvara*, the *Śekhara*, and other scriptures:
"In the case of those who have fewer [deities] than the standard, the two [deities] of the Enemy of the Cities of the Grandfather (Brahmā) are excellent;
however, for Viṣṇu (Viṣṭaraśravas), the portion must never be less nor more."
Otherwise, the *liṅga* would be encroached upon by the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), or the pedestal would be encroached upon by the *liṅga*.
When such encroachment or visibility [of the defect] occurs, one should abandon it from afar as a fault.
Having subtracted the width and length [of the base], the *liṅga* should be positioned in the middle of the portion.
"One should perform the rites prescribed for the hermitage after having consulted with one's own [preceptor] and being well-satisfied.
And likewise, Viśvakarman says:
"If the *liṅga* is deficient, there will be death; if it is excessive, there will be severe diseases."
Therefore, the pedestal (pīṭha), including the linga and other components, should be fashioned according to the measure of the maker's own body.
If the pedestal (piṇḍikā) exceeds the base (loṅga), or if the throne (pīṭha) exceeds the liṅga,
then the maker, the kingdom, and likewise the preceptor will be afflicted by diseases;
therefore, both the portions of Hara and Brahmā should be made neither deficient nor excessive.

The height of the three types of *liṅgas* should not be less than nor more than that of Śiva; the deerskin used for the length of the *liṅga* should be eight and a half cubits, and the seat should be made of *śaika* wood.
The Lord (Īśa) would consist of seven and a half [parts], while Hari himself would be from his own portion;
the Three-eyed One (Tryakṣa) would consist of eight parts plus a quarter, and the Discus-bearer (Cakrī) would be present in the mandala.
Brahmā should be made with a height of three-quarters of one-eighth [of the base];
the height of Hara (Śiva) should be one part of the house-measure, and then Viṣṇu should be made with eight parts.
One should fashion the Brahmā-portion of the deity worshipped by the gods using seven-fold cooking;
for him who thus fashions the liṅga, his desired object rests in the palm of his hand.
Brahmā should be square, and Viṣṇu should be octagonal.
"In the portion of Rudra, there shall be a circle by means of the sequence of mixed omissions. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the opinion of Piṅgalā: "Make the measurement of the pedestal (pīṭha) and the base (piṇḍikā) equal to the measurement of the liṅga;
it is held that the base should be adorned all around with bells."
But when the Liṅga exceeds the measurement of the pedestal,
then all the inhabitants of that region are constantly afflicted by diseases.
The architect, the artisan who fashioned [the image], and those together with the guardians of the idols—
all are afflicted by diseases such as consumption, leprosy, fever, and the like.
And when the linga exceeds the measurement of the pedestal (piṇḍikā),
then one incurs all the faults and the [inefficacy of the] worship that has been described.
Therefore, the pedestal should be joined to the linga in a manner that is appropriate to it. Thus [it is said].
The Brahmā-portion should be square, and above it, it should be octagonal as appropriate.
On the arm-lines, one should mark the projections using threads for half the length of the neck.
Then, with the *bāhāhu* thread, the *kaṇṭhasūtra*, and clarified butter.
One should mark the corners with whatever remains of the neck-thread; or, having divided the diameter into seven parts, one should mark from the center by three [parts] and from the two sides.
Therefore, it becomes eight-cornered; thus, it is considered the portion belonging to Viṣṇu.
Above that, in the portion belonging to Rudra, one should divide the circle into four parts;
having visualized two triangles at the corners, one should rotate the circle in due order.
And so it is stated in the Kālottara:
"The three parts of the liṅgas consist of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara;
they are respectively quadrangular, octagonal, and circular, and are designated as Ūrdhva."
By abandoning the corners and the upper part, one obtains the octagon known as Viṣṇu;
by following the sequence of omitting the horse-ears, one should bring it to the state of a circle, which is called Rudra.
And so it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"O Śatakratu, by abandoning one half of the ear [of the hand], there is the *aṅgulāśra*;
the middle [line] is formed by the three sages, and the *dhyāna* [line] is measured by the number of fingers."
"Thus, it would consist of sixteen parts; afterwards, it proceeds evenly. Thus [it is said].
And likewise, I have described the unmanifest [pedestal] as characterized by four, eight, and sixteen parts;
the height of the liṅga is [divided] by six parts, and it is joined with four parts of the base.
O best of sages, having abandoned the *sādhana-aliṅga* as the *viṣkambha*,
by discarding the *tura* above its ears, it becomes eight-sided (*aṣṭāśra*) for the *muni-bhājika*.
"One should bring about the circularity of the two upper parts of the blows on the two sections,
either by means of the ground from the station of Brahmā or by way of the removal of the corners."
Nevertheless, according to the view on the *liṅga*: "Half of the [total] height is indeed made the width; this is declared to be the 'mild' (*mṛdu*) measurement by number.
This is proclaimed as the 'abundant' (*āḍhya*) *liṅga*, O you who are worshipped by the best of gods."
Having made half of the *liṅga* like a *vasu* (eightfold), one should make it four-cornered by the number of elements (five);
this is taught as the general characteristic for all [types] that are not *anāḍhya*.
I shall now fully describe the third [mandala], which is honored by hosts of deities;
it is divided into four parts above and has four corners according to the number four.
O Goddess, everything else is equal in bringing wealth, grain, and happiness;
it is common to all principles and becomes like a treasure for various purposes.
Below and at the sixth [mark], one should again divide that [length] into three parts;
five [parts] joined with the portion of the serpent (nāga) shall clearly be the width (viṣkambha).
This measurement has been specified; now I shall describe the form:
having divided the square known as Brahmā into three equal parts, it becomes four-cornered.
"Or it may have thirty-two [parts] with a hundred [units]; the triangular liṅga is considered to be of two kinds.
One should determine the portion for worship of a circular liṅga as being equal [to its base].
Thus it is said. Furthermore, that which was stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṅgraha*:
When the [lagna] is divided by the modifications (vikāra), [the results are] six, five, and four [ghaṭīs] respectively;
these are the nāḍīs for the worship of the gods in Viṣkambha, which is equal in all respects.
The width shall be five parts combined with thirty-sixths;
one should multiply the inches of sovereignty (the height) by the inches of width of the liṅga.
One should discern the remainder by means of eight times eight heart-mantras:
in the banner (dhvaja), the mark (lakṣma), the abode of radiance (dhṛtidhāman), victory (jaya), and the lion (siṃha), there is purification.
In Taurus (Vṛṣa), there is suffering; in Leo (Gaja), there is gain; and in Sagittarius (Khaga), there is loss.
When the embrace is devoid of income, one should then cast an auspicious income [into it].
When there is no defect in the shadow, one should divide that respective linga into three parts.
A third part of the length of the linga is the piṇḍāṃśa, and it is this that moves;
in all three types of lingas, the remaining two parts are considered to be either less or more [than the piṇḍāṃśa].
In a [mandala] divided into portions consisting of the signs of the wealthy (āḍhyaliṅga), the parts of the modifications (vikāra), and the portions for worship (arcābhāga),
one should take one portion and assign it to the Brahma-portion.
Then, by means of the pedestal, the liṅga becomes a source of prosperity.
When the portion of Brahmā is divided into eight parts,
the single part joined with Rudra should be known as the Liṅga that bestows all siddhis, when it is adorned with beautiful lines.
In all types of equilateral [mandalas], the measurement should be equal across the three parts;
then the pedestal (pīṭha) is established upon the base (vaṭa) and the liṅga, together with the pedestal-base (piṇḍikā).
When the *samāpiṇḍī* is at the level of the *arcā* (the image) and is joined with a pedestal (*pīṭha*) on all sides,
it brings happiness to the gods, the asuras,
and men; however, he who out of delusion installs it otherwise in the *liṅga* shall suffer.
Both of them were evildoers, bringing harm to all the worlds.
"One should bring the two blows of the two parts upward to a circular shape,
either from the position of the *brahman* on the ground or by means of the commencement of the *āśravalopa*."
Nevertheless, according to the Liṅga-mata:
"Having made half of the navel the width, like fire, by the number of the 'mṛdu' [fingers],
this is declared to be the Āṭya-liṅga, O worshiper of the best of gods."
Having fashioned half of the *liṅga* like the Vasus (eight parts), one should make it four-cornered according to the number of elements (five);
this is designated as the general characteristic for all [types], excluding the *anāḍhya*.
I shall now fully describe the third [mandala], which is honored by the assembly of sages;
it is divided into nine parts above and has four corners according to the number four.
O Goddess, everything else is equal in bringing wealth, grain, and happiness;
it is common to all principles and becomes like various treasures for many purposes.
Below the sixth [line] and the māyā [line], one should again divide those three by two;
five, joined with the portion of the nāgas, shall clearly be the width (viṣkambha).
This measurement has been specified; now I shall describe the form:
having divided the square known as Brahmā into three equal parts, one should make it four-cornered.
"Or it may have thirty-two [parts] and be joined; the triangular liṅga is considered to be of two kinds.
Or, for a circular liṅga, one should arrange the portion for worship so that it is equal. Thus it is said. Furthermore, as stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṅgraha*:
When the [lunar] day is divided by the transformations (vikāras), [the results are] six, five, and four in sequence;
Viṣkambha occurs everywhere when they are equal among the lords of the days, the nāḍīs, and the gods.
This is declared to be the limit of the cock; for the liquor-drinker, it is not otherwise.
In a *liṅga* consisting of four parts, one should preserve the fourth part;
furthermore, another [part] is to be placed on the top of the *liṅga* when it is divided sixfold.
O Nandana, having set aside three parts, the flower should be made for one who is without a channel (anāḍya), and never for anyone else.
First, one should divide [the area] into three parts; when the side portions have been set aside, one should draw a half-moon on the ground according to the sequence of the corner-lines.
"O Ṣaṇmukha, the worship of the Liṅga must indeed be performed by one who is wealthy and devoted;
thus has the entire characteristic of the Liṅga's head (mastaka) been briefly proclaimed.
Now, it follows that for each of the four types of Liṅgas, there may be four types of heads as well. As stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
The characteristic mark has been described; now, O Hari, his head will be described in general terms:
it is the large lotus, the Śrīvatsa, and the crusher of enemies.
The *trapuṣa*, the *kukkuṭāṇḍa*, and the *khaṇḍacandra* of the Lord of Śacī—thus the seven-headed [arrangement] has been declared; now hear the procedure for its execution.
The lotus is formed by adding four units to one-eighth of the base;
the *viśāla* is formed by the reduction of the neck, and the *śrīvatsa* by the reduction of the qualities.
One should know the fourth [house], the destroyer of enemies, from the end of the corner;
it has the shape of a hundred-petaled lotus with one-quarter of a part added to each petal when divided by six.
If one abandons even a portion of what has been heard, the head becomes like a hen's egg.
"And through the abandonment of the secondary division (guṇabhakta), the young moon (bālendu) becomes clearly manifest. Thus it is said.
The parasol, the cock, the arghya vessel, the gourd, and the top of the linga—
each of these is said to have four varieties as proclaimed in the Agamas.
When the eighth part is divided by four, there is the elimination of one portion;
this is the pure and extensive [shape] named Vardhamāna, which is the third.
The Śrīvatsa is the fourth; the kukkuṭāṇḍa is of four kinds.
The gradual application [of the colors] consists of three parts and four meal-portions (caturbhakta).
The first is named Vimala, the second Vipula, and the third Vardhamāna;
the fourth should be Śrīvatsa, and the Kukkuṭāṇḍa is of four kinds. [These are obtained] by dividing the third part into four and subtracting one portion from each part.
Amṛta, Pūrṇakumbha, Bala, and the one named Kumuda—thus the fourfold Trapuṣa should be known as the granter of all desires. Thus [it is said].
The wrapping of the *brahmabhāga* and other parts of the *liṅgas*, such as the *adhi*,

should be neither deficient nor excessive, exactly as prescribed in the scriptures; when the auspicious portion corresponding to the length of the *liṅga* has been determined, [the wrapping is performed].
Brahmā was surrounded by twenty-four auspicious [deities], Viṣṇu likewise by twenty,
and Śambhu by nineteen at the beginning.
Brahmā is to be surrounded by twenty [parts], and Viṣṇu likewise by seven and one [i.e., eight] parts;
Rudra’s portion is considered to be the altar (vedi) measured in finger-breadths (aṅgula), while the sacrificial pit (sonā) is held to be sixteen [parts].
Furthermore, Brahmā is [placed] first with sixty and sixteen parts, as well as the preceding finger-breadths.
Viṣṇu is said to be with thirteen parts plus one-third;
the Brahmaveṣṭana is with twenty-one parts plus one-third.
The portion of Hari should also be surrounded by seventeen parts plus one-sixth.
That Śambhu is always to be surrounded by seventeen [deities] when all are equal;
or else, that previously mentioned Veda, who is a portion of Brahmā, is four-armed.

There, having divided one part into seven, Viṣṇu should be surrounded by three arms measuring two and a half parts; Hara should be surrounded by three arms measuring one and a quarter, one, and one-quarter parts respectively.
And so it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Having encircled the four-armed [form] with seven parts,
Viṣṇu is formed by two and a half arms, and Hara by one and a half arms."
And so it is stated in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:
"Having set aside the portion consisting of the marks [of a Great Man], one should then count [the remaining deities]:
the Victor surrounded by twenty Śārdūlas, with Brahmā and others as the primary encirclers."
Likewise, there would be no change in the state of the human channels during the eighth part of the night.
With a modified tone, joined with a third part of the vowel portion,
and combined with a division of half a part, O you who are worshipped by the gods and the Kaṇas.
With a third part of a third part, marked by a nail and the moon;
and with a third part of a portion, joined with a fourth part.
"In an equilateral [figure], the circumference shall consist of seventeen parts;
having surrounded Rāhu with four parts, the arms are made of seven parts.
Viṣṇu is formed by two and a half arms, and Hara by three and a half arms. Thus it is said.

If the *mṛtyu* [mark] is elevated, there will be great enjoyment; if it is on the back, there is the acquisition of cattle. If the *yava* [mark] is present within it, there will be rain; if the *jaṭhara* [mark] is elevated, there will be food and drink.
If all the limbs are rounded, there is happiness, worship, and the increase of fortune;
if the belly is level, it destroys fear; if the base is thick, one attains speed.
A linga that is excessively deficient in height or possesses other such defects should be avoided with great effort;
likewise, a linga with a hundred faces, a thousand limbs, or one that is indistinctly formed.
As it is stated in the venerable *Kālottara*:

"That which was previously described as 'the Abundant' (*āḍhya*) dissolves; one should fashion that as the 'Thousand-fold' (*sahasraka*), because it bestows all desires, it is therefore beneficial as the 'Thousand-fold'."
One should fashion the division of the sun like that of Rudra according to its height;
there, O twice-born one, it should be equal to the opening of the machine in terms of width.
A thousand [units] less one clearly constitute the *liṅga*;
it must not be uneven, and one should avoid placing one above the other.
Even if they are joined together, one should install those [liṅgas] that are devoid of the *lakṣa*-lines;
[likewise] thousands of breasts, the head of the Lord of the Earth (*Ṭhākekandra*),
and another liṅga, the one worshipped by the hosts of gods, numbering one hundred and eight.
Having made the height like that of the Veda, O Seven-eyed One, the width should be one-seventh of it; by that measure, O son, a liṅga of one hundred and eight [units] should be fashioned as before.
Then, O son, a face-liṅga should always be fashioned, equal in all respects;
it should be made by one who is wealthy, not by one who is poor, and the new tool should be used for the worship of the deity.
But it is not prescribed that [the offering] be equal for all, nor for those who have fallen away from their vows alone;
rather, that which is about to be described should indeed be performed in three parts.
One finger-breadth should be given for each joint, and that [measurement] should be divided by eleven;
one part of that [total] at the crossroads should be added sequentially to Brahmā and the others.
That Liṅga should be of one's own measurement, for it increases both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O child, without the correct measurement, it leads only to equal suffering.
That Liṅga of one's own measurement should be installed, or it may be marked with a face.
The measurement of the *mukhaliṅga* is now declared by me according to the tradition of Śaila. Teachers should always fashion it with four, three, or one face;
however, they should avoid those with five or two faces, as these grant undesirable results.
A portion for worship (pūjābhāga) should be prepared starting from the birth sign and the sign of misfortune;
having set aside one-twelfth part from above, one should avoid six positions.
The elevation of the head, the forehead, the nose, and likewise the face and the neck should be made with four parts each; the height of the arms is [four] parts.

Having formed the hands into a bud-like shape and measuring according to the prescribed proportions, the upward movement [of the image] should be performed; its width should be one-eighth [of the total height].
Thus the four-faced [liṅga] has been described by me; now the three-faced is being explained.
However, one should specify that his forehead and other parts are increased by a quarter;
his two arms must be made with four parts, and not otherwise.
Therefore, one should fashion him as having three faces, with the western face being omitted.
The projection of the faces should be one-seventh of the width; then,
one face should be made facing east with gentle eyes.
One should fashion the forehead, the nose, the face, and the neck;
one should fashion the shoulder portion with a fifth part, and fashion it devoid of arms.
The width of the opening for the exit should be beneficially one-sixth of the total width.
One should proclaim the faces and lingas of them all together with the cock.
The person facing east is Aghora, the southern face is Aghora,
the northern is called Vāmadeva, and the western is Sadyojāta.

"One should fashion the facial characteristics in accordance with the nature of their respective colors; their number, moreover, should be as distinct as they appear when measured by the span of a hand.
Thus it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
From that, one should manifest the Manifest (vyakta) from the Unmanifest (avyakta), [visualizing it] with one, two, three, or four faces;
for one devoted to Śakti and for those who are portions of Rudra, this head consists of the divisions of fire and so forth.
The forehead, nose, mouth,
and the city-gates such as Cinduka and others should be properly fashioned by the architect on the exterior of the temple's foundation.
One should heat the portion of the modification of the liṅga— the expansion of the liṅga— from the outside toward the four corners in the four directions, in order for it to emerge.
Having fashioned a portion [of the base], one should make it like a distinct form or a linga;
the portion at the top should resemble a linga, with its root-width forgotten.

The wise man should fashion the crown part by part, provided with a mass of matted locks; he should have it made rich in qualities, divided into nine parts and apportioned according to the aesthetic sentiments (rasas).
In the portion for worship (*pūjābhāga*), the two arms and shoulders extend out by six finger-breadths (*ṛtvaṅgula*).
The neck is external to this; the portion for the village (*grāmabhāga*) is not above the shoulders nor beyond them.
From foot to foot, the crown should be fashioned according to the characteristics of worship;
in the other portion, half the length of the linga is for the linga itself when its width is excluded from the exterior.
Therein, one should fashion everything, including the ears, nose, skull, and so forth.
When the portion of one face is divided by the qualities within the portion of Bhava in the Liṅga.
Having divided the lower portion into two, one half remains situated there;
then, with two parts, the shoulders and neck [are formed], and again in the middle, with three and a half [parts].
One should fashion the face and the rest, ending at the head, by means of each individual part;
above that, one should fashion the crown using two parts divided by the [three] qualities (guṇas).
The face, resembling the *liṅga* in appearance, is said to extend by one part;
the projection [of the neck] extending by a portion equal to the length of the *liṅga* brings about auspiciousness.
Then, as in the *Mohaśūrottara*, he caused the liṅga to revolve;
from it arose the Gaṅgā and other rivers, born of sacred fields.
Likewise, I shall describe the characteristics of the jar-liṅga and of Māyā:
having made the clay well-worn and mixed it with the powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
One should grind together realgar, orpiment, vermilion,
sulphur, gold, and mountain-ash (gairika), mixed with a small amount of guggulu,
using a fine cloth until it is well-mixed by a skillful person.
Having kept it for six months in a vessel made of *bilva* wood,
and having let it remain for seven nights immersed in water infused with a decoction, one should [use it].
With fragrant substances mixed with perfume, as well as with resinous exudate.
One should knead it thoroughly on all sides with effort using kaṣāya;
then one should fashion the auspicious liṅga according to the prescribed characteristics.
"Ripe [fruit] for the unripe [eye], well-prepared for the eye, according to what is marked in the mind. Thus it is said.
Just as the location of the *liṅga* and its fruit have been declared in the *Kālottara*,
so too is the earthen [liṅga] considered to be of two kinds, distinguished by being either baked or unbaked.
The unrefined vajra should be joined with refined gold and vermilion;
it should be fashioned with the Aghora mantra and cooked slowly in the fire of Śiva.

I shall now describe the movable and immovable lingas; listen. That which is made of clay is of two kinds: uncooked and cooked. The merit arising from a cooked one should be known as ten times greater than that of an uncooked one.
Therefore, a gift made on a mountain of pearls is said to yield ten times the fruit.
Therefore, the fruit obtained from iron, which resembles sharp-edged steel, is a hundredfold greater.
A linga made of gold bestows great lands; one made of silver increases one's progeny;
a linga made of bell-metal brings fame; and one made of copper increases one’s subjects.
A liṅga made of bell-metal leads to enjoyment and liberation; one made of fine iron destroys enemies;
a liṅga made of copper bestows desires and longevity; and one born of mixed metals grants all perfections.
From that, the fruit [obtained from] one made of precious gems is a thousandfold;
on a linga made of jewels and gems, the fruit is considered to be a hundred-thousandfold.
Among superior, inferior, and middling gems,
one should likewise accept as a true gem those jewels that possess increasingly greater brilliance.
By installing a Bāṇaliṅga, the merit becomes ten million times that of one made of jewels;
O son, the fruit of a Rasaliṅga is ten million times greater than that of a Bāṇaliṅga.
Who is capable of describing the merit of a Nṛsiṃhaliṅga in the supreme realm of Śiva?
The supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, are well-established in the non-mercurial lingas;
however, when the mercury-linga is worshipped, there shall indeed be liberation, O Śiva, which bestows auspiciousness.
