Therefore, one should diligently install that delightful linga according to the procedure taught by Vātula, and likewise effect the binding of mercury (rasabandha).
For mercury should indeed be bound with mercury; a child [mercury] should be bound with Ratnagarbha.
Alternatively, by the power of strength, one should bind it with adamantine iron (vajraloha).

One may cause it to swoon or even bind it with a flood of juice from the blazing medicinal plant; one should not calculate its weight, measure, or dimensions. However, the root of the *dhurdhūraka* plant used for the commencement [of the rite] should be black.

A wise person should cause a flower to bloom by using the root of *matsyākṣī* combined with *meghanāda*, along with breast milk and water. Having added a dose of mercury the size of a *guñjā* seed to it, one should wrap it [in the petals].
One should fashion the form of a dark man out of a lump of clay mixed with powdered black gram.
Thus it is said in the teaching on mercury that there shall be the binding of mercury (rasabandha);
for both mercury and calamine (rasaka) are these two great minerals (mahārasa).
p.
499) Mercury, produced from *rajaka*, [should be treated] with sesamum oil and one part of each [of the other ingredients];
through union with an equal amount of gold, the mercury (*sūtaka*) undergoes binding.

It should be known that [this practice], when combined with a talliṅga made of gold and provided with a golden pedestal, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it is proclaimed as yielding these results without effort.
Alternatively, one may wear on the hand a ring made of mercury-processed [gold].
Whatever one gives and whatever one offers in sacrifice, that becomes inexhaustible;
this applies even to those men who have been cremated and to those who were deprived of funeral rice-balls (piṇḍa).
Those few who were killed by infants or those who died due to miscarriages—
[he should touch] their finger-rings with his own hand while [the mantras] are established upon his teeth.

Now, O beloved, hear the measurement of the sacred field (kṣetra) for all the Liṅgas. For the self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) Liṅgas made of mercury or gems, a distance of one yojana in every direction is declared beneficial; for those made of jewels and precious stones, half of that is said to be the sacred field.
Half of that [measurement] applies to wood and metals, and likewise for earthen objects.
And by the ṛṣis, Daityas, Arcīnas, Gaṇas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas.
Or even by the Siddhas, as well as by the best among gods, asuras,
and men— O son, their form and measure should not be grasped like an arrow;
she (the Goddess) causes the arrangement of their seats and temples according to her own will.
When the defects have been worn away, one should employ [the rites] just as in the case of the arrows of Svayambhū;
just as in the field of Svayambhū, so should one arrange them for those [sites].
And the field on the bank of a great river is to be known as being like that of Svayambhū.
p.
500) It should be known that for a bow made of wood, clay, or stone, [the measurement] is thirty finger-breadths;
for those made of iron, it is double that, and from there, it is double again for each subsequent material.
In Ratnaja, Maṇiliṅga, Bāṇa, and then Rasarasa—
thus indeed has the measurement of the Citra [mandala] for the ritual means been declared;
likewise with respect to recitation, as well as in the case of transference, giving, or nourishing.
I shall explain once more that measurement as it stands:
having divided that field into five parts, one should arrange it like a lotus.
One should designate the first part as the neck (*kaṇṭhaka*), the second as the filaments (*kesara*),
the third here as the bowls (*pātra*), and the fourth as the tips of the petals (*dalāgra*).
One should likewise arrange the fifth external portion within the field (*kṣetra*).
And the previously mentioned fruit should be assigned there in five ways as follows.
Crystal is to be known as threefold, consisting of the nature of the sun, the moon, and the self;
it is white, red, and yellow, while black-shadowed [crystal] belongs to the twice-born and other classes. Indeed, its lines and colors are like those of frost and the marks of a courtesan.
One should avoid a linga that has a dark spot, is gritty, has a dot, or is stepped upon by a dog; one should fashion a crystal linga together with its pedestal as it is described.

An image measuring from one finger-breadth up to a span (vitasti) should always be worshipped in the home. Beyond that, having established it according to the sages' tradition, it should be stainless, radiant with luster, with a width at the top of the linga equal to its height.
The circumference should be three times [the diameter], and this is forgotten regarding each respective pedestal.
p.
501) The *guṇatīrtha* should be at the base, with the throat [of the liṅga] in the middle;
its measurement should be like that of the liṅga itself, just as it is intended by the Goddess.
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) for a movable liṅga should be three parts wide and two parts high,
and it may be either square or circular.
It should be very firm, free from flaws, auspicious, and possess three girdles with equanimity in the middle.
Above this, the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) should be made level, or it may also have three girdles.
For the purpose of the portion for worship, the girdle should consist of one-third of the portion.
The pit should be of that same measurement, or else reduced by one-quarter;
its height should be the measure of the image, and the water-channel should extend outwards.
Its width at the base should be that same measurement, while at the tip it should be half of that.
"In the middle, a delightful water-channel should be made, occupying one-third [of the space]. Thus it is said.
Now, in the *Kālottara*:
"A linga made of metal or gems is beneficial for householders who maintain a home."
For the sake of prosperity, [the image] should not exceed half a finger-breadth or a span in height or depth;
however, there is no such restriction for an image made of jewels—one should worship it according to what is obtained.
At that time, the intense brilliance of the jewels is praised when they are present nearby.
One should always worship with supreme devotion, as if it were a *liṅga*, a stone originating from a great river or produced in a sacred field of accomplishment (*siddhakṣetra*).
The iron liṅga is declared to have the same form as the bāṇaliṅga;
white, red, yellow, and black are the best types for the Brahmins and the other castes respectively.
Due to its absence, the black variety grants success among all castes;
that which originates from the Narmadā is called the Roha, resembling the Bāṇaliṅga.
The self-manifested (svayambhūta) Bāṇaliṅga, which is always worthy of worship and the most excellent among all liṅgas,
should likewise be known as the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Listen briefly to the origin and the characteristics of the Bāṇaliṅgas.
O Six-faced One, there are likewise Bāṇaliṅgas of the holy rivers, such as the goddess Narmadā;
they are worshipped here by Indra and the other gods, and are indeed marked with their respective signs.
The six corners are yellow, and the limbs of the vajra are especially so.
The placement of those Indraliṅgas indeed bestows imperial sovereignty;
their laughter, like a mass of snow, completely turns into a sensation of heat through touch.
Having worshipped the Śakti of the Āgneya [Liṅga], or else having installed this supreme Liṅga marked with a Śakti, one becomes the lord of splendor.
The Āyāmaya [Liṅga] is considered to have spokes shaped like staffs, or else it has the form of a tongue.
When that which was anointed [with oil] becomes free from it within a moment, then,
by the end of the destruction of the enemies' wealth, it is established;
it is like a Rākṣasa sword, bestowing the fruit of the yoga of knowledge.
If it is smeared with sugar and other such substances, then it should be made pungent.
Varuṇa is circular in shape, marked with a noose, and exceedingly radiant;
when situated in the center, it attains growth, sweetness, and purity.
That which belongs to Vāyu is black or smoky, adorned with the emblem of a smoky banner.
For indeed, living beings tremble when he has placed his foot upon their heads.
In a windless place, however, these [mantras] move; they are beneficial for exorcism (*uccāṭana*) according to the scriptures.
One should meditate on the formless, heavy-heavy [syllable] situated in the center of the north.
Whether by day or by night, it increases the prosperity and growth of those who dwell there;
it is triangular, marked with tridents, fierce, and possesses the luster of snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.
Alternatively, at the outset, it arises as the fourfold caste (caturvarṇa) during the equinox;
it is marked with the discus and conch of Viṣṇu, adorned with the mace, lotus, and so forth,
occupied by the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha gems, and marked with the throne of the Kaula lion.
Whether it bears the mark of Garuḍa (Vainateya) or is marked by Śrī and Bhūdevī,
that is declared to be a Vaiṣṇava [liṅga], which bestows the fruit of all sovereign powers.
Furthermore, one situated in Śālagrāma and the like, or at the tip of a conch, increases prosperity.
Marked with a lotus, marked with a svastika, and marked with the śrīvatsa for the sake of prosperity.
One marked with a horse, a *kola*, a lion, or the sun should be joined for the sake of prosperity; likewise one marked with the earth or a bull for Rājyavardhana.
One marked with the word "spoken" (*uktāṅka*) should be employed for welfare; one should avoid all other remaining [marks].
The *liṅga* that is lotus-colored, with a lotus on its left side, and marked with a staff and a rosary, is considered Brāhma; it bestows the attainment of knowledge.
[The *liṅga*] of Mahākāla is moon-colored, while Nadīśa is like a ruby.
All [of it] resembles topaz, has the luster of mung beans, and is worshipped by the Siddhas.
Resembling a pearl or the hue of sapphire, it was worshipped by the Rudras and Ādityas.
And that which is frequented by Vasus, Daityas, Indras, Yakṣas, Guhyakas, and Yātudhānas,
possessing the hue of men and the color of the blue lotus, with the luster of a blue water-lily.
This is the definition proclaimed by those expert in reality after examination:
for one who attains balance on the scale three or five times.
At that time, what is known as *bāṇa* [mercury] is said to be the remainder produced from stone;
one should cast it again into a river whenever it is obtained.
The Bāṇaliṅga brings success at that time; any other [liṅga] only increases suffering.
Now, the Bāṇa [liṅga] is fully described, just as the Bāṇa was taught in the beginning.
Bāṇa is Lord Sadāśiva, and Bāṇa is also the Asura Bāṇa;
because [the latter] performed [devotion] for him, it is called the Bāṇaliṅga.
Śiva, the accomplisher of all goals, is ever present for him;
that liṅga was consecrated by Śiva known as Bāṇa.
Shaped like a ripe jambu fruit and having the form of a hen’s egg,
this Bāṇaliṅga is declared to bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
If the *bāṇaliṅga* is rough, there will be the loss of sons and wife;
if it is worshipped while being flat, the ruin of the household will certainly occur.
If one side of the arrow is shattered, there is the loss of cattle and the giving away of sons; if the shaft is shattered, there is loss of wealth;
and if the head of the arrow is shattered, there is disease and even death.
If the *anyajāti* [mudrā] is placed on the ascendant (*vilagna*), there will be the wasting away of all limbs;
however, when the arrow (*bāṇa*) is worshipped with a multicolored emblem (*citraliṅga*), there will be the pacification of foreign lands.
By seeing a courtesan at a linga, a man becomes afflicted by disease;
however, for sages desiring liberation, the Kapila linga should be worshipped.
A householder should never worship a linga that is small, brown, or thick;
one should avoid a linga whose top points toward the south, whose head is crooked, or which is angular.
One who is excessively stout, excessively emaciated, very small, or afflicted by disease—
such a person a householder should avoid, for he is not beneficial to one seeking liberation.
A householder should worship that which resembles a bee in color,
together with its pedestal or even without a pedestal, provided it is free from the ritual purification of the left hand.
When the Bāṇaliṅga— which bestows both spiritual perfection and liberation, resides at the Sarvaprasāda Pīṭha,
and is held in one's hand— then one should carry it within the Suṣumṇā.
If the three forms [of the planets] do not achieve equality even after seven revolutions, then it is declared to be a *bāṇa* (arrow); otherwise, one should say it is a *pāṣāṇaka* (stone).
Or one should cast it again into a river; when that [result] is observed, then the arrow is declared successful; otherwise, it brings suffering.
In this matter, the consideration of lines is to be performed according to the prescribed rules for the *ghaṭikā*;
it is also traditionally taught in relation to the circumference of the *bāṇa*, *rohā*, and other *liṅgas*.
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) is three parts in height and divided by eight;
its base is two parts, while the neck (gala) in the form of its pedestal is two parts.
One who has mastered the text by heart should,
with devotion, offer a vessel for water according to its form, using one-third of it for Kālikā.

One should worship the linga made of fragrant substances three times a day according to the rite for one's own happiness. Then, with the offered sandalwood or saffron— prepared with the four ingredients or simply with the light substance alone— it should be applied.
Having thus fashioned the mark of fragrance and worshipped it with devotion, |||
Accompanied by his kinsmen, that man attains union with Śiva.
Now, one should fashion a very beautiful liṅga made from guggulu resin.
One should prepare it with lac and the juice of *kunda* flowers, making it firm; or one may fashion it according to the natural proportions of two fingers or even a cubit.
Having attained infinite sovereignty, one should abandon [the body]; then,
having reached the state of the Guṇatattva-pada, which is the linga born of the five elements, one shall subsequently become equal to Śiva.
And thus, an image made of sesame seeds is an object that increases one's enjoyment.
Having become the sovereign lord of the male principle (puṃstattva), one shall thereafter proceed to the state of Śiva.
A linga made of gular wood, twelve finger-breadths in length according to measurement,
bestows incomparable sovereignty as well as imperishable liberation.
The kalpa is the fruit; the liṅga is the supreme state beyond the samaya.
Having enjoyed the fruit of action, the flower of dissolution, the mark endowed with form and fragrance,
and the interior of the nine divisions, one becomes the sovereign lord of the Gaṇas.
He who worships with devotion the linga manifested from the *rajas* element shall attain the state of the principle of *vidyā-tattva*, and thereafter become equal to Śiva.
One who desires liberation should worship the laughing Liṅga; he shall attain the state of Śiva.
One should worship the Śrīkāma Oṃgośa-liṅga day after day,
fashioning it from cow dung mixed with *kastha* and *kāvilā*.
One who desires prosperity, one who desires nourishment, and one who desires a son should worship a linga made of flour, derived from barley, wheat, or rice.
A linga made of sugar candy, when worshipped, increases health;
and those desiring fame should worship the Supreme Lord in a mirror.
A linga made from salt mixed with the three pungents (trikaṭuka) and honey, or a linga made of cow's ghee, should be worshipped; it increases the intellect.
"For prosperity, a cloth-liṅga; for the destruction of what is seen [evil omens], mustard-seed [liṅgas] are auspicious.
Thus they speak of these as being for immediate purposes; one should worship them day after day.
This concludes the procedure for the characteristics of the liṅga in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
Salutations to Śrī Mahāgaṇapati.
The characteristics of the *liṅga*, as proclaimed in various scriptures, have been stated;
now they are correctly written down for worship, according to what is taught in the *Mohaśūrottara*.
I shall describe the characteristics of the image, consisting of its measurement and the door-arch;
with two horizontal units [of the door] added to the vertical, it is the most excellent of the excellent.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be made with one part; it is said that the center is drawn [downward].
Having stated that it shines like Nanda in length, one should again divide it into three parts.
One should invite the Lord of these portions and assign a portion to the seat;
furthermore, at the door divided for the Siddhis, one should set aside a bodily portion.
Having divided [the space] according to its qualities, designate the remainder as the external living beings (jīva).
By means of a fractional part, the pedestal (pīṭha) shall be formed; for each [deity], there are two below and two [above].
According to the distinctions of Jyeṣṭhā and the others, the measurements of the doors of Śakra and the proportions of the images are determined.
Beginning from one square up to as far as the range of the digits.

The measure of these [circles] is like that of the *liṅga*; Purandara [the diameter] is obtained by dividing the circumference with the noble *ari* [six] fingers; the ninth part of the sixth part [is the thickness].
The measurement of a finger (aṅgula) has been specified; by that, the movement of the cowherds is determined.
The gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are to be known as nine [tālas] in height.
Bhūtas, Vetālas, and Rākṣasas should be made eleven tālas.
The attendants (kiṅkara) should be seven tālas in height, and those on the left side five tālas.
Pākukuvau, Bhūtāśa, Kūśmāṇḍa, and Yugatālaka;
having divided the desired measurement of the form into nine parts.
O Indra, one should fashion a miniature image (rūpaka) there for whichever deity has the sky [as its element];
the height of the crown should be one and a quarter fingers (vikārāṅgula).

Regarding this, the specific characteristics of the crown are stated in the *Kālottara*: "O Six-faced One, in the images, the radiance of the crest should be fashioned. One should likewise fashion the crown of Śiva with a svastika and three peaks; it should possess a lotus and a crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*). It should have five, three, or one peak, and its tip should be shaped like a *kuṭa* (a type of vessel) and be adorned with a *kalaśa*."
Having released the cord and jewel, one should fashion them in conjunction with the morning [rite]:
a crest-jewel (mauli) should be assigned for the gods, likewise a svastika for the nāgas;
for the daityas, dānavas, and yakṣas, one should fashion the form of a weapon (astra).
The crown of Indra and the others, however, is a lotus among the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvara) and so forth.
This has been explained as incidental; now, what was introduced is set forth:
it is declared that [the height] is equal to an āsyatāla, and the neck is extended by four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula).
One should know that the heart is located below the neck, at the region of the navel.
The belly of the most excellent [consort] is measured by a *tāla* even without cause;
through fortitude, she whose form is the aesthetic essence of desire (*kāmakalā*) has her limbs fashioned with fingers.
The shanks and thighs should be made with eleven aṅgulas, while the two ankles should be four aṅgulas;
the feet should be known as eight aṅgulas in the supreme image for the removal of obstacles.
The vertical measurement has been fully described; now hear about the horizontal measurement beginning with the nose. There are three parts in the face, including the chin.
O Indra, the nose, the chin, and the forehead should each be four finger-breadths (kṛtāṅgula) in length,
and the forehead should be two finger-breadths wide across.
Below the forehead, the two eyebrows are attached at one finger-breadth;
they have one and a half eyes [in length], are twice as wide at their base, and then gradually decrease by one-quarter [of that width] from there.
At the corners, the width should be that of a barley grain, and the mouth should indeed be shaped like a bow;
the two auspicious eyes should be made with a measure of length and have pupils consisting of one-third [of the eye].
O enemy of the belly of the fish, O auspicious one in the portion of the elements and the lord of light!
Having understood the remainder [of the proportions] between the middle of the thumb and the forefinger, one should apply them;
one should direct the gaze according to the form as desired.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Kālottara*: "Having divided the height into nine parts, one should divide each ninth part like the sun [into twelve];
by that, the limbs and the minor limbs are established in twelve-finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)."
Then one should fashion the face, heart, navel, belly, and the mouth with a measure of nine [units];

the two thighs, O Lord, with two units of the sages (twenty-four); and the two shanks with two units of the face (sixteen). There, the distance from the ankle to the knee and the neck should be made four units.
This height, however, for the *śreṣṭhā* [type], without modification,
one should determine as having a measure of two beats (*dvikala*) according to the *rudratāla*.
The forehead, measuring eight finger-breadths in width, becomes shattered.
In a conch-shell horn, there should be two time-units (kala) at the base where it meets its root;
leaving one finger-breadth from the middle of that, it extends four finger-breadths.
The second [measurement] at the root region is, in order, sharp and white in appearance.
The inner bowstring is like a staff, situated between the two eyes.
Between each pair of eyes, at the center, there should be a hundred dots (*tāra*).
From one-fifth of that measure, the light (*jyotis*) should be made; the corner of the eye (*netrāṃśra*) is the size of a barley grain (*yava*).
At the tip of each eye, two pupils (*kāri*) should be made, according to the measurement of a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*).
The eye extending to the corners of the mouth, with a charming belly, is auspicious.

The eye is considered to be of five types: resembling a bow, resembling a fish, resembling the petal of a blue lotus, resembling a lotus, and having a beautiful pupil. These are measured by three, five, six, nine, and ten yavas respectively.
One should determine their width according to the appropriate requirements;
the eye, for the purpose of observing the stages of yoga, should be bow-shaped.
The supreme self, Śiva, who is changeless, resembles a fish;
he resembles a blue lotus among desires, and he should always be known as resembling a lotus.
The eye, resembling the essence of wrath, is one finger-breadth wide in its remaining parts; the various glances are to be fashioned according to the underlying rasa and bhāva.
p.

511) Thus it is said. And as for the aesthetic flavors (*rasas*) and emotional states (*bhāvas*), they are described in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* as follows: "The erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the heroic, the furious, the terrible..."
The sentiments of disgust, the marvelous, and the tranquil are not prescribed for the actor.
From the erotic (śṛṅgāra) arises the comic (hāsya), and from the furious (raudra) arises the pathetic (karuṇa) sentiment;
from the heroic (vīra) the marvelous (adbhuta) is to be known, and from the loathsome (bībhatsa) the terrifying (bhayānaka).
"Peaceful and independent," thus are the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and emotions (bhāvas) described by dancers.
Thus the incidental matter should be known; now the primary subject is being written.
O Lord of the Moon, the nose is not mixed with the two fingers at the front;
that which is on the side is superior, while below it is inferior, and at the base it is the supporting part, free from defects.
When the stars have been forgotten, one should wrap [the medicine] like a grain of *niṣpāva* pulse on the outside and place it in the nostrils;
in the fourfold sacrifice, the two valves (*avalau*) should be applied to the nostrils.
Indeed, it is not that Māyā alone is forgotten there by even a fraction [of its power];
rather, once the *tuṭi* and the finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) have been transcended, the two bonds remain merely for the sake of ornamentation.
The space between the throat is designated as the "house-ball" (gṛhakolaka) measure;
from the forehead up to the brow is the "lightning-row ball" (vidyutpaṅkti-golaka).
The two nostrils are six finger-breadths [from the corners of the mouth]; the junction from the throat to them is a sphere;
its width is that of the petals, while its length is forgotten, being one and a half finger-breadths.
That which is not forgotten is designated as such, but that which is forgotten is nine finger-breadths [in length].
Regarding this, the Atraya-viṣa states in the Kālottara (p.
"The mouth [of the conch] is four finger-breadths in length; however, half of that time [measure] is forgotten.
For those who are gentle or deformed, one should prescribe a circle of one finger-breadth. Thus it is said.
One should maintain half of that *kalā*, and they know nothing further than half of that;
therefore, its maker is like a finger, and in that context, half of a cow’s footprint is a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
The ears should extend upward from the nose, not downward, and should be free from the defects of being too large or too small;
the corners of the mouth and the eyes should lie along the same line, and the two temples should be marked by the lines of the hair-whorls.
The middle of the face, the lips, the nose, the eyebrows, and the chin should all fall along a single vertical line.
Likewise, the conventional designations such as "Kalpa-leaf" and so forth are incidental.

A small leaf-like structure is described as encircling the ear-cavity; it is known as the *śakulī*, which exists by surrounding the entire cavity. The *śakulyas* are situated all around the circular fold located at the edge of the ear.
The region situated for the purpose of looking is the cheek (gaṇḍa); the hollow of the neck is known as the avaṭu.
The junction should be known as the chin, and Kapila as the root of the eye;
the distance between the ear and the sight should be known as four finger-breadths more.
The region situated between the forehead and the eyes is declared to be the location of the conch (śaṅkha).
The cheek, measuring four and seven digits (eleven digits), is fleshy and located below the eyes.
This section concerning the measurement of the image is now written;
following that, the neck should be made nine finger-breadths long, and its circumference twelve finger-breadths.
The two *sandhau-trikola* (shoulder-joint triangles) should be made with a circumference of one *vikārāṅgula*;
both the *bāhu-bhūpa* and *aṅgula* (arm-king and finger) should be made as the *bāhu-puraṃdara* (arm-victor);
the two *dhāman* (abodes) should have *vasurūpa* (eight-form) fingers; and one should know the joint (*granthi*) to be half a *kalā*.
Similarly, the length of the upper arms and forearms is one finger-breadth (aṅgula) less;
the width at the middle is five finger-breadths, and likewise, excluding half a finger-breadth [from that].
The index finger and the ring finger [are each] half a digit [in width];
the little finger is equal to those two; the thumb is equal to that in length; and the forefinger and the others [beginning with the middle finger] are three digits [in length].
At the base, fire (Ra) is to be known as Kalā; Sasya (Sa) and Indra (La) are also displaced there. Likewise, at the root of the arm, Śakra (Va) and Arka (Ra) are free from disease.
The diameter [of the disc] ranges from one *akṣa* (two fingers) up to the corners [of the mandala], and its circumference is three times that.
The two hands should be fleshy and excellent; the fingers should be rounded and without gaps.
In the middle [of the disc], the spherical part (*golaka*) should be diminished by one, two, or four *yavas*.
The length, including the joints, should be laid out with the digits reduced by one from the *paṅkti* (ten);
excluding a fourth part, the little finger (*kanyā*) [is formed], while the joints of the forefinger and middle finger are half [the length] of the thumb-joint;
at the base, the middle finger is three *aṅgulas*, and it is devoid of barley-corns in the middle.
In the end, having abandoned even such qualities, one [attains] from another source than one's own bliss.
The two fingers at the sides and those in the middle should have their joints formed by the essence [of the proportions];
with the thumbs, there should be a barley-corn (*yava*) at each joint, extending forward from the tip of the thumb.
Starting from the neck-form, there are the two nipples, which are spheres of rasa;
the space between them should be the same [as their diameter], and the two wings (sides) of those two should be six finger-breadths.
The mandala is said to be of two kinds:
that centered on a barley grain (*yava*) for one who is capable, and the opposite for one who is not.
The two nipples are thus indicated;
next, the navel is described. The navel should be clockwise-rotating and indeed deep.
The wise man should not perform the threefold wrapping of Hari’s body with a single finger’s breadth of cloth;
he should avoid such exertion, for it is like a urinary ailment. Instead, one should wrap the waist region using eight fingers’ breadth from below, measured by the *jina-aṅgula*.

O virtuous one, the scrotum is not two digits; the testicles are measured by a yantra. At the base of the penis, the girth is three parts, while the circumference is again three times that, excluding the hands, feet, and other limbs.
Having known that [the breath] has not strayed far from the six measures, one should then practice elsewhere;
likewise, your [meditation] on the three times should be at the knees and at the root of the shanks.
The measurement of that garment is an excess of one *golaka*; its height from the toes is three units. Its covering is declared to be triple, according to what was previously stated, O Śatakratu.
The two feet should be auspicious, and the heel should then be three *aṅgulas* long.
The big toe is three finger-breadths minus one quarter; the height of the vow [the linga] is less by one barley-corn;
its covering is known to be three times that, O Śatakratu, as it was previously described.
The two feet should be made auspicious, and then the heels should be three finger-breadths [long].
O Śatakratu, the big toe is three finger-breadths long; the forefinger is one barley-corn less than that;
and each of the other fingers is successively shorter by one-quarter of a finger-breadth.
In the bulb, at the finger-breadth of the elements, and in the navel, it falls away from the middle;
with a half-measure, it is inverted and heavy, falling, and falling further in succession.
The finger-measure for the necks of the two wives of that [king] is the same as that for the crest-ornament.
p.
515) As long as one's own deposit [of mantra] has not fallen away from the portion of Māyā,
it is stated in the *Kālottara*:
The two testicles should be rounded with fingers; this is beneficial for worship performed at the three times of day.
The width should be made two finger-breadths, and the upward commencement should be made by the mouth.
The commencement of the shank is likewise prescribed to be three times [the width] at the front;
furthermore, the ankle-bone is seven angulas, and the middle of the shank is considered to be the same.
The heel should likewise be five finger-breadths long and three times that in circumference;
it is considered to be four finger-breadths [in width], and the foot should be like the face.
One should fashion the tip of that foot with a width of five finger-breadths;
therein, the thumb is three finger-breadths, the forefinger is the best of the barley-measures,
and the two feet are each equal to the measure of the forefinger, with three layers of bricks.
At the navel, at the base of the thumb, in its middle, and likewise at its tip—
these five [points] are endowed with the five forces (vegas) and the elements (bhūtas), accompanied by half a digit (vikalārdha).
The base, middle, and tip of the forefinger are endowed with digits (kalās) according to Kapila.
The circumference should be made three barley grains, or again, one barley grain.

"One should always fashion a lotus or a wheel as a mark in the middle of the foot. Thus has the incidental matter been explained; now that which is relevant is being written: "With the root mantra, it should be made slightly depressed at the base and somewhat raised at the tip."
O Namucisūdana, the characteristics of men and women have been declared;
however, I shall now explain the remainder, concerning how the measurement of a woman is determined.
A woman is not auspicious if her eight parts— feet, hands, eyes, hips,
and breasts— are too slender; nor if her eyebrows, eyes, or nose are excessive in size or height.
The mouth of the bamboo tube should be ten finger-breadths long and its width should be six finger-breadths;
the two beautiful stalks should be slightly less than that in size and pleasing to the mind.
The neck should be reduced by eight barley-corns; having measured it transversely, one should place it upwards.
Thus, the length is eight finger-breadths, measured by the *vismṛtākaraṇa* finger-breadth.
O Śatakratu, taking two pairs of spheres for the upper arms...
One should provide a height of half a finger-breadth for the thighs, knees, and calves;
the shanks should be higher than those, while the feet, moreover, should be level with the ground.
Taking four finger-breadths [for the width], the two thighs should be as long as the arms;
the buttocks should be made plump and rounded—the measurement in finger-breadths is thus declared.
Taking one-eighth part for the *svasti* (auspicious mark), one should place it extensively at the top. Making three parts, it should be elevated, smooth, and endowed with the proper characteristics;
in its center, there should be a cavity from itself, shaped like the lip of an elephant.
In this regard, it has been stated by me:
"If a woman's eyebrows exceed [the standard] by one *yava*, and the elevation of her navel is diminished by one *yava*;
if her face exceeds [the standard] by one *kalā*, then the upper part of the face is distorted horizontally."
Eyes that are three yavas long, minus one-third, are beneficial.
In the *pulya* [measurement], it is considered to be half of that plus one, with an additional *karṇapāśa*.
The measurement of the two shoulders, being one *kalā* less, is recommended;
its commencement and elevation proceed from a width of one *aṅgula* at the *śrīvatsa*.

O best of the twice-born, the calves should be full and without deficiency in their proportions; the knees and the kneecaps should be well-rounded, as should the backs of the feet and the buttocks, each according to its proper form.
The fingers are seven parts in width and length; the calves and thighs are less by one sixteenth part in length, and the hips are less by one thirty-second part.
The two breasts, situated between the cords, are increased, solid, and full;
the secret organ is exceedingly like a leaf, distinguished by all its beauty.
As it is said in the Śrī Kālottara:
Now, do not even consider the life-force of a woman as being present in her face;
for her face is not in her mouth, nor are the other [limbs] there, except for the sphere [of the heart].
The tāla measures the height of the breasts and buttocks as they emerge;
it is traversed by the five *sasyendra* [mātrās], and may consist of two or three *kalās*.
Or there is a reading stating it should be twelve finger-breadths or three times that.

With that [measurement], the ankles, knees, and neck [total] ninety-six finger-breadths; such a woman bestows auspiciousness, provided she is neither too short nor too tall. The region of the shoulders should be six finger-breadths, and each shoulder-blade (aṃsa) should be two units (kala).
O son, the neck is considered to be seven finger-breadths in width at its base;
the two hands and feet are each reduced by a seventh part from their previous measurements.
The distance between the middle of the arms is five fingers and three kalās;
however, there should be an increase of one finger for the backs of the feet and the buttocks.

The differentiation of the thighs and knees is by means of ten, six, and five [units] respectively. One should fashion the middle and the ends of the shanks like the two hands of a twice-born (brāhmaṇa).
The secret organ is considered to be six finger-breadths; it is like the back of a tortoise and hairless.
A woman twice eight years of age should be made beautiful;
the measurement of the shoulder region should be made twenty-eight finger-breadths.
The distance between the two eyes should always be made eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
while the width of the region of the breasts should be known as eight kalās.
"The daughter of Pārvatī should be made with three *kalās* at the three [joints]";
thus the characteristics of women have been declared, and now that which is relevant is being written.
The image should be fashioned according to the measurement of one's own arm-span, with the hands positioned at the level of the shoulders;
it bestows various supernatural powers (siddhis), whereas any other form would not be auspicious.
Wherever the measurement of the lakṣa (the target area) is deficient or excessive, one should perform the rite in accordance with that [proper] standard.
Since the fruit pertaining to both the next world and this one is obtained through right application,
a lotus-wood image would grant happiness equally with one made of clay.
The one made of gold is considered to bestow nourishment, while that made of grain and jewels is likewise esteemed.
The auspicious mountains are considered to follow the sequence of colors: the Śaila (stone) mountain bestows security;
the one made of copper grants victory;
the one made of silver provides a wife; and the one born of brass (pittala) yields cattle.
Those produced from lead are strong; those originating from brass or iron should not be used.
A woman with a protruding belly causes fear of hunger and other such misfortunes; one with a thin waist causes loss of wealth;
one with a humpbacked body causes disease; and one with long limbs causes fear after fear.
If she leans to the right, it kills the husband; if she leans to the left, it harms the woman.
If she has a wound, it causes death; if she is pregnant, it brings fear of miscarriage, O King. Likewise, if her gaze is directed upward, there is disease; if downward, the destruction of the people.
One with uneven lips suffers from quarrels and diseases of the mouth;
one with missing eyes attains liberation (*kaivalya*); and one with a face devoid of blood suffers from facial deformities.
Deafness, lack of a throat, and being deficient in a limb constitute a loss of one's position.
A woman with cold hands destroys the artisan; one with fierce limbs likewise destroys her husband.
One who is constantly deficient in feet or hands, whose hair is disheveled, and whose calves are stunted, brings ruin to her kin. One who lacks a nose increases her enemies.
One with a mark of terror causes fear; one with lines indicates the danger of snakes;
one lacking a waist destroys others; and one with very long arms destroys the king.
Accompanied by the *bindu*, it produces constant intoxication; of this there is no doubt.
Now, as it is said in the *Kālottara*:
"The straight [line] should be made with effort; one should avoid the slanted with effort. Likewise, the straight [line] should be avoided when it has fallen into the shadows."

"One should avoid [images] with a neck bent by devotion, with eyes turned away from the sanctuary, slightly raised, half-raised, or facing away; these eight types of images should be avoided. They should be made without illusion and without ornaments. Thus it is said.
Then, having entered the state of peaceful rectitude along with its accomplishment,
one attains that state— whether gentle or fierce— for the sake of desired goals, just as it is.
The three types of postures (sthānaka) are known as the peaceful (śānti), the gentle (saumya), and the fierce (raudra).
For one standing with straight and even feet, the distance between the feet is three finger-breadths; for one with uneven feet, that distance from the toes is known to be nine kalās.

From the middle of those two heels, one should recognize a space of two parts; that which is called *ṛtu* is of two kinds: the *śānta* (peaceful) is gentle with the left leg extended, while the *raudra* (fierce) is known by the reversal of these two; the characteristics of these two are otherwise the same.
"Among these, the first is said to bestow liberation; the second bestows both enjoyment and liberation;
and the Raudra [world] shows the way to the station for those whose passion has ceased. Thus it is said.
The sixty-four *sthānakas* have been proclaimed, as well as their many varieties;
the one hundred and eight *karaṇas* are known to have been taught by Bharata.
I have not stated its full extent here for fear of excessive length in the text.
Having understood that, one should act according to the various forms prescribed in the scriptures;
here it is first written that the body is that of Mahāsadāśiva.
The two left lotuses are situated upon the lotus of the cosmic shell (kaṭāha) beneath the universe;
the universe rests on the lotus of the shell, and he stands in the lotus posture with his two feet.
At the conclusion of Māyā is the intellect (buddhi); that is the fifth collection of arms.
Established upon the pure path, he possesses twenty-five faces.
Resembling pure crystal, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing a tiger skin as his lower garment, and having a serpent as his sacred thread—
these are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These five faces of Brahmā are the cause of creation; they are described with their respective locations and measurements, while the remaining ones possess fewer digits.
Bāla, Gaurīvatī, Rudra, and Viśvebhyo Vyomanāyaka;
one should write the measures as stated for each region in the sequence of four, two, and one.
The central face is a *tāla* in measure, while the remaining faces are devoid of *kalās*.
A trident, a goad, a sword, a discus, an arrow together with a spear,
a skull-topped staff, a great jewel, a mace, a lotus, and a crown.
A censer, an axe, the solar disc, and a pair of scissors;
a vajra, a needle, a great conch, and a jar filled with nectar.
Holding a sprout of the mango tree, an excellent pomegranate fruit,
the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and the gesture of granting boons (varada) in his right arms respectively.
The Śuka, Darpaṇa, Tarjantī, Sru, Caṇḍamaru,
Sarpika, Bījapūra, Ardhacandra, Kṣurikā, and likewise the Śabdanī.
The svastika, the water-pot and staff, the trident, and the yogic belt;
the eight great supernatural powers, the bow, the pestle, and the supreme plow.
Holding a noose and a blue lotus with his arms positioned on the left,
he has the lotus-mudrā with his two hands, while at the crown of his head there is the half-moon and at his heart the añjali-gesture.
With both hands he holds the *yonimudrā* below his navel;
he is proclaimed as Mahāsadāśiva, the Lord of Obstacles (*Vighneśvara*) who possesses a universal form.
Now, the form of Sadāśiva is described as it is taught in the *Kālottara*: "O Sadāśiva, understand specifically the measurement:
one should [represent] Sadāśiva with the Sadyojāta face measuring twenty finger-breadths."

One should determine ten *tālas* here using one's own fingers; each face [of the deity] is equal to that, while the others are reduced by half a *kalā*. Its ankles, knees, and neck are each two *kalās*, measured by the same unit as the face.
One should diligently expand the extent according to the previous method;
the arms and forearms should be made from ten and eleven cubits respectively.
The joint-form is considered to be a union situated at the measure of a *kalā*;
the shoulder and head are six finger-breadths [in length], and the hand is twenty-four finger-breadths.
With arms reaching down to his knees, he should thus become the Supreme Lord;
when he stands upright and touches his knees with his hands.
Because his arms reach down to his knees, he is called the son of Kṛttikā;
one should fashion him with five faces, endowed with fifteen eyes, with an upward-facing mouth, and lacking a digit [of the moon], turning it completely around.
The crescent moon is three finger-breadths wide, extending from the matted locks to the right edge.

One should fashion the five-crested matted locks of Īśāna; it should be known that the skull is indeed the ornament of the southern face. He has a beautiful nose, a beautiful mouth, and beautiful eyebrows, and is seated upon a lion-throne.
He who has ten arms and large eyes, with long, lotus-like eyes.
One should meditate upon Īśāna as having an upward face, detached from worldly thought and white as snow; Puruṣa, however, has the luster of saffron, is always facing east, and belongs to the Lord;
while Vikṛti has a crest of serpents and a brilliance like that of crushed collyrium.
To the south of Śambhu is Aghora, who is Sadāśiva;
he resembles the pomegranate flower and possesses the luster of lac and asafoetida.

One should always contemplate Sadyojāta, who is Sadāśiva, whose western face is adorned with many ornaments, situated in the northern direction, resembling snow, jasmine, and the moon, possessing beautiful cheeks and a well-set lower lip.
p.
523) One should observe the root door of the temple of Īśāna, who is always present;
it should be established facing east, or facing north, or facing west.
The lion throne, moreover, is four-cornered and equal to eight tālas in measurement.
Rising to half of that height, there should be a lotus-throne of six *tālas*, inlaid with the powers (*śaktis*) beginning with Vāmā; [therein resides] the God, the Lord Sadāśiva.
Likewise—
One should fashion the five-headed [form] with ten *tāla*s in height according to the measurement of a limb.
One should determine the proportions for Bhairava, Nṛsiṃha, Varāha, and Kavināyaka as being two stories (dvitala) and using the Rudratāla measure; furthermore,
Ananta and the others should be fashioned according to the medium or superior proportions.
The Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and others, as well as the Pannagas, Kinnaras, and so forth, should be made according to the medium measurement, O Guha; it must not be otherwise.
Others, headed by the Lords of the Fields (Kṣetrapālas), and the Kiṅkaras, are based on the smallest measurement.
Having understood [this] again and again with effort, one should fashion their forms.
Now, the measurements of Bhairava and the others are also written down:
the face of Bhairava has two eyes, three eyes, and so forth, all around.
The remaining height for Bhairava is also as before.
The width from the root of the arm to the elbow is seven, six, and five [units] respectively;
likewise, the chest, the heart, the navel, the secret region, and the hip follow in this same sequence.
The two thighs and the two teeth are likewise complete;
there are two faces and half a face, and the waist consists of three faces.
The thighs, the knees, the shanks, the middle,
and their tips should be two *kalās*, one full *kalā*, and one and a half *kalās* respectively; they should not be more than this.
The length of the former [the tongue] should be three times its width in circumference;
the sheath of the fangs should be one-sixteenth part of the measurement, white, smooth, and perfectly round.
The tail-hair (kūrca) and the tail (lāṅgula) should be made bushy, radiant, and likewise brilliant.
The nose situated on the upper lip is said to measure three finger-breadths.
The eyebrow should be one finger-breadth wide, curved, radiant, and auspicious;
its length is declared to be three finger-breadths, measured from the eye.
The mouth should be made wide open, provided with thirty-two teeth;
the measurement of those teeth is said to be two or three barley-corns.
The tongue should have the shape of a lotus petal, measuring three finger-breadths and possessing a reddish luster.
One should visualize Bhairava with bloodshot eyes together with Bhairavī.
She should be made eight *tālas* in height, neither less nor more.
In this same manner, Gaurī, Mahālakṣmī, Durgā, Śrī, Sarasvatī,
Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and furthermore, whatever other Mothers there may be.
Sukarī, Nārasiṃhī, Cāmuṇḍī, Kṛśodarī,
Ṛkṣakarṇā, Lampaṭā, and especially Gulagarjā.
The Vaināyakī, the Gāruḍī, and likewise another with a deformed face—
these are all declared to have a mouth exceeding that of the Trigola.
O son, one should also prescribe the remaining *tāla*s as being deficient;

however, the measurement for a deformed woman should be prescribed as one hundred [units] in height. The arrangement of the arms and weapons is to be performed according to the procedure stated in the *Kalpa*.
p.
525) And [deities] such as Ardhanārīśvara are [described] in the *Mohaśūrottara* as follows:
"Ardhanārīśvara should be depicted with half of his body unburnt and marked by the earth."
I am the moon, wearing matted locks with half adorned by a tilaka mark;
an earring on the right ear, and on the left neck a necklace beginning with a bud;
on the left side, there is one breast marked by a serpent-king as a half-necklace.
One should place a trident in the right hand and a lotus in the left.
This is known as Ardhanārīśvara; now Umēśa is described.
Umā and Īśa are seated together, appearing in the forms of both woman and man, O Śatakratu.
Wearing a crown and a mass of matted locks, the supreme Hara is three-eyed;
his neck should be adorned with ornaments, and his ears decorated with earrings.
Having two arms and wearing a sacred thread, he is seated in the vṛddhavīrāsana posture.
Gaurī stands upon the left thigh, intent on beholding his face;
her body is embraced by the arms of Soma, and a glowing tilaka adorns her forehead.
The arrangement of the hair should be done, adorned with fragrant flowers;
the ears should be made beautiful with ornaments, and the feet should be decorated with anklets.
One should show the right arm of the Goddess resting upon the shoulder of the God;
in the left hand, one should place a mirror, and on her hip, a thread together with a girdle.
Again, the Goddess should place her skillful divine hand upon the chin;
she who possesses a beautiful nose, a lovely face, and excellent breasts is the Guide.
Her arms are gracefully elegant and auspicious, marked with armlets and bracelets.
Listen, O Umeshvara, who are known as Hara and Narayana.
The form of Hari-Nārāyaṇa has half of its head with matted hair,
a single eye on the forehead, and is adorned with mudrās and earrings.
Now the Lord of Dance (Nṛtteśa), known as Four-Armed, is described.
One should fashion Nṛttarudra with his head adorned by the crescent moon.
He who maintains the Vaiśākha posture,
wearing a sacred thread of serpents, with a serene countenance, his matted hair gathered in a topknot, and girdled with a snake-belt.

One should fashion the auspicious Lord with sixteen arms— or eight arms— possessing a broad chest, thighs, and shanks, endowed with all the marks, wearing a tiger skin, seated upon a man, with a smiling face, and of beautiful form.
Adorned by the resonant sound of an ensemble of musical instruments such as the flute, lute, and drum;
his left arm is extended, while the second [right hand] bestows fearlessness.
In his hands he holds a rosary, a staff, a sword, a trident, and a spear;
he is endowed with a skull-cup, a noose, a khaṭvāṅga, a shield, armor, and a goad.
And likewise, one [should be depicted] holding a bow with the arrow drawn upward;
Umā, Brahmā, Hari, Skanda, Nandin, Kāla, and those others who are present.
While gazing [at the Lord], the dancing Bhṛṅgī should be visualized standing in front;
moreover, those bearing garlands and swords, as well as the Siddhas and others, are stationed there.
O Lord of Dance, that which is to be attained and what must be performed has been told to you.
I shall describe Viṣṇu in three ways; first, Vāsudeva with two arms—his characteristics will be declared by me in brief, O observer of good vows.
With a beautiful nose and lovely cheeks, his face is well-rounded and radiant with a crown;
adorned with a tilaka on his forehead, he is dark-complexioned and wears yellow garments. He holds a lotus.
In the case of the eight-armed Hari, the fourth right hand bestows peace and holds a mace, a sword, and a lotus;
while the left hands hold a conch, a discus, a bow, and a shield.
In the case of the four-armed [form], the conch and discus should be placed in the two left hands.
In his right hand he holds a lotus, a mace, and the gesture of threatening the three worlds;
he is two-armed, bearing a conch in his left hand, while his right hand bestows peace. Thus Viṣṇu is described; now hear about Brahmā.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) has four faces, a long beard, and four arms;
his matted locks are slightly tawny, he is seated upon a swan, and his seat is a lotus.
On his right arm is a staff, and on that staff is a measuring cord.
He should likewise hold a water-pot in his left hand, as well as sacrificial grass (barhis) and other such items.
"Sāvitrī should be placed on the right and Sarasvatī on the left";
thus Brahmā has been described, and now the Sun-god is being discussed.
The god Bhāskara, adorned with jeweled earrings, stands there upon a single-wheeled chariot drawn by seven horses, with a ruddy charioteer.
With limbs as red as a man's feet, covered by armor on all his body,
he may have beautiful hair or wear a crown, and may have two eyes or three eyes.
Carrying two lotuses with stalks and leaves upon his shoulders with both hands,
he is fair-complexioned, holds a staff, and has a beard and a protruding belly.
Holding an inkwell and a pen in his two hands,
he, the witness of the deeds of living beings, records those very actions.
Piṅgala, however, on the left side, is the doorkeeper who bears a staff.
The gatekeepers are Varuṇa, Sūryanāman, and another, Sahasrāṃśu; then Dhātṛ,
known as Tapana, and Savitṛ, Gabhastika.
Likewise, Ravi, Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, Amīśra, and Viṣṇuka—these are the twelve Suns; they have two arms and hold a boon-granting gesture and a lotus.
They have one face and three eyes, and are situated in the midst of a circle of light;
alternatively, they should be made four-armed, with the two upper hands holding an elephant.
In the right [hand] he grants boons; in the left, beginning with wisdom and ending with the weapons, they are said to be:
the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the banner, and the mace.
The trident, the mallet, likewise the goad, the radiant discus,
and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles— in this sequence, these are declared to be their suns.
In some places they are described differently; here too, they are written down according to those [other accounts]:
Pūṣan, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Bhaga, Parjanya, and Indragā.
Arthamā, Aryaman, Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu,
as well as Sāvitra and Aṃśumān— these are remembered as the twelve Bhāskaras.
"Those [deities] are considered to be situated upon a twelve-spoked wheel, resting on lotuses, with lotuses in their hands, and possessing two [lotuses]. Thus [it is said].
He stands as the manifest thread, the Moon, his own form being a beautiful water-pot;
he has red eyes, a red complexion, three eyes, and is garlanded with a multitude of powers (śaktis).
Then, having seen the son of Bhānu— Vaktrapāda,
who was extremely terrifying, cruel, long-armed, dark-complexioned, and wearing a garland of beads upon his crest— (p. 529).
O virtuous one, Rāhu is said to have a manifest face, to be terrible, with a dark middle body and fearsome; he bears a crescent moon—such is the form of Rāhu described.
One should fashion a banner adorned with three hoods, having the form of a human, a goat, or a donkey,
holding a sword and a shield, or else with hands joined in reverence; it may also have the appearance of a golden ram, or an elephant-faced head that has removed its own tusk.
He has a large belly and a massive body, is adorned with ornaments, and possesses four arms;
he wears a serpent as a sacred thread, has three eyes, and bears the crescent moon upon his crest.
The finger-breadth of the king should be measured by the expansion of the fingers of Purandara;
its mouth is eight finger-breadths wide, and the goddess Śrī is three finger-breadths in height.
The trunk [should be] six finger-breadths long, and its base one finger-breadth;
at the end, it should be one finger-breadth wide, and in between, according to proportion on the measuring line.

"Then, with those [fingers] joined at the base of the thumb in the *sarandhṛcī* [mudrā], the region of the thighs is one *tāla* in measure; the feet are raised, and those two *kumbhas* have closely joined heads. The two *kumbhas* are nine and eight fingers [in height] respectively; their middle is measured by a cord."
His teeth and hair [are as described], and his nostril cavity is one and a half finger-breadths in length.
The ears and the corners of the eyes are considered broad, measuring two finger-breadths in width.
Complete in all his limbs and endowed with every beauty, he is proclaimed as Gaṇādhipa; he is called Śarajanman (the one born from the reed).
He should have six faces well-adorned with ornaments, as well as hair, eyes, and arms.
He holds a spear, a bell, a banner, a lotus, a noose, a cock, and a staff.
One should place in his hands the gestures of boon and fearlessness, a bow and arrow, and an axe;
he may be fashioned with four arms or two, and mounted upon a peacock.
In this regard, there is a specific detail in the *Kālottara*:
"Listen briefly to the characteristics of Gaṇeśa, Vāmana, and the others.
One should designate [the posture] as 'well-established like a stake' (*supratiṣṭha*) among the *nandana* and *nanda* [mudrās]."
Their heart, navel, and abdomen should each be eight finger-breadths in measure;
the thighs and shanks should be twice that length, provided with knees and ankles.
The neck is said to be two finger-breadths [in width], and its shadow is described as that of a lotus;
together with the eyes, it is declared by me to be five tālas in height for the pratihārī.
The arms should be made with many ornaments, joined at the mouth and the joints;
the hands and feet should be eight finger-breadths [in length], and the chest should have three faces.
In this manner, one should fashion the image of Gaṇeśa, who bears the face of a leader of the hosts.
One should draw his two ears, ending at the rim, measuring eight finger-breadths;
they should be veined, delicate, and smooth, adorned with bells and chowries.
Those two [breasts] are shaped like jars with nipples, and between them is the kala-hita.
Its handle should have three faces; its base shall be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long, its tip is recommended to be four finger-breadths, and its end should be six finger-breadths.
A white girdle extending across the hips is praised; Gaṇeśvara should be seated upon a lotus.

Seated upon a lion, or standing on Indra’s mountain, or established on a pedestal, he bestows all accomplishments; he holds his own teeth, possesses excellent vessels, and is endowed with an axe and creepers.

Kārttikeya has three eyes, a protruding belly, and is stout; he is adorned with all ornaments and possesses six faces, assigning the six [deities] to his faces according to their respective directions.
"These should be performed by one who is equal [to the deity], or else with a single face, in the support. Thus it is said.
As has indeed been stated by the venerable Trilocana:
"In a village, a city, a town, or even a capital, the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) should be installed;
he is endowed with twelve arms and possesses his own characteristic form."
In the right hands, there are the Śaktis, the noose, the sword, the bow, and the raised index finger, along with the Śānti mudrā; likewise, there are six [attributes] in the left hand.
The Gaṇa [deity] is praised when depicted with a peacock-feather bow, a shield, a banner, the gesture of fearlessness, and a cock,
either in the field (kṣetra) or within a six-fingered space.
He always holds the śakti, sword, bell, and shield in his six right and left hands respectively.
Whether in a village or in a forest, he should be made two-armed and one-faced, holding a spear in his left hand,
and likewise a cock in his right.
"Red-limbed and clad in red garments, youthful in form and well-fleshed, standing upon a crest, this entire [deity] is adorned with all ornaments. Thus it is said.

One should place Nandin, who has three eyes and is accompanied by his attendants, on the right cheek; and one should remember that he has ears for arms, while on the left [cheek] one should place the skull-bowl and the trident.
"However, Mahākāla—or whichever deity Bhairava is here—should be fashioned. Thus it is said.
Vināyaka was proclaimed of old as Bhṛṅgīśa; he is the protector of the Pāṇḍavas.
532) His body is bound in a difficult posture, he has three feet, and he is endowed with a crest-lock.
Endowed with the staff and the water-pot, he becomes one whose essence is the bliss of the crest-lock.
In some traditions, Bhṛṅgin is said to have three eyes and two hands holding tridents;
the bull should be understood as being like the bull [of Śiva], and Kārttikeya is as previously described.
The goddess is four-armed and yellow in color, adorned with divine ornaments;
she holds a mirror and a blue lotus in her left hands, and likewise a thread and the gesture of granting boons in her right hands.
In ancient times, the Caṇḍeśvaras were declared to reside there: the Gaṅgā is white and youthful;
the Yamunā has a dark-blue body; the Mahī is yellow; and the Narmadā is likewise [yellow].
The Sindhu is like a dark blue cloud, Bhāratī is like crystal,
Payoṣṇī is like molten gold, and Nīlā is adorned with all ornaments.
Seated upon lotuses or crocodiles, holding water-pots and chowries in their hands,
Praśāntī and Śiśirā are considered to be yellow in color and bearers of the trident and the vajra.
Parjanya and Śoka are both lepers (kuṣṭha), holding a staff and a trident;
Bhūta and Sañjīvana are red, bearing a noose and a spear;
and Dhanada and Śrīprada are considered to be red, with hands holding a mace and a trident.
Having thus described the gatekeepers and others, the field-protectors (kṣetrapālas) are now described:
[one should visualize] Kṛṣṇa, four-armed, naked, and adorned with tinkling bells and anklets.
Adorned with armlets and bracelets, and wearing jeweled earrings and a crown.
One should visualize Kṣetrapāla as extremely fierce, with fangs bared, holding a trident and a ḍamaru drum above, as well as a skull and a small knife.
Mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, he has a thousand eyes and four arms;
his crown is golden in color, and he is adorned with all ornaments.
Holding a rosary and a vajra, with arms granting boons and fearlessness,
or else holding a vajra and a goad, the King of Gods should be surrounded by men.
One whose belly is yellowed by hair and eyes [is such];
Niṛti, situated among the pretas, is smoke-colored, fanged, and has round eyes.
Holding a sword and a shield, he is wrathful and surrounded by rākṣasas; Varuṇa stands upon the water, holding a noose, a goad, and the gesture of fear.
In some places he is the skillful wielder of the noose, holding a jar of nectar in his left hand;
he has a large belly and mighty arms, adorned with all ornaments.
Śyāma is dark-complexioned, mounted upon a deer, and adorned with a banner and a goad;
Kubera is yellow, mounted upon a ram, and endowed with an excellent mace.
Īśāna is mounted upon a bull, adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon;
he has one face and three eyes, and stands firm in his vow, clothed in a tiger skin.
The khaṭvāṅga, the ḍamaru, the trident, and the skull-cup are held in the left and right hands;
the world-protectors are likewise described, as are Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as before.
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa, Adhanya and Jaghanyaka,
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, Āvāha and Vivāhaka.
The eight Vasus are well-known, resplendent with crowns and ornaments; they have the form of Aśoka sprouts, and their attributes are a garland, the gesture of granting boons, and a vehicle.
White, yellow, reddish, and dark-blue in color, they carry the Vedas,
hold water-pots and rosaries, have matted hair and ashes as their bodily ornaments, and always stand with palms joined in reverence.
With mantras accompanied by their Upaniṣads, those auspicious ones, bearing swords and bows, also praise that God of gods, the king of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages.
Dharmamūrti was made king; others were deprived of their footstools.
They were Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, Janaḥ, Tapaḥ, Satya, and Dhruva.
They should be known as the lords of the forms [of the deities] of the worlds, possessing vehicles, weapons, and bodies;
resembling pure jasmine and the moon, these lords of forms hold tridents in their hands,
grant boons with their left arms, and wear crests of matted hair and the half-moon.
The lords of the principles (tattveśas) should likewise be known as having a fondness for garments of tiger-skin;
without meditation and worship, the deities of the site (vāstudevas) do not bestow their fruits.
I shall now describe their meditation according to the sequence of the scriptures.
The sixty-four-pada site is beneficial for the gods; no other is so.
In the center, upon four padas, is Brahmā, four-faced and four-armed.
Mounted upon a swan, with a large belly, seated upon a lotus,
he is established in the eastern quarter on a six-petalled [lotus] together with Marīci.
The glorious one holds a vajra-noose, or alternatively, he holds a leather noose.
He has one face and two eyes, possesses the luster of molten gold,
stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, and is adorned with various ornaments.
Vivasvān is situated on the right side within the six squares of the body of the site;
he has one face and three eyes, and his luster is like a mass of crushed collyrium.
In the western part of the body of the site (vāstu), within a space of six squares, is the deity named Mitra. He has two arms, is mounted upon a buffalo, and holds a staff and a noose in his hands.
He resembles snow, the kunda flower, and the moon; he has three eyes and four arms.
He holds a noose and a goad, is fierce, has a jasmine flower in his hand, and possesses great strength.
Enveloped in the ālīḍha posture, it is endowed with ten million snow peaks.
The characteristics of the ālīḍha and pratyālīḍha stances are as stated in the Dhanuḥśāstra:
"One should place the left knee slightly bent and the right leg straight, extending it forward; the right foot should be placed two cubits behind and turned sideways."

"With face turned sideways, straight and firm, with the body standing steady, that is declared to be *ālīḍha* and *pratyālīḍha* by the mere sight of the feet positioned alternately. Thus [it is said].
Now, as for the one called *prathamidhara*, it is on the sixth square to the north of *vāsetā*.
He has one face, four arms, and three eyes, and is adorned with a crown;
he is white as the moon, possesses great vital power, sits upon the Vaiṣṇava seat, and holds a lotus;
his hands carry an arrow and a bow, while another hand brandishes a mace.
Regarding the non-Vaiṣṇava tradition as described by Bharata:
"The distance between the two feet should be two tālas or one and a half tālas;
one [foot] should be placed evenly, while the other, situated on the side, forms a triangle."
And his shanks were slightly curved, endowed with the grace of well-formed arms.
"For this is indeed the station of Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity there. Thus [it is said].
And in the north-eastern direction, there is one who has the form of water (Āpa), possessing three faces and likewise six arms.
With eyes like the openings of a lotus, possessing the luster of a lotus, and bearing a discus, a jasmine flower, and a mace.
Equipped with the pacification of arrows and the like, joined with the first of ten million [years],
it should be known as the Āpavatṣa, situated in the direction of its presiding deity.
He resembles the whiteness of the moon, yet he stands situated within the mandala.
And that is written as follows:
In the eastern direction, the mandala has two feet situated at a distance of four tālas;
the two wings are likewise positioned at the level of the hips and knees.
"The maṇḍala is said to be the place, endowed with various states and flavors.
Thus [it is said]. Savitṛ carries the foot; Sāvitra is the foot below.
Indra and Jayanta are situated in that direction of the tree.
In the north-western corner is Rudra, and likewise Rudradāsa is considered [to be there];
thus these two lords occupy the squares of Śarva; and Khaḍga and Aṃśa occupy the fire-corner (south-east) cells.
In the southwest is the yellow deer, and in the northwest is the disease-bearing [wind];
I shall now describe to you in order the deities beginning with Parjanya who preside over the directions.
Parjanya, Jayanta, Indra, Sūrya, and Satya—these are situated in the east in order; now hear concerning those in the south.
Pūṣan, Vitatha, Śaṅka, and likewise Gṛhakṣata;
Gandharva and Bhṛṅgin are stationed in the southern watch (yāma),
as are Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Pracetas.
The sixteen Asrura-samjñas are situated in the western direction;
Nāśa is the primary [deity] in Calabhaṭa, and likewise Soma, Ṛg, and Yadithī.
All of them should be known as having feet; their meditation is now described.
Pavitrā is red in color and is endowed with a sword and a noose in her hands.
Likewise, there are those known as Sāvitra and Kuśapiñchalaka;
Indra should be golden-colored, three-eyed, and equipped with a thunderbolt.

The warrior Nīlendīvarahasta stands holding a *karavīra* flower; likewise, Indrajaya should be depicted, endowed with a sword and a noose in his hands. Rudra resembles a black *añjali* flower; he is three-eyed and holds a trident and a sword.
Likewise, the Rudrajaya rite should always be performed with a bow [and arrows] in the heart.
O son of Kṛttikā, those situated in the middle enclosure have been described;
now I shall describe to you those situated in the outer enclosure.
One should meditate on Īśa, who has three eyes, holds a trident, a sword, and a shield in his hands, and is accompanied by a lotus.
One should meditate on Parjanya, who has clouds for his vehicle and is practiced in various protective roles;
he has one face and beautiful eyes, and his complexion is as white as a kunda flower and a sword.
Jaya shall be lotus-colored and bear armor, arrows, a sword, and a shield;
Indra shall have a thousand eyes and be adorned with a thunderbolt and a goad.
Sūrya shall be the color of vermilion and be endowed with rays and lotuses in his hands.
The left peak is marked with a lotus banner and placed upon the left hand;
Satya has four faces, and Siddhi possesses a radiance like that of a ruby.
The western [face] is that of a bull, beautiful and endowed with youth;
it is the god holding a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), possessing large eyes and adorned with bracelets.
Seated upon a lotus throne,
with a lotus held in his hand, resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree, he possesses a most wondrous form.
The god should be fashioned with twenty-one faces and fifty arms;
his faces should face the cardinal directions, with each face positioned progressively higher than the one below.
One should assign the faces, starting from the topmost, by means of their respective portions:
the eastern face is considered Puruṣa, the southern Bhairava, the northern Vāmadeva, and the western Sadyojāta.
Thus have the faces of Bhṛgu, corresponding to the directions, been described to you:
the Atharvaveda is his eastern face, while Vāmadeva is his southern face.

The Yajurveda faces north, and the Ṛgveda faces west; however, the faces [of the other Vedas] are optionally placed according to the previously mentioned measurements. Vaikuṇṭha has the eastern face, while Nārasiṃha has the southern face.
They know the northern face to be Vāśa and the western to be Kāpila.
Indeed, they are equal to eight finger-breadths, decreasing by two at each stage;
Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera are the faces in sequence.
O son of Kṛttikā, the night must be divided into parts by a sixteenth part (kalā).
The eastern face is that of Āditya, and the southern face is that of Agni.
The northern face is moon-faced, and the western face is that of a king;
indeed, quarrels arise at intervals of four finger-breadths.
One part [is] the sky-faced, situated above all.
O Six-faced One, in this manner, one should cause a smile to appear on the faces of the others;
[and they should hold] a sword, a *kunda* flower, an arrow, a bow, a discus, and a shield in their hands.
A lotus petal, a rosary, a citron, and a water-pot; a fruit, a spear, a mace, a noose, and a staff, as well as an axe;
a lute, a harp, a flute, a tree, and a cloth marked with the half-moon.
A book, the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles, a sword, a hand-drum, and a banner;
The Kaṅkāla weapon, the Mahāstra, the Brahmāstra along with the Picchaka,
the Khātakāstra, and the Aghorāstra, accompanied by the conch and the drum.
One should likewise imagine other such forms as these for those who bear them;
thus has the universal form of the one called Bhṛśa been revealed.
One should visualize the intermediate space as resembling a mass of crushed collyrium,
filled with tridents, swords, mallets, serpents, tigers, skins, and garments, and beloved by those who delight in them.
Agni should have a spear in his hand and be seated upon a lotus throne;
Pūṣan, resembling the moon in luster, is endowed with a bow and arrows in his hands.
Falsehood has the appearance of a smoky color and is like the God of Death (Kṛtānta) in its splendor;
it is mounted upon a ghost, carries a staff, and is always intent on the destruction of one's duties.
Gṛhakṣata is likewise to be depicted as having a terrifying and massive body, mounted upon a buffalo; Yama is to be made with the luster of crushed collyrium,
clothed in white garments, and endowed with a staff and a noose in his hands.
Afflicted by ten million diseases and accompanied by the most terrifying hells,
the Gandharva is conch-colored and endowed with a banner, a bow, and a goad.
Accompanied by ten million *gandharvas*, resembling a white cloud with bees [hovering about it],
he has one face and four arms, and carries a shield, a sword, an arrow, and a bow.

He should be made dark-complexioned like a deer or a blade of dūrvā grass, with a hide fashioned upon his hand as a sword; he should be yellowish and very emaciated, adorned with a staff and a circle of flour.
He was constantly surrounded by ten million gods known as the Pitṛs.
The gatekeeper with staff in hand, Vikaṭa, Pinākin, and Kānana.
The Holder of the Noose (Pāśadhṛk) may be dark like a lotus leaf or green like a mung bean;
Mānamoha is Sugrīva, and Mukti holds a broken staff.
Puṣpadanta should be depicted as richly endowed with splendor, adorned with a face like that of an elephant,
possessing the luster of refined gold, holding a noose and a goad in his hands,
situated above the planets, and surrounded by ten million nāgas.
Akrūra, sword in hand, dark as Kṛṣṇa, and adorned with a shield,
should be depicted as emaciated from wasting disease, resembling the color of rājavarta stone.
Umā should likewise be depicted holding a staff, accompanied by ten million diseases;
Vāyu should be made cloud-colored and adorned with a banner on his foot.
The Naga should be depicted resembling a lotus, endowed with various weapons:
the Śrīphala, the goad, the Kunda-missile, the sword, the lotus, and the mace.
And on the left [side], the moon, banner, conch, bow, and spear.
Accompanied by ten million nāgas, the chief [deity] resembles Hari;
he is glorious, bearing a bow and a trident, and intent on threatening with his index finger.
Bhallāṭa is golden-hued, equipped with a spear and a bell;
he shines with a banner and earrings, and holds a bow, arrows, a lotus, and a blue water-lily.
Endowed with two hands holding a lute, beautiful and marked with auspicious signs,
he has six faces and twelve arms, and has a peacock as his vehicle.
Soma, consisting of nectar, should be known as being endowed with a water-pot and a sword;
he born of jewels should be known by the sages as holding a bow while mounted upon a horse.
He should be fashioned without a beard, surrounded by ten million suns,
possessing the luster of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and endowed with a staff, a rosary, and bracelets.
The wise one wears a bundle of *darbha* grass, holds a water-pot in his hand,
has a long beard, appears aged, and his body is marked with garlands and lotuses.
And Diti is of a luster like a precious gem, always bearing the conch and the discus;
Yamā, Jambhaka, and Pilipiñcha are in the east.
Caskī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the evil Rākṣasī—
beginning from the northeast corner, these Rākṣasīs are situated on the outside.
White, red, yellow, and black, with faces beginning from the shoulder;
holding a vajra, sword, staff, and trident, and a mace at the feet and head.
The Skandas and others have been correctly described; now listen, O Six-faced One, to the Rākṣasīs.

They are Khaḍgā, Khādyā, and so forth, ending with Kṣirikā; Muṇḍā, Khaṇḍā, Asi, and Kartarī—these should be arranged in sequence, having distorted faces, emaciated bodies, and [standing upon] their feet.
O sinless one, those deities who reside within the body of the site have been described by me.
If the meditation is disturbed, there will be the ruin of the kingdom;
if the offerings are deficient, there will be famine; and if the fire-oblations are omitted, there will be consumption by disease.
Therefore, one should perform this with effort, endowed with meditation, substances, and ritual action.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed in the center, as well as the worship of the deities.
This is indeed called "The Giver of Joy to the Deities," consisting of eight groups of eight words.
Know that the eighty-one-square grid (*ekāśītipada*) consists of excellent progeny;
know that the hundred-square grid (*śatapada*), called "the Steadfast" (*susthira*), bestows perfect accomplishment.
On paths, in difficult terrain, in forts, on ramparts, in cities, in villages, and in market towns.
One should offer the oblation upon beds, on measures of grain, as well as in houses,
in places of accomplishment, in palaces, and at the beginning of sacrifices.
O Guha, the hundred-pada rite should be performed everywhere— in ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, as well as in forests and groves, whether specifically mentioned or not.
First, during the inspection of the site; likewise again during the sprinkling of water;
similarly during the laying of the Brahma-stone; and during the installation of the door-frames.
O Six-faced One, the deities of the site (vāstudeva) are to be worshipped when establishing the layout of a building;
