that which is situated upon the surface of the earth within its various sections is known by the name "Vāstu."
In the *Vṛddhisāraka*, there is the Brahmapīṭha and so forth, as well as the vision of obstacles;
in the temple, there is the wheel called Dharmadaṇḍa at the beginning of the thread and so on.
"Śakra has been surpassed by me; the Daitya Vāstu, the stealer of sacrifices, has been struck down, and the gods stand firm"—thus was it said to the Supreme Lord.
Otherwise, as it is further described in the system known as Piṅgala:
when the Earth was uplifted by Viṣṇu in the form of a boar.
Then, all those three-eyed gods, capable of assuming any form at will, together with their attendants,
began to destroy all the hermitages of the sages.
Then the Lord of the Gods severed their wings and their heads;
they fell once more upon the earth like a great mountain. Then the subterranean nāgas from Śeṣa released a mighty poison.
And that ground, overcome by that poison, emitted hot and great winds.
Born from the union of the humors and the vital breaths, it is called the body (*vāstu*);
though this physical frame is unstable at its end, it encompasses the entire universe.
With limbs like those of a barbarian, possessing the form of a demon, with eyes red as black iron,
two-armed, terrifying, and heroic, he had tawny beard and hair.
Possessing a vajra-body, he is extremely difficult to overcome and hard even for the gods to withstand;
terrified by him, the gods fled and approached the God of Gods.
The Lord, for the sake of protecting that [city], instantly created great illusory snares of his own self and an exceedingly seductive Rudra. Rudra,
having been raised up by the gods, was cast down to the surface of the earth.
And having bound him with the snares of illusion, the gods caused him to enter therein.
"From that time forth, the auspicious deities have been worshipped within that body.
Likewise:
"The sixty-four-padded Vāstu resides in the abode of the gods."
In the square of Īśa (northeast), his head is located; in the [square of] Niṛ-ṛti (southwest), the pair of feet;
Agni (southeast) and Vāyu (northwest) should be the forearms; and Ajā (center) is the junction of the elbows.
At the time of worship, having arisen, one should honor the face with a bow; neither facing south nor north, one should offer the *arghya* according to the rule.
Lakṣmī, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Supriyā, Vimalā, Śivā,
Subhagā, and Sumatī— these are the channels (nāḍīs) that emerge from the eastern face.
Dhanyā, Prāṇā, Viśālā, Sthirā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Aniśā,
and Dvirajā— these are proclaimed as the Saumyavaktrās (those with gentle faces).
Furthermore, Durjaya and Durdhara are situated horizontally and upwards respectively upon the two bamboo-like [pillars].
Then there are Kīlanī and Bandhanī at the ears and the ankles; Saṃvartā and Vivartā at the junctions of the knees and elbows;
and Sadbhāvā and Jānunī in the regions of the heart, the secret place, and the belly.
The birds, with their beaks stained red, settled upon the remnants of the earth;
those two-footed ones stood there, and those gods remained as if fixed in their places.
The lotus, the vajra, the siddhi, the foot, and the joined ploughs.
The trident, the wrist-bind, the triple-step, and likewise the swastika;
the channels consist of twenty cords, and thirteen vital points (marmas) are recorded.
Through the conjunction of eight threads, the five lotuses are proclaimed;
[located] in the Brahma-position, the east, the south, the north, and the west.
By the conjunction of six threads, the vajra consists of twenty-eight [squares].
O fair-faced one, that place where the channels (nāḍī) meet is called the *siddhimarma*, and its number is sixteen; these are the joint-marmas (*sandhimarma*).
The pure enclosure is declared to be the "pada," and that is sixteenfold in number;
the cord-line together with its cross-beam is known as the "vaṃśa," and half of that is remembered as the "hala."
O lady of excellent hips, its number is proclaimed to be sixteen;
there is no doubt that the thread goes from corner to corner, reaching to the end of the enclosure.
That has been declared as thirty-four; no deliberation should be made here.
By the conjunction of three lines at the corner, the trident (triśūla) is proclaimed.
It is asked: what is the number four? [The directions] Īśānī, Nirṛti, and the rest; the conjunction of five threads is celebrated as the wrist-joint (maṇibandha).
The number eight is declared for the Brahmin, with pairs of squares starting from the east;
that which consists of three threads at its end is undoubtedly divided into three sections.
Its number, as before, has been illustrated in that direction.
In the center of the junction of the cords, there is undoubtedly a svastika;
the two bamboo poles were previously mentioned,
as were the eight cords and the eighteen channels— all of that has been declared as the vital points (marmas).
One should draw the thread either one finger-breadth or half of that, as previously described.
When the site has been thus cleared, the multitude of vital points (marman) becomes displaced;
therefore, one should avoid [disturbing] the Vāstu in a house or a field that has been made square.
Śāntā, Ayaśovatī, Kāntā, Viśālā, Prāṇavāhinī,
Satī, Vasumatī, Nandā, Subhadrā, Yamunā, and Ramā.
These ten channels are indeed known to extend from the west-facing and east-facing openings.
Hiraṇyā, Suprabhā, Lakṣmī, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Śrī, Jayā, Jvalā, Viśokā, and Īśā— these indeed face the north.
The two lineages are as before, and likewise there are eight cords (*rajjus*). However, O Brahmin, they consist of three quarters and six quarters; yet [the lineage] is established in nine quarters.
Those beginning with Marīci are situated in six quarters, while those beginning with Svāyaṃbhuva are considered to be in two quarters.
Īśa and the others are to be known as the lords (patika), and Skanda and the others are to be understood here as before.
I shall now describe the hundred-square site-plan (vāstu): one should divide the ground into ten parts.
Eleven channels are traditionally taught there; of those, nine have been mentioned previously.
The channel Aindrī is situated in the east, and Vijayā is considered to be in the west.
The southern channel (nāḍī) should be in the south, and the northern channel is situated in the north;
here, the placement of ropes, bamboo, and so forth is declared according to the *gṛhavāstu* (domestic architecture).
Just as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed in a temple, so too is it beneficial in the *śatapada* diagram;
here, the planets, Skanda, and others are to be understood as occupying four squares each.
The Rākṣasa and the five beginning with Carakī are situated in each of the five quarters;
one should conceive of the body of Vāstu as having the size of a house within a house.
For all these deities, one should offer milk-rice with ghee;
or alternatively, black-gram rice with clarified butter, or grains mixed with curd.
Neither meat nor liquor should be given by the instructors to the rākṣasīs.
p.
547) Now it is said: even a bull made from the substance of a *liṅga* stands before that *liṅga* when it has been fashioned in its unmanifest state and installed.
In the kingdom of the sacrificing king, there is always an auspicious cause.
And so it is said:
"Neither the Yamunā, nor untimely death, nor disease, nor fear of calamities afflicts the people where the Lord, together with Vṛṣa, resides; and there the king is victorious."
In one's own chosen liṅga, in a thousand-limbed liṅga, in a face-liṅga, in a self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga,
before an image of Advaita, or at the foot of a bull, [the act] would not be a source of fault.
That place should be known as "pierced" (kilita); no accomplishment (siddhi) exists there.

Now, one might object: "Since it was stated previously by Śrī Maya that 'the bull [statue] is prescribed for common liṅgas,' does this not mean that the bull should be installed everywhere except before an *iṣṭaliṅga*? Therefore, why should it not be said that the bull should not be placed even in front of the *mukhaliṅgas*? To this we reply: It should not be so stated. For in that context, Śrī Maya spoke of "common" [liṅgas] in brief; however, other liṅgas as well—whether manifest (*vyakta*) or unmanifest (*avyakta*)—are indeed objects of personal devotion (*abhimāna*). This has been explained in the same way by the venerable Somaśambhu in the *Maheśvaraghaṭikā*, as well as in the *Brahmayāmala*: "O wise ones, when an unmanifest liṅga is fashioned, it is common to all."
When it has been placed before him, the bull is considered to be facing him directly.
In the Bāṇerauha, which is self-manifested, marked with a thousand and a hundred signs,
as well as in a face-liṅga (mukhaliṅga) image and especially in a jewel-liṅga (ratnaliṅga).
One should not conceive of a bull in the self, its marks, or in non-duality;
when, through knowledge, one conceives of a bull before these [realities], then [error occurs].
That place should be known as "pinned down" (kīlita); no accomplishment (siddhi) exists there.
Therefore, the ritual of stabilization (saṃsthāpana) must be performed in front of the Unmanifested (Avyakta) and the Bull (Vṛṣa).
The king attains victory, and the subjects indeed rejoice there;
nor do they face the fear of untimely death, disease, or calamities.
Likewise, in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṅgraha*:
"When a manifest (*vyakta*) linga is installed upon a pedestal common to all [deities],
it should be performed before it for the pacification of all misdeeds."
"Otherwise, the Bull (Vṛṣabha) is not praised for the welfare of those desiring spiritual accomplishment. Thus it is said.
And it has been said elsewhere:
"Indeed, among common signs, the bull (vṛṣa) is considered to be foremost;
[it is not so] in the case of Raudra, Lobhana, Bāṇa, Sva, Bhūti, and Acala."

"O Bull, there is certainly no [need for] a bull in an image that possesses a hundred lingas, a thousand limbs, a face-linga marked with weapons, and which is perfected and worshipped by the world-protectors. Thus it is said.
And so it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:

"For the fierce [deities], there is no poison-offering; nor indeed is there one for those whose nature is specific. In a Bāṇaliṅga, there is no bull-offering; nor indeed is there one for a self-manifested (svayaṃbhūta) liṅga."
A bull should never be fashioned at Rauhiṇa, Śataliṅga, Mukhaliṅga, Sahasraka, nor likewise at Lokapālārccita.
There is no bull at a non-Śiva-liṅga; indeed, there is no bull at a Siddha-liṅga.
There is no bull before an image, nor at another's [liṅga], nor at a solitary liṅga.
The bull-weapon (vṛṣāstra) must never be employed during the offering of the flagstaff;
rather, it should be performed before the jars that are common to all.
"A stone [image] should be made from stones; for one made of wood, it should be made of wood;
for metals, it should be made of metal; and for clay, it should consist of clay. Thus it is said.
Moreover, it has been stated in the Piṅgalāgamas that "the one [pillar] at the base is five cubits high";
this is described here just as the bull [is described].
For a liṅga measuring one cubit, the bull should be equal in height to the pedestal.
For a *karaliṅga* of one unit, the bull (*vṛṣa*) is twenty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
for a *liṅga* of one and a half units, the bull is twenty-four finger-breadths.
For a bull [image] of one and three-quarter cubits, it should be thirty finger-breadths;
for a linga of two cubits, the bull should be two cubits.
Furthermore, for a liṅga measuring four cubits, the bull should have two and a half cubits for its horns and two cubits for its eyes; it should be eight and a half cubits in total height.
For a height of four and a quarter cubits, there are eighteen eyes and two cubits [in width];
for a height of five and a half cubits, there are ten eyes and two cubits [in width].
For a five-cubit linga, the bull should be three cubits; for a two-cubit linga, it should be two cubits, according to the number of Rudra's eyes (eleven).
For a five-cubit linga, the bull should be three cubits.
For a bull five and a quarter cubits [in height], the bull should have two eyes and three horns;
for one five and a half cubits, the bull should have two eyes and three horns.
Then, for a six-cubit [liṅga], the bull should be three-eyed and three-armed;
for this six-cubit liṅga, it should be endowed with two eyes and three arms.
Then, for a six-and-a-quarter-cubit [liṅga], it should be three-armed and five-eyed.
For a liṅga measuring six and a half cubits, there should be six eyes and three hands;
for one measuring six and three-quarter cubits, there should be three hands and seven eyes.
For a *liṅga* measuring seven cubits, the bull (*vṛṣa*) is three cubits high and has nine eyes;
for one measuring seven and a quarter cubits, the bull is two and a quarter cubits high and possesses divine eyes.
Then, the Rudra-eye [liṅga] shall measure seven and a half cubits and have three arms;
furthermore, the bull shall stand at seven and three-quarter cubits and be four cubits in height.
Now, for a linga measuring eight and a half cubits, the circumference is four cubits and six and a half eyes;
for one measuring nine cubits less a quarter, the circumference is four cubits and six eyes.
"For a liṅga of nine cubits, the bull (vṛṣa) should be five cubits [in height].
It should not exceed five cubits, nor should it be less than one cubit on the left side.
Thus the height of the bull has been declared; its length should be double that.
And so it is stated in the *Kālottara*: "In the case of common (*sādhāraṇa*) liṅgas, a bull must be fashioned, and not otherwise;
its installation is like that of the liṅga, and its ritual procedure extends up to the limit of Śakti."
Up to the principle of Īśvara—the Liṅga is triangular and eternal; its effect should be double its extent.
And so it is stated in the Kālottara:
When the characteristic marks are common [to both], a bull should be made, and not otherwise;
its installation, like that of the linga, extends to the sphere of the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
Up to the level of the Īśvara-tattva, thirty liṅgas should be fashioned with vigor; they should be twice as long [as wide],
and their alignment must be such that they are level with the back of the pedestal.
The bull should be depicted as having abandoned its horns, with its head touching the head of Lakṣmī;
its gaze should be fixed upon half of Lakṣmī’s body—this is said to be the remaining characteristic.
O Six-faced One, the measure *vṛṣadairghya* is divided by the portion of the gods (*devavasvaṃśa*). A finger-measure (*aṅgula*) is one such portion, and twice that is considered a *kalā*.
The *tāla* is said to consist of six *kalās*, while the *tāraka* consists of three parts (*tryaṃśa*).
It is well known as the *khaṇḍadvitāra*; the pair of *keratālas* is considered [to be part of it].
The face of the bull should be sixteen finger-breadths in measure;
likewise, one should determine that same width for the region of the horns.
One should determine the space between the ears as seven units in width;
including the two side-lobes and the central protrusion, the total width shall be complete.
One should conceive of two *kalās* for that which resides within the nostrils;
one should likewise assign ten *aṅgulas* to the two eyes of the Bull.
The region of the cheek is three digits from the tip of the nose and half a digit from the eye, measured by rotation.
The eyes should be equal in number to the number of eyes [on the face], yet they are considered superior when the pupils are prominent;
auspicious eyes resembling the crescent moon should have a width of one finger-breadth.
The pinnacle [should be] half a digit [in size], elevated by two digits and two eyes [from the base].
One should rotate the *nācikīrṣa* by half a *kalā* at the tip of the horn;
it should be devoid of the space between the horns, consist of three *kalās*, and be provided with a pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
The ears should be five finger-breadths in length, elevated and beautifully curved;
one should prescribe the middle width of the ear as five finger-breadths.
Furthermore, the two ears should be made thin at the tip, measuring three barley-corns in width;
however, at the base they should be three units wide, straight, and provided with lines.
The region of the *kakut* is three units; the height of the *vrata* is two units; it has two girdles (*mekhalā*);
the neck is considered to be eight units; and likewise, the left and right jaws are [the same].
The five eyes are at the front; the shanks have a joint of one finger-breadth;
the lower shanks are eight finger-breadths long; and the two ankles are considered to be three finger-breadths each.
The hooves are praised when they measure four finger-breadths;
furthermore, the height from the hoof up to the top of the forehead is said to be three and a half faces.
The head has eight eyes, and likewise the neck is forgotten;
the measurement of the hump has two eyes, and the bull should have three eyes.
The back [of the diagram] consists of eighteen petals; the waist is a single petal that has been forgotten [as separate];
then, extending from there to the end of the tail, it shall be six units (kalās) in length.
The three corners and the root of the tail—these may be deficient or forgotten;
thus has it been stated by way of summary, and now the detailed characteristics are being described.
At the commencement of the shanks, the circumference is sixteen finger-breadths and half a kalā.

The base should be fourteen finger-breadths wide, and the joint fifteen finger-breadths; from there, the circumference of the lower leg should be seven kalās, and thus the cavity of the shank is formed.

The measurement of the tail at the ankle is eleven finger-breadths; now hear the measurement of the tail itself: the base of the tail should be two eye-breadths (four fingers), and its tip is one finger-breadth less.
The tail is shaped like a chowrie and has three faces hanging down.
Listen now to the measurement of the width of the back from the base to the middle:
the widths at the base, the middle, and the end are ten, eight, and seven *netras* respectively.
O Six-faced One, the circumference at the base of the central pillar should be fourfold;
however, the circumference at the middle and the top is proclaimed to be threefold.

The navel should be located in the middle part; likewise, the neck (kambala) should measure two *kalās*. At the end of the navel, the testicles should be fashioned, hanging down and measuring two *palas* in width.
The fore-shank is ten finger-breadths, and the lower shank is likewise;
the joint at the navel and the two ankles should each be four finger-breadths.
The blade should be five fingers long and the handle one and a half fingers;
the hilt at the base of the blade should be one finger, and it should be provided with a guard.
The circumference at the base of the shank is considered to be twenty-two finger-breadths;
at its upper end, the circumference is reduced by eight kalās, and the joint itself measures exactly one finger-breadth.
The shank should be eleven finger-breadths, and the great ankle fourteen finger-breadths;
having understood this according to worldly convention, one should avoid any defective limb.
Or one may likewise fashion a bull seated [in the same manner] according to the prescribed rule;
having thus completed [the image], one should perform the ritual consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the bull within the boundary according to the injunctions.
By establishing oneself in the yogas for the sake of the goal, one attains the fundamental fruit;
untimely death is pacified, and no calamity causes affliction.
The king attains victory, while they constantly revile his caste,
according to the scripture which describes the characteristics of a bull as being like those of a son.
Thus ends the procedure for the classification of forms in the *Śrījñānaratnāvalī*.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
The classification of the forms has been fully explained; now the [classification] of the sacred seats (pīṭha) and so forth is being described.
Since a Linga installed upon a pedestal that has not been consecrated does not bestow success,
one should therefore fashion a pedestal consisting of the power (śakti) and action (kriyā).
Likewise, in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"O Śakra, just as the entire world, including all that is stationary and moving, is deluded by the power called Kriyā, that very [power] is proclaimed to be the pedestal (piṇḍikā)."
Having thus known the supreme seat situated within the body, one who is well-composed should contemplate the lower seat according to the distinctions of name, measure, and so forth.
When a Linga installed according to the prescribed rite is devoid of its pedestal (piṇḍikā),
it does not accept the commencement of worship, nor does it attain proximity [to the deity], and it is not purified.

"Therefore, O observer of excellent vows, one should construct the pedestal with great effort, by which the attainment of all fruits arises for the souls of practitioners. Thus it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The pedestal [should be made] according to the measurement of the interior of the temple."
When the embryo is divided into eight parts, the smallest part shall consist of four such portions.
When the portion of Tāra is further divided by five, the middle [portion] arises.
"The Vasubhāga [pīṭha], consisting of the portions of the qualities, is declared to be the Jyeṣṭha seat;
two each should be made for the middle ones, and likewise two for the Kanyā. Thus it is said.
For those [images] made according to the measurement of the cubit (hastamāna), the pedestal (pīṭha) is forgotten as being equal to that;
its height, including the pedestal (piṇḍikā), should consist of nine parts.
The pedestal (pīṭha) is considered to consist of many sections, while the base (piṇḍikā) consists of a single section;
however, because of the inability [to fashion it] in the case of face-liṅgas (mukhaliṅga), the base is considered to consist of two sections.
And so it is stated in the Kālottara:
"The height of the *liṅga* is the measure for the length of the pedestal on all sides;
that [measurement] should extend from the manifest (*vyakta*) up to the unmanifest (*avyakta*), reaching as far as Viṣṇu."
For all [deities], the pedestal (piṇḍikā) may consist of a single block, or it may consist of many blocks;
it may always be manifest as a single unit, or at other times as separate parts.
In the case of a *mukhaliṅga*, it may consist of two pieces or many pieces;
one should fasten it together with copper pegs, or those made of gold or silver.
"The pedestal-base should be made of iron, or it should be prepared for the sake of minor accomplishments.
Likewise:
"One should first install the *liṅga* upon the forehead of the *brahmaśilā* according to the prescribed rite."
Having thus performed the binding of the pedestal, one should lower the pedestal-base (piṇḍikā).
Thus, stability is prescribed for unmanifest lingas that are small;
likewise for those with a hundred or a thousand parts, or even for large mukhalingas. The pedestal (pīṭha) is considered to consist of either a single block or many pieces.
Because it is impossible otherwise, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is considered to be divided into two parts upon entry;
in those works of Viśvakarman, there exists no other way for both.
The fourfold elongated mass is prescribed for images;
it is equal to the brush (kūrca) in length, half of that in width,
and its height is considered to be either equal to the measurement of the image's torso or equal to its navel.
The length of the calves is considered to be half of that [the height], while the length of the thighs is forgotten.
The height should be half the width, and the water-channel is likewise prescribed;
now the method for fashioning the pedestals and the *piṇḍikās* is being described.
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be located in the middle part [of the base], elevated like the back of a tortoise;
its width should be one-sixth [of the total height], and the thickness of the pedestal should enter into that proportion.
And likewise in the *Kiraṇa*:
"The abundance of the water-receptacle [is determined] by half or one-third of the *liṅga*."

In that manner, one should worship the characteristic marks. It is as wide as the circumference of the linga and elevated up to the portion of Viṣṇu; its width is one-sixth [of the height], and it is raised to the same degree by its thickness. Thus it is said.
The procedure for the arrangement of the pedestal (pīṭhavartana), as taught in the Mohaśūrottara, is now written:
one should fashion the pedestal (piṇḍikā) with eight pieces of cloth from the Mohaśūrottara.
Their names shall now be told to you, O Lord of Śacī:
the first here is Kalamātrā, the second is Payodharā,
the third shall be Vāpi, and the fourth is Vajrasaṃsthitā.
The fifth is known as Candra, and the sixth is Amṛtā;
O Śakra, Saṃvartā is the seventh, while the eighth is called Nandikā.
In this regard, there may be a face-linga; these are known by the various names such as Kapiṇḍīka and so forth.
As it is said in the *Kālottara*:
"In the first [case], the measurement of the breasts is praised as one thousand and one hundred [aṅgulas].
Therefore, [the measurement] should be made equal in all respects, especially in the case of the *mukhaliṅga*.
Established in the non-wealthy (anāḍhya), she is known as the one considered to be the digit of the moon (candrakalā).
"O son of Pārvatī, on the upper part [of the pedestal], an *amṛtā* should be made, as well as a *padmā* and a *saṃvartikā*; and a *nandyāvarta* should also be made, but not others.
One should allot one-twelfth of the length of the *liṅga* for the purpose of the girdle (*mekhalā*).
One should turn the solar portion, which rests upon the *liṅga*, behind the golden [pedestal];
in some cases, it is taught that the pedestal's thickness is measured in proportion to the *liṅga*.
p. 557) The girdle (mekhalā) is also considered by some to be one-sixteenth of the pedestal (pīṭha). And likewise, in the Kālottara:
And for all the pedestals (pīṭhas), the width of the water-reservoir (jalādhāra) shall be one-sixteenth of the height; from the base, it should be double that.
"It should be extensive, well-known, and one should lead it up from within the pit.
Herein, various types of characteristics for what is called the *mekhalā* (girdle) have been proclaimed in the *Mayadīpikā*.
In the southern direction, the one known as Mekhalādi is indeed remembered;
he is either deprived of a fourth part or devoid of a third part.
In some places it is taught by half [the measure], and in others by a third part.

"According to the division of the youngest, middle, and eldest [brothers], each separately; however, that which exceeds by two *yavas* in the eastern [channel] and likewise in the western one, is known as being at the base of the water-conduit (*praṇāla*), and is considered to be greater by two *yavas*. Thus it is said.
Having understood the thickness of the pedestal, the removal of the eight-sided [member],
and the entry into the Brahma-portion, one should fashion the throne.

Having abandoned the space occupied by the *liṅga* in the center, the wise one should divide the width on the sides according to the ritual requirements; the remainder should be executed as prescribed in the *sūtras*.
When the field has been divided into fifteen parts (*bhūta-indu*), one part is for the pedestal (*pāda*) and likewise for the lotus (*padma*).
One who is well-composed should fashion both the pericarp and the region,
according to sequence, with forms, white rays, the moon, and fortunes.
Just as the two moons are equal to the two lotuses arising from the water— each placed in its own respective place—
so too are the Siddhas, Suras, Daityas, and Munis free from envy.
Among these, this [mandala] is renowned as Padma; it is the ground that bestows great accomplishment (mahāsiddhi).
It is divided into sixteen parts according to the sequence of one, two, three, four, three, two, and one units.
O King, the neck consists of four parts, including the noose, the pitcher, and the womb;
the altar is one part higher than that, and the two fillets consist of two parts.
One should know this as the *vajra* [pedestal], which bestows sons and sovereignty.

This six-sided [Vajra] has been described; furthermore, in the Kālottara, its height is divided by the portions of the Nāgas (eight), and its form is measured by the years of the eyes (two). The foot, the shank, the base, the ear, and the upper fillet are likewise [measured].
Bestowing peace and nourishment, granting all accomplishments, she is this digit of the moon; she is considered the fallen glory, the glorious one, and the nectar.

In a field divided into six parts, there shall be the *jaṅghā* (shank), the *kumbha* (pitcher), and above that the *paṭṭikā* (band); the *kaṇṭha* (neck), *upakaṇṭha* (sub-neck), and *paṭṭa* (band) shall also be present; and for Hari, there shall be the *saṃvarta* and the *piṇḍikā* (pedestal).
When the height is adorned with eight parts, the two wings are divided by the horse-portion (seven);
starting from the foot up to the neck, one should decrease by one part at each stage.
The entry through the two necks and the shanks is by the number of sages (seven);
the exit is by the portion of the chest, following the path to the edge of the pedestal.
Bestowing all accomplishments, auspicious, and always beneficial to all,
the auspicious one marked with the *nandyāvarta* is renowned as Nandyāvarta.
Thus the Piṇḍī has been fully described; now I shall explain the Brahmaśilā to you.
Have an auspicious Brahmaśilā fashioned, equal in measure to the Brahmabhāga.
Just as divine [measurement] is superior due to its digits, so too is the *jyeṣṭhā* [measure] superior in the *jyeṣṭhaka* [temple].
One should decrease it by one digit for each of the others in successive order.
The girdle should be made according to that measurement; it is declared to be equal to the girdle [in width].
That is specified as "deep"; now I shall tell you the "expansion" (vyāsa).
The Brahmavyāsa extends outward by one and a half [units];
furthermore, for the others, one should gradually decrease it by half a barley-corn (yava) at each step.
In even greater detail, there should be two [mandalas] for the lowest [class].
Having measured it accurately with a cord, one should draw a well-proportioned and level circle.
One should carefully carve out the jewel-designs in the center, as they are known.
Then, one should arrange it in the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as in the center, in a circular manner.
Just as one should extract the portion for Brahmā and so forth from the Brahma-stone, so too should the Kūrma-stone be prepared; however, it must be larger than the Brahma-stone.
Thus has the Brahma-stone been described; now the water-channel (praṇāla) is discussed. The pedestal, together with its channel, may be made of clay, gems, or stone.
The earthly [portion] itself is beneficial when devoid of a conduit;
having reached the portion of Rudra at the end, half of it is forgotten.
Always superior above the ear, with water emerging from one-third of that [height],
the spout above the ear is effective for the rite, since it provides comfort.
Thereafter, for men, there may be a deficiency or excess of suffering in the performance of sacrifice.
On the pedestal, according to the division of Brahmā and Acyuta, the cavity should be eight-cornered;
and in the case of stone slabs, the pit should be of a measurement corresponding to the thickness of the linga.
On the uppermost part of the best liṅga, there should be a visible eight-sided [section] consisting of five barley-corns;
for the others, it should be reduced successively by half a barley-corn each.
"In brief, the pedestal (pīṭha) beginning with the Brahma-stone has been thus indicated.
In this manner, the remainder regarding the Linga should be understood; likewise, the pedestal for the planets and for Śiva and others [is to be understood].
And so it is stated in the Pārameśvara:
"The Devapīṭha [is located] in the northeast, as are the bull and the Brahmaśilā;
likewise the Ekaja and Karṇa; anything other than these is auspicious. Thus it is said. The pedestal (piṇḍikā), joined with the base (pīṭha), may be made either of stone or of metal.
Is it not the case that, according to some doctrines, it has been stated that the Brahmaśilā is to be grasped?
The Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) may sometimes be equal in measurement to the ear-measure of the Brahmāṃśa; or it may be one-fourth of that, or even greater than the width of the Liṅga.
Even by a mere fraction of an arrow’s length, it may extend beyond the limbs of Brahmā;
it may be a Vākṣī-Brahmaśilā, or it may be a Liṅga, and even a Piṇḍikā.
For lingas with one hand (hasta) and so forth, starting from two finger-breadths (aṅgula) apart,
there is an increase of one finger-breadth for each up to ten; however,
in some traditions, the stone slab (kaśilā) is considered to be greater in width.
The determination of the height for the entrance of the Brahma-section should be understood as follows:
the entrance [should be] by one-eighth, or by a quarter, or by a third,
or by half, or even by the full length of the Brahma-section.
... as [it is] in the higher [teachings].
p.
561) Up to the half-measure, by an increase of one *tara*, the sixty [units] are the best for the excavation (*khāta*).
The pedestal (*pīṭhana*) should consist of three sections, as should the *piṇḍikā* and the *ghaṇḍikā*.
Whether in the section on impossibility and so forth, or even in the great [section] on the primary and secondary marks.
The width of both the pedestals (*pīṭha*) and the bases (*piṇḍikā*) is equal to the length of the linga.
The water-channel (praṇālaka) should be one-third of that height;
thus it has been declared in various ways in the *Tattvakālottara*,
just as success was attained when this Liṅga was installed by the lords of the Daityas.
A water-strainer made of barley-grass, provided it is without a frame, bestows success.
Know that for an image made of stone, the benefit is derived from stone;
for one made of clay, from clay; and for one made of wood, from wood.
That which is produced from iron is effective against iron, likewise that produced from gems against gems;
that produced from jewels is praised against jewels, and everything is established as effective against arrows.
... [it] would be without support.
On a silk cloth, a throne, or the like, or upon a garment that has been spread out,
or on a seat of flowers, one should worship the arrow even without a physical support.

For metals, that which is of their own origin is best; it is not desirable when from a different source. Likewise, [an image] made of copper, or one with a copper pedestal, or one with a crystal [pedestal], or a binding made of silver.
One should fashion a pedestal for the jewels made of gold or silver;
likewise, the binding for all of them should be made of gold or silver.
"One should place two goads (aṅkuśas) in the excavation, or else one-fifth;
having divided the lingas into three parts, one should install one part. Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the mobile linga as well, in the *Mayadīpikā*—for example:
The lengths of arrows and other such weapons are proclaimed to be equal to their respective breadths.
The height of the jewel-born [pedestals] should likewise be determined according to their beauty or their proportions;
they should be equal in height to three parts of the width.
Having divided the portion for the form (rūpāṃśa) like a treasure, one should fashion the hoof (khura) with one part;
the fillet (paṭṭikā) and the base-moulding (jagatī) should likewise be made with two parts each, as well as the neck (gāla).
The emergence of the God of gods is by a tenth part, and the girdle is likewise declared; the pedestal for the five lingas bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Thus ends the procedure for the characteristics of the seats (*pīṭha*) in the glorious *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
Thus concludes the brief enumeration.
Now, the determination of the marks on the lingas and the pedestals is being written.
The body is sometimes abandoned by certain subtle characteristics previously mentioned.
Śambhu is endowed with a hundred thousand marks; otherwise, he is not one's own deity.
For a linga may indeed be without marks, or it may possess other marks.
"Because the deities reside here upon a support that is neither too long nor too thin, one should therefore, with every effort, extract the auspicious *lakṣaṇa*. Thus it is said.
Likewise, a linga characterized by the absence of the *aṇu* (the subtle point), when installed by one who is self-restrained,
shall always cause terror to the lords of that region.

"Therefore, exerting effort, one should fashion the *liṅga* according to its characteristics. Thus it is said. It should be known that the installation [is performed] by one born under the *Tala* [constellation]. And likewise in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
That splendor which is the majesty of Śiva and which illuminates the Self—that is declared to be the City characterized by that; it should be extracted by the wise man.
"...the distinction is not discerned. Thus it is said.
Having correctly laid out the Brahma-sūtra through the middle of the portion for the image (arcā), one aṅgula is prescribed for the liṅga by means of a division into one hundred and eight parts.
One should cause the marks on the forehead, nose, mouth, and so forth to descend from the position of the image's [original] marks;
likewise, in the Piṅgalāmata it is said:
"A distinction in the mouth, nose, and forehead would result in the destruction of prosperity."

Since it has perished from that [place], the wise one should cause the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*)—the portion for the image—to descend by means of the third [finger] and the two [others] measuring a *lakṣa*. Otherwise, it would bring about defects. It was declared thus:
"For others, [it is] nine [units] less than eight *aṅgulas*."
The lines extend for a width of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), measured by eight times eight barleycorns (*yava*).
As follows:
The *lira* [is so called]; likewise, it gives half [the share].
In some places it is thus designated; therefore, O Father, act accordingly as if it were dead.
O Beloved, that pair [of measurements] should be extended in the middle; a plumb-line between the two [should be applied].
In the case of the best liṅga, the width is eight barley-corns (*yava*);
the entire breadth of the base is seven barley-corns plus one *yūka*, in a liṅga measuring seven cubits.
A *tri-yūka* consists of five barley grains; a *veda-yūga* consists of four barley grains.
In a measure of four cubits there are three finger-breadths and five yūkas;
in one cubit there are six yūkas and [three] yavas.
"One *yava* and seven *yūkas* [is the measure] for that which is situated below the *māraṇa*.
"When the field of the *lakṣma* is divided into eight parts, the descent of the wings occurs from two parts;
the width of the wing-field is by the measure of half the field of the *lakṣma*."
As it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"For one desiring prosperity, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) consists of the dual and the single; that which is divided by the single mark (*lakṣma*) brings about the form of Rāma.
[If] the line of the mark (*lakṣmarekhā*) is one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*)... fallen from elsewhere."
There should be twelve lines for the divisions when divided by eight;
from the two divisions above, due to rotation, [the lines] extend equally behind at both ends.
Above, however, there are two spiral lines situated behind and below the knot;
as the head of the *liṅga* has been described, so too is the head of the *lakṣa* characterized.
"O Śakra, this auspicious characteristic, which bestows all accomplishments, brings good fortune, strikes fear into all obstacles, and is common to all, is a mark of auspiciousness. Thus it is said.
The specific rules for the wealthy and others are as stated in the Kālottara:
according to the teaching on proportions, the height of the *liṅga* is divided into three parts, and one part is taken as the measure for the modifications.
The other type of line is considered common to all lingas;
it is omitted from twenty-four parts of the height of the linga.
In the case of the best linga, which measures eight *yavas*, the deep line is omitted.
She [wrote] a letter with an extensive seal, measuring one finger-breadth of Jyeṣṭharudra.
Then, a line reduced by one-ninth [of its length] should be drawn across the two liṅgas;
having likewise carved out the *lakṣma*-line of the middle [liṅga],
the line of the smallest [liṅga] is reduced by one barley-corn at the ninth part.
The first five parts, beginning with the modification of the Rudra-portion, are to be abandoned.
Within the Rudra-portion, one should divide the Rudra-portion by day and night.
The female portion consists of four equal quarters, while the elevated portion consists of five and a half parts.
The characteristics have been correctly described for one who is wealthy; for one who is not wealthy, worship of the gods is prescribed.
The projection from the side-lines shall be half of that, and not otherwise.
When divided by eight, nine, and three, [the measurements] are obtained respectively by the multipliers of the plumb-lines.
By two and a half parts, success is granted in the first [sections] beginning with "surāḍhya."

Alternatively, when dividing by *kṛti* (four), one should discard two parts; then, by means of the *randhra* (nine), *arka* (twelve), and *kendra* (four), the two fortnights are obtained in sequence— this is the third method, common to all.
A junction should be made by means of two lines, or else it may be a serpent-noose (*nāgapāśa*);
however, some authorities maintain that at the sixth part, it should have the measure of a *bhāga* and the shape of a barley grain (*yava*).
The seventh house is beneficial when it is devoid of its own lord or when its lord is in the seventh house.
A single line, perfectly complete and ending at the portion of Viṣṇu,
characterized by a measure of one hundred barley-corns (*barha*), one part (*tāṃśa*), one hundred parts,
or two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); this is the opening of the eyes for images that possess both natures.
Nor by arrows, nor by a linga made of jewels, nor by one made of metal, nor by one made of earth.
However, it should be performed when [the food] is cooked, so that no odor may arise.
In the Piṇḍīkā, the preceptor should first mark the characteristic form of the yoni (bhaga) moving at a moderate speed; thereafter, the artisan should carve it.
In the *Ratnaliṅga*, the mark of the creeper is a light that is utterly stainless;
this is the statement from the *Sarvajñānottara* concerning the left and the middle [channels], as it truly is.
And it is said:
"Two parts of the jewel-liṅgas should be visible, while the third part, which is the entry-point, is prescribed for the cavity adorned with gold."
And one should diligently extract their defining characteristic from among them.

"Having joined [the height] at three parts, one should abandon the upward connection. Thus it is written; and the characteristic of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) is described in terms of its proportional form, so that the characteristic of the *bhaga* (the vulva) may be situated near the splendor of the *liṅga*.
The *piṇḍikā* in the middle of the pit should be half the measure [of the base] in size;
it should be fashioned like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, in the shape of a womb (*yoni*), and provided with a perforation.
The opening should be two yūkās long and five līkṣās wide;
externally, the depth and width of the line should be two and a half līkṣās.
"One should increase [the measurement] by one *yūkā* and one *līkṣā* for each of the two-kara units and so forth;

the wise man should apply the remaining characteristics in conjunction with the proportions. Thus it is said: "One should not pierce the vital points (*marman*) when laying down the side-lines (*pakṣasūtra*)."
If there should be [a mark] at the head-end of the lakṣasūtra, death is certain.
And likewise in the Piṅgalāmata: "The thread which is declared to be the pedestal (pīṭhaka) should be fixed at the vital points (marman), both below and above;
having properly laid it out, one should draw [the mandala] auspiciously, bound with dhava-wood. Thus it is said.
In various scriptures, the characteristics have been proclaimed in many different ways;
what is the use of that multiplicity if there were but one [method] that grants all accomplishments?
The scattering of a hundred thousand [offerings] has been declared in the *Adhivāsa* chapter of the *Khilāgama*;
nevertheless, it is also fully explained here as the cause for the manifestation of the face.
Because the presence of the two tips, the primary limbs, and so forth exists at that time, the Guru should perform the consecration with mantras using a golden needle.
Thus, all the characteristics conducive to happiness have been briefly explained. Now, for the sake of accomplishing the temple (prāsāda), the determination of the site is being written.
Having abandoned a space of one, two, or three hundred *dhanus* from the site of the city,
and having constructed a beautiful city there, he should begin the construction of the palace.
And likewise in the Kālottara (p. 568): "A field of one, two, or three hundred [verses] is inferior, middling, or superior."
O Śikhidhvaja, it should be measured by the length of a bow.
In that regard, one should examine the ground according to its respective colors. Thus it is said.
One should abandon [the site] at a distance of one hundred and fifty bows;
temples should be constructed facing their own proper sites and never turned away from them.
They should never be made facing north or facing south;
however, with the exception of the Caityas, the Assembly Hall, the Mothers, the Yakṣas, and the Vināyakas,
they should be turned away from the donor according to the requirements of the site.
Then, the wise man, knowing this, should employ this means appropriate for his aspiration:
[an image] endowed with the colors and ornaments of that [deity], and possessing its dress, weapons, and vehicle.
"One should paint that [deity] upon the wall facing the city;
this very procedure is declared for those engaged in the art of painting. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa and Yāmadeva are also depicted here in this context.
Viṣṇu, Śakra, and Bhānu were established in the eastern abode.
Agni stands in the southeast, and Hanuman, like the sun, is in the south; likewise are Bhūta, Vetāla, Tāra, and Yamuna.
The Pitṛs, Bhadrakālī, the Daityas, and the Rākṣasas are in the southwest;
the ocean, Varuṇa, and the rivers, as well as Viśvāmitra, are likewise situated in the west. Now hear again concerning those in the northwest corner.
Vāyu, Kātyāyanī, the Nāgas, Gaṇeśa, and Śanaiścara.
In the north reside the Yakṣas, the Grahas, Skanda, and Pārvatī;
in the northeast are Bhairava, Rudra, Caṇḍeśa, and Kṣetrapālaka.
O Brahmins, Brahmā and Nayanā were auspicious and facing toward that city;
for Śiva is omnipresent and bestows auspiciousness in every place.
And so it is stated in the Bāṇamata:
"A rule regarding the location of the quarters has been proclaimed specifically for the [other] gods;
however, there is no such restriction for Śiva concerning the construction of his temple."
"Beginningless, all-pervading, and worthy of worship with devotion in all directions;
in villages and other places, situated upon earth and fire, the abodes of the gods face west, extending from south to north, established facing the east, and auspicious. Thus it is said.
And likewise, in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"Outside the royal palace, in the various directions and on both sides,
the king should have palaces constructed, each demarcated by its own distinct boundary."
In a place presided over by a deity, there is an increase of Dharma; therefore, [reside] with the king.
For indeed, by the power of the agent's desire, there is a distinction between actions performed face-to-face and those performed from behind;
yet among the various faces [of action], the face of formative activity (rūpa-karma-mukha) is for the sake of battle.
Endowed with that form, its ornaments, dress, weapons, and vehicle,
or with hands granting boons and fearlessness, one should, with a concentrated mind, install the deity.
Since the two faces of the two [buildings] are equally defective,
other palaces situated outside them are screened from view by those [defects].
"Facing forward or turned away, they should be made according to the will of the performer.
O leader of the gods, this rule does not apply to the arrow that has become self-manifested;
for in that case, the two [ends] should be made facing forward and turned away, since it bestows grace upon all."
Having established [the two points], if the distance between the two established locations is equal to five arrows (five yojanas),
or if it is greater, equal, or less, then the eastern length and so forth will be obstructed.
One should not construct palaces and such; if one should do so, he would meet with death.
One should construct them with twice the height of both [the previous structures], leaving a space on the ground in front.
If the navel is pierced from behind, on both sides, at the tips of its feet, or on its flanks, this is the rule for a pierced navel; it is not a defect in the case of a pierced navel.
"Starting from the corner [of the mandala] and so forth, it leads to the defect of the principal deity's limbs. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṅgraha*:
"When a deity previously installed— whether it be one's own [personal deity] or a manifest [public image]—
one should not perform the piercing of its vital points (*marmavedha*), nor likewise the piercing of its boundaries (*sīmāvedha*)."
The vital point where the threads of the southern, northern, and intermediate directions intersect is called the *marman*.
One should construct [the layout] on both sides of that thread, even for houses, villages, and so forth.
In the case of a field of *sūma* grass, when two [boundary stones] are being set up for one who has been accused,
one should leave a space twice as large as the interval between them, equal to the height of both.
One should first mark the front, and then the back, with an interval twice that of the width.
Having set aside this cloth and other such items, one should prepare the sacred space on both sides;
otherwise, death occurs for the performer and great suffering arises.
The king [should consider] the oppression of the kingdom, its forms, and fears;
there shall be no fault in the triple-junctions, nor any fault in the corner-houses.
Since the *pradhāna* is subordinate to it, the *jagatī* meter is indeed one;
for if this [world] has arisen again from that which was commenced through knowledge.
When the basis is not yet perfected, it would then be a basis of non-existence;
[one should perform] the "perfection" of the agent's death in order to remove that fault.
By means of oblations to each respective guardian of the directions and by the gift of their respective vehicles.

"One should always perform the Rudra-śānti daily according to the prescribed rule; in this way, peace shall come to the performer through great worship, recitation, and other rites. Thus [it is said].
Or rather, the *Kālottara* describes the defects as follows:
When the god who wields the Pināka bow is to be depicted together with Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
he should always be made facing east, as should his attendants and the great lords.
One should avoid the two deities Sumukha and Deva, as well as those positioned back-to-back;
thereafter, I shall describe the front and back of the bow using one-third of its length.
It is beneficial to re-install with effort an image that was previously installed;
however, it should be placed in a higher location, excluding the Vedic [mantras].
Leaving a space equal to twice the height of both, one should establish the boundary.
Having constructed palaces in this manner, they will become sources of suffering in the end.
Otherwise, suffering arises for both the practitioner and the patron when there is the appearance of a great pillar,
a crossroads, a wheel, or similar forms;
or when [the site] is pierced by a large mountain, a cow-path, or a three-footed path, and so forth.
Since it bestows death upon the performer, one should therefore avoid this [act].
In cities, villages, sacrificial grounds, and so forth, one should install that [deity] facing forward;

however, when the deity is situated with its back turned, it bestows auspiciousness upon the region. Therefore, [one should place] the base facing forward and the deity itself with its back turned toward the center.
The deity situated in the center of the region removes the fear of enemy armies;
therefore, one should proceed toward the center and not toward the southern direction.
In the north-eastern region of that country, there shall be weapons;
in the western direction, sovereignty; and in the eastern quarter, [prosperity]; while in the south-eastern direction, [there shall be] that [destruction].
In the southern direction, in the domain of Nirṛti, there is suffering;
in the western region, there is prosperity; in the northwest, there is the utterance [of obstacles];
in the north, there is partial success; and in the northeast, for the sake of all success.
One who is a destroyer of Krauñca should install Mahādeva and Viśākha in the east,
and Hutāśana and Brahmā in the southeast.
The Mothers, Bhairaveśa, and others are beneficial in the south as Guhyakas;
in the southwest (Rakṣasī direction) are the Kṣetrapālas and likewise the deformed Kiṅkaras.
All those beginning with the western direction are beneficial for both the village and the city;
the Kṣetrapālas are in the north-west, and the Mothers are in the north;
in the north-east is the divine Yogin, as well as Mṛtyujihva and Ṭaṅkin.
Furthermore, Kṛṣṇā spoke to Vināyaka when she was indeed engaged in her proper range:
"In cities, villages, hamlets, and market-towns it is exactly thus and not otherwise;
so too in palaces, trees, sacrificial posts, and the like, as well as in monasteries, shrines, houses, and so forth."
One should diligently construct temples and even houses for the Gaṇas;
the Sun should be placed in the southwest, and Durgā in the northwest region. For a house shaded [by a tree] brings about death with certainty, whereas one [properly situated] brings sovereignty.
"O Śikhidhvaja, just as a shadow does not obstruct an effect that has been shaped by a wall, this definition has been declared according to the sequence [of topics]. Thus [it is said].
Thus, the ritual procedure that must necessarily be performed has been demonstrated.

Now, the examination of the ground (*bhūparīkṣā*) and other matters according to various established doctrines are being written down. When a Brahmin resides [there], the ground is red; when a king, it is yellow; when a Vaiśya, it is white.
A Śūdra, without the Veda, should perform the worship of the golden lotus feet;
having dug up the clay and extracted it, he should fill [the cavity] with the desired earth.
It should be sweet, sour, pungent, bitter, and likewise astringent.
It is indeed characterized by the successive odors of feces, urine, blood, and semen.
A Brāhmaṇī woman [is known] by the growth of *kāśa* grass; a Kṣatriyā woman by the growth of *uśīra*;
a Vaiśyā woman by the growth of *dūrvā* grass; and a Śūdrī woman by the growth of *kāśa* grass.
A woman who has a depression on the left side is said to belong to a king; one with a depression on the right side is a Vaiśyā.
For the twice-born and others, the float is on the water; for Śūdras, the float is at the rear.
The earth is most excellent at Śatoniṃna and common to all;
for these [regions], the respective constellations are Uttarāṣāḍhā and Kṛttikā.
When Jyeṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, the gods, Varuṇa, Agni, Indra, and Vāyu [are present],
the earth becomes most manifest in the third month, with the seeds sown having sprouted.

In the west, the middle [quality] is declared; in the seventh [direction], the lowest is remembered. To the south, there is pasture; to the east, grain; to the north, crops, iron, and water. It is neither too soft nor too hard, pleasant to the touch, and level.
It is smooth, heavy, firm, pure, fragrant, free from defects,
possessing sweet water, uncracked, and delightful in its natural form and other qualities.
[One should visualize] the winnowing basket and so forth, the peaks and lips and so forth, and the hearth as having a uniform form.
One that is circular or elongated, triangular, or possessed of wandering eyes and so forth; one that is hollow, porous, perforated, censurable, or bloody.
One should abandon a site known to be inhabited by outcastes, frequented by those such as the *asaṅga*, or infested with foul odors and the like; instead,
one should accept ground that is free from all defects, possessing roots and insects, and for which witnesses are available.
Or he should acquire land through means such as requests, or by lawful means alone.
In the center, covered with cloths and other materials, placed upon an auspiciously adorned base,
and atop a raw clay pot, there is a lamp filled with ghee.
One should arrange the four continents in the four directions for the twice-born,
either consecrated with the Jātīśa mantra or empowered with the Praṇava.
One should protect and preserve one's reputation, which is guarded and shielded by the armor of weapons;
when all things are blazing among all classes, it is auspicious;
but when they have subsided in a particular case, then for that person it is not auspicious.
Whether completely extinguished or even if it flares up again, this [fire] is not recommended;
one should dig a pit one cubit deep all around and fill it with water.
Having gone a hundred steps away, one should return and observe it once more.
The ground with abundant water is the best; that which lacks two finger-breadths [of water] is middling;
below that is to be known as the inferior. It should be purified with great effort.
First, upon the acquisition of the site, then during the placement of the foundation stones,
and especially at the commencement of the walls, one should worship Vāstu at the three times of day.
Having leveled the site and worshiped it as previously described,
one should then satisfy all the deities with oblations and ritual offerings.
Then, having offered the *digbali* and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the prescribed rule.
One should place two auspicious jars in the central and northeastern squares;
one should dig a pit in the southeastern square, measuring one cubit on all sides.

If [the soil] is not in season, one should wash the earth of the field with water; for purification in the case of a field, one should throw water in succession into a dug pit and moisten the ground with that.
Having placed another jar, covered with two cloths, upon the shoulder of a Brahmin,
he should lead it to the eastern boundary amidst auspicious sounds and the chanting of the Vedas;
having stood there for a moment, he should properly circumambulate the city in every direction.
The preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should mark the boundary lines;
this is called the "taking of the horse" (aśvādāna), performed by the circumambulation of the Īśa-pitcher.
In some cases, the digging is performed without the ritual pot (kumbha), while in others, the acceptance (parigraha) is omitted;
in certain instances, only the worship of the site (vāstupūjana) is prescribed, even without the ritual image (bimba).
One should dig down to the level of a pebble or to the level of a stone,
depending on the obstruction of the foundation, using stones that fill the hand and with soil placed at intervals of eight finger-breadths.
One should fill the excavation until one-quarter [of the total volume] has been reached.
596) Regarding what is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata* concerning the desired and undesired [proportions] for the wings:
one should excavate a depth exceeding one-fourth of the intended measurement.
It is declared that [the ground] should be leveled on all sides until it reaches the edge of the water;

then the wise man should either dig down to pure consciousness (cinmātra) or to the level of a man's height. Once the excavation has reached three-quarters of its depth, the wise man should fill it with five parts [of materials].
Once it has been baked, neither armor nor even a stone-binding is desired, because both would shift; therefore, O Lord of Serpents, one should withdraw.
It is not desired [to build] with mere clay using carts,
chariots, elephants, or even by manual labor; rather,
one should fill the pit with care after sprinkling it with water, using clay that is free from gravel, stones, and saline soil, and leveled to a depth of eight finger-breadths.
With hands and feet made from the wood of the Palāśa and Aśvattha trees on all sides.
Having filled one hut with the other hut, one should create a state of agitation.
There, having worshipped the site (vāstu) and performed the laying of the foundation stones (śilānyāsa) in due order as will be described,
one should establish a firm binding with the stones.
When the back has become level, made like the surface of a mirror,
then the preceptor, surrounded by artisans, should extend the measuring cord.
One should determine the northern direction by means of the pole star (dhruva), or the eastern direction by means of the steady flow [of water],
or by the conjunction of Puṣya, Revatī, and Maghā, or by means of instruments such as the conch-shell;
having thus known the east and west, one should establish the center between the two sides.
With a cord equal in measure to that, one should mark the south and north;
then, taking half of that as well, one should mark the intermediate corners.
Then, having made it square according to one's own preference,
one should worship Vāstu there and perform the arrangement of offerings corresponding to that.
Having constructed the pedestal-base according to the measurement of the *dīpikā* as desired, one should then form the pedestal-base according to the proportions of the *madaprāsāda*.
"A pedestal elevated by half the height of the temple is [the] medium;
one reduced by a quarter is [the] best; and one [reduced] by half is the smallest.
Thus it is stated, and also in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṅgraha*:
The best pedestal-base (pīṭhabandha) should be half the height of the pinnacle (śikhara) and three-quarters of its width; one-quarter less than that would be the middling.
The lowest [measurement] is said to be by means of the *argha*; it is equal to the fruit for both [types].
Furthermore, the height of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is to be known from the elevation of the *ja* [syllable] and so forth.
In the highest [scale], it is equal to the *dhāma*; in the middle, it is devoid of a quarter.
O Jagatīraja, the measurement of the field for the smallest [mandala] is as follows;
and as stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"The pedestal is proclaimed to be elevated by its height, measuring half that of the palace."
The middle [measurement] shall be one-quarter less than that, and the smallest shall be half of the largest.
I shall now describe the construction of the *jagatī* along with the temples for the deities in the cardinal directions.
It should be made half the size of the temple, or three-quarters, or equal to it;

in front of the pavilion, it should be square and beautifully adorned, equal in size to that [temple]. Outside of that, at half the distance from the temple, there should be eight shrines for deities in the cardinal directions.
Having abandoned half of that on the exterior, one should cause the wall-binding to be made;
the binding of the jagatī-wall should be constructed like the divisions of a temple.
Then Nandi and Mahākāla [should be placed] in the east, or Vajrapāṇi;
Ardhanārīśvara and Sūrya in the southeast, or Hutāśana.
One should place Mātṛśakra or Gaṇeśa, or Kṛtānta, stationed in the south;
one should place the two Aśvins [in their respective places];
and one should place the god Mṛtyuñjaya, the Yogin, or Varuṇa in the western quarter.
One should place Kubera, endowed with the power of yoga, and the goddess Umā in the north.
One should place the discus, or the one named Khaṇḍana, or Īśāna within one's own domain;
it may be equal to the temple itself, or equal to its inner sanctum.
The width of the residential quarters is prescribed to be twice their height;
the temples dedicated to Īśa and the other deities, ending with Pāvaka, face the west.
The temples beginning with Nairṛta and ending with Tilā are prescribed to face the east;
likewise, those beginning with Pāvaka and ending with Nairṛta should face the north.
All the temples in the north are traditionally said to face the south.
In some traditions, the foundation of the pedestal (pīṭhabandha) is considered to be either at the base or at the top of the jagatī;
in others, the footstool (pādapīṭha) should be constructed above the foundation of the pedestal. That sanctum (dhāma) should be raised by one-third of its width.
It is turned [into a circle] by means of a sixth part or, in some cases, a fifth part;
therein, it is called "the revolving" (āvartin) in the Viśvakarmāgama and other such texts.
One should assign one-eighth for the youngest [pillars], one-sixteenth for those of middle size,
and having given one-twelfth for the exterior, one should proceed there with the largest ones;
above the portion of Rudra, one should divide the width into four parts.

One should make the hundred [units] equal to half a khura; the kumbha [should be] from two parts including the feet (aṅghri); the pāṭhī of the kumbha is by one quarter, while the neck (kaṇṭha) is by two parts. Then, having divided that part into three, one should fashion three paṭṭikās.
By means of the *bhoga*, it should be a square; the *haṃsa* should be one and three-quarter parts. The *haṃsapadī* should be one-quarter part, and above that, there should be a lotus.
Then, O Śivā, by entering the middle of the *kura*, one reaches the single *kumbha*;
by reciting that with half an entry, there is an entry into the throat by means of two.
A set of four *pāṭikās* should be made, each emerging by half of its own width;
the *haṃsa* enters by half its own width, and that *paṭṭī* enters by a quarter.
Above that, one should fashion a lotus in such a way as to be beautiful;
it should be adorned with rows of men and swans, and likewise with rows of lions and elephants.
One should diligently and respectfully construct this for the sake of the beauty of the pedestal (pīṭha).
In some places it is called *dhārāpīṭha*, in others it is considered *pādaśilā*;
and *bādha*, *jagatī*, and *padma* are mentioned briefly in various contexts.
And in some traditions, it is held that [the base consists of] a foot, a *jagatī*-shaped pitcher, and a lotus.
In some places it is said that one should fashion a pedestal (*pīṭha*) at the ankle-joints (*jaṅghāvarta*);
in other places it is stated that the pedestal should be like a *piṇḍikā*.
This method of constructing the pedestal (pīṭhabandha) extends through a hundred varieties; however, for fear of excessive length in this work, it is described here in brief by way of summary.
A quarter of the *jagatī* should be made into a lotus, a water-lily, and the pericarp of the lotus;
these are to be fashioned upon the pedestal-base according to what is beautiful in form.
One should divide the height and width of thirty-four units by eight;
one quarter [of that] by four is the *paṭṭī*, which is raised by one part;
the *jagatī* is considered to be raised by four parts and projected out by one part.
Having entered with two [lines], that stripe emerges from one part;
the lotus is formed by four [lines], and the stripe emerges from two parts of the hand.
One [part] is the neck; then, from the two [parts] emerging, there are two bands;
by means of two [parts], both in their emergence and their height, it is called the *kumuda*.

The country (deśa) is formed by two [parts], the double-band (dvipaṭṭī) by two, and the neck (kaṇṭha) by one part; the two strips (paṭṭikā) are formed by those two, and the lotus (padma) by four parts.
Having entered from the lotus by means of a portion, there shall be the expansion of the pericarp.
Having entered either one part of the circumference of the pericarp or half a part,
one should subsequently construct the temple, just as it is described in the Kālottara.
The first Veda (4) increased by the Vedas (4), or the first taste (6) increased by the fires (3), is the number of the mantra;
or the first pentad (5) increased by the pentads (5), or the five oceans (5) increased by the mantra (1).

One should not construct a house for Śambhu that is less than four cubits in height, nor one where the five [measures] beginning with the *paṅkti* increase up to the limit of the sky and the elements (*viyat-bhūta-kara*).
Fifty is prescribed for the Nāgas; the remainder is considered the abode of the Bhūtas.
O Six-faced One, for manifest images made of clay, stone, wood, or metal, they must indeed be constructed according to the specific measurements of the temple door.
O son of Kṛttikā, a temple with a common foundation must never be constructed for deities who are manifest or unmanifest, nor for those made of wood, stone, or clay; however,
such a construction exists according to the prescribed rule for those made of gold and jewels.
Thus indeed, among the Bāṇaliṅgas, those that are self-manifested (svayambhū) are especially [sacred].
Listen to the characteristics of the pedestals and sanctums according to the dimensions of the palaces; O Guha, the specific features of the doors are also described here in brief.
When the field is divided into eight parts, the pedestal portion consists of four parts;
the inner sanctum is twelve parts, and the wall is two parts.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should have a width equal to twice the width of the door, and its height should be double that;
the height of the plinth (jaṅghā) is declared to be according to the measurement of its width.
One should fashion the pinnacle (śikhara) as twice that [height] and in the shape of a trident; likewise, when the field is divided into nine parts, the pedestal (pīṭha) shall be one equal part.

It should be constructed with the *garbha* as the base unit; the internal partitioning is likewise measured by the *pada*. The hollow space should be measured in *bhāgas*, while the outer wall consists of one *pada*. The four doors in the cardinal directions are to be made according to the measurement of the width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
On the outer wall, however, it may be double [the thickness], or perhaps one and a half parts;
its height should be double its width, or even two and a half times its width.
O son, the measurement of the shikhara should be made for the shanks as before;
when the heap of cubits for those increasing by one from the Paṅkti onwards is divided into two.
The three enclosures on the pedestal should be proportionate to the length of the liṅga;
one should arrange the exterior according to that measurement of the liṅga which includes its own share.
The width of the door should be equal to the [width of the] *liṅga*, and its height should be twice that;

the height of the *jaṅghā* (pedestal/base) should be made equal to the width of the *jaṅghā*. The *nāsā* (nose/ornamental projection) should be according to the measurement of the inner sanctum (*garbha*), and the inner sanctum of the *nāsā* should not be otherwise.

The bud-like nose-ornament (nāsāmañjarī) is praised when it reaches half the height of the pinnacle (śikhara); the pilasters (nāḍyas) should extend out by half the interior depth, and the pavilion (maṇṭapa) should be like the interior, except for its absence.
"O son of Kṛttikā, this general characteristic has been declared: that [the deity] has emerged from the pavilion along with a portion of the essential essence of the elements."
Now, as it is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"In a temple dedicated to Nāga, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be made with eight divisions and the inner sanctum (*garbha*) with twelve;
the plinth (*jaṅghā*) and the wall (*bhitti*) should be equal in height, each consisting of eight and four divisions respectively."
The pinnacle (śikhara) should be made double [the height of the base], with the tip of the parrot-nose (śukāgra) measuring half the pinnacle.
One should construct it as previously described according to the dimensions of the womb-chamber (garbha), with a projection (nirgama) of one-third [of that].
Alternatively, on the pedestal (pīṭha), the linga may be measured according to the size of the pedestal, and the circumambulatory path (paribhrama) should be half the size of the pedestal.
The door is remembered as being like a pedestal, twice as high [as the width], with the others [the side walls] being the thicknesses of the two walls.
The *śukagrā* (beak-portion) is to be understood as before, and likewise the *jaṅghā* (shank) and the *śikhara* (spire).
When the square base is divided into four parts, the four [parts] constitute the pedestal (*pīṭhaka*) within the womb-chamber (*garbha*).
The door should be equal in measure to the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the walls should likewise be of that same proportion.
Therein, the nose (the central projection) should be like the womb (*garbha*), emerging from within the corners of the pedestal.
In the *samaṇḍapa*, the *vedī* (altar) extends out by one-eighth of the shaft (*śara*) from the center of the womb (*garbha*).

When the [width] is divided by the number of openings (*randhra*), the *pada* (unit), the *pīṭha* (pedestal), the *garbha* (womb), and the wall (*bhitti*) reach the edge of the circumambulatory path (*bhrama*).
The *patikā* (fillet) is to be made outside; and at the tip of the *śuka-nāsa* (the crow-beak projection), it extends... [as previously specified].
This [method] has been declared for the sake of protecting the lingas made of gold and other precious gems.
When the arrows have increased from Āśā (the tenth house) and so on, and the Hand-constellation (Hasta) has been divided into three parts,
the three enclosures are formed by the middle of the pedestal (pīṭha) together with one [additional part], like a linga.
With an increased number [of cubits], there is external devotion; as previously stated, starting from the Śuka and others,
having established the Veda [four] cubits and so forth, it grants an increase of one cubit for each corner,
following the sequence of the temples [measuring] six and four [cubits].

The pedestal (pīṭha) should be equal in length to the liṅga; it should have three circular tiers (vṛttika), each one-third of that size, and an outer molding (bhakti) for the sake of the pedestal, when the total height is divided by eight and multiplied by one.

The measurement from the end of the wall to the end of the opening is the "equal measure" (dhāmatulya); the measurement of the opening up to the end of the wall is the "opening-measure" (randhramānaka). One should lay out the lines for the length of the temple and its corners.

These twelve types of pavilions (*maṇṭapa*), which have openings and are square with four corners, are like the "Destroyers of Cities" (*purandara*); when constructed in the same proportions as the temple (*prāsāda*), they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, in brief, [it is established] in all abodes.
O Purandara, for the sake of manifesting the distinction, that which is capable [of differentiation] is declared to be separate; one should offer the sixteenth part externally.
"In order to establish the forms of Jyeṣṭhā and the others in sequence, [they are placed] upon Maurya and the rest. Thus [it is said].
And as it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Now I shall fully explain the characteristics of temples:
having made [the ground] square and level, marked with the cardinal and intermediate directions."
One should divide the wealth equally into horizontal and vertical sections according to sequence;
by the horizontal portion there shall be the pedestal (pīṭha), and by the vertical portion there shall be the ornament (bhūṣaṇa).

The wall should have forty-eight [parts], and the nose-projection (nāsāgra) should be fashioned accordingly. The external upper member (ūrdhvaja) should be equal to the field (kṣetra), and that above the plinth (jaṅghā) should be double [that].
O lady of excellent hips, the spire (śikhara) and the top of the parrot-ornament (śukāgra) should be measured according to the interior sanctum (garbha).
It proceeds from the front of the exit, whether from one-third or even from half of the height.
The width of the inner sanctum (garbha) should be one-eighth of the [total] height, including the pinnacle;
having made the width eightfold, the inner sanctum is said to be one-sixth [of that].
The *pragrīva* (neck-projection) is known as the extension from the tip of the *śukāgra*;
this is indeed remembered as the measurement of the site (*vāstu*) when devoid of the characteristics of pavilions (*maṇṭapa*).
Now I shall describe the measurement of the *liṅga*: the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the *liṅga* should be equal.
O you of excellent vows, the inner sanctum (garbha) should be half the size of the pedestal (pīṭha) on all sides;
the wall should be twice that [thickness], and the plinth (jaṅghā) should have the same width as the wall.
O fair-faced one, the height of the *śikhin* (the spire) is said to be twice that of the *jaṅghā*;
the interior of the pedestal up to the neck is of that same measure, and by that same proportion is the *śukāṅghrikā*.
And having emerged, O lady of excellent hips, one should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
This is remembered as the measurement for the *liṅga*; now the measurement for the door is being stated.
Having made it four-cornered like the Vedas, the door should be equal to one part;
its width has been fully described as being twice the length of the base.

In the center of the Dvāravat-pīṭha, there should be the Śeṣa, and the Ṛṣika should be located there. The wall should be divided into eleven parts, with the door occupying four and a half parts. The height of the spire (śikhara) should be twice its width.
The *śukāgrā* should be understood as before, both in its projection and its elevation;
this *śukāgrā* has also been described along with pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) characterized by the *mīna* (fish) motif.
I shall now describe the *śukāgrā* according to the proper rule for that pavilion.
O Dear One, whether by a portion of two cubits or even a portion of one cubit,
the Śukāgra should be constructed at the front, provided with a pavilion.
The remaining details regarding the calculation of width and height have been explained as before;
this method has been proclaimed for those [images] that rest without a physical support.
For lingas measuring from one cubit up to five cubits,
it is proclaimed that they may be without a surrounding platform (maṇṭapa) and even without a sacrificial fire-pit (nirādhāna).
O Suranāḍika, for one who sees [the deity] from the womb-thread, the tip of a parrot's beak, or the excellent pavilion,
it is declared that the pavilion is of middling size.
