The width of the two wings for the sake of the womb [sanctum] is equal to that in front;
this is declared to be the smallest [size], while the half-maṇḍapa is half of that.
The Pādamaṇṭapa should be understood as being either equal in size to the Śukaprayāsa on all sides, or equal to the Garbhasūtra.

The meaning of this is as follows: "The four-pillared pavilion (*catuṣkikā*) for the bull. What is this four-pillared pavilion? O Goddess, there should be a pavilion below; a pavilion facing downwards at half the height of the womb-chamber (*garbha*); and a mound of earth (*mṛtkhaṇḍa*) at half the pavilion's extent, even in front of the bull's four-pillared pavilion.
The distance from the center to each side of the square should be one-fourth of the total;
this entire measurement of the pavilion is declared to be that of the flagstaff.
At the end of the three pavilions, the location of the flagstaff should be known;
the flagstaff pillar should be constructed from solid heartwood.
The bull should be fashioned with four Vedas on its ears, a lotus above its ears, and its own weapon upon its back;
it should be made standing and facing the temple.

Then, the altar-platform (vedikā) should be one cubit, and the seat for Kujā (Mars) should be half that; the pedestal for offerings (balipīṭha), however, should be at a distance of four cubits from that.
It should be made square, circular, or in the shape of a lotus;
O beloved, one should always install Mṛtyu, Bālya, and Hara situated therein.
The circumambulation should be understood as one-fourth of the height of the pinnacle.
O Dear One, in front of the pavilion (maṇṭapa), there should be a rampart (ṛgadigbandhaka) equal [in size] to it;
the enclosure wall (prakāra) should be known as being on both sides, like the walls of a temple (prāsāda).
And that height is pure consciousness alone, or it consists of half a *kauśika*.
O beloved goddess, I shall describe the proportions for the *sandhārikā*—the support and foundation for fame—as well as for those with equal relatives; listen, O Goddess, just as it is.
This applies to the six types of lingas, starting from one cubit up to nine cubits.
O lady of excellent limbs, the *sandhāra* is proclaimed for temples of Gaurī and others, as well as for those with great images, and for palaces.
It should not be performed for others unless it is for the sake of the Buddha;
and that [measurement] should be divided equally into eight parts according to the dimensions of the site.

One part shall be the outer wall; in the second [part] there should be a supporting beam (dhārikā); and in the third, again, there should be a decorative band (bhakti). One should measure the inner sanctum (garbhakoṣṭha) with [the remaining] parts.
In the center, a pedestal (pīṭha) should be made with an extent of one part, ending at the boundary of the Vijā.
The tip of the beak should be fashioned according to the measurement of its interior;
devotion and liberation are to be understood as before, with the exit and height being as previously described.
Alternatively, one may construct it in another way, making it four-cornered like a star.
Likewise, the interior of the pedestal and the supporting walls;
furthermore, the walls are divided according to the midday [measurement], each having its own characteristic.
The front of the parrot [pedestal] should be made as before, provided with an interior and joined with decorative divisions.
O lady of beautiful countenance, these are indeed remembered as the sustainers of the world, not those who possess pride.
588) Now I shall describe the measurement of the linga; listen accordingly.
The pedestal and the linga should be made equal, and the womb-chamber (garbha) should likewise be so.
The division by half of the womb (*garbha*) constitutes the *bhakti*; such is the verse [describing] that which is equal.
The outer wall is like a pedestal (*pīṭha*), as previously stated in the section on the "Hole for the Parrot" (*śukandhra*) and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: first, the *liṅga* is measured by four [units] and so forth, and the *pīṭha* (pedestal) is measured all around by that same measure; the *garbha* (inner sanctum) is half of that, and the wall (*bhitti*) is half of that—this is the measurement of the temple site (*kṣetra*). Having again assigned that same site-measure, one should construct there a blind wall (*andhakārikā*) like the inner wall and an outer wall like the pedestal. Now, for those measuring five cubits and increasing by five cubits, within their own respective sites, the pedestal and the *liṅga* are like the *piṅga* [measurement], the wall is half of that, and likewise the blind wall; having assigned another site-measure outside of that, the outer wall should be constructed according to the measure of the pedestal. Then, for those increasing by five [cubits] starting from ten cubits, within each of their own sites, the pedestal, the *garbha*, the blind wall, and the wall are as before. Whatever circular area occurs among the *āpāda* [elements], that is the blind wall (*andhakārikā*) for each; one should distribute it appropriately among the outer walls. And it has been said:

In all types of temples, the architects should ensure that the outer walls are made either slightly larger or slightly smaller than the inner darkness of the sanctum (pīṭhagarbha). Thus the measurement of the liṅga has been fully explained; now the measurement of the door (dvāra) is being stated.
The door should be half the size of the sanctum, and the central pedestal should be like the door.
Know the Vāyavya to be hollow; its wall is said to be equal to that.
Its support is to be known as equal to that on all sides, O fair-faced one.

However, there may be an exit for it [the shrine] at half the measure of the door, O Goddess; for the measurement of the doors of the pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) has indeed been thus prescribed. Now, the [measurement] of the pavilions is being described.
One should extend the measurement of the field outward from the two wings of the śukanāsā.
Its width should be equal to its height, and it should be symmetrical and square;
this pavilion is declared to be the best, possessing auspicious characteristics.
Having provided a supporting ledge (sandhāra) on both sides with a width equal to that [of the base],
and making it square on all sides, this is proclaimed as the middle [type].

One should worship the tip of the śūka and the wings with a thread equal to the inner wall (garbha). Know that its width at the front should also be equal to that; this is the smallest [type]. Furthermore, the mukhamaṇḍapa should be equal to the central axis (sūtra) of the womb-chamber at the front.
O lady of virtuous vows, the wall of the pavilion (maṇṭapa) should be understood to be like the wall of the temple (prāsāda);
the circumambulatory path (pradakṣiṇā) should be known to be one-third of the temple's size,
and the foundation (jagatībandha) of the pavilion is considered to be one-third of the pavilion's size.
Having left a space for the four-sided platform (catuṣkikā) of the bull at the front of the pavilion,
one should construct the flagstaff situated according to the measurement of two pavilions.
On each side, temples measuring one-fourth of the temple's height are prescribed;
being joined to the walls of the main temple, they do not obstruct the circumambulation.
The four goddesses, beginning with Avalī, are situated in the directions starting from the east;
they have the form of peaks at the end of the fourth [layer] and extend outwards from the southeast and the other intermediate directions.
The gables mentioned previously are to be placed in the center, along with the excellent doors.
Outside the front pavilion (mukhamaṇṭapa), which is provided with four supports,
the divine ground above the door is called the "ghaṭikā."
One should place Nandin and Mahākāla at the entrance;
one should install Rudra as Ardhanārīśvara, situated in the south-eastern direction.
I go to the Mother in the south; in the southwest is he whose form is like a bhr̥ṅgin.
The wise one, worshipping the divine Lord of Yoga, should place him in the west;
if the two door-keepers are not worshipped in the east,
then he should worship the Lord as the Master in the northwest and Goddess Umā likewise in the north.
Likewise, one should place Caṇḍeśa in the northeast, and Lokeśa as shown by Īśa;
[and the guardians] Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Anila, Soma, and Gā.
And Īśāna—these are indeed remembered as having the directions from the east to the northeast as their domain.
"If there is no [specific] division, O auspicious one, one should thus arrange those situated on the temple platform.
Thus it is said that [the general rule] is common to all; however, as for the remainder, according to the *Kālottara*, I shall now fully explain the specific characteristics of the temples.
Meru should be fifty cubits [in height], while [the next] is five less;
Kailāsa, the favorite of Śaṅkara, should be made with space as its measure (ten cubits);
the fourth, Sarvatobhadra, is considered to be thirty-five cubits.
The *vināma* should be thirty cubits, and the second [type] is exactly like that.
There are four varieties of *śrīvatsa*, which are considered to be twenty-five cubits;
it should be made like Mount Gairika or Elāsa, and not otherwise, O son of Kṛttikā.
The Haṃsa, Suvarṇa, Kamala, Aṣṭāśra, Ṣoḍaśāśra, and Aṣṭaka [mandalas] should be made with two rows [of bricks], and not otherwise, by one desiring prosperity.
The king of planets (Graharāja) should be fashioned measuring fifteen cubits;
its length is ten cubits, and its height is eighteen cubits, O son.
From the "Valaya" (the circle) at the hand of the Bhūta up to the limit of the two rows,
the temples should be constructed according to the measurement of the Liṅga and its proportions;
herein is written that which is declared as the "Lakṣa" (the defining characteristic) in other scriptures.

"The temple for lingas with one hand [of measurement] and so forth should be four times that size; in the smallest [temple], the inner sanctum (garbha) should be three times [the linga]; in the medium, it should be four and a half times;
and in the largest, it should be known as twice [the linga]. In the remaining cases, one should fashion the walls accordingly. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"From the mixed [plan] with manifest characteristics, the interior [sanctum] is three, two, and one and a half [parts], respectively, by means of two parts;
in some cases, there is an increase of the wall starting from the smallest [size]. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the Asura [mandala], there are two intermediate wombs together with the [other] half, while the eldest [womb] consists of two parts.
"But with three [parts], the womb (garbha) is the smallest; the remainder is the wall (bhitti) in some cases.
Likewise, in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṅgraha*:
"For a liṅga of the three smallest types, the womb is desired to be threefold [of the base]."
The superior [length] is twice that of the medium three-fold liṅga, plus one and a half [units].
"The embryo of the three qualities is said to be tripled for the sign of the three supreme [levels];
in the remaining portion, there shall be devotion, as previously stated for Śuka, Agrya, and so forth.
And as it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
Furthermore, O Skanda, the preceptor [should fashion] the Dhāmagarbha [pedestal], which is three times the size of the liṅga.
O Six-faced One, one should place [the deity] in the middle portion of the wall-section;
one should fashion the two middle [sections] extending upwards as far as the door.
"Having set aside one part consisting of clay, the remaining three parts made of the two [other materials] shall be the best. Thus it is said.

Thus should this incidental matter be understood; furthermore, as stated in the *Kālottara*, [the divisions] are the modifications, the sun, the eightfold parts, and the superior, middling, and inferior.
Having assigned the form-portion (rūpāṃśa) to the side, one should construct the kala-chanda there with equal width and height according to the procedure to be described;
following the sequence of the nāla-chanda, one should proceed to the upper chanda.
From the upper limit of the *ūrdhvacchanda* up to the edge of the altar (*vedikā*),
one should rotate [the measurement] after excluding a fourth part of the height of the *śikhā*.
Therein, one should arrange the neck (*grīvā*), the dome (*kumbha*), and so forth, within that fourth part.

The *mañjarī* (flower-cluster) should consist of three parts, resembling the leaf of the blue lotus (*nīlendīvara*). Having divided its shank (*jaṅghā*) into seven parts, one should arrange the divisions therein:
the *masūrika* (knee-cap) should be one part, and the shank itself should be five parts.
The cheek is said to be one part; its curvature is described as follows. One should turn out the fourth part, the peacock-feather ornament (*mayūraka*), which is equal in measure.
Above that, one should fashion three bands (tripaṭṭa) measuring one-quarter of a foot;
from there, one should fashion the neck by entering into its middle portion.
Then, a circular portion measuring one part should be made with three folds as before;
thereafter, the wise should fashion the garment according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
The *masūraka* has been fully described; now the characteristics of the shanks (*jaṅghā*) are stated:
the *nāgarī*, the *lalāṭī*, the *vairāgī*, and likewise the *prāvanī*.
The Lāṭī [script] is pure, like a city free from ornamentation;
it consists of pairs of male and female [letters], is devoid of passion, and is crowded with leaves.
The *mañjarī* is characterized by many ornaments; that *jaṅghā* is always *drāviḍā*.
The *nāgarī* is in the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*), while the *lāṭī* is proclaimed to be in Lāṭa.
The *drāviḍī* is in the southern region, and the *vairāgī* is found in all countries.
Thus, O Guha, the general rule for the two parts of the shank has been stated;
now, briefly set forth the form of the cheek-ridge.
One should arrange ten fillets on the portion of the parapet;
having arranged the ten fillets, [one should proceed with] the [remaining] construction.
One should arrange lotuses on the *nalinī* [line], lotuses empty [of other marks] along the path,
and likewise a swan’s wing and a swan; there, one should place the *nalinī* [line] at intervals,
either at every foot or even at half a foot.
The [stages] from Āma to Asura and ending with Akapota have been told to you in brief;
the decrease and increase of the stages, however, is said to be common to all.
The wise man should divide the field of the ground into sections;
having established the middle ground, he should count the ground above it.
One should take a portion equal to whatever number is produced;
having taken it, one should apply it to the lower level from the surrounding ground.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāpārameśvara*:
"For all temples, however, the levels of the ground-floor (bhūmikā) are traditionally held to be uneven."
For those who have not yet entered the stages, the Great Gone One has taught thirteen;
having set aside the middle stage, one should count the higher stages.
For as many units as the number that arises, so many finger-breadths (aṅgula) should be taken from the upper level and caused to be placed upon the lower level.
"For the remaining fingers, there is an increase of half a finger-measure.
Thus, when the decrease and increase of all the stages (bhūmikās) have been revealed,
one should conceive of the stage as endowed with eight characteristics.
Having divided the height of the base into three parts, one should turn it upward;
or, the *īśa* (the lord/central part) should be fashioned with equal *sūras* and *kapotikās*.
With two parts, the *śikhara* (spire), together with its neck (*kaṇṭha*) and *malasāraka*, is formed.
The ground-levels of the peaks are described as being like outlines.
Likewise, Mallikā, Kośala, Pañcaśṛṅgalaka, Ṣaḍbindu, Maudara, Puṣkara, and Candraśālaka are to be drawn.
One should draw the design known as Ardhapuṣkara, complete with ears and a crest.
Having understood them thoroughly, one should not employ those that are pure or mixed.
The characteristics of the ground have been explained; now hear again concerning the pitchers.
One should draw the various components of the structure in the form of root-blossoms;
this is generally beneficial for all types of temples.
The specific characteristic is clearly stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"When the field is divided by the sun and moon, and divided crosswise by the Vedas..."
Having omitted the *rasa* (six) from the four corners, that *piṇḍī* (syllabic cluster) would be formed by the reversals;
O Śakra, having understood the remainder as emerging from the union, one should transpose it.

The entrance [should be adorned] with the arrows of contentment and fire; the movement [should be provided] by the fierce Pāragaṇas. In the fourth [section], one should create a central chariot-design rich in leaf-patterns;
the remainder should be arranged thus with twelve parts starting from the direction of the sun.
It has four doors and four nostrils, sixteen peaks, and twenty-four noses;
it possesses five archways with foundations numbering fifty-two.
"Kāma, arka, īśa, dik, ambhodhi, and yudhi-śṛṅgas in sequence;
above the vedī, together with one more, it shall be one hundred and a quarter. This is the meaning of this [verse]:

thus, in the five āghāṭas there are eight śṛṅgas, sixteen in the śukanāsikās, and one principal [śikhara]; thus combined, there would be one hundred and a quarter śikharas. The meaning is that there are one hundred and twenty-five śikharas.
Between the two pillars of the Vedas, the space is divided by two [lines];
there, the first stage (bhūmikā) should be made with twenty parts above that.
O Hari, the sixteen levels should be adorned with ornaments, arranged in sequence one by one from the base upward out of fear [of instability].
Above the tips of the śūkas, in the four directions, there should be the vowels, the apas, and the animals and so forth;
above the altar (vedikā), on the necks, they should be placed according to one-third of the Vedavyāsa.
O Hari, lions should be fashioned adorned with manes;
they should have fierce, distorted fangs and their tails placed upon their heads.
Complete in all their limbs and endowed with every beauty,
there are four figures in human form on the four sides above the altar.

Adorning the stage with the guardians of the directions, the lords of the asuras, the lords of the vidyās, the lords of the mṛts, the lords of the grahas, the singers, and the lords of the gaṇas and vidyās.
There would generally be a danger of the falling of the clusters of buds within the womb;
therefore, one should make two holes in the ground at each interval within the water.
Meru has been described according to its true nature; now hear about Mandara.
When the field is divided by eight and the Vedas (four), and marked across by the faces of Brahmā,
the corner-piṇḍīs are formed by the movement of the cords and the removal of the *nala* lines, consisting of three parts.
The descent and exit should be performed; one should remove [the excess] with the "corner-makers" (sarakoṇakara).
The central emergence should be made with the "world-suns" (bhuvanabhāskara) as the arms.
By this method, all the remaining parts of the structure are placed upon the arms;
and fourteen [parts] of the earth are joined with supports at the corners.
Even for one who possesses four *āghaṭakas*, there are one hundred and sixty-one [units] between the two buttocks, calculated by the elements (5), the Vedas (4), the fires (3), and the eyes (2).
The first eighteen are the ground, while the others are obtained by reducing [the total] by one at each step.
It also has four doors and four *śukanāsikās*;
there are twenty-three [units] in the first enclosure and twenty-one in the second.
In the third [section], there are nineteen; in the fourth, seventeen;
one is the primary awn, and there are sixteen at the tips of the awns.
O Lord of the Suras, this ninety-seventh Mandāravarta is beautiful in form and endowed with the previously mentioned ornaments.
When the field is divided by thirty-six and the horizontal is divided by four,
its emergence occurs in the middle region through eight parts:
first three horizontally from the center, then one, and likewise three at the end.
Having erased [the previous marks], one should exit from the Veda-line until reaching the corner.
Then, one should fashion the corner known as Kailāsa with four faces.
In this regard, there is a specific detail stated in the *Kālottara*: "The length and width should be thirty-six *gaja*s."
A son should cause a medium-sized chariot to be turned out with eight horses.
The *paṭṭikā* (fillet) is beneficial when measured by three, four, three, or four [units];

"When the field has been made square and divided into eighteen parts,
having assigned three regions for the corners, the binding of the corners is established by means of the three [sides]."

this is declared to be the Bhadra, considered suitable for all.
One should construct a four-gated structure with a continuous foundation that bestows all accomplishments;
likewise, the characteristics of hundreds of levels of the enclosure should be established.
O auspicious one, bestower of auspicious success, the celestial chariot (vimāna) has been forgotten;

599) "The younger brother, Bhadra, declared: 'By means of lotuses, Nalina shall become [the king];
his palace, constructed with a foundation of solid earth, shall be like a celestial chariot. Thus it is said.
From the four-sided [base], by means of the portion of the elements, through the rotation of the neck-sides,

Thus, the four types of resentment (*āghāta*) are indeed pride (*mānana*).

"A great celestial palace (mahāvimāna) must be constructed," thus [he said].
With four corners having the form of the Vedas and the Rāmas, they constructed the four gates;
in the hall, which measures one unit less than the tip of the parrot (the Śuka-śikhara), is the residence of Nāṭyeśa.
On the summit of the Bhūtāṅgabhakta [mountain], the first stage is established by the Purandaras;

In this regard, there is a specific detail in the *Kālottara*:

The fetus is four-footed, or else it moves on its wings.

It is covered with cloths (*paṭṭa*) and those [ornaments]; in the wheel-base (*cakraṇa*), it is joined with the *ārābāli*. Adorned with ornaments such as the *candraśālā* and the *śṛṅgas*, this [temple] is thus embellished.
Wherein the Siddhas and the god Śakra [dwell], and wherein the Moon himself attained perfection.
This same rule applies even to a field divided into shares of profit or to a house with partitioned walls;

half a part extends outward from that, and with three [parts], Indra forms the corner.
Adorned with ornaments like those of Śāla, he is the leader who perceives all distinctions;
he is endowed with qualities such as those of the Rudras, Yakṣas, and gods, which abound in playful diversion.
The Śrīvatsa, which increases joy, is produced by divine splendors for the Creator;
it occupies a fourth part in the field of Kṛta, and its wall is shaped like a boar. It is the fourteenth [mark].
All those [elements] are indeed [formed] by a quarter of the expansion of the *dhāman*;
its central womb has six corners, while the arrangement of pillars and so forth is on the exterior.
His hips and ears are entwined by serpents, and he possesses ten stages along with the crown-protrusion;
Viṣṇu is in his center, Śiva is on the right, and the Grandfather (Brahmā) is on the left.
Having established Lakṣmī upon his tail, this Garuḍa, the beloved of Hari,
stands with his beak raised high and his wings spread at the tips, indeed as a destroyer.
Because sixteen [units] are subtracted from the Nāga portion, there is an increase by the month;
through the prior giving of the Yugas, success is achieved at the top of the parrot on the eaves of Hari.
This [measurement] should be applied to manifest lingas, especially to those of Caṇḍikā and others;
its height is double its width, it is enclosed by a haṃsa-motif and other designs,

Likewise, in the Kālottara: "The *balabhī* (pavilion) should be made long, either double or triple [the width];
its length should be divided by five and measured by those parts."
The wall is one square (pāda); its door is made with two squares. The nose-projection (nāsā) extends out by one square, and it is two squares in width.
It should be made twice the height of the base, according to the elevation of the *balabhī*.
"One should cause the covering of the *bhairī* to revolve within it like a conch shell.

He who restrains his topknot with his feet, who is free from transformation, is dear to Śiva.
The meaning of this is as follows:

the temple known as Vedāśra is likewise square in shape; however, on the ground level (bhūtapradeśa), it is provided with features such as the plinth (khura), the dome (kumbha), and the frieze (paṭṭikā).
Above that, it is "unmodified," meaning it is devoid of elements such as the chariot-pavilion (rathaka) and so forth.

When the field has been made square, that which is half the length of the diagonal is called the eighth part. One should project the diagonal in the cardinal directions with a measurement equal to that;
when the lines have fallen [in place], the eight-cornered [mandala] is thus adorned here.
Having placed Caraka in the center of that, one should mark the middle from the eight [directions].
Having made that measurement on the exterior and doubled it from the thickness of the two-edged [blade],
that too should be known as bestowing prosperity, O Purandara, when used for ornaments and the like.
Square-shaped, possessing four auspicious features, with a central hall and three stories,
this palace made of wood is praised as the king of palaces;
yet, though equal to the king of palaces, it is Indra’s [palace] without its auspicious features.
Even when endowed with a silk-clothed mansion, he is proclaimed as the lord of the planets.
O Śakra, all divine abodes— except for the pavilions consisting of one or two stories— are especially [prohibited] for the Sun.
O Lord of the Gods, because it remains at half the distance from the neck and revolves therefrom, this circular vessel, richly adorned with beautiful ornaments, is known as the *kumbha*.
The bull-shaped [mandala] is joined at the front with a pointed tip and is square within;
it is circular on the outside and adorned with decorative bands (*paṭṭaka*).
The *gāvṛkṣa* is indeed circular; without the bull, it belongs to Rudra.
O Lord of the Gods, this temple has been described by you from its very beginning.
Through the mutual blending of these types, the fruit for the sacrificers is likewise blended.
Among these, light-structured palaces named after perfumes were described.
Below the four cubits is the palace named Kṣudra;
now I shall describe to you the arrangement of the spires.
When the height above the shanks is doubled and its width is divided into ten parts,
and the fourth part of that height is further divided into four;
The height of the ear is one *indu* (one-sixteenth), the thickness at its base is one *sāra* (one-eighth), and the elevation of the *kumbha* is one *pada* (one-fourth).
The neck measures six *vedas* (fourths) and three *tribhis* (thirds); the remainder is occupied by the *śikhara* and the *saṃvṛti*.
When the portion has been divided by the elemental parts both horizontally and vertically,
it may likewise become manifold through the distinction of the divisions of the portions.
Or, having made the cord fourfold horizontally, one should increase it, O Hari.
Regarding the bases of the *sāndhārika* [style], such as the *maurvī* and others, in due order,
there is the characteristic of being provided with a pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) in a place devoid of darkness;
the sanctuaries (*dhāma*), the inner sanctums (*garbha*), and their corners (*karṇa*) extend from the neck of the inner sanctum (*garbhakaṇṭha*) up to the tips of the *śuka* [pediments].
Having taken the thread from the lotus-born one— that is, from the central thread—
and having placed it on both sides, one should construct the pavilion in front.
The front portico at its front should have half the width of the temple.
For those [temples] whose spire (śikhara) is three times [the base], their pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) is three-quarters, one and a half, or two and a quarter [times the base];
or else, for those [others], it is one-third [of the height].
Above that, having divided [the remaining height] into three equal parts, one should allocate one part for the neck,
three-fourths for the head, and half of that (one-eighth) for the forehead.
The base should be shaped like a rounded pitcher (kumbha) with a foot-like projection; the remainder should be executed as previously described.
Above the neck, one should cause supports for the flagstaff to be made in the four directions.
The placement of all four types of pillars should be upon the altar;
for all pavilions, however, the height of the pinnacle extends to the end of the nose (the spire).
In its lap, it is adorned with *rauhaka* [ornaments],

and with four [faces] beginning with Tandinī, as well as with their heads.
When combined with the number of pillars, they each become a separate number.
Beginning from sixty-four [pillars], excluding two pillars,

Now the description of the doors is declared to be equal in the Sāktatantra;
it is incomparable, excluding the portion of modification, and its width exceeds that by eight parts.

Its height is double [the width], but the ground area is provided with pot-bands (*kumbha-paṭṭikā*) and other ornaments; above that, it is fashioned as a chariot and so forth, meaning it is constructed without any distortion.
When the field has been made square, having subtracted one-eighth of half the neck (kaṇṭha), one should project the neck of the directions onto the four-cornered [area] of that same measurement.
When the lines have been cast in the eight directions, adorning them with ears,

Having made that measurement the base, by doubling it and adding two corners,
that too is to be known as the *puraṃdara* [altar], which bestows prosperity and is adorned with ornaments and the like.
Quadrangular, possessing four auspicious features, and supported by three stories;

O Purandara, although it is equal to the king of planets, it is devoid of auspiciousness; yet, even if it is provided with a portico (paṭṭaśālā), it is proclaimed as the "king of planets. A [house] consisting of one or two stories that is devoid of a portico [is likewise so called].

Thus, it should be circular on the outside and adorned with bands;

O Lord of the Gods, this temple has been described by you from its very beginning.

Above that, having divided [the height] into three parts, one part is for the thighs (*rāma*),

The base should be like a pot with a rounded form; the remainder should be executed as previously described.
Above the neck, one should cause banners and supports to be made in the four directions.
The base for all four types of pillars should be situated upon the altar (vedi). For all pavilions (maṇṭapa), the height of the spire (śikhā) should extend to the end of the nose (nāsikā).
The pedestal (pīṭha) and its enclosure (varaṇa) should be constructed at the end of the krova and the eka-rohaka.
They are resplendent with six pillars, [adorned] with the *krāda* and other [deities], with the four means of accomplishment beginning with the *kumbha*,
and with their heads [crowned] by the four [goddesses] beginning with *Nṛtyā*.
Those [temples] possessing a number of pillars equal to the count of the constellations (twenty-seven) are designated as "useless" (vṛthā),

The twenty-seven pavilions, beginning with the Śrīvatsa and ending with the Sarutsūtra.

"And at the front of the door, one should fashion a half-moon and a pair of conch shells;

Thus it is said, and likewise in the *Kālottara*:

Having fashioned the pinnacle (*śikhara*) according to the Vedas, each quarter-part (*vedāṃśa*) should likewise be made according to the Vedas.
One should make the neck one part in height, and the shaft (sāra) two parts high;
