The *cūlaka* is like a water-jar; the *padma* and the *liṅgaka* are made of clay.

The winding [of the cord] is done with a fourfold thread, while for those of threefold [thickness], the winding is done with a threefold thread. For bodies that are one and a half times [the standard size], the winding is done with a threefold thread.
In the case of a double-threaded cord, there is a contraction of the doubled threads;
likewise, the turning of bodies endowed with beauty and fame is equal.
When the *skandha* is divided tenfold or alternatively fivefold,
one should indicate the width of the *skandha* by reducing it by two parts at each stage.
The width of the altar (vedī) is said to be either six or three [units];
one should divide that into nine parts, consisting of two parts, one part, or [the remaining] seven.
Likewise, with devotion, one should measure from the height of the *jaṅghā* up to the *kapota* and the *vedikā*,
omitting one part at a time from both the width and the height.
Alternatively, the daily consumption is determined by calculation through the method of proportion (cakrāṃśika);
the portion for the *tuṇḍikā* is likewise established as a twentieth part.

One must certainly not perform [this] with the tips of spikes, for it causes destruction by Yama. O Six-faced One, the *saṃvṛti* should be made with the tips of bamboo shoots, without a stalk; it is traditionally taught that it resembles the petal of a blue lotus at the nose.

The height of the neck (kaṇṭha) should be made from half of the remainder; the height of the capital (sāraka) is one-fifth [of the total]. The height of the finial (cūlikā) above the neck is two and a half parts.
And one-third of that should be forgotten, or it may be made according to the measurement of the linga;
likewise, two parts of it should be Viṣṇu and two [parts] Brahmā.
In the *sāraka* style, one-sixth should be reduced; it should have a height of one and a half parts.
Without employing the measurement-line (*lakṣmasūtra*), it should be established like a *liṅga*.
In the *valabhī* style, a lion should be fashioned, and likewise a bull for Śaṅkara.
The [deity] Śrīkarī should be fashioned, and likewise the [deity] Sūrya in due order;
with effort, they should be placed above the nose, somewhere upon the central axis (sāra).
The trident of Śaṅkara, as well as that of the Goddess especially, should be made according to the measurement of the central part in three portions.
One should assign the discus as the weapon for the right hands;
the *añjarī* is considered to have a width equal to one-eighth of the *bhūtādi*.
The meaning of this is as follows:
the characteristics of the door-crests and so forth are determined by dividing the area of the altar into five parts.
The width of the two door-panels (śākhā) is considered to be three-quarters of the door's width;
the upper and lower lintels (ūrdhvadumbara and adhodumbara) should be made half the width of the door, O Six-faced One.
To the north, on the branch of Dakṣa, there should be Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and the daughter of the Sun (Savitṛ);
and eight figures of me, created from lotuses, accompanied by jars of nectar;
three men adorned with ornaments should be fashioned there.
The Gandharvas hold lutes in their hands, and likewise, they bear the knowledge of garlands.
Having given pairs of cows, elephants, horses, as well as pairs of rams and so forth—
the best being nine branches, the middling seven branches,
and the lowest thirty-five branches— one should perform the offering that bestows prosperity.
One should fashion the door-chamber with leaf-patterns, svastikas, and creepers; the branches should be made wide, and the central part should have an abundance of finials.
Thus the *cāra* has been fully explained; now hear about the external *sandhāra*.
The largest is forty-nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and by decreasing one row at a time, there are seven [sizes].
Now, O Six-faced One, the width of the door should be made with sixty finger-breadths (60 aṅgulas), and its height should be double that; this is the measurement remembered by the wise.
The placement of the *udumbara* [vessels] above and below should be performed according to their own measurements.
Gaṇeśa, Śobhā, Bhāratī, and Lakṣmī stand upon the upper arms with udumbara fruits;
likewise, the eight planets are there, as well as the seven Mothers.
Likewise, Īśvara should be made here, together with Vālmīki and Vyāsa.
And at the front of the door, there should be a half-moon shaped ornament, measured according to the width of the door.
The central pillars (sāraka) should be made of *bhārata* wood, and those called *kapittha* should be six parts [in measurement].
At the midpoint of the door-jamb, a strong pillar made of *argaja* wood should be constructed.
One should not construct a door that is crooked, deficient, or lacking;
rather, two door-panels made of wood should be carefully fashioned so that they are firm.

Door-panels that are joined with wooden pegs (kūrcikā), those that are defective, or those that have risen up on their own should be avoided with effort; even in private houses, panels that are split into many pieces must be shunned.
In this context, the relevant details as declared by Piṅgala and others are recorded here.
The width of the two rafters should be one-fourth of the total width;
the thickness of the two branches should be determined as half of that.
And the *ūrdhvodumbaraka* should be made by omitting one-eighth of that [measurement];
it should be fashioned for each branch, being three parts less than the others.
O beloved, for the sake of a temple, a palace, or a hermitage, the branches should be uneven;
they are traditionally remembered as being nine at the end and never more than that.
At the fourth part of the height of the branches, the two door-keepers (pratīhārau) were formerly remembered;
likewise the river, the pair, the bearers of burdens,
and furthermore the Vidyādharas and again the Kinnaras.
The Bhāva mountain, as well as the Nāgas, are assigned to the nine branches;
the nine branches end with the Nāgas, while the ritual for the cow consists of seven branches.

Ending with the Vidyādharas, it is called Bhūta, concluding with the Triśikhā-mithuna; O Dear One, it should be a simple Pratihāra with a single branch, adorned with the remaining [ornaments]: the Vivabhaṅga, Śrīvatsa, Svastika, and a garland of skulls.
With conch shells, elephant-herds, and likewise with *śriyāvarta* motifs,
and with serpent-nooses rich in beauty, let there be an ornamentation of the branches as if they were [the limbs of] a tree;
and in the center of the *dumbara* beam, let there be the *śrīgaja* and likewise Hari.
The Yakṣiṇī, Śaṅkarā, and the eight Grahas are situated in a row.

Śrīkaṇṭha is intent on exposition, as is the auspicious Nāṭyeśvara; they are established in the [mudrās] beginning with Taraḥ-paṅ* and ending with Nava, beautified by their sequence. [The mandala] is new, constructed with ancient bricks or with similar stones.

If, through negligence, the door-bolt or the door-panel is not secured, one's own enjoyment [of the house] shall cease; furthermore, it is another view that one should rotate [the structure] by one-quarter of the width along the central axis. A *candraśālā* (moon-chamber) should be constructed for the sake of providing stability.
The palaces do not collapse even due to earthquakes or great winds;
therefore, a flagstaff-support must be constructed for the altar according to the measurement of the staff.
In this regard, the turning of the stainless essence is performed through action as previously described.
The field of the Āmala-sāra should be divided into seven parts;
upon it, the spires (śṛṅgas) are to be constructed with a height and width of three-fourths [of the unit].
The candrikā should be made with three [units], while the circle there should indeed be made with two.

On the third [section] above the *sāra*, the upward-facing rotation is prescribed; then, by means of that same measure, a perfectly even *amalasarikā* should be made. Thus, according to the statement in the *Mohaśūrottara*, the pitcher (*kalaśa*) is now described.
O Hari, one should increase the height of the *kalaśa* in a field divided into six parts;
its length should be equal to the length of the *liṅga*, and its width should be half of that.
It is said that the [other] dimensions are reduced by one-fourth, while the width is reduced by one-sixth.
The foot-molding (pādapaṭṭī) is prescribed to be made of one part less than the lāsa;
its height and width, O observer of noble vows, are each one-fourth of that [lāsa].
That molding is raised by one-quarter of a part and extends outward according to its beauty.
The Kumbhikā [turret] is raised to half a part by means of raw flesh portions.
The left and right elbows should be raised by one and a half units;
this should be done by means of the movement of the thread, and from there one should fashion the shoulder.
At the end of the second part of the *kūrpa*, the left [hand]...
[is placed]; by means of the circumambulation itself, O Śatakratu, the *apasavya* [position is formed] at the end of the second part.
The elevated neck is forgotten; thereafter, the throat-portion (sārakaṇṭha) should be one-sixteenth [of the total height].
The cheeks should be formed by the Brahma-faces, raised by two parts.
One should cause the pitcher to shine with the mantra alone, its lotus-like eyes forgotten by the rays [of light],
and adorn it with handfuls [of flowers] suspended from the strands of the qualities.
One should decorate the mouth of the jar with variegated *aśoka* sprouts or those produced from the *cūta* (mango) tree, according to one's ability and as they are available.

The form of the jar (kumbha) should be fashioned according to its specific characteristics; its features have been described as being slightly diminished. Now I shall describe the characteristics of the trident (triśūla).
O best of sons, the trident should measure twelve finger-breadths in the superior [size], sixteen with the Vedas (four) in the middling,
and sixteen with the tastes (six) and the moon (one) in the inferior.
By abandoning the six *aragolaka*s, two by two, from below;
at the tips of the corners, in the portions of *tuṣṭi* and *atuṣṭi*; and with the portions of the planets, there is a central trident (*madhyaśūla*).
The middle portion should have the wings and flanks forgotten [i.e., tapered], with a sharp point resulting from proportional calculation;
it should be broad at the base or according to the desired form.
If the long portion [of the thread] is forgotten due to the parts of the measures, by means of the parts of the flavors (rasas) through the winding of the thread;
having fixed the hand in the middle, it becomes a beautiful circular shape.
Or else—
Placing the hand outside the center and keeping it situated at the seventh part of the middle,
one should rotate it with the right hand for the sake of curing pain in the side.
Furthermore, O Hari, two lines resembling a half-moon should be drawn;
the [first] line is measured by a cord of one and a half *patra* units, and the [second] line is equal to one *bhāga*.
Or one should place the lines of the two horns by means of an outer circle;
and one should apply two lines situated in the middle to the middle circle.
One should rotate two lower parts, positioned with a slight interval between them,
according to the method of the half-moon, so that the movement occurs as intended.

The trident (triśūla) is described as being adorned with a *gaṇḍikā* at its base, while the *kuśa* [blade] below occupies one-fourth of that; the remainder is for the lines (*rekhā*), excluding the point of destruction.
One should place [the thread] upon the jar along the two side-dwelling-threads;
and that thread which is at the front and the back, joined with the central pin. Thus it is said.
Now, I shall speak briefly: if the *nirmita* and other [deities] constantly quarrel, they will desire the pitcher of a friend.
If the door of the *sakala* and *sākaya* deities is honored by the gods, then poverty will befall the performer and his kin.
Furthermore, one should indicate the fickleness of women from a wide doorway;
there will be great wealth for the sake of the door, and authority over women. If the door is situated on a pedestal in the middle, there will be the loss of wealth, grain, and sons.
When it is "barley-shaped" (yavamadhya), there will then be an increase in disease;
if, however, it is devoid of the thread (sūtra), O observer of good vows, the doors will stand [unopened].

There will be agitation for buffaloes and other such animals, and the destruction of those things that are pleasing; when the lord of the birth sign is of a different caste, he becomes the ender of one's lineage.

One should avoid an inauspicious site characterized by such features as: being surrounded by trees, having deep pits, being filled with tree roots, having four or three paths, peaks, and the like, or being enclosed by a peaked house, or any other such irregularities.
In the middle of that, the central thread should be moved so that it becomes aligned; one should lead the thread, or even half of the thread, toward the northern direction.
Within the womb is the syllable *vaṃ*, which is armor; from that, one should likewise lead [the breath] forth. Thus it is said.
In this context, the *vartanā* (the method of drawing) on the door-panels is described here incidentally:

one should divide the width of the panel (*vyāsa*) by twenty with devotion, and its thickness (*tad-sthaulya*) by fifteen. With six parts, there shall be the staff (*daṇḍa*), and it should be filled with leafy creepers (*patravalī*).
One part would be in darkness; then, having entered with five [fingers], it would be so.
The branch of form (rūpa-śākhā) that has emerged should be forgotten by means of the three elemental portions (bhūtāṃśa).
And darkness was introduced by one part, by the fiery portion;
and those rays which emerged were forgotten by the portion of the eyes.
The root branch should have five [sub-branches] inserted into four parts;
that which has three branches is known as the door, and now the five-branch [structure] is described.
The width should be thirty-two [parts], the thickness eighteen;
the staff and branches should be six parts, and the *andhārikā* is considered to be one part.
And having entered, she emerged from the Kalpa-branch by means of seven parts.

And that [mandala] has five wide entrances consisting of portions of darkness; it has five exits, and its pillars and branches are composed of the elements (bhūta-aṃśa). One should know that the blindfold (andhārikā) is formed by one [element], and it is entered by the elements.
The form emerged from the fourteenth part, and the five branches were clearly manifested.
Andhārikā is to be known as that which has been introduced with one part in four parts.
The two branches of the *marīci* (flame-ornament), having an extent equal to two parts, emerge from the fire-part;
the mouth-branch, measuring five parts, is inserted at the fourth part.
This door has five branches, and it is also said to have seven branches;
one should indeed divide the space of its mouth into eighteen parts according to its thickness.
The Andhārikā [digit] is considered to be the portion of the sap of the staff-branch (daṇḍaśākha) associated with the moon;
it enters for nine parts and then emerges for six parts.
The serpent-shaped railing is like a branch of the Naga-tree; it is forgotten by the ocean, yet each supporting pillar is established by six, while the branch of its form serves as the foundation.
Extended by five parts and emerging from one part of fire,
it should be known as supported by one part and entered by three parts.
The leaf-branch is known to extend out by one-fifth part like the ocean;
from there, the pillar-ocean should be made to extend out by fifteen parts.
Its width should likewise be known by means of the numbers ten, one, and four;
darkness (tamas) is known by three, two, and fire (three); and the mirage (marīcikā) by three and two.
The root-branches are pervaded by three, while five parts are forgotten.
This [mandala] is to be known as having seven branches; now it is described as having nine branches:
when the thickness of the face is divided into three parts and then further divided by eleven (rudra).
With fifty [units] there is the *vāsa* in the staff (*daṇḍa*); with one hundred arrows (*śara*) there is the branch (*śākhā*).
With one [unit] it is known as the *andhārikā*, and when it has entered, it is called *rucyate*.
O Brahmin, one part is to be known as the *andhārikā* which has entered; then, with seven parts, it has emerged. The portion called the pillar (*stambha*) was forgotten by the Sage.
Darkness is described as before; that which is called the lotus-fiber is described as before;
and from that darkness, as previously stated, the manifestation of form has emerged.
It is spread out over four parts; darkness is described as before. The leaf and the branch are as before, and the Andhārikā is considered to be likewise.
The element called form (rūpa) emerged from the portion of taste (rasa), diminished by five parts;
from that, darkness (tamas) emerged as four parts, diminished by the ocean of the branches of form (rūpa).
She emerged from the two gates of the Tamomara and was likewise forgotten.
Then, the branch and the leaf enter through the two [gates] by those who have forgotten the oceans;
a wise man should fashion this nine-branched door.
One should adjust the proportions to be less or more according to the requirements of the artisan's work;
all that has been declared in the scriptures of Viśvakarman and others is known by me,
and it is now written down for the present purpose as it is set forth in the *Kālottara*.
The sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) should be constructed outside, in accordance with the Mūlāyana tradition;
one should fashion a flagstaff marked with a trident and the bull-emblem,
and it should be made to encircle the spire at one-fourth of its height.
And it is measured by half a laya, a third part, and a quarter;
then, according to the divisions of the smallest and so forth, the temples of the deities [are constructed].
O Six-faced One, they must be constructed facing toward the temple,
starting from five and extending as one desires up to a hundred.
The arrangement of the assembly hall (*gaṇāyatana*) is conceived in the form of a main temple (*mūlaprāsāda*).
Listen briefly to [the description of] the pavilions (*maṇṭapa*) at the front of the temple.
By means of a four-gated temple, four pavilions (maṇḍapas) are prescribed;
however, at a single-gated temple, only one pavilion should be constructed.
Having placed the *garbha* (central core) within the two wings, it is beneficial for a four-faced temple;
thus, with great care, one should construct four porticoes (*mukhamanṭapa*).
One may fashion them from the *garbha*, from the wall, or from the entire well-constructed structure.
Having combined the total length of both wings, one should determine the overall length;
a pavilion with a width reduced by one-thirtieth of that length is beneficial.
The arrangement for a single-faced [pavilion] and also for a three-faced one is as previously described.
The designations and distinctions of the pillars of the pavilions are now declared:
Hara, Śiva, Nanda, Dharmadeva, Śikhī, and Īśa.
The nine types of pavilions (maṇḍapas) are proclaimed as Priya and Mahāpriya;
they should be employed for the smallest [shrines], increasing up to twelve [pillars].
Furthermore, I shall describe the auspicious ones beginning with Vasunemi in the middle [cycle]:
Sunandana, Nandana, Variṣṭha, Varada, Viśāla, Suśīla, Śrutīśa, Hara, and Bhadraka.
By doubling that twice, one is considered a master of the four Vedas among those of middling capacity;
furthermore, O Vasudeva, I shall now describe [the requirements] for those of superior capacity.
Jaya and Jayabhadra, Buddhi and likewise Buddhidhara;
Ānanda and Nandana, as well as Puṣpabhadraka and Puṣpaka.
And [the pavilion] is called Bhadra; by increasing [the measurements] up to sixty-four,
there are eight pillars in the ten directions, and the maṇḍapas have six pillars.
Two pillars and a kumārikā should be placed, established by Śukanāsa. Thus it is said.
And as it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Therefore, the classification of the pavilions (*maṇṭapa*) is described by their names:
Puṣpaka, Puṣpabhadra, Puṣpānanta, and Kuśasyasa."
Therefore, the one named Saṃkīrṇaka is Jayabhadra, which brings victory;
Śrīvatsa is the seed-syllable (bīja) of the two, and Saṃkīrṇa is the neck of the sacrificial ladle (śruk).
Yajñabhadra, Viśāla, Suśīla, Kramardaka,
Bhāva, Candana, Vṛddhi, and likewise Māṇibhadraka.
Sugrīva, Harṣa, Karṇikāra, Padadvaka, Siṃha, Vāmabhadra, and Susūtra are thus proclaimed.
Now, the division known as the twenty-seven-fold is being described.
With sixty-four pillars, there is the Puṣpadṛkarāmā; with sixty-two pillars, it becomes the Yugma.
That is declared to be the Mandaraga, established according to the [rules of] prosody.
O God, that which is joined with sixty pillars is proclaimed as Puṣpānanda;
it is also called Kailāsaka, and its form is described according to that [same] pattern.
Kuśalya is celebrated as having one hundred and eight pillars.
That [temple] for an elephant is also quadrangular and possesses those same characteristics;
it is considered to be filled with wisdom when it has three hundred pillars.
The Sarvatobhadraka is likewise situated as the Sarvatobhadra;
Jayabhadra is proclaimed to consist of fifty-four pillars.
That [hall] was also followed by the Vimāna style, and its floor was like that of the Pināka;
it was celebrated as being joined with fifty-two [pillars], and that floor was also followed by the Jayāvananda style. The one renowned by the name Śrīvatsa was joined with fifty pillars.
He too, following Nandivṛddha, remained established in the increase of joy.
With forty-eight [verses], the one named Vijaya is proclaimed;
that king’s follower, the twice-born, is also established like the king of the twice-born.
With forty-six [verses], he is celebrated by the name Vāstu.

That [deity] who has attained grace through the lotus remains in the form of a lotus; he is renowned by the name *Asaṃkīrṇa*, famous for his forty [faces]. He, too, having sixteen faces as his attendants, is remembered as the pure one with six faces.
But the pavilion, which maintains the sacred tradition, consists of forty-two yāmas.
That [altar] also, following the eight-sided form, should be eight-sided in appearance;
with forty pillars, it is proclaimed as the Yajñabhadra.
The king of houses, though being a householder,
is established in that form with thirty-six pillars, known by the name Suśīla.
That [mountain] also, following the half-section, is situated like a half-section;
it is celebrated as Nandana, supported by thirty pillars.
In front of the Vardhamāna [stūpa], that one also stands like a Vardhamāna;
Sugrīva, however, is proclaimed to have twenty-eight pillars.
He too stood upon the tip of the bull, in the very form and nature of a bull.
The one renowned by the name Harṣa stands before Nṛsiṃha with twenty-two pillars, established in that very form;
Karṇikāra, moreover, stands before Bhāsa with twenty pillars.
That pavilion should be constructed in the form of a swan and be beautiful;
it should consist of eighteen cubits of pillars and measure two paces [in width]. It should also be followed by lotuses, arranged symmetrically from the lotuses themselves.
O Goddess, with sixteen pillars, the pavilion known as Haṃsa was brought forth; that too, accompanied by various Śrīs, stood firm under the name Nāga.
The Bhadra is proclaimed as being dark-colored with pillars numbering nine (Indra);
it stands like a dog or a wolf positioned in front of a bull.
O Goddess, it is proclaimed that [the mandala] with twelve pillars is called Susūtra;
it should also be made with its front side measuring four [units], and it should be square-shaped.
In this context, as a related point, the characteristics of the *stambha* (pillar) beginning with *rūcaka* are described.
As stated in the *Kāmika-saṃhitā* and other texts:
"A *rūcaka* pillar should be made with four corners, and that known as *vajra* should have eight corners."
A sixteen-sided [vajra] should be a vajra, while a thirty-two-sided one is called a *pralīnaka*.
If the first two feet are maṇḍana and the last two are vṛtta, it is known as mamatha.
The sun [mandala] measures sixteen and twenty finger-breadths starting from the smallest;
their width shall be as follows, while their height is equal to the door.

In some traditions, the height of the pillar is considered to be three-quarters of the width of the base; the wise should construct the pillar with a square top and *rucikās* (ornamental projections) equal to it. The third part [of the pillar] is proclaimed to be square, serving as the "thunderbolt-maker" (*vajrakāra*).
The second is said to be double [the first], and the third is sixteen-sided;
then follow the eight-sided, the sixteen-sided, and the circular [mandalas] in sequence.
The parts of the double-vajra [pedestal] are three from the trident;
the third part of the dissolved [portion] is proclaimed as the thirty-two-sided [octagonal] section.
Then, increased by half a part, the kalaśa is said to be half a part.
Endowed with four corners, the third [mandala] is circular;
it is further adorned with four downward-facing corners.
But for the *mandhana* [drum], all parts are considered to have sixty-four sides;
the *manmatha* is an even meter (*samavṛtta*), and its head is said to be like a jar (*kumbha*).
The height of the pillar and so forth should be determined in sequence by adding one-sixteenth part to the *vasu* (eight) [units], starting from the smallest size;
the capital (*śiras*) should be adorned with a pitcher (*kumbha*), a necklace (*hāra*), and a supporting beam (*vāhaka*).
The artisan should execute it with beauty according to his own craft and intelligence.
In some Āgamas, the pavilion (maṇṭapa) is said to be equal to the hall (dhāman), half its size, one-quarter less, double, or even twice that; furthermore,
in the smallest [structure], there should be four pillars and the door-decorations should be of the kumārikā type.
And there are eight pillars in the middle, arranged in two rows;
likewise, twelve young maidens are said to be situated at the corners.
In the middle, however, two *kumārikā* pillars should be joined against each wall;
thus, as previously stated, there are eight pillars situated in the center.
"The charming young maidens, stationed in two rows and leaning against the wall,
are traditionally said to be sixteen in number, or else according to the weight [of the offering].
Thus has this section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) been proclaimed by the most excellent gurus as consisting of fifteen [chapters].
Having carefully deliberated, it should be executed by artisans who are most proficient in the technical scriptures.
Thus ends the procedure for the characteristics of the temple in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
And it is written that this *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) is fivefold for Śiva;
it is twofold for an image and likewise fivefold for temples.
Thus it has been said: "Pratiṣṭhāna, likewise sthāpana, and avya;
the fourth is called āsthāpana, and after that utthāpana."
Thus, the determination of that consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is declared to be fivefold.
There, having first placed the *liṅga* within the *brahmaśilā*,
it should be an unmanifest-faced (*avyaktamukha*) *liṅga*; then, having performed the construction of the pedestal (*pīṭhabandha*),
one should attain a pure conjunction with the *piṇḍikā*.
That which is performed is the *pratiṣṭhā*; furthermore, it is called *sthāpana*.
A linga made of the jewels of the elements, or one made of Bāṇa or Rauha;
having divided that linga into five parts and further subdivided the abode into three.
Having understood the relative strength or weakness of two parts or even one, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is established in the center; this is declared to be the "establishment" (sthāpana).
In the case of a linga that is a single solid mass, such as one made of crystal and the like,
where the consecration is performed by means of the mind, that is called "sthāpana" (installation).
This applies whether the linga is four cubits in height or even a manifest linga (*vyaktaliṅga*).
Having prepared the pedestal together with its base (piṇḍikā) to be situated in the center of the temple,
the consecration performed therein is called installation (sthāpana).
Having carefully extracted that which is defective from a displaced [liṅga] and having installed another in its place, that is called "re-establishment" (utthāpana).
Thus, the characteristics of the Śiva-liṅga have been declared by the wise to be fivefold;
those of the forms beginning with Rudra are twofold, according to whether they are installed or raised up.
The *āsana* (seat) and *āvapana* (receptacle) are the most excellent for all *liṅgas*, bringing about auspiciousness;
for other [types of *liṅgas*], due to the proximity of time and the possibility of deficiency at the two tips, they are not so.
The installation of the Dhamni-pāda, the Śilā-nyāsa, the Dvāra-hṛt-kumbha, the Cūlikā,
and the Dhvaja-roha are renowned as the fivefold types of Pratiṣṭhā.
Or, on a level surface or in a field that has been dug and refilled to three-quarters of its depth,
having worshipped and offered libations there according to the prescribed rite.
The laying of the foundation stones should be performed, and those stones should be placed according to the scriptures.
627) In a stone temple, stones measuring one cubit on all sides are recommended;
in some cases, they may be one cubit in length, with a width and height of half that measure.
Half of that [measure] is recommended for bricks used in a temple made of brick.
The nine [mandalas] are auspicious, square in shape, and marked in their centers with the vajra and other symbols;
they are Nanda, [Nandottarā], Jayā, Pūrṇā, Ajitā, and Parājitā.
Vijayā, Maṭhalā, and Dharaṇī as the ninth;
the jars should be made of gold or silver, or in its absence, of copper.
For a cubit [of length], eight finger-breadths are recommended, with a weight of fifteen palas;
for each subsequent cubit, there is an increase of one finger-breadth and five palas.
They are endowed with various artistic designs and marked with the weapons of the world-protectors.
Subhadra, Vibhadra, Sunanda, Puṣpanandana, Jaya, Vijaya, Kumbha, Pūrṇa, and likewise Uttara.
Thus, the nine pitchers are proclaimed; likewise, when there are nine stones, they are Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā—these being the five stones.
Of these, there are Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, and likewise Makara.
There should be jars representing the ocean, all marked with lotuses;
jars filled with red minerals, medicinal herbs, pits, honey, and clarified butter;
or, in the middle of the stone slabs, jars that are capable and well-arranged.
Having constructed the pavilion and other structures according to the procedure to be described,
one should worship the archways, the gates, the guardians of the directions, the water-jars, the weapons, and so forth.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the ritual rules, including the satiation and kindling of the mantra,
and having ensured the perfection of place, time, and other necessary factors, the preceptor (deśika) proceeds.
For the sake of the worshiper’s attainment of the goal, the priests (mūrtipās) should establish the pavilion for the ritual site;
there, one should arrange the stone slabs and water-pots starting from the middle and proceeding toward the east and other directions.
Then the Guru should place it upon a bed of kuśa grass;
having scraped it with kuśa grass and then with a ritual blade, he should worship it by name, beginning with the mantra "dhruva."
Having adorned [the image] with the five products of the cow, decoctions, and so forth, as well as earth, fragrant water, and scents, one should then wrap it in a red cloth.

Having led the sacrifice around clockwise to the accompaniment of the auspicious sounds of musical instruments, and having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite, one should place it facing the west.

In the pavilion and on the altar, one should sequentially assign the principles (tattvas), beginning with Intellect (buddhi) and ending with Earth (nidharā), to those [locations] such as the Kulika and others.
Having placed the Lords of the Principles (tattveśas) in the heart with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should then deposit the three principles there:

the principle of Intellect (*buddhi*), the principle of Ego (*ahaṃkṛti*), and within those, the Principle of Śiva along with Śaṅkara; and one should deposit the Principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*) and Viṣṇu upon the eleven sense organs.

He should again place Brahmā, the Self-principle (ātmatattva), and the subtle elements (tanmātras) therein; he should then place the deities of each principle (*tattva*) and the [deities of] knowledge in their proper order.
There, one should worship five or eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas);
then, one should place the seed-syllable of Māyā, ending with Śakti, at a distance upon the [five] fingers of the right hand.
And having prepared a triple offering with treatises that possess the pride of worldly prosperity.
Then, having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and performed the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rule,
one should perform that which will be described regarding each of the three portions.
In the central jewel-pot shall be Ananta, the leader of the nāgas;
and the eight pots beginning with Subhadra are worshipped by the guardians of the world.
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the jar spoken of as the Lord of Ananta; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the auspicious jar (subhadrakalaśa) as the Lord of I [the Earth]," and so forth are the mantras.

Having offered a hundred, a thousand, or half that number of oblations according to one's capacity, one should conclude the rite after offering incense, lamps, and other food offerings upon the ground of the temple.

Having fully worshipped the Vāstu deities, offered oblations, and presented the *digbali* offerings, the sequence for the Vāstu-pūjā mantras is obtained as follows: In the sixty-four squares divided by eight times eight, [the following are] the abodes of the gods: — *Oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*, in the central four squares; — *Oṃ hāṃ marīcaye namaḥ*, in the six eastern squares; — *Oṃ hāṃ ādityāya namaḥ*, likewise in the south; — *Oṃ hāṃ mitrāya namaḥ*, likewise in the west; — *Oṃ hāṃ dahrādharāya namaḥ*, likewise in the north; — *Oṃ hāṃ āpāya namaḥ*; — *Oṃ hāṃ āpavatsāya namaḥ*, in each square in the northeast corner.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Savitṛ. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Savitrāya. Likewise, in the southwest corner (Nirṛti): Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudradāsa. Likewise, in the northwest corner. Thus, there are thirteen deities in the middle enclosure (*madhyāvaraṇa*). Then, in the second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*), in the eastern position of the northeast corner: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśāna; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahendra.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ravi; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Parjanya; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yantṛ; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahendra; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ravi; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Satya; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Āpa. Then, in the middle of the southeast corner: oṃ, obeisance to Antarikṣa. Then, in the space to the south of that: oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vahni; then, oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Pūṣan.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vitatha; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gṛhakṣaya; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yama; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gandharva; oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Bhṛṅga—at the object in the southwest (nairṛta). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mṛga; then at the object in the west: oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Pitṛ; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dauvārika; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sugrīva; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Puṣpadanta; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vratasa; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Asura.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śeṣa; then, at the location of wind, Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Roga; at the northern location, Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu; and then, Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nāga.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mukhya; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhallāṭa; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Soma; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ṛgi; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Aditi. Then, in the northeast corner (īśānakoṇa), [obeisance] to Padārtha. Thus, there are thirty-two deities in the second enclosure (dvitīyāvaraṇa). Then, outside of that, in the four directions starting from the east: oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Skanda; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Asyama; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jambhaka; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Piṅgalapiñchaka. Then...
In the corners starting from Īśāna: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Carakī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vidyā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Pūtanā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Pāparākṣasī.
Having thus sprinkled [the area] according to rule with cow-dung water, one should perform the *bhūta-śuddhi* (purification of the elements).
When the auspicious lagna has arrived, the learned priest, accompanied by Vedic recitations and other auspicious rites,
should place the jars upon the supporting powers (ādhāra-śaktis) with their respective mantras.

The *dhāraṇī* should be placed in the center; the remaining [mantras] are based on the Dharma and so forth, as appropriate. Alternatively, one should superimpose them according to the method taught by the venerable Somaśambhu.
One should place the Śakti in the central pit, and the final Kumbha with Ananta;
upon this Kumbha, one should place the stone of the earth (Dharaṇī) by means of the root-mantra mounted on the letter *la*.
Having installed the mantras of the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the eight auspicious directions starting from the east, within their respective pits where the Śaktis have been placed,
one should then sequentially install the stones known as Nandā and the others upon them.
The installation of the image should be performed so that it may be situated within the devotion of those who possess it.
The eight [deities] beginning with Āsudharma arise from the division of corner to corner;
among Subhadrā and the others, the four beginning with Nandā reside in the corners starting with the southeast (Agni).
One should place Ajitā and the others in the east and other directions, or alternatively, one may assign them to Jayā and the others.
Thus, when the śāla tree has nine stone sections and five [sections],
one should place the eastern stone in the center and then those stones extracted from the ocean-vases.
And having placed Nandā and the others in the lotuses and so forth, in the corners starting from the southeast in due order—
or alternatively, having placed four [deities] in the centerless [lotuses] starting from the Svayambhū [lotus].
Having performed their ablutions in divine forms, the presiding deities of the stones remained in the temple with joyful minds for as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist.
"Remaining here, may you always respectfully bring about the fulfillment of all goals.
Having thus informed them, one should worship Brahmā above the heads of them all.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the all-pervading Śiva, offered oblations, and thoroughly restrained [the senses],
the wise one should mentally contemplate the celestial palace (vyomaprāsāda) therein;
he should then meditate upon the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), beginning with Śiva and ending with primordial nature (prakṛti).
O Lord, may the completion of this palace be immediate and free from obstacles;
may there always be the attainment of long life, health, and prosperity for the patron.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra, as well as the Pāśupata caru,
and having especially given the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should cast the bali offering toward those who hate poison.
An image made of stone is praised over one made of wood; one made of metal is beneficial over one made of stone;
one made of gems is praised over one made of metal; and one made of precious jewels is beneficial over one made of gems.
Having understood this, one should diligently remove a worn-out image and install a new one.
Just as one might extract a gem that has lost its luster after it has been touched by fire,
so too is a Linga that has been served by dogs and other such beings, and left unworshipped for a long time.

Having extracted that which is deficient in ritual procedure, and especially that which contains an embryo; likewise, one should extract that which is slightly crooked, unworthy, or lacking in measurement.
The Pāśupata [system] established by the Śaivas is to be worshipped even by those who follow the Bhautika and Aindrika [schools],
but it should always be avoided when one is established in the Somasiddhānta.
Likewise, having approached the time [of death], and by those established in the fourth stage of life (śramaṇa)—by these, the Liṅga has been established; one should neither worship nor salute it.
Having removed [the previous image] and established another that possesses its qualities— or whatever else [is suitable]—
the Guru, having consecrated that very [new image] with mantras, should install it once again.
That linga which is defiled by faults is considered the abode of the elements (*bhūtālaya*).
Depending upon it, there arise the great elements, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas,
vetālas, kṣetrapālas, fevers, bhasmārakas, and so forth.
Famine, difficult-to-conquer epidemics, bad dreams, and ill omens;
suffering for the subjects, suffering for the fetus, and suffering for the king [occur] during the Dvika and other such periods.
In that region, fear arises from thunderclaps, serpents, and other such dangers;
there is also fear of foreign kingdoms. Maheśvara is the one who restores what is decayed. The houses of Maheśvara there collapse on all sides.

If there is a fall of meteors or a thunderous crash (*nirghāta*) during that time, a great conflict will arise for one who is deprived of his windows; cattle-plague and human-mortality will occur among those [who are] unprotected.
Indeed, other such evils as these arise;
therefore, with every effort, one should never disturb that which is well-established.
One should never hold onto what has arisen; having recognized it again and again, one should completely uproot it.
I shall now declare its extraction as it was spoken in former times:
one should first worship the teachers with milk-rice and clarified butter.
Gold, jewels, and so forth, as well as vehicles and other such items, should be given to them.
O Lord, one should worship the water-pot (kalaśa) situated on the right side of the pavilion (maṇṭapa) as previously described.
Then, the worship of Śiva on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be performed as before.
Having performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule, one should cast the outer and inner offerings; then,
having bathed the worn-out [image] with the Astra-mantra and having released it with a sincere heart.
Having worshipped the *liṅga* and offered libations endowed with the three principles (*tritatva*) and so forth,
one should offer a thousand oblations (*āhuti*) for each portion with the *asta-mantra*,
and while touching the portion with *kuśa* grass, one should likewise mutter the *śastra-mantra*.
O son of Kṛttikā, having performed the recitation (japa) five hundred or one hundred and fifty times,
and having then offered the *viloma-arghya*, one should dismiss the image and the guardians of the image.
Just as [the offering] is beneficial for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra according to their respective functions,
so too is it beneficial for the pedestal, the stone slab, and the front of the wooden structure.
In the Cūlaka-prāsāda, the dismissal (*visarjana*) should indeed be performed;
for by means of the *praṇava* alone, there is the dismissal of the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Indeed, one should effect the dismissal of all this through the *praṇava* alone.

One should avoid Śīla, who is the Lord of the forms of the three principles (tritatva) and is auspicious; likewise, one should avoid the god Caṇḍeśvara, who is both manifest and unmanifest and the restrainer.
Having extracted [the victim] by means of a bond consisting of gold and iron, as well as one that has entered the vital channels,
and by means of the bonds of the sacrificial fire-offerings (homapāśa), one should lead him outside.
The sacrificial ground should be prepared by means of artistic skills, and one should subsequently place it upon the chariot.
Having cast a stone or a wooden vessel into the water, one should burn it;
likewise, one may cast an iron deposit into the water or dissolve it again.
One should also cast objects made of gems, jewels, and earth into the water.
And the casting [of the offering] into the water shall burn away the bonds in the fire of Śiva.
Having purified those qualities up to the limit of their establishment,
one should extract twice as many and then join other [qualities] once again.
One should extract that linga which is twice the size of the original linga;
likewise, if the pedestal is devoid of qualities, one should discard that pedestal as well.
The same rule should apply to the gate-towers, and likewise to the pinnacle on the palace;
one should indeed avoid doubling [the dimensions] there, but rather preserve the structural integrity.
It must be worshipped with great effort, otherwise by means of the central guardian deity (Vāstu).
"O son, for those who desire to establish [the image] again after it has fallen, one attains supreme sovereignty by moving the worn-out [image].
Thus is written the restoration of the worn-out [image], as stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*."
Once the consecrated [image] has decayed, one should not perform [the rite] again;
therefore, the wise man should carefully remove the decayed image and install a new one endowed with excellent qualities.
Worn out and bringing about great existence, assuming an exceedingly cruel form,
it constantly inflicts manifold harm upon the kingdom and the king.
Then, seeing that the linga was devoid of the deity and stripped of its qualities, those gods [beheld] the defective linga.
Relying upon those who are victorious, they produce great fear;
one should discard what is deficient, worn out, made, burnt, or gross, as well as pride and the like.
A linga that is devoid of its characteristic marks, has a broken half of its womb, is cracked, shattered, or pierced;
likewise one that is rubbed away by winds, or where the pedestal and other parts have fallen away;
as well as one that is loose, moved from its place, or has fallen—such a linga should be removed.
If these [sites]— namely, one that is level, uneven, low-lying, or confused in its orientation, as well as one that is elevated—
are not of the prescribed dimensions, they should be established right there.
Having abandoned the application of stones, he possesses the characteristic of being free from wounds;
he may extract what is stuck, but never for the purpose of implanting it.
A worn-out [liṅga], when worshipped, destroys [the worshipper], and if not worshipped, it utterly annihilates him;
therefore, one should have that liṅga removed according to the scriptures and in accordance with the prescribed rites.
A *liṅga* that has been removed without the prescribed ritual by preceptors ignorant of the scriptures truly brings ruin from kingdom to king; one should therefore avoid such a thing.
If the *liṅga* is extracted according to the prescribed rite by preceptors who have fallen from their commitments (*samaya*),
then through that specific fault, there shall be either victory or destruction.
To the right, in a portion of the pavilion, there should be one door with a single archway;
here, the worship of the door and so forth is performed, while the worship of Śiva takes place upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the kindling (*dīpana*) of the mantras as before,
O best of the twice-born, having offered [the oblation] to Śiva and the Lingins, and to Viṣṇu and the others,
and having given the *bali* offering to the spirits (*bhūta*s) and so forth, one should perform the rite for peace (*śāntika*) in the center of the Śiva[-liṅga].
Having prepared [the offering] with milk, clarified butter, honey, and dūrvā grass along with well-kindled fuel-sticks,
one should go to the vicinity of the liṅga, bathe it with the mantra, and worship it accordingly.
*Oṃ vyāpakeśvarāya*, ending with *namaḥ*, is the root mantra. *Oṃ vyāpaka hṛdayāya*, ending with *namaḥ*, is known as the heart mantra (*hṛdaya*).
In this same manner, one should assign the *jvālinī*, the armor (*varma*), and the eyes (*netra*) in their proper sequence.
p.
637) One should worship the *liṅga* and the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) upon a seat of stars;
there, while pronouncing the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should cause the disciple to hear the supreme reality (*tattva*).
A certain being here, some horse, remains resorting to a linga;
having fashioned the linga within the mechanisms, it moves through the threads by the command of Śiva.
Having spoken thus and having offered the oblation with the Śivāstra mantra, he should dismiss the Ācārya.
Then, with the Pāśupatāstra mantra, he should perform the distribution of portions according to his own devotion.
Having touched [the site] with the roots of darbha grass and other materials, one should recite the Astra-mantra twenty-one times.
Having offered the *arghya* with the face turned away, one should dismiss the *tatvapa*s;
likewise, in the case of a transgression, one should dismiss the *pīṭhamantra*s and the mantras of the three portions.

One should diligently dig up the Lord, together with Śiva and his limbs, along with the three-fold path, the lord of the path, and the path itself, using one’s own golden spade and the weapon-mantra; having bound him with the noose of *kāñcana* and the rope of strength.

The preceptor should diligently extract the linga, the pedestal, and the image of Śivā from the temple of Śiva’s mantra, whether they are situated together as a pair or as a single unit; he should cause the people to cast them away and threaten them.
Having again offered oblations for nourishment and for the propitiation of the lords of the directions,
one should offer one hundred oblations each for the purification of the site of the temple and for the removal of obstacles.
One should employ [the mantras] ending with the Mahāpāśupata for protection;
one should not install another *pāśa* or *liṅga*, except for our own.
The *liṅga* endowed with the previous measure, having been consecrated in that form, should then be installed in its respective place and always worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
O Goddess, that which was established by the gods and sages who know the truth—
whether it be broken or decayed— one should not move it even according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform the restoration of the decayed [temple] only according to the prescribed rite.
One should join the mantras thirty-three times in a mirror or in something very pure.
Furthermore, one should subsequently begin so that it may take on its former form;
when completed, the application of the mantra and the consecration are as previously described.
One should make the *vākṣa* and the *yāma* out of brick, and one should take eight stones;
with materials that are inferior or superior, one should fashion that auspicious [image] consisting of those very substances.
In whatever manner the site is situated— whether long or of equal extent—
one should construct the wall right there, avoiding both reduction and increase.
If it is broken, death will occur; if it grows, there will be loss of wealth. Therefore, with every effort, one should cause neither its diminution nor its growth.
Having given the teacher a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of garments, gold, and other gifts, he should satisfy him;
he should say the words "Forgive me," and the teacher should then say "May there be auspiciousness."
Thus, by resorting to the *liṅga* endowed with ritual action,
the practitioner attains the perfection of equanimity and liberation, which is the ultimate goal of liberation;
just as water on a lotus leaf is extremely flickering when stirred by the wind.
O Śakra, the life of living beings is as fickle as that;
youth is unstable, and wealth is likewise unstable.
O son, this lineage beginning with your own sons and grandsons is unstable, like the fleeting beauty of a plantain tree.
Therefore, having abandoned sons, wives, friends, companions, wealth,
and the nets of delusion, one should undertake the adoption of the ascetic marks.
Whether on Mount Kālāñjara, Mahendra, Sahya, or Malaya;
or on the banks of the Gaṅgā, at the ocean, or on the shores of the rivers of Śrīśaila— provided it is auspicious, endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits, and strewn with earth and kuśa grass.
On an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, in a favorable yoga, and endowed with a favorable karaṇa.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods, one should fashion a liṅga made of gold,
which is always most excellent and [honored] by the gods.
One should resort to a sacred site established by sages in the past and endowed with all auspicious characteristics, or one that has been personally prepared by oneself.

The practitioner shall always conquer by means of Gaurī, Heramba, Durgā, and the other Lords of the Field (Kṣetrapālas) stationed within the womb, [and] by that which is above, completely surrounding the liṅga.

O Hari, O performer of a hundred sacrifices, the two excellent Liṅgas facing east and west are praised for the sake of spiritual perfection; likewise, those facing south and north are recommended for the attainment of success. One should accept a Liṅga that is desired for one's own possession.
The practitioner of mantra should worship constantly, having realized that the body is impermanent.
Thus concludes the procedure for the restoration of dilapidated [shrines] in the *Śrīmajjñānaratnāvalī*.
Salutation to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
The installation of the *liṅga*, the temple, and so forth has been declared in eight ways, as well as in five ways;
the installation of this *liṅga* is also written down here, as stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*.
And the monastery is situated outside on the southern side of the lingas, because you,
O Śiva-blessed one, wish to dwell in the southern direction.

Having instructed that one should cause the palace, the extent of the sūtra, its measurement, the terrace outside, and the enclosure wall to be constructed, he then [instructed] the building of the dwellings for those in the stages of life (āśramins).
Having abandoned that which is equal to the monastery, one should place a lion on the south;
a bull as the *arghya* [offering] on the north, and an elephant situated to the east of the banner.
Or rather, it should be made extensive according to the desire of the builder.
Divided by four-sided arrows, they fall from there, leaving the center behind.

The placement of the planets may be done according to one's own preference; the entry and exit should be in the north. One may construct a long hall with one, two, or three stories as is convenient, and one should arrange the placement for the vow according to the specific requirements.
The previously mentioned interval is to be established, as well as its meaning exactly as it is.
Three small cells should be constructed here, while the *paṭṭsālā* [is to be] ... [as follows].
First, the ground was designated; [then] a small hut was built, well-proportioned with level lines, preceded by the worship of the site (vāstupūjā).
"With the desire to perform a great meritorious act, that temple for the *liṅgas* should be constructed;
having installed [the stationary image] in the shrine, one should install the mobile [image]. Thus it is said.
The Guru should again construct various temples so that those [deities] may be worshipped as their respective lords.
Having first prepared the property of the deity, one should employ it for the rites of the deity;
that is called a "grove of penance," and they go to the supreme state.
Having delighted the monastery with garments and other gifts, that [transaction] shall be preceded by a fee of one paṇa.
O Vaiśya, the third part of Vyāsa’s [share] shall be the first; the second shall be one-quarter less than that;
the third shall be by half a share—this is declared to be the measure of the fine.
Having taken up [the vessel] marked with a banner, sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra, and covered it with a cloth,
the wise one should deposit the three principles (tattvas) according to the division of the Śiva-tattva. Then, having deposited the Astra-mantra, he brings about the presence [of the deity].
One should place the *tattva* in the temple, having first placed the sustaining *śakti*.

Then, one should place the *ātmatattva* in the lower portion, extending as far as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). One should place the *vidyātattva* in the middle, following the positions of the *buddhitattva*.
Above Śiti is the Śivatattva, which extends as far as Śuddhavidyā.
Having meditated upon that causal principle, one should [worship] Śiva along with his limbs (*aṅgas*).
For each respective Tattva, there is presence (*sānnidhya*), confinement (*rodhana*), worship (*pūjā*), and unification (*sandhāna*).
In this manner, the ritual procedure shall reach completion everywhere according to the rules.
Having secured an auspicious moment, one should respectfully install the flagstaff;
thereafter, one should establish the temple with auspicious items such as fruits and the like.

In a hut constructed of wood or grass, however, the ritual deposit (*nyāsa*) is performed [as follows]. That which pertains to the metallic [elements] should be applied to the staffs (*daṇḍaka*), and so forth. One should then again perform the installation (*nyāsa*) of Śiva along with his limbs (*sāṅga*), characterized by the pillars and the solar expanse.
Having honored him with wealth, grain, and other offerings, and having constructed a monastery for him who is endowed with virtues,
one should offer that [monastery] to him— who is worshipped like Śiva— with water containing the *tattvas*.
By the grace of Śiva and Śakti,
[this work] of the ocean of the Śrī Saiva Āgamas has been composed for the sake of those who,
though they have entered upon the royal road [of the tradition], still stumble at every step.
In the same way, if the virtuous here, through negligence, [fail to attain] the state that is the abode of peace;
At the illustrious seat of Āmārdaka, there was the great sage Śrī Durvāsas,
the bringer-down of the Śiva scriptures for the sake of protecting the world. His disciple was the glorious Araṇabhadra, who was like Indra, the lord of the immortals.
The ornament of that lineage, Śrī [Name], did not equal him in meditative concentration.
This Śiva, established at the site of Golakī, was Śrīprabhāva;
his lineage-sun was Śrīsomaśambhu;
and this one was ŚrīDharmaśambhu, renowned as Lakṣādhyāyin.
His disciple was Jñānalashambhu, and from him came Vyomashamkara.

O you who have been cleansed by initiation, you who were previously obscured by the darkness of ignorance and led along wrong paths—listen now! You have come into the presence of Vyomashambhu, the supreme teacher of the world.

By his most eminent disciple, Śrī Jñānaśiva— who dwells in Vārāṇasī, whose mind is filled with the overflowing nectar of the supreme Siddhānta, and who finds his sole abode in the supreme bliss of awakening—
this [work] was composed at the feet of the lotus-like feet of Śambhu.
The Illustrious *Jñānaratnāvalī* is completed.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
